Bare Metal to GPU University

From a curious kid who has never programmed to an engineer who can build an operating system for any hardware, write GPU kernels in CUDA C++ and ROCm/HIP, and build the software of robots and drones. Thirteen faculties, 87 courses, 603 chapters, 10 bridge chapters and 8 mega projects, all in this one page.

Welcome

Build status of this edition

81 of 603 chapters are written as drafts; the others are listed in the catalogue as planned. Status counts: planned 522, draft · code run 81.

Every code listing in a written chapter was compiled and run in this build and its real output is pasted in. This build had no internet access, so no official document could be opened: sources are named by title and marked pending verification, and no chapter is yet "published" in the sense of the guide (gates G1, G6–G8 are open). Each chapter links to its QA record.

The promise, stated kindly and truthfully. No curriculum by itself can guarantee that someone becomes a "senior engineer". Seniority is not a certificate. It is deep knowledge plus years of building, debugging, reviewing and owning real systems together with other people: shipping things that others depend on, being woken by an incident and fixing it, explaining a design to a sceptical colleague, mentoring a beginner, and being wrong in public and learning from it.

What a university can do is give the learner the knowledge, the habits and a very large amount of realistic practice. That is why this one is built around practice: every chapter has a lab, every course has forensic labs (diagnosing real-looking broken systems from evidence), exams that test doing rather than remembering, projects, design reviews and post-mortems, and the final years are mostly mega projects. A learner who completes it honestly will be ready to grow into a senior engineer much faster, and will have a portfolio that proves it. The last step still happens in real teams on real systems.

Hallucination: the honest engineering view. Agents that write chapters can produce text that sounds right and is wrong: an API name that does not exist, a register that belongs to another chip, a version number that was never released, a performance figure from nowhere. No wording in a prompt can eliminate this. "Please do not hallucinate" does not work on its own. Hallucination can only be made rare by a process: read the official source first and write down what it says (the source dossier), tag every claim with its source, compile and run every code listing with a named toolchain and paste the real output, have an independent agent fact-check against the sources, and keep a corrections log for whatever still slips through. Section 3 is that process, and it is the most important section of this guide.

Safety: read before any robot, drone, firmware or GPU lab.

  • Robots and drones can hurt people. Propellers cut skin and eyes; motors pinch fingers and can start unexpectedly; robot arms move with force. Every physical lab starts in a simulator; real hardware only after the simulator lab passes. Remove propellers for all bench tests; use a physical kill switch or arming switch; keep a clear zone around the vehicle.
  • LiPo batteries (lithium polymer) can catch fire if punctured, over-charged, over-discharged, short-circuited or charged unattended. Use a charger made for LiPo, a fire-resistant charging bag or container, never charge unattended, store at the storage voltage the battery maker documents, and dispose of damaged batteries according to local rules. The chapter quotes the battery and charger manufacturers' instructions, never numbers from memory.
  • Young learners (levels L0–L2) do physical labs only with adult supervision, at low voltages, with kits designed for their age. No mains-voltage work at any level of this university.
  • Drone flights are regulated in most countries (registration, where and how high you may fly, line of sight, flying near people or airports). Before any outdoor flight lab, the chapter tells the learner to read the current rules of their national aviation authority and to fly only where allowed, with permission of the land owner, and supervised. Agents never write rule details (heights, weights, distances) from memory: they cite the authority's current document or say "check your national aviation authority's current rules".
  • Firmware and bricking: develop firmware and kernels in QEMU with OVMF first (curriculum safety box); move to spare hardware only after the emulator milestone passes; never flash a machine the learner depends on; keep a recovery path (SD-card boot, USB recovery mode, external SPI programmer with a backup image).
  • GPU labs need a GPU. CUDA labs need an NVIDIA GPU; ROCm/HIP labs need an AMD GPU that appears in the ROCm documentation's compatibility list (HIP can also compile for NVIDIA GPUs, which is enough to learn the syntax but not AMD-specific performance). A cloud GPU instance is an acceptable alternative. Every GPU lab states its hardware requirement at the top, and labs that can run without a GPU (reading profiler output, forensic labs on recorded traces) say so.

Start here

A curious kid (about 10–12)

Start with KID101 How computers think, chapter F0-01. Go at your own pace, in short sessions, with a grown-up for anything physical.

A teen who already codes

Read the Foundation-year chapters you need, then start SP101 C++ I. (The SP101 placement quiz is planned.)

An adult engineer

Use the goal paths and enter where your skills end; the upper years follow the Systems Curriculum milestones.

The learner ladder

Every chapter states its level. The level decides the reading level, the maths allowed, the share of analogy, depth and code, and the kind of lab. Early chapters are fully kid-friendly; later chapters keep the analogy first (one short paragraph at least), then go to full engineering depth. Ages are indicative only: an adult beginner starts at L0 or L1 too, and a gifted twelve-year-old may climb faster. The level describes what the learner can do, not how old they are.

2.2 The maths ladder and where the university teaches each rung

Maths is taught just before it is needed and always with a use case from the five goals. Each maths course belongs to the maths spine of F0 (5.4). A chapter may only use maths whose course is in its prerequisites; otherwise it includes a short "maths you need here" box that teaches the minimum and links the full course.

RungWhat exactlyCourseLevelFirst used for

2 · AlgebraVariables, expressions, equations, functions, graphs, inequalities, powers and logarithms of 2MA101L1Loop counts, index formulas such as i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x, the line a robot should follow

2.3 Level rules every agent applies

  1. State the level in the chapter front matter (one of L0–L5, or a range of two adjacent levels such as L1–L2 when a chapter serves both).
  2. Never jump more than one level between consecutive chapters of a course. If a jump is needed, insert a bridge chapter (section 6).
  3. Prerequisites are explicit: chapter ids and course codes, never "you should know some C++".
  4. L0–L2 chapters pass the reading-level checks of 10.4 before publication.
  5. From L3 upwards, the analogy is still first: every chapter opens with a story hook and every major section opens with one analogy sentence, then the precise engineering text follows.
  6. Each level has a "can do" exam: the practical exams of the courses at that level test the "Can do" column of the table above.

Years, semesters and the prerequisite graph

  • One credit hour = about 30 hours of total learner work (reading, labs, forensic labs, quizzes, project time). A 4-credit course is therefore about 120 hours. The curriculum's timeline ranges (18.1) were used to size the L3–L4 courses; they are estimates, not promises, and the course page says so.
  • Semester = a planning unit of about 15–18 credits for a full-time learner; part-time learners take half. Kids in the Foundation year go at their own pace, in short sessions.
  • Year 0 is the Foundation year (L0–L1). Years 1–5 build to L4. Years 6–7 are the advanced year and the residency (L4–L5), dominated by mega projects.
  • Honest pacing note (on every course page): a full-time adult learner might move through Years 1–6 in five to eight years; a kid starting at 11 who studies part-time grows with the school over their teenage years and continues into university age. Nobody is "late".

Safety

Read before any robot, drone, firmware or GPU lab. Every lab links here.

Safety: read before any robot, drone, firmware or GPU lab.

  • Robots and drones can hurt people. Propellers cut skin and eyes; motors pinch fingers and can start unexpectedly; robot arms move with force. Every physical lab starts in a simulator; real hardware only after the simulator lab passes. Remove propellers for all bench tests; use a physical kill switch or arming switch; keep a clear zone around the vehicle.
  • LiPo batteries (lithium polymer) can catch fire if punctured, over-charged, over-discharged, short-circuited or charged unattended. Use a charger made for LiPo, a fire-resistant charging bag or container, never charge unattended, store at the storage voltage the battery maker documents, and dispose of damaged batteries according to local rules. The chapter quotes the battery and charger manufacturers' instructions, never numbers from memory.
  • Young learners (levels L0–L2) do physical labs only with adult supervision, at low voltages, with kits designed for their age. No mains-voltage work at any level of this university.
  • Drone flights are regulated in most countries (registration, where and how high you may fly, line of sight, flying near people or airports). Before any outdoor flight lab, the chapter tells the learner to read the current rules of their national aviation authority and to fly only where allowed, with permission of the land owner, and supervised. Agents never write rule details (heights, weights, distances) from memory: they cite the authority's current document or say "check your national aviation authority's current rules".
  • Firmware and bricking: develop firmware and kernels in QEMU with OVMF first (curriculum safety box); move to spare hardware only after the emulator milestone passes; never flash a machine the learner depends on; keep a recovery path (SD-card boot, USB recovery mode, external SPI programmer with a backup image).
  • GPU labs need a GPU. CUDA labs need an NVIDIA GPU; ROCm/HIP labs need an AMD GPU that appears in the ROCm documentation's compatibility list (HIP can also compile for NVIDIA GPUs, which is enough to learn the syntax but not AMD-specific performance). A cloud GPU instance is an acceptable alternative. Every GPU lab states its hardware requirement at the top, and labs that can run without a GPU (reading profiler output, forensic labs on recorded traces) say so.

Analogy registry

Each faculty has one analogy world, used consistently across all its courses, with an explicit mapping table. Analogies make ideas sticky for a kid and remain the first paragraph for an engineer; they are never a substitute for the precise definition. The tables below are the registry: authors use these mappings, and a new mapping is added only through the Dean (who updates analogies.html and this table's copy) so that two chapters never use two different analogies for the same thing.

8.1 Analogy worlds and mapping tables

F0 Foundations — everyday life at home

ConceptAnalogyWhat maps exactlyWhere it breaks
Program / algorithmA recipeExact steps in order; the cook (computer) does exactly what is writtenA human cook fills gaps with common sense; a computer never does
BitA light switch: on or offTwo states, nothing in betweenA real switch can be broken or half-pressed; a bit is always exactly 0 or 1 when read
Byte, binary numberA row of eight switches; each switch is worth double the one to its rightPlace values 1, 2, 4, 8…Meaning (number, letter, colour) is decided by the program, not by the switches
VariableA labelled jarA name, and something inside that can changeA jar can hold anything; a variable has a type and a fixed size
Loop"Stir 20 times"Repetition with a count or a conditionA loop that forgets to change its condition runs forever; a cook would stop
BugA mistake in the recipeThe program does what was written, not what was meantSome bugs come from the machine or other programs, not the recipe
Network messageA postcard with an addressSender, receiver, content, may get lostPackets can be duplicated and reordered too; postcards rarely are

F1 and F2 — the restaurant building and its kitchen

ConceptAnalogyWhat maps exactlyWhere it breaks
Voltage, current, resistanceWater pressure, flow, and a narrow pipe in the building's plumbingMore pressure pushes more flow; narrow pipes resist flowElectricity needs a closed loop; charge does not "leak out" of an open wire like water; capacitors and inductors have no simple pipe equivalent
TransistorA tap opened by a small control valveA small signal controls a larger flowReal transistors have analog behaviour, thresholds and switching time
CPU coreThe head chefVery fast, very clever, does one dish's steps at a time (or a few at once)A core executes instructions with pipelining and speculation that no chef does
RegistersThe chef's hands and the cutting boardTiny, instantly reachableRegister counts and names are fixed by the instruction set
Caches (L1, L2, L3)Shelves near the stove, then along the wall, then in the back roomCloser is faster but smallerCaches fill automatically by lines and evict by policy; the chef does not choose
Main memory (DRAM)The big pantry down the corridorLarge, slow to reachDRAM has banks, rows and refresh; "distance" is about time, not metres
Storage (SSD, disk)The warehouse across townHuge, slowest, keeps things when the restaurant closesSSDs have internal processors and queues
BusCorridors and service liftsPaths shared by many deliveriesModern links such as PCIe are point-to-point serial lanes, not one shared corridor
InterruptThe doorbellThe chef stops, handles the visitor, returns to cookingInterrupts have priorities, can be masked, and can arrive while another is being handled
DMAA delivery truck that unloads straight into the storeroomThe chef does not carry each boxDMA needs addresses set up correctly and cache coherence considered; a wrong address overwrites anything
PointerA note with a shelf number written on itIt tells where something is, not what it isThe note can point to an empty or reused shelf (dangling pointer) and nothing warns you
RAIIBorrowing a tool from the tool wall, which is returned automatically when you leave the roomClean-up is tied to leaving the scopeOnly works if every resource has an owner object
ThreadsSeveral cooks in one kitchenThey share the kitchen and can bump into each otherThe OS can pause a cook at any instant, mid-step
MutexThe single key to the spice cabinetOnly the holder may use what it protectsForgetting to return the key (unlock) blocks everyone forever
Atomic operationA tally counter that clicks in one movementNobody can see a half-clickMemory orders add rules about what others see before and after the click
Data raceTwo cooks writing on the same order slip at onceThe result is garbledIn C++ a data race is undefined behaviour: anything may happen, not just a garbled slip
CompilerA translator who rewrites the recipe into the chef's exact languageInput language to machine instructionsThe compiler may reorder and remove steps as long as the language rules allow

F3 and F4 — the school (and its visitors)

ConceptAnalogyWhat maps exactlyWhere it breaks
Operating systemThe school principal and the timetableDecides who uses which room and when; settles conflictsThe OS is software running on the same CPUs it manages
SchedulerThe timetableWho runs now, for how longTimetables are fixed in advance; schedulers decide continuously
ProcessA class with its own roomIts own space, its own belongingsProcesses can share memory if they ask
ThreadA student working in that roomSeveral in one room share its contents—
FirmwareThe building's caretaker who opens the doors in the morningFirst to arrive; switches on lights and heating; hands overFirmware stays partly resident (runtime services, SMM) after the OS starts
BootloaderThe person who unlocks the classroom and lets the principal inLoads the OS and hands over the keys—
InterruptThe doorbell (same as F1)——
System callAsking at the office windowStudents cannot enter the office; they ask through a window with a formThe CPU switches privilege level; it is not a polite request
User mode / kernel modeStudent areas / staff-only roomsSome rooms and actions are forbidden to studentsEnforced by hardware, not by a sign on the door
Page tableThe map of lockers: locker number to real cupboardEach class sees its own numberingMulti-level tables, permissions bits and TLB caching
TLBThe principal's sticky note of recently looked-up lockersFast lookupsMust be cleared when the map changes (TLB shootdown)
DriverAn interpreter for a visitor who speaks another languageTranslates between the OS and the deviceDrivers also manage memory, interrupts and errors for the device
DMAThe delivery truck to the storeroom (same as F1)——
File systemThe library catalogue and shelvesNames to locations; order on the shelvesMust survive a power cut in the middle of shelving (crash consistency)
DeadlockTwo students each holding a book the other needsBoth wait forever—
Virtual machine / hypervisorA school inside a school, with the real principal aboveThe inner principal thinks it runs everythingHardware support makes most actions direct, not relayed

F5 — friends in different towns

ConceptAnalogyWhat maps exactlyWhere it breaks
Message passingLetters between friendsDelay, possible lossNetworks also duplicate and reorder messages
RPCPhoning a friend and asking them to do somethingRequest and replyIf the line drops you do not know whether they did it
ConsensusFriends agreeing on one pizza by voteOne choice, everyone ends with the same answer, even if some friends are slowReal protocols must work when friends crash and messages are lost, which voting rules alone do not handle
Leader (Raft)The friend who writes the orderOne coordinator at a timeTerms and elections are formal rules, not popularity
Replicated logEveryone's copy of the shared notebookSame entries in the same order—
Clock skewEveryone's watch is a little differentYou cannot order events by watches alone—
Network partitionThe phone lines between two towns are downGroups cannot talk—
Cluster schedulerThe organiser who assigns choresMatches jobs to available peopleHas rules for priorities, fairness and resources

F6, F7, F8 — the great kitchen hall

ConceptAnalogyWhat maps exactlyWhere it breaks
CPUThe head chef (same as F1)Few, fast, flexible—
GPUA hall of thousands of kitchen helpersMany simple workers doing the same kind of step on different ingredientsHelpers are grouped in hardware units and scheduled by hardware; there is no "manager" walking around
Kernel (GPU)The recipe card every helper followsSame instructions, each helper on its own itemUnrelated to the operating-system "kernel" of F3 (say so in every F6 chapter that uses the word)
ThreadOne helperHas its own number and its own hands (registers)A GPU thread is not an OS thread
Warp (32) / wavefront (64 on CDNA)A row of helpers that move together, step by stepOne instruction for the whole row at onceIf some helpers must do something different, the others in the row wait (divergence)
Block / workgroupA group of rows sharing one tableThey can share things on the table and wait for each otherBlocks cannot rely on other blocks running at the same time
GridAll the table groups for one jobThe whole jobNot all of the grid is in the hall at once if it is large
RegistersEach helper's handsFastest, privateUsing more per helper means fewer helpers fit in the hall (occupancy)
Shared memory / LDSThe table in the middle of a row groupFast, shared within the groupOrganised in banks; helpers reaching into the same drawer must take turns (bank conflicts)
Global memoryThe big pantry far awayEveryone can reach it, slowlyHas caches in front of it
CoalescingFetching neighbouring jars in one tripNeighbouring helpers asking for neighbouring jars → one tripThe exact rules depend on the hardware generation (cite the vendor guide)
Latency hiding / occupancyWhile one row waits for the pantry, another row cooksMany rows keep the hall busyMore rows is not always faster (instruction-level parallelism can matter more)
AtomicsOne shared tally counter that every helper may clickEach click counted onceMany clicks on one counter form a queue
StreamsSeparate order queues at the passOrders in one queue run in order; different queues can overlap—
Tensor / matrix coresA machine that multiplies a whole small tray of numbers at onceBig speed-up for the right shapes and typesOnly for specific sizes, layouts and number formats
Multi-GPU, NCCL/RCCLA chain of kitchen halls with a delivery service between themHalls must share resultsDelivery roads have very different speeds (topology)
Ring all-reducePassing bowls around a round table, each person adding their partAfter two laps everyone has the totalMessages are split into chunks and pipelined, so all bowls move at once

F9 — riding a bicycle; a body with senses and muscles

ConceptAnalogyWhat maps exactlyWhere it breaks
Control loopRiding a bicycle and correcting your balanceSense, compare, correct, again and againA computer loop runs at a fixed rate and sees only what its sensors measure
PIDSteering back into your laneP: how far off you are; I: how long you have been off; D: how fast you are driftingReal systems saturate and have delays; the gains interact
Sensors / actuatorsSenses / musclesInput and output of the bodySensors are noisy and biased in specific, measurable ways
EncoderCounting the turns of a wheelDistance from rotationWheels slip
IMUThe balance sense in your inner earFeels turning and accelerationDrifts over time without other references
Kalman filterCombining two friends' guesses, trusting the more reliable one moreWeighted by uncertaintyOptimal only under its assumptions (linear, Gaussian)
SLAMDrawing the map of a dark house while walking through it with a torchMap and position built togetherErrors accumulate until you recognise a place you have seen (loop closure)
ROS 2 node / topicTeam members / notice boards they pin messages toPublish and subscribeDelivery guarantees depend on QoS settings
DDSThe postal service behind the notice boardsFinds receivers, delivers messagesDiscovery and QoS are configurable and can fail silently if mismatched
Real-timeA drummer who must hit every beatLate is wrong, even if correct"Fast" and "real-time" are different things

F10 — carrying a tray of drinks while walking

ConceptAnalogyWhat maps exactlyWhere it breaks
Attitude estimationKeeping a tray of drinks level while walkingFeeling tilt and correcting continuouslyThe drone has no eyes on the tray: it infers tilt from sensors that drift and vibrate
Complementary filterTrusting your quick sense of tilt for fast changes and your slow sense of "down" for the long runHigh-pass the gyro, low-pass the accelerometerAcceleration during manoeuvres fools the "down" sense
Cascaded controlA chain: manager (where to go) → team leader (how fast) → worker (which tilt) → hands (how quickly to rotate)Each level gives the next a targetInner loops must be faster and well tuned first
ESCThe nerve controller for each muscleTurns commands into motor powerProtocol, timing and calibration matter
uORBA notice board inside the drone's brainModules publish and read topics—
MAVLinkWalkie-talkie code words between drone and groundAgreed message setMessage definitions come from XML dialects; versions matter
FailsafeThe rule "if you get lost, go back to the meeting point"Pre-agreed action on lossMust be configured and tested; defaults may not suit your field

F11 — a castle with gates and guards; F12 — building a house as a team

ConceptAnalogyWhat maps exactlyWhere it breaks
Chain of trust / secure bootEach gate guard checks the badge of the next person before letting them inEvery stage verifies the nextBadges are cryptographic signatures; a stolen key breaks everything after it
Memory safetyWriting only on your own page of the notebookOut-of-bounds writes damage others' pagesAttackers aim at specific pages on purpose
Threat modelThinking like a burglar about your own houseAssets, entrances, attackersSoftware has many more entrances than a house
Functional safetySeatbelts and airbags, designed and tested to rulesMechanisms for when things go wrongCertification needs evidence, not just mechanisms
Design docThe house blueprintAgree before buildingSoftware blueprints change more often; keep them alive
Code reviewA second carpenter checks your jointsFresh eyes find defectsReviews also share knowledge, not only find bugs
Post-mortemAfter a fire drill went wrong, the team asks "what failed?" without blaming a personLearning, not punishment—

8.2 Analogy rules

  1. Analogy first. Introduce the analogy before the precise term, in the story hook or the first paragraph of the section.
  2. Map every part explicitly. Use a small mapping list or table: "helper = thread; row = warp; table = shared memory". No silent mappings.
  3. State where it breaks. Every chapter has the "Where the analogy breaks" section with at least two concrete points; the Fact-Checker checks they are correct (FC-12).
  4. Never let the analogy replace the precise definition. Every term the analogy introduces is followed by its precise, tagged definition.
  5. Keep the same analogy across a course (and across the faculty, as registered above). A chapter that needs a new mapping asks the Dean to register it.
  6. Age-appropriate. No violence, danger glorification, romance, fear, or adult themes; analogies a 10-year-old understands at L0–L1.
  7. Culturally neutral. Everyday activities common to many cultures (cooking, school, walking, cycling, friends sharing food); no religious or political content, no national sports or holidays, no brand names, no assumptions about family structure or wealth; names in stories are varied and not stereotyped.
  8. One analogy per idea per chapter. Do not mix worlds inside one explanation (no "the GPU kitchen's principal").
  9. Analogies carry no hidden technical claims. If the analogy implies a number or a behaviour ("the pantry is 100 times farther"), that claim must be tagged or removed.
  10. Engineer-level chapters keep it short: one paragraph, then the specification.

Glossary

Each entry has the four parts of guide 10.2: simple words, analogy, precise definition and source. Entries written in this build are drafts whose sources are pending verification (no official source could be opened in this build). Entries seeded from the Systems Curriculum glossary (section 20) are shown below them with their original one-line definition; they still need the four-part rewrite (guide 15.1, step 5).

Entries written with the chapters

Actuator
Simple words: A part that makes something move or happen. Analogy: A muscle. Precise: A device that turns a command from the computer into a physical action, such as a motor turning a wheel. Source: D1 of F0-10 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Motor, Output. Chapters: F0-10, F9-01, F9-03.
Address
Simple words: The number or name that says which computer a packet is for, and which sent it. Analogy: The address written on a postcard, and the sender's name. Precise: An identifier of a computer (or a part of one) on a network, carried in each packet so it can be delivered, and so the reply can find its way back. Source: D1 of F0-09 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Packet. Chapters: F0-09.
Algorithm
Simple words: A list of clear steps that solves a problem, every time. Analogy: A recipe that always makes the same dish if you follow it exactly. Precise: A finite list of exact steps that, followed in order, solves a problem. It can be written in words, drawn, or written as a program. Source: D1 of F0-01 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Program, Instruction, Loop, Decision. Chapters: F0-01, F0-04.
Allowed range
Simple words: All the numbers that are permitted, from a lowest to a highest. Analogy: The jar spots that exist on the shelf: 0 to 9. Precise: The set of values satisfying one or more inequalities; the half-open range 0 ≤ i < n holds exactly n whole numbers, 0 to n − 1. Source: D1 of F0-19 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Inequality, Bounds check. Chapters: F0-19, F0-18.
ALU (arithmetic logic unit)
Simple words: the part of a processor that does arithmetic and logic on two numbers, choosing the operation from a code. Analogy: Ines's prep station with its tools and the selector dial. Precise: a combinational circuit with two N-bit operands, an operation code (opcode) and an N-bit result plus status flags; it computes several functions and selects one with a multiplexer. Source: D2, D1 of F1-14 (pending verification). Related: Opcode (operation code), Status flags (Z, N, C, V), Multiplexer (mux). Chapters: F1-14.
Ammeter (in series)
Simple words: the current mode: you open the loop and let the current pass through the meter. Analogy: the flow meter fitted into the cut pipe. Precise: a current measurement is made with the meter in series, so the circuit's current flows through the meter's small internal (shunt) resistance; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance. Source: D2 of F1-07 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Multimeter, Voltmeter (in parallel), Ohmmeter. Chapters: F1-07.
Analog and digital signal
Simple words: Analog is a number that can take many values; digital here means only two, yes or no. Analogy: A dimmer knob versus a light switch. Precise: An analog signal varies continuously; a digital signal has two levels (high and low). A microcontroller turns an analog voltage into a number with an analog-to-digital converter. Source: D2 of F0-43 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: High and low, Sensor. Chapters: F0-43.
Analog signal
Simple words: a signal that can take any value in a range. Analogy: the oven thermometer's needle. [proposed mapping, awaiting registration in guide 8.1; see HW101 NOTES.md] Precise: a signal whose value varies continuously and whose exact value carries the information. Source: D2 of F1-08 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D3 of F1-08 (Petzold, "Code") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Signal, Digital signal, Threshold. Chapters: F1-08.
AND
Simple words: True only when both inputs are true. Analogy: Two switches one after the other in the same wire (in series). Precise: the Boolean function with output 1 exactly when all inputs are 1; in C++, && for bool values and & bit by bit (F0-25). Source: W1 of F0-26 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); R1 of F0-26 (lab run in this build). Related: OR, NOT, Truth table. Chapters: F0-26.
Anode and cathode
Simple words: the diode's two ends: current goes in at the anode and out at the cathode. Analogy: the inlet and outlet side of the flap. Precise: in the forward direction, conventional current enters the anode and leaves the cathode; the symbol's triangle points from anode to cathode, towards the bar. Source: D2 of F1-06 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Diode, Forward voltage, LED. Chapters: F0-40, F1-06.
Argument
Simple words: The actual value you hand to a function when you call it. Analogy: The word you write in the blank: "add salt to the pot". Precise: An expression in a function call whose value initialises the matching parameter, such as "salt" in add_to_pot("salt"). Source: R1 of F0-34, D1 of F0-34 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Parameter. Chapters: F0-34.
Assignment
Simple words: Putting a new value into a variable. The old value is gone. Analogy: Emptying the jar and filling it with something new. Precise: The operator = in a statement such as apples = apples + 2; the right side is worked out first, then its value replaces the variable's old value. It is not the "is equal to" of maths; that is == (F0-32). Source: R1 of F0-30, D1 of F0-30 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Variable, Comparison operator. Chapters: F0-30, F0-32.
Axis
Simple words: One of the two number lines at the edge of a graph. Analogy: The edge of the kitchen floor where you count tiles. Precise: A number line measuring one coordinate; the horizontal and vertical axes cross at (0, 0). Source: D1 of F0-18 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Coordinates, Number line. Chapters: F0-18.
Base
Simple words: How many different digit symbols a number system uses. Analogy: How many positions each switch (or dial) has. Precise: the number of distinct digits in a place-value system, and the factor by which each position's value grows to the left: 10 for decimal, 2 for binary. Source: W1 of F0-20 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter). Related: Binary, Decimal, Hexadecimal (hex). Chapters: F0-20, F0-22.
Battery
Simple words: A store of energy that pushes electricity around a loop. Analogy: A pump that makes pressure. Precise: One or more electrochemical cells that keep a voltage between two terminals, marked + and −. Source: D1 of F0-39 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Voltage, LiPo battery. Chapters: F0-39, F0-46.
Binary
Simple words: A way of writing numbers using only the two digits 0 and 1. Analogy: A row of switches where each switch is worth double the one to its right. Precise: The base-2 number system: each position has a place value that is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8 and so on). Source: D1 of F0-02 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Bit, Place value. Chapters: F0-02, F0-20, F0-21, F0-22.
Bit
Simple words: The smallest piece of information: on or off, 1 or 0. Analogy: One light switch. Precise: A binary digit, which has exactly one of two values, written 0 and 1. Source: D1 of F0-02 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Byte, Binary. Chapters: F0-02, F0-20, F0-23.
Bit and byte symbols (b, B)
Simple words: Small b means bits, capital B means bytes. Analogy: One switch versus one whole row. Precise: 1 B = 8 b; this university spells out "Gbit/s" and "GB/s" at levels L0–L2 so the two cannot be mixed up (guide 13.3). Source: W1 of F0-23 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter). Related: Bit, Byte. Chapters: F0-23.
Bit field
Simple words: A group of neighbouring bits that together hold a small number. Analogy: Three switches side by side used as a dial from 0 to 7. Precise: a contiguous range of bits within a value, read by shifting it down to bit 0 and masking off the other bits. Source: W1 of F0-25 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); D1 of F0-25 (title only, pending verification). Related: Flag, Mask, Shift. Chapters: F0-25.
Bit number
Simple words: The name of a bit's position, counted from the right, starting at 0. Analogy: The room number of each switch on Zara's panel: kitchen is 0, garden is 7. Precise: bit k has place value 2; bit 0 is the least significant bit and bit 7 the most significant bit of a byte. Source: W1 of F0-25 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter). Related: Least significant bit (LSB), Mask. Chapters: F0-25.
Bitwise operator
Simple words: An operation that works on each pair of bits separately. Analogy: Doing the same thing to every switch at once, switch by switch. Precise: in C++, & (AND: 1 only if both bits are 1), | (OR: 1 if at least one is 1), ^ (XOR: 1 if they differ) and ~ (NOT: flip every bit). F0-26 gives their full truth tables. Source: R1 of F0-25 (lab run in this build); D2 of F0-25 (title only, pending verification). Related: AND, OR, NOT, XOR (exclusive OR), Mask. Chapters: F0-25, F0-26.
Block
Simple words: A group of statements inside curly braces { }. Analogy: A boxed group of steps in a recipe that belong together. Precise: A sequence of statements enclosed in braces; the whole block belongs to the if, else, loop or function written in front of it. Source: R1 of F0-32, D1 of F0-32 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: if statement, Statement. Chapters: F0-32.
bool
Simple words: The type for yes/no answers: true or false. Analogy: A light switch: on or off. Precise: The Boolean type with the two values true and false; std::cout prints them as 1 and 0 unless std::boolalpha is used (R1). Source: R1 of F0-31, D1 of F0-31 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Type, Condition. Chapters: F0-31, F0-32.
Boolean algebra
Simple words: Rules for rewriting true/false sentences, like the rules for rewriting sums. Analogy: Tidying the house rules on the fridge without changing what they mean. Precise: the algebra of the values 0 and 1 with the operations AND, OR and NOT, and the laws they satisfy; named after the mathematician George Boole. Source: W1 of F0-27 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); D1 of F0-27 (title only, pending verification). Related: De Morgan's laws, Expression (Boolean), Equivalent expressions. Chapters: F0-27.
Boolean value
Simple words: A value that is either true or false. Analogy: A switch is on or off; a lamp is lit or dark. Precise: a value of a two-element set {false, true}, written 0 and 1; in C++ the type bool, which prints as 0 or 1 by default (run R1). Source: R1 of F0-26 (lab run in this build); D1 of F0-26 (title only, pending verification). Related: Truth table, Boolean algebra. Chapters: F0-26.
Bounds check
Simple words: Checking that a number is inside the allowed range before using it. Analogy: "Is my ticket less than 10?" before walking to the shelf. Precise: A test such as if (i < n) that guards every use of position i in a list of n items numbered from 0; every GPU kernel whose grid can exceed its data needs one (guide 13.4). Source: D1 and R1 of F0-19 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Allowed range, Off-by-one error, Rounding up. Chapters: F0-19.
Breakdown (reverse)
Simple words: what happens if you push a diode backwards too hard: it suddenly conducts and can be destroyed. Analogy: the flap torn off by too much back-pressure. Precise: the reverse voltage above which reverse current rises sharply; the datasheet gives the maximum reverse voltage, which for LEDs can be low. Source: D2 of F1-06 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D4 of F1-06 (datasheets/manual of the kit chosen by the owner) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Diode, Anode and cathode, Forward voltage. Chapters: F1-06.
Breakpoint
Simple words: A place in your program where the debugger will pause. Analogy: A sticky note on step 9: "stop here and check". Precise: A location set with the gdb command break (help text: "Set breakpoint at specified location.", R5); the program stops each time it reaches that line (R4). Source: R4 of F0-37, R5 of F0-37, D2 of F0-37 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Debugger. Chapters: F0-37.
Bug
Simple words: A mistake that makes a program do the wrong thing. Analogy: A mistake in the recipe. Precise: A fault in a program (or in the data, the hardware or another program it depends on) that makes it behave differently from what was intended. Source: D1 of F0-08 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Debugging, Symptom, Root cause. Chapters: F0-08.
Bump sensor
Simple words: a sensor that only says "I touched something" or "I did not". Analogy: the skin on your hand feeling a wall. Precise: a contact switch that closes (or opens) when pressed; its reading has only two values. Source: D4 of F9-02 (pending verification). Related: Sensor. Chapters: F9-02.
Burden (shunt) resistance
Simple words: the small resistance inside the meter in current mode. Analogy: the slight narrowing the flow meter adds to the pipe. Precise: the series resistance an ammeter adds to the circuit; the voltage across it (the burden voltage) slightly reduces the current being measured. Source: D2 of F1-07 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Multimeter, Voltmeter (in parallel), Ammeter (in series). Chapters: F1-07.
Bus
Simple words: The paths that carry information between the parts. Analogy: Corridors and service lifts. Precise: A set of connections that carries data, addresses and control signals between the processor, memory and devices. Source: D2 of F0-05 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: CPU (central processing unit), Input and output (I/O). Chapters: F0-05.
Byte
Simple words: A group of eight bits. Analogy: A row of eight light switches. Precise: A unit of eight bits; it can hold 256 different patterns, so one byte can stand for a whole number from 0 to 255. Source: D1 of F0-02 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Bit, Binary. Chapters: F0-02, F0-03, F0-23, F0-24.
Cache
Simple words: A small, fast store near the CPU for things used often. Analogy: Shelves near the stove. Precise: A small, fast memory between the processor and main memory that keeps copies of recently used data, so it can be reached sooner. Source: D3 of F0-05 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Main memory, Register. Chapters: F0-05.
Calibrate
Simple words: to measure known things first, so you can set your numbers well. Analogy: looking at the white line and the grey yard before the race starts. Precise: to determine how a sensor's readings relate to known conditions (here: readings on floor and on line) and set the program's constants from those measurements. Source: D3 of F9-02 (pending verification). Related: Threshold, Sensor noise. Chapters: F9-02.
Capacitance
Simple words: how much charge a capacitor holds for each volt. Analogy: how big and how stretchy the tank's rubber wall is. [proposed mapping, awaiting registration in guide 8.1; see HW101 NOTES.md] Precise: C = Q ÷ V, measured in farads (F); one farad is one coulomb per volt; practical values use µF (10−6 F), nF (10−9 F) and pF (10−12 F). Source: D2 of F1-05 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D3 of F1-05 (BIPM, "The International System of Units (SI)") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Capacitor, RC circuit, Time constant (τ). Chapters: F1-05.
Capacitor
Simple words: a part that stores charge on two plates that do not touch. Analogy: the basement tank with a stretchy rubber wall. [proposed mapping, awaiting registration in guide 8.1; see HW101 NOTES.md] Precise: a two-terminal component made of two conductors separated by an insulator; when a voltage V is applied, charges +Q and −Q collect on the two sides, with Q = C × V. Source: D2 of F1-05 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Capacitance, RC circuit, Time constant (τ). Chapters: F1-05.
Carry
Simple words: The extra 1 you pass to the next column when a column adds up to too much. Analogy: When 9 + 3 = 12, you write 2 and "carry the 1". Precise: The value moved into the next place when the sum of one place is at least the base (10 in decimal, 2 in binary). Source: D2 of F0-07 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Binary. Chapters: F0-07.
Carry in, carry out (cin, cout)
Simple words: the carry arriving from the column to the right, and the carry leaving to the column to the left. Analogy: the token the runner brings, and the token sent on. Precise: the carry input and carry output of a full adder; chaining cout of one bit to cin of the next makes a multi-bit adder (F1-14). Source: D2 of F1-13 (pending verification). Related: Full adder, Ripple-carry adder. Chapters: F1-13.
char
Simple words: The type for one single character, like 'A'. Analogy: One fridge-magnet letter. Precise: A type that holds one character, written in single quotes; the character 'A' printed as the number 65 when converted to int on the build machine (R1). Source: R1 of F0-31, D1 of F0-31 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Type, std::string. Chapters: F0-31.
Character code
Simple words: A table that gives every letter, digit and sign its own number. Analogy: The fridge note, but agreed by the whole world. Precise: A mapping from characters to numbers. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is an early example; Unicode is a larger one for the writing systems of the world. Source: D1 of F0-03 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Code (for information). Chapters: F0-03.
Charge
Simple words: the "stuff" of electricity: tiny particles carry it, and it can be positive or negative. Analogy: the water itself in the restaurant's pipes. Precise: electric charge is a property of particles such as electrons (negative) and protons (positive); it is measured in coulombs (C). Source: D2 of F1-01 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D3 of F1-01 (BIPM, "The International System of Units (SI)") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Current, Voltage, Potential. Chapters: F1-01.
Checklist
Simple words: A list you go through, item by item, before you start. Analogy: Checking you have every ingredient before you cook. Precise: A written list of conditions that must all be confirmed before an activity begins. Source: R1 of F0-46 (lab run in this build). Related: Fail-safe default. Chapters: F0-46.
Circuit
Simple words: A complete loop that electricity can travel around. Analogy: A closed loop of pipe with a pump. Precise: A closed path of conductors and parts through which current can flow from one terminal of a source back to the other. Source: D1 of F0-39 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Switch, Short circuit. Chapters: F0-39, F0-40, F0-41.
Clear zone
Simple words: an empty space around the robot that people stay out of while it can move. Analogy: the path being clear before you ride fast. Precise: a marked area around a robot that is kept free of people, animals and objects whenever the robot is powered and able to move. Source: S1 of F9-07 (pending verification). Related: Supervision, Emergency stop. Chapters: F9-07.
CMOS
Simple words: a way of building logic where every output has pMOS switches to the supply and nMOS switches to ground. Analogy: each sink has one set of taps from the roof tank and a matching set of taps to the drain, and only one set is open at a time. Precise: complementary MOS: logic built from a pull-up network of pMOS transistors and a complementary pull-down network of nMOS transistors, so that for every input exactly one network conducts. Source: D2 of F1-09 (pending verification). Related: nMOS and pMOS, Pull-up and pull-down network, Inverter (NOT gate). Chapters: F1-09, F1-10.
Code (for information)
Simple words: An agreement about which number stands for which thing. Analogy: Jun and Priya's "A is 1, B is 2" note on the fridge. Precise: A fixed rule that matches each symbol (a letter, a colour, a sound level) with a pattern of bits, so both writer and reader get the same meaning. Not the same as "code" meaning a program's text. Source: D1 of F0-03 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Character code, Byte. Chapters: F0-03.
Combinational circuit
Simple words: a circuit whose outputs depend only on its inputs right now, with no memory. Analogy: the pass: what goes through depends only on the plates and the ticket in front of Mateo, not on yesterday's orders. Precise: a digital circuit without feedback or storage, whose outputs are a Boolean function of its current inputs (after the outputs settle, F1-15). Circuits with memory are sequential (HW201). Source: D2 of F1-12 (pending verification). Related: Multiplexer (mux), Decoder, Propagation delay. Chapters: F1-12.
Command
Simple words: one instruction for the robot, like "go forward one square". Analogy: "turn right at the bakery". Precise: in this chapter's simulator, one character: F moves forward one cell, L turns 90 degrees left, R turns 90 degrees right, on the spot. Source: R1 of F9-06 (pending verification). Related: Grid world, Heading. Chapters: F9-06.
Comparison
Simple words: Looking at two things and deciding which is bigger. Analogy: Holding two cards side by side. Precise: A test between two values whose answer is yes or no, such as "is the left one bigger than the right one?". Counting comparisons is one way to measure how much work a sorting method does. Source: D2 of F0-04 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Sorting, Condition. Chapters: F0-04.
Comparison operator
Simple words: Signs that compare two values: <, >, <=, >=, == and !=. Analogy: Holding two jars side by side to see which one has more. Precise: Operators that compare two values and give a bool. == means "is equal to" and != means "is not equal to"; a single = is assignment, which g++ flagged inside an if with the course flags (R3). Source: R2 of F0-32, R3 of F0-32, D1 of F0-32 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Condition, Assignment. Chapters: F0-32.
Compiler
Simple words: A program that turns the text you wrote into a program the computer can run. Analogy: A helper who rewrites your recipe in the only language the cook can read, and refuses if the recipe makes no sense. Precise: A program (here g++) that checks C++ source code against the rules of the language and translates it into machine instructions stored in an executable file; it reports errors and warnings when it cannot. Source: R4 of F0-29, D2 of F0-29 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Source code, Executable, Compiler error. Chapters: F0-29, F0-36.
Compiler error
Simple words: A message from the compiler that says it cannot build your program, and where it got stuck. Analogy: The helper saying: "I cannot rewrite this recipe; step 6 is missing its end." Precise: A diagnostic that stops compilation; g++ prints file:line:column: error: followed by a description and the source line with a marker (R2). Source: R2 of F0-36, D2 of F0-36 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Warning, Compiler. Chapters: F0-36.
Computer
Simple words: A machine that follows a list of exact steps to work with information. Analogy: A cook who follows a recipe word for word. Precise: A machine that carries out a stored list of instructions, one at a time, on data such as numbers and letters. Source: D1 of F0-01, D2 of F0-01 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Instruction, Program, CPU (central processing unit). Chapters: F0-01.
Condition
Simple words: A question whose answer is yes or no. Analogy: "Is the cup full?" Precise: An expression that is either true or false, used to decide which step comes next. Source: D1 of F0-07 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Decision, Loop. Chapters: F0-07, F0-32, F0-33, F9-04.
const
Simple words: A word that makes a variable unchangeable after its first value. Analogy: A jar with its lid glued shut: you can look, but not change what is inside. Precise: A qualifier on a declaration (const int baked = 12;); the compiler rejects any later assignment to that variable. Source: R3 of F0-30, D1 of F0-30 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Variable. Chapters: F0-30.
Contamination delay
Simple words: the shortest time before an output can start to change after an input changes. Analogy: how soon the first cook can touch the plate after the order arrives. Precise: the minimum time from an input change until any output begins to change; together with the propagation delay it bounds when an output may be changing. Source: D2 of F1-15 (pending verification). Related: Propagation delay. Chapters: F1-15.
Control loop
Simple words: The robot's repeating cycle: sense, think, act, and again. Analogy: Amira's "feel, decide, move" in the dark hallway. Precise: A loop in which a program reads sensors, decides on commands from what it read, sends the commands to the actuators, and repeats, so that each action is based on fresh measurements. Source: D1 of F0-10, D4 of F0-10 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Loop, Sensor, Actuator. Chapters: F0-10, F0-45, F9-05.
Conventional current
Simple words: the direction engineers draw current: from + to − outside the battery. Analogy: drawing the water's direction on the building plan. Precise: the direction positive charge would move; in metal wires the electrons actually move the opposite way, and circuit diagrams use the conventional direction. Source: D2 of F1-01 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Charge, Current, Voltage. Chapters: F1-01.
Coordinates
Simple words: A pair of numbers that says where a point is: across first, then up. Analogy: "Third tile from the door, fifth tile from the wall." Precise: An ordered pair (x, y): x along the horizontal axis, y along the vertical axis. Source: D1 of F0-18 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Axis, Graph. Chapters: F0-18.
Counter
Simple words: A variable that counts how many times something happened. Analogy: Counting stirs on your fingers. Precise: A variable, usually an int, that is increased (for example with ++day) on each iteration and often used in the loop's condition. Source: R1 of F0-33, D1 of F0-33 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: for loop, Variable. Chapters: F0-33.
Counterexample
Simple words: One case that shows a claim is wrong. Analogy: One open window under a green light. Precise: an assignment of input values for which two expressions claimed equal give different outputs; one counterexample is enough to disprove equivalence. Source: W1 of F0-27 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter). Related: Equivalent expressions. Chapters: F0-27.
CPU (central processing unit)
Simple words: The part that carries out the program's steps. Analogy: The head chef. Precise: The processor: the circuit that fetches instructions from memory and carries them out, one after another, working on data. A CPU can contain one or more cores; each core is like one head chef. Source: D1 of F0-05, D3 of F0-05 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Register, Cache, Main memory. Chapters: F0-05.
Critical path
Simple words: the slowest route from any input to any output. Analogy: the order that has to visit every station in the row. Precise: the path through a combinational circuit with the largest sum of gate delays; it sets the circuit's propagation delay. Source: D2 of F1-15 (pending verification). Related: Propagation delay, Ripple-carry adder. Chapters: F1-15.
Current
Simple words: how much charge flows past a point each second. Analogy: how much water flows through a pipe each second. Precise: the rate of flow of charge, I = Q ÷ t for a steady flow; measured in amperes (A); one ampere is one coulomb per second. Source: D2 of F1-01 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D3 of F1-01 (BIPM, "The International System of Units (SI)") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Charge, Voltage, Potential. Chapters: F0-39, F0-40, F0-44, F1-01, F1-02.
Current limit
Simple words: The most current a part may safely give or take. Analogy: The most water a small pipe can carry before it bursts. Precise: A maximum rating stated in the part's datasheet; exceeding it can damage the part. Source: D3 of F0-44 (kit datasheets, not yet chosen). Related: Datasheet, Motor driver. Chapters: F0-44, F0-40.
Datasheet
Simple words: The instruction sheet a maker writes for a part, with its true numbers. Analogy: The label on a food packet that says what is inside. Precise: The manufacturer's document that states a part's ratings, limits and behaviour. Source: D3 of F0-40 (kit datasheets, dossier part F, not yet chosen). Related: Current limit, Forward voltage. Chapters: F0-40, F0-42, F0-43, F0-44.
De Morgan's laws
Simple words: To push a NOT inside a bracket, flip each part and swap AND with OR. Analogy: "not (open door or open window)" means "closed door and closed window". Precise: NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B); named after the mathematician Augustus De Morgan. Source: W1 of F0-27 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); R1 of F0-27 (lab run in this build); D1 of F0-27 (title only, pending verification). Related: Boolean algebra, NOT, Equivalent expressions. Chapters: F0-27.
Debugger
Simple words: A program that runs your program one step at a time, so you can look inside. Analogy: A pause button for the kitchen: everything freezes and you can look into every jar. Precise: A tool (here GNU gdb 15.1) that starts or attaches to a program, stops it at chosen places and shows the values of its variables (R3, R5). Source: R3 of F0-37, R5 of F0-37, D2 of F0-37 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Breakpoint, Step. Chapters: F0-37.
Debugging
Simple words: Finding and fixing bugs. Analogy: Hana checking the recipe and the jars. Precise: The process of locating the cause of a wrong behaviour, correcting it, and checking that the correction works. Source: D1 of F0-08 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Bug, Test. Chapters: F0-08.
Decimal
Simple words: A number with a point, where the digits after the point are tenths, hundredths, thousandths. Analogy: Cutting each slice into ten smaller pieces, and each of those into ten again. Precise: Base-ten place value continued to the right of the ones place: places worth 1/10, 1/100, 1/1,000, ... Computers usually store such numbers in base two as close copies (MA302). Source: D1 of F0-13; R1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Place value, Fraction, Percentage. Chapters: F0-13, F0-21.
Decision
Simple words: A step that chooses what to do, using a yes-or-no question. Analogy: "If it is too hot, wait one minute." Precise: A branch in an algorithm: if the condition is true, one set of steps runs; otherwise another set (or nothing) runs. In C++ it is written with if and else. Source: D1 of F0-07, D3 of F0-07 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Condition. Chapters: F0-07.
Declaration
Simple words: The line where you first tell the computer a variable's name and type. Analogy: Putting a new empty jar on the shelf and writing its label. Precise: A statement that introduces a name and its type, such as int apples = 3; a name must be declared before it is used (F0-36 shows the error when it is not). Source: R1 of F0-30, D1 of F0-30 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Variable, Initialise. Chapters: F0-30, F0-36.
Decoder
Simple words: a circuit that turns a binary number into one active line out of many. Analogy: the ticket board lighting exactly one station lamp. Precise: a combinational circuit with n inputs and 2n outputs, of which exactly the output whose index equals the input number is 1 (when enabled). Source: D2 of F1-12 (pending verification). Related: One-hot, Enable, Multiplexer (mux). Chapters: F1-12.
Denominator
Simple words: The bottom number of a fraction: how many equal parts make the whole. Analogy: How many slices the bread was cut into. Precise: b in the fraction a/b; it must not be zero. Source: D1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Fraction, Numerator. Chapters: F0-13.
Device
Simple words: A piece of equipment connected to the computer. Analogy: A tool or helper in the house. Precise: A hardware unit that the computer communicates with, such as a keyboard, screen or sensor. Source: D1 of F0-06 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Input, Output. Chapters: F0-06.
Difference
Simple words: The answer when you take away; how far apart two numbers are. Analogy: How many more spoons one jar holds than another. Precise: The result of subtraction; 12 − 5 = 7. Source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Sum, Distance between numbers. Chapters: F0-12, F0-14.
Differential drive
Simple words: steering by turning two side wheels at different speeds. Analogy: Kofi and Ines pushing the two cart wheels. Precise: a wheeled robot with two independently driven wheels on one axle; equal wheel speeds drive straight, different speeds turn it toward the slower wheel's side. Source: D2 of F9-03 (pending verification). Related: Motor, Encoder, Heading. Chapters: F9-03.
Digit
Simple words: One of the ten symbols 0 to 9 that we use to write numbers. Analogy: A single count of beans, cups or bowls on the table: never more than nine of one kind. Precise: A symbol standing for a whole number from 0 to 9; a base-ten numeral is a row of digits. Source: D1 of F0-11 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Place value, Placeholder. Chapters: F0-11, F0-13.
Digital signal
Simple words: a signal that is read as one of a few values, usually just HIGH or LOW. Analogy: the order bell: ringing or not. [proposed mapping, awaiting registration in guide 8.1; see HW101 NOTES.md] Precise: a signal interpreted as one of a finite set of levels, in binary logic two (1 and 0), each corresponding to a range of voltages. Source: D2 of F1-08 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D3 of F1-08 (Petzold, "Code") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Signal, Analog signal, Threshold. Chapters: F1-08.
Diode
Simple words: a part that lets current through one way and blocks it the other way. Analogy: the one-way flap valve in the restaurant's drain. [proposed mapping, awaiting registration in guide 8.1; see HW101 NOTES.md] Precise: a two-terminal semiconductor device that conducts readily when its anode is more positive than its cathode (forward bias) and passes only a tiny current in the opposite direction (reverse bias), up to its breakdown voltage. Source: D2 of F1-06 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Anode and cathode, Forward voltage, LED. Chapters: F0-40, F1-06.
Dissipation
Simple words: electrical energy turning into heat inside a part. Analogy: the mill's iron body getting warm. Precise: the conversion of electrical power into heat in a resistive part; for a resistor all of P = I² × R is dissipated. Source: D2 of F1-03 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Energy, Power, Power rating. Chapters: F1-03.
Distance between numbers
Simple words: How many steps apart two numbers are on the number line, never negative. Analogy: How many floors the lift travels. Precise: The larger number minus the smaller one; from −4 to 3 it is 3 − (−4) = 7. Source: D1 of F0-14 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Number line, Difference. Chapters: F0-14.
Distance sensor
Simple words: a sensor that tells how far away the nearest thing in front is. Analogy: judging with your eyes how far the wall is. Precise: a range sensor; some send out a signal (sound or light) and measure the echo that comes back from an object. Source: D3 of F9-02 (pending verification). Related: Sensor, Reading. Chapters: F9-02.
double
Simple words: The type for numbers with a decimal point, like 1.5. Analogy: A measuring jug that can hold 1.5 litres. Precise: A floating-point type; many decimals, such as 0.1, are stored only approximately, which is why 0.1 + 0.2 printed as 0.30000000000000004 with 17 digits (R2). Source: R1 of F0-31, R2 of F0-31, D1 of F0-31 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Type, int. Chapters: F0-31.
Drone
Simple words: A flying robot, often with spinning propellers. Analogy: A body that must keep its balance in the air all the time. Precise: An unmanned aircraft; a multirotor drone uses a computer (the flight controller) that reads its sensors and changes the speed of its motors to stay balanced and move. Source: D3 of F0-10 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Robot, Motor. Chapters: F0-10.
Electricity
Simple words: Tiny charged particles moving through a material, carrying energy to a lamp or a motor. Analogy: Water moving through the pipes of a house. Precise: The flow of electric charge (in metal wires the charge carriers are electrons) driven by a voltage. Source: D1, D2 of F0-39: Platt, "Make: Electronics"; Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics" (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Voltage, Current, Circuit. Chapters: F0-39.
Element
Simple words: One value inside a list. Analogy: One jar in the row. Precise: One of the values stored in a container such as std::vector. Source: R1 of F0-35, D1 of F0-35 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Index, std::vector. Chapters: F0-35.
Emergency stop
Simple words: a big, easy button or switch that makes the robot stop at once. Analogy: the brakes on your bicycle. Precise: a stop control that removes the power to the robot's motors (or otherwise forces them to stop) immediately and stays active until a person deliberately resets it; in this university it must be a physical switch that does not rely on the robot's program. Source: S1 of F9-07 (pending verification). Related: Latched, Speed limit, Supervision. Chapters: F9-07.
Enable
Simple words: an on/off input that lets a circuit work or keeps all its outputs off. Analogy: the main switch of the ticket board: when it is off, no lamp lights. Precise: an input that, when inactive, forces a decoder's outputs to their inactive value (here 0) regardless of the other inputs. Source: D2, R1 of F1-12 (pending verification). Related: Decoder. Chapters: F1-12.
Encoder
Simple words: a sensor that counts how much a wheel has turned. Analogy: counting the turns of a wheel. Precise: a sensor on a motor or wheel shaft that produces counts as the shaft rotates; distance travelled is estimated from the counts and the wheel size. Source: D2 of F9-03 (pending verification). Related: Motor, Differential drive, Sensor. Chapters: F9-03.
Energy
Simple words: the ability to do work, such as making light, movement or heat. Analogy: the total effort Kwame spends at the mill during a shift. Precise: a quantity measured in joules (J); in a circuit, each coulomb moved through a voltage V transfers V joules. Source: D2 of F1-03 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D3 of F1-03 (BIPM, "The International System of Units (SI)") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Power, Dissipation, Power rating. Chapters: F1-03.
Equation
Simple words: A statement that two amounts are equal, with an = sign in the middle. Analogy: A balance scale with its beam level. Precise: A statement expression = expression, such as 3x + 2 = 14; true for some values of its variables and false for others. Source: D1 of F0-17 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Unknown, Solution, Inequality. Chapters: F0-17, F0-18.
Equivalent expressions
Simple words: Two rules that always give the same answer. Analogy: Two ways of saying the same house rule. Precise: two Boolean expressions are equivalent when their outputs agree in every row of their truth table. Source: W1 of F0-27 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter). Related: Truth table, Counterexample, De Morgan's laws. Chapters: F0-27, F0-28.
Equivalent fractions
Simple words: Different-looking fractions that are the same amount. Analogy: Half a bread is the same as 4 slices out of 8. Precise: a/b and c/d are equivalent when a × d = b × c; multiplying or dividing top and bottom by the same non-zero number gives an equivalent fraction. Source: D1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Fraction. Chapters: F0-13.
Equivalent resistance
Simple words: one resistor that would do the same job as a group. Analogy: one pipe that lets through the same flow as a whole set of pipes. Precise: the single resistance that draws the same current from a source as the network it replaces; series: R1 + R2; parallel: 1 ÷ (1/R1 + 1/R2). Source: D2 of F1-04 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Series, Parallel, Node. Chapters: F1-04.
Error (control)
Simple words: How far you are from where you want to be. Analogy: How far the ribbon is from your feet. Precise: The difference between the wanted value and the measured value; not the same as a bug or a compiler error. Source: D1 of F0-45 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Control loop, Feedback. Chapters: F0-45, F9-05.
Estimate
Simple words: A sensible "about" answer you can get quickly. Analogy: Guessing the rice in a jar from one spoonful. Precise: An approximate result, usually found by rounding the inputs before calculating; used to check exact answers. Source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Rounding. Chapters: F0-12.
Executable
Simple words: The finished program file that the computer can start. Analogy: The recipe after it was rewritten for the cook: ready to use, but no longer easy for you to read. Precise: A file of machine instructions and data produced by the compiler; on the Linux build machine of this course the file tool describes it as an ELF 64-bit executable, and its first bytes are 7f 45 4c 46. Source: R4 of F0-29, D3 of F0-29 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Compiler. Chapters: F0-29.
Exhaustive test
Simple words: trying every possible input and checking every output. Analogy: tasting every dish on the menu, not only the favourites. Precise: a test whose vectors cover all 2n combinations of n binary inputs; for small combinational circuits this proves the circuit matches its truth table. Source: D1, W1 of F1-10 (pending verification). Related: Logic simulator, testbench, Pseudo-random test vectors. Chapters: F1-10.
Exit code
Simple words: A number a program gives back when it ends. 0 means "all went well". Analogy: The cook saying "done, no problems" or "something went wrong" at the end. Precise: The value returned by main (or set when a program is stopped); run_lab.sh records it in each .log file, for example "exit code: 0". Source: R1 of F0-29 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: main function. Chapters: F0-29, F0-33.
Expanded form
Simple words: A number written as the sum of what each digit is worth. Analogy: Saying "3 bowls and 4 cups and 7 beans" instead of 347. Precise: The sum of each digit times its place value, for example 3,407 = 3,000 + 400 + 0 + 7. Source: D1 of F0-11 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Place value. Chapters: F0-11.
Exponent
Simple words: The small raised number that says how many times to multiply. Analogy: The number of folds. Precise: n in a^n (also written a^n in plain text and program output). Source: D1 of F0-15 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Power, Logarithm (base two). Chapters: F0-15, F0-16.
Exponential curve
Simple words: a curve that changes fast at first and then slower and slower. Analogy: the tank fills quickly at first, then creeps towards full. Precise: here V(t) = Vs × (1 − e−t/τ), where e ≈ 2.718 is the base of natural logarithms; in each further τ the remaining gap shrinks by the same factor e−1 ≈ 0.368. Source: D2 of F1-05 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Capacitor, Capacitance, RC circuit. Chapters: F1-05.
Expression
Simple words: A recipe for a number made of numbers, letters and operations, with no equals sign. Analogy: The note "2 × batches" before you know the batches. Precise: A combination of numbers, variables and operations, such as 3n + 2, that has a value once every variable has a value. Source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Variable (maths), Term, Equation. Chapters: F0-16, F0-17.
Expression (Boolean)
Simple words: A rule written with letters, AND, OR, NOT and brackets. Analogy: "NOT (door open OR window open)" written short as NOT (D OR W). Precise: a formula built from Boolean variables, the constants 0 and 1, the operators AND, OR, NOT and brackets; it has one output value for each combination of variable values. Source: W1 of F0-27 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter). Related: Boolean algebra, Truth table. Chapters: F0-27.
Expression width (Verilog)
Simple words: how many bits Verilog uses to work out an expression. Analogy: a board that only has room for one digit: a total of 3 is written as 1 and the rest is lost. Precise: Verilog sizes an expression from its operands and its context; adding three 1-bit values in a 1-bit context keeps only the low bit. The run width_demo shows it. Source: D5, R3 of F1-13 (pending verification). Related: Reference model. Chapters: F1-13.
Fail-safe default
Simple words: If you are not sure, choose the safe answer. Analogy: If you do not know whether the stove is off, treat it as on. Precise: A design rule: when information is missing or a part fails, the system goes to its safe state. Source: R1 of F0-46 (lab run in this build). Related: Checklist. Chapters: F0-46.
Feedback
Simple words: Using what you sense now to choose what you do next. Analogy: Looking at the ribbon after every step. Precise: Using a measurement of a system's output to adjust its input. Source: D1 of F0-45 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Control loop. Chapters: F0-45, F9-01, F9-05.
Firmware
Simple words: The program that lives inside a small device. Analogy: The recipe card glued inside the cook's cupboard. Precise: Software stored in a device's non-volatile memory that runs when the device starts. Source: D2 of F0-42 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Microcontroller. Chapters: F0-42.
Flag
Simple words: One bit that answers a yes/no question. Analogy: One light: on means yes. Precise: a single bit in a larger value whose 1 or 0 records whether a condition is true. Source: D1 of F0-25 (title only, pending verification). Related: Bit field, Mask. Chapters: F0-25.
Floating (Z) and short (X)
Simple words: floating means the output is connected to nothing; a short means it is connected to 1 and 0 at the same time. Analogy: a sink with every tap shut, so nobody can say how full it is; or a sink with the roof tank and the drain both open, so water rushes straight through. Precise: Verilog writes a floating (high-impedance) value as z and an unknown value, such as two strong drivers in conflict, as x; in a real circuit a short between supply and ground draws a large current. Source: D5, R3 of F1-09 (pending verification). Related: Pull-up and pull-down network, Logic simulator, testbench. Chapters: F1-09.
Follow-on error
Simple words: An extra error message caused by an earlier mistake, not by a new one. Analogy: One missing step that makes the next three steps confusing too. Precise: A diagnostic that appears only because the compiler was already confused by an earlier error; fixing the first error usually removes it, as in R3 and R6. Source: R3 of F0-36, R6 of F0-36 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Compiler error. Chapters: F0-36.
for loop
Simple words: A loop with a counter built in: start, keep going while, and step. Analogy: Counting your stirs out loud: "one, two, three…" up to five. Precise: for (start; condition; step) { ... } runs start once, then checks the condition before each iteration and runs step after each one (R1). Source: R1 of F0-33, D1 of F0-33 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Loop, Counter. Chapters: F0-33, F0-35.
Formula
Simple words: A rule that says how to work out one quantity from others. Analogy: The fridge note "eggs = 2 × batches". Precise: An equation giving one variable in terms of others, such as ticket = table × seatsPerTable + seat (the F6 index formula in disguise). Source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Expression, Equation. Chapters: F0-16, F0-19.
Forward voltage
Simple words: the voltage across a diode when it conducts. Analogy: the pressure needed to hold the flap open. Precise: the voltage across a forward-biased diode at a stated current; it changes only a little over a wide range of current, and its value for a given part comes from the datasheet. Source: D2 of F1-06 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D4 of F1-06 (datasheets/manual of the kit chosen by the owner) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Diode, Anode and cathode, LED. Chapters: F0-40, F1-06.
Fraction
Simple words: A number that says "this many parts out of that many equal parts". Analogy: 3 slices of a bread cut into 8 equal slices. Precise: A number a/b with whole numbers a and b, b not zero; it means a ÷ b. Source: D1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Numerator, Denominator, Decimal. Chapters: F0-13.
Full adder
Simple words: a circuit that adds three bits: two digits and a carry coming in. Analogy: a board whose cook also takes the runner's token. Precise: a combinational circuit with inputs a, b, cin and outputs s = a XOR b XOR cin and cout = (a AND b) OR (cin AND (a XOR b)), so that 2·cout + s = a + b + cin. Source: D2, R1 of F1-13 (pending verification). Related: Half adder, Ripple-carry adder, Carry in, carry out (cin, cout). Chapters: F1-13, F1-14.
Function
Simple words: A named group of steps that you can use again by calling its name. Analogy: A small recipe inside a bigger recipe: "make the sauce (see page 12)".
