Precise: A named block of code with a return type and parameters, for example int double_it(int number); calling it runs its body and may give back a value. Source: R1 of F0-34, D1 of F0-34 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Parameter, Return value, Function call. Chapters: F0-18, F0-34, F0-38.
Function call
Simple words: Using a function by writing its name with round brackets. Analogy: Turning to the sauce page and following it, then coming back. Precise: An expression such as double_it(3) that runs the function body with the given arguments and then continues after the call (R1). Source: R1 of F0-34, D1 of F0-34 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Function, Argument. Chapters: F0-34.
Functionally complete (universal gate)
Simple words: a set of gates is complete if you can build every logic function from it; a gate that is complete on its own is called universal. Analogy: Zofia's one knife that can do every kitchen job, with enough moves. Precise: a set of Boolean operations is functionally complete if every Boolean function can be expressed using only operations from the set; {NAND} and {NOR} are each functionally complete. Source: D1, D2 of F1-11 (pending verification). Related: NAND gate, NOR gate. Chapters: F1-11.
Fuse
Simple words: a weak link that breaks on purpose when the current is too high. Analogy: a pipe section designed to burst first, safely, before anything else does. Precise: a protective device that opens the circuit when its current exceeds its rating for long enough; meters usually protect their current inputs with fuses whose ratings are in the manual. Source: D1 of F1-07 (Platt, "Make: Electronics"); D4 of F1-07 (datasheets/manual of the kit chosen by the owner) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Multimeter, Voltmeter (in parallel), Ammeter (in series). Chapters: F1-07.
Gain
Simple words: a number that says how strongly to correct. Analogy: how hard Lucía turns the handlebars for each bit she is off. Precise: the constant that multiplies the error to produce the correction; in a proportional rule, correction = − gain × error. Source: D1 of F9-05 (pending verification). Related: Proportional correction, Over-correction. Chapters: F9-05.
Gate symbol
Simple words: the standard drawing for each kind of gate, with inputs on the left and the output on the right. Analogy: the little picture on a kitchen door that tells you what happens in that room. Precise: a schematic shape: a triangle for a buffer, a D shape for AND, a curved shield for OR; a small circle (bubble) on an output or input means inversion. Source: D2 of F1-10 (pending verification). Related: Logic gate. Chapters: F1-10.
Gate, source, drain (of a transistor)
Simple words: the three wires of a transistor: one that controls it, and two that are joined when it is on. Analogy: the thin control pipe (gate), and the two ends of the big pipe through the tap (source and drain). Precise: in a MOS transistor the gate terminal controls whether a conducting channel forms between the source and drain terminals. The word "gate" also names a whole logic circuit (F1-10); the context says which one is meant. Source: D2 of F1-09 (pending verification). Related: Transistor, Logic gate. Chapters: F1-09.
Glitch (hazard)
Simple words: a short wrong pulse on an output that should not have changed. Analogy: a plate that briefly disappears from the counter while two cooks swap places, then comes back. Precise: an unwanted transient on a combinational output caused by different path delays; a static-1 hazard is a momentary 0 on an output whose correct value stays 1. Source: D2, R3 of F1-15 (pending verification). Related: Settle, Timing diagram. Chapters: F1-15.
Graph
Simple words: A picture of a function made of all its points. Analogy: Dots on squared paper, one per row of a table. Precise: The set of points (x, f(x)) for all allowed inputs x, drawn on a pair of axes. Source: D1 of F0-18 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Function, Slope. Chapters: F0-18.
Grid world
Simple words: A pretend world made of squares, printed as text. Analogy: A floor of square tiles. Precise: A simulation in which positions are whole-number cells of a grid and the robot moves one cell per step. Source: R1 of F0-45 (lab run in this build). Related: Simulator. Chapters: F0-45, F9-06.
Ground (reference)
Simple words: the point we agree to call 0 V. Analogy: the basement floor from which every height in the building is measured. Precise: the node of a circuit chosen as the 0 V reference for all other potentials; in battery circuits it is usually the battery's − terminal by the designer's choice. Source: D2 of F1-01 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Charge, Current, Voltage. Chapters: F1-01.
H-bridge
Simple words: Four switches around a motor that let it turn either way. Analogy: Four valves around the water wheel that choose which side the water enters. Precise: A circuit of four switches (in practice transistors) arranged in an H with the motor as the crossbar; closing opposite corners drives current through the motor in one direction or the other. Source: D2 of F0-44 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open); truth model R2 of F0-44. Related: Motor driver, Short circuit. Chapters: F0-44.
Half adder
Simple words: a circuit that adds two bits and gives a sum bit and a carry bit. Analogy: one board with no runner arriving. Precise: a combinational circuit with inputs a, b and outputs s = a XOR b and c = a AND b, so that 2c + s = a + b. Source: D2, R1 of F1-13 (pending verification). Related: Full adder, XOR (exclusive OR). Chapters: F1-13.
Hardware description language (HDL)
Simple words: a language for writing down a circuit as text: its parts and the wires between them. Analogy: the written plan of the building's pipes, which a practice kitchen can follow exactly. Precise: a computer language whose descriptions specify the structure and behaviour of digital hardware so that tools can simulate it or turn it into gates; Verilog is the HDL used in this course. Source: D2, D5 of F1-09 (pending verification). Related: Logic simulator, testbench, Structural description. Chapters: F1-09.
Heading
Simple words: the direction the robot is facing. Analogy: which way your bicycle's front wheel points. Precise: the robot's orientation; in the grid world one of east, south, west or north. "Left" and "right" are measured from the robot's own heading, not from the map. Source: D2 of F9-06 (pending verification). Related: Command, Differential drive. Chapters: F9-06.
Hex digit
Simple words: One symbol of a hexadecimal number. Analogy: The nickname for one group of four switches. Precise: one of the sixteen symbols 0–9, A–F; it stands for exactly four bits, because 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. Source: W1 of F0-22 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter). Related: Hexadecimal (hex), Nibble. Chapters: F0-22.
Hex prefix
Simple words: A label in front of a number that says "this is written in hex". Analogy: A sticky note on the row saying "read me with nicknames". Precise: the prefix 0x marks a hexadecimal literal in C++ (for example 0x2A is 42); this university also writes hex as 0x2A in running text (guide 13.3). Source: R1 of F0-22 (lab run in this build); D2 of F0-22 (title only, pending verification). Related: Hexadecimal (hex). Chapters: F0-22.
Hexadecimal (hex)
Simple words: A way of writing numbers with sixteen symbols: 0 to 9, then A to F. Analogy: A one-symbol nickname for every group of four hallway switches. Precise: the base-16 place-value system; the digits A–F stand for 10–15, and each position is worth 16 times the one to its right. Source: W1 of F0-22 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); R1 of F0-22 (lab run in this build). Related: Hex digit, Nibble, Hex prefix, Binary. Chapters: F0-22.
High and low
Simple words: On and off for a pin. Analogy: The light switch up or down. Precise: The two voltage levels of a digital signal; the actual voltages are given in the microcontroller's datasheet. Source: D2, D3 of F0-42 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Pin (input/output). Chapters: F0-42, F0-43.
Hysteresis
Simple words: using two thresholds: a higher one to switch on, a lower one to switch off. Analogy: the bell only rings after a firm pull, and only resets after the rope is fully let go. Precise: a property of a circuit whose switching threshold depends on its present state; a Schmitt trigger has an upper threshold for rising inputs and a lower one for falling inputs. Source: D2 of F1-08 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Signal, Analog signal, Digital signal. Chapters: F0-43, F1-08.
if statement
Simple words: A way to say "only do this when the condition is true". Analogy: "If it is raining, take an umbrella." Precise: A statement that runs its block only when its condition is true; an optional else block runs otherwise, and else if chains test conditions in order until one is true (R1). Source: R1 of F0-32, D1 of F0-32 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Condition, Block. Chapters: F0-32.
Index
Simple words: The position number of an element. Counting starts at 0. Analogy: The number painted on a jar: jar 0, jar 1, jar 2. Precise: The position of an element in a container, from 0 up to size() − 1; list[0] is the first element (R1). Source: R1 of F0-35, D1 of F0-35 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Element, Off-by-one error. Chapters: F0-35.
Inequality
Simple words: A statement that one amount is bigger or smaller than another. Analogy: A balance scale that is tipped, not level. Precise: A statement using <, >, ≤, ≥ or ≠, such as x + 3 ≤ 7; multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses it. Source: D1 of F0-19 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Allowed range, Equation. Chapters: F0-19, F0-11, F0-14.
Infinite loop
Simple words: A loop that never stops. Analogy: "Add milk until the cup is full", but nobody ever adds milk. Precise: A loop whose condition never becomes false, usually because nothing inside the loop changes what the condition tests. Source: D1 of F0-07 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Loop, Bug. Chapters: F0-07, F0-33.
Initialise
Simple words: To give a variable its first value at the moment you create it. Analogy: Filling the jar the moment you put it on the shelf. Precise: Giving a variable a value in its declaration (int apples = 3;). With the course flags, g++ refused to build a program that used a variable before giving it a value (R4). Source: R1 of F0-30, R4 of F0-30, D1 of F0-30 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Declaration, Variable. Chapters: F0-30.
Input
Simple words: Information that goes into the computer. Analogy: What your ears and eyes take in. Precise: Data that a program receives from outside itself, for example from a keyboard, a mouse, a microphone, a sensor or a file. Source: D1 of F0-06 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Output, Sensor, Device. Chapters: F0-06.
Input and output
Simple words: What goes into a rule, and what comes out. Analogy: The time you ask about, and the distance the simulator tells you. Precise: For y = f(x), x is the input (independent variable) and y the output (dependent variable). Source: D1 of F0-18 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Function. Chapters: F0-18.
Input and output (I/O)
Simple words: Information coming into the computer, and results going out. Analogy: Order slips through the order window; plates out through the serving hatch. Precise: The transfer of data between the computer and the outside world through devices such as a keyboard (input) or a screen (output). Source: D2 of F0-05 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Input, Output, Device. Chapters: F0-05, F0-06.
Input resistance
Simple words: how much the voltmeter itself resists current; bigger is better. Analogy: how little water the gauge's hoses let through. Precise: the resistance a voltmeter presents between its probes; it appears in parallel with the measured part and causes loading (F1-04); its value is given in the meter's manual. Source: D2 of F1-07 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D4 of F1-07 (datasheets/manual of the kit chosen by the owner) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Multimeter, Voltmeter (in parallel), Ammeter (in series). Chapters: F1-07.
Instruction
Simple words: One single step that tells the machine to do one thing. Analogy: One line of a recipe, like "crack the egg". Precise: One command that a computer can carry out; a program is made of many of them. Source: D2 of F0-01 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Program, Algorithm. Chapters: F0-01.
int
Simple words: The type for whole numbers, like 7 or -3. Analogy: A jar for whole eggs: no half eggs allowed. Precise: The basic signed integer type; on the build machine it used 4 bytes and its largest value printed as 2147483647 (R3). Source: R1 of F0-31, R3 of F0-31, D1 of F0-31 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Type, Integer division. Chapters: F0-31.
Integer
Simple words: A whole number that may be positive, negative or zero. Analogy: A lift button: no half floors. Precise: Any of ..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ...: the whole numbers together with their opposites. Not the same as the C++ type int, which holds only a limited range of integers (MA102). Source: D1 of F0-14 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Negative number. Chapters: F0-14.
Integer division
Simple words: Dividing whole numbers in C++ gives a whole number: the part after the point is dropped. Analogy: Sharing 7 eggs between 2 boxes: each box gets 3 whole eggs, and 1 egg is left over. Precise: When both operands of / are integers, the result is an integer and the fractional part is discarded: 7 / 2 printed 3 and 7 % 2 printed the remainder 1 (R2). Source: R2 of F0-31, R5 of F0-31, D1 of F0-31 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: int, Remainder operator. Chapters: F0-31, F0-38.
Invariant
Simple words: A sentence about a process that stays true at every step. Analogy: "the two jars together hold twenty marbles", whatever moves are made. Precise: a condition (a Boolean expression about the state, F0-27) that holds in the starting state and is preserved by every allowed step, so it holds in every state reached. Source: W1 of F0-28 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); D1 of F0-28 (title only, pending verification). Related: Loop invariant, Invariant check, Parity. Chapters: F0-28.
Invariant check
Simple words: A line in a program that tests the invariant and complains if it is false. Analogy: Counting all the marbles after each turn. Precise: code that evaluates the invariant at chosen points and reports a failure; in larger C++ programs this can be written with assert (introduced in later courses). Source: R1 of F0-28 (lab run in this build); D2 of F0-28 (title only, pending verification). Related: Invariant, Loop invariant. Chapters: F0-28.
Inverse operation
Simple words: The operation that undoes another one. Analogy: Taking marbles off undoes putting them on. Precise: Subtraction undoes addition; division by a non-zero number undoes multiplication; applying the same inverse operation to both sides keeps an equation true. Source: D1 of F0-17 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Equation. Chapters: F0-17, F0-12.
Inverter (NOT gate)
Simple words: a circuit whose output is the opposite of its input. Analogy: a sink that fills when the control pipe is empty and drains when it has pressure. Precise: the logic function y = NOT a; in CMOS, one pMOS pull-up and one nMOS pull-down with their gates joined to the input. Source: D2, R2 of F1-09 (pending verification). Related: CMOS, NAND gate. Chapters: F1-09.
Iteration
Simple words: One round of a loop. Analogy: One stir of the spoon. Precise: A single execution of a loop's block. Source: R1 of F0-33, D1 of F0-33 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Loop. Chapters: F0-33.
I–V curve
Simple words: a graph of how much current flows at each voltage. Analogy: a chart of flow against pressure for the stiff flap. Precise: the plot of current against voltage for a part; a resistor's is a straight line (F1-02), a diode's is nearly flat and then rises very steeply. Source: D2 of F1-06 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Diode, Anode and cathode, Forward voltage. Chapters: F1-06.
Kibibyte (KiB)
Simple words: 1024 bytes. Analogy: Felix's box of 1024 cookies. Precise: 1 KiB = 2 B = 1024 B, using the binary prefix kibi; MiB = 1024 B, GiB = 1024 B. Source: W1 of F0-23 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); D3 of F0-23 (title only, pending verification). Related: Kilobyte (kB), Byte. Chapters: F0-23.
Kilobyte (kB)
Simple words: One thousand bytes. Analogy: Ana's box of 1000 cookies. Precise: 1 kB = 1000 B, using the decimal (SI) prefix kilo = 10; MB = 1000 B, GB = 1000 B. Source: W1 of F0-23 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); D2 of F0-23 (title only, pending verification). Related: Kibibyte (KiB), Byte. Chapters: F0-23.
Kirchhoff's laws
Simple words: two bookkeeping rules: voltages round a loop add to zero; currents into a joint equal currents out. Analogy: water going round the building ends where it started; water into a pipe joint equals water out. Precise: the voltage law: the sum of potential differences around any closed loop is zero; the current law: the sum of currents into any node equals the sum out. Source: D2 of F1-04 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Series, Parallel, Node. Chapters: F1-04.
Latched
Simple words: once switched on, it stays on until someone switches it off on purpose. Analogy: a door that locks when it shuts, and needs a key to open. Precise: a state that, once set by an event, remains set after the event ends, until an explicit reset. Source: R1 of F9-07 (pending verification). Related: Emergency stop. Chapters: F9-07.
Least significant bit (LSB)
Simple words: The bit on the far right, worth 1. Analogy: The switch at the right end of the hallway, the one that flips most often. Precise: the bit with the smallest place value, 2 = 1; it decides whether the number is odd (1) or even (0). Source: W1 of F0-21 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter). Related: Most significant bit (MSB), Bit number, Parity. Chapters: F0-21, F0-25.
LED
Simple words: a diode that gives off light when current flows forward. Analogy: a flap valve that glows while water flows through it. Precise: a light-emitting diode; its colour and forward voltage depend on its semiconductor material, and its brightness rises with forward current up to the datasheet's maximum. Source: D1 of F1-06 (Platt, "Make: Electronics"); D2 of F1-06 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Diode, Anode and cathode, Forward voltage. Chapters: F0-40, F0-41, F0-42, F1-06.
Light sensor
Simple words: a sensor that tells how bright something is. Analogy: your eyes telling light from dark. Precise: a sensor whose output changes with the amount of light reaching it; pointed at the floor, often next to a small lamp, it reports how much light the floor reflects. Source: D4 of F9-02 (pending verification). Related: Threshold, Calibrate, Line follower. Chapters: F9-02.
Like terms
Simple words: Terms with exactly the same letters, which can be added together. Analogy: 4 cups of rice and 3 cups of rice make 7 cups of rice; rice and milk do not combine. Precise: Terms whose variable parts are identical; 4a + 3a = 7a, but 3a + 2b cannot be combined. Source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Term. Chapters: F0-16.
Line follower
Simple words: A robot that drives along a line drawn on the floor. Analogy: Walking along a ribbon while looking at your feet. Precise: A mobile robot whose program uses downward-facing sensors to detect a line and steers to keep the line under its sensors. Source: D2 of F0-45: Lynch and Park, "Modern Robotics" (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Control loop, Sensor. Chapters: F0-45, F9-05.
LiPo battery
Simple words: A kind of rechargeable battery that can catch fire if mistreated. Analogy: A pressure cooker: useful, but only with strict rules. Precise: A lithium polymer battery; it can catch fire if punctured, over-charged, over-discharged, short-circuited or charged unattended. Not used in F0. Source: S1 of F0-46: University Authoring Guide, Honesty first (opened in this build). Related: Battery. Chapters: F0-46.
Loading
Simple words: when connecting something to a circuit changes the circuit's voltages. Analogy: opening an extra tap halfway down a pipe lowers the pressure there. Precise: the change in a circuit's behaviour caused by the current drawn by a connected load; a load across R2 of a divider forms R2 ∥ Rload and lowers Vout. Source: D2 of F1-04 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Series, Parallel, Node. Chapters: F1-04, F1-07.
Log (trace)
Simple words: the lines a program prints about what it did, one after another. Analogy: a diary of the ride. Precise: a time-ordered record of a program's actions and values, used to understand and debug its behaviour. Source: R1 of F9-04 (pending verification). Related: Test run. Chapters: F9-04.
Logarithm (base two)
Simple words: How many times you must double 1 to reach a number, or halve the number to get back to 1. Analogy: How many folds made 1,024 layers. Precise: log2(x) is the exponent n with 2^n = x; log2(1,024) = 10. Source: D1 of F0-15 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Power of two, Exponent. Chapters: F0-15.
Logic gate
Simple words: a small circuit that computes one logic function, such as NOT or AND, from its inputs. Analogy: one sink with its own set of taps, whose fill level answers one yes/no question. Precise: an electronic circuit implementing a Boolean function of one or more binary inputs; in CMOS, a pull-up and a pull-down network of transistors. "Gate" also names one terminal of a transistor (F1-09). Source: D2, D1 of F1-10 (pending verification). Related: NAND gate, NOR gate, Gate symbol. Chapters: F1-10.
Logic simulator, testbench
Simple words: a program that pretends to be a circuit; a testbench is the extra code that tries inputs and checks outputs. Analogy: a practice kitchen where you test a recipe before the real dinner, and a tasting checklist. Precise: a simulator computes the values of the wires of a circuit description over time; a testbench is a description that applies input values (test vectors) to the design under test and compares its outputs with expected values. Source: D1, D5 of F1-09 (pending verification). Related: Exhaustive test, Reference model. Chapters: F1-09.
Logical operator
Simple words: Words that join conditions: and (&&), or (||), not (!). Analogy: "Homework done AND it is after school." Precise: The operators && (true only if both sides are true), || (true if at least one side is true) and ! (turns true into false and false into true) (R2). Source: R2 of F0-32, D1 of F0-32 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Condition, bool. Chapters: F0-32.
Loop
Simple words: Steps that are repeated. Analogy: "Stir 20 times." Precise: A part of an algorithm that runs again and again, either a set number of times or while a condition stays true. In C++, for and while make loops. Source: D1 of F0-07, D3 of F0-07 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Condition, Infinite loop. Chapters: F0-07, F0-33, F9-04.
Loop invariant
Simple words: An invariant for a repeating part of a program. Analogy: The marble total checked after every turn of the game. Precise: a condition that is true before a loop starts and remains true after each pass of the loop body; together with the loop's stopping condition it proves what the loop computes. Source: W1 of F0-28 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); D1 of F0-28 (title only, pending verification). Related: Invariant, Invariant check. Chapters: F0-28.
main function
Simple words: The place where every C++ program starts. Analogy: The first line of the recipe: "start here". Precise: The function named main, which the program runs first; the value it returns (0 here) becomes the exit code that the run log records. Source: R1 of F0-29, D1 of F0-29 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Function, Exit code. Chapters: F0-29, F0-34.
Main memory
Simple words: The big workspace that holds the program and its data while it runs. Analogy: The big pantry down the corridor. Precise: The computer's large working memory (built from DRAM chips, dynamic random-access memory), where running programs and their data are kept; its contents are lost when the power goes off. Source: D3 of F0-05 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Storage, Cache. Chapters: F0-05.
Mains electricity
Simple words: The electricity in the wall sockets of a building. Analogy: The high-pressure water main under the street, not the garden hose. Precise: The building's alternating-current supply from the electricity network; dangerous, and never used in any lab of this university. Source: S1 of F0-46 (opened in this build); D1 of F0-46 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Supervision. Chapters: F0-46, F0-39.
Mask
Simple words: A pattern of bits that picks which bits you want to touch. Analogy: The card with holes over some switches. Precise: a value combined with data by a bitwise operator so that only the bit positions selected by the mask are set, cleared, toggled or kept. Source: W1 of F0-25 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); D1 of F0-25 (title only, pending verification). Related: Bitwise operator, Shift, Bit field. Chapters: F0-25.
Microcontroller
Simple words: A very small computer on one chip, made to control things like lights and motors. Analogy: A cook who only knows one short recipe card and repeats it all day. Precise: An integrated circuit that contains a processor, memory for the program and data, and input/output pins on one chip. Source: D2 of F0-42 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Pin (input/output), Firmware. Chapters: F0-42, F0-43, F0-44.
Million
Simple words: A thousand thousands. Analogy: A thousand bowls of a thousand beans each. Precise: 1,000,000 = 1,000 × 1,000, a 1 followed by six zeros. In this university a billion means a thousand millions, 1,000,000,000. Source: D1 of F0-11 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Power of ten. Chapters: F0-11, F0-15.
Millisecond (ms)
Simple words: A very short time: one second cut into a thousand parts. Analogy: A tiny tick of the kitchen timer. Precise: One thousandth of a second; 1,000 ms = 1 s. Source: Definition; D1 of F0-42 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: —. Chapters: F0-42.
Most significant bit (MSB)
Simple words: The bit on the far left, worth the most. Analogy: The switch at the left end, the one with the biggest number written above it. Precise: the bit with the largest place value in a number of a given width; in 8 bits it is worth 2 = 128. Source: W1 of F0-21 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter). Related: Least significant bit (LSB), Sign bit. Chapters: F0-21.
Motor
Simple words: A part that spins when it gets electricity. Analogy: The muscle that turns a wheel or a propeller. Precise: An electric machine that turns electrical energy into turning motion; the most common actuator in small robots and drones. Source: D2 of F0-10 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Actuator. Chapters: F0-10, F0-44, F0-45, F9-03.
Motor command
Simple words: the instruction the program gives a motor, such as "turn this fast". Analogy: your brain telling a leg how hard to push the pedal. Precise: the value a control program sends to a motor driver; what the motor then really does also depends on the load, the battery and friction. Source: D2 of F9-03 (pending verification). Related: Motor, Encoder, Speed limit. Chapters: F9-03.
Motor driver
Simple words: A helper circuit that lets a weak signal switch a strong motor current. Analogy: A tap opened by a small control valve. Precise: A circuit (it can be a single chip) that uses a low-current control input to switch the motor's higher current from a separate supply. Source: D2 of F0-44 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Transistor, H-bridge, Current limit. Chapters: F0-44, F0-45.
Multimeter
Simple words: one meter that can measure voltage, current and resistance. Analogy: the plumber's pressure gauge, flow meter and pipe tester in one box. [proposed mapping, awaiting registration in guide 8.1; see HW101 NOTES.md] Precise: a test instrument with selectable modes and ranges (at least voltage, current and resistance), connected through two probes to sockets chosen for the mode; the exact sockets, ranges and limits are given in its user manual. Source: D1 of F1-07 (Platt, "Make: Electronics"); D4 of F1-07 (datasheets/manual of the kit chosen by the owner) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Voltmeter (in parallel), Ammeter (in series), Ohmmeter. Chapters: F0-40, F1-07.
Multiplexer (mux)
Simple words: a circuit that chooses one of several inputs and passes it to the output. Analogy: Mateo sliding one station's plate through the hatch. Precise: a combinational circuit with 2n data inputs, n select inputs and one output, whose output equals the data input whose index is the binary number on the select inputs. Source: D2, D1 of F1-12 (pending verification). Related: Select input, Decoder, ALU (arithmetic logic unit). Chapters: F1-12.
NAND gate
Simple words: "not and": the output is 0 only when all inputs are 1. Analogy: Kenji's sink: it drains only when both drain taps are open. Precise: the Boolean function y = NOT (a AND b); in CMOS, two nMOS in series to ground and two pMOS in parallel to the supply. Source: D2, R1 of F1-10 (pending verification). Related: NOR gate, Functionally complete (universal gate). Chapters: F1-10, F1-11.
Negative number
Simple words: A number less than zero, written with a minus sign in front. Analogy: A floor below the street, or a temperature below zero. Precise: For every number a > 0, its opposite −a satisfies a + (−a) = 0; numbers below 0 are negative. Source: D1 of F0-14 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Integer, Opposite, Number line. Chapters: F0-14, F0-16, F0-19.
Netlist
Simple words: the list of every gate in a circuit and the wires that join them. Analogy: the plumber's parts list with every pipe connection written down. Precise: a description of a circuit as instances (cells) and the nets (wires) connecting their pins. Source: D6 of F1-11 (pending verification). Related: Synthesis tool. Chapters: F1-11.
Network
Simple words: Computers joined together so they can send each other messages. Analogy: The postal service, with post offices and roads between them. Precise: A set of computers and connecting devices, linked by cables or radio, that pass data from one computer to another. Source: D1 of F0-09 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Packet, Router, Protocol. Chapters: F0-09.
Newline
Simple words: The invisible character that says "start a new line here". Analogy: Pressing the Enter key on a typewriter or keyboard. Precise: The character written '\n' in C++; without it, the next output continues on the same line (R3 shows two messages glued together). Source: R3 of F0-29, D1 of F0-29 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: String literal, std::cout. Chapters: F0-29.
Nibble
Simple words: Half of a row of eight bits: four bits. Analogy: One group of four switches. Precise: a group of 4 bits; one hex digit writes one nibble. The word is an informal engineers' name. Source: W1 of F0-22 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); D1 of F0-22 (title only, pending verification). Related: Hex digit, Byte. Chapters: F0-22.
nMOS and pMOS
Simple words: the two kinds of transistor switch: nMOS turns on when its gate is 1, pMOS turns on when its gate is 0. Analogy: two kinds of tap: one opens when the control pipe has pressure, the other opens when it has none. Precise: n-channel and p-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors; in the ideal-switch model of digital logic, an nMOS conducts when its gate is at logic 1 and a pMOS conducts when its gate is at logic 0. Source: D2, R2 of F1-09 (pending verification). Related: Transistor, CMOS, Pull-up and pull-down network. Chapters: F1-09.
Node
Simple words: a meeting point of wires. Analogy: a pipe joint where several pipes meet. Precise: a point (or a set of points joined by wire) in a circuit, which has one potential. Source: D2 of F1-04 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Series, Parallel, Equivalent resistance. Chapters: F1-04.
Noise
Simple words: unwanted wiggles added to a signal. Analogy: Kemal's trembling hand on the bell rope. Precise: unwanted random or interfering variations superimposed on a signal. Source: D2 of F1-08 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Signal, Analog signal, Digital signal. Chapters: F0-43, F1-08.
NOR gate
Simple words: "not or": the output is 1 only when all inputs are 0. Analogy: a sink with two drain taps side by side and two roof taps one after the other. Precise: the Boolean function y = NOT (a OR b); in CMOS, two nMOS in parallel to ground and two pMOS in series to the supply. Source: D2, R1 of F1-10 (pending verification). Related: NAND gate, Functionally complete (universal gate). Chapters: F1-10.
NOT
Simple words: Turns true into false and false into true. Analogy: A push button that breaks the circuit while you press it. Precise: the one-input Boolean function with output equal to the opposite of the input; in C++, ! and bitwise ~. Source: W1 of F0-26 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); R1 of F0-26 (lab run in this build). Related: AND, OR, De Morgan's laws. Chapters: F0-26.
Number line
Simple words: A straight line where every number has its own spot, smaller on the left and bigger on the right. Analogy: The lift shaft lying on its side: street floor at 0. Precise: A line with a chosen point for 0 and a fixed spacing for 1, so that each number corresponds to one point; moving right adds, moving left takes away. Source: D1 of F0-14 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Negative number, Axis, Allowed range. Chapters: F0-12, F0-14, F0-18, F0-19.
Numerator
Simple words: The top number of a fraction: how many parts you have. Analogy: The slices Hana ate. Precise: a in the fraction a/b. Source: D1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Fraction, Denominator. Chapters: F0-13.
Off-by-one error
Simple words: A mistake where something happens one time too many or one time too few. Analogy: Stirring 19 times when the recipe says 20. Precise: A bug in which a count, a limit or a position is wrong by exactly one, often from choosing "less than" instead of "less than or equal". Source: D2 of F0-08 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Bug, Loop. Chapters: F0-08, F0-19, F0-35, F0-37, F0-38.
Ohm (Ω)
Simple words: the unit of resistance. Analogy: a "narrowness number" for a pipe. Precise: one ohm is the resistance through which one volt drives one ampere (1 Ω = 1 V/A). Source: D3 of F1-02 (BIPM, "The International System of Units (SI)") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Resistance, Ohm's law, Resistor. Chapters: F1-02.
Ohm's law
Simple words: for many parts, the current is proportional to the voltage. Analogy: twice the pressure through the same pipe gives twice the flow. Precise: V = I × R with R constant; parts that obey it over their working range are called ohmic. Source: D2 of F1-02 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Resistance, Ohm (Ω), Resistor. Chapters: F0-39, F0-40, F1-02, F1-03.
Ohmmeter
Simple words: the resistance mode: the meter sends its own small current through a part. Analogy: testing how narrow a pipe is after taking it out of the building. Precise: a resistance measurement in which the meter applies a known small current or voltage from its own battery; it is valid only with the circuit unpowered, and the part should be isolated from parallel paths. Source: D1 of F1-07 (Platt, "Make: Electronics"); D2 of F1-07 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Multimeter, Voltmeter (in parallel), Ammeter (in series). Chapters: F1-07.
One-hot
Simple words: a group of wires where exactly one is 1. Analogy: one lit lamp on the ticket board. Precise: an encoding in which exactly one bit of a group is 1; a decoder's outputs are one-hot when enabled. Source: D2 of F1-12 (pending verification). Related: Decoder. Chapters: F1-12.
Opcode (operation code)
Simple words: a small binary number that says which operation the ALU should do. Analogy: the dial position on Ines's station. Precise: the select input of the ALU's result multiplexer and of any operation-specific logic; this chapter's ALU uses a 3-bit code with eight operations. Source: W1 of F1-14 (pending verification). Related: ALU (arithmetic logic unit). Chapters: F1-14.
Opposite
Simple words: The number the same distance from zero on the other side. Analogy: Floor 3 and floor −3 are both three floors from the street. Precise: The opposite of a is −a, with a + (−a) = 0; subtracting a number is adding its opposite. Source: D1 of F0-14 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Negative number. Chapters: F0-14.
OR
Simple words: True when at least one input is true. Analogy: Two switches side by side (in parallel): either one can light the lamp. Precise: the Boolean function with output 1 when one or more inputs are 1; in C++, || and bitwise |. It is "inclusive": both on also gives 1. Source: W1 of F0-26 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); R1 of F0-26 (lab run in this build). Related: AND, XOR (exclusive OR), Truth table. Chapters: F0-26.
Order of operations
Simple words: The agreed order for doing the steps of a calculation. Analogy: A recipe that says "mix the dry things first, then add the milk". Precise: Brackets first; then multiplication and division from left to right; then addition and subtraction from left to right. Source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Expression. Chapters: F0-12, F0-16.
Oscillator
Simple words: a circuit that keeps switching back and forth on its own. Analogy: a kitchen timer that rings, resets itself and rings again. Precise: a circuit that produces a periodic output without a periodic input; a relaxation oscillator does it by charging and discharging a capacitor between two thresholds. Source: D2 of F1-08 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Signal, Analog signal, Digital signal. Chapters: F1-08.
Out of range
Simple words: Asking for a list position that does not exist. Analogy: Reaching for jar 3 on a shelf that has only jars 0, 1 and 2. Precise: Using an index that is not less than size(); the member function at() checks and throws std::out_of_range, which stopped the program in R4 with exit code 134. Source: R4 of F0-35, D1 of F0-35 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Index, Off-by-one error. Chapters: F0-35, F0-37.
Output
Simple words: Information or action that comes out of the computer. Analogy: Your voice and your hands. Precise: Data or signals that a program sends out, for example to a screen, a speaker, a printer, a lamp, a motor or a file. Source: D1 of F0-06 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Input, Actuator, Device. Chapters: F0-06.
Over-correction
Simple words: correcting so hard that you shoot past the target to the other side. Analogy: Lucía yanking the handlebars and zig-zagging. Precise: a response that crosses the target (overshoot) because the correction is too large for the system; with this chapter's rule it happens when the gain is larger than 1. Source: R3 of F9-05 (pending verification). Related: Gain. Chapters: F9-05.
Overflow
Simple words: What happens when a number is too big for the switches you have. Analogy: Trying to show 8 with only three switches: there is no switch worth 8, so the row goes back to all off. Precise: the result of a calculation needs more bits than the storage has; the extra high bits are lost and the stored value wraps around. Source: R3 of F0-20 (lab run in this build). Related: Wrap-around, Bit. Chapters: F0-20, F0-24.
Overflow (signed)
Simple words: the true answer is too big or too small to fit, so the bits show a wrong signed number. Analogy: a four-board row asked to show a count that needs five boards, read as a signed count. Precise: in N-bit two's complement, the representable range is −2N−1 to 2N−1 − 1; a signed sum outside that range overflows; this happens exactly when the carry into the top bit differs from the carry out of it. Source: D2, W1, R3 of F1-14 (pending verification). Related: Status flags (Z, N, C, V). Chapters: F1-14.
Packet
Simple words: One small piece of a message that travels on its own. Analogy: One postcard of Ines's story. Precise: A unit of data sent across a network, made of a header (with information such as the addresses) and a piece of the message. Source: D1 of F0-09 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Address, Network. Chapters: F0-09.
Parallel
Simple words: parts connected side by side between the same two points, so they share the same voltage. Analogy: way two: the pipe splits, feeds both, and joins again. Precise: components connected between the same two nodes, so they have the same voltage; their currents add. Source: D2 of F1-04 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Series, Node, Equivalent resistance. Chapters: F0-41, F1-04.
Parameter
Simple words: A variable in a function that receives a value from the caller. Analogy: The blank in "add ___ to the pot". Precise: A variable declared in a function's parameter list; it starts as a copy of the argument when the parameter is a plain type such as int, so changing it does not change the caller's variable (R4). Source: R1 of F0-34, R4 of F0-34, D1 of F0-34 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Argument, Function. Chapters: F0-34.
Parity
Simple words: Whether a number is odd or even. Analogy: Whether the marbles can be paired off with none left over. Precise: the remainder of a whole number after dividing by 2: 0 (even) or 1 (odd); for a binary number it is the least significant bit (F0-21). Source: W1 of F0-28 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter). Related: Least significant bit (LSB), Invariant, XOR (exclusive OR). Chapters: F0-28.
Percentage
Simple words: "Out of a hundred". Analogy: Pretending the bread was cut into 100 tiny equal slices and counting how many you ate. Precise: p % means p/100; 37.5 % = 0.375 = 3/8. Percentages above 100 are allowed. Source: D1 of F0-13 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Fraction, Decimal. Chapters: F0-13.
Pin (input/output)
Simple words: A little metal leg of the chip that the program can switch on or off, or read. Analogy: A light switch the cook can flip, or a doorbell the cook can listen to. Precise: A terminal connected to the chip's input/output circuits; as a digital output the program drives it high or low, as an input the program reads its level. Source: D2 of F0-42 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: High and low, Microcontroller. Chapters: F0-42, F0-43, F0-44.
Pixel
Simple words: One tiny dot of a picture. Analogy: One tile in a mosaic on a kitchen wall. Precise: A picture element: one point of an image, stored as numbers that describe its colour. Source: D1 of F0-03 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Code (for information). Chapters: F0-03.
Place value
Simple words: How much a digit is worth because of where it sits. Analogy: The price tag stuck under each switch. Precise: The number a position stands for; in our usual decimal numbers the places are 1, 10, 100; in binary they are 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. Source: D1 of F0-02 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Binary. Chapters: F0-02, F0-11, F0-13, F0-15, F0-20, F0-21.
Placeholder
Simple words: A zero that keeps the other digits in their right places. Analogy: An empty cup spot on the table that says "no cups here". Precise: A digit 0 in a numeral; it adds nothing to the value but fixes the position, and so the place value, of every digit to its left. Source: D1 of F0-11 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Digit, Place value. Chapters: F0-11.
Polarised capacitor
Simple words: a capacitor with a + leg and a − leg that must not be swapped. Analogy: a tank whose rubber wall may only be pushed from one side. Precise: a capacitor type (for example an electrolytic) that is designed to be used with one terminal always positive; its datasheet gives the polarity marking and the maximum voltage. Source: D1 of F1-05 (Platt, "Make: Electronics"); D4 of F1-05 (datasheets/manual of the kit chosen by the owner) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Capacitor, Capacitance, RC circuit. Chapters: F1-05.
Potential
Simple words: the "height" of one point, compared with a chosen zero point. Analogy: how high a tap is above the basement floor. Precise: the voltage of a point measured from a chosen reference point; only differences of potential have physical meaning. Source: D2 of F1-01 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Charge, Current, Voltage. Chapters: F1-01.
Power
Simple words: how fast energy is delivered or used. Analogy: how hard and how fast Kwame turns the mill at this moment. Precise: the rate of energy transfer, P = E ÷ t; in a part with voltage V across it and current I through it, P = V × I; measured in watts (W), one watt being one joule per second. Source: D2 of F1-03 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D3 of F1-03 (BIPM, "The International System of Units (SI)") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Energy, Dissipation, Power rating. Chapters: F0-15, F1-03.
Power of ten
Simple words: 1, 10, 100, 1,000 and so on: a 1 followed by zeros. Analogy: The bowls and cups of F0-11, ten of each making the next. Precise: 10^n, written as 1 followed by n zeros; the place values of base ten. Source: D1 of F0-15 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Power, Place value, Million. Chapters: F0-15, F0-11.
Power of two
Simple words: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on: each one double the one before. Analogy: The layers of paper after each fold; a row of switches, each worth double the one to its right. Precise: 2^n for a whole number n; the place values of base two; n on/off switches make 2^n patterns. Source: D1 of F0-15 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Power, Logarithm (base two), Bit. Chapters: F0-15, F0-19.
Power rating
Simple words: the most power a part may take without damage, as its maker says. Analogy: the mill's sign "do not turn faster than this". Precise: the maximum continuous power dissipation stated in a part's datasheet, under the conditions the datasheet states. Source: D4 of F1-03 (datasheets/manual of the kit chosen by the owner) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Energy, Power, Dissipation. Chapters: F1-03.
Processing
Simple words: The work the computer does between the input and the output. Analogy: Your thinking: "the bell rang, so it is Grandma". Precise: The steps of the program that turn input data into output data. Source: D2 of F0-06 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Input, Output. Chapters: F0-06.
Product
Simple words: The answer when you multiply. Analogy: The rice in many spoons when each spoon holds the same number of grains. Precise: The result of multiplication; for whole numbers 3 × 4 means 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. Source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Quotient, Power. Chapters: F0-12.
Program
Simple words: An algorithm written in a language a computer can follow. Analogy: The recipe, translated into the cook's own language. Precise: A list of instructions written in a programming language, such as C++, that is turned into instructions the computer can carry out. Source: D2 of F0-01, D3 of F0-01 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Algorithm, Instruction. Chapters: F0-01, F0-29, F9-04.
Program loop
Simple words: Steps that repeat again and again. Analogy: Knead, rest, repeat on the recipe card. Precise: A sequence of instructions that the processor carries out again and again; the main loop of a blink program has no end condition. Source: D4 of F0-42: Petzold, "Code" (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Control loop. Chapters: F0-42.
Propagation delay
Simple words: the time from an input changing to the output reaching its new, final value. Analogy: the time between an order arriving and the plate being finished on the counter. Precise: the maximum time from a change at a circuit's input until its output is stable at the new value; for a path through several gates it is the sum of the gate delays along the path. Source: D2 of F1-15 (pending verification). Related: Contamination delay, Critical path, Settle. Chapters: F1-15.
Proportional correction
Simple words: a little off, steer a little; far off, steer a lot. Analogy: Arjun's advice, "gently". Precise: a control law in which the command is proportional to the error; it is the P of PID, taught fully in F9-17. Source: D1 of F9-05 (pending verification). Related: Gain, Control loop. Chapters: F9-05.
Protocol
Simple words: Agreed rules for how computers talk. Analogy: Ines and Tomás agreeing to write "card n of 5" and to ask for missing cards. Precise: A set of rules that sender and receiver both follow: what a message looks like, in what order things are sent, and what to do when something goes wrong. Source: D1 of F0-09 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Packet, Code (for information). Chapters: F0-09.
Pseudo-random number generator
Simple words: A recipe that produces numbers that look random. Analogy: A very long, fixed shuffled list of numbers that you start reading at some place. Precise: An algorithm that produces a sequence of numbers from a starting value (the seed); the same seed gives the same sequence, as R3 shows with seed 2026. This course uses std::mt19937 with std::uniform_int_distribution. Source: R3 of F0-38, D2 of F0-38 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Seed. Chapters: F0-38.
Pseudo-random test vectors
Simple words: test inputs that look random but come from a formula, so the same list appears every run. Analogy: a tasting list drawn by lottery, but from a lottery whose draw can be repeated exactly. Precise: inputs produced by a deterministic generator from a fixed seed; used when exhaustive testing is too large; the run is repeatable because the seed is fixed. Source: D5, R4 of F1-14 (pending verification). Related: Reference model, Exhaustive test. Chapters: F1-14.
Pull-up and pull-down network
Simple words: the switches that connect the output to 1 (pull-up) or to 0 (pull-down). Analogy: the taps between the sink and the roof tank (pull-up), and between the sink and the drain (pull-down). Precise: in a CMOS gate, the pull-up network joins the output to the supply rail and the pull-down network joins it to ground; their switch patterns are complements of each other. Source: D2 of F1-09 (pending verification). Related: CMOS, Floating (Z) and short (X). Chapters: F1-09, F1-10.
Push button
Simple words: A switch that is on only while you press it. Analogy: A doorbell button. Precise: A momentary switch: a spring returns its contacts to their rest position when released. Source: D1 of F0-41 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Switch, Toggle. Chapters: F0-41.
Quotient
Simple words: The answer when you divide: how many in each share, or how many shares. Analogy: How many full cars of four children you can make. Precise: The result of division; in whole-number division 23 ÷ 4 has quotient 5 and remainder 3. Source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Remainder, Rounding up. Chapters: F0-12, F0-16.
Range-based for loop
Simple words: A for loop that visits every element of a list, one by one, without an index. Analogy: Walking along the shelf and looking into each jar in turn. Precise: for (int score : scores) { ... } runs the block once for each element, with the loop variable holding that element (R2). Source: R2 of F0-35, D1 of F0-35 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: for loop, std::vector. Chapters: F0-35.
RC circuit
Simple words: a resistor and a capacitor together, used to make a delay. Analogy: the rubber-wall tank filled through a narrow pipe. [proposed mapping, awaiting registration in guide 8.1; see HW101 NOTES.md] Precise: a circuit in which a capacitor charges or discharges through a resistance, so its voltage changes gradually rather than at once. Source: D2 of F1-05 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Capacitor, Capacitance, Time constant (τ). Chapters: F1-05.
Reading
Simple words: One number the program gets from a sensor at one moment. Analogy: One look at the thermometer. Precise: A single sampled value of a sensor's output, in units stated by its datasheet (or, in the course simulator, made-up units). Source: R1 of F0-43 (lab run in this build). Related: Sensor, Noise. Chapters: F0-43, F9-02.
Reference model
Simple words: a second, simpler description of what the answer should be, used to check the circuit. Analogy: the head chef's recipe card that the tasting checks against. Precise: an independent implementation of the specification (here, integer arithmetic in the testbench) whose outputs are compared with the design under test for every applied vector. Source: D1, D2 of F1-14 (pending verification). Related: Exhaustive test, Pseudo-random test vectors. Chapters: F1-14.
Register
Simple words: A tiny place inside the CPU that holds a number it is working on right now. Analogy: The chef's hands and the cutting board. Precise: A small, very fast storage place inside the processor that holds one value; instructions work on values in registers. Source: D1 of F0-05 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: CPU (central processing unit). Chapters: F0-05.
Remainder
Simple words: What is left over when things do not share out exactly. Analogy: The three children still waiting after five cars are full. Precise: For whole numbers a and b (b not zero), the r with a = quotient × b + r and 0 ≤ r < b; 23 = 5 × 4 + 3. C++ computes it with %. Source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Quotient, Rounding up. Chapters: F0-12, F0-16, F0-21.
Remainder operator
Simple words: The % sign: it gives what is left over after a whole-number division. Analogy: The egg that does not fit in the boxes. Precise: The operator % on integers; 7 % 2 printed 1 in this build (R2). Source: R2 of F0-31, D1 of F0-31 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Integer division. Chapters: F0-31.
Resistance
Simple words: how strongly a part holds back the current. Analogy: how narrow a pipe in the restaurant's plumbing is. Precise: the ratio of the voltage across a part to the current through it, R = V ÷ I; measured in ohms (Ω). Source: D2 of F1-02 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D3 of F1-02 (BIPM, "The International System of Units (SI)") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Ohm (Ω), Ohm's law, Resistor. Chapters: F0-39, F0-40, F1-02, F1-03.
Resistor
Simple words: a part made to have a known resistance. Analogy: a pipe section deliberately made narrow. Precise: a two-terminal component manufactured with a stated nominal resistance, a tolerance and a power rating (values from its datasheet). Source: D1 of F1-02 (Platt, "Make: Electronics"); D4 of F1-02 (datasheets/manual of the kit chosen by the owner) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Resistance, Ohm (Ω), Ohm's law. Chapters: F0-40, F0-41, F1-02.
Return value
Simple words: The answer a function gives back to the code that called it. Analogy: The sauce the helper hands back when the sauce recipe is done. Precise: The value given by a return statement; a function whose return type is not void must return a value, and g++ refused one that did not (R3). Source: R1 of F0-34, R3 of F0-34, D1 of F0-34 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Function, void. Chapters: F0-34, F0-38.
Ripple-carry adder
Simple words: a multi-bit adder made by chaining full adders, each passing its carry to the next. Analogy: the row of counting boards, with the runner's token travelling from right to left. Precise: an N-bit adder of N full adders in which the carry out of bit i is the carry in of bit i + 1; the carry may have to pass ("ripple") through every bit. Source: D2, R1 of F1-14 (pending verification). Related: Full adder, Critical path, Propagation delay. Chapters: F1-14, F1-15.
Robot
Simple words: A machine with a computer inside that senses the world and moves in it by itself. Analogy: A body with senses, a brain and muscles. Precise: A machine that uses sensors, a computer running a program, and actuators to act in the physical world, following that program rather than direct moment-by-moment human control. Source: D1 of F0-10 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Sensor, Actuator, Control loop, Drone. Chapters: F0-10, F9-01.
Root cause
Simple words: The real reason behind the symptom. Analogy: The swapped jar labels. Precise: The underlying fault that, once fixed, makes the symptom go away and stay away. Source: D1 of F0-08 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Symptom. Chapters: F0-08.
Rounding
Simple words: Swapping a number for a nearby friendly one. Analogy: Saying "about 90 grains" when you counted 87. Precise: Replacing a number by the nearest multiple of 10 (or 100, 1,000, ...); in this university a number exactly halfway rounds up (45 → 50). Source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Estimate, Rounding up. Chapters: F0-12.
Rounding up
Simple words: Taking the next whole number when anything is left over, so that everything fits. Analogy: One more car for the last three children. Precise: The smallest whole number of groups of size b that holds a items; with whole-number division, (a + b − 1) ÷ b. Also called ceiling division. It is the number of blocks in a GPU launch (F6). Source: D1 of F0-12; R1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Quotient, Remainder, Bounds check. Chapters: F0-12, F0-11, F0-15, F0-18, F0-19.
Router
Simple words: A box that passes packets along towards where they are going. Analogy: A post office that sorts postcards and sends each one onwards. Precise: A network device that receives packets and forwards each one towards its destination address. Source: D1 of F0-09 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Network, Packet. Chapters: F0-09.
Safety limit (step limit)
Simple words: a rule that stops the robot after too many rounds, even if the job is not done. Analogy: "I have gone much too far, I will stop and call home." Precise: a maximum number of loop iterations (or a maximum time) after which the program stops on purpose, so that a wrong rule cannot make the robot run forever. Source: R2 of F9-04 (pending verification). Related: Loop, Emergency stop. Chapters: F9-04.
Sample (of a sound)
Simple words: One measurement of a sound at one moment. Analogy: One frame of a flip book. Precise: A number that records the level of a sound wave at one instant; a recording is a long list of samples taken at regular times. Source: D1 of F0-03 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Code (for information). Chapters: F0-03.
Sampling and quantisation
Simple words: reading an analog voltage at moments in time and rounding it to one of a fixed set of steps. Analogy: Aiko writing down the thermometer every few minutes, to the nearest mark. Precise: sampling takes values at discrete times; quantisation maps each value to one of 2n codes for an n-bit converter (an analog-to-digital converter, ADC). Source: D2 of F1-08 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Signal, Analog signal, Digital signal. Chapters: F1-08.
Seed
Simple words: The starting number for a pseudo-random number generator. Analogy: The page where you start reading the shuffled list. Precise: The value given to a generator when it is created; with seed 2026 the game's secret was 22 in every recorded run of this build (R1, R3). Source: R1 of F0-38, R3 of F0-38 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Pseudo-random number generator. Chapters: F0-38.
Select input
Simple words: the input that says which choice to make, written as a binary number. Analogy: the order number on the ticket. Precise: the control inputs of a multiplexer or decoder; with n select bits there are 2n choices. Source: D2 of F1-12 (pending verification). Related: Multiplexer (mux), Decoder. Chapters: F1-12.
Sense–think–act
Simple words: the three jobs a robot does over and over: notice, decide, do. Analogy: Amara noticing the bend, deciding to steer, and steering. Precise: a way to describe a robot's work as a repeating cycle of measuring (sense), computing a decision (think) and commanding its actuators (act). Source: D2 of F9-01 (pending verification). Related: Robot, Loop, Control loop. Chapters: F9-01, F9-04.
Sensor
Simple words: A part that measures something about the world, like light or heat, and turns it into a number. Analogy: One of your senses. Precise: A device that responds to a physical quantity (light, temperature, sound, movement) and produces a signal that the computer can read as a value. Source: D3 of F0-06 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Input, Actuator. Chapters: F0-06, F0-10, F0-43, F0-45, F9-01, F9-02.
Sensor noise
Simple words: small random wobbles in a sensor's readings. Analogy: the line looking slightly different every time a cloud moves. Precise: the part of a measurement that differs from the true value in ways that change from reading to reading; real sensors always have some. Source: D3 of F9-02 (pending verification). Related: Reading, Calibrate. Chapters: F9-02.
Series
Simple words: parts connected one after another, so the same current passes through all of them. Analogy: Mr Okafor's way one: one pipe through the sink tap and then the dishwasher valve. Precise: components connected end to end with no branch between them, so they carry the same current; their voltages add. Source: D2 of F1-04 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Parallel, Node, Equivalent resistance. Chapters: F0-41, F1-04.
Series and parallel (switches)
Simple words: series means one after another, so all must be on; parallel means side by side, so any one is enough. Analogy: two taps on one pipe, one after the other, or two pipes joined side by side. Precise: switches in series conduct only if every switch conducts (an AND of their conditions); switches in parallel conduct if at least one conducts (an OR). Source: D2, D3 of F1-10 (pending verification). Related: CMOS, NAND gate, NOR gate. Chapters: F1-10.
Settle
Simple words: to stop changing and show the final answer. Analogy: the moment the last cook puts down the spoon. Precise: a combinational output has settled when, after an input change, no further change will happen until the inputs change again; before that it may show wrong intermediate values. Source: W1, R2 of F1-15 (pending verification). Related: Propagation delay, Glitch (hazard). Chapters: F1-15.
Shift
Simple words: Sliding all the bits left or right by some places. Analogy: Moving every light's setting a few rooms along the panel; settings that fall off the end are lost, and empty places get "off". Precise: x << n moves the bits of x n places left (multiplying an unsigned value by 2 while it fits); x >> n moves them n places right (dividing an unsigned value by 2, dropping the remainder). Source: W1 of F0-25 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); R1 of F0-25 (lab run in this build). Related: Mask, Bit field. Chapters: F0-25.
Short circuit
Simple words: a path with almost no resistance straight across a source. Analogy: a burst pipe that lets the tank empty at once. Precise: an unintended low-resistance connection between two points at different potentials, which lets a large current flow; the current is limited only by the source's internal resistance and the wiring. Source: D1 of F1-03 (Platt, "Make: Electronics"); D2 of F1-03 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Energy, Power, Dissipation. Chapters: F0-44, F0-46, F1-03.
Sign bit
Simple words: The leftmost bit, which tells you if a signed number is negative. Analogy: The leftmost switch, now worth −128 instead of +128. Precise: in two's complement, the most significant bit; it is 1 exactly when the value is negative. Source: W1 of F0-24 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter). Related: Two's complement, Most significant bit (MSB). Chapters: F0-24.
Signal
Simple words: a voltage that changes over time to carry information. Analogy: any message reaching Aiko: the needle's position or the bell's ringing. Precise: a quantity, here a voltage, whose variation in time represents information. Source: D2 of F1-08 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Analog signal, Digital signal, Threshold. Chapters: F1-08.
Signed
Simple words: A number that can be negative or positive. Analogy: The counter read with Jonas's agreement: 999 means −1. Precise: an integer type that can represent negative values; in C++, std::int8_t is a signed 8-bit type holding −128 to 127. Source: R1 of F0-24 (lab run in this build); D1 of F0-24 (title only, pending verification). Related: Unsigned, Two's complement, Sign bit. Chapters: F0-24.
Simulator
Simple words: A program that pretends to be the real world, so you can test a robot safely. Analogy: Practising a dance in your room before the show. Precise: Software that models a robot and its surroundings well enough to run the robot's program and observe what would happen, without real hardware. Source: D1 of F0-10 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Robot. Chapters: F0-10, F0-40, F0-42, F0-45, F9-01, F9-06, F9-07.
Slope
Simple words: How much the output changes when the input goes up by 1. Analogy: How many centimetres the robot moves each second. Precise: For y = mx + c, the number m; between two points, (change in y) ÷ (change in x). It can be negative. Source: D1 of F0-18 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Graph, Function. Chapters: F0-18.
Solution
Simple words: The number that makes an equation true. Analogy: The count that, put in every bag, keeps the beam level. Precise: A value of the unknown for which both sides of the equation have the same value; x = 4 solves 3x + 2 = 14. Source: D1 of F0-17 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Equation, Substitute. Chapters: F0-17.
Sorting
Simple words: Putting things in order, like smallest to biggest. Analogy: Lining up cards in your hand from low to high. Precise: Rearranging a list so that each item is no bigger than the next one (or no smaller, for the other direction). Source: D2 of F0-04 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Comparison, Swap, Sorting network. Chapters: F0-04.
Sorting network
Simple words: A fixed plan of "compare these two, swap if needed" stations that always sorts. Analogy: A chalk path on the floor where people meet at boxes, compare, and step left or right. Precise: A fixed sequence of compare-and-swap operations on fixed positions, chosen so that any starting order comes out sorted. Source: R1 of F0-04 (lab run in this build: all 24 starting orders sorted); the name itself is pending an algorithms textbook in the registry. Related: Sorting, Comparison. Chapters: F0-04.
Source code
Simple words: The text of a program, written by a person in a programming language. Analogy: The recipe written in your own handwriting on a card. Precise: The human-readable text of a program, stored in files such as hello.cpp; the compiler reads it and either reports errors or produces an executable. Source: R1 of F0-29, D1 of F0-29 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Compiler, Program. Chapters: F0-29.
Speed limit
Simple words: the fastest the robot is allowed to go, whatever its program asks for. Analogy: riding slowly near the playground. Precise: an upper bound applied to every motor command before it is sent, so that no part of the program can command a faster speed. Source: R1 of F9-07, S1 of F9-07 (pending verification). Related: Emergency stop, Motor command. Chapters: F9-07.
Statement
Simple words: One instruction in a program. In C++ most statements end with a semicolon. Analogy: One step of the recipe. Precise: A single instruction inside a function body, such as std::cout << "Hello"; statements run one after another, from top to bottom, unless a statement such as if or a loop changes the order. Source: R2 of F0-29, D1 of F0-29 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Program. Chapters: F0-29, F0-30, F0-36.
Status flags (Z, N, C, V)
Simple words: extra one-bit outputs that report facts about the result: is it zero, is it negative, did the addition carry out, did it overflow? Analogy: the four lamps on the station's panel. Precise: Z = 1 when every result bit is 0; N = the top bit of the result (its sign in two's complement); C = the carry out of the top bit for ADD and SUB; V = 1 when a signed (two's complement) ADD or SUB gives a result outside the range of N bits. Source: D2, R3 of F1-14 (pending verification). Related: Overflow (signed), ALU (arithmetic logic unit). Chapters: F1-14.
std::array
Simple words: A list with a fixed number of values. Analogy: An egg box: always the same number of places. Precise: The standard library container from <array> whose size is part of its type, for example std::array<std::string, 3> (R3). Source: R3 of F0-35, D1 of F0-35 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: std::vector. Chapters: F0-35.
std::cin
Simple words: The name C++ uses for "read what the person types". Analogy: The cook listening to an order. Precise: The standard input stream from <iostream>; the operator >> reads a value into a variable. In the lab runs the input comes from a .in file instead of a keyboard. Source: R3 of F0-30, D1 of F0-30 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: std::cout, Variable. Chapters: F0-30.
std::cout
Simple words: The name C++ uses for "print this on the screen". Analogy: The cook calling out loud what is happening. Precise: The standard output stream from the header <iostream>; the operator << sends text and numbers to it, and the run log captures what it printed. Source: R1 of F0-29, D1 of F0-29 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: String literal, Newline. Chapters: F0-29, F0-30.
std::string
Simple words: The type for a piece of text, like a name or a sentence. Analogy: A string of fridge-magnet letters in a row. Precise: The standard library type from <string> that holds a sequence of characters; it can be joined with + and knows its length through size() (R1, R4). Source: R1 of F0-31, R4 of F0-31, D1 of F0-31 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: char, String literal. Chapters: F0-31.
std::vector
Simple words: A list of values of the same type that can grow. Analogy: A row of numbered jars on a shelf, and you can add more jars at the end. Precise: The standard library container from <vector> that stores elements in order; size() gives the number of elements and push_back adds one at the end (R1). Source: R1 of F0-35, D1 of F0-35 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Element, Index, std::array. Chapters: F0-35.
Step
Simple words: Running exactly one more line of the program, then pausing again. Analogy: Doing one recipe step and freezing again. Precise: gdb's next runs one line and treats a function call as one line ("proceeding through subroutine calls"); step goes into the called function (R3, R5). Source: R3 of F0-37, R5 of F0-37, D2 of F0-37 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Debugger, Breakpoint. Chapters: F0-37.
Storage
Simple words: Where files and programs are kept, even when the computer is off. Analogy: The warehouse across town. Precise: A device such as an SSD (solid-state drive) or a hard disk that keeps data without power; it is larger and slower to reach than main memory. Source: D3 of F0-05 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Main memory. Chapters: F0-05.
String literal
Simple words: Text written inside double quotes in your program. Analogy: Words copied exactly onto a label. Precise: A sequence of characters between double quotes in source code, such as "Hello, world!\n"; the program uses it exactly as written. Source: R1 of F0-29, D1 of F0-29 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: std::string, Newline. Chapters: F0-29.
Structural description
Simple words: describing a circuit by listing its parts and how they are wired, not by writing a formula. Analogy: a floor plan showing every pipe and tap, instead of a sentence saying "the sink fills when…". Precise: an HDL description built from instances of gates or modules connected by named wires; the opposite style, describing what the output should be, is called behavioural. Source: D2, D5 of F1-11 (pending verification). Related: Hardware description language (HDL), Netlist. Chapters: F1-11.
Substitute
Simple words: Put a number in place of a letter. Analogy: Dropping counters into the labelled jar. Precise: Replace each occurrence of a variable by a given value (in brackets if needed) and evaluate with the order of operations. Source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Expression, Solution. Chapters: F0-16, F0-17.
Sum
Simple words: The answer when you add. Analogy: Putting two piles of rice together into one pile. Precise: The result of addition; 12 is the sum of 7 and 5. Source: D1 of F0-12 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Difference. Chapters: F0-12.
Sum bit and carry bit
Simple words: when you add one column, the sum bit is the digit you write down and the carry bit is what you pass to the next column. Analogy: Hana's board after the flip (sum) and the runner's token (carry). Precise: for inputs whose total in one column is T (0 to 3), the sum bit is T mod 2 and the carry bit is T div 2 (integer division). Source: W1, D3 of F1-13 (pending verification). Related: Half adder, Full adder. Chapters: F1-13.
Supervision
Simple words: A responsible adult is with you, watching, the whole time. Analogy: An adult staying in the kitchen while the stove is on. Precise: In this university, an adult present for every physical activity at levels L0–L2, able to stop the activity at once. Source: S1 of F0-46: University Authoring Guide, Honesty first and 5.5 (opened in this build). Related: Checklist. Chapters: F0-40, F0-46, F9-07.
Swap
Simple words: Two things change places. Analogy: Two children in a line trading spots. Precise: Exchanging the values in two positions of a list. Source: D2 of F0-04 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Sorting. Chapters: F0-04.
Switch
Simple words: A part that opens or closes a gap in a circuit. Analogy: A tap on a pipe (careful: a closed switch lets current through, a closed tap stops water). Precise: A component with contacts that connect (closed) or disconnect (open) a conducting path. Source: D1 of F0-41 (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Push button, Series, Parallel. Chapters: F0-41, F0-40.
Symptom
