Simple words: What you notice is wrong. Analogy: "the bread is flat and salty". Precise: An observable sign of a fault, such as wrong output, a crash or a program that never ends; it is not the cause itself. Source: D1 of F0-08 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Root cause, Bug. Chapters: F0-08.
Synthesis tool
Simple words: a program that turns a circuit description into a list of gates. Analogy: a head chef who reads "make soup for twelve" and writes the exact steps and tools. Precise: software that translates an HDL description into a netlist of cells from a target library (here, NAND and NOT cells), usually trying to reduce some cost. Source: D6, D2 of F1-11 (pending verification). Related: Netlist, Structural description. Chapters: F1-11.
Target (setpoint)
Simple words: where you want to be. Analogy: right on the chalk line. Precise: the desired value of the controlled quantity; here, a distance from the line of zero. Engineers call it the setpoint. Source: D1 of F9-05 (pending verification). Related: Error (control), Control loop. Chapters: F9-05.
Term
Simple words: One piece of an expression that is added or taken away. Analogy: One line of a recipe. Precise: A product of a number (its coefficient) and variables, such as 3n; in 3n + 2 the terms are 3n and 2. Source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Like terms, Expression. Chapters: F0-16.
Test
Simple words: A small try that checks if something works. Analogy: Tasting a pinch from each jar. Precise: Running a program (or part of it) with chosen inputs and comparing what it does with what it should do. Source: D1 of F0-08 (pending verification: title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Debugging. Chapters: F0-08.
Test function
Simple words: A function that checks other functions by comparing their answers with answers you worked out by hand. Analogy: Tasting the sauce before you serve it. Precise: A function that calls the code under test with known inputs, compares the results with expected values, reports PASS or FAIL and counts failures (R2). Source: R2 of F0-34 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Function. Chapters: F0-34, F0-38.
Test run
Simple words: trying the program to see if it does what you wanted. Analogy: tracing the route on the map with your finger. Precise: an execution of a program with known inputs whose output is compared with the expected result. Source: R1 of F9-06 (pending verification). Related: Simulator, Log (trace). Chapters: F9-06.
Threshold
Simple words: the line between "counts as LOW" and "counts as HIGH". Analogy: how hard the rope must be pulled before the bell rings. Precise: the input voltage at which a digital input's interpretation changes; real logic families specify ranges guaranteed to be read as LOW or HIGH in their datasheets. Source: D2 of F1-08 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D4 of F1-08 (datasheets/manual of the kit chosen by the owner) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Signal, Analog signal, Digital signal. Chapters: F0-43, F0-45, F1-08, F9-02.
Time constant (τ)
Simple words: the "speed setting" of an RC circuit: bigger means slower. Analogy: how long the tank takes to fill most of the way. [proposed mapping, awaiting registration in guide 8.1; see HW101 NOTES.md] Precise: τ = R × C, in seconds when R is in ohms and C in farads; after one τ a charging capacitor has covered 1 − e−1 ≈ 63.2 % of the way to the supply voltage. Source: D2 of F1-05 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); R1 of F1-05 (lab run in this build) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Capacitor, Capacitance, RC circuit. Chapters: F1-05, F1-08.
Timing diagram
Simple words: a picture of signals changing over time, one row per signal. Analogy: the kitchen's order log with a time for every step. Precise: a plot of signal values against time; high and low levels for single bits, and labelled segments for multi-bit values (buses). Source: D2 of F1-15 (pending verification). Related: Propagation delay, Glitch (hazard). Chapters: F1-15.
Toggle
Simple words: Change to the other state: on becomes off, off becomes on. Analogy: Pressing the hallway light switch once more. Precise: An operation that inverts a two-state value; here it happens once per new button press. Source: R1 of F0-41 (lab run in this build). Related: Push button. Chapters: F0-41.
Tolerance
Simple words: how far a real part may be from the number written on it. Analogy: pipes from the same shop are never exactly the same width. Precise: the maximum allowed difference between the actual and nominal value, usually given as a percentage in the datasheet. Source: D2 of F1-02 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D4 of F1-02 (datasheets/manual of the kit chosen by the owner) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Resistance, Ohm (Ω), Ohm's law. Chapters: F1-02.
Toolchain
Simple words: The set of programs you use to turn source code into a running program. Analogy: Your kitchen tools: the same recipe needs the right pots and an oven. Precise: The compiler and the programs that work with it (and, in F0-37, the debugger). This course records the exact versions the tools print, for example "g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0". Source: R4 of F0-29, D2 of F0-29 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Compiler, Debugger. Chapters: F0-29, F0-37.
Trace
Simple words: Extra printed lines that show what the program is doing, step by step. Analogy: The cook saying each step out loud while cooking. Precise: Output added only for debugging, such as [trace] i = 3, which shows the order of events and the values of variables (R2). Source: R2 of F0-37 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Debugger. Chapters: F0-37.
Transistor
Simple words: a tiny electrical switch with no moving parts, turned on and off by a voltage. Analogy: a tap in the building's plumbing, opened by a small control valve. Precise: a semiconductor device with three terminals in which the voltage on one terminal controls the current between the other two; in digital logic it is used as an on/off switch. Source: D2, D3 of F1-09 (pending verification). Related: nMOS and pMOS, CMOS, Gate, source, drain (of a transistor). Chapters: F0-44, F1-09.
Truth table
Simple words: A table that lists every combination of inputs and the result. Analogy: A chart on the fridge: if this and that, then …. Precise: A table giving the output of a logic function for every combination of its inputs. Source: D4 of F0-41: Petzold, "Code" (pending verification; title only, dossier gate G1 open). Related: Series, Parallel. Chapters: F0-26, F0-27, F0-41.
Two's complement
Simple words: The usual rule for writing negative numbers in binary. Analogy: Going backwards from 000 on the counter. Precise: an n-bit representation where the most significant bit has place value −2 and all others are positive; −x is written as the pattern of 2 − x, found by inverting all bits of x and adding 1. Source: W1 of F0-24 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); D1 of F0-24 (title only, pending verification). Related: Signed, Sign bit, Wrap-around. Chapters: F0-24.
Type
Simple words: The kind of value a variable can hold: whole number, decimal, true/false, letter or text. Analogy: The shape of a jar: an egg box holds eggs, a bottle holds liquids. Precise: The property of a variable or value that decides which values it can hold and which operations work on it, for example int, double, bool, char and std::string. Source: R1 of F0-31, D1 of F0-31 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: int, double, bool, char, std::string. Chapters: F0-31.
Unknown
Simple words: The number you are trying to find. Analogy: The marbles hidden inside one closed bag. Precise: A variable in an equation whose value is to be determined, often called x. Source: D1 of F0-17 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Equation, Variable (maths). Chapters: F0-17.
Unsigned
Simple words: A number that can never be below zero. Analogy: The bicycle counter read plainly: 000 to 999. Precise: an integer type whose bit pattern is read with all place values positive; with 8 bits it holds 0 to 255. In C++, std::uint8_t is an unsigned 8-bit type. Source: R1 of F0-24 (lab run in this build); D1 of F0-24 (title only, pending verification). Related: Signed, Two's complement. Chapters: F0-24.
Variable
Simple words: A named place that holds a value, which can change while the program runs. Analogy: A labelled jar: the label is the name, the contents are the value. Precise: A named object with a type, for example int apples = 3; reading the name gives its current value, and assignment replaces the value. Source: R1 of F0-30, D1 of F0-30 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Type, Assignment, Declaration. Chapters: F0-30, F0-31.
Variable (maths)
Simple words: A letter or name that stands for a number. Analogy: A labelled jar: the label is the name, the counters inside are the number. Precise: A symbol such as n that represents a number, either one not yet known or any number from a range. Not the same as a variable in a program (KID102 F0-30), which is a named storage place whose contents can change. Source: D1 of F0-16 (pending verification; arithmetic checked by the chapter's number-check run). Related: Expression, Unknown, Formula. Chapters: F0-16, F0-17.
void
Simple words: The word for "this function gives nothing back". Analogy: A step like "boil the water" that does not hand you anything. Precise: The return type of a function that returns no value, such as void boil_water(). Source: R1 of F0-34, D1 of F0-34 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Return value. Chapters: F0-34.
Voltage
Simple words: the push that makes charge move, measured between two points. Analogy: the difference in water pressure between two places in the plumbing. Precise: the potential difference between two points: the energy given to (or taken from) each coulomb of charge that moves between them; measured in volts (V), where one volt is one joule per coulomb. Source: D2 of F1-01 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics"); D3 of F1-01 (BIPM, "The International System of Units (SI)") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Charge, Current, Potential. Chapters: F0-39, F0-40, F0-42, F1-01, F1-02.
Voltage divider
Simple words: two resistors in series that give a smaller voltage from their middle point. Analogy: a tap halfway down a pipe gives part of the full pressure. Precise: a series pair R1, R2 across Vin whose junction has Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2) when nothing draws current from the junction. Source: D2 of F1-04 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Series, Parallel, Node. Chapters: F1-04.
Voltmeter
Simple words: a tool that shows the voltage between its two probes. Analogy: the plumber's pressure gauge with two hoses. Precise: an instrument (often one mode of a multimeter, F1-07) that displays the potential of its red probe minus the potential of its black probe. Source: D1 of F1-01 (Platt, "Make: Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Charge, Current, Voltage. Chapters: F1-01.
Voltmeter (in parallel)
Simple words: the voltage mode: probes touch the two ends of a part. Analogy: the pressure gauge's two hoses on two joints. Precise: a voltage measurement is made with the meter connected in parallel with the part; an ideal voltmeter draws no current; a real one has a large but finite input resistance. Source: D2 of F1-07 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Multimeter, Ammeter (in series), Ohmmeter. Chapters: F1-07.
V–I graph
Simple words: a drawing of voltage against current for a part. Analogy: Aiko's table of pressure and cups per minute, drawn as dots. Precise: a plot of the voltage across a part against the current through it; for an ohmic part the points lie on a straight line through the origin whose slope is R. Source: D2 of F1-02 (Horowitz and Hill, "The Art of Electronics") — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open). Related: Resistance, Ohm (Ω), Ohm's law. Chapters: F1-02.
Warning
Simple words: A message from the compiler that says "this is allowed, but it looks like a mistake". Analogy: The helper saying: "You bought pears but never used them. Did you mean to?" Precise: A diagnostic about legal but suspicious code, enabled by flags such as -Wall and -Wextra; with -Werror ("Treat all warnings as errors", R7) every warning stops the build (R5). Source: R5 of F0-36, R7 of F0-36, D2 of F0-36 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Compiler error. Chapters: F0-36.
while loop
Simple words: A loop that checks its condition before every round, and stops when it is false. Analogy: "While the timer is above zero, wait one more second." Precise: while (condition) { ... } evaluates the condition before each iteration and runs the block only while it is true (R2). Source: R2 of F0-33, D1 of F0-33 (R = lab run in this build; D = book or manual cited by title only, pending verification at dossier gate G1). Related: Loop, Condition. Chapters: F0-33, F0-38.
Word
Simple words: The size of number a computer likes to work with in one go. Analogy: How many rows of switches the house's control panel flips at once. Precise: a machine-dependent group of bytes that a processor handles as one unit; its size is set by the processor's architecture manual, not by a universal rule. Source: D1 of F0-23 (title only, pending verification). Related: Byte. Chapters: F0-23.
Wrap-around
Simple words: Going past the end of the numbers and coming back at the other end. Analogy: The counter going from 999 to 000, or from 000 back to 999. Precise: arithmetic modulo 2: a result that does not fit in n bits keeps only its low n bits. It is one form of overflow (F0-20). Source: W1 of F0-24 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); R1 of F0-24 (lab run in this build). Related: Overflow, Two's complement. Chapters: F0-24.
XNOR
Simple words: the opposite of XOR: 1 when the inputs are equal. Analogy: a "same?" checker for two switches. Precise: y = NOT (a XOR b); truth table 1, 0, 0, 1. Source: W1 of F1-11 (pending verification). Related: XOR (exclusive OR). Chapters: F1-11.
XOR (exclusive OR)
Simple words: True when the two inputs are different. Analogy: The stair light: flipping either switch changes the lamp. Precise: the two-input Boolean function with output 1 exactly when the inputs differ; for bool values in C++, a != b, and bitwise ^. Source: W1 of F0-26 (worked arithmetic shown in the chapter); R1 of F0-26 (lab run in this build). Related: OR, Parity, Truth table. Chapters: F0-26.

Seeded from the Systems Curriculum (section 20) — needs verification

ACPI
Advanced Configuration and Power Interface: tables and bytecode through which firmware describes the platform and its power management to the OS. needs verification
ACS / AER / DPC
PCI Express Access Control Services (which devices may talk to each other directly), Advanced Error Reporting, and Downstream Port Containment (isolating a failed link). needs verification
AHCI
Advanced Host Controller Interface: the standard register interface for SATA controllers. needs verification
ALSA / ASoC
Linux's sound architecture and its System-on-Chip layer, which splits SoC audio into codec, CPU interface (I2S) and machine drivers. needs verification
AML / ASL
ACPI Machine Language (bytecode in the DSDT/SSDTs) and ACPI Source Language (its human-readable form). needs verification
AP / BSP
Application processor / bootstrap processor: the BSP runs firmware and early kernel code; APs are started later. needs verification
APIC, local APIC, IOAPIC, x2APIC
x86 interrupt controllers: one local APIC per CPU (timer, IPIs, interrupt acceptance), IOAPICs routing device interrupts, x2APIC as the MSR-based mode of the local APIC. needs verification
APLIC / IMSIC
The two parts of the RISC-V Advanced Interrupt Architecture: a wired-interrupt controller and a per-hart controller for message-signalled interrupts. needs verification
BAR
Base Address Register: PCI configuration field giving the address range of a device's registers or memory. needs verification
BDS
Boot Device Selection, the UEFI PI phase that chooses and launches a boot option. needs verification
Bank conflict
Two or more threads of a warp/wavefront accessing different addresses in the same shared-memory/LDS bank, which serializes the accesses. needs verification
BL31 / BL32 / BL33
Trusted Firmware-A stage names: the EL3 runtime, the secure payload (for example OP-TEE) and the non-secure firmware (for example U-Boot). needs verification
Block cache
Kernel cache of disk blocks shared by file systems. needs verification
Boot ROM
Code fixed in an SoC at manufacture that runs first after reset and loads the next stage from a boot medium, often with a USB recovery mode. needs verification
Bus bandwidth (busbw)
The nccl-tests metric that normalizes collective throughput so that it can be compared with link bandwidth. needs verification
Cache-as-RAM
Using the CPU cache as memory before DRAM is initialized during early firmware. needs verification
CAN
Controller Area Network: a robust multi-drop bus used in vehicles and industry, standardised as ISO 11898. needs verification
CCID
The USB class for smart-card readers. needs verification
CDNA / RDNA
AMD's GPU architecture families for compute accelerators (Instinct) and for graphics (Radeon). needs verification
Class code
The three-byte PCI field (base class, subclass, programming interface) that says what kind of device a function is and, for standard interfaces, which programming model it follows. needs verification
Clean-room implementation
Reimplementation in which one party writes a specification from observation and another implements from that specification only. needs verification
Coalescing
Combining the memory accesses of a warp/wavefront into few wide transactions. needs verification
Collective
A communication operation involving a whole group of processes or GPUs (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter, broadcast). needs verification
Common clock framework
Linux's model of an SoC's clock tree (rates, parents, gating), the usual reference for clock drivers. needs verification
Compatible string
The devicetree property ("vendor,device", most specific first) used to match a device node to a driver. needs verification
Compute Unit (CU)
AMD's basic GPU core block, comparable to NVIDIA's SM. needs verification
Connection manager (USB4)
The software or firmware that discovers USB4 and Thunderbolt routers and sets up tunnels for PCIe, DisplayPort and USB 3. needs verification
coreboot
Open-source firmware that initializes hardware and then runs a payload (for example SeaBIOS, an EDK II payload or LinuxBoot). needs verification
CPPC
Collaborative Processor Performance Control: an ACPI interface through which the OS requests abstract performance levels from the platform. needs verification
cpufreq / cpuidle
Linux's frameworks for choosing CPU frequency and idle-state depth; good conceptual references for your own power management. needs verification
CPUID / MIDR / misa
The CPU identification mechanisms of x86, Arm (Main ID Register) and RISC-V (machine ISA register, with mvendorid, marchid and mimpid). needs verification
Crash consistency
The property that a file system returns to a valid state, without losing synced data, after a power cut at any moment. needs verification
CRC32
The checksum used in GPT headers and partition arrays. needs verification
CSI-2 / DSI

DART

The identifier strings Windows builds from bus IDs (for example from PCI vendor and device IDs) and matches against INF files to choose a driver. needs verification

On this page: the design-log entry the agent opens for every new device (identification, tier, documents, design, tests, status). needs verification

A data structure describing hardware for platforms without ACPI, passed by firmware to the kernel. needs verification
DMA
Direct Memory Access: a device reading or writing memory without the CPU. needs verification

On this page: the 1–6 scale from "open class standard" to "locked" that predicts the effort a device will need (section 5.2). needs verification

The open-source reference implementation of UEFI and PI; OVMF is built from it. needs verification

ELF

EPT / NPT

Errata
A vendor's list of known deviations between hardware and its documentation, with workarounds (Intel "specification update", Arm "Software Developer Errata Notice"). needs verification

ARM64 privilege levels: user, kernel, hypervisor, secure monitor. needs verification
exFAT
Microsoft's FAT successor for large removable media; its specification was published openly in 2019. needs verification
ExitBootServices
The UEFI call by which the OS loader takes ownership of the machine; boot services are gone afterwards. needs verification

The USB recovery mode in Allwinner boot ROMs, used with the sunxi-tools. needs verification

An object signalled when the GPU finishes a piece of work, used for synchronization. needs verification

A C++ implementation without a hosted OS: only a minimal set of standard headers is guaranteed. needs verification
FullMAC / SoftMAC
Wi-Fi designs in which the 802.11 MAC layer runs in the chip's firmware (FullMAC) or in the host driver (SoftMAC). needs verification

Global Descriptor Table: x86 segment descriptors; in long mode mainly code/data privilege and the TSS. needs verification

Arm Generic Interrupt Controller. needs verification

GPUDirect P2P / RDMA
NVIDIA technologies for direct GPU-to-GPU transfers and for network adapters accessing GPU memory directly. needs verification
GSP

GuC / HuC / DMC
Firmware-driven microcontrollers in Intel GPUs: command submission scheduling, media authentication, and display power management. needs verification
H extension
The RISC-V hypervisor extension adding HS, VS and VU modes and G-stage translation. needs verification

A region of kernel virtual address space mapping all physical memory at a fixed offset. needs verification

AMD's C++ GPU programming interface, closely mirroring the CUDA runtime, part of ROCm. needs verification

Two-wire low-speed buses for sensors, EEPROMs and controllers; SMBus is a stricter subset of I2C, I3C a faster MIPI successor. needs verification

The Windows driver-package description listing supported hardware IDs, services and settings. needs verification

The C++ ABI used by GCC and Clang on x86-64, ARM64 (with small variations) and RISC-V: mangling, vtables, runtime support functions. needs verification

The standards body for memory (DDR, LPDDR, SPD), flash storage (eMMC, UFS) and related interfaces. needs verification

C libraries commonly ported to new operating systems (Linux-ABI oriented, embedded oriented, and designed for hobby systems respectively). needs verification

Story hook

Analogy

Maya wants to make a cheese sandwich. Her little brother Teo has never made one. So Maya writes the steps on a card: "Put butter and cheese on the bread."

Teo reads the card very carefully. He puts the butter dish on top of the bread bag. Then he puts the cheese on top of the butter dish. He did exactly what the card said! But it is not a sandwich.

Maya laughs and tries again. This time she writes small steps, one at a time. Open the bag. Take out one slice. Put it on the plate. Teo follows every step, and out comes a real sandwich.

A computer is like Teo on his very first day, every day. It does exactly what the steps say. It never guesses what you meant. This chapter is about writing steps so clear that even a computer gets them right.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain that a computer follows exact steps, one after another, and never guesses.
  • Write an algorithm in words that another person can follow without asking questions.
  • Test your algorithm by having someone follow it exactly, and fix the steps that fail.
  • Find a missing or wrong step by comparing the steps with the result.
  • Say where the "computer is a cook with a recipe" idea stops being true.
Jargon box
Computer
Simple words: a machine that follows a list of exact steps to work with information. Analogy: a cook who follows a recipe word for word. Precise: a machine that carries out a stored list of instructions, one at a time, on data such as numbers and letters. D1 D2
Instruction
Simple words: one single step that tells the machine to do one thing. Analogy: one line of a recipe, like "crack the egg". Precise: one command that a computer can carry out; a program is made of many of them. D2
Algorithm
Simple words: a list of clear steps that solves a problem, every time. Analogy: a recipe that always makes the same dish if you follow it exactly. Precise: a finite list of exact steps that, followed in order, solves a problem. It can be written in words, drawn, or written as a program. D1
Program
Simple words: an algorithm written in a language a computer can follow. Analogy: the recipe, translated into the cook's own language. Precise: a list of instructions written in a programming language, such as C++, that is turned into instructions the computer can carry out. D2 D3

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the big idea of this chapter. A recipe goes in at the left. The cook does one step at a time, in order. The result comes out at the right.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Think about the last time you followed a recipe. Each line told you one thing to do. You did the lines in order. If you skipped a line, the cake came out flat.

A computer works the same way. It gets a list of steps. Each step is called an instruction. The computer does the first instruction, then the next one, then the next. It never skips one, and it never adds one of its own. D1 D2

A list of clear steps that solves a problem is called an algorithm. A recipe for a sandwich is an algorithm. So are the steps for tying a shoe or brushing your teeth. You already know hundreds of algorithms. You never wrote them down.

Here is the hard part. People are clever at filling gaps. If a recipe says "add the egg", you know to crack it first. A computer does not know that. It will try to add the whole egg, shell and all. So the steps for a computer must be complete, exact and in the right order.

What makes a good step?

A good step does one thing. It uses words with one meaning. It says what to use and where to put it. "Put one slice of bread on the plate" is a good step. "Make it nice" is not, because nobody knows what "nice" means.

When you write an algorithm in a computer's language, it becomes a program. You will write real programs in KID102. In this course, you write algorithms in words first. That is how many programmers start, too: on paper.

How do you test an algorithm?

You give it to a friend. Your friend plays the computer. They must do exactly what the words say, and nothing else. They may not ask you questions. Where they get stuck, your algorithm has a gap. You fix that step and try again. That is the "be the robot" lab of this chapter.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Note

For the curious. A computer keeps its program in its memory, as a list of instructions. A part called the processor fetches one instruction, carries it out, and then moves on to the next one. This repeats very many times every second. D2 Some instructions say "jump to another step", which is how a program can repeat steps or choose between them. You will meet repeating and choosing in F0-07, and the parts inside the computer in F0-05.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

At this level, the deeper story is kept for later courses. In HW102 you will see how real instructions are coded as patterns of bits and carried out by circuits. The one idea to keep from today is that the machine does what is written, not what is meant. D2

How the hardware actually does it

Inside a computer, the instructions are stored as patterns of tiny on-and-off signals. You will learn this "light-switch alphabet" in F0-02. A part called the processor reads one instruction at a time and does what it says, very fast. It does not understand the goal of the program at all. It only follows the steps. D1 D2

Worked example

Ravi writes steps for pouring a glass of water. Let us test his first try, step by step, like a computer would.

Ravi's stepWhat a "literal" helper doesProblem?
1. Pour water.Stands still. Pour from what? Into what?Yes: says nothing about the jug or the glass.
2. Stop.Stops. But nothing happened in step 1.Yes: stop when?

Ravi fixes it. Now each step does one thing and says exactly what to use.

Ravi's better stepWhat the helper doesProblem?
1. Put an empty glass on the table.Puts the glass down.No.
2. Pick up the water jug by its handle.Holds the jug.No.
3. Tip the jug over the glass until the water is one finger from the top.Pours, watches, stops at the line.No: "one finger from the top" is clear.
4. Put the jug back on the table.Puts the jug down.No.

Notice step 3. It says when to stop. A good algorithm always says when a step is finished.

Code walk-through

You do not need to write code in this course. Real coding starts in KID102. But here is a peek: a tiny C++ program that prints a sandwich recipe, step by step, in order.

Listing 1 — recipe.cpp

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    const std::vector<std::string> steps = {
        "Open the bread bag.",
        "Take one slice and put it on the plate.",
        "Take a second slice and put it next to the first one.",
        "Spread butter on the first slice.",
        "Put one piece of cheese on the buttered slice.",
        "Put the second slice on top of the cheese.",
    };

    int number = 1;
    for (const std::string& step : steps) {
        std::cout << "Step " << number << ": " << step << '\n';
        number = number + 1;
    }
    std::cout << "Finished: " << steps.size() << " steps, done in order.\n";
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined recipe.cpp -o recipe, then run ./recipe.

Output of the real run in this build:

Step 1: Open the bread bag.
Step 2: Take one slice and put it on the plate.
Step 3: Take a second slice and put it next to the first one.
Step 4: Spread butter on the first slice.
Step 5: Put one piece of cheese on the buttered slice.
Step 6: Put the second slice on top of the cheese.
Finished: 6 steps, done in order.

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-01/recipe.out; run record recipe.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:31:28Z; exit code: 0.

LinesCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–3#include …Brings in ready-made tools: printing, text, and lists.The program can use them without writing them again. D3
5–6int main() and {Marks where the program starts.The computer always begins at main. D3
7–14const std::vector<std::string> steps = { … };Makes a list of six steps, written as text, in order.This is the recipe, stored inside the program.
16int number = 1;Starts a step counter at 1.So each printed step gets its number.
17for (const std::string& step : steps) {Goes through the list, one step at a time, from first to last.The order in the list is the order of the work. D3
18std::cout << "Step " << …Prints "Step", the number and the step's words.You can see each step being followed.
19number = number + 1;Adds one to the counter.The next step gets the next number.
20}Ends the repeated part.Everything between the braces is done once per step.
21std::cout << "Finished: " …Prints how many steps the list has.A last check that every step was used.
22–23return 0; and }Ends the program and reports "all fine".Zero means success to the computer. D3

Look at the output. The steps come out in exactly the order of the list. Try to predict: if you swapped two lines in the list, what would the output show?

Where the analogy breaks

  • A cook has common sense; a computer has none. A cook who reads "add the egg" cracks it first. A computer never fills a gap. It does only what the instructions say. D1
  • A cook can stop and ask. A cook can say "I don't understand step 3". A computer cannot ask what you meant. A wrong program still runs, and gives a wrong result.
  • A recipe is read once. A real computer can jump back and repeat steps, or skip steps when a test says so. Recipes rarely work like that. You will see this in F0-07. D2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Your friend stops and says "I can't do this step".A step uses a thing that is not there yet, like "spread butter" before the tub is open.Ask: what must be true before this step can work?Add the missing step before it.
The result is wrong, but every step was done.Two steps are in the wrong order.Act out the steps slowly. Watch where it first goes wrong.Swap the steps.
Two friends get two different results.A word with two meanings, like "a bit of cheese".Circle words that could mean more than one thing.Use exact words: "one slice of cheese".
Your friend never stops.A step does not say when it is finished, like "stir".Look for steps with no end.Say when to stop: "stir ten times".
Transition box

Where you came from: everyday life. You have followed recipes and instructions all your life, and you fill gaps without noticing. What carries over: the idea of steps done in order, and checking the result at the end. What changes: a computer never fills gaps, never asks, and never guesses, so every step must be written down exactly. D1 What comes next: F0-02 shows how a computer stores steps and information, using rows of on-and-off switches called bits.

Check yourself

  1. What does a computer do when a step is missing from its instructions? (a) It adds the step itself. (b) It asks you. (c) It does the steps it has, and nothing else.
  2. Which is a better step for a computer: "Make the bed nicely" or "Pull the blanket up to the pillow"? Why?
  3. What is the difference between an algorithm and a program?
  4. Explain in your own words why "add the egg" is a fine step for a person but a bad step for a computer.
  5. Apply it to a new case: write three exact steps for putting a sock on a foot.
  6. In Listing 1, if the list had "Spread butter" before "Open the bread bag", in which order would the program print them?
  7. Look at Figure 1. What does the dashed note say, and why does it matter?

Lab

Be the robot

Goal: write an algorithm in words that a friend can follow exactly, without asking you anything.

You need: paper, a pencil, a friend or family member, two cups and some dry beans or buttons. No computer is needed.

Safety

No sharp knives, hot water or stove in this lab. Use dry beans or buttons, not food you will eat. If young children are nearby, keep small items away from them.

  1. Put one cup with ten beans on the left. Put one empty cup on the right.
  2. Write steps that move exactly five beans into the right cup. Number every step.
  3. Give the paper to your friend. Your friend is now the robot. The robot does only what the words say. The robot may not ask questions. You may not talk.
  4. Watch. Make a mark next to any step where the robot got stuck or did something odd.
  5. Fix the marked steps. Try again. Repeat until the robot gets it right the first time.
  6. Swap roles. Now you are the robot for your friend's steps.

What you should see: the first try almost always fails somewhere. That is normal. Programmers fix their steps many times too.

Check you succeeded: a new person, who has not seen the lab, follows your steps once and ends with exactly five beans in the right cup.

If something goes wrong:

  • The robot picks up all the beans at once → your step did not say "one bean" → write "pick up one bean".
  • The robot keeps going after five → no step says when to stop → add "stop when you have moved five beans".
  • The robot laughs and guesses → remind them to act like a machine: only the words count.

Extension: change your steps so they work for any number of beans your friend chooses.

Forensic lab

The sandwich went wrong

Scenario. Our "literal cook" is a tiny program the university wrote for this lab. It reads steps and does exactly what each line says. If a step cannot be done, it does nothing for that step and moves on. Sami gave it his sandwich steps. He says: "The cook made the sandwich, but it is dry! There is no butter on it."

Questions.

  1. What is wrong with Sami's sandwich? Use the words of the evidence.
  2. Write down two ideas (guesses) about why it went wrong, before you decide.
  3. Which step is missing or wrong? Prove it by pointing at lines in the evidence.
  4. How would you fix Sami's steps?
  5. What could Sami do next time to find this kind of mistake sooner?

Method hints. Put the two lists of steps side by side. Find the first place where they are different. Then look at the last line of each "plate" description. Is there a clue there?

Mini-project

Pick something you do every morning, like packing your school bag. Write it as an algorithm of eight to fifteen steps. Test it with someone who does not know the task. Fix it until they succeed on the first try. Then draw your algorithm as boxes and arrows, like Figure 1.

Rubric (4 points): every step does one thing (1); words have one meaning (1); the tester succeeded with no questions (1); your drawing matches your steps (1).

Summary

  • A computer follows exact steps, one after another.
  • Each step is an instruction; a list of clear steps that solves a problem is an algorithm.
  • An algorithm written in a computer language is a program.
  • A computer never fills gaps, never asks and never guesses.
  • You test an algorithm by having someone follow it exactly.
  • When the result is wrong, compare the steps with the result to find the missing or wrong step.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. (c). It does the steps it has, and nothing else. (a) is wrong: a computer never adds steps. (b) is wrong: a computer cannot ask what you meant.
  2. "Pull the blanket up to the pillow." It says exactly what to do and when it is done. "Nicely" has no exact meaning.
  3. An algorithm is the list of clear steps, in any form, even in words. A program is an algorithm written in a language a computer can follow.
  4. Your own words. A good answer says: a person fills the gap and cracks the egg first; a computer does only what is written, so it would add the whole egg.
  5. One example: 1. Hold the sock open at its top with both hands. 2. Put your toes into the opening. 3. Pull the sock up over your heel until the heel part is on your heel. Any exact steps that work are right.
  6. In the order of the list: "Spread butter" first, then "Open the bread bag". The program prints the list in its order; it does not know that this order makes no sense.
  7. It says a missing step is never added. It matters because you must write every step yourself.

Forensic lab answer key

Root cause: the step "OPEN THE BUTTER TUB" is missing in Sami's steps. Without it, "DIP THE KNIFE IN THE BUTTER" cannot work, so the knife stays clean, and "SPREAD THE KNIFE ON THE FIRST SLICE" spreads nothing.

Evidence: Nadia's list has "OPEN THE BUTTER TUB" as step 4; Sami's list goes straight from the bread to "DIP THE KNIFE IN THE BUTTER". Sami's plate says "first slice has butter: no" and "butter tub left open: no". Nadia's says "yes" for both. The tub was never opened.

Fix: add "OPEN THE BUTTER TUB" before "DIP THE KNIFE IN THE BUTTER". Run the steps again and check that the plate says "first slice has butter: yes".

How the fault was made: the Lab Engineer deleted one line from Nadia's steps to make Sami's steps. The cook's program is the same for both runs.

Wrong answers and why: "The knife is broken" is wrong: the knife step worked in Nadia's run with the same program. "The spread step is wrong" is wrong: the spread step is the same in both lists; it had nothing on the knife. Prevention: before each step, ask "what must be true for this to work?", and test with a literal helper.

Extra find: Nadia's sandwich is right, but she left the butter tub open. A careful detective can suggest one more step: "CLOSE THE BUTTER TUB".

Story hook

Analogy

Lena and her grandfather live in two flats that face each other across a small yard. At night, they send signals with their bedroom lights. One light on means "Good night". Light off means "I am still awake".

One evening Lena wants to say more. "How can I tell you what I had for dinner with one light?" she asks. Grandfather smiles. "Use more lights," he says. "Two lights give four patterns. Three lights give eight."

So they tape a code to their windows. Off-off means soup. Off-on means rice. On-off means pasta. On-on means pizza. Now two simple lights can say four different things.

Computers talk in exactly this kind of light-switch alphabet. Every number, letter and picture inside a computer is made of on-and-off switches. This chapter shows you how.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain a bit using a light switch: on or off, one or zero, nothing in between.
  • Count in binary from 0 to 15 with four switches, and back again.
  • Use place values (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128) to turn a row of switches into a number.
  • Turn a number up to 255 into a row of eight switches.
  • Find a mistake caused by reading switches from the wrong end.
Jargon box
Bit
Simple words: the smallest piece of information: on or off, 1 or 0. Analogy: one light switch. Precise: a binary digit, which has exactly one of two values, written 0 and 1. D1
Binary
Simple words: a way of writing numbers using only the two digits 0 and 1. Analogy: a row of switches where each switch is worth double the one to its right. Precise: the base-2 number system: each position has a place value that is a power of two (1, 2, 4, 8 and so on). D1
Place value
Simple words: how much a digit is worth because of where it sits. Analogy: the price tag stuck under each switch. Precise: the number a position stands for; in our usual decimal numbers the places are 1, 10, 100; in binary they are 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. D1
Byte
Simple words: a group of eight bits. Analogy: a row of eight light switches. Precise: a unit of eight bits; it can hold 256 different patterns, so one byte can stand for a whole number from 0 to 255. D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows a row of eight switches, a byte. Under each switch is its place value. Each switch is worth double the one to its right. You add up the values of the switches that are on.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A light switch has two positions: on and off. There is no "a little bit on". That makes switches very easy to read. You never have to guess.

Computers store information in tiny parts that act like switches. Each one is either on or off. We write on as 1 and off as 0. One switch is called a bit. D1

One bit can only say two things, like yes or no. That is not much. So computers use many bits side by side, like Lena's two lights. Two bits give four patterns. Three bits give eight. Every new switch doubles the number of patterns.

Counting with switches

Now the clever part. Give each switch a price tag. The switch on the right is worth 1. The next one is worth 2. Then 4, then 8. Each tag is double the one to its right. This tag is the switch's place value.

To read a row, add up the tags of the switches that are on. Off switches count as nothing. With switches worth 8, 4, 2 and 1, the pattern on-off-on-on means 8 + 2 + 1. That is 11. Writing numbers this way is called binary. D1

You already use place values every day. In the number 352, the 3 is worth three hundred, because of where it sits. Binary works the same way. It only uses doubling instead of "times ten".

A byte: eight switches

A row of eight bits has its own name: a byte. Its place values are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1, as Figure 1 shows. When all eight are off, the byte means 0. When all eight are on, it means 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1. Add them up, and you get 255. D1 R1

So one byte can stand for any whole number from 0 to 255. That is 256 different patterns, because zero counts too. Bigger numbers need more bytes. You will see in F0-03 that a byte can also stand for a letter.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Note

For the curious. Why does every new switch double the patterns? Each old pattern can now come in two versions: with the new switch off, and with it on. So one switch gives 2 patterns, two give 2 × 2 = 4, three give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, and eight give 2 multiplied by itself eight times, which is 256. Mathematicians write this as 2 to the power 8. D1 You will practise powers of two in MA101 and binary conversion in MA102.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

At this level, Layer 3 waits for later courses. MA102 covers bytes and words, hexadecimal and negative numbers in binary. HW102 shows how circuits store and add bits. Keep one idea: a pattern of bits has no meaning by itself; a program decides what it means. D1

How the hardware actually does it

A computer does not have tiny light switches with plastic handles. It has electronic parts that can be in one of two states, such as a higher or lower voltage. The computer treats one state as 1 and the other as 0. Billions of these two-state parts together store all of a computer's numbers, letters and pictures. D1

Not verified — check before relying on this

The word "billions" above is a sense of scale, not a measured number. The exact count of bits in any real computer depends on its memory and storage size. Check the datasheet of a named memory part (or the computer's own system information) before quoting a number.

Worked example

From switches to a number

Read the byte 00101101 from Figure 1. Go from left to right.

SwitchBitPlace valueCounts?
1st0128no
2nd064no
3rd132yes: 32
4th016no
5th18yes: 8
6th14yes: 4
7th02no
8th11yes: 1

Add the "yes" values: 32 + 8 = 40, 40 + 4 = 44, 44 + 1 = 45. So 00101101 is 45. The real run of Listing 2 printed the same total. R1

From a number to switches

Now go the other way with 13 and four switches (8, 4, 2, 1). Start at the biggest switch.

  1. Is 13 at least 8? Yes. Switch 8 on. 13 − 8 = 5 left.
  2. Is 5 at least 4? Yes. Switch 4 on. 5 − 4 = 1 left.
  3. Is 1 at least 2? No. Switch 2 off.
  4. Is 1 at least 1? Yes. Switch 1 on. 1 − 1 = 0 left. Done.

So 13 is on-on-off-on, written 1101. Check: 8 + 4 + 1 = 13. Listing 1 uses exactly this method, and its row for 13 says "ON ON off ON". R1

Code walk-through

Real coding starts in KID102. These two small programs show the switch method from the worked example. You can read them like recipes.

Listing 1 — count_switches.cpp: counts from 0 to 15 with four switches.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

std::string switchesFor(int number)
{
    const std::vector<int> placeValues = {8, 4, 2, 1};
    std::string row;
    for (const int value : placeValues) {
        if (number >= value) {
            row += " ON ";
            number = number - value;
        } else {
            row += " off";
        }
    }
    return row;
}

int main()
{
    std::cout << "number | 8s  4s  2s  1s\n";
    for (int number = 0; number <= 15; ++number) {
        std::cout << "  " << number << (number < 10 ? " " : "") << "   |" << switchesFor(number) << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined count_switches.cpp -o count_switches

Listing 2 — bit_board.cpp: reads rows of eight switches, typed as 0 and 1, and adds up their place values. Its input file bit_board.in holds five rows, the last one with only four switches on purpose.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    const std::vector<int> placeValues = {128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1};
    std::string board;
    while (std::cin >> board) {
        if (board.size() != placeValues.size()) {
            std::cout << board << " has " << board.size() << " switches, not 8. Skipped.\n";
            continue;
        }
        int total = 0;
        std::cout << board << " = ";
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < board.size(); ++i) {
            if (board[i] == '1') {
                std::cout << placeValues[i] << " ";
                total = total + placeValues[i];
            }
        }
        if (total == 0) {
            std::cout << "(no switch is on) ";
        }
        std::cout << "-> total " << total << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined bit_board.cpp -o bit_board, run as ./bit_board < bit_board.in.

Where the analogy breaks

  • A real switch can be broken or half-pressed. A bit, when the computer reads it, is always exactly 0 or 1. There is no "half on". D1
  • Switches do not know what they mean. In Lena's code, on-on meant pizza. In binary, on-on means 3. The same switches can mean a number, a letter or a colour. The program decides the meaning, not the switches. D1
  • You can see a light switch. You cannot see a bit. It is far too small, and it is an electrical state, not a moving part.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Your answer is far too big, for 6 you got 96.You read the switches from the wrong end.Check: is the 1 switch on the right?Always put the smallest place value on the right.
Your answer is off by one place, for 5 you got 10.A switch is missing, so everything slid one place.Count the switches: a byte has exactly eight.Write all eight, including the leading zeros.
Two place values are the same, or one is 6.The doubling went wrong when you wrote the tags.Each tag must be double the one to its right.Write 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 from right to left.
The program says "has 4 switches, not 8. Skipped."The row typed into Listing 2 was too short.Count the 0s and 1s in that row.Type all eight digits, as in the last line of the Listing 2 output.
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-01: a computer follows exact steps. What carries over: exact steps still matter; the switch method in the worked example is itself an algorithm. What changes: now you see what the computer works on: everything is stored as bits, and a bit has only two values. Reading switches from the wrong end gives a very different number. D1 What comes next: F0-03 shows how the same switches can stand for letters, colours and sounds.

Check yourself

  1. How many different patterns can three switches make? (a) 3 (b) 6 (c) 8
  2. What number is the four-switch pattern 1010?
  3. Write 9 with four switches.
  4. What is the biggest number one byte can hold? Show the sum.
  5. Explain in your own words why each new switch doubles the number of patterns.
  6. Apply it to a new case: Lena has a row of five switches. What are the five place values, and what is the biggest number she can show?
  7. Is it true that a bit can be "half on"? Why or why not?

Lab

A paper bit board

Goal: build an eight-switch bit board on paper and use it to show any number from 0 to 255.

You need: a strip of paper, a pencil, eight coins or paper squares. No computer is needed. (Listings 1 and 2 above are optional extras.)

Safety

None beyond normal paper and pencil work. Keep coins away from very young children.

  1. Draw eight boxes in a row. Under them, write 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 from left to right.
  2. A coin heads-up in a box means "on" (1). An empty box, or tails, means "off" (0).
  3. Show 5. You should have coins on 4 and 1.
  4. Show 45. Check with Figure 1.
  5. Ask a friend for a secret number up to 255. Show it on the board. Your friend checks by adding.
  6. Count from 0 to 15 on the four right-hand boxes. Compare with the Listing 1 output.

What you should see: the rightmost box flips every time you count up by one. The next box flips every second count. That is the doubling pattern.

Check you succeeded: you can show 0, 1, 100 and 255 without mistakes, and read back any row your friend makes.

If something goes wrong: a total too big → you read from the wrong end → put 1 on the right. A number you cannot make → you skipped a box → use all eight. A friend gets a different total → one of you added wrongly → add again, one "yes" box at a time.

Extension: what happens if you add a ninth box on the left? What is its place value, and what is the new biggest number?

Forensic lab

The numbers that grew too big

Scenario. Ama sends three numbers to Kofi, written as bytes. She wants to send 6, 12 and 20. Kofi types her rows into Listing 2. He is puzzled: "Your numbers are huge!"

Evidence. Kofi's run, using the same program as Listing 2 (copied as forensic_board.cpp), with Ama's three rows as input:

01100000 = 64 32 -> total 96
00110000 = 32 16 -> total 48
00101000 = 32 8 -> total 40

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-02/forensic_board.out; run record forensic_board.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:31:31Z; exit code: 0.

Questions.

  1. Which numbers did Kofi get, and which did Ama mean?
  2. Give two possible ideas for what went wrong.
  3. Write 6 as a byte yourself. Compare it with Ama's first row. What do you notice?
  4. Is the program wrong, or the rows? Prove it.
  5. Write Ama's three rows correctly.

Method hints. Work out the right byte for each number by hand, using the worked example. Then lay it next to Ama's row. Read one of them backwards.

Mini-project

Start the course project: a paper computer that adds two small binary numbers. Today, make two four-switch boards (8, 4, 2, 1) and a third board with five switches for the answer (16, 8, 4, 2, 1). Show 5 on the first board and 3 on the second. Work out the answer in your usual way and show it on the third board. You will write the adding rules in F0-07.

Rubric (4 points): place values correct (1); 5 and 3 shown correctly (1); answer board shows 8 (1); neat labels a friend can read (1).

Summary

  • A bit is like a light switch: on or off, written 1 or 0.
  • Every extra switch doubles the number of patterns.
  • In binary, each switch has a place value: 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on, doubling to the left.
  • To read a row, add the place values of the switches that are on.
  • A byte is eight bits and can show any number from 0 to 255.
  • Reading the switches from the wrong end gives a very different number.
  • The switches have no meaning by themselves; the program decides.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. (c) 8, because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. (a) counts the switches, not the patterns. (b) adds instead of doubling.
  2. 8 + 2 = 10.
  3. 1001: 8 + 1 = 9.
  4. 255: 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255.
  5. Your own words. A good answer: every old pattern can appear twice, once with the new switch off and once with it on.
  6. 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. The biggest is 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 31.
  7. No. When the computer reads a bit, it is always exactly 0 or 1. Only a real, broken light switch can be "half on".

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: Kofi got 96, 48 and 40. Ama meant 6, 12 and 20.

Root cause: Ama wrote each byte backwards, with the 1 switch on the left. 6 is 00000110; written backwards it is 01100000, which the program reads as 64 + 32 = 96. 12 is 00001100; backwards, 00110000 = 48. 20 is 00010100; backwards, 00101000 = 40.

Proof that the program is fine: the same program read 00000101 as 5 and 00101101 as 45 in the Listing 2 run, and those are correct.

Fix: the rows should be 00000110, 00001100 and 00010100.

How the fault was made: the Lab Engineer reversed the three correct rows by hand and fed them to an unchanged copy of Listing 2.

Wrong answers and why: "The program adds wrongly": ruled out above. "One switch was missing": each row has eight switches and the program did not print "Skipped". Prevention: agree on "smallest place value on the right" and send one test number first, such as 1.

Story hook

Analogy

Jun and his cousin Priya share a secret code. A is 1, B is 2, C is 3, and so on. Priya leaves a note on the fridge: 8, 9. Jun counts on his fingers. H, I. "Hi!"

The next week, Priya's friend finds a note: 8, 9. She has no idea what it means. Is it two shoe sizes? A phone number? Without the code, the numbers are only numbers.

That is the whole secret of this chapter. A computer can only store numbers made of bits. To store a letter, a colour or a sound, everyone must agree on a code first. Then numbers become messages.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain that letters, colours and sounds are stored as numbers, using an agreed code.
  • Encode a short word as bytes, using a real letter table printed by a computer.
  • Decode bytes back into a word.
  • Describe a colour as three numbers: how much red, green and blue.
  • Find the cause of a scrambled message.
Jargon box
Code (for information)
Simple words: an agreement about which number stands for which thing. Analogy: Jun and Priya's "A is 1, B is 2" note on the fridge. Precise: a fixed rule that matches each symbol (a letter, a colour, a sound level) with a pattern of bits, so both writer and reader get the same meaning. Not the same as "code" meaning a program's text. D1
Character code
Simple words: a table that gives every letter, digit and sign its own number. Analogy: the fridge note, but agreed by the whole world. Precise: a mapping from characters to numbers. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is an early example; Unicode is a larger one for the writing systems of the world. D1
Pixel
Simple words: one tiny dot of a picture. Analogy: one tile in a mosaic on a kitchen wall. Precise: a picture element: one point of an image, stored as numbers that describe its colour. D1
Sample (of a sound)
Simple words: one measurement of a sound at one moment. Analogy: one frame of a flip book. Precise: a number that records the level of a sound wave at one instant; a recording is a long list of samples taken at regular times. D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows three kinds of message. Each one is a list of numbers. The code next to it tells you how to read them.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

In F0-02 you learned that a computer stores numbers as rows of switches. But computers also show words, photos and music. How?

The answer is a code. A code is an agreement: "this number means that thing". The computer stores only the number. A program uses the code to turn the number back into a letter, a colour or a sound. D1

Letters

For letters, people agreed on tables called character codes. Each letter, digit and sign gets its own number. We asked a computer in this build which number it uses for each capital letter. It printed A = 65, B = 66, and so on up to Z = 90. R1

So the word "HI" is stored as 72, 73. Each number fits in one byte. In switches, H is 01001000. Check it with your bit board: 64 + 8 = 72.

Small letters have different numbers from capitals. The space between words has a number too. In our run, a space was 32 and "!" was 33. R1

Colours

A picture on a screen is made of tiny dots called pixels. Each dot has one colour. A common way to describe a colour is with three numbers: how much red, how much green and how much blue light to mix. D1

In this chapter we use our own paper code. Each of the three amounts goes from 0 (none) to 255 (full), so each fits in one byte. Red 255, green 0, blue 0 is bright red. All three at 0 is black. All three at 255 is white.

Sounds

Sound is air that wobbles very fast. A microphone turns the wobble into a changing signal. The computer measures that signal again and again, at equal steps in time. Each measurement is a number, called a sample. A song is a very long list of samples. D1

To play the song, the computer sends the numbers to a speaker, in order and at the same speed. The speaker wobbles the air again, and you hear the sound.

Not verified — check before relying on this

How many samples per second real recordings use, and how many bytes real image files use per pixel, depend on the file format and device. This chapter gives no such numbers. Check: D1 (sections on sound and pictures), or the specification of the named file format, before quoting any.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Note

For the curious. One byte has 256 patterns, which is plenty for English capital and small letters, digits and signs. But the world has many writing systems with thousands of characters. Unicode gives each of them its own number, and some numbers need more than one byte. D1 Also, the same byte can mean different things: 72 can be the letter H, the number 72, or a dark shade of red. Only the program knows which code to use.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

At this level, Layer 3 waits for later courses. MA102 covers bytes, units and hexadecimal colour numbers. KID102 uses char and std::string for text. The key idea to keep: bits never carry their own meaning; the code is an agreement between the writer and the reader. D1

How the hardware actually does it

Memory stores only bits. It does not know if a byte is a letter or a colour. When you press a key, the keyboard sends a number to the computer. A program looks up which character that is, and finds which dots on the screen to light to draw its shape. Every step is numbers and agreed codes. D1

Worked example

Encode the word "HI"

  1. Look up H in the letter table from Listing 3: H = 72.
  2. Turn 72 into switches. Is 72 at least 128? No: 0. At least 64? Yes: 1, and 72 − 64 = 8 is left. 32? No: 0. 16? No: 0. 8? Yes: 1, nothing left. 4, 2, 1: all 0. So H is 01001000.
  3. I = 73. That is 72 + 1, so the same pattern with the last switch on: 01001001.
  4. The message is 01001000 01001001.

Decode a message

Decode 01001100. The switches that are on are worth 64, 8 and 4. 64 + 8 + 4 = 76. The table says 76 is L. Listing 2 decoded the same byte as L in its real run. R1

Mix a colour

Using our paper code, orange is red 255, green 128, blue 0. In bits, 255 is 11111111, 128 is 10000000 and 0 is 00000000. So one orange dot takes three bytes in our code: 11111111 10000000 00000000.

Code walk-through

Coding starts for real in KID102. Here, three small programs let the computer show you its own letter numbers.

Listing 1 — letters.cpp: shows the number and bits stored for each character of "Hi A!".

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

std::string eightSwitches(int number)
{
    const std::vector<int> placeValues = {128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1};
    std::string bits;
    for (const int value : placeValues) {
        if (number >= value) {
            bits += '1';
            number = number - value;
        } else {
            bits += '0';
        }
    }
    return bits;
}

int main()
{
    const std::string word = "Hi A!";
    for (const char letter : word) {
        const int number = static_cast<int>(letter);
        std::cout << "'" << letter << "' is stored as number " << number
                  << " = bits " << eightSwitches(number) << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined letters.cpp -o letters

'H' is stored as number 72 = bits 01001000
'i' is stored as number 105 = bits 01101001
' ' is stored as number 32 = bits 00100000
'A' is stored as number 65 = bits 01000001
'!' is stored as number 33 = bits 00100001

Listing 2 — decode.cpp: reads groups of eight bits from decode.in and turns them back into letters.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    const std::vector<int> placeValues = {128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1};
    std::string group;
    std::string message;
    while (std::cin >> group) {
        int number = 0;
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < group.size() && i < placeValues.size(); ++i) {
            if (group[i] == '1') {
                number = number + placeValues[i];
            }
        }
        const bool printable = number >= 32 && number <= 126;
        const char letter = printable ? static_cast<char>(number) : '?';
        std::cout << group << " -> " << number << " -> " << letter << '\n';
        message += letter;
    }
    std::cout << "Message: " << message << '\n';
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined decode.cpp -o decode, run as ./decode < decode.in.

01000101 -> 69 -> E
01001100 -> 76 -> L
01001100 -> 76 -> L
01001111 -> 79 -> O

Where the analogy breaks

  • A fridge-note code is private; computer codes are shared. Jun and Priya made up their own code. Computers must use the same agreed tables, or a message from one computer turns into nonsense on another. D1
  • Jun's code used A = 1; the computer's does not. In our run, A is 65. Do not mix the two codes. R1
  • A mosaic tile is a solid object. A pixel on a screen is light, and its colour is only numbers until the screen shows it. Our paper code of three numbers from 0 to 255 is a teaching code; real file formats have their own exact rules.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Your decoded word is all "?" or odd signs.The bits were read from the wrong end.Decode one byte by hand with 128 on the left.Keep the biggest place value on the left.
Every letter is one place off, H became I.You started the table at the wrong number.Check one letter in the Listing 3 table.Use the real table: A = 65.
The message has no gaps between words.The space was not encoded.Count the bytes; there should be one for each space.Encode the space too: 32.
Small letters decode to the wrong letters.Small and capital letters have different numbers.Check: in our run "i" was 105, not 73.Use the right number for each case.
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-02: bits, place values and bytes as numbers. What carries over: the bit board and the method for turning switches into numbers and back. What changes: now a number can stand for something else, a letter, a colour or a sound, and you need the agreed code to read it. Using the wrong code, or reading from the wrong end, scrambles the message. D1 What comes next: F0-04 goes back to algorithms, with sorting socks and cards.

Check yourself

  1. Why do a writer and a reader need the same code?
  2. Using the letter table from Listing 3, what is the number for C? For Z?
  3. Decode 01000010. (a) A (b) B (c) 2
  4. In our paper colour code, what colour is red 0, green 0, blue 255?
  5. What is a sample of a sound?
  6. Explain in your own words why the byte 72 might not mean H.
  7. Apply it to a new case: encode the word "OK" as bytes.

Lab

Secret bit messages

Goal: send a short word to a friend as bytes and have them decode it.

You need: paper, a pencil, your bit board from F0-02, the letter table (the output of Listing 3). No computer is needed.

Safety

None beyond normal paper and pencil work.

  1. Choose a word of three to five capital letters.
  2. Look up each letter's number in the table.
  3. Turn each number into eight bits. Write them in groups of eight with a gap between groups.
  4. Give the bits, and only the bits, to your friend.
  5. Your friend decodes each group and writes the word.
  6. Compare. If it is wrong, find which group went wrong and why.

What you should see: every capital letter starts with 010 in its eight bits, because they are all between 64 and 95. Look for that pattern in your message.

Check you succeeded: your friend reads the word correctly with no hints.

If something goes wrong: a group gives a number below 65 → a switch was dropped → count to eight. A letter is one off → adding slip → add again. A group gives a huge number → read from the wrong end → put 128 on the left.

Extension: design a colour message: three bytes for one dot, using our paper code. Can your friend say the colour?

Mini-project

Make a pixel picture on squared paper, eight squares by eight. Use only two colours. Write each row as one byte: 1 for coloured, 0 for empty. Give the eight bytes to a friend. Can they redraw your picture from the bytes alone?

Rubric (4 points): eight rows of exactly eight bits (1); bytes match the picture (1); friend redraws it correctly (1); you wrote the code you used ("1 means coloured") on the sheet (1).

Summary

  • A computer stores only numbers, as bits.
  • A code is an agreement about what each number means.
  • Letters use a character code; in this build's run, A was 65 and H was 72.
  • A picture is made of pixels; a colour can be described as amounts of red, green and blue.
  • A sound is stored as a long list of samples.
  • The same byte can mean different things; the program decides which code to use.
  • The wrong code, or the wrong reading direction, scrambles a message.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. The bits carry only numbers. Without the same code, the reader turns the numbers into the wrong things.
  2. C = 67, Z = 90 (from the Listing 3 output).
  3. (b) B. 01000010 is 64 + 2 = 66, and 66 is B. (a) would be 65. (c) mixes up the number 2 with the bits: only one switch, worth 2, is not the whole story.
  4. Bright blue.
  5. One measurement of the sound's level at one moment. A recording is a long list of them.
  6. Your own words. A good answer: 72 is only a number; it is H only if the reader uses the letter code. With another code it could be a colour amount or a plain number.
  7. O = 79 = 01001111; K = 75 = 01001011. So "OK" is 01001111 01001011.

Forensic lab answer key

Root cause: in the friend's decoder, line 7 lists the place values smallest first, so each group is read from the wrong end.

Evidence: 01001000 read with values 1, 2, 4, …, 128 from the left: the 1s are in the 2nd and 5th places, worth 2 and 16, so 18. That is exactly what the bad run printed. The good run printed 72 for the same bits. The only different line is line 7.

Why both L's became "2": L is 01001100 in both places; read backwards it is 2 + 16 + 32 = 50, and 50 is the digit "2" in the character code. Same input, same wrong rule, same wrong answer.

Fix: change line 7 back to {128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1}; run again and check that the message is "HELLO".

How the fault was made: the Lab Engineer copied Listing 2 and reversed the list on line 7, then ran both with the same input file.

Wrong answers and why: "Zainab sent the wrong bits": the good decoder read the same bits as HELLO. "The letter table is wrong": 72 is H in the Listing 3 table. Prevention: test a decoder on a known message first, such as one letter you can check by hand.

Algorithms at home: sorting socks and cards

← F0-03 · course KID101 · catalogue · F0-05 →
