Story-level preparation for HW101–HW102; no curriculum milestone

Story hook

Analogy

It is laundry day. Omar tips a basket of clean socks onto the bed. There are blue ones, striped ones, and one lonely green one. His job is to pair them all.

His sister Aiko watches. Omar grabs a sock, then digs through the whole pile for its partner. Then he grabs another and digs again. "That takes forever," Aiko says. "Try my way. Pick up a sock. If its partner is already on the bed, join them. If not, lay it out on its own."

Both ways work. Both end with neat pairs. But Aiko's way needs far less digging. Two good algorithms can solve the same problem, and one can be much faster. That is what this chapter is about.

What you will be able to do

  • Write a sorting algorithm in words that someone else can follow.
  • Test an algorithm by acting it out with cards, and count its steps.
  • Compare two algorithms for the same job by counting their comparisons.
  • Play a sorting-network game on the floor and explain why it works.
  • Find the missing piece in a sorting network that does not always work.
Jargon box
Sorting
Simple words: putting things in order, like smallest to biggest. Analogy: lining up cards in your hand from low to high. Precise: rearranging a list so that each item is no bigger than the next one (or no smaller, for the other direction). D2
Comparison
Simple words: looking at two things and deciding which is bigger. Analogy: holding two cards side by side. Precise: a test between two values whose answer is yes or no, such as "is the left one bigger than the right one?". Counting comparisons is one way to measure how much work a sorting method does. D2
Swap
Simple words: two things change places. Analogy: two children in a line trading spots. Precise: exchanging the values in two positions of a list. D2
Sorting network
Simple words: a fixed plan of "compare these two, swap if needed" stations that always sorts. Analogy: a chalk path on the floor where people meet at boxes, compare, and step left or right. Precise: a fixed sequence of compare-and-swap operations on fixed positions, chosen so that any starting order comes out sorted. R1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the sorting network you will play on the floor. Four lines are four "spots". Each bar joining two lines is a station: the two cards there are compared, and the smaller goes to the upper line.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Sorting means putting things in order. You sort when you line up from shortest to tallest, or put books from A to Z. Computers sort all the time: names in a contact list, songs by title, scores from best to worst.

Here is the surprise. A computer cannot look at a whole pile and "see" the order. It can only do one small thing at a time. It looks at two items and asks: "Is this one bigger than that one?" That is a comparison. Then it may swap them. Sorting a list is many comparisons and swaps, in a clever order. D2

Method 1: find the smallest

Lay five cards in a row, face up. Look along the row and find the smallest card. Swap it with the first card. Now the first card is done. Do the same for the rest of the row, starting at the second card. Keep going until one card is left. That card is the biggest, and it is already in its place.

This is an algorithm. It is exact. It always ends. It works for any five cards, and for fifty too. You will act it out in the worked example.

Method 2: the sorting network

A sorting network is a fixed plan. Draw four lines on the floor, as in Figure 1. Four friends each hold a card and stand on a line. At each station, two friends meet and compare cards. The smaller card steps to the upper line. The bigger card steps to the lower line. R1

The plan never changes, whatever cards people hold. That is why it is a great game: nobody has to think, only compare. And it always works. Our computer tried every possible starting order of four cards, all 24 of them, and every one came out sorted. R1

Which method is better?

A good way to compare algorithms is to count their work. For sorting, we count comparisons. Fewer comparisons for the same job means less work. In the worked example you will count both methods for yourself.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Note

For the curious. Count the "find the smallest" method for five cards. The first look compares the first card with 4 others. The next look compares 3 pairs, then 2, then 1. That is 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 comparisons, every time, whatever the cards are. With ten cards it is 9 + 8 + … + 1 = 45. The work grows much faster than the number of cards. The sorting network has another advantage: its stations 1 and 2 use different spots, so two pairs of friends can compare at the same moment. Doing work at the same time like this is called working in parallel, and it is the big idea behind GPUs much later in this university.

Not verified — check before relying on this

Computer-science books give these methods names: "find the smallest" is known as selection sort, and the floor game is a sorting network. This chapter's registry of sources has no algorithms textbook yet, so these names and any claims about which method real programs use are not checked here. The Dean must add an algorithms textbook to the source registry, and the Source Researcher must confirm the names.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

At this level, the deeper story waits. You will measure the speed of real sorting code in later courses, and in the GPU faculty you will see work split across many helpers at once. Keep one habit from today: to compare algorithms, count their steps on the same input. R1

How the hardware actually does it

Inside the computer, a comparison is one tiny step done by the processor: it checks whether one number is bigger than another and remembers the yes-or-no answer. A swap moves two numbers between places in memory. A sorting program is a long list of these small steps. The processor never sees "the whole list" at once. D1 You will meet the processor and memory in F0-05.

Worked example

"Find the smallest" with five cards

Start: 7 2 9 4 5. Done cards are in brackets.

RoundLook atComparisonsSmallestSwapRow after
17 2 9 4 5422 with 7[2] 7 9 4 5
27 9 4 5344 with 7[2 4] 9 7 5
39 7 5255 with 9[2 4 5] 7 9
47 917none[2 4 5 7] 9

Total comparisons: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. The last card, 9, is in place without a check.

The sorting network with four cards

The real run of Listing 1 traced 9 4 7 2 through the five stations of Figure 1. R1

  1. Station 1 (spots 0 and 1): 9 and 4. Swap. Row: 4 9 7 2.
  2. Station 2 (spots 2 and 3): 7 and 2. Swap. Row: 4 9 2 7.
  3. Station 3 (spots 0 and 2): 4 and 2. Swap. Row: 2 9 4 7.
  4. Station 4 (spots 1 and 3): 9 and 7. Swap. Row: 2 7 4 9.
  5. Station 5 (spots 1 and 2): 7 and 4. Swap. Row: 2 4 7 9. Sorted!

The network used 5 comparisons for 4 cards. "Find the smallest" would use 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 for 4 cards. And stations 1 and 2 can happen at the same moment.

Code walk-through

Real coding starts in KID102. This program plays the floor game, then tests every possible starting order. You may find it harder than the earlier listings; read the table slowly.

Listing 1 — network.cpp

#include <algorithm>
#include <array>
#include <iostream>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

using Cards = std::array<int, 4>;

const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> comparators = {{0, 1}, {2, 3}, {0, 2}, {1, 3}, {1, 2}};

Cards runNetwork(Cards cards, bool show)
{
    for (const auto& [left, right] : comparators) {
        if (cards[left] > cards[right]) {
            std::swap(cards[left], cards[right]);
        }
        if (show) {
            std::cout << "compare spots " << left << " and " << right << ": ";
            for (const int card : cards) {
                std::cout << card << ' ';
            }
            std::cout << '\n';
        }
    }
    return cards;
}

int main()
{
    runNetwork({9, 4, 7, 2}, true);

    Cards order = {1, 2, 3, 4};
    int tried = 0;
    int sorted = 0;
    do {
        tried = tried + 1;
        const Cards result = runNetwork(order, false);
        if (std::is_sorted(result.begin(), result.end())) {
            sorted = sorted + 1;
        } else {
            std::cout << "NOT sorted: " << order[0] << ' ' << order[1] << ' ' << order[2]
                      << ' ' << order[3] << '\n';
        }
    } while (std::next_permutation(order.begin(), order.end()));
    std::cout << sorted << " of " << tried << " starting orders came out sorted.\n";
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined network.cpp -o network

compare spots 0 and 1: 4 9 7 2 
compare spots 2 and 3: 4 9 2 7 
compare spots 0 and 2: 2 9 4 7 
compare spots 1 and 3: 2 7 4 9 
compare spots 1 and 2: 2 4 7 9 
24 of 24 starting orders came out sorted.

Where the analogy breaks

  • You can see the whole pile of socks at once. A computer cannot. It only compares two items at a time, so "look for the partner" is not a step it can do in one go. D1
  • Friends on the floor may take shortcuts. Someone might say "I can see 2 is smallest, I'll go first". A computer follows the plan exactly, every time, even if the cards were already sorted.
  • Socks have no single "order". Pairing socks is matching, not sorting by size. Computers sort by a rule you choose, like "smaller number first". Without a rule, there is no sorting.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
The row is almost sorted, but two middle cards are swapped.A station is missing, or done in the wrong order.Act it out with cards and write the row after every station.Follow Figure 1's order: five stations.
The biggest card ends at the top.The rule was flipped: bigger to the upper line.Check one station by hand.Smaller card goes to the upper spot.
Your method works on one example but fails on another.You tested only one easy case.Try many orders, including "backwards" (4 3 2 1).Test every order, as Listing 1 does.
Your friend skips a round of "find the smallest".Your written steps did not say when to stop.Read the steps aloud: when does it end?Write "repeat until one card is left".
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-01 (exact steps) and F0-03 (everything is numbers). What carries over: algorithms are exact steps; letters are numbers, so sorting names is sorting numbers. What changes: now several algorithms solve the same problem, and you can compare them by counting work. A plan that "looks right" must be tested on every case you can. R1 What comes next: F0-05 opens the box: the kitchen inside a computer where comparisons and swaps really happen.

Check yourself

  1. What two small actions is sorting made of?
  2. How many comparisons does "find the smallest" use for six cards? Show the sum.
  3. At a station, which card goes to the upper spot? (a) the bigger (b) the smaller (c) the one that arrived first
  4. Why is testing all 24 orders a strong test for a four-card network?
  5. Explain in your own words why the sorting network is good for a group of people.
  6. Apply it to a new case: sort 3 1 4 2 with the network of Figure 1. Write the row after each station.
  7. Why is pairing socks not really sorting?

Lab

The sorting-network game on the floor

Goal: play the network of Figure 1 with four people and show that it always sorts.

You need: chalk or tape, a floor or a playground, four players and one caller, cards with numbers (any four different numbers).

Safety

Walk, do not run. Play on a dry, flat floor with space around the lines. Use tape or chalk that an adult says may be used on that floor.

  1. Draw four long lines next to each other. Mark five stations as in Figure 1: short marks joining spots 0–1 and 2–3 near the start, then 0–2, then 1–3, then 1–2.
  2. Each player takes a card and stands at the start of a line.
  3. The caller says "station 1". The two players on spots 0 and 1 meet, compare, and the smaller goes to spot 0.
  4. Continue through stations 2 to 5, always in order.
  5. At the end, check: are the cards in order from spot 0 to spot 3?
  6. Shuffle the cards and play again. Try "backwards" (biggest on spot 0) too.

What you should see: every game ends sorted. Stations 1 and 2 can happen at the same time, because they use different players.

Check you succeeded: five different games all end sorted, and you can explain the station rule to someone new.

If something goes wrong: not sorted at the end → a station was skipped → replay with the caller ticking each one. Big card on top → rule flipped → "smaller goes up". Players argue → write the rule on a card at each station.

Extension: play with the cards of the forensic lab. What do you notice?

Questions.

  1. How many orders failed? How many worked?
  2. Look at the trace for 9 4 7 2. How many stations are there? Is the result sorted?
  3. Give two possible ideas for what is wrong with the plan.
  4. Take one failing order, like 1 3 2 4. Act it out. Where are the cards at the end?
  5. Which station is missing? How would you prove the fix works?

Method hints. Compare the trace with the one in the worked example. Which step is missing at the end? For the failing orders, look at which two spots are wrong.

Mini-project

Write the "find the smallest" method as numbered steps for a friend. Test it on five cards, then on eight. Count the comparisons each time and make a small table: number of cards, number of comparisons. Can you see a pattern?

Rubric (4 points): steps are exact and say when to stop (1); friend sorts correctly without questions (1); comparisons counted correctly (1); a pattern is described in your own words (1).

Summary

  • Sorting puts things in order by a rule.
  • A computer sorts by many comparisons and swaps of two items at a time.
  • Different algorithms can solve the same problem with different amounts of work.
  • Count comparisons to compare sorting methods.
  • A sorting network is a fixed plan of compare-and-swap stations.
  • Testing every possible starting order is the strongest test for a small problem.
  • One missing step can make a plan work only sometimes.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Comparisons (which of two is bigger?) and swaps (two items change places).
  2. 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15.
  3. (b) the smaller. (a) would sort the other way round. (c) is not a rule about the numbers at all; the order of arrival does not matter.
  4. Four cards can start in only 24 orders, and the run tried every one. If all 24 come out sorted, no starting order can fail.
  5. Your own words. A good answer: the plan is fixed, so nobody has to decide anything; each pair only compares two cards; and some pairs can work at the same time.
  6. Start 3 1 4 2. Station 1 (0,1): swap → 1 3 4 2. Station 2 (2,3): swap → 1 3 2 4. Station 3 (0,2): 1 and 2, no swap → 1 3 2 4. Station 4 (1,3): 3 and 4, no swap → 1 3 2 4. Station 5 (1,2): 3 and 2, swap → 1 2 3 4.
  7. There is no "smaller" sock. You are matching equal things, not putting them in order by a rule.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: only 8 of 24 orders came out sorted; 16 failed. The trace for 9 4 7 2 has only four stations and ends 2 7 4 9, which is not sorted.

Root cause: station 5 (compare spots 1 and 2) is missing. After the first four stations, the smallest card is always on spot 0 and the biggest on spot 3, but the two middle cards can still be in the wrong order. For 1 3 2 4, nothing swaps at all, and 3 and 2 stay wrong in the middle.

Fix and proof: add the station for spots 1 and 2 at the end. Listing 1 has exactly that one extra station and its run shows 24 of 24 sorted.

How the fault was made: the Lab Engineer copied Listing 1 and deleted the last pair, {1, 2}, from line 9.

Wrong answers and why: "The swap rule is wrong": the first four stations swap correctly in the trace. "Station 3 is in the wrong place": with it in place, 2 still reaches spot 0 in the trace. Prevention: never trust one game; test every order, or as many as you can.

Story-level preparation for HW101–HW102; no curriculum milestone

Story hook

Analogy

Elif's aunt runs a small restaurant. One Saturday, Elif is allowed to watch the kitchen from a stool in the corner.

The head chef stands at the stove. She works with her hands on a small cutting board. On shelves near the stove are the things she uses most: salt, oil, a few onions. Down the corridor is a big pantry full of jars and boxes. Every morning a van brings sacks of flour and rice from a warehouse across town.

An order slip comes in through the order window. The chef reads it, fetches what she needs, cooks, and passes a plate out through the serving hatch.

Elif thinks: "It is like a machine." She is right, in a way. A computer has a part like each of these. This chapter opens the box and shows you the kitchen inside.

What you will be able to do

  • Name the main parts inside a computer: CPU, registers, cache, main memory, storage, bus, and input and output.
  • Match each part to its place in the kitchen map.
  • Explain why the closest storage places are the smallest and the fastest to reach.
  • Trace a tiny "load, add, store" recipe step by step on paper.
  • Find the step in the wrong order when a toy computer gives a wrong answer.
Jargon box
CPU (central processing unit)
Simple words: the part that carries out the program's steps. Analogy: the head chef. Precise: the processor: the circuit that fetches instructions from memory and carries them out, one after another, working on data. A CPU can contain one or more cores; each core is like one head chef. D1 D3
Register
Simple words: a tiny place inside the CPU that holds a number it is working on right now. Analogy: the chef's hands and the cutting board. Precise: a small, very fast storage place inside the processor that holds one value; instructions work on values in registers. D1
Cache
Simple words: a small, fast store near the CPU for things used often. Analogy: shelves near the stove. Precise: a small, fast memory between the processor and main memory that keeps copies of recently used data, so it can be reached sooner. D3
Main memory
Simple words: the big workspace that holds the program and its data while it runs. Analogy: the big pantry down the corridor. Precise: the computer's large working memory (built from DRAM chips, dynamic random-access memory), where running programs and their data are kept; its contents are lost when the power goes off. D3
Storage
Simple words: where files and programs are kept, even when the computer is off. Analogy: the warehouse across town. Precise: a device such as an SSD (solid-state drive) or a hard disk that keeps data without power; it is larger and slower to reach than main memory. D3
Bus
Simple words: the paths that carry information between the parts. Analogy: corridors and service lifts. Precise: a set of connections that carries data, addresses and control signals between the processor, memory and devices. D2
Input and output (I/O)
Simple words: information coming into the computer, and results going out. Analogy: order slips through the order window; plates out through the serving hatch. Precise: the transfer of data between the computer and the outside world through devices such as a keyboard (input) or a screen (output). D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 is the kitchen map of a computer. Read it from the chef outwards. The closer a place is to the chef, the smaller it is and the quicker she can reach it.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Every computer, from a phone to a laptop, has the same main parts. Let us walk through the kitchen.

The head chef: the CPU

The CPU is the head chef. It carries out the program's steps, one after another. It is very fast, but it can only work on what it is holding right now. D1

The chef's hands: registers

What the chef is holding goes in her hands and on her cutting board. In the CPU, these are the registers. There are only a few. They hold the numbers being worked on this very moment. D1

Shelves near the stove: the cache

The chef keeps salt and oil on shelves right next to the stove. She uses them all the time, so she does not walk to the pantry each time. The CPU has the same trick, called a cache. It keeps copies of things used often, close by. D3

The big pantry: main memory

Down the corridor is the big pantry. It holds everything needed for today's cooking. That is main memory. While a program runs, the program and its data live here. But this pantry has a strange rule. When the power goes off, it forgets everything. D3

The warehouse: storage

Across town is the warehouse. It is huge, and it keeps things safe even at night. That is storage. Your photos, games and documents stay there when the computer is off. Before a program runs, it is brought from storage into main memory. D3

Corridors, window and hatch

Things move between all these places along the bus, like corridors and service lifts. New information arrives as input, like order slips at the window: a key you press, a mouse click. Results leave as output, like plates through the hatch: letters on the screen, a sound from the speaker. D2

The big rule of the kitchen

Look at Figure 1 again. The closer a place is to the chef, the smaller it is. And the faster it is to reach. Hands are tiny but instant. The warehouse is huge but slow. Good programs try to keep what they need close to the chef. D3

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Note

For the curious. Main memory is a long row of numbered boxes. Each box has an address, like a house number. To fetch a number, the CPU sends the address along the bus, and the memory sends back what is in that box. Instructions are stored in memory as numbers too, so the CPU fetches them the same way. D1 D2 A cache works by itself: the chef does not decide what goes on the shelves; the hardware does. D3

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

At this level, the depth waits for HW102 and the F1 faculty, where the same kitchen map is used again with more detail: several levels of cache, how memory is organised, and how real processors read and run their instructions. Real sizes and speeds are only quoted there from the datasheet of a named product. D3

How the hardware actually does it

All these parts are made of electronic circuits that store and move bits, as in F0-02. The registers are part of the CPU itself, and the caches are built close to it. Main memory is made of separate memory chips. Storage is another device. The bus is made of wires and connections on the board that joins them. D2 D3

Not verified — check before relying on this

How many registers a CPU has, how large its caches are, and how much faster a register is than main memory or storage are different for every product. This chapter gives no such numbers on purpose. To find real ones, use the datasheet or manual of a named processor and memory part (guide rule AH-21), or ask a grown-up to show you the system information of your own computer and write your own numbers here: ____.

Worked example

Let us cook "7 + 5" in a toy kitchen. The pantry has three boxes. Box 0 holds 7, box 1 holds 5, and box 2 is empty (0). The chef has two hands. Here is the recipe.

StepRecipe lineLeft handRight handPantry boxes 0, 1, 2
start—007, 5, 0
1LOAD_LEFT 0: fetch box 0 into the left hand707, 5, 0
2LOAD_RIGHT 1: fetch box 1 into the right hand757, 5, 0
3ADD: left = left + right1257, 5, 0
4STORE_LEFT 2: put the left hand's number in box 21257, 5, 12

The answer, 12, ends up in box 2 of the pantry. Notice that the chef never adds things in the pantry. She brings them to her hands first. Real CPUs work in the same "load, work, store" way, with registers as the hands. D1 Listing 1 runs this toy recipe, and its real output matches the table. R1

Code walk-through

Real coding starts in KID102. This program is a toy model of the kitchen. It is not a real CPU: real processors have their own exact list of instructions, which you meet in HW102.

Listing 1 — kitchen.cpp

// A toy model of the kitchen map in chapter F0-05. It is NOT a real CPU:
// real processors have their own exact instruction lists (HW102 and HW202).
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Step
{
    std::string action;
    int box;
};

int main()
{
    std::vector<int> pantry = {7, 5, 0};
    int leftHand = 0;
    int rightHand = 0;

    const std::vector<Step> recipe = {
        {"LOAD_LEFT", 0}, {"LOAD_RIGHT", 1}, {"ADD", 0}, {"STORE_LEFT", 2},
    };

    for (const Step& step : recipe) {
        if (step.action == "LOAD_LEFT") {
            leftHand = pantry[step.box];
        } else if (step.action == "LOAD_RIGHT") {
            rightHand = pantry[step.box];
        } else if (step.action == "ADD") {
            leftHand = leftHand + rightHand;
        } else if (step.action == "STORE_LEFT") {
            pantry[step.box] = leftHand;
        }
        std::cout << step.action << " " << step.box << "  -> hands: " << leftHand << ", "
                  << rightHand << "  pantry boxes: " << pantry[0] << ", " << pantry[1]
                  << ", " << pantry[2] << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined kitchen.cpp -o kitchen

LOAD_LEFT 0  -> hands: 7, 0  pantry boxes: 7, 5, 0
LOAD_RIGHT 1  -> hands: 7, 5  pantry boxes: 7, 5, 0
ADD 0  -> hands: 12, 5  pantry boxes: 7, 5, 0
STORE_LEFT 2  -> hands: 12, 5  pantry boxes: 7, 5, 12

LinesCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters

3–5#include …Tools for printing, text and lists.Ready-made parts of C++. D4
7–11struct Step { std::string action; int box; };Describes one recipe line: an action word and a box number.Each step of the toy recipe has this shape.
15std::vector<int> pantry = {7, 5, 0};The pantry: three boxes holding 7, 5 and 0.Toy main memory.
16–17int leftHand = 0;, int rightHand = 0;The chef's two hands, empty at the start.Toy registers.
19–21const std::vector<Step> recipe = { … };The four recipe lines, in order. ADD ignores its box number.The order of these lines is the order of the work.
23for (const Step& step : recipe) {Takes each recipe line in turn.Like a CPU fetching one instruction after another. D1
24–27LOAD_LEFT, LOAD_RIGHTCopies a number from a pantry box into a hand.Load: memory to register.
28–29ADDAdds the right hand to the left hand.The work happens in the hands, not in the pantry.

36–38}, return 0;, }Ends the loop and the program.Zero means success.

Where the analogy breaks

  • The chef chooses what goes on her shelves; a CPU does not. A cache fills and empties by itself, following fixed rules in the hardware. D3
  • "Down the corridor" is about time, not metres. Main memory is not far away in distance. It takes longer to reach because of how it works, not because the CPU walks there. D3
  • A real chef understands food. The CPU does not understand anything. It only follows its instructions very fast, as in F0-01.
  • A pantry does not empty itself at night. Main memory loses everything when the power is off. Only storage keeps it. D3

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
You think a file is saved, but it is gone after the power goes off.It was only in main memory, which forgets without power.Ask: did I save it to storage?Save to storage before switching off.
You mix up "memory" and "storage".People often use the words loosely.Ask: does it keep things with the power off?Yes: storage (warehouse). No: main memory (pantry).
Your toy kitchen gives the wrong answer.A step is in the wrong order, like storing before adding.Trace hands and boxes after every step, as in the worked example.Put the steps in the right order.
You draw the warehouse right next to the chef.The map is about how quick things are to reach.Ask: which is fastest to reach?Hands, then shelves, then pantry, then warehouse.
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-01, F0-02 and F0-04: exact steps, bits, and comparisons and swaps. What carries over: the computer still follows steps exactly, and everything it holds is bits. What changes: now the steps happen in places: numbers must be brought to the CPU's registers before any work, and results must be stored back. Main memory forgets without power; storage does not. D1 D3 What comes next: F0-06 looks closely at the order window and the serving hatch: inputs and outputs.

  1. Match each part to the kitchen: CPU, registers, cache, main memory, storage, bus.
  2. Which keeps your files when the computer is off? (a) registers (b) main memory (c) storage
  3. Why does the chef keep salt on a shelf near the stove? What computer part is like that shelf?

Lab

Be the kitchen

Goal: act out the toy kitchen with people and paper, and get the right answer for 7 + 5 and for a sum of your own.

You need: three paper cups labelled box 0, box 1, box 2; small slips of paper; a pencil; two or three people. No computer is needed.

Safety

None beyond normal paper and pencil work.

  1. One person is the head chef, with two hands. Another is the pantry keeper, with the three cups. A third person, if you have one, reads the recipe aloud.
  2. Write 7 on a slip in box 0, 5 in box 1, and 0 in box 2.
  3. The reader reads one line at a time: LOAD_LEFT 0, LOAD_RIGHT 1, ADD, STORE_LEFT 2.
  4. For LOAD, the chef walks to the pantry keeper, copies the number onto a slip, and holds it in that hand. For ADD, the chef adds in her head and writes the new number on the left-hand slip. For STORE, the chef walks back and puts a copy into the box.
  5. After every line, write the hands and the boxes in a table like the worked example.
  6. Change the numbers and run it again.

What you should see: the chef walks to the pantry for every LOAD and STORE, but not for ADD. That walking is the slow part.

Check you succeeded: your table matches the Listing 1 output for 7 + 5, and box 2 ends with the right sum for your own numbers.

If something goes wrong: box 2 has the wrong number → STORE came too early → check the order. A hand has an old number → a LOAD was skipped → reload. The chef adds in the pantry → remind her: work happens only in the hands.

Extension: write a recipe for 7 + 5 + 4, using a fourth box. How few lines can you use?

Forensic lab

The sum that came out as 7

Scenario. Noor wrote her own toy recipe for 7 + 5. The program ran without errors, but box 2 ended with 7, not 12.

Evidence: real run of Noor's version, kitchen_bad.cpp:

LOAD_LEFT 0  -> hands: 7, 0  pantry boxes: 7, 5, 0
LOAD_RIGHT 1  -> hands: 7, 5  pantry boxes: 7, 5, 0
STORE_LEFT 2  -> hands: 7, 5  pantry boxes: 7, 5, 7
ADD 0  -> hands: 12, 5  pantry boxes: 7, 5, 7

Questions.

  1. At which step does box 2 change? What number goes in?
  2. Give two possible ideas for why the answer is 7.
  3. Does the ADD step work? Look at the hands after it.
  4. Which steps are in the wrong order? Write the correct order.
  5. Why did the program not complain?

Method hints. Read the trace one line at a time. For each line, ask: what was in the left hand at this moment?

Mini-project

Draw your own kitchen map of a computer, like Figure 1, from memory. Label every part twice: with its kitchen name and its computer name. Add one real example of input and one of output from your home. Then explain your map to someone in two minutes.

Rubric (4 points): all seven parts present (1); kitchen and computer names match the map in this chapter (1); closer-is-faster idea shown (1); clear two-minute explanation (1).

Summary

  • The CPU is the head chef: it carries out the steps.
  • Registers are the chef's hands and cutting board: tiny and fastest.
  • The cache is the shelves near the stove: small, fast, filled by the hardware.
  • Main memory is the big pantry: it holds running programs and data, and forgets without power.
  • Storage is the warehouse across town: huge, slowest, keeps files with the power off.
  • The bus is the corridors; input is the order window; output is the serving hatch.
  • Work happens in the registers: load, work, store.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: box 2 changes at the third line, STORE_LEFT 2, and gets 7. The ADD comes last and makes the left hand 12, but nothing stores it afterwards.

Root cause: STORE_LEFT 2 and ADD are in the wrong order. The store copied the left hand before the addition.

Evidence: in the bad run, the line "STORE_LEFT 2 → hands: 7, 5, pantry boxes: 7, 5, 7" comes before "ADD 0 → hands: 12, 5". In Listing 1's run, ADD comes first and box 2 gets 12.

Fix: the order LOAD_LEFT 0, LOAD_RIGHT 1, ADD, STORE_LEFT 2. Run again and check that box 2 holds 12.

Why no complaint: every step was a valid step. The computer did exactly what was written, as in F0-01; only the order was wrong.

How the fault was made: the Lab Engineer swapped the last two recipe lines (line 20) of Listing 1.

Wrong answers and why: "ADD is broken": the trace shows ADD made 12. "The pantry lost the number": box 2 holds exactly what the left hand held at the store. Prevention: trace hands and boxes after every step before trusting the answer.

Story hook

Analogy

Kwame is reading on the sofa. Ding-dong! His ears hear the doorbell. His brain thinks: "That must be Grandma." He calls out with his voice: "Coming!" Then his legs carry him to the door.

Something came in (the sound of the bell). Something happened inside (Kwame thought about it). Something went out (his voice, his legs). In, inside, out.

A computer does the same three things all day long. It takes things in through its "senses", works on them inside, and sends results out through its "voice". This chapter is about the in and the out.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain the input → processing → output pattern with an everyday example.
  • Sort devices into input devices and output devices, and name some that do both.
  • Explain what a sensor does: it measures something and turns it into a number.
  • Trace a night-light program: light level in, decision inside, lamp on or off out.
  • Find whether a fault is in the input, the processing or the output.
Jargon box
Input
Simple words: information that goes into the computer. Analogy: what your ears and eyes take in. Precise: data that a program receives from outside itself, for example from a keyboard, a mouse, a microphone, a sensor or a file. D1
Output
Simple words: information or action that comes out of the computer. Analogy: your voice and your hands. Precise: data or signals that a program sends out, for example to a screen, a speaker, a printer, a lamp, a motor or a file. D1
Processing
Simple words: the work the computer does between the input and the output. Analogy: your thinking: "the bell rang, so it is Grandma". Precise: the steps of the program that turn input data into output data. D2
Sensor
Simple words: a part that measures something about the world, like light or heat, and turns it into a number. Analogy: one of your senses. Precise: a device that responds to a physical quantity (light, temperature, sound, movement) and produces a signal that the computer can read as a value. D3
Device
Simple words: a piece of equipment connected to the computer. Analogy: a tool or helper in the house. Precise: a hardware unit that the computer communicates with, such as a keyboard, screen or sensor. D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the pattern of this chapter: input on the left, processing in the middle, output on the right. The night-light program of this chapter is drawn underneath as an example.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A computer on its own is like a person in a dark, silent room. It can think very fast. But it cannot know anything about the world, and nobody can know what it thought. It needs ways in and ways out.

Ways in: input

Anything that goes into the computer is input. When you press a key, the keyboard sends a number for that key. When you click, the mouse sends where it is and which button. A microphone sends sound, as a list of numbers like the samples in F0-03. A camera sends the colours of many pixels. D1

Each of these is a device: a piece of equipment joined to the computer. Input devices are like the computer's senses.

Ways out: output

Anything that comes out of the computer is output. The screen shows letters and pictures. The speaker plays sounds. A printer puts ink on paper. A computer can also switch on a lamp or turn a motor. Output devices are like the computer's voice and hands. D1

Some devices do both. A touch screen shows pictures (output) and feels your finger (input). A headset has speakers and a microphone.

In between: processing

Between input and output is processing. That is the program, running in the kitchen of F0-05. It reads the input, follows its steps, and makes the output. Without the program, the input would go nowhere. D2

Sensors: senses that measure

Some input devices measure the world. They are called sensors. A light sensor measures how bright it is. A temperature sensor measures how warm it is. Each one turns what it measures into a number the computer can read. D3

Think of a night light. A light sensor says how bright the room is, as a number. The program decides: "Is it dark?" If yes, the output turns the lamp on. In, inside, out, again and again.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Note

For the curious. A sensor does not send "dark" or "bright". It sends a number, and the program decides what the number means. The limit between dark and bright is a choice written in the program. In Listing 1 that choice is 30, on our own made-up scale from 0 to 100. A real light sensor has its own range and units, given in its datasheet. D3 Also, a program's input does not always come from a device. In Listing 1, the "sensor readings" come from a text file, so that everyone gets the same run.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

At this level, the depth waits for later courses. In HW101 you will see how a sensor makes an electrical signal, and in the F1 and F4 faculties how the CPU talks to devices through the bus. Keep this: devices send and receive numbers; programs give them meaning. D1

How the hardware actually does it

Every device is connected to the computer, by wires or by radio. Input devices turn something from the world, a key press or light, into electrical signals that become numbers in memory. Output devices do the reverse: the computer sends numbers, and the device turns them into light, sound or movement. The CPU reaches the devices through the bus, the corridors of F0-05. D1 D3

Worked example

Trace the night light by hand. The limit is 30. The rule is: if the light level is less than 30, lamp ON; otherwise, lamp off.

Input: light levelProcessing: is it less than 30?Output
80 (sunny room)Nolamp off
31No (31 is more than 30)lamp off
30No (30 is not less than 30)lamp off
12 (evening)Yeslamp ON
0 (dark)Yeslamp ON

Look closely at 30. It is exactly on the limit. "Less than 30" means 29 or below, so 30 gives "off". Edge cases like this are where many mistakes hide. The real run of Listing 1 gives the same outputs. R1

Code walk-through

Real coding starts in KID102. Here is the night light as a tiny program. It uses an if, a choice; F0-07 explains choices properly.

Listing 1 — night_light.cpp. Its input file night_light.in holds six pretend sensor readings: 80, 55, 31, 30, 12 and 0.

#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    const int darkLimit = 30;
    int light = 0;
    while (std::cin >> light) {
        std::cout << "input: light level " << light << "  ->  output: ";
        if (light < darkLimit) {
            std::cout << "lamp ON\n";
        } else {
            std::cout << "lamp off\n";
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined night_light.cpp -o night_light, run as ./night_light < night_light.in.

input: light level 80  ->  output: lamp off
input: light level 55  ->  output: lamp off
input: light level 31  ->  output: lamp off
input: light level 30  ->  output: lamp off
input: light level 12  ->  output: lamp ON
input: light level 0  ->  output: lamp ON

LinesCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1#include <iostream>Brings in the tools for input and output.std::cin reads input; std::cout writes output. D4
3–4int main(), {The program starts here.As in every listing.
5const int darkLimit = 30;Stores the limit, 30, with a name.The meaning of "dark" is a choice made in the program.
6int light = 0;A place for one light reading.Each new reading goes here.
7while (std::cin >> light) {Reads the next number from the input. Repeats while there are numbers.This is the input step.
8std::cout << "input: light level " …Prints the reading.So you can see what came in.
9if (light < darkLimit) {Asks: is the reading less than the limit?This is the processing step: the decision.
10std::cout << "lamp ON\n";If yes: output "lamp ON".In a real night light, this would switch the lamp.
11–13} else { … "lamp off" … }If no: output "lamp off".Every reading gets exactly one output.
14–16}, return 0;, }Ends the loop and the program.Zero means success.

Where the analogy breaks

  • Your senses come with meaning; a sensor does not. When you see darkness, you know it is dark. A light sensor gives only a number. The program decides what counts as dark. D3
  • You can tell when your eyes are tired. A broken or dirty sensor still sends numbers, and the program may trust wrong ones. Real sensors can be noisy or off by some amount; you will measure that in later courses.
  • Your voice and hands are part of you. A computer's outputs are separate devices. If the speaker is unplugged, the program still "says" its sound, and nobody hears it.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Nothing happens when you type.The input device is not connected, or the program is not reading input.Check one step at a time: is the input arriving?Reconnect, or make the program read.
The program works, but you see nothing.The output device is off or unplugged.Check the output on its own.Switch it on or plug it in.
The lamp does the opposite of what it should.The decision is flipped.Make a table of inputs and outputs, as in the worked example.Fix the decision in the processing.
It works for 80 and 0, but is wrong exactly at 30.The edge case: "less than" versus "less than or equal".Test the limit itself and the numbers next to it.Decide what the limit should do, and write it exactly.
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-05: the kitchen inside the computer, with the order window (input) and the serving hatch (output). What carries over: the CPU and memory do the processing; everything is still numbers. What changes: now the computer meets the real world: devices turn the world into numbers and numbers into light, sound and movement. A sensor gives only numbers; the program decides what they mean. D1 D3 What comes next: F0-07 looks at the "if" in the middle: decisions and loops, without a computer.

Check yourself

  1. Sort these into input and output: keyboard, screen, microphone, speaker, mouse, printer.
  2. Name one device that does both input and output.
  3. What does a light sensor give the computer? (a) the word "dark" (b) a number (c) a picture of the room
  4. In the night light, what output does a reading of 29 give? And 30?
  5. Explain in your own words the three parts: input, processing, output.
  6. Apply it to a new case: a microwave oven. Name one input, the processing, and one output.
  7. The lamp is on in the daytime. Which part might be wrong? Give two possibilities.

Lab

Input–processing–output hunt

Goal: find five machines at home or school and describe each one as input → processing → output.

You need: paper, a pencil, and a grown-up to walk around with you. No computer is needed.

Safety

Look, do not open. Never open a machine, touch wires, or poke into sockets or vents. Ask a grown-up before pressing buttons on any machine.

  1. Draw a table with four columns: machine, input, processing, output.
  2. Find five machines, for example a doorbell, a lift, a washing machine, a phone, a street crossing button.
  3. For each one, write what goes in (a button, a sound, a temperature), what it decides, and what comes out.
  4. Mark any input that comes from a sensor with an "S".
  5. Choose one machine and play "be the machine": a friend gives you inputs, you say the outputs.

What you should see: almost every machine has the same three parts. Many have sensors you did not notice before.

Check you succeeded: five complete rows, and a friend agrees with your input and output for each.

If something goes wrong: you cannot tell the input → ask "what makes it start?". You cannot tell the output → ask "what changes when it works?". You are not sure about the processing → write what it seems to decide, and mark it with "?".

Extension: write the night-light rule for a fan instead: what is the input, what is the limit, and what is the output?

  2. Is the problem in the input, the processing or the output? Give your reasons.
  3. Which line causes it?
  4. Look at the reading 30. Why is the output the same in both runs?
  5. How would you fix Leo's program, and how would you check the fix?

Method hints. Line up the two runs reading by reading. If the inputs match and the outputs differ, where must the difference be?

Mini-project

Invent a helpful home machine on paper, like a plant-watering helper. Draw it as input → processing → output, like Figure 1. Write its rule as one sentence with a limit, for example "if the soil wetness is less than 20, water for a short time". Make a table of five test inputs, including the limit itself, and the outputs you expect.

Rubric (4 points): clear input, processing and output (1); rule with an exact limit (1); five test inputs including the edge case (1); expected outputs match the rule (1).

Summary

  • Computers work in three parts: input, processing, output.
  • Input devices are the computer's senses: keyboard, mouse, microphone, camera, sensors.
  • Output devices are its voice and hands: screen, speaker, printer, lamp, motor.
  • Some devices do both, like a touch screen.
  • A sensor turns something it measures into a number.
  • The program decides what the numbers mean, and limits are choices written in the program.
  • To find a fault, check input, processing and output one at a time.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Input: keyboard, microphone, mouse. Output: screen, speaker, printer.
  2. A touch screen, or a headset with a microphone. Other correct answers are fine.
  3. (b) a number. (a) is wrong: the program decides what is "dark". (c) is what a camera gives, not a light sensor.
  4. 29: lamp ON, because 29 is less than 30. 30: lamp off, because 30 is not less than 30.
  5. Your own words. A good answer: input is what comes in; processing is the program working on it; output is what comes out.
  6. Example: input = the buttons you press (time, start) and the door sensor; processing = the program counts down the time; output = the heating, the light inside, the beep.
  7. Two possibilities: the decision is flipped (processing), or the sensor gives wrong numbers (input). The forensic lab shows how to tell them apart.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: both runs show the same six inputs (80, 55, 31, 30, 12, 0). Leo's outputs are ON for 80, 55 and 31, and off for 30, 12 and 0. Listing 1 gives the opposite for every reading except 30.

Root cause: processing. Line 9 of Leo's program uses "greater than" (>) instead of "less than" (<), so the decision is flipped.

Why not input or output: the input lines are identical in both runs, so the sensor readings are not the cause. The output prints both "lamp ON" and "lamp off" when asked, so the output works.

Why 30 is the same: 30 is neither less than 30 nor greater than 30, so both programs choose the "else" branch: lamp off.

Fix and check: change line 9 to if (light < darkLimit) {; run again with the same input and compare with the worked-example table.

How the fault was made: the Lab Engineer copied Listing 1 and changed only the comparison on line 9.

Wrong answers and why: "The sensor is upside down": the inputs are the same as in the good run. "The lamp is broken": the program printed both outputs. Prevention: test with a dark reading, a bright reading and the limit itself before using a new program.

Story hook

Analogy

Sofia is making hot chocolate with her dad. The recipe card says: "Stir 20 times." She counts out loud: one, two, three… all the way to twenty. Then she stops.

Next, the card says: "Add milk, one spoon at a time, until the cup is full." Sofia does not know how many spoons that will be. So she adds one, looks, adds another, looks again. When the cup is full, she stops.

Last line: "If it is too hot, wait one minute." Sofia touches the cup. It is warm, not hot. So she skips the waiting and drinks.

That one small recipe had three big ideas: repeat a number of times, repeat until something is true, and choose what to do. Every computer program is built from these ideas. You can learn them with no computer at all.

What you will be able to do

  • Write a decision as an "if … then … otherwise …" step with a yes-or-no question.
  • Write a loop that repeats a fixed number of times, and one that repeats until something is true.
  • Explain why a loop that never changes its question runs forever.
  • Add two small binary numbers on paper by following written rules (the paper computer).
  • Find the cause of a loop that never ends from its output.
Jargon box
Condition
Simple words: a question whose answer is yes or no. Analogy: "Is the cup full?" Precise: an expression that is either true or false, used to decide which step comes next. D1
Decision
Simple words: a step that chooses what to do, using a yes-or-no question. Analogy: "If it is too hot, wait one minute." Precise: a branch in an algorithm: if the condition is true, one set of steps runs; otherwise another set (or nothing) runs. In C++ it is written with if and else. D1 D3
Loop
Simple words: steps that are repeated. Analogy: "Stir 20 times." Precise: a part of an algorithm that runs again and again, either a set number of times or while a condition stays true. In C++, for and while make loops. D1 D3
Infinite loop
Simple words: a loop that never stops. Analogy: "Add milk until the cup is full", but nobody ever adds milk. Precise: a loop whose condition never becomes false, usually because nothing inside the loop changes what the condition tests. D1
Carry
Simple words: the extra 1 you pass to the next column when a column adds up to too much. Analogy: when 9 + 3 = 12, you write 2 and "carry the 1". Precise: the value moved into the next place when the sum of one place is at least the base (10 in decimal, 2 in binary). D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 draws "add milk until the cup is full" as a flowchart. Boxes are actions. The diamond is a decision. Follow the arrows with your finger.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

In F0-01, every algorithm went straight from the first step to the last. Real recipes are not always like that. Sometimes you repeat. Sometimes you choose. A computer can do both, as long as you write exactly how.

Decisions: if, otherwise

A decision is a step that chooses. It always starts with a yes-or-no question, called a condition. "If it is raining, take an umbrella. Otherwise, take a cap." The question is "Is it raining?" The answer picks one path. D1

The question must have a clear yes or no. "Is it cold?" is unclear: cold for whom? "Is the temperature below 10?" is clear. You saw this in the night light of F0-06: "Is the light level less than 30?"

Loops: repeat a number of times

A loop repeats steps. "Stir 20 times" is the simplest kind. You know before you start how many times. You count each one and stop at 20. D1

Loops: repeat until something is true

"Add milk until the cup is full" is a different kind. You do not know how many spoons. So each time round, you ask a question: "Is the cup full?" If no, add a spoon and ask again. If yes, stop. Figure 1 draws this loop.

Look at the question in Figure 1. Each time you add a spoon, the answer gets closer to "yes". That is what makes the loop end. D1

The loop that never ends

Now imagine a helper who asks "Is the cup full?" but never adds any milk. The answer is always "no". The helper asks forever. That is an infinite loop. A person would notice and stop. A computer does not notice. It keeps asking until someone stops the program. D1 R1

Here is the rule for every "until" loop. Something inside the loop must change what the question looks at.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Note

For the curious. With three tools, steps in order, decisions and loops, you can already write a great many algorithms. Inside the computer, both decisions and loops are made from one kind of instruction: "jump to another step if a condition is true". A loop is a jump backwards. A decision is a jump forwards over steps you skip. D2 You will write if, for and while yourself in F0-32 and F0-33.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

At this level, the depth waits for KID102 (writing loops and decisions in C++) and HW102 (the jump instructions and the adder circuits that do what our paper computer does). Keep this habit: for every loop, say what makes it end. D2

How the hardware actually does it

The CPU answers a condition by comparing two numbers, such as "spoons" and 4, and remembering the yes-or-no result. A following "jump if" instruction then goes either back to the top of the loop or on to the next step. Adding binary numbers is done by circuits that follow rules like the ones in our worked example, column by column, with a carry. D2

Worked example

The paper computer adds 5 + 3

This is the heart of the course project. The paper computer adds two four-switch numbers using only these written rules. Work from the right-hand column to the left. In each column, count the 1s: the two bits plus the carry from the column before (start with carry 0).

Number of 1s in the columnWrite in the answerCarry to the next column
000
110
201
311

5 is 0101 and 3 is 0011, as in F0-02.

ColumnBitsCarry in1sWriteCarry out
1s1 and 10201
2s0 and 11201
4s1 and 01201
8s0 and 01110

The last carry out is 0. Put it in front: 0 1000, which is 8. And 5 + 3 = 8. The rules worked!

Notice the shape: a loop ("for each column, from right to left") with decisions inside ("if there are 2 ones, write 0 and carry 1"). Listing 2 follows exactly these rules. Its real run printed 0101 + 0011 = 01000, then tested all 256 pairs of four-switch numbers against ordinary adding and found 0 wrong. R1

Code walk-through

Real coding starts in KID102. These programs show the same ideas you did by hand.

Listing 1 — stir_and_fill.cpp: a "repeat 5 times" loop, then an "until full" loop with a decision inside.

#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    for (int stir = 1; stir <= 5; ++stir) {
        std::cout << "stir number " << stir << '\n';
    }

    const int full = 4;
    int spoons = 0;
    while (spoons < full) {
        spoons = spoons + 1;
        std::cout << "added a spoon of water, cup has " << spoons << '\n';
        if (spoons == full - 1) {
            std::cout << "  almost full: go slowly\n";
        }
    }
    std::cout << "cup is full\n";
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined stir_and_fill.cpp -o stir_and_fill

Listing 2 — add_rules.cpp: the paper computer's rules, checked against every pair of four-switch numbers.

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

// Adds two 4-switch numbers using only the written rules of the paper computer.
std::string addByRules(const std::string& a, const std::string& b)
{
    std::string answer = "0000";
    int carry = 0;
    for (int column = 3; column >= 0; --column) {
        const int ones = (a[column] == '1') + (b[column] == '1') + carry;
        if (ones == 0) { answer[column] = '0'; carry = 0; }
        if (ones == 1) { answer[column] = '1'; carry = 0; }
        if (ones == 2) { answer[column] = '0'; carry = 1; }
        if (ones == 3) { answer[column] = '1'; carry = 1; }
    }
    return std::to_string(carry) + answer;
}

std::string fourSwitches(int n)
{
    std::string s;
    for (const int value : {8, 4, 2, 1}) {
        if (n >= value) { s += '1'; n = n - value; } else { s += '0'; }
    }
    return s;
}

int main()
{
    std::cout << "0101 + 0011 = " << addByRules("0101", "0011") << '\n';

    int checked = 0;
    int wrong = 0;
    for (int x = 0; x <= 15; ++x) {
        for (int y = 0; y <= 15; ++y) {
            const std::string sum = addByRules(fourSwitches(x), fourSwitches(y));
            const int expected = x + y;
            const std::string expectedBits = (expected >= 16 ? "1" : "0") + fourSwitches(expected % 16);
            checked = checked + 1;
            if (sum != expectedBits) { wrong = wrong + 1; }
        }
    }
    std::cout << "checked " << checked << " sums, " << wrong << " wrong\n";
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined add_rules.cpp -o add_rules

checked 256 sums, 0 wrong

10ones = (a[column] == '1') + (b[column] == '1') + carry;Counts the 1s in this column, plus the carry.Each yes counts as 1, each no as 0.

Where the analogy breaks

  • A cook would stop. If Sofia added no milk, she would notice after a few tries. A computer running a loop that forgets to change its condition keeps going until someone stops the program. R1
  • "Full" is a feeling for a person. Sofia looks at the cup and judges. A computer needs an exact test, such as "spoons is 4 or more". If the test is fuzzy, it cannot be written at all.
  • People skip pointless steps. If the cup was already full, Sofia would not even ask. A computer asks the question every time, exactly as written.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
The loop never ends; the same line repeats with the same number.Nothing inside the loop changes what the condition tests.Look at the printed numbers: does the tested value change?Add the step that moves it towards the end.
The loop runs one time too many or too few."Less than" and "less than or equal" were mixed up.Count the outputs; test the edge case by hand.Choose the exact test (see F0-08).
The decision always picks the same path.The question can never be true, or is always true.Try inputs on both sides of the limit.Fix the question.
Binary adding gives a wrong answer.A carry was forgotten.Write the carry above each column, as in the worked example.Count the carry as one of the 1s.
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-01 (steps in order), F0-02 (binary) and F0-06 (a decision in the night light). What carries over: steps are still exact and done in order. What changes: now an algorithm can jump: repeat steps (loops) and skip steps (decisions). The most dangerous new mistake is a loop that never ends; next is a loop that runs one time too many or too few. D2 What comes next: F0-08 teaches you to be a code detective and hunt such bugs.

Check yourself

  1. Which is a good condition for a computer? (a) "Is it late?" (b) "Is the time after 20:00?" (c) "Should I go to bed?"
  2. What is the difference between "stir 20 times" and "add milk until full"?
  3. Explain in your own words why a loop can run forever.
  4. Add 6 + 7 with the paper computer's rules: 0110 + 0111. Show each column.
  5. In Listing 1, which line makes the "until full" loop end?
  6. Apply it to a new case: write a loop and a decision for brushing teeth: "brush each of the 4 sides of your mouth; if a side still feels rough, brush it again".
  7. Look at Figure 1. What would happen if the "add one spoon" box were missing?

Lab

Run the paper computer

Goal: add small binary numbers by following only the written rules, as the course project's paper computer will.

You need: paper, a pencil, two four-switch boards and one five-switch answer board from the F0-02 mini-project (or draw them), a friend.

Safety

None beyond normal paper and pencil work.

  1. Copy the rule table from the worked example onto a card. This card is the paper computer's "program".
  2. Your friend picks two numbers from 0 to 15 and writes them in binary on the two boards.
  3. Follow the card exactly, column by column from right to left. Write the carry above the next column each time.
  4. Read the answer board as a number, using place values 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
  5. Check by adding the two numbers in the usual way.
  6. Do at least five sums, including 15 + 15 and 0 + 0.

What you should see: the rules always give the right answer, even though you never "add" in your head; you only count 1s and look up the card. That is how a machine can add without understanding.

Check you succeeded: five sums correct, and 15 + 15 gives 11110, which is 30.

If something goes wrong: answer too small → a carry was lost → write carries above columns. Answer has only four switches → you forgot the last carry → put it in front. Your number board is wrong → check it with F0-02.

Extension: write the "stir 20 times" and "until full" loops as flowcharts, like Figure 1, and test them with a friend acting as the computer.

Forensic lab

The cup that never fills

Scenario. Musa wrote a program to fill a cup with four spoons of water. He ran it, waited, and nothing finished. The university's lab runner stops any program after a time limit, so it stopped Musa's program after 3 seconds.

Evidence: the real output of Musa's program, fill_forgot.cpp, with the run record. Exit code 124 is how the runner reports "stopped by the time limit".

start filling the cup
still not full, cup has 0
still not full, cup has 0
still not full, cup has 0
still not full, cup has 0
still not full, cup has 0
still not full, cup has 0

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-07/fill_forgot.out; run record fill_forgot.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:31:39Z; exit code: 124 (stopped by the 3 s time limit).

Musa's program (his loop is lines 10 to 13):

#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

int main()
{
    const int full = 4;
    int spoons = 0;
    std::cout << "start filling the cup" << std::endl;
    while (spoons < full) {
        std::cout << "still not full, cup has " << spoons << std::endl;
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(500));
    }
    std::cout << "cup is full" << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Questions.

  1. What number does every "still not full" line show? What should happen to it?
  2. Did the line "cup is full" ever print? What does that tell you?
  3. Give two possible ideas for why the program never ends.
  4. Compare Musa's loop with lines 11 to 17 of Listing 1. Which line is missing?
  5. How would you fix it, and how would you check that the fix works?

Method hints. In a loop that never ends, look at the value the condition tests. Does anything inside the loop change it?

Mini-project

Design a "morning routine" algorithm with at least one counted loop, one "until" loop and two decisions. Draw it as a flowchart like Figure 1. Then test it: a friend follows the flowchart with your choices of weather and time.

Rubric (4 points): one counted loop and one "until" loop (1); two decisions with clear yes-or-no questions (1); every "until" loop has a step that makes it end (1); a friend followed it without questions (1).

Summary

  • A condition is a yes-or-no question; a decision uses it to choose what to do.
  • A loop repeats steps: a set number of times, or until something is true.
  • Something inside an "until" loop must change what the question looks at, or the loop never ends.
  • Decisions and loops are jumps: forwards to skip, backwards to repeat.
  • The paper computer adds binary numbers with a loop over columns and four rules.
  • A machine can add correctly by following rules, without understanding.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. (b). It has an exact yes-or-no answer. (a) "late" means different things to different people. (c) is a decision, not a question that can be checked.
  2. "Stir 20 times" repeats a known number of times. "Until full" repeats an unknown number of times and asks a question each time.
  3. Your own words. A good answer: if nothing inside the loop changes what the question looks at, the answer never changes, so the loop never stops.
  4. 1s column: 0 and 1, carry 0 → one 1 → write 1, carry 0. 2s: 1 and 1, carry 0 → two → write 0, carry 1. 4s: 1 and 1, carry 1 → three → write 1, carry 1. 8s: 0 and 0, carry 1 → one → write 1, carry 0. Answer 01101 = 8 + 4 + 1 = 13. And 6 + 7 = 13.
  5. Line 12, spoons = spoons + 1;.
  6. Example: "For each of the 4 sides: brush the side. Repeat until it feels smooth: if it still feels rough, brush it again." Any version with a counted loop and a question is fine.
  7. The number of spoons would stay 0, the answer would always be "no", and the loop would never end.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: every "still not full" line says "cup has 0". "cup is full" never printed. The run record says exit code 124: the program was stopped by the time limit, not finished.

Root cause: the loop has no step that adds a spoon. spoons stays 0, so spoons < full is always true and the loop never ends.

Evidence: Listing 1 has spoons = spoons + 1; inside its loop (line 12) and its output counts 1, 2, 3, 4. Musa's loop has only the print and a short wait.

Fix and check: add spoons = spoons + 1; inside the loop. The run should then print the cup filling to 4, print "cup is full", and end with exit code 0.

How the fault was made: the Lab Engineer wrote the loop without the adding step. The short wait (line 12 of Musa's file) slows the printing so the evidence stays short.

Wrong answers and why: "The computer is too slow": in 3 seconds it printed the same value many times, so it was running, only never changing. "The limit 4 is too big": even a limit of 1 would never be reached from 0 without adding. Prevention: for every "until" loop, point to the line that moves it towards the end.

Bugs: being a code detective

← F0-07 · course KID101 · catalogue · F0-09 →

Story-level preparation for HW101–HW102; no curriculum milestone

Story hook

Analogy

Hana's family has a recipe for banana bread. This time it comes out of the oven flat and salty. Everyone is puzzled. Her uncle says, "The oven is broken!" Her cousin says, "The bananas were bad!"

Hana does not guess. She gets out the recipe card and reads it, line by line. Then she checks the salt jar and the sugar jar. The labels have been swapped! The recipe was right. The ingredients were not what the labels said.

Hana did not shout the first idea that came to mind. She collected clues. She tested each idea. She found the real cause, and she fixed it. That is exactly what programmers do when a program goes wrong. They become detectives.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a bug is: the program does what was written, not what was meant.
  • Use the detective method: symptom, guesses, test, cause, fix, check, prevent.
  • Spot an off-by-one bug in a counting loop.
  • Trace a robot's route step by step and find the first step where it goes wrong.
  • Write a short bug report that someone else can act on.
Jargon box
Bug
Simple words: a mistake that makes a program do the wrong thing. Analogy: a mistake in the recipe. Precise: a fault in a program (or in the data, the hardware or another program it depends on) that makes it behave differently from what was intended. D1
Debugging
Simple words: finding and fixing bugs. Analogy: Hana checking the recipe and the jars. Precise: the process of locating the cause of a wrong behaviour, correcting it, and checking that the correction works. D1
Symptom
Simple words: what you notice is wrong. Analogy: "the bread is flat and salty". Precise: an observable sign of a fault, such as wrong output, a crash or a program that never ends; it is not the cause itself. D1
Root cause
Simple words: the real reason behind the symptom. Analogy: the swapped jar labels. Precise: the underlying fault that, once fixed, makes the symptom go away and stay away. D1
Test
Simple words: a small try that checks if something works. Analogy: tasting a pinch from each jar. Precise: running a program (or part of it) with chosen inputs and comparing what it does with what it should do. D1
Off-by-one error
Simple words: a mistake where something happens one time too many or one time too few. Analogy: stirring 19 times when the recipe says 20. Precise: a bug in which a count, a limit or a position is wrong by exactly one, often from choosing "less than" instead of "less than or equal". D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the detective method as a circle of steps. You go round it once for each bug. If the check fails, you go round again.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A bug is a mistake that makes a program do the wrong thing. Remember F0-01: the computer does exactly what is written. So when a program goes wrong, the computer is usually doing what we wrote. We wrote something different from what we meant. D1

Bugs are normal. Everyone who writes programs makes them, including the people who wrote this course. What matters is how calmly and cleverly you find them. Finding and fixing bugs is called debugging.

Clues first, guesses second

The thing you notice is the symptom. "The bread is flat." "The program prints 9 numbers, not 10." A symptom is a clue, not the answer. The real reason is the root cause. Hana's symptom was salty bread; the root cause was swapped labels. D1

A good detective makes at least two guesses before deciding. Then they test one guess at a time. A test is a small try with a known right answer. If the result matches the guess, good. If not, cross that guess off and try the next.

The bug with a famous name

One bug is so common that it has its own name: the off-by-one error. Something happens one time too many or one time too few. You want to print 1 to 10, and you get 1 to 9. You fence a garden with 10 metres of fence and posts every metre, and you buy 10 posts instead of 11. D2

Off-by-one errors hide at the edges: the first item, the last item, the limit. That is why good testers always test the edges.

Fix, check, prevent

When you find the cause, fix it. Then run the same test again. Did the symptom go away? If not, back to guessing. If yes, do one last thing: keep that test, so the bug can never sneak back without you noticing.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Note

For the curious. A true story from building this course. One of our own lab programs, the postcard program of F0-09, had a bug in its first version: it tried to read a fifth postcard when the message had only made four. A checking tool that the university's lab runner switches on for every program, called AddressSanitizer, stopped the program and reported a read outside the list. We changed the message and made the program check the card number. The finished version is the one in F0-09. Tools like this are detective helpers; you will use them from KID102 on. D3

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

At this level, the depth waits for F0-36 (reading compiler errors) and F0-37 (the debugger, which pauses a program so you can look inside). Later faculties use the same detective method on crash dumps, slow boots and GPU programs. Keep one rule: never fix what you have not first explained with evidence.

How the hardware actually does it

Most bugs live in the program: the computer carried out wrong steps correctly. But not all. Some faults come from the hardware, from wrong data, or from another program. A detective keeps all of these on the list of guesses, and lets the evidence decide. D1

Worked example

The poster that stopped at 9

Ali wants a poster with the numbers 1 to 10. His program (Listing 1) prints only 1 to 9. Let us use the detective method.

  1. Symptom: the output is "1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9". The 10 is missing. Nothing else is wrong. R1
  2. Guesses: (a) the loop starts at the wrong number; (b) the loop stops too early; (c) the printing drops the last number.
  3. Test guess (a): the output starts with 1. So the start is right. Cross off (a).
  4. Test guess (b): read the loop's condition: n < 10. Try it by hand at the edge. When n is 9: is 9 less than 10? Yes, print 9. When n is 10: is 10 less than 10? No, stop. So 10 is never printed. Guess (b) explains the symptom exactly.
  5. Root cause: the condition says "less than 10" but Ali meant "up to and including 10". An off-by-one error.
  6. Fix: change it to n <= 10 ("less than or equal to 10").
  7. Check: the fixed program prints 1 to 10. R1
  8. Prevent: a test that counts the numbers printed: there must be exactly 10.

Code walk-through

Real coding starts in KID102. Here is Ali's program, with the bug, and the one-character fix.

Listing 1 — count_bug.cpp

#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    // Goal: print the numbers 1 to 10 for a number poster.
    for (int n = 1; n < 10; ++n) {
        std::cout << n << ' ';
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined count_bug.cpp -o count_bug

1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-08/count_bug.out; run record count_bug.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:31:43Z; exit code: 0.

LinesCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–4#include <iostream>, int main()Printing tools and the start of the program.As in every listing.
5// Goal: print the numbers 1 to 10 …A comment: what Ali meant.Writing the goal down lets you compare it with the output.
6for (int n = 1; n < 10; ++n) {Counts n from 1, while n is less than 10.The bug: when n reaches 10, the loop stops before printing it. D4
7–8std::cout << n << ' ';, }Prints the number and a space.One number per time round the loop.
9–11std::cout << '\n';, return 0;, }Ends the line and the program.Zero means success, even though the output is wrong: the computer cannot know what Ali meant.

Listing 2 — count_fixed.cpp: the same file with one change on line 6, n <= 10.

#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    // Goal: print the numbers 1 to 10 for a number poster.
    for (int n = 1; n <= 10; ++n) {
        std::cout << n << ' ';
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined count_fixed.cpp -o count_fixed
