Story hook

Analogy

Grandma Rosa keeps her buttons in a tin. Her grandson Kai wants to tell his friend how many buttons there are, using only the hallway switches from F0-20. There are 45 buttons.

Kai looks at the switches: 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. "Which switches do I turn on to make 45?" he wonders. He tries the big one first. 32 fits. 13 buttons are left over. 16 is too big. 8 fits, so 5 are left. 4 fits, so 1 is left. 2 is too big. 1 fits. Done!

Kai turned on 32, 8, 4 and 1. The row reads 101101. His friend reads it back by adding the switches that are on. Both of them get 45. In this chapter you will learn two quick ways to go from a number to switches, and two quick ways back.

What you will be able to do

  • Convert a decimal number up to 255 into binary, by taking away place values.
  • Convert a decimal number into binary by dividing by 2 and reading the remainders.
  • Convert a binary number into decimal, by adding place values or by doubling.
  • Name the least significant bit and the most significant bit of a binary number.
  • Diagnose a converter that writes its bits in the wrong order (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Decimal
Simple words: the everyday way of writing numbers with the ten digits 0 to 9. Analogy: a dial with ten positions instead of a switch with two. Precise: the base-10 place-value number system; each position is worth ten times the one to its right. W1
Least significant bit (LSB)
Simple words: the bit on the far right, worth 1. Analogy: the switch at the right end of the hallway, the one that flips most often. Precise: the bit with the smallest place value, 20 = 1; it decides whether the number is odd (1) or even (0). W1
Most significant bit (MSB)
Simple words: the bit on the far left, worth the most. Analogy: the switch at the left end, the one with the biggest number written above it. Precise: the bit with the largest place value in a number of a given width; in 8 bits it is worth 27 = 128. W1
Remainder
Simple words: what is left over after sharing out equally. Analogy: sharing buttons between two jars: if one button is left over, the remainder is 1. Precise: for whole numbers, n = 2 × q + r with r equal to 0 or 1 when dividing by 2; in C++ the operator % gives the remainder and / between whole numbers gives the whole-number quotient q. W1 R1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the "divide by 2" method for 45. Each row halves the number and writes down the remainder. You then read the remainders from the bottom up. The bottom remainder is the most significant bit.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

There are two easy ways to turn a number into switches. The first is Kai's way: take away the biggest place value that fits. Turn that switch on. Then do the same with what is left. Switches you skip stay off.

The second way is halving. Split the buttons into two equal piles. Is one button left over? Write 1. Nothing left over? Write 0. Keep one pile, and halve it again. Stop when nothing is left to halve.

The leftover buttons are the bits. But the first leftover belongs to the switch worth 1, on the right. So you write each new bit on the left of the ones you already have. Or you read your list from the bottom up, as in Figure 1.

Going back is easy too. Add the place values of the switches that are on, as in F0-20. There is also a fun "doubling" way. Start at zero. Read the bits from the left. For each bit, double what you have, then add the bit. When the bits run out, you have the answer.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Subtracting place values. List the place values up to the first one bigger than your number. Go from the largest down. If the place value fits in what is left, write 1 and subtract it; otherwise write 0. Each number has exactly one binary pattern, so you always reach 0. W1

Repeated division by 2. Any whole number n can be written as n = 2 × q + r, where r is 0 or 1. The remainder r is the least significant bit (LSB): it says whether n is odd. The quotient q holds all the other bits, shifted one place to the right. So you repeat the step on q. The last remainder you get is the most significant bit (MSB). W1 R1

Adding place values. A binary number is the sum of the place values of its 1 bits. You already know this from F0-20. W1

Doubling (left to right). Read the bits from the MSB. Keep a running value. For each bit: value = value × 2 + bit. Doubling moves every bit already read one place to the left. That is the same as multiplying it by 2. So by the end, each bit has been doubled exactly the right number of times. W1 R1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. The doubling method is known as Horner's rule (name to be confirmed against D1). It needs no table of powers: only "multiply by the base and add". It works for any base, so the same loop reads decimal text (value × 10 + digit) or hexadecimal text (value × 16 + digit, F0-22). Programs that read numbers typed by a user work this way. Division by 2 and multiplication by 2 are also exactly a shift right and a shift left by one bit; F0-25 uses that. W1 D1

How the hardware actually does it

A computer does not convert its numbers to binary: they are binary from the start. Conversion happens at the edges. When you type "45", the keyboard sends the characters '4' and '5'; a program turns those into bits with the doubling rule. When the program prints a number, it turns bits back into decimal characters with the division rule. The circuits that do the arithmetic itself are built in HW102. D1 D2

Worked example

45 to binary, by subtracting place values

Place valueFits in what is left?BitLeft over
3245 ≥ 32: yes145 − 32 = 13
1613 ≥ 16: no013
813 ≥ 8: yes113 − 8 = 5
45 ≥ 4: yes15 − 4 = 1
21 ≥ 2: no01
11 ≥ 1: yes10

Reading the bit column from top to bottom: 101101. The division method in Figure 1 gives the same answer. W1

200 to binary, by dividing by 2

200 ÷ 2 = 100 r 0; 100 ÷ 2 = 50 r 0; 50 ÷ 2 = 25 r 0; 25 ÷ 2 = 12 r 1; 12 ÷ 2 = 6 r 0; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 r 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 r 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1. Reading the remainders from the last to the first: 11001000. Check: 128 + 64 + 8 = 200. It needs all eight bits. W1

10110 to decimal, by doubling

Start with 0. Read 1: 0 × 2 + 1 = 1. Read 0: 1 × 2 + 0 = 2. Read 1: 2 × 2 + 1 = 5. Read 1: 5 × 2 + 1 = 11. Read 0: 11 × 2 + 0 = 22. Check with place values: 16 + 4 + 2 = 22. W1

All three answers are confirmed by the real run of Listing 1 below. R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 does the Worked example for you and prints every step. You only need to read it; writing C++ starts in KID102.

Listing 1 — convert.cpp

// Decimal to binary by dividing by 2, and binary to decimal by doubling.
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

std::string toBinary(int number)
{
    if (number == 0) {
        return "0";
    }
    std::string bits;
    while (number > 0) {
        int remainder = number % 2;
        std::cout << "  " << number << " / 2 = " << number / 2
                  << " remainder " << remainder << '\n';
        bits = std::to_string(remainder) + bits;  // new bit goes on the LEFT
        number = number / 2;
    }
    return bits;
}

int toDecimal(const std::string& bits)
{
    int value = 0;
    for (char bit : bits) {
        value = value * 2 + (bit - '0');  // double what you have, add the new bit
        std::cout << "  read " << bit << ", value is now " << value << '\n';
    }
    return value;
}

int main()
{
    std::cout << "45 to binary:\n";
    const std::string a = toBinary(45);
    std::cout << "45 = " << a << " in binary\n\n";

    std::cout << "200 to binary:\n";
    const std::string b = toBinary(200);
    std::cout << "200 = " << b << " in binary\n\n";

    std::cout << "10110 to decimal:\n";
    const int c = toDecimal("10110");
    std::cout << "10110 = " << c << " in decimal\n";
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Halving buttons always works; halving in a computer drops the remainder. With real buttons, the leftover one sits on the table where you can see it. In C++, 45 / 2 is 22 and the leftover disappears unless you ask for it with %. If you forget, you lose a bit. R1
  • Kai can see all the switches at once; the division method produces them backwards. In the hallway every switch has a fixed place. The division method gives you the rightmost bit first, so you must put each new bit on the left. Forgetting this is exactly the bug in the forensic lab. R2
  • Real buttons can be any number; a computer's row has a fixed length. 200 needs eight switches. A number like 300 would need nine, and would overflow an 8-bit row (F0-20). W1

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
6 comes out as 011 (the forensic lab's real output).Remainders written left to right in the order they came.Convert your answer back; does it give the starting number?Read remainders from the bottom up, or put each new bit on the left.
A bit is missing: 45 becomes 10110.A division step was skipped or the last "1 ÷ 2" was not done.Count the rows: keep going until the quotient is 0.Stop only when the number left is 0.
Subtracting gives a negative leftover.A place value that did not fit was used.Check "fits?" before subtracting.Write 0 for that place and move to the next smaller one.
Doubling gives a far too big answer.The bits were read from the right.Which end did you start at?Doubling starts at the MSB (the left).
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-20 showed that binary is place value with base two. MA101 (F0-12) taught division with remainders. What carries over: place values, and "divide, keep the remainder". What changes: you now have methods that work for any number, not only by counting; and order matters, because the division method gives the LSB first. What comes next: binary numbers get long. F0-22 introduces hexadecimal, a short way to write them. W1

Check yourself

  1. Convert 13 to binary by subtracting place values.
  2. Convert 100 to binary by dividing by 2. Show the ladder.
  3. Convert 110010 to decimal in two ways: adding place values and doubling.
  4. Which bit tells you whether a number is odd? (a) the MSB (b) the LSB (c) the middle bit (d) none of them
  5. Explain in your own words why the division method gives the bits from right to left.
  6. Apply it to a new case: a game stores a player's level in binary as 1000001. What level is it?
  7. Predict: what will Listing 1 print as its first step for toBinary(9)?

Lab

Goal

Play a conversion race with binary cards and check your answers with Listing 1.

Hardware and software needed

The five binary cards from the F0-20 lab (or make them now), a partner, paper. Optional: a computer with a C++ compiler; our run's toolchain is recorded under Sources, R1.

Safety

None beyond normal paper and computer use.

Steps

  1. Your partner writes five numbers between 1 and 31 on slips and turns them over.
  2. Turn over a slip. Convert the number with the subtracting method, using the cards. Write the pattern.
  3. Convert the same number with the dividing method, on paper. Do the two patterns match?
  4. Swap: your partner writes five binary patterns. Convert each back with the doubling method.
  5. Optional: change the numbers in lines 34, 38 and 42 of Listing 1 to your numbers, run it, and compare.

Expected observations

Both methods always give the same pattern. The division ladder for each number has as many rows as the pattern has bits. If you run Listing 1 unchanged, your output matches the one shown above. R1

Verification

For each answer, convert it back the other way. You must land on the number you started with.

Troubleshooting

  • The two methods disagree. A common slip: the division bits were read top-down. Read them bottom-up.
  • The program prints nothing new after editing. You must build again after every change, then run the new program.
  • The build fails after your edit. Check that each number is a plain whole number and that the quotes around "10110" are still there.

Extension

Convert 255 and 256. Why does 256 need nine bits?

Forensic lab

Scenario

Priya wrote her first converter. Her friend Ben tested it and said: "It's great, 1, 3, 5 and 9 are all right!" Then her teacher tried 6 and got a strange answer. Is the program right or wrong? Find out from the evidence.

// Evidence program for the forensic lab: Priya's first converter.
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

std::string toBinary(int number)
{
    std::string bits;
    while (number > 0) {
        bits = bits + std::to_string(number % 2);
        number = number / 2;
    }
    return bits;
}

int main()
{
    for (int n : {1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 12, 13}) {
        std::cout << n << " -> " << toBinary(n) << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Questions

Method hints

Do the division ladder for 6 by hand. Write the remainders in the order you get them. Then compare with the program's output. Grade yourself with the forensic rubric of the course (observation, hypotheses, evidence, fix, prevention).

Mini-project

Design a "secret door code" game for a friend. Write five clues as binary numbers (for example, "the code's first number is 1011"). Your friend converts them to decimal to open the door. Include an answer card that shows your working with both methods.

Rubric (4 points): five correct clues (2); working shown with both methods (1); neat answer card a friend can follow (1).

Summary

  • Decimal to binary: subtract the biggest place value that fits, or divide by 2 and keep remainders.
  • The first remainder is the LSB; read the remainders from the bottom up.
  • Binary to decimal: add the place values of the 1 bits, or double-and-add from the left.
  • The LSB says odd (1) or even (0); the MSB has the biggest place value.
  • Always check a conversion by converting it back.
  • Test with numbers that are not the same backwards, such as 6 or 12.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. 13: 8 fits (5 left), 4 fits (1 left), 2 does not, 1 fits. 1101.
  2. 100 ÷ 2 = 50 r 0; 50 ÷ 2 = 25 r 0; 25 ÷ 2 = 12 r 1; 12 ÷ 2 = 6 r 0; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 r 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 r 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1. Bottom up: 1100100. Check: 64 + 32 + 4 = 100.
  3. Place values: 32 + 16 + 2 = 50. Doubling: 1, 3, 6, 12, 25, 50.
  4. (b) the LSB: it is worth 1, and every other place value is even. (a) The MSB only tells you about size. (c) No single middle bit decides it. (d) is wrong because (b) works.
  5. Any answer that says: the remainder after halving is the bit worth 1 (odd or even), so the first bit you find is the rightmost one; each later bit belongs one place further left.
  6. 1000001 = 64 + 1 = 65.
  7. 9 / 2 = 4 remainder 1 (with two spaces in front), because 9 = 2 × 4 + 1.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: 1, 3, 5 and 9 are right. 2 → 01, 6 → 011, 12 → 0011 and 13 → 1011 are wrong: 01 is 1, 011 is 3, 0011 is 3 and 1011 is 11. Pattern: each wrong answer is the right answer written backwards (10, 110, 1100, 1101). The right ones (1, 11, 101, 1001) read the same in both directions, so the bug cannot show on them. Hypotheses: (1) the division is wrong; (2) the bits are in the wrong order. Reversing each wrong answer gives the correct pattern, so the remainders are right and only the order is wrong: hypothesis 2. Root cause: Listing 2, line 9, bits = bits + … puts each new bit on the right; the first remainder is the LSB and must end up on the right, so later bits must go on the left. Fix: bits = std::to_string(number % 2) + bits;, exactly line 15 of Listing 1, whose run gives 45 = 101101 and 200 = 11001000 R1. Prevention: test with numbers that are not palindromes in binary (2, 6, 12), and test by converting every answer back. How the evidence was made: Listing 1's toBinary with the join order swapped and the printing removed, run in this build R2. Wrong answers: "the program fails for even numbers" (9 is right but 13, odd, is wrong); "numbers above 10 fail" (9 is right, 2 is wrong).

Story hook

Analogy

Mei is reading out the hallway switches to her dad over the phone. "On, on, off, off, off, on, off, off." Her dad is writing it down. "Slow down!" he laughs. "That's too many words for one row."

So they invent a trick. Mei splits the row into two groups of four switches. Each group of four can only make sixteen patterns. They give each pattern one short name: 0 to 9, and then the letters A to F. Now Mei only says two symbols: "C, 8." Her dad writes "C8" and later turns it back into switches.

Engineers use exactly this trick every day. It is called hexadecimal. It is not a new kind of number. It is a short way to write binary.

What you will be able to do

  • Write the sixteen hexadecimal digits 0–9 and A–F, with their 4-bit patterns.
  • Convert between binary and hexadecimal by grouping bits in fours.
  • Convert a two-digit hexadecimal number to decimal and back.
  • Mix a colour on paper as three amounts and write it as a code like #0A00F0, then check it with a small C++ program.
  • Diagnose a missing leading zero in a hexadecimal colour code (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Hexadecimal (hex)
Simple words: a way of writing numbers with sixteen symbols: 0 to 9, then A to F. Analogy: a one-symbol nickname for every group of four hallway switches. Precise: the base-16 place-value system; the digits A–F stand for 10–15, and each position is worth 16 times the one to its right. W1 R1
Hex digit
Simple words: one symbol of a hexadecimal number. Analogy: the nickname for one group of four switches. Precise: one of the sixteen symbols 0–9, A–F; it stands for exactly four bits, because 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. W1
Nibble
Simple words: half of a row of eight bits: four bits. Analogy: one group of four switches. Precise: a group of 4 bits; one hex digit writes one nibble. The word is an informal engineers' name. W1 D1
Hex prefix
Simple words: a label in front of a number that says "this is written in hex". Analogy: a sticky note on the row saying "read me with nicknames". Precise: the prefix 0x marks a hexadecimal literal in C++ (for example 0x2A is 42); this university also writes hex as 0x2A in running text (guide 13.3). R1 D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows a row of eight switches split into two groups of four. Each group becomes one hex digit. The left group 1100 is C (twelve). The right group 1000 is 8. So the row is 0xC8.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Four switches make sixteen patterns, from 0000 to 1111. Hexadecimal gives each pattern a one-symbol name. The first ten names are the digits you know: 0 to 9. We have no single digit for ten, so we borrow letters. A means ten, B eleven, C twelve, D thirteen, E fourteen and F fifteen.

Now a long row of switches is easy to say. Cut it into groups of four, starting from the right. Name each group. Eight switches become two symbols. Thirty-two switches become eight symbols.

Going back is as easy. Take each symbol and write its four switches. Put the groups side by side. No adding or dividing is needed.

Hex is a shorthand, like writing "km" instead of "kilometre". The switches underneath are exactly the same.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Hexadecimal is place value with base 16. From the right, the positions are worth 1, 16, 256 and so on, each 16 times the last. A hex digit runs from 0 to F (fifteen). W1

Why does grouping in fours work? Because 16 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2. One hex position covers exactly four binary positions. The place values inside one group are 8, 4, 2, 1. The next group to the left is worth 16 times as much, which is exactly where the binary places 128, 64, 32, 16 sit. So you can convert one group at a time, and the groups never mix. W1

A group of four bits is called a nibble (an informal name), and two nibbles make a byte (bytes are the subject of F0-23). So one byte is always exactly two hex digits, from 00 to FF. FF is 15 × 16 + 15 = 255, the biggest number eight switches can hold. W1 R1

Because "10" could mean ten, two or sixteen, we mark the base. This university writes hex with the hex prefix 0x: 0x10 is sixteen. In C++, a number written 0x2A in the code is read as hexadecimal; Listing 1 shows it equals 42. R1

Converting hex to decimal uses place value: 0x2A = 2 × 16 + 10 = 42. Converting decimal to hex divides by 16: 200 ÷ 16 = 12 remainder 8, so 200 = 0xC8. This is the same ladder as F0-21, with 16 instead of 2. W1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Engineers read memory addresses, register values and file contents in hex because each digit lines up with four bits, so you can see individual bits without counting long rows of 0s and 1s. Later courses use this constantly: register fields in HW102 and beyond, and memory addresses in the systems courses. Octal (base 8, groups of three bits) is another shorthand of the same kind. Modern C++ also accepts binary literals such as 0b1010 and digit separators such as 0b1011'0110; which version of the standard added them is a question for the standard itself (D3). Listing 1 of F0-25 uses both, and its clean build with -std=c++20 in this course is the evidence that our compiler accepts them. D2 D3

How the hardware actually does it

Hardware never stores hex. It stores bits. Hex exists only for people: in a program's text, in a tool's display, in a printout. When Listing 1 prints C8, the program is turning the bits 11001000 into the two characters 'C' and '8' so that you can read them. R1 D1

Worked example

Binary to hex: 11001000

  1. Split into fours from the right: 1100 | 1000.
  2. 1100 = 8 + 4 = 12 = C. 1000 = 8.
  3. Answer: 0xC8.
  4. To decimal: 12 × 16 + 8 = 192 + 8 = 200, the same number as in F0-21.

Hex to binary: 0x2A

  1. 2 = 0010. A = ten = 8 + 2 = 1010.
  2. Put them together: 0010 1010, which is 00101010.
  3. To decimal: 2 × 16 + 10 = 42.

Mixing a colour on paper

In this lab a colour is three amounts of light: red, green and blue, each from 0 to 255. The colour code writes each amount as two hex digits, in the order red, green, blue, after a # sign.

  1. Choose red 10, green 0, blue 240 (a deep blue).
  2. 10 ÷ 16 = 0 remainder 10, so 10 = 0x0A. Write two digits: 0A.
  3. 0 = 00.
  4. 240 ÷ 16 = 15 remainder 0, so 240 = 0xF0: F0.
  5. The code is #0A00F0. Notice the zero in front of A: it keeps every amount two digits wide.

Listing 1 checks the first two examples and Listing 2 the colour code. W1 R1 R2

Not verified — check before relying on this

Codes of the form #RRGGBB are also used outside this course, for example by web pages and drawing programs. This build could not open the document that defines that use (for web pages, the World Wide Web Consortium's CSS colour specification, cited by title only). In this chapter, #RRGGBB is our own exercise rule, defined above; treat any claim about other software as unverified until the Source Researcher checks it.

// Show 0 to 15 in decimal, binary and hexadecimal, then some whole bytes.
#include <bitset>
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    std::cout << "dec  binary  hex\n";
    for (int n = 0; n <= 15; ++n) {
        std::cout << n << (n < 10 ? "    " : "   ")
                  << std::bitset<4>(n) << "    "
                  << std::hex << std::uppercase << n << std::dec << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
    for (int byte : {0x2A, 0xC8, 0xFF}) {
        std::cout << std::bitset<8>(byte) << " = 0x" << std::hex << std::uppercase
                  << byte << std::dec << " = " << byte << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

// Hex colour mixer: read red, green and blue (each 0 to 255) and print #RRGGBB.
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>

void printTwoHexDigits(int amount)
{
    std::cout << std::hex << std::uppercase << std::setw(2) << std::setfill('0')
              << amount << std::dec;
}

int main()
{
    int red = 0;
    int green = 0;
    int blue = 0;
    while (std::cin >> red >> green >> blue) {
        if (red < 0 || red > 255 || green < 0 || green > 255 || blue < 0 || blue > 255) {
            std::cout << red << ' ' << green << ' ' << blue
                      << " -> each amount must be from 0 to 255\n";
            continue;
        }
        std::cout << red << ' ' << green << ' ' << blue << " -> #";
        printTwoHexDigits(red);
        printTwoHexDigits(green);
        printTwoHexDigits(blue);
        std::cout << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Nicknames can be a free choice; hex digits are not. Mei and her dad could have picked any sixteen names. Hex uses exactly 0–9 and A–F, and A always means ten. If you invent your own names, nobody else can read your rows.
  • The groups of four must start at the right. In the hallway it seems natural to group from the left. But for a row of, say, six switches, 101101, grouping from the left gives 1011 | 01 and a wrong answer. Group from the right: 10 | 1101, padded to 0010 1101 = 0x2D = 45. W1
  • Saying "C8" is short, but it is not a new switch. A hex digit is not stored anywhere as a single thing: the computer still holds eight separate bits. Hex is only for writing and reading.

Transition box

Where you came from: F0-21 converted between binary and decimal. What carries over: place value and the division ladder, now with 16 instead of 2. What changes: there are digits beyond 9 (A–F), and you must always say which base you mean (0x for hex). Hex and binary convert by grouping, with no arithmetic. What comes next: F0-23 names the rows of bits computers use (bytes and words) and shows the two different meanings of "kilo" for memory and storage. W1

Check yourself

  1. Write the hex digit for each of: 1010, 1111, 0111, 1100.
  2. Convert 0x3F to binary and to decimal.
  3. Convert 10110110 to hex.
  4. Convert 175 to hex using the division ladder.
  5. Which colour code is correctly written for red 0, green 128, blue 15? (a) #08015 (b) #0080F (c) #00800F (d) #0080015
  6. Explain in your own words why one hex digit always matches exactly four bits.
  7. Apply it to a new case: a robot's eight-switch status row reads 0x81. Which switches are on?
  8. Predict: what would Listing 2 print for the input line 0 0 0?

Lab

Goal

Mix three colours on paper, write their codes in hex, and check them with the colour-mixer program (Listing 2).

Hardware and software needed

Paper and coloured pencils. A computer with a C++ compiler for steps 4–6, or use the recorded output above. Our run used the toolchain recorded under Sources, R2.

Safety

None beyond normal paper and computer use.

Steps

  1. Draw three boxes. In each, decide on three amounts between 0 and 255 for red, green and blue. Write them down.
  2. Convert every amount to two hex digits with the division ladder (÷ 16). Keep the leading zero.
  3. Write each colour code as # followed by six hex digits.
  4. Put your three colours, one per line, into the input file colour_mixer.in next to Listing 2.
  5. Build and run the program with the build command shown above (or with university/labs/run_lab.sh on the lab folder).
  6. Compare each printed code with your paper code, digit by digit.

Expected observations

Every code has exactly six digits. Amounts below 16 start with 0. An amount above 255 is refused with the message "each amount must be from 0 to 255", as in the recorded run. R2

Verification

All your paper codes match the program's codes. Convert one code back to three decimal amounts to prove you can go both ways.

Troubleshooting

  • The program prints nothing. The input file is empty or in the wrong folder; it must sit next to the listing with the same name.
  • Your code and the program's differ in one digit. Recheck that division step; 16 × 15 = 240 is a common place to slip.
  • Lowercase letters appear. The std::uppercase tool was removed; lowercase hex means the same value.

Extension

Add a fourth line with a "half" colour, such as 128 64 0. Then change the program so it also prints each amount in binary (hint: Listing 1, line 10).

Forensic lab

Scenario

Tomas wrote a colour mixer before he learned about leading zeros. His friend typed in six colours. Some codes look fine. Others look too short. Tomas says "the computer must be skipping digits". Find the real cause.

Evidence pack

Tomas's program (Listing 3), and the real output for the same first six colours used by Listing 2.

    int green = 0;

        std::cout << red << ' ' << green << ' ' << blue << " -> #"
                  << std::hex << std::uppercase << red << green << blue << std::dec << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Questions

  1. Which codes are correct? Compare each with the output of Listing 2.
  2. Count the digits of each wrong code. What is missing, and where?
  3. State two hypotheses before you decide: one about the input, one about the printing.
  4. Why is the line for 128 128 128 correct while the line for 255 0 0 is wrong?

Method hints

Convert each amount to hex by hand and write it with two digits. Then write the three pairs side by side and compare with the evidence. Grade yourself with the forensic rubric of the course.

Mini-project

Make a "colour of the week" chart: seven colours, one for each day, with their amounts in decimal, their codes in hex, and a coloured patch drawn by hand. Choose at least two colours with an amount below 16, so the leading zero matters.

Rubric (4 points): seven correct codes (2); at least two codes with a leading zero, correct (1); one sentence explaining why each amount needs exactly two hex digits (1).

Summary

  • Hexadecimal is base 16, with digits 0–9 and A–F (ten to fifteen).
  • One hex digit is exactly four bits, a nibble; one byte is exactly two hex digits.
  • Binary to hex: group bits in fours from the right; hex to binary: write each digit as four bits.
  • Hex to decimal: place values 1, 16, 256; decimal to hex: divide by 16.
  • Write hex with the 0x prefix, as C++ does: 0x2A is 42.
  • Keep leading zeros when a fixed number of digits is expected.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. 1010 = A, 1111 = F, 0111 = 7, 1100 = C.
  2. 0x3F: 3 = 0011, F = 1111, so 00111111. Decimal: 3 × 16 + 15 = 63.
  3. 1011 | 0110 = B6 (0xB6).
  4. 175 ÷ 16 = 10 remainder 15, so A then F: 0xAF. Check: 10 × 16 + 15 = 175.
  5. (c) #00800F: 0 = 00, 128 = 80, 15 = 0F. (a) and (b) dropped leading zeros (five digits cannot be split into three pairs). (d) wrote 15 in decimal.
  6. Any answer that says: four bits make 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 patterns, and hex has exactly 16 digits, so each pattern has one digit and each digit one pattern.
  7. 0x81 = 1000 0001: the switch worth 128 (the MSB) and the switch worth 1 (the LSB) are on.
  8. 0 0 0 -> #000000: each 0 is printed two digits wide with '0' fill.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: only 128 128 128 -> #808080 is correct. The others are short: #FF00 (4 digits), #0FF0, #FFFF0, #A0F0, #FFA50. In each wrong line, an amount below 16 lost its leading zero (0 printed as "0", 10 as "A"). Hypotheses: (1) the input was read wrongly; (2) the printing drops digits. The decimal amounts printed before the arrow are correct, which rules out (1). Root cause: Listing 3, line 11, prints each amount with std::hex but without a width of 2 and a '0' fill, so amounts below 16 print one digit. 128 = 0x80 already has two digits, so it looks right. Ambiguity: #FFFF0 could be 255 255 0 (FF FF 0) or 255 15 240 (FF F F0): the code cannot be decoded. Fix: print each amount with std::setw(2) << std::setfill('0'), as Listing 2 does; its run prints #0A00F0 and #FF0000 R2. Prevention: a test that checks every code has exactly 7 characters (# plus six digits), and test inputs with small amounts (0 and 10). How the evidence was made: Listing 2 with the width and fill removed and the range check removed, run on its first six input lines in this build R3. Wrong answers: "the computer skips digits at random" (the run is repeatable, and only amounts below 16 are affected); "hex cannot show 0" (it can: 0x00).

Story hook

Analogy

Ana and her cousin Felix each bake cookies for a school sale. Ana packs them in boxes of 1000. Felix packs them in boxes of 1024, because he likes doubling: 2, 4, 8, … all the way to 1024.

At the sale, both cousins write "1 thousand-box" on their labels. A customer buys one box from each and counts. "These boxes are different!" she says. "One has 24 more cookies."

Ana and Felix were both honest. They used the same word for two different sizes. Computers have exactly this problem with the word "kilo". In this chapter you will learn the names for groups of bits, and how to label sizes so nobody is confused.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a byte is, and show one byte as a row of eight switches.
  • Explain what a word is, and why its size depends on the machine.
  • Convert sizes with decimal prefixes (kB, MB, GB: powers of 1000) and binary prefixes (KiB, MiB, GiB: powers of 1024).
  • Tell bits (b) from bytes (B), and convert between them.
  • Diagnose a size report that uses the wrong unit name (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Byte
Simple words: a group of eight bits. Analogy: one row of eight hallway switches, each worth double the one to its right. Precise: a group of 8 bits that holds one of 256 patterns (0 to 255 when read as an unsigned number); the unit symbol is B. The C++ constant CHAR_BIT printed 8 in our run. W1 R1
Word
Simple words: the size of number a computer likes to work with in one go. Analogy: how many rows of switches the house's control panel flips at once. Precise: a machine-dependent group of bytes that a processor handles as one unit; its size is set by the processor's architecture manual, not by a universal rule. D1
Kilobyte (kB)
Simple words: one thousand bytes. Analogy: Ana's box of 1000 cookies. Precise: 1 kB = 1000 B, using the decimal (SI) prefix kilo = 103; MB = 10002 B, GB = 10003 B. W1 D2
Kibibyte (KiB)
Simple words: 1024 bytes. Analogy: Felix's box of 1024 cookies. Precise: 1 KiB = 210 B = 1024 B, using the binary prefix kibi; MiB = 10242 B, GiB = 10243 B. W1 D3
Bit and byte symbols (b, B)
Simple words: small b means bits, capital B means bytes. Analogy: one switch versus one whole row. Precise: 1 B = 8 b; this university spells out "Gbit/s" and "GB/s" at levels L0–L2 so the two cannot be mixed up (guide 13.3). W1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 compares the decimal and binary sizes, drawn to scale. Each pair starts equal on the left. The binary bar is always a little longer, and the gap grows with every step.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

One switch is a bit. A row of eight switches is a byte. A byte can show 256 different patterns, from 00000000 to 11111111. That is enough for a small number, or for one letter of the alphabet.

Computers handle bytes in bigger bundles too. A word is the bundle size a particular computer likes best. Different computers like different sizes, so always ask "a word on which machine?"

Files and memory hold many bytes, so we use bigger units. Here is the tricky part. In everyday life, "kilo" means 1000: a kilometre is 1000 metres. But in binary, round numbers are powers of two. The power of two nearest to 1000 is 1024.

So people made two sets of names. kB (kilobyte) means 1000 bytes, like Ana's box. KiB (kibibyte, said "kibby-byte") means 1024 bytes, like Felix's box. The little "i" means "the binary one". Use the right name, and nobody gets confused.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A byte is 8 bits; it is written B. A bit is written b. So a speed in "Mbit/s" and a size in "MB" differ by a factor of 8 before you even think about prefixes. Our run printed CHAR_BIT, the number of bits in the smallest C++ unit of storage, as 8. W1 R1

Decimal prefixes multiply by 1000 each step: kilo (k) = 1000, mega (M) = 1000 × 1000, giga (G) = 1000 × 1000 × 1000. Binary prefixes multiply by 1024 = 210 each step: kibi (Ki), mebi (Mi), gibi (Gi). The run of Listing 1 prints all six values. W1 R1

This university follows one rule (guide 13.3): binary prefixes for memory sizes where the quantity is binary; decimal prefixes only where the source document uses decimal units, and then it says so. A size without a clear unit is a bug waiting to happen.

A word has no single size. Its size is set by each processor's own manual. Our program cannot print "the word size" directly, but it printed two related sizes on the machine that ran it: an int took 4 bytes and a pointer (a memory address) took 8 bytes. Your machine may print different numbers: run the listing and write yours down. R1 D1

Not verified — check before relying on this

The names kibi, mebi and gibi (Ki, Mi, Gi) and the definition of kilo, mega and giga as powers of 1000 come from standards that this build could not open: the binary prefixes from IEC 80000-13 (title only), and the decimal prefixes from "The International System of Units (SI)", the SI Brochure published by the BIPM (title only). The arithmetic in this chapter (1024 = 210, 1000 = 103) is true by definition; the naming convention is tagged to these standards pending verification by the Source Researcher (dossier gate G1 open).

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. The word "word" is especially slippery. Some processor manuals keep an old meaning (a fixed small size) even on machines whose registers are much wider, and then use names like "double word" and "quad word" for bigger units. Always read the size from the manual of the exact processor family, and in C++ prefer types whose size is in their name, such as std::uint8_t, std::uint32_t and std::uint64_t, which F0-24 and F0-25 use. D1 D4

Not verified — check before relying on this

That a specific processor family's manual uses "word" for a size smaller than its register width is a claim about that manual. Check the processor vendor's architecture manual (for example the software developer's manual of the processor family recorded in the dossier) before giving any specific size.

How the hardware actually does it

Memory is organised as a long list of numbered places. In the computers this university studies, each number (an address) picks out one byte. The processor moves several bytes together when it loads a word. How many bytes, and how memory chips are counted, comes from the product's own documentation; that is the subject of HW102 and later hardware courses. This chapter does not quote any real product's sizes. D1

Worked example

How big is a file of 5,000,000 bytes?

  1. In MB: 5,000,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 5 MB exactly.
  2. In MiB: 1 MiB = 1024 × 1024 = 1,048,576 B. 5,000,000 ÷ 1,048,576 ≈ 4.77 MiB.
  3. In bits: 5,000,000 × 8 = 40,000,000 bits.

The run of Listing 1 prints 5 MB, 4.76837 MiB and 40000000 bits. W1 R1

How much bigger is each binary unit?

  1. KiB versus kB: 1024 − 1000 = 24; 24 ÷ 1000 = 0.024 = 2.4 %.
  2. MiB versus MB: 1,048,576 − 1,000,000 = 48,576; ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.048576 ≈ 4.9 %.
  3. GiB versus GB: 1,073,741,824 − 1,000,000,000 = 73,741,824; ÷ 1,000,000,000 ≈ 7.4 %.

Each step multiplies by 1024 instead of 1000, so the extra 2.4 % is multiplied again at every step. W1

How many bytes in 3 KiB? In 3 kB?

3 × 1024 = 3072 B. 3 × 1000 = 3000 B. A label that says only "3K" could mean either. W1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — units.cpp

// Bits, bytes and the two kinds of "kilo": 1000 (kB) and 1024 (KiB).
#include <climits>
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    std::cout << "bits in one byte on this machine: " << CHAR_BIT << '\n';
    std::cout << "bytes in an int on this machine: " << sizeof(int) << '\n';
    std::cout << "bytes in a pointer on this machine: " << sizeof(void*) << "\n\n";

    const long long kB = 1000;
    const long long KiB = 1024;
    std::cout << "1 kB  = " << kB << " bytes\n";
    std::cout << "1 KiB = " << KiB << " bytes\n";
    std::cout << "1 MB  = " << kB * kB << " bytes\n";
    std::cout << "1 MiB = " << KiB * KiB << " bytes\n";
    std::cout << "1 GB  = " << kB * kB * kB << " bytes\n";
    std::cout << "1 GiB = " << KiB * KiB * KiB << " bytes\n\n";

    const long long fileSize = 5000000;  // a file of five million bytes
    std::cout << "a file of " << fileSize << " bytes is\n";
    std::cout << "  " << static_cast<double>(fileSize) / (kB * kB) << " MB\n";
    std::cout << "  " << static_cast<double>(fileSize) / (KiB * KiB) << " MiB\n";
    std::cout << "  " << fileSize * 8 << " bits\n";
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Cookie boxes can be any size; computer units are fixed by definition. Ana could pack 999 cookies if she liked. A kB is exactly 1000 B and a KiB exactly 1024 B, always. W1
  • A row of eight switches looks like a number, but a byte is not always a number. The same byte can be a letter, part of a colour (F0-22) or part of a bigger number. The program decides. D4
  • A "word" has no fixed size in the house. The analogy of "how many rows the control panel flips at once" hides that every processor family chooses its own size, and that manuals do not even agree on what to call it (see Layer 3). D1

Transition box

Where you came from: F0-22 wrote one byte as two hex digits, and F0-15 compared powers of ten with powers of two. What carries over: bits and place values; 1024 is 210. What changes: sizes now need units, and the same prefix letter can mean two sizes; always write the "i" for binary units, and b versus B. What comes next: F0-24 uses one byte to hold negative numbers, and shows why a byte value can suddenly print as negative. W1

Check yourself

  1. How many bits are in 3 bytes? How many different patterns can one byte hold?
  2. How many bytes are in 2 KiB? In 2 kB?
  3. Which is bigger: 1 GB or 1 GiB? By how many bytes?
  4. A message is 4096 bytes. Write its size in KiB and in kB.
  5. Which label is clearest for 1,048,576 bytes? (a) 1 MB (b) 1 M (c) 1 MiB (d) 1 Mb
  6. Explain in your own words why computer people wanted a "kilo" of 1024 at all.
  7. Apply it to a new case: a robot sends readings at 8000 bits per second. How many bytes per second is that?
  8. Predict: if Listing 1 ran on a different computer, which output lines might change, and which never can?

Lab

Goal

Measure the sizes of a few things on your own computer and label every size with the right unit.

Hardware and software needed

Paper. Optional: a computer with a C++ compiler to run Listing 1. Our run's machine and toolchain are recorded under Sources, R1.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use. Do not delete or move files to "make space" during this lab.

Steps

  1. Write a table with columns: thing, bytes, kB, KiB, bits.
  2. Fill in by hand: one byte; the word "binary" stored as one byte per letter; a file of 5,000,000 bytes.
  3. If you can, run Listing 1. Write your machine's numbers for CHAR_BIT, sizeof(int) and sizeof(void*). Label them "measured on my machine".
  4. With an adult's help, look at the size of one of your own files in your computer's file viewer. Write the number and the unit exactly as shown. Note whether it says kB, KB, KiB or something else.
  5. Convert that size into bytes twice: once as if the unit were 1000-based and once as if it were 1024-based.

Expected observations

The hand-made rows match the arithmetic of the Worked example. The values for kB through GiB match the run above exactly; the first three lines may differ on your machine. The file viewer's unit may not say which "kilo" it means, which is the point of the lab. R1

Verification

Every number in your table has a unit, and every "k" says whether it is 1000 or 1024.

Troubleshooting

  • Your MiB number has many decimals. That is expected: 1,048,576 rarely divides evenly. Round to two decimals and say so.
  • Your file viewer uses a capital K. Some programs do. Record it exactly, then add a note: "unit meaning not stated".
  • Your sizeof(int) differs from ours. That is allowed; types can have different sizes on different machines.

Extension

Add a row for 1 TB and 1 TiB (the next prefixes, tera and tebi). Work out the percentage gap. Does the pattern from Figure 1 continue?

Forensic lab

Scenario

Nadia downloaded a song for a school project. One program said the download was 3.14573 MB. Another said 3 MB. Her friend says "one of them is broken". Is that true?

Evidence pack

Listing 2 — two_reports.cpp (evidence)

// Evidence program for the forensic lab: two size reports for the same download.
#include <iostream>

void reportA(long long bytes)
{
    std::cout << "Report A: " << static_cast<double>(bytes) / 1000000 << " MB\n";
}

void reportB(long long bytes)
{
    std::cout << "Report B: " << static_cast<double>(bytes) / (1024 * 1024) << " MB\n";
}

int main()
{
    const long long download = 3145728;
    std::cout << "download size: " << download << " bytes\n";
    reportA(download);
    reportB(download);
    return 0;
}

Method hints

Compute 3,145,728 ÷ 1,000,000 and 3,145,728 ÷ 1,048,576 on paper. Then compare each result with its label. Grade yourself with the forensic rubric of the course.

Mini-project

Make a "unit translator" card that fits in a pencil case. One side: kB, MB, GB with their byte counts. Other side: KiB, MiB, GiB with their byte counts. Add one example of each and the rule "b = bit, B = byte".

Rubric (4 points): six correct byte counts (2); one correct example per side (1); the bit/byte rule stated clearly (1).

Summary

  • A byte is 8 bits (B versus b); it holds 256 patterns.
  • A word is a machine-dependent group of bytes; read its size from the processor's manual.
  • kB, MB, GB are powers of 1000; KiB, MiB, GiB are powers of 1024 = 210.
  • The gap grows: 2.4 % at kilo, 4.9 % at mega, 7.4 % at giga.
  • Always write which unit you mean; measure type sizes with sizeof instead of guessing.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. 3 × 8 = 24 bits. One byte holds 28 = 256 patterns.
  2. 2 KiB = 2048 bytes; 2 kB = 2000 bytes.
  3. 1 GiB is bigger, by 1,073,741,824 − 1,000,000,000 = 73,741,824 bytes.
  4. 4096 ÷ 1024 = 4 KiB; 4096 ÷ 1000 = 4.096 kB.
  5. (c) 1 MiB is exact. (a) 1 MB is 1,000,000 bytes, so it is wrong here. (b) "1 M" says neither bytes nor which prefix. (d) Mb means megabits, a unit 8 times smaller than megabytes.
  6. Any answer that says: memory sizes and addresses come in powers of two, because each extra bit doubles the count; 1024 = 210 is the power of two closest to 1000, so it was convenient, and the "i" names were added to keep the two meanings apart.
  7. 8000 ÷ 8 = 1000 bytes per second, which is 1 kB/s (decimal; 1000 is not 1 KiB).
  8. The first three lines (CHAR_BIT, sizeof(int), sizeof(void*)) describe the machine and compiler and might change. The prefix lines and the file-size lines are pure arithmetic and cannot change.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: the byte count is the same for both reports: 3,145,728. Report A says 3.14573 MB; Report B says 3 MB. Hypotheses: (1) one program computes wrongly; (2) both compute correctly but one uses the wrong unit name. Evidence: 3,145,728 ÷ 1,000,000 = 3.145728, so Report A is right: it is about 3.15 MB. 3,145,728 ÷ 1,048,576 = 3 exactly (3,145,728 = 3 × 1024 × 1024), so Report B's arithmetic is right too, but the answer is in MiB. Neither program is "broken" in its arithmetic; hypothesis 2. Root cause: Listing 2, line 11 labels a 1024 × 1024 division as "MB". Fix: change the label to "MiB". The fixed program (two_reports_fixed.cpp in the lab folder, one changed line) printed:

Report B: 3 MiB

Negative numbers in binary: two's complement

Story hook

Analogy

Jonas has an old bicycle counter on his handlebars. It counts the turns of the wheel and shows three digits. One day it shows 000. Jonas pushes the bike backwards by one turn. The counter does not show "minus one". It shows 999.

Jonas thinks about it. "If I go backwards one turn from 000 and get 999, then 999 is a lot like minus one. And 998 is like minus two!" His sister Aisha adds: "So we could agree that the top half of the numbers mean negative ones."

That agreement is exactly how computers store negative numbers. A row of eight switches can show 256 patterns. We agree that the top half of the patterns stand for the negative numbers. The rule has a funny name: two's complement.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain the difference between an unsigned and a signed reading of the same eight bits.
  • Read an 8-bit two's complement number by giving the leftmost switch the value −128.
  • Find the pattern for a negative number with the rule "flip all bits, then add one".
  • State the range of an 8-bit signed number (−128 to 127) and of an unsigned one (0 to 255).
  • Diagnose the forensic case "Why is my number negative?": a byte printed through a signed type.
Jargon box
Unsigned
Simple words: a number that can never be below zero. Analogy: the bicycle counter read plainly: 000 to 999. Precise: an integer type whose bit pattern is read with all place values positive; with 8 bits it holds 0 to 255. In C++, std::uint8_t is an unsigned 8-bit type. R1 D1
Signed
Simple words: a number that can be negative or positive. Analogy: the counter read with Jonas's agreement: 999 means −1. Precise: an integer type that can represent negative values; in C++, std::int8_t is a signed 8-bit type holding −128 to 127. R1 D1
Two's complement
Simple words: the usual rule for writing negative numbers in binary. Analogy: going backwards from 000 on the counter. Precise: an n-bit representation where the most significant bit has place value −2n−1 and all others are positive; −x is written as the pattern of 2n − x, found by inverting all bits of x and adding 1. W1 D1
Sign bit
Simple words: the leftmost bit, which tells you if a signed number is negative. Analogy: the leftmost switch, now worth −128 instead of +128. Precise: in two's complement, the most significant bit; it is 1 exactly when the value is negative. W1
Wrap-around
Simple words: going past the end of the numbers and coming back at the other end. Analogy: the counter going from 999 to 000, or from 000 back to 999. Precise: arithmetic modulo 2n: a result that does not fit in n bits keeps only its low n bits. It is one form of overflow (F0-20). W1 R1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the same row of switches as in F0-20, with one change. The leftmost switch is now worth −128 instead of +128. The row 11111011 then means −5.

Figure 2 shows all 256 patterns of one byte as a wheel, like the bicycle counter. Going forward one step from 127 lands on −128.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Eight switches make 256 patterns. So far we used them for 0 to 255. But what about negative numbers, like a temperature of −5 degrees on a winter night?

We have no extra switch for a minus sign. So we make an agreement, like Jonas and Aisha. Patterns that start with 0 are the ordinary numbers 0 to 127. Patterns that start with 1 are the negative numbers −128 to −1.

Here is the neat part. The leftmost switch is worth −128 instead of +128. Everything else stays the same. To read a pattern, add the place values as usual, but count the leftmost one as −128.

The same eight switches can therefore mean two different numbers. If the program says "unsigned", 11111011 means 251. If the program says "signed", it means −5. The switches never change. Only the way we read them changes.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

An unsigned 8-bit number gives every switch a positive place value: 128, 64, …, 1. Its range is 0 to 255. A signed 8-bit number in two's complement gives the leftmost switch −128 instead. Its range is −128 to 127. Both use all 256 patterns; they only split them differently. W1 R1

The leftmost bit is called the sign bit. If it is 1, the signed value is negative, because −128 is bigger in size than all the other place values together (64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 127). W1

Flip and add one. To write −x, take the pattern of x, flip every bit (0 ↔ 1), then add 1. For 5: 00000101 → 11111010 → 11111011. Why does it work? Flipping every bit of x gives 255 − x, because x plus its flip is 11111111. Adding 1 gives 256 − x. In 8 bits, 256 is the same as 0 (it needs a ninth switch, which is lost). So the pattern behaves like −x. W1 R1

The quick rule for reading a signed byte: if the sign bit is 1, read it as unsigned and subtract 256. 11111011 is 251 unsigned, so it is 251 − 256 = −5 signed. 200 unsigned (11001000) is 200 − 256 = −56 signed. W1 R1

Wrap-around follows from the wheel in Figure 2. Adding 1 to 127 (01111111) gives 10000000. Read as signed, that is −128. Our run shows exactly this: "127 + 1 stored in a signed byte reads as -128". R1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Two's complement is popular in hardware because addition does not need to know whether the numbers are signed: the same adder circuit adds 251 + 6 = 257 → 1 (unsigned, wrapped) and −5 + 6 = 1 (signed), with the same bits. Only comparison and widening (copying a byte into a bigger type) need to know. When a signed byte is widened, its sign bit is copied into all the new high bits ("sign extension"), which is why −56 stays −56 in an int. HW102 builds the adder. D1 D3

Not verified — check before relying on this

The C++20 standard (ISO/IEC 14882:2020, "Programming languages — C++", title only) is understood to require signed integers to use two's complement and to define the conversion of an out-of-range value to a signed type as wrapping modulo 2n. This build could not open the standard. What is verified is behaviour: with g++ -std=c++20 and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer enabled, Listing 1 converted 200 to −56 and 128 to −128, and the sanitizer printed no message (run R1). Whether plain char is signed or unsigned is also left to each platform; check the compiler's documentation for your target before relying on it, and prefer std::uint8_t or std::int8_t, which say what they are.

How the hardware actually does it

The memory holding a byte stores only its eight bits. It does not store "signed" or "unsigned". The program's types decide which instructions the processor uses to compare or widen the value, and so which reading you get. That is why the same byte can print as 200 in one program and −56 in another. D1 R1

Worked example

Write −5 in 8-bit two's complement

  1. 5 = 00000101.
  2. Flip every bit: 11111010.
  3. Add one: 11111010 + 1 = 11111011.
  4. Check with place values: −128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 2 + 1 = −5. Unsigned: 251, and 251 − 256 = −5.

Read 11001000 as signed

Unsigned it is 128 + 64 + 8 = 200 (F0-21). The sign bit is 1, so signed it is 200 − 256 = −56. With place values: −128 + 64 + 8 = −56.

Check that 5 + (−5) = 0

00000101 + 11111011 = 1 00000000. The ninth bit does not fit in the byte and is lost, leaving 00000000 = 0. Wrap-around makes the sum come out right.

The run of Listing 1 confirms every number above. W1 R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — twos.cpp

// The same eight switches read two ways: unsigned (0 to 255) and signed (-128 to 127).
#include <bitset>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

void show(std::int8_t value)
{
    const auto pattern = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(value);
    std::cout << std::bitset<8>(pattern)
              << "  signed: " << static_cast<int>(value)
              << "  unsigned: " << static_cast<int>(pattern) << '\n';
}

int main()
{
    for (int n : {0, 1, 5, 127, -1, -5, -128}) {
        show(static_cast<std::int8_t>(n));
    }
    std::cout << '\n';

    const std::uint8_t five = 5;
    const auto flipped = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(~five);
    const auto plusOne = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(flipped + 1);
    std::cout << "5            " << std::bitset<8>(five) << '\n';
    std::cout << "flip all     " << std::bitset<8>(flipped) << '\n';
    std::cout << "add one      " << std::bitset<8>(plusOne)
              << "  read as signed: " << static_cast<int>(static_cast<std::int8_t>(plusOne))
              << '\n';
    std::cout << '\n';

    const std::uint8_t fromSensor = 200;
    const auto asSigned = static_cast<std::int8_t>(fromSensor);
    std::cout << "200 stored in a signed byte reads as " << static_cast<int>(asSigned) << '\n';
    const auto wrapped = static_cast<std::int8_t>(127 + 1);
    std::cout << "127 + 1 stored in a signed byte reads as " << static_cast<int>(wrapped) << '\n';
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • The bicycle counter is decimal; a byte is binary. On the counter, "flip each digit" would mean 9 minus each digit. In binary, flipping means 0 ↔ 1. The idea (counting backwards from zero wraps to the top) is the same; the details are not. W1
  • The counter has one reading; a byte has two. Jonas's counter always shows 999. A byte does not "show" anything: the program's type chooses whether 11111111 is 255 or −1 (F0-20 said the switches do not know their meaning). R1
  • Negative numbers are not symmetrical. On a number line (F0-14), −128 and +128 are mirror images. In a signed byte, −128 exists but +128 does not: the range is −128 to 127. W1

Transition box

Where you came from: F0-14 introduced negative numbers on a number line; F0-23 defined the byte. What carries over: place values and bytes; addition works exactly as before. What changes: one place value becomes negative (−128), the range is no longer symmetrical, and the same bits can now mean two numbers, so types matter. What comes next: F0-25 works on single switches inside a byte with masks and shifts. W1

Check yourself

  1. What are the smallest and largest values of an 8-bit unsigned number? Of an 8-bit signed number?
  2. Write −1, −2 and −128 as 8-bit two's complement patterns.
  3. Read 10000011 as unsigned and as signed.
  4. Which pattern is −12? (a) 10001100 (b) 11110100 (c) 11110011 (d) 00001100
  5. Show that −12 + 12 = 0 by adding the two patterns.
  6. Explain in your own words why the same eight bits can print as 200 in one program and −56 in another.
  7. Apply it to a new case: a 4-bit signed number. What is the place value of its leftmost bit, and what is its range?
  8. Predict: Listing 1 is changed to also show -2. What line will it print?

Lab

Goal

Build a paper "byte wheel" and use it with Listing 1 to explore signed and unsigned readings.

Hardware and software needed

Paper, a pencil, a plate or compass to draw a circle. Optional: a computer with a C++ compiler; our run's toolchain is under Sources, R1.

Safety

Take care with the point of a compass. Otherwise none beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Draw a large circle. Mark 16 evenly spaced points, like a clock with 16 hours.
  2. Use 4-bit patterns (a "half byte"): write 0000 at the top and go clockwise to 1111.
  3. Next to each pattern write its unsigned value (0 to 15) and its signed value (leftmost bit worth −8).
  4. Find the place where adding one makes the signed value jump from 7 to −8. Mark it.
  5. Pick three numbers and use "flip and add one" to find their negatives. Check them on your wheel.
  6. Optional: add -2, -100 and 100 to the list in line 16 of Listing 1, run it, and check the printed patterns by hand.

Expected observations

Patterns starting with 0 have equal signed and unsigned values; patterns starting with 1 differ by exactly 16 on your 4-bit wheel (and by 256 for a byte, as in the run of Listing 1). The jump sits between 0111 and 1000. R1

Verification

For each of your three numbers, x + (−x) adds to 0000 on paper once the fifth bit is dropped.

Troubleshooting

  • Your negatives are off by one. You flipped the bits but forgot to add one.
  • Your wheel has 17 points or 15. Count again: 4 bits make exactly 16 patterns.
  • The program fails to build after your edit. Numbers in the list need commas between them, and the minus sign must touch the number.

Extension

Find a number that is its own negative in 8-bit two's complement, apart from 0. (Hint: try −128.) Explain why.

Forensic lab

Scenario: "Why is my number negative?"

Leila and Marco are building a model kitchen display for a school fair. A pretend oven sends one byte per reading: the temperature in degrees Celsius, from 0 to 250. Their program prints the readings. Cool readings look fine. Hot ones come out negative, which is impossible for a hot oven.

Evidence pack

The program (Listing 3) with the readings it was given (line 9), and the real output of one run.

Listing 3 — temperature.cpp (evidence)

// Evidence program for the forensic lab "Why is my number negative?".
// The oven sends one byte per reading: the temperature in degrees Celsius, 0 to 250.
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    const std::vector<std::uint8_t> packet = {20, 65, 110, 127, 128, 150, 180, 200, 250};
    for (std::uint8_t byte : packet) {
        std::int8_t temperature = static_cast<std::int8_t>(byte);
        std::cout << "oven temperature: " << static_cast<int>(temperature) << " C\n";
    }
    return 0;
}

Questions

  1. List the readings that are wrong. What is the first wrong one?
  2. For each wrong reading, compute "printed value + 256". What do you notice?
  3. State at least two hypotheses (for example: "the oven sends wrong bytes" and "the program reads the bytes wrongly"). Which one does the evidence support, and why?
  4. Which line of Listing 3 causes the problem? Explain with two's complement.
  5. Give a fix, and say how you would verify it.
  6. Suggest a test that would have caught this before the fair.

Method hints

Compare the printed values with the bytes in line 9, one by one. Find where they start to differ: what is special about that number? Then read the type of every variable the value passes through. Hypothesis → test → conclusion. Grade yourself with the forensic rubric of the course (observation, hypotheses, evidence, fix, prevention).

Mini-project

Make a 4-bit "signed number wheel" poster (from the lab) and a short comic, four boxes long, in which a character discovers that 7 + 1 = −8 on a 4-bit wheel and works out why.

Rubric (4 points): all 16 patterns with correct signed and unsigned values (2); the comic explains the jump with the place value −8 (1); clear, neat, readable by a classmate (1).

Summary

  • Unsigned byte: 0 to 255. Signed byte (two's complement): −128 to 127.
  • In two's complement the leftmost bit (the sign bit) is worth −128.
  • To negate: flip every bit, then add one.
  • Reading a signed byte with sign bit 1: unsigned value − 256.
  • Past the end, values wrap around: 127 + 1 → −128 when stored in a signed byte.
  • Bits have no sign of their own: the type decides the reading. Keep unsigned data in unsigned types.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Unsigned: 0 to 255. Signed: −128 to 127.
  2. −1 = 11111111; −2 = 11111110; −128 = 10000000.
  3. Unsigned: 128 + 2 + 1 = 131. Signed: −128 + 2 + 1 = −125 (or 131 − 256).
  4. (b) 11110100: 12 = 00001100, flipped 11110011, plus one 11110100. (a) only sets the sign bit (that is −116 in two's complement). (c) forgot to add one (that is −13). (d) is +12.
  5. 00001100 + 11110100 = 1 00000000; the ninth bit is dropped, leaving 0.
  6. Any answer that says: memory stores only the bits 11001000; one program's type reads them unsigned (200), the other's reads them as two's complement with the leftmost bit worth −128 (−56).
  7. Leftmost bit worth −8; range −8 to 7.
  8. 11111110 signed: -2 unsigned: 254.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: 20, 65, 110 and 127 are printed correctly. From 128 onwards every reading is wrong: 128 → −128, 150 → −106, 180 → −76, 200 → −56, 250 → −6. Pattern: each wrong value + 256 gives the true reading (−106 + 256 = 150, −6 + 256 = 250). Hypotheses: (1) the oven sends wrong bytes; (2) the program reads correct bytes wrongly. The bytes in line 9 are correct, and every error is exactly 256, the signature of a signed reading of a byte whose sign bit is 1: hypothesis 2. Root cause: Listing 3, line 11, stores the reading in std::int8_t, a signed byte whose range is −128 to 127. Readings of 128 and above have the leftmost bit 1, which two's complement reads as −128 plus the rest. Fix: keep the reading unsigned, for example int temperature = byte;. The fixed program (temperature_fixed.cpp in the lab folder, two lines changed) printed:

oven temperature: 20 C
oven temperature: 65 C
oven temperature: 110 C
oven temperature: 127 C
oven temperature: 128 C
oven temperature: 150 C
oven temperature: 180 C
oven temperature: 200 C
oven temperature: 250 C

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-24/temperature_fixed.out; run record temperature_fixed.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:31:00Z; exit code: 0.

Verification: all nine values now match line 9. Prevention: a test with the boundary values 127, 128 and 250 (the top of the stated range); and a rule: data described as "0 to 250" goes into an unsigned or wider type. How the evidence was made: nine made-up readings, stored through a signed byte on purpose, run in this build R3. Wrong answers: "the oven is broken above 127" (the bytes in line 9 are right); "the printing with static_cast<int> is the bug" (that conversion keeps the value; the damage is already done on line 11); "the readings overflow 255" (none is above 250).

Story hook

Analogy

Zara's family has a little control panel by the front door with eight switches, one for each light in the house. The rightmost is the kitchen. Then the hall, the living room, the bathroom, two bedrooms, the porch, and on the far left, the garden.

At bedtime Zara's grandfather wants to turn off only the bathroom light. He must not touch the other seven. Zara has an idea. She cuts a piece of card with one hole in it, right over the bathroom switch. She lays the card on the panel. Now only one switch can be reached.

That card is a mask. Computers use masks all the time, to change one bit of a byte without disturbing the others. In this chapter you will make masks, and learn to slide bits left and right with shifts.

What you will be able to do

  • Number the bits of a byte from bit 0 (the LSB) to bit 7 (the MSB).
  • Build a mask with a shift, such as 1u << 3, and use it to set, clear, toggle and test one bit.
  • Use a right shift and a mask to pull a field of several bits out of a byte.
  • Decode a made-up 8-bit status byte from a written description of its fields.
  • Diagnose a mask that clears the wrong lights (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Bit number
Simple words: the name of a bit's position, counted from the right, starting at 0. Analogy: the room number of each switch on Zara's panel: kitchen is 0, garden is 7. Precise: bit k has place value 2k; bit 0 is the least significant bit and bit 7 the most significant bit of a byte. W1
Mask
Simple words: a pattern of bits that picks which bits you want to touch. Analogy: the card with holes over some switches. Precise: a value combined with data by a bitwise operator so that only the bit positions selected by the mask are set, cleared, toggled or kept. W1 D1
Bitwise operator
Simple words: an operation that works on each pair of bits separately. Analogy: doing the same thing to every switch at once, switch by switch. Precise: in C++, & (AND: 1 only if both bits are 1), | (OR: 1 if at least one is 1), ^ (XOR: 1 if they differ) and ~ (NOT: flip every bit). F0-26 gives their full truth tables. R1 D2
Shift
Simple words: sliding all the bits left or right by some places. Analogy: moving every light's setting a few rooms along the panel; settings that fall off the end are lost, and empty places get "off". Precise: x << n moves the bits of x n places left (multiplying an unsigned value by 2n while it fits); x >> n moves them n places right (dividing an unsigned value by 2n, dropping the remainder). W1 R1
Flag
Simple words: one bit that answers a yes/no question. Analogy: one light: on means yes. Precise: a single bit in a larger value whose 1 or 0 records whether a condition is true. D1
Bit field
Simple words: a group of neighbouring bits that together hold a small number. Analogy: three switches side by side used as a dial from 0 to 7. Precise: a contiguous range of bits within a value, read by shifting it down to bit 0 and masking off the other bits. W1 D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows two jobs. On top, a mask clears only bit 3. Below, a shift and a mask pull out a field of three bits.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Each switch on Zara's panel has a number, counted from the right and starting at 0. The kitchen is switch 0. The bathroom is switch 3. The garden is switch 7. These numbers are called bit numbers.

To work on one switch, you make a mask: a row of eight bits with a 1 only where you want to work. To make a mask with a 1 at position 3, start with a single 1 at position 0 and slide it three places left. That slide is a shift.

Now there are three tricks. To turn a light on, use OR with the mask: switches under a 1 come on, the rest stay as they were. To flip a light, use XOR with the mask: switches under a 1 change, the rest stay. To turn a light off, flip the mask first so it has a 0 in that place and 1s everywhere else; then use AND. Under a 1, a switch keeps its state. Under the 0, it goes off.

To test one light, AND it with its mask. If the answer is not zero, that light is on.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

The bitwise operators work on each pair of bits in the same position, independently. For one pair of bits: AND (&) gives 1 only if both are 1; OR (|) gives 1 if at least one is 1; XOR (^) gives 1 if they are different; NOT (~) flips a single bit. F0-26 writes these rules as truth tables. R1 D2

Four patterns cover almost every job with a single bit k. The mask is 1u << k. R1

JobCodeWhy it works
Set bit k (turn on)x = x | (1u << k)OR with 1 gives 1; OR with 0 keeps the bit.
Clear bit k (turn off)x = x & ~(1u << k)The flipped mask has 0 at k: AND with 0 gives 0; AND with 1 keeps the bit.
Toggle bit k (flip)x = x ^ (1u << k)XOR with 1 flips; XOR with 0 keeps the bit.
Test bit k(x & (1u << k)) != 0Every other bit is cleared; what is left is non-zero only if bit k is 1.

A mask can select several bits at once: 0b1000'0001 selects bits 7 and 0. The 0b prefix writes a number in binary, and the ' is only a separator for your eyes. R1

A shift moves every bit. x << n moves bits n places left and fills the right with 0s, so for an unsigned value that fits, it multiplies by 2n: 1u << 20 printed 1048576 = 220. x >> n moves bits n places right, and bits that fall off the right end are lost, so it divides an unsigned value by 2n and drops the remainder. W1 R1

A bit field is read in two steps: shift it right until its lowest bit is at position 0, then AND with a mask of as many 1s as the field is wide. For bits 6..4: (x >> 4) & 0b111. A single-bit field is a flag. W1 R1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. In C++, the operands of these operators are first widened to at least int (or unsigned int). So ~(1u << 3) is a full-width unsigned value with many 1s, not an 8-bit one; that is fine for AND, but it is why Listing 1 converts some results back to std::uint8_t before printing them as eight bits. Use unsigned types for bit work: shifting into or out of the sign bit of a signed type is a trap for the next reader. Hardware registers in later courses (device registers, page-table entries) are described exactly as "bit 7: flag; bits 6..4: field", and drivers read them with these same shifts and masks. D2 D3

Not verified — check before relying on this

The exact C++ rules for widening ("integral promotion") and for shifting signed values are set by the C++ standard (ISO/IEC 14882, title only), which this build could not open. What is verified here is that Listing 1, built with -std=c++20 and both sanitizers, produced the output shown with no warnings and no sanitizer messages (R1).

How the hardware actually does it

A processor has instructions that apply AND, OR, XOR and NOT to all the bits of a register at the same moment, and instructions that shift a register's bits. One mask operation is therefore one step for the machine, not eight. How a particular processor encodes these instructions is in its architecture manual; HW102 builds the gates they are made from. D1 D3

Worked example

Decode a made-up status byte

A pretend robot vacuum describes its status byte like this (we invented it for practice; no real product uses it):

BitsNameMeaning
7DOOR1 = dust door open
6..4SPEEDspeed level 0–7
3LOWBAT1 = battery low
2..0MODE0 = off, 1 = sweep, … 6 = edges, 7 = return home

The byte reads 0b1011'0110 (0xB6).

  1. Write the bits under their numbers: bit 7 = 1, bits 6..4 = 011, bit 3 = 0, bits 2..0 = 110.
  2. DOOR: (x >> 7) & 1 = 1, so the door is open.
  3. SPEED: (x >> 4) & 0b111 = 011 = 3.
  4. LOWBAT: (x >> 3) & 1 = 0, so the battery is fine.
  5. MODE: x & 0b111 = 110 = 6, edges.

The run of Listing 1 prints the same byte, the shift by 4 (00001011), the low four bits (00000110) and "bits 6..4 as a number: 3". W1 R1

Shift arithmetic

0b1011'0110 = 182. Shifting right by 4 divides by 16: 182 ÷ 16 = 11 remainder 6, and indeed 00001011 = 11 while the lost bits 0110 = 6. W1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — masks.cpp

// Eight room lights in one byte: bit 0 is the kitchen, bit 7 is the garden.
#include <bitset>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

void show(const char* what, std::uint8_t lights)
{
    std::cout << std::bitset<8>(lights) << "  " << what << '\n';
}

int main()
{
    std::uint8_t lights = 0b0000'0000;
    show("all off", lights);

    lights = lights | (1u << 3);            // set bit 3: turn ON the bathroom light
    show("set bit 3 (OR)", lights);

    lights = lights | 0b1000'0001;          // set bits 7 and 0 at once
    show("set bits 7 and 0 (OR)", lights);

    lights = lights & ~(1u << 3);           // clear bit 3: turn OFF the bathroom light
    show("clear bit 3 (AND with NOT)", lights);

    lights = lights ^ 0b0000'0011;          // toggle bits 1 and 0
    show("toggle bits 1 and 0 (XOR)", lights);

    const bool gardenOn = (lights & (1u << 7)) != 0;  // test bit 7
    std::cout << "garden light on? " << (gardenOn ? "yes" : "no") << "\n\n";

    const std::uint8_t status = 0b1011'0110;
    show("status byte", status);
    show("shifted right by 4", static_cast<std::uint8_t>(status >> 4));
    show("low four bits (AND 0x0F)", static_cast<std::uint8_t>(status & 0x0F));
    std::cout << "bits 6..4 as a number: " << ((status >> 4) & 0b111) << '\n';
    std::cout << "1 shifted left by 20 = " << (1u << 20) << '\n';
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • A card with holes only stops you touching switches; a mask does the work. With AND, OR and XOR, the mask is combined with every bit, even the ones you "do not touch"; they stay the same only because the operation leaves them alone under that mask value. Pick the wrong operation and the "covered" switches change too. W1
  • Lights do not move between rooms; bits move in a shift. Moving every room's setting along the panel makes no sense in a house, but it is exactly what a shift does, and settings that slide off the end are lost forever. R1
  • A real panel's switches are all the same; bit numbers carry value. Switch 3 is worth 8 and switch 7 is worth 128. Mixing up "bit 3" and "the value 3" is the bug in the forensic lab. R2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
The wrong bits change (forensic lab: 00001011 becomes 00001000).The value 3 was used as a mask instead of bit 3 (1u << 3).Write the mask in binary: 3 = 0b0000'0011.Build masks from bit numbers with a shift.
Clearing a bit turns everything else off.AND with 1u << k instead of ~(1u << k).Print the mask in binary.Flip the mask before AND.
A field reads too big, for example 11 instead of 3.Shifted but forgot the mask; higher bits are still there.Count the 1s you kept.AND with as many 1s as the field is wide.
A test like x & 1u << k != 0 stops the build with "suggest parentheses" (Listing 3).Operator order: != is grouped before &.Read the compiler message: it names the line and column.Write (x & (1u << k)) != 0.

The fourth row is easy to check with our own compiler. Listing 3 writes the test without brackets. With the university's flags it is expected not to compile, and the compiler's real message explains why: the comparison != is grouped before &. R3

Transition box

Where you came from: F0-22 wrote bytes in hex and F0-24 showed that the type decides how a byte is read. What carries over: place values, bit numbers from the right, hex for writing masks (0x0F). What changes: you now operate on single bits inside a byte, and you must use unsigned types and brackets carefully. What comes next: F0-26 writes AND, OR, NOT and XOR as truth tables and builds them as light circuits with two switches. W1

Check yourself

  1. What is 1u << 5 in binary and in decimal?
  2. Start with 0b0101'0101. Set bit 1. What do you get?
  3. Start with 0b1111'0000. Clear bit 6. What do you get?
  4. Which expression tests bit 2 of x? (a) x & 2 (b) (x & (1u << 2)) != 0 (c) x | (1u << 2) (d) x >> 2
  5. What is 200 >> 3? Show it with bits and with division.
  6. Explain in your own words why clearing a bit needs the flipped mask.
  7. Apply it to a new case: the robot vacuum's byte is 0x9A. Decode all four fields.
  8. Predict: in Listing 1, if line 25 used the mask 0b0000'0001 instead, what would line 26 print?

Lab

Goal

Make a paper light panel with masks, practise the four jobs, then check them with Listing 1.

Hardware and software needed

Paper or card, scissors, a pencil. Optional: a computer with a C++ compiler; our toolchain is under Sources, R1.

Safety

Use child-safe scissors, with an adult nearby for younger learners.

Steps

  1. Draw eight boxes in a row and number them 7 to 0 from left to right. Label each with a room.
  2. Use a coin in a box for "on". Set the panel to 1000 1001.
  3. Cut a strip of card with a window over box 3. Using the rules in Layer 2, write the mask and the result of setting, clearing and toggling bit 3. Move the coins to match.
  4. Write the result of each step as bits, then compare with lines 2–5 of Listing 1's output.
  5. Write the made-up status byte 1011 0110 and decode its fields on paper with the Worked example's steps.
  6. Optional: change line 31 of Listing 1 to another byte, such as 0b0101'1001, predict line "bits 6..4 as a number", then run it.

Expected observations

Your paper results match the real output above, row for row. Every mask touched only the boxes under its 1s (or its 0, for clearing). R1

Verification

For your own byte in step 6, your prediction equals the program's printed field value.

Troubleshooting

  • Your bit numbers are mirrored. Bit 0 is always on the right.
  • Clearing turned off everything. You used the mask without flipping it.
  • Your edited program does not build. A binary number needs the 0b prefix, and the separator ' must sit between digits.

Extension

Write on paper the one line that turns on bits 4 and 5 and turns off bit 0 in two steps. Then add those two lines to Listing 1 and run it.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Bruno programmed the "goodnight" button: it should turn off the bathroom light (bit 3) and leave everything else alone. His sister reports: "The bathroom light is still on, and now the kitchen and the hall are dark!"

Evidence pack

Listing 2 — light_bug.cpp (evidence)

// Evidence program for the forensic lab: "the bathroom light will not turn off".
#include <bitset>
#include <cstdint>
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    std::uint8_t lights = 0b0000'1011;  // kitchen (0), hall (1) and bathroom (3) are on
    std::cout << "before: " << std::bitset<8>(lights) << '\n';
    lights = lights & ~3u;              // meant: turn off the bathroom light (bit 3)
    std::cout << "after:  " << std::bitset<8>(lights) << '\n';
    return 0;
}
