Questions

  1. Which bits changed, and which should have changed?
  2. Write 3u and ~3u (only the low eight bits) in binary.
  3. State two hypotheses (for example "the AND is wrong" and "the mask is wrong") and choose one using the evidence.
  4. Give the corrected line and the output you expect from it.
  5. Suggest a habit that prevents this mistake.

Method hints

Write the before value, the mask and the after value in three rows, as in Figure 1. Look at which columns hold the 0s of the mask. Grade yourself with the forensic rubric of the course.

Mini-project

Invent your own 8-bit status byte for a pretend device (a fish tank, a bike computer, a plant waterer). Write its field table with at least one flag and one field of two or more bits. Give a friend three bytes in hex to decode, and an answer card with the shifts and masks.

Rubric (4 points): clear field table that uses all 8 bits (1); three correct answer cards with shifts and masks (2); a friend decoded at least one byte using only your table (1).

Summary

  • Bits are numbered from 0 at the right; bit k is worth 2k.
  • Make a mask for bit k with 1u << k.
  • Set with OR, clear with AND of the flipped mask, toggle with XOR, test with AND.
  • << n multiplies by 2n and >> n divides by 2n (unsigned, while the value fits).
  • Read a field: shift right to bit 0, then AND with a mask of 1s as wide as the field.
  • Use unsigned types and brackets for bit work.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. 0b0010'0000 = 32.
  2. 0b0101'0101 | 0b0000'0010 = 0b0101'0111.
  3. 0b1111'0000 & ~0b0100'0000 = 0b1011'0000.
  4. (b). (a) tests bit 1, because 2 = 0b10 (the value-versus-bit-number mix-up). (c) sets bit 2 instead of testing it. (d) moves bit 2 down but keeps all higher bits too, so it can be non-zero when bit 2 is 0.
  5. 200 = 1100 1000; shifted right by 3: 0001 1001 = 25. Division: 200 ÷ 8 = 25 exactly.
  6. Any answer that says: AND keeps a bit where the mask has 1 and clears it where the mask has 0, so the mask needs a single 0 at the bit to clear and 1s everywhere else, which is the flipped single-bit mask.
  7. 0x9A = 1001 1010. DOOR (bit 7) = 1, open. SPEED (6..4) = 001 = 1. LOWBAT (bit 3) = 1, battery low. MODE (2..0) = 010 = 2.
  8. Line 26 would toggle only bit 0: from 10000001 to 10000000.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: before 00001011, after 00001000. Bits 1 and 0 (hall, kitchen) went off; bit 3 (bathroom) stayed on, the opposite of the intent. Hypotheses: (1) AND is the wrong operation; (2) the mask has its 0s in the wrong place. Evidence: 3u = 0000 0011, so ~3u ends in 1111 1100: its 0s are at bits 1 and 0. AND clears exactly those, matching the output. AND with a correct mask is the right operation (Listing 1, line 22), so hypothesis 2. Root cause: Listing 2, line 10, uses the value 3 instead of the bit number 3; the mask must be 1u << 3 = 0000 1000. Fix: lights = lights & ~(1u << 3);. The fixed program (light_fixed.cpp in the lab folder, one changed line) printed:

before: 00001011
after:  00000011

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-25/light_fixed.out; run record light_fixed.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:31:02Z; exit code: 0.

Verification: only bit 3 changed (00001011 → 00000011). Prevention: always build single-bit masks with 1u << k, or give each mask a name such as bathroomMask; print masks in binary while testing. How the evidence was made: Listing 1's clear-bit line rewritten with the value 3 as the mask, run in this build R2. Wrong answers: "the program ran the wrong line" (only one line changes the lights); "use OR instead of AND" (OR can only turn lights on).

Story hook

Analogy

Kwame's family has a big cupboard with a light inside. The light has two switches. One is on the wall, and one is a little button inside the door frame that is pressed only when the door is open. The light comes on only when the wall switch is on and the door is open.

At the stairs it is different. There is one switch at the bottom and one at the top. Kwame can turn the light on downstairs and off again upstairs. His cousin Sofia wonders: "How does the light know which switch I used?"

Both puzzles have the same answer. A light that depends on two switches follows a rule, and the rule can be written as a small table. In this chapter you will write those tables, called truth tables, and test them with a tiny circuit model.

What you will be able to do

  • Write the truth tables of AND, OR, NOT and XOR from memory.
  • Explain AND and OR with two light switches in a row (series) and side by side (parallel).
  • Explain XOR with the two switches of a stair light.
  • Build a truth table for a new rule by listing every combination of inputs.
  • Diagnose a stair-light model that uses the wrong rule (the forensic lab).
Safety

The light circuits in this chapter are models only: drawings and a small C++ program. Never open a wall switch, a lamp holder or a socket. House lights run on mains electricity, which can kill, and this university does no mains work at any level. Real circuits with switches and lamps are built later, in KID103, with battery kits designed for children and an adult present (see the safety rules).

Jargon box
Boolean value
Simple words: a value that is either true or false. Analogy: a switch is on or off; a lamp is lit or dark. Precise: a value of a two-element set {false, true}, written 0 and 1; in C++ the type bool, which prints as 0 or 1 by default (run R1). R1 D1
Truth table
Simple words: a table that lists every possible input and the output for each. Analogy: a chart by the cupboard that says, for each position of the two switches, whether the light is on. Precise: a complete listing of a Boolean function: one row for each of the 2n combinations of its n inputs, with the output value. W1
AND
Simple words: true only when both inputs are true. Analogy: two switches one after the other in the same wire (in series). Precise: the Boolean function with output 1 exactly when all inputs are 1; in C++, && for bool values and & bit by bit (F0-25). W1 R1
OR
Simple words: true when at least one input is true. Analogy: two switches side by side (in parallel): either one can light the lamp. Precise: the Boolean function with output 1 when one or more inputs are 1; in C++, || and bitwise |. It is "inclusive": both on also gives 1. W1 R1
NOT
Simple words: turns true into false and false into true. Analogy: a push button that breaks the circuit while you press it. Precise: the one-input Boolean function with output equal to the opposite of the input; in C++, ! and bitwise ~. W1 R1
XOR (exclusive OR)
Simple words: true when the two inputs are different. Analogy: the stair light: flipping either switch changes the lamp. Precise: the two-input Boolean function with output 1 exactly when the inputs differ; for bool values in C++, a != b, and bitwise ^. W1 R1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows two circuits drawn as blocks. On the left, switches A and B are in series: the current must pass through both. On the right, they are in parallel: either path will do. Under each is its truth table.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Think of the cupboard light. Current must flow through the wall switch and then through the door button. If either one is open, the path is broken. So the light is on only when both are on. That rule is called AND.

Now imagine a lamp with two switches side by side, like two doors into the same room. The current can go through either one. If at least one is closed, the lamp lights. That rule is called OR.

A push button that breaks the circuit while you press it does the opposite of your finger. Pressed means dark. Not pressed means lit. That rule is called NOT.

The stair light is the cleverest. Flipping either switch changes the lamp. If both switches are the same, the lamp is off. If they are different, it is on. That rule is called XOR, short for "exclusive OR": one or the other, but not both.

A truth table writes such a rule down completely. With two switches there are four combinations: off-off, off-on, on-off, on-on. The table has one row for each. Nothing is left out, so nothing is left to guess.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A Boolean value is either false (0) or true (1). A logic rule takes Boolean inputs and gives a Boolean output. A truth table lists all 2n input combinations for n inputs, in counting order: 00, 01, 10, 11 for two inputs, the binary numbers 0 to 3 (F0-20). W1

ABA AND BA OR BA XOR B
00000
01011
10011
11110

NOT has one input: NOT 0 = 1 and NOT 1 = 0. These four tables match the output of Listing 1. R1

Some facts you can read straight from the tables. AND is 1 in only one row; OR is 0 in only one row. OR and XOR differ only in the last row, where both inputs are 1. XOR is 1 exactly when the inputs differ, so for two Boolean values it is the same as "not equal". W1

In C++, the logical operators on bool values are && (AND), || (OR) and ! (NOT); Listing 1 writes XOR as a != b. On whole bytes, the bitwise operators of F0-25 apply the same tables to each pair of bits. R1 D3

To build a truth table for any new rule: list the inputs in counting order, then work out the output for each row. Example: "the porch lamp is on if it is dark AND (someone is at the door OR the alarm is set)" has three inputs, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 rows. W1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. With two inputs there are 4 rows, and each row's output can be 0 or 1, so there are 24 = 16 different two-input rules. AND, OR and XOR are three of them; NAND (NOT AND) and NOR (NOT OR) are two more that hardware designers like, because every other rule can be built from NAND alone. HW102 builds all the gates from NAND. In C++, && and || also "short-circuit": if the left side already decides the answer, the right side is not evaluated; that matters when the right side has an effect, and is taught with conditions in KID102. W1 D4 D3

How the hardware actually does it

Inside a chip, the switches are tiny electronic switches (transistors), and small groups of them form gates that compute AND, OR, NOT and XOR on electrical signals. The idea is the same as Figure 1: arrangements of switches decide whether a signal gets through. The gates themselves are the first topic of HW102. D1 D2

Worked example

The porch lamp

Rule: lamp = DARK AND (VISITOR OR ALARM). Work out the bracket first, then the AND.

The lamp is lit in three rows: it is dark and at least one of the other two is true. W1

The stair light, step by step

Start with both switches down (0, 0): lamp off. Flip the bottom one (1, 0): different, so on. Walk up and flip the top one (1, 1): same, so off. Flip the bottom one again (0, 1): different, so on. Each single flip changes the lamp, which is what XOR gives you. The fixed model in the forensic answer key prints exactly this sequence. W1 R2

Code walk-through

Listing 1 is the university's own tiny text model of light circuits. It does not simulate electricity; it applies the rule of each circuit and prints the truth table.

Listing 1 — switch_circuits.cpp

// The university's tiny text model of light circuits with two switches, A and B.
// true means a switch is pressed (closed) or the lamp is lit; false means open or dark.
#include <iostream>

bool seriesCircuit(bool a, bool b)    // A and B one after the other: AND
{
    return a && b;
}

bool parallelCircuit(bool a, bool b)  // A and B side by side: OR
{
    return a || b;
}

bool stairCircuit(bool a, bool b)     // two-way switches at the bottom and top of a stair: XOR
{
    return a != b;
}

bool pushToBreak(bool a)              // a button that breaks the circuit when pressed: NOT
{
    return !a;
}

int main()
{
    std::cout << "A B | AND OR XOR\n";
    for (bool a : {false, true}) {
        for (bool b : {false, true}) {
            std::cout << a << ' ' << b << " |  " << seriesCircuit(a, b) << "   "
                      << parallelCircuit(a, b) << "   " << stairCircuit(a, b) << '\n';
        }
    }
    std::cout << "\nA | NOT\n";
    for (bool a : {false, true}) {
        std::cout << a << " |  " << pushToBreak(a) << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Real switches can bounce, stick or be half pressed; a Boolean value cannot. The model's inputs are always exactly true or false. Turning a real, noisy switch into a clean 0 or 1 is an engineering job of its own (later, in hardware courses).
  • In a real stair circuit, "same means off" depends on how it was wired. An electrician could wire it so that "same" means on; then the rule would be NOT XOR. Either way, flipping one switch changes the lamp. Our model fixes the XOR version by definition. D2
  • Lamps take time to light; logic in the model is instant. The model prints the result immediately. Real gates take a short time to switch, which matters a lot in HW102 and later courses.
  • A truth table with many inputs is not practical as a wall chart. Each extra switch doubles the rows. With 10 inputs there are 1024 rows (F0-23); engineers then use algebra instead (F0-27). W1

Transition box

Where you came from: F0-25 used AND, OR, XOR and NOT on the bits of a byte. What carries over: the same four rules; a byte operation is eight truth-table lookups side by side. What changes: you now write each rule completely, as a table with every combination, and connect it to switches in series and parallel. What comes next: F0-27 shows how to rewrite and simplify rules with Boolean algebra, including De Morgan's laws, and how to prove two rules are equal with a truth table. W1

  1. Write the truth tables of AND, OR, XOR (two inputs) and NOT.
  2. Two switches in series control a lamp. Switch A is closed and B is open. Is the lamp lit?
  3. Which rule gives 1 only when the inputs differ? (a) AND (b) OR (c) XOR (d) NOT
  4. How many rows does a truth table with 4 inputs have?
  5. In which single row do OR and XOR give different answers?
  6. Explain in your own words why switches in parallel behave like OR.
  7. Apply it to a new case: a garden sprinkler runs if it is morning AND NOT raining. Write its truth table.
  8. Predict: if line 17 of Listing 1 were changed to return a == b;, what would the XOR column print?

Lab

Goal

Build truth tables for two light switches in the university's text circuit model (Listing 1), then design and test a circuit rule of your own.

Hardware and software needed

Paper and pencil. A computer with a C++ compiler for steps 4–6 (or read the recorded output). Our toolchain is under Sources, R1. No electrical parts: this lab is a model.

Safety

Do not touch real house wiring (see the Safety box at the top of this chapter). Otherwise none beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. On paper, draw the series and parallel circuits of Figure 1 and fill in their tables without looking.
  2. Draw the stair light as two switches and write its table.
  3. Predict the output of Listing 1, line by line.
  4. Build and run Listing 1 (build command above, or university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F0-26). Compare with your prediction.
  5. Add a new function to the model for the cupboard light with a push-to-break child lock: lamp = WALL AND DOOR AND NOT LOCK. Print its 8-row table.
  6. Check your 8 rows against a table worked out on paper.

Expected observations

Listing 1 prints the four-row table with AND = 0 0 0 1, OR = 0 1 1 1, XOR = 0 1 1 0, and NOT = 1 0, as in the recorded run. Your cupboard rule has exactly one row with a lit lamp: wall 1, door 1, lock 0. R1

Verification

Your paper tables and the program's tables agree in every row, and your new table has 8 rows.

Troubleshooting

  • The output shows "true" and "false" instead of 1 and 0. Someone added std::boolalpha; that is allowed and means the same.
  • Your new table has only 4 rows. Three inputs need three nested loops.
  • The build fails with an "unused" error. With -Werror, a function or variable you wrote but did not use stops the build; call it or remove it.

Extension

Write the truth table for NAND (NOT AND) and show that NAND of A with itself gives NOT A.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Amara modelled her stair light for a school project. Her brother tested it: he turned the light on downstairs, walked up, and flipped the top switch to turn it off. In the model, the light stayed on. Find out why from the model's record.

Evidence pack

Listing 2 — hall_light.cpp (evidence)

// Evidence program for the forensic lab: Amara's model of the stair light.
// Each line is one moment: someone flips one switch, and the model prints the lamp.
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

bool lamp(bool bottom, bool top)
{
    return bottom || top;
}

int main()
{
    bool bottom = false;
    bool top = false;
    const std::string flips = "BTBTTB";  // B = flip the bottom switch, T = flip the top switch
    std::cout << "start          bottom=" << bottom << " top=" << top
              << " lamp=" << lamp(bottom, top) << '\n';
    for (char flip : flips) {
        if (flip == 'B') {
            bottom = !bottom;
        } else {
            top = !top;
        }
        std::cout << "flip " << flip << "         bottom=" << bottom << " top=" << top
                  << " lamp=" << lamp(bottom, top) << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

<< " lamp=" << lamp(bottom, top) << '\n';

Questions

  1. A stair light must change every time any switch is flipped. Mark every evidence line where the lamp did not change.
  2. Write the four (bottom, top) combinations that appear and the lamp value for each. Which truth table is that?
  3. State two hypotheses (for example "the flips are recorded wrongly" and "the lamp rule is wrong") and test them with the evidence.
  4. Which line of Listing 2 must change, and to what?
  5. Predict the fixed model's output for the same flips.

Method hints

Build a truth table from the evidence itself, then compare it with the four tables in Layer 2. Grade yourself with the forensic rubric of the course.

Mini-project

Design a "secret clubhouse light" for three switches (one at each of three doors) so that flipping any single switch changes the light. Write its 8-row truth table and explain your rule. Hint: try XOR twice.

Rubric (4 points): correct 8-row table (2); rule written with AND, OR, NOT or XOR (1); clear explanation of why every single flip changes the light (1).

Summary

  • A truth table lists every input combination (2n rows) and the output.
  • AND: 1 only if both are 1 (switches in series).
  • OR: 1 if at least one is 1 (switches in parallel); it includes the "both" case.
  • NOT: the opposite (a push-to-break button).
  • XOR: 1 if the inputs differ (the stair light).
  • In C++: &&, ||, ! and != for bool; &, |, ~, ^ bit by bit.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: the lamp did not change on the third line (flip T: 1,1 → lamp stays 1), the fourth (flip B: 0,1 → stays 1) and the last (flip B: 1,1 → stays 1). Evidence table: (0,0) → 0, (1,0) → 1, (0,1) → 1, (1,1) → 1: that is the OR table. Hypotheses: (1) flips are recorded wrongly: ruled out, because each line shows exactly one switch changing, as the flip letter says; (2) the lamp rule is wrong: supported, because the rule's table is OR, while a stair light needs XOR. Root cause: Listing 2, line 8, return bottom || top;. With both switches on, OR still gives 1, so the second switch cannot turn the lamp off. Fix: return bottom != top; (XOR). The fixed model (hall_light_fixed.cpp in the lab folder, one changed line) printed:

start          bottom=0 top=0 lamp=0
flip B         bottom=1 top=0 lamp=1
flip T         bottom=1 top=1 lamp=0
flip B         bottom=0 top=1 lamp=1
flip T         bottom=0 top=0 lamp=0
flip T         bottom=0 top=1 lamp=1
flip B         bottom=1 top=1 lamp=0

Story hook

Analogy

Before bedtime, Hana's mum checks the house. By the front door there is a small green light. It should glow only when everything is shut: "NOT (the door is open OR the window is open)".

Hana says it differently: "The light is green when the door is closed AND the window is closed." Her older brother Kofi says it a third way: "The light is green when the door is closed OR the window is closed." All three sound sensible at bedtime.

But are they the same rule? Two of them are. One is not, and it could leave a window open all night with a green light glowing. In this chapter you will learn the rules for rewriting such sentences safely, and how to prove that two rules really are the same.

What you will be able to do

  • Write logic rules as expressions with AND, OR and NOT, using letters for the inputs.
  • Use the basic laws of Boolean algebra (identity, complement, double negation, commutative, associative, distributive) to rewrite an expression.
  • State and apply De Morgan's two laws.
  • Prove that two expressions are equal with a complete truth table, and show that two are different with one counterexample row.
  • Diagnose a wrong "simplification" of a safety rule (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Boolean algebra
Simple words: rules for rewriting true/false sentences, like the rules for rewriting sums. Analogy: tidying the house rules on the fridge without changing what they mean. Precise: the algebra of the values 0 and 1 with the operations AND, OR and NOT, and the laws they satisfy; named after the mathematician George Boole. W1 D1
Expression (Boolean)
Simple words: a rule written with letters, AND, OR, NOT and brackets. Analogy: "NOT (door open OR window open)" written short as NOT (D OR W). Precise: a formula built from Boolean variables, the constants 0 and 1, the operators AND, OR, NOT and brackets; it has one output value for each combination of variable values. W1
Equivalent expressions
Simple words: two rules that always give the same answer. Analogy: two ways of saying the same house rule. Precise: two Boolean expressions are equivalent when their outputs agree in every row of their truth table. W1
Counterexample
Simple words: one case that shows a claim is wrong. Analogy: one open window under a green light. Precise: an assignment of input values for which two expressions claimed equal give different outputs; one counterexample is enough to disprove equivalence. W1
De Morgan's laws
Simple words: to push a NOT inside a bracket, flip each part and swap AND with OR. Analogy: "not (open door or open window)" means "closed door and closed window". Precise: NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B), and NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B); named after the mathematician Augustus De Morgan. W1 R1 D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows De Morgan's two laws as a recipe. The NOT outside the bracket moves inside: each letter gets its own NOT, and the AND or OR in the middle swaps.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

In F0-17 you rewrote number sentences without changing their meaning: 3 + 4 is the same as 4 + 3. True/false sentences have rewriting rules too. Together, those rules are called Boolean algebra.

Some rules are easy to believe. "Door shut AND window shut" means the same as "window shut AND door shut". "NOT NOT open" means "open", as "it's not true that the door isn't open" means it is open.

The most useful rules are De Morgan's laws. They tell you what happens when a NOT sits outside a bracket. "It is NOT true that (the door is open OR the window is open)." That means neither is open. So the door is closed AND the window is closed.

See what happened? The NOT went inside and touched each part. And the OR turned into an AND. That is the whole trick: flip each part, and swap AND with OR.

How can you be sure two rules mean the same? Try every case. With two inputs there are only four cases. If the rules agree in all four, they are the same. If they disagree in even one case, they are different. That one case is a counterexample.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A Boolean expression uses letters for inputs (A, B, C), the constants 0 and 1, and AND, OR, NOT. Two expressions are equivalent when they give the same output in every row of the truth table. Because there are only 2n rows for n inputs, you can always check by trying them all. This is a complete proof, not a guess. W1

Each law below can be checked with a truth table of at most 8 rows. W1 D2

LawAND formOR form
IdentityA AND 1 = AA OR 0 = A
Null (dominance)A AND 0 = 0A OR 1 = 1
IdempotentA AND A = AA OR A = A
ComplementA AND (NOT A) = 0A OR (NOT A) = 1
Double negationNOT (NOT A) = A
CommutativeA AND B = B AND AA OR B = B OR A
Associative(A AND B) AND C = A AND (B AND C)(A OR B) OR C = A OR (B OR C)
DistributiveA AND (B OR C) = (A AND B) OR (A AND C)A OR (B AND C) = (A OR B) AND (A OR C)
De MorganNOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B)NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B)

Look at the pattern: every law has a twin made by swapping AND with OR and 0 with 1. The second distributive law has no twin in ordinary arithmetic: 2 + (3 × 4) is not (2 + 3) × (2 + 4). Be careful not to carry number habits across without checking. W1

Listing 1 checks both De Morgan laws in all four rows. Listing 2 checks the first distributive law and De Morgan's law for three inputs in all eight rows. Both report zero failures. R1 R2

In C++ the same laws hold for bool values with &&, || and !, and bit by bit for &, | and ~ (F0-25): ~(a | b) equals ~a & ~b in every bit. D3

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Proving by trying every row is sometimes called "perfect induction". It works because the input space is finite; it stops being practical when there are many inputs (each extra input doubles the rows), and then engineers use algebraic steps, or tools that reason about the expressions. Our compiler did some of this reasoning by itself. Listing 3 compares !(a || b) with !a && !b in one expression. With our flags it refused to build: it reported that the comparison "always evaluates to true", which means it had worked out that the two sides are the same. R3 D2

            std::cout << (!(a || b) == (!a && !b)) << '\n';

How the hardware actually does it

De Morgan's laws let hardware designers build one kind of gate from another: an OR of inputs can be made from an AND of flipped inputs, followed by a NOT. Chip design tools use Boolean algebra to replace expressions with equivalent ones that need fewer or cheaper gates. You will use the laws by hand when you build gates in HW102. D2 D4

Worked example

Prove De Morgan's second law with a truth table

ABA OR BNOT (A OR B)NOT ANOT B(NOT A) AND (NOT B)
0001111
0110100
1010010
1110000

The fourth and seventh columns agree in all four rows, so the expressions are equivalent. W1 R1

Simplify with algebra

Simplify NOT (NOT A OR B) AND B.

  1. De Morgan on the bracket: NOT (NOT A OR B) = (NOT NOT A) AND (NOT B).
  2. Double negation: = A AND (NOT B).
  3. So the whole expression is A AND (NOT B) AND B.
  4. Associative and commutative laws let us group (B AND NOT B).
  5. Complement: B AND (NOT B) = 0. Null: A AND 0 = 0.
  6. Answer: the expression is always 0, whatever A and B are.

Disprove with one counterexample

Claim: NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B). Try A = 1, B = 0. Left: NOT (1 AND 0) = NOT 0 = 1. Right: (NOT 1) AND (NOT 0) = 0 AND 1 = 0. They differ, so the claim is false. One row is enough. W1

Listing 1 — demorgan.cpp

// Check De Morgan's laws by trying every combination of A and B.
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    int rowsChecked = 0;
    int rowsWhereLaw1Fails = 0;
    int rowsWhereLaw2Fails = 0;
    std::cout << "A B | !(A&&B) !A||!B | !(A||B) !A&&!B\n";
    for (bool a : {false, true}) {
        for (bool b : {false, true}) {
            const bool left1 = !(a && b);
            const bool right1 = !a || !b;
            const bool left2 = !(a || b);
            const bool right2 = !a && !b;
            std::cout << a << ' ' << b << " |    " << left1 << "       " << right1
                      << "    |    " << left2 << "       " << right2 << '\n';
            ++rowsChecked;
            if (left1 != right1) {
                ++rowsWhereLaw1Fails;
            }
            if (left2 != right2) {
                ++rowsWhereLaw2Fails;
            }
        }
    }
    std::cout << "rows checked: " << rowsChecked << '\n';
    std::cout << "law 1 failed in " << rowsWhereLaw1Fails << " rows\n";
    std::cout << "law 2 failed in " << rowsWhereLaw2Fails << " rows\n";
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Everyday sentences are fuzzy; Boolean expressions are not. "Shut the door or the window" might mean "one of them" or "at least one". In Boolean algebra, OR always includes the "both" case (F0-26). Translate carefully before you apply a law.
  • Tidying the fridge rules can change their spirit; equivalent expressions never change their output. Rewriting a house rule in nicer words sometimes changes what people do. A correct algebraic rewrite gives the same output in every row, guaranteed by the truth table. W1
  • Number habits do not all carry over. In numbers, 1 + 1 = 2; in Boolean algebra, 1 OR 1 = 1. The second distributive law works for Boolean values but not for numbers. W1

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
A safety light shows "all clear" while something is open (forensic lab).NOT pushed inside without swapping OR to AND.Compare the two versions in all four rows.NOT (A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.
A rewrite "works" in the cases you tried but fails later.Only some rows were tested.Count rows: are there 2n?Test every row, or prove with laws.
NOT applied to only one letter of a bracket.The NOT was not distributed to every part.Underline each letter inside the bracket: does each get a NOT?Each part gets its own NOT.
The compiler stops with "self-comparison always evaluates to true" (Listing 3).Two equivalent expressions compared directly.Read the message; it names the line.Store each side in a named variable, or remove the needless check.
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-26 wrote AND, OR, NOT and XOR as truth tables; F0-17 rewrote equations without changing their meaning. What carries over: truth tables, which now serve as proofs; the habit of rewriting step by step. What changes: you now transform whole expressions with laws, and some laws (1 OR 1 = 1, the second distributive law) differ from number arithmetic. What comes next: F0-28 uses logic to state invariants: sentences that must stay true while a program runs. W1

Check yourself

  1. Write both of De Morgan's laws.
  2. Use De Morgan to rewrite NOT (hungry AND tired) in words.
  3. Simplify A OR (NOT A AND B). (Hint: use the second distributive law.)
  4. Which is equivalent to NOT (A OR B)? (a) NOT A OR NOT B (b) NOT A AND NOT B (c) A AND B (d) NOT A OR B
  5. Find a counterexample to the claim A OR (B AND C) = (A OR B) AND C.
  6. Explain in your own words why a complete truth table is a proof, but a few test rows are not.
  7. Apply it to a new case: a robot may move when NOT (battery low OR bumper pressed). Rewrite the rule with AND, and say when the robot may move.
  8. Predict: if Listing 1 compared !(a && b) with !a && !b instead, how many rows would "law 1" fail in?

Lab

Goal

Prove two laws by hand with truth tables, disprove one false "law" with a counterexample, and check all three with a small program.

Hardware and software needed

Paper and pencil. Optional: a computer with a C++ compiler; our toolchain is under Sources, R1.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Draw a truth table for De Morgan's first law with columns A, B, A AND B, NOT (A AND B), NOT A, NOT B, (NOT A) OR (NOT B). Fill in all four rows.
  2. Draw an 8-row table for the second distributive law A OR (B AND C) = (A OR B) AND (A OR C).
  3. Check the false law "NOT (A AND B) = NOT A AND NOT B" and circle the rows where it fails.
  4. Compare step 1 with the output of Listing 1.
  5. Optional: copy Listing 2 and change it to test the second distributive law instead of the first. Run it with run_lab.sh.

Expected observations

Steps 1 and 2: the two sides agree in every row. Step 3: the false law fails in exactly two rows (A, B = 0, 1 and 1, 0). Listing 1 reports zero failures for both real laws. R1

Verification

Your hand tables match the program's rows, and your edited program (step 5) prints "combinations where a law failed: 0".

Troubleshooting

  • Your table for step 2 has 4 rows. Three inputs need 8.
  • The build stops with "self-comparison always evaluates to true". You compared two equal expressions in one line; store each side in a named variable, as Listing 2 does.
  • A law "fails" in your hand table. Recheck the NOT columns first; that is where slips happen.

Extension

Prove the "absorption" law A AND (A OR B) = A, first with a table, then with algebra.

Forensic lab

Scenario

The "all closed" green light from the story hook is controlled by a small program. Kofi "simplified" the rule. That night the light glowed green while the window was wide open. Find what went wrong.

Evidence pack

Listing 4 — alarm.cpp (evidence; the program prints both versions side by side)

// Evidence program for the forensic lab: the "all closed" light by the front door.
// Original rule: the green light is on when NOT (door open OR window open).
// Kofi "simplified" it before this run.
#include <iostream>

bool greenLightOriginal(bool doorOpen, bool windowOpen)
{
    return !(doorOpen || windowOpen);
}

bool greenLightSimplified(bool doorOpen, bool windowOpen)
{
    return !doorOpen || !windowOpen;
}

int main()
{
    std::cout << "door window | original simplified\n";
    for (bool door : {false, true}) {
        for (bool window : {false, true}) {
            std::cout << "  " << door << "     " << window << "    |    "
                      << greenLightOriginal(door, window) << "         "
                      << greenLightSimplified(door, window) << '\n';
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

Questions

  1. In which rows do the two versions disagree? What does each of those rows mean in the house?
  2. State two hypotheses: "the original rule is wrong" and "the simplification is wrong". Which does the evidence support?
  3. Which law did Kofi try to use, and what mistake did he make?
  4. Write the correct simplified rule and predict the program's output with it.
  5. What check should be part of every rewrite of a safety rule?

Method hints

Read each output row as a sentence ("door closed, window open: original says …"). Then apply De Morgan's law to the original rule on paper and compare with Kofi's line. Grade yourself with the forensic rubric of the course.

Mini-project

Collect three rules from your own home or school ("you may go out if NOT (raining OR homework not done)"). Write each as a Boolean expression, rewrite it with De Morgan's laws, and prove each rewrite with a truth table. Present them as a "rule book" page.

Rubric (4 points): three correct expressions (1); three correct rewrites (1); three complete truth tables as proofs (1); clear everyday wording of each rewritten rule (1).

Summary

  • Boolean algebra rewrites true/false expressions without changing their outputs.
  • Every law has a twin: swap AND with OR and 0 with 1.
  • De Morgan: NOT (A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B; NOT (A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B.
  • A complete truth table (2n rows) is a proof; one disagreeing row is a counterexample.
  • Some laws differ from number arithmetic: 1 OR 1 = 1, and OR distributes over AND.
  • Check every rewrite of a safety rule in every row.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. NOT (A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B); NOT (A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B).
  2. "Not hungry OR not tired" (at least one of the two is not true).
  3. A OR (NOT A AND B) = (A OR NOT A) AND (A OR B) = 1 AND (A OR B) = A OR B.
  4. (b). (a) is De Morgan's other law applied to the wrong bracket (it equals NOT (A AND B)). (c) has no NOT at all. (d) only flips A.
  5. A = 1, B = 0, C = 0: left = 1 OR 0 = 1; right = (1 OR 0) AND 0 = 0. (Any row with A = 1 and C = 0 works.)
  6. Any answer that says: the expressions have only 2n possible inputs, so checking every row leaves no case unchecked; a few rows leave untested cases where they might differ.
  7. NOT battery low AND NOT bumper pressed: the robot may move only when the battery is not low and the bumper is not pressed.
  8. Two rows: (0, 1) and (1, 0), where the left side gives 1 and the right side gives 0.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: the versions disagree in rows (door 0, window 1) and (door 1, window 0): the original gives 0 (not all closed), the simplified gives 1 (green light) while something is open. Both agree when both are closed (1) and when both are open (0), which is why a quick test with "everything shut" and "everything open" passed. Hypotheses: (1) the original is wrong: ruled out, its column is 1 only when both are closed, which is the stated meaning; (2) the simplification is wrong: supported. Root cause: Listing 4, line 13: Kofi pushed the NOT inside the bracket but kept the OR: !doorOpen || !windowOpen. De Morgan's second law requires swapping OR to AND. Story hook

Analogy

Luca and his grandmother Ines play a game with two jars of marbles: a red jar and a blue jar. On each turn, one of them moves some marbles from one jar to the other. The jars fill and empty, back and forth.

"Here's a riddle," says Ines. "After a hundred turns, how many marbles are there in total?" Luca does not need to watch the hundred turns. "Twenty," he says, "the same as at the start. We only move marbles. We never add or take any away."

Luca has found something that stays true while everything else changes. Engineers call that an invariant. When a program breaks an invariant, you know there is a bug, and the first broken step shows where to look. In this chapter you will learn to state invariants and to use them as bug detectors.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what an invariant is, with an everyday example.
  • State an invariant for a simple process, such as moving marbles or converting a number to binary.
  • Check that an invariant is true at the start and is kept by every step, and use it to prove a result.
  • Use a parity (odd/even) invariant to show that some goals can never be reached.
  • Diagnose a bug by finding the first step where an invariant breaks (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Invariant
Simple words: a sentence about a process that stays true at every step. Analogy: "the two jars together hold twenty marbles", whatever moves are made. Precise: a condition (a Boolean expression about the state, F0-27) that holds in the starting state and is preserved by every allowed step, so it holds in every state reached. W1 D1
Loop invariant
Simple words: an invariant for a repeating part of a program. Analogy: the marble total checked after every turn of the game. Precise: a condition that is true before a loop starts and remains true after each pass of the loop body; together with the loop's stopping condition it proves what the loop computes. W1 D1
Parity
Simple words: whether a number is odd or even. Analogy: whether the marbles can be paired off with none left over. Precise: the remainder of a whole number after dividing by 2: 0 (even) or 1 (odd); for a binary number it is the least significant bit (F0-21). W1
Invariant check
Simple words: a line in a program that tests the invariant and complains if it is false. Analogy: counting all the marbles after each turn. Precise: code that evaluates the invariant at chosen points and reports a failure; in larger C++ programs this can be written with assert (introduced in later courses). R1 D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 follows the two jars through four moves of the game. The jars change every time. The total under them does not.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Most things in a process change. Marbles move. Numbers get halved. Switches flip. An invariant is something that does not change. You say it as a sentence, and the sentence stays true at every step.

To be sure a sentence is an invariant, you check two things. First: is it true at the start? Second: if it is true before a step, is it still true after the step? If both answers are yes, it stays true forever, however many steps there are. It is like a row of dominoes: the first one falls, and each one knocks over the next.

Invariants are great bug detectors. If a program should keep "twenty marbles in total", let it count after every move. The first time the count is wrong, you know which move has the bug.

Invariants also answer "is this possible?" questions. Suppose you may only flip two switches at a time, and all eight start off. Can you end with exactly one switch on? Each move changes the number of "on" switches by 2, 0 or −2. So the number stays even. One is odd. So it can never happen, and you did not have to try every move.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

An invariant is a Boolean expression about the state of a process (the jars, the variables of a program). Proving that it is an invariant takes two steps. Start: show it is true in the starting state. Step: show that every allowed step, starting from any state where it is true, ends in a state where it is still true. Then it is true in every state the process can reach. W1 D1

For the jars: at the start, red + blue = 12 + 8 = 20. A move of m marbles from red to blue changes red to red − m and blue to blue + m, and (red − m) + (blue + m) = red + blue. A move from blue to red is the same with the roles swapped. So red + blue = 20 is an invariant. W1

A loop invariant does the same job for a loop in a program. Listing 1 converts 45 to binary as in F0-21. Its invariant is: original = rest × placeValue + doneSoFar. Here rest is the part not yet converted, placeValue is the value of the next bit to write, and doneSoFar is the value of the bits already written. R1

  • Start: rest = 45, placeValue = 1, doneSoFar = 0, so 45 × 1 + 0 = 45. True.
  • Step: rest = 2 × (rest ÷ 2) + bit. The loop adds bit × placeValue to doneSoFar, doubles placeValue and halves rest. The new rest × placeValue + doneSoFar equals (rest ÷ 2) × 2 × placeValue + doneSoFar + bit × placeValue = rest × placeValue + doneSoFar, unchanged.
  • End: the loop stops when rest = 0. The invariant then says original = 0 + doneSoFar. So the bits written are worth exactly the original number: the conversion is correct.

The run of Listing 1 checks the invariant at every pass and prints "holds" seven times. W1 R1

Parity invariants are common. If every step changes a count by an even amount, the count's parity (its LSB) never changes. Then any goal with the other parity is impossible. W1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. The "start plus step" argument is mathematical induction. A loop invariant, together with the condition that stops the loop, is a standard way to prove what a loop computes; the same idea is used to argue that a loop finishes at all (here, rest gets smaller at every pass). Larger systems state invariants about their data: "this list is always sorted", "this counter equals the number of items", and, in the concurrency courses, "only the thread holding the lock changes the shared data". In C++, invariant checks can be written with assert, which stops the program with a message when its condition is false; it is introduced with the tooling in the systems programming courses. D1 D2

How the hardware actually does it

Hardware relies on invariants too. Some memory and communication systems store an extra parity bit with each group of bits, chosen so that the number of 1s is always even (or always odd). If a single bit flips by accident, the count's parity changes and the check fails, so the error is noticed. How a particular device does this is in its own documentation; the idea is the parity invariant of this chapter. D3

Worked example

The two-switch puzzle

Eight switches start off. A move flips exactly two different switches. Can you reach a state with exactly three switches on?

  1. Count the switches that are on: call it n. At the start, n = 0, which is even.
  2. A move flips two switches. Each flip changes n by +1 (off to on) or −1 (on to off). Two flips change n by +2, 0 or −2.
  3. Adding an even number to an even number gives an even number. So "n is even" is an invariant.
  4. Three is odd. So three switches on can never be reached.

The conversion invariant, row by row

restplaceValuedoneSoFarrest × placeValue + doneSoFar
451045 × 1 + 0 = 45
222144 + 1 = 45
114144 + 1 = 45
58540 + 5 = 45
2161332 + 13 = 45
1321332 + 13 = 45
064450 + 45 = 45

Every row gives 45, and the last row says the bits written are worth 45: 101101. These rows are exactly the values printed by Listing 1. W1 R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — invariant.cpp

// Converting 45 to binary while checking a sentence that must stay true at every step:
//   original == rest * placeValue + doneSoFar
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main()
{
    const int original = 45;
    int rest = original;   // what is still left to convert
    int placeValue = 1;    // the value of the next bit we will write
    int doneSoFar = 0;     // the value of the bits already written
    std::string bits;

    while (rest > 0) {
        const bool holds = (original == rest * placeValue + doneSoFar);
        std::cout << "rest=" << rest << " placeValue=" << placeValue
                  << " doneSoFar=" << doneSoFar << " bits=" << (bits.empty() ? "-" : bits)
                  << "  invariant " << (holds ? "holds" : "BROKEN") << '\n';
        const int bit = rest % 2;
        bits = std::to_string(bit) + bits;
        doneSoFar = doneSoFar + bit * placeValue;
        placeValue = placeValue * 2;
        rest = rest / 2;
    }
    const bool holds = (original == rest * placeValue + doneSoFar);
    std::cout << "rest=" << rest << " placeValue=" << placeValue << " doneSoFar=" << doneSoFar
              << " bits=" << bits << "  invariant " << (holds ? "holds" : "BROKEN") << '\n';
    std::cout << original << " = " << bits << " in binary\n";
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Real marbles can roll under the sofa; program variables are changed only by the program. If Luca's total drops, a marble may be lost in the room. If a program's invariant breaks, the program itself changed something wrongly (or, much more rarely, the hardware failed). The program's bug is the first thing to look for. R2
  • Counting marbles is the check; in a program the check is extra code. Luca can see the jars. A program only checks an invariant if someone writes the check, and a check written wrongly can hide a bug. Keep checks simple and close to the definition.
  • An invariant can be true and still not enough. "Twenty marbles in total" stays true even if all the marbles end up in one jar when they should not. An invariant rules out some mistakes, not all; you choose invariants that capture what matters. W1

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
A total that should never change does change (forensic lab: sum 20 → 16 at move 2).One kind of step does not preserve the invariant.Find the first step where the check fails; look at that kind of step only.Correct the step; rerun with the check.
An "invariant" is false at the very start.Starting values chosen wrongly, or the invariant stated wrongly.Check the start before any step.Fix the starting values or restate the invariant.
The check passes but the answer is wrong.The invariant is too weak (true, but does not imply the result).Ask: at the end, does the invariant prove the answer?Choose an invariant that, with the stop condition, gives the result.
The check itself crashes or is always true.A bug in the check, for example comparing a value with itself.Break the program on purpose: does the check notice?Test the check with a known bad state.
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-21 converted numbers with a loop; F0-27 wrote and proved Boolean expressions; F0-17 kept equations balanced. What carries over: an invariant is a Boolean expression, and its proof is a careful check, like a balanced equation. What changes: you now reason about a whole process, step by step, instead of one expression at a time. What comes next: this is the last chapter of MA102. The course project (a binary-to-hex-to-decimal converter with tests, written in KID102) uses the round-trip invariant "converting there and back gives the start number" as a test. HW102 builds gates and adders from the logic of this course. W1

Check yourself

  1. What two things must you check to show that a sentence is an invariant?
  2. In the marble game, is "the red jar has more marbles than the blue jar" an invariant? Why or why not?
  3. A machine adds 3 to a counter or takes 6 away, nothing else. The counter starts at 9. Find an invariant, and decide whether the counter can ever show 10.
  4. Which is a loop invariant of Listing 1? (a) rest is even (b) placeValue is a power of two (c) doneSoFar is 0 (d) bits has 6 characters
  5. At the end of Listing 1's loop, why does doneSoFar equal the original number?
  6. Explain in your own words how an invariant check helps you find a bug.
  7. Apply it to a new case: in a class, pupils swap stickers one for one. State an invariant about the total number of stickers.
  8. Predict: if line 21 of Listing 1 were removed, at which printed line would the invariant first say "BROKEN"?

Lab

Goal

Play the marble game with an invariant check, then break and fix the invariant in Listing 1.

Hardware and software needed

Two jars or cups and 20 small objects (marbles, buttons, dried beans), paper. Optional: a computer with a C++ compiler; our toolchain is under Sources, R1.

Safety

Small objects such as marbles and beans are a choking risk for very young children: play away from toddlers and keep them out of mouths.

Steps

  1. Put 12 objects in one jar and 8 in the other. Write "red + blue = 20" at the top of a page.
  2. Take ten turns with a partner. After each turn, count both jars and write the counts and the sum.
  3. Now let your partner secretly add or remove one object during one turn. Find the turn from your table.
  4. Play the two-switch puzzle with eight coins (heads = on): flip exactly two coins per move. Try to reach exactly one head. Explain why you cannot.
  5. Optional: in Listing 1, change line 22 to placeValue = placeValue * 3;. Predict which output line first says "BROKEN", then run it. Change it back and run again.

Expected observations

The sum is 20 after every honest turn and differs from 20 starting at the turn your partner cheated. The coin puzzle never reaches one head. Unchanged, Listing 1 prints "invariant holds" on every line, as in the recorded run. R1

Verification

You name the cheating turn correctly, and you can explain the coin puzzle with the words "the number of heads stays even".

Troubleshooting

  • Your sum is wrong on an honest turn. Recount both jars; a miscount is a bug in the check, not in the game.
  • You cannot find the cheating turn. Count after every turn, not only at the end.
  • After the edit, the output looks the same. Build again before running; the old program is still the one being run.

Extension

Change the puzzle: a move flips exactly three coins. Is "the number of heads is even" still an invariant? What is?

Forensic lab

Scenario

Wei wrote a program to play the marble game automatically. After four moves it reports only 14 marbles. Nobody touched the jars. The program even has a built-in invariant check. Find the bug.

Evidence pack

Listing 2 — marbles.cpp (evidence)

// Evidence program for the forensic lab: moving marbles between two jars.
// Rule of the game: marbles move between jars; none are added or taken away.
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    int red = 12;   // marbles in the red jar
    int blue = 8;   // marbles in the blue jar
    const int total = red + blue;
    // positive: move that many from red to blue; negative: from blue to red
    const std::vector<int> moves = {3, -2, 4, -1};
    std::cout << "start   red=" << red << " blue=" << blue << " sum=" << red + blue << '\n';
    int step = 0;
    for (int move : moves) {
        ++step;
        if (move > 0) {
            red = red - move;
            blue = blue + move;
        } else {
            blue = blue + move;
            red = red + move;
        }
        std::cout << "move " << step << "  red=" << red << " blue=" << blue
                  << " sum=" << red + blue
                  << (red + blue == total ? "" : "   <-- sum changed") << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Questions

  1. At which move does the invariant first break? By how much does the sum change there, and at the later moves?
  2. Which moves keep the sum and which do not? What do the breaking moves have in common?
  3. State two hypotheses for the cause, then use the evidence to choose one.
  4. Which line of Listing 2 is wrong? Work out the correct line by checking the invariant algebraically, as in Layer 2.
  5. Predict the fixed program's output.

Method hints

Make a table of moves: move value, sign, change in sum. Look for a pattern linking the sign to the change. Then trace one negative move by hand through lines 20–22. Grade yourself with the forensic rubric of the course.

Mini-project

Invent a game for a younger child with a hidden invariant (for example, a card swap where the number of red cards in your hand always stays even). Write the rules, let someone play it, and then reveal and prove the invariant in three sentences: start, step, conclusion.

Rubric (4 points): clear rules (1); a correct invariant (1); a proof with start and step (1); a report of what the player noticed (1).

Summary

  • An invariant is a sentence that stays true at every step of a process.
  • To prove one: it is true at the start, and every step keeps it true.
  • A loop invariant plus the stopping condition proves what a loop computes.
  • Parity invariants show that some goals can never be reached.
  • An invariant check in a program finds the first step that breaks it, which points at the bug.
  • An invariant can be true and still too weak; choose ones that capture what matters.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. That it is true at the start, and that every allowed step keeps it true.
  2. No. It is true at the start (12 > 8), but a single move of 3 makes it 9 and 11, so a step can make it false.
  3. Every step changes the counter by a multiple of 3, and 9 is a multiple of 3, so "the counter is a multiple of 3" is an invariant. 10 is not a multiple of 3, so it can never show 10.
  4. (b) placeValue starts at 1 and is only doubled. (a) is false at the start (45 is odd). (c) is false after the first pass. (d) is only true at the end.
  5. The invariant original = rest × placeValue + doneSoFar holds at every pass; the loop stops when rest = 0, which leaves original = doneSoFar.
  6. Any answer that says: the program checks the invariant after each step, so the first failed check shows the first step that went wrong, and you only need to look at that kind of step.
  7. The total number of stickers in the class stays the same (each swap gives one and takes one).
  8. Without line 21, doneSoFar stays 0. The first line (45 × 1 + 0) still holds; the second line (22 × 2 + 0 = 44) is the first "BROKEN".

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: move 1 (+3) keeps the sum at 20. Move 2 (−2) drops it to 16. Move 3 (+4) keeps it at 16. Move 4 (−1) drops it to 14. Pattern: only negative moves break the invariant, and each loses twice the number of marbles moved. Hypotheses: (1) the starting values are wrong: ruled out, the first line shows 12 + 8 = 20; (2) the negative-move branch is wrong: supported, because every break happens on a negative move. Root cause: Listing 2, line 22, red = red + move;. For a negative move m, blue changes by m (line 21, correct: blue loses |m|), and red also changes by m, so red also loses |m|. Algebra: (red + m) + (blue + m) = red + blue + 2m, not red + blue. The line must be red = red - move;, giving (red − m) + (blue + m) = red + blue. Fix verified: the fixed program (marbles_fixed.cpp in the lab folder, one changed line) printed:

start   red=12 blue=8 sum=20
move 1  red=9 blue=11 sum=20
move 2  red=11 blue=9 sum=20
move 3  red=7 blue=13 sum=20
move 4  red=8 blue=12 sum=20

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-28/marbles_fixed.out; run record marbles_fixed.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:31:09Z; exit code: 0.

Prevention: keep the invariant check (it found the bug at the first bad move), and test both kinds of move in every new version. How the evidence was made: the marble program written with the negative branch wrong on purpose, run on four moves in this build R2; the fix run is R3 R3. Wrong answers: "the total variable is wrong" (it is computed once from 12 + 8 = 20); "the check line is buggy" (the printed jars themselves add up to the printed sums).

Story hook

Analogy

Ana wants her grandfather to make her favourite pancakes. She writes the recipe on a card in her neat handwriting. But her grandfather reads only one language, and it is not the one Ana writes.

So Ana asks her cousin Tomás for help. Tomás reads the card very carefully. If a step makes no sense, he hands the card back and says exactly which line is wrong. If every step makes sense, he copies the recipe into the language her grandfather reads.

Now her grandfather follows the new card, word for word. The pancakes appear. Ana never had to learn her grandfather's language at all.

Writing a computer program works the same way. You write the recipe. A helper program checks it and rewrites it. Then the computer follows it exactly. In this chapter you will do all three steps yourself, for the first time.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain, with the recipe story, the three steps from source code to a running program: write, compile, run.
  • Build and run a C++ program that prints text, using the course's build command.
  • Check which toolchain you have by asking the compiler for its version, and write that version down.
  • Change the text a program prints, predict the new output, run it and compare.
  • Find a missing \n and steps in the wrong order by reading a program's output and its source.
Jargon box
Program
Simple words: A list of exact steps that a computer follows. Analogy: A recipe that the cook follows word for word. Precise: A set of instructions for a computer; in this course it starts as C++ source code and is turned by a compiler into an executable that the operating system can run. R1, D1
Source code
Simple words: The text of a program, written by a person in a programming language. Analogy: The recipe written in your own handwriting on a card. Precise: The human-readable text of a program, stored in files such as hello.cpp; the compiler reads it and either reports errors or produces an executable. R1, D1
Compiler
Simple words: A program that turns the text you wrote into a program the computer can run. Analogy: A helper who rewrites your recipe in the only language the cook can read, and refuses if the recipe makes no sense. Precise: A program (here g++) that checks C++ source code against the rules of the language and translates it into machine instructions stored in an executable file; it reports errors and warnings when it cannot. R4, D2
Executable
Simple words: The finished program file that the computer can start. Analogy: The recipe after it was rewritten for the cook: ready to use, but no longer easy for you to read. Precise: A file of machine instructions and data produced by the compiler; on the Linux build machine of this course the file tool describes it as an ELF 64-bit executable, and its first bytes are 7f 45 4c 46. R4, D3
Toolchain
Simple words: The set of programs you use to turn source code into a running program. Analogy: Your kitchen tools: the same recipe needs the right pots and an oven. Precise: The compiler and the programs that work with it (and, in F0-37, the debugger). This course records the exact versions the tools print, for example "g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0". R4, D2
main function
Simple words: The place where every C++ program starts. Analogy: The first line of the recipe: "start here". Precise: The function named main, which the program runs first; the value it returns (0 here) becomes the exit code that the run log records. R1, D1
Statement
Simple words: One instruction in a program. In C++ most statements end with a semicolon. Analogy: One step of the recipe. Precise: A single instruction inside a function body, such as std::cout << "Hello"; statements run one after another, from top to bottom, unless a statement such as if or a loop changes the order. R2, D1
std::cout
Simple words: The name C++ uses for "print this on the screen". Analogy: The cook calling out loud what is happening. Precise: The standard output stream from the header <iostream>; the operator << sends text and numbers to it, and the run log captures what it printed. R1, D1
String literal
Simple words: Text written inside double quotes in your program. Analogy: Words copied exactly onto a label. Precise: A sequence of characters between double quotes in source code, such as "Hello, world!\n"; the program uses it exactly as written. R1, D1
Newline
Simple words: The invisible character that says "start a new line here". Analogy: Pressing the Enter key on a typewriter or keyboard. Precise: The character written '\n' in C++; without it, the next output continues on the same line (R3 shows two messages glued together). R3, D1
Exit code
Simple words: A number a program gives back when it ends. 0 means "all went well". Analogy: The cook saying "done, no problems" or "something went wrong" at the end. Precise: The value returned by main (or set when a program is stopped); run_lab.sh records it in each .log file, for example "exit code: 0". R1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the whole journey of a program. You write text. The compiler checks it and turns it into an executable. The computer runs the executable, and you see the output.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A computer follows steps exactly. You learned that in KID101 with recipes and robots. Now you will write steps that a real computer follows.

You write your steps as text in a file. The file is like Ana's recipe card. People can read it. The computer cannot follow it yet. We call this text source code.

Next, a helper program reads your text. This helper is called the compiler. It checks every line against the rules of the language. If something is wrong, it stops and tells you where. If all is well, it writes a new file. That new file is the program the computer can run.

Then you run the new file. The computer follows the steps, one after another, from top to bottom. Our first program has one main step: show the words "Hello, world!" on the screen.

"Hello, world" is a small program. But it proves that the whole chain works: your text, the compiler, and the computer.

Three ideas matter most today. First, the computer does exactly what you wrote, not what you meant. Second, the compiler is your helper, not your judge. Third, every run leaves a record, so you can compare what you expected with what really happened.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A C++ program is one or more text files whose names end in .cpp. Our first one is hello.cpp. It contains a main function: the place where the program starts. Inside main there are statements. Each statement is one instruction and ends with a semicolon. R1, D1

To print, the program sends text to std::cout with the << sign. The text is a string literal: characters between double quotes. The two characters \n inside it mean "start a new line". They are one invisible character, the newline. R1, R3, D1

The last statement, return 0;, ends main. The number 0 goes back to the system as the program's exit code. Zero means "everything went well". Our lab runner writes it into a log file after every run. R1

You build the program with the compiler g++. The course runner uses this exact command:

g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined hello.cpp -o hello

That is long, so here is what each part does. -std=c++20 picks the version of the C++ rules. -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic turn on many warnings. -Werror turns every warning into an error, so nothing suspicious slips through. -g keeps information for the debugger (F0-37). -fsanitize=address,undefined adds extra checks while the program runs. -o hello names the output file. R4, D2

The compiler can also be called the short way, g++ hello.cpp -o hello. We tried that too, and it worked: the transcript is in the Lab section below. The course uses the long form because it catches more mistakes early. R4

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. "Compiling" is really several jobs in a row. g++ first prepares the text (it pulls in the contents of headers such as <iostream>), then translates C++ into machine instructions, and finally joins your code with ready-made library code into one executable. That last job is called linking. You will study each job in SP101 (chapter F2-01). D1, D2

The file our compiler made is not text any more. The tool file described it as an "ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64". ELF is the name of the file format on this Linux machine. Its first four bytes, shown by od, are 7f 45 4c 46. When od shows the same four bytes as characters, the last three appear as the letters E, L and F. R4

How the hardware actually does it

Inside the computer, the processor cannot read C++. It reads machine instructions: numbers that stand for tiny steps such as "add" or "copy". That is why the compiler is needed. The executable is a long list of such numbers, plus the text "Hello, world!" stored as bytes. When you run it, the operating system loads the file into memory, and the processor follows the instructions one by one. You met the processor and memory as the kitchen's cook and pantry in F0-05. R4, D3

Worked example

Let us predict the output of Listing 2 before running it. We read the program like the computer does: from top to bottom, one statement at a time.

  1. Line 5 prints Sandwich recipe, then \n. So the next text starts on a new line.
  2. Line 6 prints Step 1: take two slices of bread and a newline.
  3. Lines 7 and 8 print steps 2 and 3 the same way, each on its own line.
  4. Line 9 prints Done. Enjoy! and a newline.
  5. Line 10 returns 0, so the exit code should be 0.

Prediction: five lines of text, in the same order as in the source, and exit code 0. The real run below matches this. If you swap lines 7 and 8, step 3 will be printed before step 2. The computer does not know that the numbers are out of order. It follows the order of the statements, not the meaning of the words. R2

Where the analogy breaks

  • Tomás, the helper, would fix a small spelling mistake himself. The compiler never guesses what you meant. It stops and reports, and you fix it. (It may suggest a fix, as F0-36 shows, but it does not apply it.) R4, D2
  • Ana's grandfather could notice that "step 3" comes before "step 2" and fix the order. The computer cannot. It runs statements in the order written, whatever the words say (the forensic lab shows this). R3
  • A rewritten recipe card is still a card someone could read. The executable is a file of numbers. You read your program in the source file, never in the executable. R4

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Two messages appear glued on one line.A missing \n at the end of the first message.Find the line that printed the first message. Look at the end of its string literal.Add \n before the closing quote.
The output shows old text after you changed the source.You ran the old executable without compiling again.Compare the time you saved the file with when you last compiled.Compile again, then run.
The compiler prints an error and no executable appears.A rule of C++ was broken (often a missing ; or ").Read the first error: file, line and column (F0-36).Fix the first error, then compile again.
The command is "not found".No compiler is installed, or it is not where the system looks for commands.Type g++ --version.Ask an adult to install the toolchain chosen in the dossier.
Transition box

Where you came from: In KID101 (F0-01, F0-04) you wrote algorithms in words that a person followed exactly. What carries over: Exact steps, in order, with nothing left to guess; the habit of predicting the result before trying it. What changes: Now the reader is a machine. It needs a strict language (C++), a translator (the compiler) checks every line before anything runs, and every run is recorded with its exit code. R1, R4 What comes next: F0-30 gives your programs memory: labelled jars called variables.

Check yourself

  1. Put these in the right order: run the executable; write the source code; compile.
  2. In the recipe story, who plays the part of the compiler?
  3. What does \n do inside a string literal?
  4. A program ends with return 0;. What exit code will the log show? What does it mean?
  5. Which line of Listing 1 would you change to print "Hello, Ana!"? Write the new line.
  6. Multiple choice. You edit hello.cpp, then run ./hello at once. The old text appears. Why? (a) The compiler is broken. (b) You did not compile again. (c) The computer remembers old programs on purpose.
  7. Explain in your own words why the computer needs a compiler before it can run your program.
  8. Apply to a new case: a program prints "Step 3" before "Step 2". Where would you look first, and what would you change?

Lab

Goal

Build and run your first programs, record your toolchain, and practise "change, predict, run, compare".

Hardware and software needed

A computer with a C++ toolchain. This build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 on Linux x86_64, as printed by g++ --version. R4

Not verified — check before relying on this

How to install a C++ toolchain depends on your operating system. This build only used a Linux computer where g++ was already installed; no installation steps were tested. The Source Researcher adds the official installation instructions of the toolchain chosen for your computer to the dossier, and your teacher or parent records its name and version there.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use. Ask an adult before installing any software.

Steps

  1. Type g++ --version. Write the first line it prints in your notebook. This is your toolchain record. In this build it printed the line shown above.
  2. Save Listing 1 as hello.cpp. Build it the short way: g++ hello.cpp -o hello. You should see no messages at all. Silence means success.
  3. Run it: ./hello. You should see Hello, world!.
  4. Build it the course way, with the full command from the Code walk-through. Run it again. The output is the same.
  5. Change, predict, run, compare: change the text to greet yourself. Before you run it, write down exactly what you expect. Then compile, run, and compare letter by letter.
  6. Remove the \n. Predict: what happens to the next thing your terminal shows? Run and compare.
  7. Save Listing 2. Swap lines 7 and 8. Predict the output, then run it.

Troubleshooting

  • "command not found" → no compiler, or not on the command path → type g++ --version → ask an adult to install the toolchain from the dossier.
  • "No such file or directory" when compiling → you are in a different folder from hello.cpp → list the folder's files → move to the right folder.
  • Output did not change → old executable → compile again before running.

Extension

Print a small picture made of characters, such as a house drawn with /, \ and |. Hint: a backslash inside a string literal must be written twice, \\. Predict, run, compare.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Kwame wrote a program to print his breakfast steps. His little sister says, "Your computer is confused! It says Good morning and Breakfast together, and it wants me to pour milk into an empty bowl." Kwame insists the computer is broken. You are the code detective.

Evidence pack

Evidence 1 — the source, breakfast.cpp:

#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    std::cout << "Good morning!";
    std::cout << "Breakfast steps:\n";
    std::cout << "Step 2: pour the milk on the cereal\n";
    std::cout << "Step 1: put cereal in the bowl\n";
    std::cout << "Step 3: eat with a spoon\n";
    return 0;
}

Evidence 2 — the real output, from the lab run in this build:

Good morning!Breakfast steps:
Step 2: pour the milk on the cereal
Step 1: put cereal in the bowl
Step 3: eat with a spoon

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-29/breakfast.out; run record breakfast.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:46:32Z; exit code: 0.

Questions

  1. Describe precisely what is wrong in the output. Name the output line.
  2. Which source line causes the glued words? What is missing?
  3. Why is step 2 printed before step 1? Is the computer confused?
  4. Write the fixed program and predict its output.
  5. How could Kwame catch this kind of mistake next time before his sister does?

Method hints

Match each output line with the statement that printed it. Then make two guesses about the cause before you decide. Remember the rule from this chapter: the computer follows the order of the statements, exactly as written. The answer key is at the end of the page.

Mini-project

Write a program that prints the recipe for something you like to make at home: a title, at least four numbered steps, and a closing line. Then ask a friend to read only your output and follow it in their head.

Rubric: builds with the course command and no errors (2 points); output matches your written prediction exactly (1 point); steps are in a sensible order and each on its own line (1 point); you recorded your toolchain version line (1 point).

Summary

  • You write a program as text: the source code, in a .cpp file.
  • The compiler checks the text and translates it into an executable, or reports errors.
  • You run the executable; the computer follows the statements from top to bottom.
  • Every C++ program starts at main; return 0; gives exit code 0.
  • std::cout << prints; \n starts a new line.
  • Always record your toolchain with g++ --version.
  • Change, predict, run, compare: this habit is the heart of the whole course.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Write the source code, compile, run the executable.
  2. Cousin Tomás: he checks the card and rewrites it in the language the cook reads.
  3. It is one invisible character, the newline: the next output starts on a new line.
  4. Exit code 0, which means the program ended normally ("all went well"). The run logs show exit code: 0. R1
  5. Line 5: std::cout << "Hello, Ana!\n";
  6. (b). The executable is only rebuilt when you compile. (a) is wrong because a broken compiler would print errors, not old text. (c) is wrong: the computer runs whatever executable file is there; it has no wish to keep old programs.
  7. Any answer that says: the processor only follows machine instructions, not C++ text, so the compiler checks the text and translates it into an executable.
  8. Look at the order of the statements that print the steps; swap them so they appear in the order you want. The computer follows statement order, not the step numbers in the text.

Forensic lab answer key

  • Observation: output line 1 reads Good morning!Breakfast steps: (two messages glued); output lines 2–3 show step 2 before step 1. R3
  • Root cause 1: source line 5 has no \n at the end of "Good morning!", so the next output continues on the same line.
  • Root cause 2: source lines 7 and 8 are in the wrong order. The computer is not confused: it runs statements top to bottom, exactly as written.
  • Fix: write "Good morning!\n" on line 5 and swap lines 7 and 8. Predicted output: Good morning!, Breakfast steps:, then steps 1, 2, 3 in order.
  • Prevention: write the expected output down before running, and compare line by line. Reading the output aloud also helps.
  • How the evidence was made: the newline was removed and the two statements were swapped on purpose; the output is the real run R3.
  • Wrong answers: "the computer is broken" (the same computer printed Listing 2 correctly, R2); "the compiler mixed up the lines" (the compiler keeps statement order; it was the source).
