Story hook

Analogy

In Priya's kitchen there is a shelf of glass jars. Each jar has a label: "rice", "sugar", "buttons". You can look inside a jar without changing it. You can empty a jar and fill it with something new. But the label stays the same.

One day Priya's dad says, "Swap the rice and the sugar. Rice goes in the sugar jar, sugar goes in the rice jar." Priya thinks for a moment. If she pours the rice into the sugar jar, the sugar is still in there. What a mess!

So she fetches a third, empty jar. Rice goes into the spare jar. Sugar goes into the rice jar. Then the rice goes from the spare jar into the sugar jar. Done, with nothing spilled.

A program needs jars too. It needs places to keep numbers and words while it works. In C++ these jars are called variables. And yes, swapping two of them needs a spare jar, exactly like Priya's.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a variable is, using the labelled-jar picture and the precise words name, type and value.
  • Write a program that creates variables, changes their values and prints them.
  • Predict, line by line, the value inside every variable, then check your prediction with a real run.
  • Swap two variables correctly with a spare variable, and explain why the two-line swap fails.
  • Read a number typed by the user (or from an input file) into a variable.
Jargon box
Variable
Simple words: A named place that holds a value, which can change while the program runs. Analogy: A labelled jar: the label is the name, the contents are the value. Precise: A named object with a type, for example int apples = 3; reading the name gives its current value, and assignment replaces the value. R1, D1
Declaration
Simple words: The line where you first tell the computer a variable's name and type. Analogy: Putting a new empty jar on the shelf and writing its label. Precise: A statement that introduces a name and its type, such as int apples = 3; a name must be declared before it is used (F0-36 shows the error when it is not). R1, D1
Initialise
Simple words: To give a variable its first value at the moment you create it. Analogy: Filling the jar the moment you put it on the shelf. Precise: Giving a variable a value in its declaration (int apples = 3;). With the course flags, g++ refused to build a program that used a variable before giving it a value (R4). R1, R4, D1
Assignment
Simple words: Putting a new value into a variable. The old value is gone. Analogy: Emptying the jar and filling it with something new. Precise: The operator = in a statement such as apples = apples + 2; the right side is worked out first, then its value replaces the variable's old value. It is not the "is equal to" of maths; that is == (F0-32). R1, D1
std::cin
Simple words: The name C++ uses for "read what the person types". Analogy: The cook listening to an order. Precise: The standard input stream from <iostream>; the operator >> reads a value into a variable. In the lab runs the input comes from a .in file instead of a keyboard. R3, D1
const
Simple words: A word that makes a variable unchangeable after its first value. Analogy: A jar with its lid glued shut: you can look, but not change what is inside. Precise: A qualifier on a declaration (const int baked = 12;); the compiler rejects any later assignment to that variable. R3, D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows Listing 1 as jars on a shelf. Each picture is a moment in the program. Read it from left to right, like a comic strip.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A program often needs to remember things. How many apples are left? What is the player's name? What is the score? It keeps each of these in a variable.

Think of a variable as a jar with a label. The label is the variable's name, like apples. What is inside is its value, like 3. You choose the name once. The value can change many times.

When the program reads a variable, it looks inside the jar. Looking does not change anything. When the program puts a new value in, the old value is gone. The jar holds only one thing at a time.

Each jar also has a shape. A jar for whole numbers holds whole numbers only. You will meet the other shapes, called types, in F0-31.

Now Priya's puzzle makes sense. To swap two jars, you need a spare jar for a moment. Otherwise one value is poured away before you can save it.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

You create a variable with a declaration. The line int apples = 3; says three things: the type is int (a whole number), the name is apples, and the first value is 3. Giving the first value at once is called to initialise the variable. R1, D1

Later you can change the value with an assignment: apples = apples + 2;. The computer works out the right side first. It reads the old value 3, adds 2, and gets 5. Only then does it put 5 into apples. So the same name can appear on both sides. R1, D1

Watch out: in C++ the sign = does not mean "is equal to". It means "put the value on the right into the variable on the left". The question "is equal to?" is written ==, and you will use it in F0-32. D1

Assignment copies values. After int pears = apples;, the variable pears holds its own copy of 5. When apples becomes 0 on the next line, pears still holds 5. The real run shows exactly this. R1

A program can also read a value from the person using it. std::cin >> cookies; waits for a number and puts it into cookies. In our lab runs the "typing" comes from a small file, cookies.in, which contains the number 5. R3, D1

Some values should never change. Writing const in front, as in const int baked = 12;, glues the lid shut. If a later line tries to change baked, the compiler refuses. R3, D1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. What is in a jar that was never filled? In C++, a plain int declared without a value does not start at 0 by itself; reading it before giving it a value is a mistake. With the course flags, g++ refused to build such a program and named the variable (Listing 4 in "Common mistakes"). Always initialise your variables. R4, D1

Names have rules too. A name is made of letters, digits and the underscore _, and it must not start with a digit. Names are case-sensitive: apples and Apples are two different jars. Good names say what is inside: cookies is better than c. D1

How the hardware actually does it

A computer's memory is a long row of numbered boxes, each holding a small number. You met it as the pantry in F0-05. When your program creates a variable, a few of these boxes are set aside for it. The name is for you and the compiler. The running program finds the variable by its place in memory. The jar picture hides this: real memory has no labels written on it. D2

Worked example

We trace Listing 1 by hand. A trace table has one row per line that changes something. We write what is in each jar after that line runs. A dash means "the jar does not exist yet".

Our prediction is three lines: "The apple jar holds 3", "After adding 2, it holds 5" and "Apples: 0, pears: 5". The real run of Listing 1 printed exactly these three lines. R1

Now the swap in Listing 2. Start: left holds 4, right holds 9. Line 9 copies 4 into spare. Line 10 copies 9 into left, so both hold 9 for a moment. Line 11 copies the saved 4 from spare into right. Result: left is 9 and right is 4. The real run agrees. R2

Where the analogy breaks

  • A real jar can hold rice and buttons at the same time if you are careless. A variable holds exactly one value of its type. A new value replaces the old one completely. R1
  • Copying a jar's contents in a kitchen leaves the first jar emptier. Copying a variable (int pears = apples;) leaves the first variable unchanged: both now hold the same value. R1
  • A new kitchen jar is empty. A new C++ variable without a first value is not "empty" or zero: its contents are unknown, and the compiler with our flags refuses to let you read it. R4, D1
  • Real jars can hold anything. A variable has a fixed type, and the compiler checks that you only put suitable values in it (F0-31).

Transition box

Where you came from: F0-29: programs that only print fixed text. What carries over: Statements run top to bottom; the build command and the "change, predict, run, compare" habit. What changes: The program now remembers values, and the same line can print different things depending on what is in a variable at that moment; the order of assignments now matters a lot, as the swap shows. R1, R2 What comes next: F0-31 gives jars different shapes: whole numbers, decimals, true/false, letters and text.

Check yourself

  1. In the jar picture, what are the label, the contents and the shape of the jar in C++ words?
  2. What is printed by: int a = 2; a = a * 3; std::cout << a;?
  3. Multiple choice. After int x = 5; int y = x; x = 1;, what is y? (a) 1 (b) 5 (c) 6
  4. Why does apples = apples + 2; make sense in C++ but not as a maths equation?
  5. What does const do? Give an example of a value that should be const.
  6. Explain in your own words why a swap needs a third variable.
  7. Apply to a new case: three jars hold a = 1, b = 2, c = 3. Write lines that rotate them so that a = 2, b = 3, c = 1. Use one spare variable.
  8. What did g++ say about Listing 4, and on which line?

Lab

Goal

Predict, then check, the value in every variable of three small programs, and build a working swap.

Hardware and software needed

The toolchain from F0-29; this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 on Linux x86_64 (recorded in every .log file). R1

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Copy Listing 1. Before running, fill in a trace table like the one in the Worked example. Run it and compare.
  2. Change line 8 to apples = apples * 4;. Predict all three lines of output. Run and compare.
  3. Copy Listing 2. Change the starting values to your age and a friend's age. Predict, run, compare.
  4. Copy Listing 3 and run it. Type a number when it asks. (With the course runner, put your number in cookies.in.)
  5. Add the line baked = 20; after line 10 of Listing 3. Predict what the compiler says. Compile and read the message. Then remove the line.
  6. Remove = 0 from line 5 of Listing 3. Does it still build? Then try Listing 4 and compare: why does one fail and not the other? (Hint: in Listing 3 a value is read in before the variable is used.)

Expected observations

Steps 1–4: the outputs match the trace tables you wrote, as the real runs above did. Step 4 in this build, with input 5, printed "Now there are 17." R3

Verification

For every run, your written prediction matches the output exactly, and the log shows exit code: 0. Run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F0-30 to check the given listings; Listing 4 must be reported as "compile failed as expected".

Troubleshooting

  • "was not declared in this scope" → the variable's name is misspelled or used before its declaration → compare names letter by letter → fix the spelling or move the declaration up.
  • The program seems to "hang" → it is waiting for you to type a number (std::cin) → type a number and press Enter.
  • The output says 12 instead of 17 → the input was not a number, so the read failed and cookies held 0 (in this build, the input abc gave "Now there are 12.", file cookies_letters.cpp) → type digits only. R8

Extension

Write a program with jars a, b and c that rotates their values (Check yourself question 7). Print before and after. Then try to swap two variables using only additions and subtractions, with no spare variable, and explain how it works.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Lucía wrote a program to swap the juice in a red cup and a blue cup. Her teacher ran it and said, "Now both cups hold the same juice. Where did the other juice go?" Lucía is sure her two lines are correct.

Evidence pack

Evidence 1 — the source, swap_bug.cpp:

#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    int red_cup = 7;
    int blue_cup = 2;
    std::cout << "Before: red cup = " << red_cup << ", blue cup = " << blue_cup << '\n';

    red_cup = blue_cup;
    blue_cup = red_cup;
    std::cout << "After:  red cup = " << red_cup << ", blue cup = " << blue_cup << '\n';
    return 0;
}

Evidence 2 — the real output of the run in this build:

Before: red cup = 7, blue cup = 2
After:  red cup = 2, blue cup = 2

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-30/swap_bug.out; run record swap_bug.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:46:36Z; exit code: 0.

Questions

  1. What exactly does the "After" line show? Which value is missing?
  2. Make a trace table for lines 5–11. After which line is the value 7 lost for ever?
  3. Write the fixed lines.
  4. Why did the compiler not warn about this mistake?

Method hints

Do not guess. Trace the program on paper, one line at a time, writing both jars after each line. Compare your table with the evidence. State two possible causes before you choose one.

Mini-project

Write a "pocket money" program. It reads how much money you have now (from std::cin), adds a weekly amount stored in a const variable four times, one line per week, and prints the total after each week.

Rubric: builds with the course command (1 point); uses at least one const and one variable that changes (1 point); a written trace table matches the real output (2 points); good variable names (1 point).

Summary

  • A variable is a named place for a value: a labelled jar.
  • A declaration such as int apples = 3; gives the type, the name and the first value.
  • Assignment = works out the right side first, then replaces the old value.
  • = means "put into"; "is equal to?" is ==.
  • Assigning copies a value; the two variables stay separate.
  • A swap needs a spare variable.
  • std::cin >> reads a value; const makes a value unchangeable.
  • Always initialise variables; g++ with our flags refuses to read an unset one.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Label = the variable's name; contents = its value; shape = its type (here int).
  2. 6: the right side 2 * 3 is worked out first, then stored in a.
  3. (b) 5. y got a copy of 5; changing x later does not change y. (a) would be true only if the two jars were linked, and they are not. (c) mixes up the two values. R1
  4. In maths, a = a + 2 has no solution. In C++, = means "work out the right side, then put the result into the left side".
  5. It makes the variable unchangeable after its first value. Examples: the number of days in a week, the number of cookies baked per tray.
  6. When you copy one value into the other, the first value is overwritten and lost. The spare variable keeps a copy until it is needed.
  7. One answer: int spare = a; a = b; b = c; c = spare; Trace: spare 1; a 2; b 3; c 1.
  8. Line 6: "'sugar' is used uninitialized [-Werror=uninitialized]", with a note pointing to the declaration on line 5. R4

Forensic lab answer key

  • Observation: before the swap the cups hold 7 and 2; after it, both hold 2. The value 7 has disappeared. R5
  • Trace: after line 9, red_cup = 2 and blue_cup = 2. The 7 is lost here. Line 10 then copies 2 into blue_cup, which already held 2.
  • Root cause: the swap has no spare variable, so the first assignment destroys a value that is still needed.
  • Fix: int spare = red_cup; red_cup = blue_cup; blue_cup = spare; (as in Listing 2, whose real run swapped correctly). R2
  • Why no warning: every line is legal C++ and every variable is used; the compiler checks the rules, not your intention.
  • Prevention: trace tables before running; a test that checks both values after a swap (functions and tests arrive in F0-34).
  • How the evidence was made: the spare variable was removed from a correct swap on purpose; the output is real run R5.

Story hook

Analogy

Yusuf is helping in the kitchen. He has an egg box, a measuring jug, a light switch, a fridge magnet with one letter, and a long row of magnet letters that spells "SOUP".

His aunt says, "Put three and a half eggs in the egg box." Yusuf laughs. An egg box has places for whole eggs only. Half an egg does not fit. The measuring jug is different. It can hold 1.5 litres of water, no problem.

The light switch can only be on or off. The single magnet shows one letter. The row of magnets can spell a whole word, as long or as short as you like.

Every container is good at one kind of thing. A program's jars are the same. Each one has a shape, called its type, and the shape decides what can go inside. Today you meet the five shapes you will use most.

What you will be able to do

  • Choose the right type for a value: int, double, bool, char or std::string.
  • Predict what C++ prints for whole-number division and remainders, and check it with a run.
  • Explain why 7 / 2 gives 3 but 7.0 / 2 gives 3.5.
  • Read a word and a number from input, join text with + and count its characters.
  • Find a "lost half" bug caused by whole-number division.
Jargon box
Type
Simple words: The kind of value a variable can hold: whole number, decimal, true/false, letter or text. Analogy: The shape of a jar: an egg box holds eggs, a bottle holds liquids. Precise: The property of a variable or value that decides which values it can hold and which operations work on it, for example int, double, bool, char and std::string. R1, D1
int
Simple words: The type for whole numbers, like 7 or -3. Analogy: A jar for whole eggs: no half eggs allowed. Precise: The basic signed integer type; on the build machine it used 4 bytes and its largest value printed as 2147483647 (R3). R1, R3, D1
double
Simple words: The type for numbers with a decimal point, like 1.5. Analogy: A measuring jug that can hold 1.5 litres. Precise: A floating-point type; many decimals, such as 0.1, are stored only approximately, which is why 0.1 + 0.2 printed as 0.30000000000000004 with 17 digits (R2). R1, R2, D1
bool
Simple words: The type for yes/no answers: true or false. Analogy: A light switch: on or off. Precise: The Boolean type with the two values true and false; std::cout prints them as 1 and 0 unless std::boolalpha is used (R1). R1, D1
char
Simple words: The type for one single character, like 'A'. Analogy: One fridge-magnet letter. Precise: A type that holds one character, written in single quotes; the character 'A' printed as the number 65 when converted to int on the build machine (R1). R1, D1
std::string
Simple words: The type for a piece of text, like a name or a sentence. Analogy: A string of fridge-magnet letters in a row. Precise: The standard library type from <string> that holds a sequence of characters; it can be joined with + and knows its length through size() (R1, R4). R1, R4, D1
Integer division
Simple words: Dividing whole numbers in C++ gives a whole number: the part after the point is dropped. Analogy: Sharing 7 eggs between 2 boxes: each box gets 3 whole eggs, and 1 egg is left over. Precise: When both operands of / are integers, the result is an integer and the fractional part is discarded: 7 / 2 printed 3 and 7 % 2 printed the remainder 1 (R2). R2, R5, D1
Remainder operator
Simple words: The % sign: it gives what is left over after a whole-number division. Analogy: The egg that does not fit in the boxes. Precise: The operator % on integers; 7 % 2 printed 1 in this build (R2). R2, D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the five types as kitchen containers. Under each one is a value it can hold, taken from Listing 1.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

In F0-30 every jar held whole numbers. But programs need other things too. A recipe needs 1.5 litres of water. A game needs to know "is the door open: yes or no?" A greeting needs a name.

So each jar gets a shape. The shape is called its type. You choose the type when you create the jar, and it never changes.

Whole numbers go in an int. Numbers with a decimal point go in a double. Yes-or-no answers go in a bool. One single letter or sign goes in a char. Words and sentences go in a std::string.

The type matters when you do sums. Share 7 whole eggs between 2 boxes. Each box gets 3 eggs, and 1 egg is left over. C++ does the same with whole numbers: 7 divided by 2 gives 3. If you want 3.5, you must use decimal numbers.

The type also matters when you print. A bool prints as 1 or 0 unless you ask for the words. And a letter is secretly stored as a number. You will see both in the real run.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

An int holds whole numbers, positive or negative. A double holds numbers with a fractional part, such as 1.5. A bool holds true or false. A char holds one character, written in single quotes: 'A'. A std::string holds text in double quotes; you need #include <string> for it. R1, D1

When both numbers in a division are int, the result is an int too. The part after the decimal point is thrown away. So 7 / 2 printed 3. The remainder operator % gives the leftover: 7 % 2 printed 1. If at least one number is a double, the division keeps the fraction: 7.0 / 2 printed 3.5. R2, D1

Printing true showed 1. After std::boolalpha was sent to std::cout, the same value printed as true. Printing the char 'A' showed the letter, but converting it to int with static_cast<int> showed 65. A character is stored as a number code, the idea you met in F0-03. R1, D1

Strings can be joined with + when at least one side is a std::string: "Hello, " + name + "!" works because name is a std::string. The function size() counts the characters: "soup" has 4. R1, R4, D1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Each type uses a fixed number of bytes in memory. Listing 3 asked this machine with sizeof: a bool and a char used 1 byte, an int 4 bytes and a double 8 bytes. The biggest int was 2147483647 and the smallest −2147483648. These are measurements on this build machine, not promises for every computer. R3

A double cannot store most decimals exactly, because it stores numbers in binary. 0.1 + 0.2 printed as 0.3 with the normal number of digits, but as 0.30000000000000004 when 17 digits were requested. So never test whether two double values are exactly equal; you will learn the safe way in later courses (MA302). R2, D1

Not verified — check before relying on this

This build measured the sizes of int and double on one machine only. Whether the C++ rules allow other sizes on other kinds of computers was not checked here. Check the C++ standard (ISO/IEC 14882 working draft, the clause on fundamental types), record the answer in the dossier, and until then treat Listing 3's numbers as "measured on this machine".

How the hardware actually does it

Memory stores only bits: rows of switches, as in F0-02. The type tells the program how to read a row of bits. The same bits could mean a number, a letter or true/false; the type decides which. That is why the letter 'A' could be printed as the number 65: same bits, different reading. Whole numbers and decimal numbers are stored in quite different bit patterns, which is one reason C++ keeps their types apart. R1, D2

Worked example

Three friends share 10 biscuits fairly. How many does each get, and how many are left? We predict each line of a tiny calculation, then compare with what Listing 2 showed for the same kind of sum.

  1. With whole numbers: 10 / 3. 3 × 3 = 9, and 3 × 4 = 12 is too many. So each friend gets 3. The fraction is thrown away.
  2. The remainder: 10 % 3. 10 − 9 = 1 biscuit is left.
  3. Check: 3 × 3 + 1 = 10. The share and the remainder always rebuild the starting number.
  4. With a decimal: 10.0 / 3. Now the answer keeps its fraction: 3.333… C++ prints a rounded version of it.

Listing 2 did the same kind of sum with 7 and 2: 7 / 2 printed 3, 7 % 2 printed 1, and 3 × 2 + 1 = 7. With 7.0 / 2 it printed 3.5. R2

In the lab you will change Listing 2 to 10 and 3 and check this prediction.

Where the analogy breaks

  • A real measuring jug can hold any amount, as exactly as you can pour. A double stores many decimals only approximately: 0.1 + 0.2 was not exactly 0.3 (Listing 2). R2
  • An egg box cannot take half an egg, and you would notice at once. In C++, int cups = 2.9; built without any message and stored 2: the fraction vanished silently. The forensic lab shows how sneaky that is. R5, R6
  • A magnet letter is only a letter. A char is really a small number with a letter meaning on top: 'A' printed as 65 when read as a number. R1
  • An egg box has as many places as you can see. An int has a hidden limit: on this machine nothing above 2147483647 fits. R3

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
A share or average is too small, with no fraction.Whole-number division: both sides are int.Look at every /: are both sides whole numbers?Make one side a double, e.g. static_cast<double>(slices) / friends.
A bool prints as 1 or 0.That is the default way std::cout prints a bool.Look for std::boolalpha.Send std::boolalpha to std::cout first.
error: invalid operands of types 'const char [8]' and 'const char [7]' to binary 'operator+'Two string literals joined with +.The message points at the + and names both sides.Make one side a std::string, or write the text as one literal.
Only the first name is read.>> stops reading text at a space.Print the variable right after reading it.Read one word at a time, or learn std::getline in SP101.
A char prints as a number, or a number as a strange letter.The value was converted between char and int.Check the declared type of the variable you print.Use the type you mean; convert on purpose with static_cast.
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-30: variables of one kind, whole numbers. In F0-02 and F0-03 you learned that everything inside a computer is bits, and that letters are stored as numbers. What carries over: Declaring, initialising and assigning work the same for every type; letters really are numbers inside (65 for 'A' in this run). R1 What changes: Every variable now has a type you must choose, and the type changes results: whole-number division drops the fraction, and a double is only approximate. R2 What comes next: F0-32 uses bool values to make decisions with if and else.

Check yourself

  1. Which type would you choose for: the number of people at a table; the temperature 21.5; whether the oven is on; the first letter of your name; your full name?
  2. What does C++ print for 9 / 4 and for 9 % 4?
  3. Multiple choice. What does 9.0 / 4 print? (a) 2 (b) 2.25 (c) 2.0
  4. Why did is_hot print as 1 at first, and as true later?
  5. What number did the run print for the letter 'A'? Where else in the university did you meet number codes for letters?
  6. Explain in your own words why "Hello, " + "world!" fails but "Hello, " + name works.
  7. Apply to a new case: 25 sweets are shared by 4 children. Write two C++ expressions: one for the sweets each child gets, one for the sweets left over. What do they give?
  8. Why is it risky to check whether 0.1 + 0.2 is exactly equal to 0.3?

Lab

Goal

Predict and check how each type stores, prints and calculates.

Troubleshooting

Extension

Write a program that converts minutes into hours and minutes using / and % (for example 135 minutes → 2 hours and 15 minutes). Test it with 59, 60 and 61 minutes.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Mateo and Hana share 3 slices of pizza. Mateo's program says each of them gets 1 slice. "Then where is the third slice?" asks Hana. Mateo points at his code: "Look, I even used a double for the answer!"

Evidence pack

Evidence 1 — the source, pizza.cpp:

#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    int slices = 3;
    int friends = 2;
    double each = slices / friends;
    std::cout << "Slices: " << slices << ", friends: " << friends << '\n';
    std::cout << "Each friend gets " << each << " slices\n";
    return 0;
}

Evidence 2 — the real output of the run in this build:

Slices: 3, friends: 2
Each friend gets 1 slices

Questions

  1. What value would a person expect for "each", and what was printed?
  2. On which line is the half slice lost? Explain why the double on the left did not help.
  3. Propose a fix and predict its output.
  4. Why did the compiler not complain, although we use strict warning flags?

Method hints

The computer works out the right side of = first, and only then stores the result (F0-30). Ask: what are the types of the two numbers being divided? Write two hypotheses before deciding.

Mini-project

Write a "recipe scaler". It reads the number of guests (an int), uses a const double for litres of soup per guest, prints the litres needed, and prints whether a large pot is needed as a bool with std::boolalpha (you may set it with bool big_pot = litres > 5.0;, a preview of F0-32).

Rubric: builds with the course command (1 point); uses at least three different types correctly (2 points); no whole-number division where a fraction is needed (1 point); prediction written before the run matches it (1 point).

Summary

  • Every variable has a type that decides what it can hold: int, double, bool, char, std::string.
  • Whole-number division drops the fraction: 7 / 2 is 3; % gives the remainder.
  • Use a double on at least one side to keep fractions.
  • A double is approximate; never test decimals for exact equality.
  • A bool prints as 1/0 unless you use std::boolalpha.
  • A char is a number code underneath ('A' printed as 65).
  • Strings join with + when one side is a std::string; size() counts characters.

Forensic lab answer key

  • Observation: 3 slices and 2 friends, but "Each friend gets 1 slices". A person expects 1.5. R5
  • Hypotheses: (a) the double cannot hold 1.5; (b) the division itself already lost the fraction. Hypothesis (a) is ruled out: Listing 1 printed a double holding 1.5 correctly.
  • Root cause: line 7 divides two int values, so slices / friends is worked out as whole-number division, giving 1. Only then is 1 stored in the double. The type on the left cannot bring back the lost half.
  • Fix: double each = static_cast<double>(slices) / friends; The fixed program pizza_fixed.cpp printed "Each friend gets 1.5 slices" in this build. R5
  • Why no warning: whole-number division is legal and often wanted (Listing 2 used it on purpose); the flags used by this course did not warn about it.
  • Prevention: for every /, ask "are both sides whole numbers, and is that what I want?"; test with numbers that do not divide evenly.
  • How the evidence was made: a correct program was changed to divide two int values; the output is real run R5.

Story hook

Analogy

Every morning, Noor looks out of the window before getting dressed. If it is freezing, she takes her warm coat, a hat and gloves. Otherwise, if it is cool, she takes a jumper. Otherwise, a T-shirt is fine.

Noor does not take all three. She asks the questions in order and stops at the first "yes". The order matters. If she first asked "Is it colder than a summer day?", the answer would be "yes" on a freezing morning too, and she would go out in a jumper and shiver.

Her little brother has a different rule for snacks: "If it is after school and my homework is done, I may have a snack." Both parts must be true.

Programs make decisions like this all the time. In C++, the words are almost the same as Noor's: if and else.

What you will be able to do

  • Write if, else if and else statements that choose what a program does.
  • Write conditions with the comparison operators < > <= >= == != and join them with &&, || and !.
  • Predict which branch runs for a given input, including the edge values, and check with real runs.
  • Explain why the order of an else if chain matters, and find a branch that can never run.
  • Read the compiler's warning about = inside a condition and fix it.
Jargon box
Condition
Simple words: A question with a yes or no answer that the program checks. Analogy: "Is the water boiling?" in a recipe. Precise: An expression whose value is converted to bool, used by if and by loops to decide what to do next, for example temperature < 5. R1, D1
Comparison operator
Simple words: Signs that compare two values: <, >, <=, >=, == and !=. Analogy: Holding two jars side by side to see which one has more. Precise: Operators that compare two values and give a bool. == means "is equal to" and != means "is not equal to"; a single = is assignment, which g++ flagged inside an if with the course flags (R3). R2, R3, D1
if statement
Simple words: A way to say "only do this when the condition is true". Analogy: "If it is raining, take an umbrella." Precise: A statement that runs its block only when its condition is true; an optional else block runs otherwise, and else if chains test conditions in order until one is true (R1). R1, D1
Block
Simple words: A group of statements inside curly braces { }. Analogy: A boxed group of steps in a recipe that belong together. Precise: A sequence of statements enclosed in braces; the whole block belongs to the if, else, loop or function written in front of it. R1, D1
Logical operator
Simple words: Words that join conditions: and (&&), or (||), not (!). Analogy: "Homework done AND it is after school." Precise: The operators && (true only if both sides are true), || (true if at least one side is true) and ! (turns true into false and false into true) (R2). R2, D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 is a map of Listing 1. The program walks down from the top. At each diamond it asks one question and follows the "yes" or "no" path. Exactly one of the three boxes runs.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Up to now, every program did the same thing every time. Every line ran, from top to bottom. That is fine for a recipe card, but life needs choices.

An if lets a program choose. It asks a question with a yes-or-no answer. If the answer is yes, the steps inside its curly braces run. If the answer is no, those steps are skipped.

An else says what to do when the answer is no. And else if asks the next question. The program asks the questions in order, from top to bottom. It stops at the first yes. Only one of the choices runs.

Questions can be joined, as in the snack rule: "after school AND homework done". Both must be true. Another rule might say "at noon OR at six o'clock". Then one true part is enough.

One small sign causes many bugs. In C++, = means "put into the jar". To ask "is it equal?", you write two signs: ==. Luckily, with our flags, the compiler catches this mix-up inside an if.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

An if statement has a condition in round brackets and a block in curly braces: if (temperature < 5) { ... }. The condition is worked out to true or false, the bool values from F0-31. The block runs only when the condition is true. R1, D1

The comparison operators are < (less than), > (greater than), <= (less than or equal), >= (greater than or equal), == (equal) and != (not equal). Each one compares two values and gives a bool. You can store that bool in a variable, as Listing 2 does with bool after_school = hour >= 15;. R2, D1

An else if chain tests its conditions in order. The first true condition wins; its block runs, and all the later tests are skipped. A final else catches every case that no condition matched. With 12 degrees, the first test (12 < 5) was false and the second (12 < 18) was true, so the program printed "Wear a jumper." With exactly 18, both tests were false, and the else ran. R1, R5, D1

The logical operators join conditions. a && b is true only if both are true. a || b is true if at least one is true. !a turns true into false and false into true. In Listing 2, hour 16 with homework done made after_school && homework_done true. R2, D1

If you write if (eggs = 6), you put 6 into eggs instead of comparing. With our flags, g++ refused: "suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value". Read that as: "did you mean ==?" R3, D2

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. With &&, if the left side is already false, the result must be false, so C++ does not even work out the right side. With ||, a true left side makes the right side unnecessary. This is called short-circuit evaluation, and later you will use it to guard a risky check, for example "the list is not empty AND its first item is …". D1

A condition does not have to be a comparison: any value that can turn into a bool works. A number counts as false when it is 0 and as true otherwise. That is exactly why if (eggs = 6) is legal C++ (6 counts as true) and why the compiler only warns about it, here turned into an error by -Werror. R3, D1

How the hardware actually does it

The processor follows instructions one after another, as you saw in F0-29. For an if, the compiler produces a compare instruction and a "jump" instruction. If the condition is false, the jump makes the processor skip over the instructions of the block and continue further down. So a decision is, underneath, "compare, then maybe skip ahead". D3

Worked example

We predict what Listing 1 prints for four temperatures, then check each prediction against a real run.

Inputtemperature < 5?temperature < 18?BranchPredicted middle line

18falsefalse (18 is not less than 18)elseA T-shirt is fine.

The input 18 is an edge value: it sits exactly on a boundary. Edge values catch most mistakes with < and <=. All four runs printed the predicted lines; the runs for 2, 18 and 25 are shown in the Lab section, and the run for 12 below Listing 1. R1, R5

Next, Listing 2 with the input 16 1 (hour 16, homework done). after_school is 16 >= 15, so true. true && true is true, so "Yes, you may have a snack." Then hour == 12 || hour == 18 is false || false, so nothing more is printed. The real run agrees. R2

Listing 1 — clothes.cpp (input file clothes.in contains 12)

#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    int temperature = 0;
    std::cin >> temperature;
    std::cout << "It is " << temperature << " degrees outside.\n";

    if (temperature < 5) {
        std::cout << "Wear a warm coat, a hat and gloves.\n";
    } else if (temperature < 18) {
        std::cout << "Wear a jumper.\n";
    } else {
        std::cout << "A T-shirt is fine.\n";
    }
    std::cout << "Have a good day!\n";
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Noor can answer "sort of cold" or "not sure". A condition is always exactly true or false. D1
  • Noor would notice if two of her questions overlapped badly and fix the order herself. The computer asks in the written order, even if a later branch can never be reached (the forensic lab). R4
  • When Noor hears "is it 6?", she never changes the number of eggs. In C++, eggs = 6 inside an if really changes the variable; only the compiler's warning stopped it here. R3

Transition box

Where you came from: In F0-07 you made decisions without a computer ("if it rains, take an umbrella"); in F0-31 you met bool. What carries over: A yes/no question decides what happens next; bool values hold the answers. What changes: The question must be exact C++ (<, ==, &&); the order of an else-if chain is followed blindly; = and == are different, and only the compiler's warning catches the mix-up. R3, R4 What comes next: F0-33 uses conditions to repeat steps: loops.

Lab

Goal

Predict and test every branch of two decision programs, including edge values.

Hardware and software needed

The toolchain from F0-29; this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 on Linux x86_64. R1

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Copy the prediction table from the Worked example. Run Listing 1 with 2, 12, 18 and 25 (type them, or put them in clothes.in one at a time). Compare.
  2. Add a fourth branch: below −10, print "Stay inside if you can." Where must it go in the chain? Predict, then test with −15 and −5.

Troubleshooting

  • "error: expected '(' before 'temperature'", followed by "'else' without a previous 'if'" → the condition is missing its round brackets (the second message is a follow-on error, see F0-36) → look at the if line → write if (condition). Real messages: file no_brackets.out. R6

Extension

Write a program that reads three whole numbers and prints the largest, using only if and else. Test it with the largest number in each of the three positions, and with two equal numbers.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Ms Okafor's class uses a star program for spelling tests. After a week, Wei notices something odd: "I got 95 and only one star. Nobody has ever got three stars!" The class thinks the test is too hard. You suspect the program.

Evidence pack

Evidence 1 — the source, stars.cpp:

#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    int score = 0;
    std::cin >> score;
    std::cout << "Score: " << score << '\n';

    if (score >= 50) {
        std::cout << "Good work: one star.\n";
    } else if (score >= 90) {
        std::cout << "Excellent: three stars!\n";
    } else {
        std::cout << "Keep practising.\n";
    }
    return 0;
}

Questions

  1. Which output is wrong, and what should it have been?
  2. Is there any score that could ever print "Excellent: three stars!"? Prove your answer.
  3. Which lines cause the problem? Write the fixed chain.
  4. Which inputs would you use to test the fixed program, and why?

Method hints

Trace the chain for 95 the way the computer does: first condition first. Then ask the key question: for a score to reach the second branch, what must be true about the first condition? Write two hypotheses ("the test is too hard", "the program is wrong") and use the evidence to decide.

Mini-project

Write a "what shall we cook?" program. It reads how many minutes you have and whether there are eggs at home (1 or 0), and suggests a dish using at least one && or || and an else-if chain with at least three branches.

Rubric: builds with the course command (1 point); every branch reached by a test input you list (2 points); edge values tested (1 point); one sentence per branch explaining its condition (1 point).

Summary

  • if (condition) { ... } runs its block only when the condition is true.
  • else if asks the next question; else catches everything left; the first true condition wins.
  • Comparisons: < > <= >= == !=; each gives a bool.
  • && needs both; || needs at least one; ! flips.
  • = assigns, == compares; our flags turn the mix-up into an error.
  • Test every branch and every edge value.
  • In a chain, put narrower conditions first, or a branch may never run.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. 4 degrees: "Wear a warm coat, a hat and gloves." (4 < 5). 5 degrees: "Wear a jumper." (5 < 5 is false, 5 < 18 is true).
  2. = puts a value into a variable; == asks whether two values are equal and gives a bool.
  3. (b) false: 11 >= 15 is false, and && needs both parts true.
  4. (a) true: homework_done is true, and || needs only one true part.
  5. It is written after the whole chain, outside every block, so it runs whichever branch was taken. R1, R5
  6. The program tests the conditions top to bottom and takes the first true one; a wide condition placed first can "steal" all the cases of a narrower one below it.
  7. if (age < 2) {...} else if (age < 13) {...} else if (age < 20) {...} else {...}. Test the edges 1, 2, 12, 13, 19, 20, and one value inside each range.
  8. "error: suggest parentheses around assignment used as truth value [-Werror=parentheses]". It means: you assigned inside a condition; you probably meant ==. R3

Forensic lab answer key

  • Observation: 95 printed "Good work: one star." where "Excellent: three stars!" was expected; 60 and 30 printed the expected lines. R4
  • Proof that three stars is impossible: to reach the second branch, score >= 50 must be false, so the score is below 50. But the second branch needs score >= 90. No number is both below 50 and at least 90, so line 12 can never run.
  • Root cause: lines 9–12: the wide test (>= 50) comes before the narrow one (>= 90).
  • Fix: test score >= 90 first, then score >= 50, then else. The fixed program stars_fixed.cpp printed "Excellent: three stars!" for 95 in this build. R4
  • Tests: 89, 90, 95 (around the top edge), 49, 50, 60 (around the lower edge), 30: every branch and every edge.
  • Wrong hypothesis ruled out: "the test is too hard" — a score of 95 was entered and still got one star, so the scores are not the problem.
  • How the evidence was made: the two tests of a correct chain were swapped on purpose; the outputs are real runs R4.

Story hook

Analogy

Grandma Ama's soup recipe says: "Stir 20 times." It does not say "stir, stir, stir, stir…" twenty times on the card. One short line is enough, because everybody understands "repeat this".

The egg timer works in a different way. Nobody says "wait 5 seconds" five times. You say: "While the timer is above zero, wait one more second." When it reaches zero, it rings, and you stop.

Then there is Kofi's job: "Fill the bowl with 20 spoons of flour, 3 spoons at a time." Kofi counts: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21… Wait! Kofi is a person, so he notices that he went past 20 and stops. A computer would not notice. It would keep spooning flour forever, and the kitchen would disappear under a white mountain.

This chapter is about repeating steps. You will learn the two main loops of C++, and how to make sure they stop.

What you will be able to do

  • Write while and for loops that repeat a block a counted number of times or until a condition changes.
  • Trace a loop by hand in a table, iteration by iteration, and predict its output.
  • Use a counter and a running total inside a loop.
  • Explain how a loop ends, and recognise one that runs zero times or one time too many.
  • Diagnose a loop that never ends from its output and its source.
Jargon box
Loop
Simple words: A part of a program that repeats. Analogy: "Stir 20 times." Precise: A statement (while, for) that runs its block again and again as long as its condition is true. R1, D1
while loop
Simple words: A loop that checks its condition before every round, and stops when it is false. Analogy: "While the timer is above zero, wait one more second." Precise: while (condition) { ... } evaluates the condition before each iteration and runs the block only while it is true (R2). R2, D1
for loop
Simple words: A loop with a counter built in: start, keep going while, and step. Analogy: Counting your stirs out loud: "one, two, three…" up to five. Precise: for (start; condition; step) { ... } runs start once, then checks the condition before each iteration and runs step after each one (R1). R1, D1
Iteration
Simple words: One round of a loop. Analogy: One stir of the spoon. Precise: A single execution of a loop's block. R1, D1
Counter
Simple words: A variable that counts how many times something happened. Analogy: Counting stirs on your fingers. Precise: A variable, usually an int, that is increased (for example with ++day) on each iteration and often used in the loop's condition. R1, D1
Infinite loop
Simple words: A loop that never stops by itself. Analogy: A cook told "stir until the soup is purple" who keeps stirring forever. Precise: A loop whose condition never becomes false; in R4 the time limit stopped the program and the log recorded exit code 124. R4

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the path the computer takes through a for loop. The arrow back to the condition is the "repeat". The only way out is a false condition.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A loop repeats some steps. Instead of writing the same line twenty times, you write it once and say how often to repeat it, or until when.

A while loop is like the egg timer. Before each round, it asks a question: "Is the timer still above zero?" If yes, it does the steps inside once more. If no, it stops and the program carries on below the loop.

A for loop is like counting your stirs out loud. It has three parts in one line: where to start counting, when to keep going, and how to count up. "Start at 1. Keep going while the count is 5 or less. Add 1 each time."

Every loop needs a way out. Something inside the loop must change, so that one day the question gets the answer "no". If nothing changes, or if the change jumps over the stopping point, the loop never ends. Kofi's flour is a famous kitchen example, and you will investigate it in the forensic lab.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A while loop has the form while (condition) { block }. The condition is checked before every iteration. If it is true, the block runs, and then the condition is checked again. In Listing 2, seconds starts at 5 and the block subtracts 1 each time; when it reaches 0, seconds > 0 is false, and the loop ends after 5 iterations. R2, D1

A for loop packs the three loop parts into one line: for (start; condition; step). The start runs once. Then, as long as the condition is true, the block runs and then the step runs. Listing 1 uses int stir = 1, stir <= 5 and stir = stir + 1. R1, D1

Programmers usually write the step stir = stir + 1 more shortly as ++stir; Listing 3 uses that form with ++day. Both add 1 to the counter. R3, D1

Because the condition is checked first, a loop can run zero times. When Listing 2 started with seconds = 0, the program printed only the "Ding!" line. R6

A loop whose condition never becomes false is an infinite loop. With while (spoons != 20) and steps of 3, spoons goes 18, 21, 24… and is never exactly 20. Our lab runner stops any program after a time limit; for that program the log recorded exit code 124. R4

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Choosing between while and for is about clarity, not power: any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop with the start before it and the step at the end of its block. Use for when you know how many times to repeat, and while when you repeat until something happens, such as "until the player guesses right" in F0-38. D1

A safer stopping condition uses <, <=, > or >= rather than !=, because a step can jump over a single exact value but cannot jump over a whole range. Changing != to < made the flour loop stop (at 21 spoons) in this build. R5

The forensic program uses std::endl instead of '\n'. std::endl also pushes the text out at once. That matters here: the runner stops the program from outside, and text still waiting inside the program would be lost (F0-35 shows this happening). D1

How the hardware actually does it

A loop is built from the same pieces as an if (F0-32): a compare instruction and a jump. At the end of the block there is a jump backwards, to the compare at the top. When the compare says "false", a jump forwards skips past the loop. The processor has no idea it is "in a loop"; it follows jumps. That is also why it never gets bored or tired, and why it will happily run an infinite loop until something stops it. D2

Worked example

Ife saves money for 10 days: 1 coin on day 1, 2 coins on day 2, and so on. How many coins after 10 days? We trace Listing 3, which adds each day's coins to a running total.

Iterationdayday <= 10?total after the block
11true0 + 1 = 1
22true1 + 2 = 3
33true3 + 3 = 6
44true6 + 4 = 10
5–95…9true15, 21, 28, 36, 45
1010true45 + 10 = 55
—11false: leave55

Prediction: the last line says 55. A quick check by pairing: 1 + 10, 2 + 9, 3 + 8, 4 + 7 and 5 + 6 are five pairs of 11, and 5 × 11 = 55. The real run printed "Saved in 10 days: 55". Notice that the condition is checked 11 times but the block runs only 10 times. R3

Where the analogy breaks

  • A cook told to "fill to 20 spoons" stops at 21 and says "close enough". A loop with spoons != 20 never stops, because 21, 24, 27… are all "not 20" (forensic lab). R4
  • A cook gets tired and slows down. The processor repeats the thousandth iteration exactly like the first; it never gets tired and never gets bored. D2
  • "Stir 20 times" counts from 1 in a kitchen. Programmers often count from 0 (for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i) also runs 20 times), which you will need for lists in F0-35. D1

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
The program never finishes; output keeps growing or stops changing.The condition never becomes false: the loop variable is not changed, or it jumps over the stop value.Print the loop variable in every iteration; look at the condition and the step together.Change the variable in the block; prefer </> to !=.
One iteration too few: "Stir number 5" is missing.< written where <= was meant (this build printed only stirs 1 to 4 with stir < 5).Trace the last two iterations by hand.Choose the operator that includes the last value you want.
The loop body never runs.The condition is already false at the start (Listing 2 with 0 seconds printed only "Ding!").Check the start value against the condition.Fix the start value or the condition.
The total is reset to the last value only.The total was declared or set to 0 inside the loop.Is int total = 0; inside the braces?Declare it before the loop.

The "one too few" and "zero times" rows come from real runs of two small variations (stir_less.cpp and timer_zero.cpp), shown in the Lab section. R6

To stop a program that never ends on your own computer, press Ctrl and C together in the terminal window.

Transition box

Where you came from: F0-07 (loops without a computer: "repeat until the basket is empty") and F0-32 (conditions). What carries over: Conditions are the same bool questions as in if; a loop is "an if that goes back up". What changes: The computer never stops on common sense: the loop variable must change so that the condition becomes false, or the program runs forever (exit code 124 in our runner). The same block now runs many times, with different values each time. R4 What comes next: F0-34 puts steps into named recipes, called functions, that you can use again and again.

  4. Why is while (spoons != 20) with steps of 3 dangerous, but while (spoons < 20) safe?

  6. Explain in your own words the difference between a while loop and a for loop.
  7. Apply to a new case: write a loop that prints the 3 times table from 3 × 1 to 3 × 10 (one line each, such as 3 x 4 = 12).
  8. What exit code did the log record for the program that never ended, and who stopped it?

Troubleshooting

  • The terminal fills with lines and does not stop → infinite loop → press Ctrl+C → print the loop variable and check the condition and the step.
  • Nothing is printed at all → the loop ran zero times, or the program is waiting for input → check the start value against the condition.
  • The last number is missing → < instead of <= → trace the last iteration.

Extension

Write a loop that doubles a number, starting at 1, while it is less than 1000, and prints every value. Predict how many lines you will see. Then write the same loop as a for loop.

Forensic lab

The course forensic lab of KID102: "The loop that never ends".

Scenario

Kofi wrote a program to help in the bakery: "Fill the bowl with 20 spoons of flour, 3 spoons at a time." He ran it, and it never printed "The bowl is full." The lab runner had to stop it. Kofi says the computer must be too slow.

Evidence pack

Evidence 1 — the source, never_ends.cpp (it pauses 200 milliseconds per iteration, like a cook taking a moment for each spoon; this also keeps the evidence short):

#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>
#include <thread>

int main()
{
    std::cout << "Fill the bowl with 20 spoons of flour, 3 spoons at a time." << std::endl;
    int spoons = 0;
    while (spoons != 20) {
        spoons = spoons + 3;
        std::cout << "Spoons in the bowl: " << spoons << std::endl;
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(200));
    }
    std::cout << "The bowl is full." << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Evidence 2 — the real output and run record. The runner gave the program 2 seconds (file never_ends.timeout) and then stopped it; how many lines appear before that can differ slightly from run to run:

Fill the bowl with 20 spoons of flour, 3 spoons at a time.
Spoons in the bowl: 3
Spoons in the bowl: 6
Spoons in the bowl: 9
Spoons in the bowl: 12
Spoons in the bowl: 15
Spoons in the bowl: 18
Spoons in the bowl: 21
Spoons in the bowl: 24
Spoons in the bowl: 27
Spoons in the bowl: 30

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-33/never_ends.out; run record never_ends.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:46:48Z; exit code: 124 (stopped by the 2 s time limit).

Questions

  1. Which line of the output shows the first sign of trouble?
  2. Which line of the program is supposed to end the loop, and why does it never do so?
  3. Is "the computer is too slow" a good explanation? Use the evidence.
  4. Propose a fix. What will the last "Spoons in the bowl" line say after your fix?
  5. How could Kofi have caught this before running it?

Method hints

Write the values of spoons after each iteration next to the condition spoons != 20, and mark true or false. Look at the exit code in the record. Form at least two hypotheses (slow computer, wrong condition, wrong step) and test each one against the evidence.

Mini-project

Write a "count the stairs" program: a while loop counts up from 1 step to the number of stairs in your home (a const int), printing "Step n", and prints "Top!" at the end. Then add a running total of the "calories" (1 per step) and print it.

Rubric: builds with the course command (1 point); the loop ends correctly at the top, checked by a trace table (2 points); a running total declared in the right place (1 point); tested with 0 and 1 stairs (1 point).

Summary

  • A loop repeats a block; each round is an iteration.
  • while (condition) checks before every iteration and can run zero times.
  • for (start; condition; step) keeps the three counting parts in one line.
  • Something inside the loop must change, so that the condition becomes false.
  • Prefer <, <=, >, >= to != for stopping: steps can jump over one value.
  • Running totals are declared before the loop.
  • Test the edges: zero iterations, the last iteration.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. The block runs 3 times; the condition is checked 4 times (for i = 1, 2, 3 and finally 4, which is false).
  2. "Timer: 2", "Timer: 1", then "Ding! The eggs are ready."
  3. (b): i = 0, 1, 2, 3. (a) runs 5 times (0 to 4). (c) runs 3 times (1 to 3).
  4. With steps of 3 from 0, spoons is never exactly 20 (18, then 21), so != stays true forever; < 20 becomes false at 21. R4, R5
  5. Before the loop. Inside, it would be created again (or reset) in every iteration and lose the sum.
  6. Both repeat while a condition is true. A for loop gathers start, condition and step in its first line, which suits counting; a while loop has only the condition, which suits "repeat until something happens".
  7. for (int n = 1; n <= 10; ++n) { std::cout << "3 x " << n << " = " << 3 * n << '\n'; }
  8. Exit code 124; the lab runner's 2-second time limit stopped it, not the program itself. R4

Forensic lab answer key

  • Observation: the output goes 18, then 21, 24, 27…; it passes 20 without stopping, "The bowl is full." never appears, and the record says exit code 124 (stopped by the time limit). R4
  • First sign: the line "Spoons in the bowl: 21".
  • Root cause: line 9, while (spoons != 20). The step of 3 from 0 gives 3, 6, …, 18, 21; it never equals 20 exactly, so the condition is always true.
  • "Too slow" is ruled out: the values passed 20 and kept growing; a slow program would still stop at 20. The program was doing exactly what it was told.
  • Fix: while (spoons < 20). The fixed program never_ends_fixed.cpp stopped in this build, with the last line "Spoons in the bowl: 21" and then "The bowl is full." (If the bowl must hold exactly 20, the step itself has to change near the end: a design question for Kofi.) R5
  • Prevention: trace the loop on paper around the stop value; use a range condition; test with a step that does not divide the target.
  • How the evidence was made: a < was replaced by != on purpose; the output and the exit code are the real run R4.

Story hook

Analogy

Mrs Haddad's family cookbook has a page called "Tomato sauce". Many other recipes use it. The lasagne recipe says: "Make the tomato sauce (page 12)." So does the pizza recipe, and the soup recipe.

Nobody copies the whole sauce recipe into every page. You turn to page 12, follow it, and come back with a pot of sauce. Then you continue where you left off.

Some small recipes need to know something first. "Add ___ to the pot" works for salt, for pasta, for carrots. You fill in the blank each time. Other small recipes hand you something back: the sauce, or the answer to "how many plates do we need?"

When the sauce recipe is right, every dish that uses it is better. When it is wrong, you only need to fix one page. And you can taste the sauce on its own, before it goes into the lasagne. Programs are built exactly like this, from small named recipes called functions.

What you will be able to do

  • Write functions with parameters and a return value, and call them from main.
  • Explain what happens during a call: the jump into the function, the copy of the arguments, and the return.
  • Predict the output of a program with several functions, in the order the calls happen.
  • Write a test function that checks another function with answers worked out by hand.
  • Explain why changing a parameter inside a function does not change the caller's variable.
Jargon box
Function
Simple words: A named group of steps that you can use again by calling its name. Analogy: A small recipe inside a bigger recipe: "make the sauce (see page 12)". Precise: A named block of code with a return type and parameters, for example int double_it(int number); calling it runs its body and may give back a value. R1, D1
Function call
Simple words: Using a function by writing its name with round brackets. Analogy: Turning to the sauce page and following it, then coming back. Precise: An expression such as double_it(3) that runs the function body with the given arguments and then continues after the call (R1). R1, D1
Parameter
Simple words: A variable in a function that receives a value from the caller. Analogy: The blank in "add ___ to the pot". Precise: A variable declared in a function's parameter list; it starts as a copy of the argument when the parameter is a plain type such as int, so changing it does not change the caller's variable (R4). R1, R4, D1
Argument
Simple words: The actual value you hand to a function when you call it. Analogy: The word you write in the blank: "add salt to the pot". Precise: An expression in a function call whose value initialises the matching parameter, such as "salt" in add_to_pot("salt"). R1, D1
Return value
Simple words: The answer a function gives back to the code that called it. Analogy: The sauce the helper hands back when the sauce recipe is done. Precise: The value given by a return statement; a function whose return type is not void must return a value, and g++ refused one that did not (R3). R1, R3, D1
void
Simple words: The word for "this function gives nothing back". Analogy: A step like "boil the water" that does not hand you anything. Precise: The return type of a function that returns no value, such as void boil_water(). R1, D1
Test function
Simple words: A function that checks other functions by comparing their answers with answers you worked out by hand. Analogy: Tasting the sauce before you serve it. Precise: A function that calls the code under test with known inputs, compares the results with expected values, reports PASS or FAIL and counts failures (R2). R2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 follows Listing 1 as it runs. main is the big recipe. Each call jumps to a small recipe and comes back to the next line.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Your programs are growing. Soon main will be long and hard to read. Functions fix that. A function is a small recipe with a name. You write it once, and use it as often as you like.

Using a function is called calling it. You write its name and round brackets, like boil_water();. The program jumps into the small recipe, follows it to the end, and comes back to the next line of the big recipe.

Some functions need information. add_to_pot needs to know what to add. You put it inside the brackets: add_to_pot("salt"). Inside the function, that value has a name, like the blank on the recipe card.

Some functions give an answer back. double_it(3) gives back 6, and you can store it in a jar: int plates = double_it(3);.

Best of all, you can test a small recipe on its own. You work out a few answers by hand, ask the function, and compare. If they match, you can trust it in the big program. If not, you know exactly which page to fix.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A function definition has four parts: a return type, a name, a parameter list in round brackets, and a body in braces. In int double_it(int number) { return number * 2; }, the return type is int, the name is double_it, there is one parameter number of type int, and the body returns twice the number. R1, D1

A function call such as double_it(3) gives each parameter its first value from the matching argument: here number starts as 3. The body runs. The return statement ends the function and hands its value back to the caller, so the call itself is worth 6. R1, D1

A function that hands nothing back has the return type void, like boil_water. A function whose return type is not void must return a value. When one did not, g++ with our flags refused to build it: "no return statement in function returning non-void". R3, D1

A parameter of a plain type such as int is a copy of the argument. Changing the copy inside the function does not change the caller's variable. In the forensic evidence, add_sugar made its own spoons 3, but the caller's spoons stayed 2. To get a result out, return it. R4, R5, D1

A function must be declared before the line that calls it. Listing 1 defines its functions above main for that reason. When a call came first, g++ said "'double_it' was not declared in this scope". R6, D1

A test function calls the function under test with inputs whose answers you worked out by hand. Listing 2's test function prints PASS or FAIL for each case and counts the failures; main stops with exit code 1 if any test failed. R2, R7

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Passing std::string thing by value makes a copy of the text for every call. For short texts that does not matter. Later (SP101) you will meet const std::string&, a way to let the function read the caller's string without copying it and without being allowed to change it. D1

Each call gets its own fresh set of parameters and local variables. They exist only while that call runs. That is why two calls of add_to_pot do not mix up "salt" and "pasta", and why a function's local variable is gone after it returns. Debuggers show this as a list of active calls, the call stack (you will see one call inside another in F0-37). D1, D2

Good functions do one job, have a name that says what that job is, and can be tested alone. Tests are written with values you can check by hand, including edge cases such as 0 guests. R2

How the hardware actually does it

A call is a special jump. Before jumping into the function, the processor remembers where to come back to: the address of the next instruction. The return is a jump back to that remembered address. Arguments and the return value are passed in agreed places, such as small storage spots inside the processor or a reserved area of memory. Because the return address is remembered, one function can call another, which calls another, and every one finds its way home. D2

Worked example

We predict Listing 2 line by line. The function cups_needed(guests) returns guests * 2 + 1: two cups per guest, plus one spare.

  1. By hand first: 0 guests need 0 × 2 + 1 = 1 cup. 1 guest needs 1 × 2 + 1 = 3. 4 guests need 4 × 2 + 1 = 9. These are the expected values in the test function.
  2. main calls test_cups_needed(). It calls check(0, 1), which calls cups_needed(0) and gets 1. 1 equals 1, so it prints "PASS: cups_needed(0) = 1, expected 1" and returns 0.
  3. The same happens for 1 guest (3) and 4 guests (9). failures stays 0 + 0 + 0 = 0.
  4. Back in main: 0 > 0 is false, so it prints "All tests passed." and then the party line: 6 × 2 + 1 = 13 cups.

Prediction: three PASS lines, "All tests passed.", and "For a party of 6 we need 13 cups." The real run printed exactly that, with exit code 0. R2

Now break it on purpose: forget the spare cup (return guests * 2;). Prediction: 0 guests gives 0 (expected 1), 1 gives 2 (expected 3), 4 gives 8 (expected 9). Every check should fail, "Some tests failed." should appear, and the exit code should be 1. The real run in the Lab section agrees. R7

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

void boil_water()
{
    std::cout << "Boil a big pot of water.\n";
}

void add_to_pot(std::string thing)
{
    std::cout << "Add the " << thing << " to the pot.\n";
}

int double_it(int number)
{
    return number * 2;
}

int main()
{

    add_to_pot("salt");
    add_to_pot("pasta");
    int plates = double_it(3);
    std::cout << "Make enough for " << plates << " plates.\n";
    return 0;
}

Listing 2 — cups.cpp, a function with its test function

#include <iostream>

// Each guest drinks 2 cups of juice, and we keep 1 extra cup just in case.
int cups_needed(int guests)
{
    return guests * 2 + 1;
}

// Returns 0 when the answer is right and 1 when it is wrong.
int check(int guests, int expected)
{
    int got = cups_needed(guests);
    if (got == expected) {
        std::cout << "PASS: ";
    } else {
        std::cout << "FAIL: ";
    }
    std::cout << "cups_needed(" << guests << ") = " << got << ", expected " << expected << '\n';
    if (got == expected) {
        return 0;
    }
    return 1;
}

int test_cups_needed()
{
    int failures = 0;
    failures = failures + check(0, 1);
    failures = failures + check(1, 3);
    failures = failures + check(4, 9);
    return failures;
}

int main()
{
    if (test_cups_needed() > 0) {
        std::cout << "Some tests failed.\n";
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "All tests passed.\n";
    std::cout << "For a party of 6 we need " << cups_needed(6) << " cups.\n";
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • When you write "salt" into the blank of a paper recipe, the card is changed. A function call does not change the function: each call gets a fresh copy of its parameters (R1 used add_to_pot twice with different values). R1, D1
  • In a kitchen, the helper who makes the sauce can add salt to your soup on the side. A C++ function with plain parameters gets copies; it cannot change your variables, as the forensic lab shows. The only way out for a result is the return value (or techniques you will learn in SP101). R4, R5
  • A cook can look ahead in the book for a page that comes later. The compiler reads the file from top to bottom and refused a call to a function it had not seen yet. R6

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
error: no return statement in function returning non-voidA function with a return type does not return a value.The message points at the closing brace of the function.Add return value;, or make the function void if it should not return anything.
error: '…' was not declared in this scopeThe function is called above its definition (or its name is misspelled).Search the file for the definition; is it below the call?Move the function above main.
A variable does not change after a function "changed" it.The parameter is a copy (forensic lab).Print the variable inside and after the function.Return the new value and assign it: spoons = add_sugar(spoons);
The result of a call is ignored.The call was written alone, like double_it(3);.Look for calls whose value is not stored or printed.Store or use the value: int plates = double_it(3);
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-33: one long main with loops and decisions. What carries over: Everything inside a function is the same C++: variables, if, loops; statements still run top to bottom inside each function. What changes: The program now jumps between named functions and comes back; parameters are copies, so a function's changes stay inside it unless they are returned; a function must appear above its first call; and each function can be tested on its own. R1, R4, R6 What comes next: F0-35 stores many values in one variable: lists, with std::vector.

Check yourself

  1. In int area(int width, int height), name the return type, the function name and the parameters.
  2. What is the value of double_it(double_it(2))?
  3. What is the difference between a parameter and an argument? Use add_to_pot("salt") as the example.
  4. Multiple choice. After int n = 5; add_sugar(n); with the forensic lab's add_sugar, what is n? (a) 6 (b) 5 (c) it depends on the compiler
  5. Why does Listing 2 run its tests before it prints the party line?
  6. Explain in your own words why programmers split a program into functions.
  7. Apply to a new case: write a function int minutes_to_cook(int potatoes) that returns 20 plus 2 minutes per potato, and three test cases with answers worked out by hand.
  8. What does "void" mean in front of a function name?

Lab

Goal

Write, call and test functions, and watch a test catch a broken function.

Hardware and software needed

The toolchain from F0-29; this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 on Linux x86_64. R1

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Run Listing 1. Add a call add_to_pot("tomatoes"); between the two existing calls. Predict the output order, run, compare.
  2. Write int triple_it(int number) and use it to print the plates for 3 tables. Predict, run.
  3. Run Listing 2. Then break cups_needed by deleting + 1. Before running, predict which checks fail and what the exit code will be.
  4. Add a fourth check to test_cups_needed for 10 guests. Work out the expected answer by hand first.
  5. Move double_it below main in Listing 1. Predict the compiler's message, then compare with Listing 4's real message.

Every check failed, exactly as predicted, and main stopped before the party line. The log recorded exit code 1. The test caught the missing spare cup before any party was planned with it.

Verification

All your tests print PASS and the program's exit code is 0; the broken version's exit code is 1 (recorded in cups_broken.log). university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F0-34 reproduces the recorded runs.

Troubleshooting

  • "was not declared in this scope" → function defined below its call → move it above main (Listing 4).
  • "no return statement" → a non-void function without return → add one (Listing 3).
  • Tests pass but the program is still wrong → the expected values in the test are wrong too → work them out again by hand, slowly, and have a friend check them.

Extension

Write bool is_even(int number) using % from F0-31, with a test function that checks 0, 1, 2 and 7. Then use it in a loop that prints the even numbers from 1 to 20.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Zara likes her tea sweet. Her program has a function add_sugar that is supposed to add one spoon. The program says the function added a spoon, but at the end there are still only 2 spoons. "The function works on the inside but not on the outside!" says Zara.

Evidence pack

Evidence 1 — the source, sugar.cpp:

#include <iostream>

void add_sugar(int spoons)
{
    spoons = spoons + 1;
    std::cout << "Inside add_sugar: spoons = " << spoons << '\n';
}

int main()
{
    int spoons = 2;
    std::cout << "Before: spoons = " << spoons << '\n';
    add_sugar(spoons);
    std::cout << "After:  spoons = " << spoons << '\n';
    return 0;
}

Evidence 2 — the real output of the run in this build:

Before: spoons = 2
Inside add_sugar: spoons = 3
After:  spoons = 2

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-34/sugar.out; run record sugar.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:46:59Z; exit code: 0.

Questions

  1. Which two lines of output disagree, and by how much?
  2. There are two variables called spoons. Where does each one live, and what happens to each during the call?
  3. Rewrite add_sugar and the call so that the caller's spoons becomes 3.
  4. Why did the compiler not warn about this?

Method hints

Draw two jars: one for main's spoons, one for the parameter. Follow the call from the Layer 2 explanation: what is copied, and when? State two hypotheses before you decide (for example "the function is never called" and "the function changes a copy") and check each against the output.

Mini-project

Write a "party planner" with at least three functions besides main: for example cups_needed, slices_needed and print_shopping_list. Add a test function for each function that returns a value. main runs all tests first and stops with exit code 1 if any fails.

Rubric: builds with the course command (1 point); at least three functions with clear names (1 point); a test function with hand-worked expected values, including an edge case (2 points); a failing test was tried on purpose and seen to fail (1 point).

Summary

  • A function is a named recipe: return type, name, parameters, body.
  • A call jumps into the function and comes back to the next step.
  • Arguments give the parameters their first values; plain parameters are copies.
  • return hands a value back; void functions hand nothing back.
  • Define a function above its first call.
  • A test function compares answers with values worked out by hand and counts failures.
  • Run the tests first; never use a function whose tests fail.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Return type int; name area; parameters width and height, both int.
  2. 8: the inner call gives 4, and double_it(4) gives 8.
  3. The parameter is the named blank in the definition (thing); the argument is the value given in the call ("salt").
  4. (b) 5. The function changes its own copy. (a) would need the result to be returned and assigned. (c) is wrong: this is how C++ passes an int by value, and the run showed it. R4
  5. So that a broken cups_needed is never used to plan a real party: if a test fails, main stops with exit code 1. R7
  6. Any of: to reuse steps without copying them, to give steps a clear name, to fix a mistake in one place, to test each part on its own.
  7. int minutes_to_cook(int potatoes) { return 20 + 2 * potatoes; }; tests: 0 → 20, 1 → 22, 5 → 30.
  8. The function returns no value.

Forensic lab answer key

  • Observation: "Inside add_sugar: spoons = 3", but "After: spoons = 2". The change of 1 spoon is lost when the function returns. R4
  • Hypotheses: "the function is never called" is ruled out by the "Inside" line, which only the function prints. The remaining hypothesis: the function changes a copy.
  • Root cause: add_sugar(int spoons) takes its parameter by value. On the call, the parameter spoons starts as a copy of main's spoons (2); line 5 changes the copy to 3; when the function ends, the copy disappears. main's jar was never touched.
  • Fix: return the new value and assign it: int add_sugar(int spoons) { spoons = spoons + 1; ...; return spoons; } and spoons = add_sugar(spoons);. The fixed program sugar_fixed.cpp printed "After: spoons = 3" in this build. R5
  • Why no warning: changing a parameter is legal, and the parameter is used (it is printed), so nothing looked suspicious to the compiler.
  • Prevention: a test that checks the caller's value after the call; the rule "results come out through return".
  • How the evidence was made: a correct function that returned its result was changed to return nothing; the output is the real run R4.
