Story hook

Analogy

Before the big family dinner, Aiko writes a shopping list: rice, beans, onions. Her brother shouts from the other room, "Add lemons!" She writes "lemons" at the bottom. One list, four items, in order.

Imagine keeping the list as separate jars instead: item1, item2, item3. Then the fourth item needs a new jar with a new name, and every part of the program must learn about it. That would be silly.

In the pantry there is a long shelf of identical jars with numbers painted on them. The first jar has the number 0. Aiko's grandmother says, "Bring me jar 2." Aiko counts: 0, 1, 2. That is the third jar.

And then there is the egg box. It always has exactly six places, no more, no fewer. In this chapter you will meet both kinds of list: the growing shelf, called std::vector, and the fixed box, called std::array.

What you will be able to do

  • Create a std::vector, read its elements by index, ask for its size and add elements with push_back.
  • Visit every element with a counting loop and with a range-based for loop.
  • Compute a total, a count and a best value from a list.
  • Use std::array for a list whose length never changes.
  • Explain what "out of range" means, and find a loop that skips the last element.
Jargon box
std::vector
Simple words: A list of values of the same type that can grow. Analogy: A row of numbered jars on a shelf, and you can add more jars at the end. Precise: The standard library container from <vector> that stores elements in order; size() gives the number of elements and push_back adds one at the end (R1). R1, D1
std::array
Simple words: A list with a fixed number of values. Analogy: An egg box: always the same number of places. Precise: The standard library container from <array> whose size is part of its type, for example std::array<std::string, 3> (R3). R3, D1
Element
Simple words: One value inside a list. Analogy: One jar in the row. Precise: One of the values stored in a container such as std::vector. R1, D1
Index
Simple words: The position number of an element. Counting starts at 0. Analogy: The number painted on a jar: jar 0, jar 1, jar 2. Precise: The position of an element in a container, from 0 up to size() − 1; list[0] is the first element (R1). R1, D1
Range-based for loop
Simple words: A for loop that visits every element of a list, one by one, without an index. Analogy: Walking along the shelf and looking into each jar in turn. Precise: for (int score : scores) { ... } runs the block once for each element, with the loop variable holding that element (R2). R2, D1
Out of range
Simple words: Asking for a list position that does not exist. Analogy: Reaching for jar 3 on a shelf that has only jars 0, 1 and 2. Precise: Using an index that is not less than size(); the member function at() checks and throws std::out_of_range, which stopped the program in R4 with exit code 134. R4, D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the shopping list of Listing 1 as a shelf of numbered jars, before and after push_back("lemons").

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

So far, each jar held one value. But many things come in lists: shopping items, scores in a game, guests at a party. A list keeps many values of the same kind together, in order, under one name.

Each value in the list has a position number. Programmers count positions from 0, not from 1. So the first item is at position 0, the second at position 1, and so on. It feels strange at first. Think of the numbers painted on the pantry jars, starting with 0.

A std::vector is a list that can grow. You can ask how many items it holds, and you can add a new item at the end. A std::array is a list with a fixed length, like an egg box.

Lists and loops are best friends. A loop can visit every item, one after another: add them up, find the biggest, print them all. That works for 3 items or for 3,000.

There is one danger. If you ask for a position that does not exist, like jar 3 on a shelf of three jars (0, 1, 2), something must go wrong. You will see what the computer does in that case.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A vector is declared with the type of its elements in angle brackets: std::vector<std::string> list = {"rice", "beans", "onions"};. You need #include <vector>. Each value in it is an element. list.size() gives the number of elements: 3 here. R1, D1

You read an element by its index in square brackets: list[0] is "rice". Valid indexes go from 0 to size() - 1. list.push_back("lemons") adds a new element at the end; afterwards the size was 4 and "lemons" had index 3. R1, D1

To visit every element, you can count through the indexes: for (std::size_t i = 0; i < list.size(); ++i). The type std::size_t is a whole-number type made for sizes and indexes; it matches the type that size() returns. Note the <: the last index used is size() - 1. R1, D1

If you do not need the index, a range-based for loop is shorter and cannot go out of range: for (int score : scores) runs once per element, with score holding a copy of that element. Listing 2 uses it to compute a total, a count and the best score. R2, D1

A std::array has its length in its type: std::array<std::string, 3> meals always holds exactly 3 strings. It has size() and can be visited with the same loops, but it has no push_back. R3, D1

Square brackets do not check the index. The member function at() does: eggs_per_box.at(3) on a vector of size 3 stopped the program with the message "vector::_M_range_check: __n (which is 3) >= this->size() (which is 3)" and exit code 134. R4, D1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Look closely at the run of Listing 4: the line "Box 0 has 6 eggs" is missing from the output, although that statement ran before the crash. The program collected its output in a waiting area (a buffer) to print it later, and the crash came first. When the same program used std::endl, which empties the buffer at once, the line appeared. So when a program crashes, its last printed lines may be missing: the crash may have happened later than the output suggests. R4, R5, D1

What about square brackets with a bad index? The C++ rules do not promise any particular result: the program might print a strange value, crash, or seem to work. That is why this course uses at() when an index could be wrong, and why our build uses AddressSanitizer (-fsanitize=address), a tool that watches memory use while the program runs. D1, D2

In for (const std::string& meal : meals) (Listing 3), the & lets the loop look at each string in place, without copying it, and const promises not to change it. You will learn this properly in SP101. D1

How the hardware actually does it

A vector keeps its elements next to each other in memory, like jars side by side on one shelf. To find element i, the program starts at the address of element 0 and moves forward i element-widths. That is why counting starts at 0: element 0 is zero steps from the start. When a vector grows beyond the space it has, it moves its elements to a bigger shelf; you do not see this happen. D1, D3

Worked example

We trace Listing 2 by hand. The scores are 7, 9, 4, 10, 6. best starts as the first score, 7.

scoretotalgamesscore > best?best
7717 > 7: false7
91629 > 7: true9
42034 > 9: false9
1030410 > 9: true10
63656 > 10: false10

Average: 36 / 5 in whole numbers is 7 (5 × 7 = 35, remainder 1), the integer division of F0-31. Prediction: 5 games, 36 points, best 10, average 7. The real run printed exactly these values. R2

Why start best at scores[0] and not at 0? If every score were negative, a start of 0 would wrongly "win". Starting with a real element is always safe, as long as the list is not empty.

Where the analogy breaks

  • Real shelves are numbered from 1 by most people. C++ indexes start at 0, so "jar 3" is the fourth jar. Many bugs come from this difference. R1
  • A shopping list can hold rice and a phone number at the same time. A vector holds elements of one type only: std::vector<int> holds only whole numbers. D1
  • Reaching for a jar that is not there, you would feel the empty shelf and stop. In C++, square brackets do not check; only at() checks, and it stops the program when the index is bad. R4, D1
  • Adding a jar to a real shelf never moves the other jars. A growing vector may move all its elements to a new place in memory, which matters in later courses. D1

The last element is never used.The loop stops one too early (forensic lab).Print i and size() in each iteration.Loop while i < size(), or use a range-based for loop.
error: comparison of integer expressions of different signednessAn int counter compared with size().The message names the comparison.Use std::size_t for the counter, or a range-based for loop.
The first item is missing from a printed list.The loop started at 1, as people count.Look at the start of the loop.Start at 0.

The signedness message in the third row is real: when the counter in Listing 1 was an int (file int_counter.cpp), our flags turned the warning into this error: R7

Transition box

Where you came from: F0-33 (loops) and F0-34 (functions): one jar per value. What carries over: Loops, totals, "best so far" and the habit of tracing in a table; each element behaves like an ordinary variable. What changes: One name now holds many values, found by index; counting starts at 0 and the last index is size − 1; a wrong index is a new kind of bug that the compiler cannot see, which at() catches while the program runs (exit code 134 here). R1, R4 What comes next: F0-36 teaches you to read the compiler's messages calmly, because by now you have met quite a few.

Check yourself

  1. A vector holds 5 elements. What are its first and last valid indexes?
  2. What does list.size() print after std::vector<int> list = {4, 8}; list.push_back(15); list.push_back(16);?
  3. Multiple choice. Which loop visits every element of v exactly once? (a) for (std::size_t i = 1; i <= v.size(); ++i) (b) for (std::size_t i = 0; i <= v.size(); ++i) (c) for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i)
  4. When would you choose std::array instead of std::vector?
  5. What is the difference between v[3] and v.at(3) when v has 3 elements?
  6. Explain in your own words why the "Box 0" line was missing from Listing 4's output.
  7. Apply to a new case: write a loop that finds the smallest value in {12, 5, 8, 3, 9}. What start value do you use and why?
  8. Why does Listing 2 start best at scores[0]?

Lab

Goal

Build, change and loop over lists, and see an out-of-range index caught.

Hardware and software needed

The toolchain from F0-29; this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 on Linux x86_64. R1

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Run Listing 1. Add two more items with push_back. Predict the size and the last index, run, compare.
  2. In Listing 2, add the score 12. Update the trace table first, then run.
  3. Add a "worst score" to Listing 2 (the smallest). Predict it, run.
  4. In Listing 3, try meals.push_back("snack");. Predict what the compiler says, then read the real message.
  5. In Listing 4, change at(3) to at(2). Predict the output and the exit code.
  6. Write a function int total_of(std::vector<int> numbers) and a test function for it with three lists you add up by hand (one of them empty).

Expected observations

Steps 1–3 and 5: your predictions match your runs. Step 6: an empty list must give 0. The given listings' outputs are shown above. R1, R2, R3

Step 4: the build fails, because a std::array cannot grow. The real message in this build (file array_push.cpp): R7

Verification

Every prediction is written before the run and agrees with it; your test function prints only PASS lines. university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F0-35 reproduces the recorded runs (the two out-of-range programs end with exit code 134 on purpose).

Troubleshooting

  • "error: 'vector' is not a member of 'std'", with a note "did you forget to '#include <vector>'?" → the include is missing (real message: no_vector_include.out) → add it at the top. R7
  • "comparison of integer expressions of different signedness" → int counter compared with size() → use std::size_t or a range-based for loop.
  • Program stops with std::out_of_range → bad index given to at() → the message names the index and the size.

Extension

Read 5 numbers from input into a vector with a loop and push_back, then print them in reverse order. Careful with the loop that counts down: a std::size_t can never be below 0.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Lena is organising a party for four friends. Her program prints a name card for every guest. At the party, Ravi has no name card. "I was invited," he says, "the list says four guests!" Lena checks: the list does say four.

Evidence pack

Evidence 1 — the source, guests.cpp:

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    std::vector<std::string> guests = {"Lena", "Kofi", "Mei", "Ravi"};
    std::cout << "Guests invited: " << guests.size() << '\n';
    std::cout << "Name cards printed:\n";
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i + 1 < guests.size(); ++i) {
        std::cout << "  [" << guests[i] << "]\n";
    }
    return 0;
}

Evidence 2 — the real output of the run in this build:

Guests invited: 4
Name cards printed:
  [Lena]
  [Kofi]
  [Mei]

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-35/guests.out; run record guests.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:47:00Z; exit code: 0.

Questions

  1. How many guests does the program report, and how many cards does it print?
  2. Which guest is missing, and what is that guest's index?
  3. Trace the loop condition for each value of i. For which i does it first become false?
  4. Write two different fixes. Which one cannot make this mistake again?

Method hints

Make a table with the columns i, i + 1, guests.size() and "condition true?". Compare the printed names with the indexes 0 to 3. Write down two hypotheses first (for example "Ravi is not in the vector" and "the loop stops early") and test each one against the evidence.

Mini-project

Write a "pantry stock" program: a vector of item names and a second vector of amounts (same order). Print every item with its amount, the total number of items, and the name of the item with the smallest amount ("buy more of this!"). Put the search into a function with its own test function.

Rubric: builds with the course command (1 point); correct loops with no index out of range (1 point); the search function has a test with values worked out by hand (2 points); handles a list where two items have the same smallest amount, with your rule written down (1 point).

Summary

  • A std::vector holds many elements of one type, in order, and can grow with push_back.
  • Indexes start at 0; the last valid index is size() - 1.
  • Count through indexes with std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(), or use a range-based for loop.
  • Totals, counts and "best so far" are loop patterns over a list.
  • std::array has a fixed size that is part of its type.
  • at() checks the index and stops the program with std::out_of_range; [] does not check.
  • After a crash, the last printed lines may be missing.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. 0 and 4.
  2. 4: two elements at the start, plus two added.
  3. (c). (a) skips index 0 and reads index size(), which does not exist. (b) also reads index size(): one step too far.
  4. When the number of elements is fixed and known when you write the program, such as the 3 meals of a day or the 7 days of a week.
  5. v.at(3) checks and stops the program with std::out_of_range (R4); v[3] does not check, and the result is not defined by the C++ rules. R4, D1
  6. The text was waiting in the program's output buffer, to be printed later; the program was stopped before the buffer was emptied. With std::endl the line appeared. R4, R5
  7. Start smallest at the first element (12), then for each element, if it is smaller, remember it; the result is 3. A start of 0 would be wrong, because 0 is smaller than every element but is not in the list.
  8. Because it is a real value from the list; a fixed start such as 0 could be better than every real score and give a wrong "best".

Forensic lab answer key

  • Observation: "Guests invited: 4" but only three cards: Lena, Kofi, Mei. Ravi, the last guest, index 3, is missing. R6
  • Hypotheses: "Ravi is not in the vector" is ruled out: line 7 lists him and the size is 4. The remaining hypothesis: the loop stops early.
  • Trace: i = 0: 1 < 4 true; i = 1: 2 < 4 true; i = 2: 3 < 4 true; i = 3: 4 < 4 false. The loop ends before index 3 is printed.
  • Root cause: line 10, the condition i + 1 < guests.size(), which is one step too strict: an off-by-one error.
  • Fixes: for (std::size_t i = 0; i < guests.size(); ++i), or better for (const std::string& guest : guests), which visits every element and cannot be off by one. The fixed program guests_fixed.cpp printed all four cards in this build. R6
  • Prevention: compare the number of printed items with size(); test with lists of 0, 1 and several elements; prefer range-based for loops.
  • How the evidence was made: the correct condition i < guests.size() was changed on purpose; the output is real run R6.

Story hook

Analogy

Sofia hands her recipe card to cousin Tomás, the helper from F0-29 who rewrites recipes for Grandpa. Tomás hands it straight back with a note: "Line 7: I expected a full stop before 'std'."

Sofia's first feeling is panic. Her second feeling is annoyance: "Line 7 is fine!" Then she looks at line 6. "Put 3 apples in the bowl" has no full stop at the end. Tomás only noticed the problem when he reached the next line, because that is where the sentence suddenly made no sense.

Tomás is not angry, and he is not judging Sofia. He is telling her exactly where he got stuck. Sometimes his note is slightly off target, and sometimes one mistake makes him write three notes. But every note is a clue.

Real programmers see error messages every day, even after many years. The difference is that they read them calmly, from the top, like a detective. This chapter teaches you how.

What you will be able to do

  • Read a g++ message and name its parts: file, line, column, error or warning, and the description.
  • Find the real mistake, which may be on the line before the reported one.
  • Fix the first error first, and recognise follow-on errors that disappear with it.
  • Explain what the warning flags -Wall, -Wextra and -Werror do, using g++'s own help text.
  • Use the compiler's suggestions ("did you mean …?") as hints, not as orders.
Jargon box
Compiler error
Simple words: A message from the compiler that says it cannot build your program, and where it got stuck. Analogy: The helper saying: "I cannot rewrite this recipe; step 6 is missing its end." Precise: A diagnostic that stops compilation; g++ prints file:line:column: error: followed by a description and the source line with a marker (R2). R2, D2
Warning
Simple words: A message from the compiler that says "this is allowed, but it looks like a mistake". Analogy: The helper saying: "You bought pears but never used them. Did you mean to?" Precise: A diagnostic about legal but suspicious code, enabled by flags such as -Wall and -Wextra; with -Werror ("Treat all warnings as errors", R7) every warning stops the build (R5). R5, R7, D2
Follow-on error
Simple words: An extra error message caused by an earlier mistake, not by a new one. Analogy: One missing step that makes the next three steps confusing too. Precise: A diagnostic that appears only because the compiler was already confused by an earlier error; fixing the first error usually removes it, as in R3 and R6. R3, R6

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 takes one real message from this chapter apart. Every g++ message has the same shape, so once you can read one, you can read them all.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

When the compiler cannot understand your program, it does not build it. Instead it prints messages. They look scary at first: long lines, strange words, little arrows. But each message is a note from a helper, and it says where the helper got stuck.

Read the first message first. It has the file name, the line number and the position on the line. Go to that line. If it looks fine, look at the line right above it. Very often the mistake is a missing semicolon or a missing quote at the end of the line before.

One mistake can confuse the compiler so much that it prints several messages. Fix the first one, build again, and see what is left. Often the other messages disappear by themselves.

Some messages are warnings, not errors. A warning says: "This is allowed, but it looks like a mistake." In this course, we ask the compiler to treat every warning as an error. That sounds strict, but it catches many bugs before the program ever runs.

And the most important rule: an error message is not a bad mark. It is free help. Read it slowly. Be a detective.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A g++ message starts with file:line:column:, then the kind (error, warning or note), then a description. Below it, g++ prints the source line with the line number and a marker (^~~~) under the place it means. Often the first line says which function the problem is in: "In function 'int main()'". R2, R3, D1

The compiler reports where it noticed the problem, which can be later than the mistake. In Listing 2 the semicolon is missing at the end of line 6, but the error is reported at line 7, column 5, where std appeared although a ; was expected. Then a second error followed: "'fruit' was not declared in this scope" at line 8, because line 7 was never understood as a declaration. Adding the ; fixes both. R2

A follow-on error is such a second message caused by the first mistake. Listing 3 shows another kind: apple is misspelled on line 8, and the compiler then also says "unused variable 'apples'", because the real apples is now never used. Fix the spelling and both messages go away. R3

Some messages contain suggestions. In Listing 3, g++ wrote "did you mean 'apples'?" and showed the corrected word. That suggestion was right. In F0-34, for a function used before its definition, g++ suggested "did you mean 'double'?", which was wrong. Suggestions are guesses based on spelling. R3, D1

Error messages use precise words for types. In Listing 4, the text "three" is described as const char*, which is how C++ sees a string literal here. You do not need to understand every word. "invalid conversion from … to 'int'" already says: "this kind of value does not fit into an int jar". R4, D1

Warnings are switched on with flags. g++'s own help describes them: -Wall "Enable most warning messages", -Wextra "Print extra (possibly unwanted) warnings", and -Werror "Treat all warnings as errors". With -Werror, the unused variable in Listing 5 stopped the build, and the message ends with the flag in square brackets: [-Werror=unused-variable]. R5, R7

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. The square brackets at the end of a warning name the flag that controls it, such as [-Werror=parentheses] in F0-32 or [-Werror=uninitialized] in F0-30. That lets you look the warning up in the GCC manual by name. A line "cc1plus: all warnings being treated as errors" means the build failed only because of -Werror. R5, D2

The compiler is not the only tool that can complain. In SP101 you will meet the linker, which joins pieces of a program together and has its own messages, such as "undefined reference". They look different because a different tool prints them. D1, D2

Not every mistake produces a message. A program can compile perfectly and still be wrong: the loop that never ends (F0-33) and the missing name card (F0-35) compiled without a single warning. For those, you need tests and the debugger of F0-37.

How the hardware actually does it

Compiler errors happen before your program ever reaches the processor. The compiler is itself a program running on the processor, reading your text from top to bottom. When it cannot fit the next word into the rules of C++, it stops translating and writes messages instead. No executable is produced, so there is nothing for the processor to run. That is why a program with a compiler error can never cause a crash: it never starts. D2, D3

Worked example

We solve Listing 2 the detective way, step by step.

  1. Read only the first error. "missing_semicolon.cpp:7:5: error: expected ',' or ';' before 'std'". File: missing_semicolon.cpp. Line 7. Column 5.
  2. Go to the place. Line 7 is std::string fruit = "apples";. Column 5 is where std starts (the first four columns are spaces). The line looks correct.
  3. Read the description as a sentence. "Before 'std', I expected a ',' or a ';'." So something before std was not finished.
  4. Look one line up. Line 6 is int apples = 3 without a semicolon. Found it.
  5. Predict the effect of the fix. With the ; added, line 7 becomes a proper declaration, so the second error about fruit should disappear too.
  6. Fix and build again. The result is fixed.cpp, which built and printed "We have 3 apples.".

Both errors came from one missing character. The real messages are under Listing 2 below; the fixed program's run is under Listing 1. R1, R2

g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0
$ g++ -v --help   (filtered to the flags used in this course)
  -Wall                       Enable most warning messages.
  -Werror                     Treat all warnings as errors.
  -Wextra                     Print extra (possibly unwanted) warnings.
  -Wparentheses               Warn about possibly missing parentheses.
  -Wpedantic                  Issue warnings needed for strict compliance to
                              the standard.
  -Wreturn-type               Warn whenever a function's return type defaults
                              to "int" (C), or about inconsistent return types
                              (C++).
  -Wuninitialized             Warn about uninitialized automatic variables.
  -Wunused-variable           Warn when a variable is unused.

Where the analogy breaks

  • Tomás could read the whole card first and then point at the real mistake. The compiler reports where it got stuck while reading, which can be a line after the mistake (Listing 2). R2
  • Tomás writes one note per mistake. The compiler may write several messages for one mistake (follow-on errors), or one message for a line that is fine. R2, R3
  • Tomás would never refuse a recipe only because you bought pears you did not use. With -Werror, the compiler does exactly that, because we asked it to be that strict. R5
  • Tomás would also notice that "fill the bowl until exactly 20 spoons, 3 at a time" can never finish. The compiler checks the rules of the language, not whether your plan makes sense (F0-33).

Common mistakes and debugging

These are mistakes in reading messages, not in writing code.

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
You fix the reported line, but the error stays.The mistake is on an earlier line (often a missing ;, " or }).Read the description: "expected … before …" points backwards.Look one or two lines up.
Fifty messages appear, and you give up.One early mistake caused many follow-on errors.Scroll to the very first message.Fix only the first; build again.
You accept a "did you mean …?" and it gets worse.The suggestion was a spelling guess (F0-34's "did you mean 'double'?").Ask: does the suggestion make sense here?Fix what you meant, not what was suggested.
You run the program and see old behaviour.The build failed, so the old executable was run.Read the build output before running.Only run after a build with no errors.
You delete the warning flags to "make it build".The warnings were pointing at real problems.Read each warning's description and flag name.Fix the code; keep the flags.

The "old executable" row is about the short build from F0-29, where you choose the output file yourself; our lab runner deletes its programs after each run. R1

Transition box

Where you came from: Chapters F0-29 to F0-35, where you met single error messages along the way (uninitialised jar, = in an if, missing return, out-of-range index). In F0-08 you learned to be a code detective without a computer. What carries over: The detective method: observe, form two hypotheses, test, conclude. What changes: Now the clues are written by a tool, in a fixed format (file:line:column: kind: description), and they point to where the compiler got stuck, not always to where you went wrong; one mistake can produce several messages. R2, R3 What comes next: F0-37 handles the bugs the compiler cannot see, with a debugger that pauses your program while it runs.

Check yourself

  1. Name the five parts of the message "missing_semicolon.cpp:7:5: error: expected ',' or ';' before 'std'".
  2. The compiler reports line 12, but line 12 is correct. Where do you look next, and why?
  3. What is a follow-on error? Give the example from Listing 3.
  4. Multiple choice. What does -Werror do? (a) It hides all errors. (b) It treats all warnings as errors. (c) It prints extra warnings.
  5. Why is "did you mean 'double'?" in F0-34 a bad suggestion?
  6. Explain in your own words why we turn warnings into errors in this course.
  7. Apply to a new case: a message says "error: expected ';' before '}' token" on line 9. Line 9 contains only }. What is the most likely mistake, and on which line?
  8. Can a program that compiles without any message still be wrong? Give an example from this course.

Lab

Goal

Break a working program in planned ways, predict the compiler's message each time, and compare with the real one.

Hardware and software needed

The toolchain from F0-29; this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 on Linux x86_64. R1

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Build Listing 1 and run it. It must work before you break it.
  2. Make a "prediction card" with three columns: what I changed, the message I expect (line and kind), the real message.
  3. Remove the semicolon on line 6. Predict, build, compare with Listing 2's real messages.
  4. Misspell apples on line 8. Predict, build, compare with Listing 3.
  5. Remove the closing } on line 10. Predict which line the message will name.
  6. Remove #include <string>. Predict. (Careful: in F0-31, one program still built without it.)
  7. For every message, write one calm sentence in your own words: "The compiler is telling me that …".

Expected observations

Steps 3 and 4: the same messages as Listings 2 and 3 (shown above). R2, R3

Step 5 in this build (file missing_brace.cpp): the message names line 9, the last line of the file, and a note points back to the { on line 5 that was never closed. R8

missing_brace.cpp: In function 'int main()':
missing_brace.cpp:9:14: error: expected '}' at end of input
    9 |     return 0;
      |              ^
missing_brace.cpp:5:1: note: to match this '{'
    5 | {
      | ^

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-36/missing_brace.out; run record missing_brace.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:47:06Z; result: compile failed as expected (messages saved in missing_brace.out).

Step 6 in this build (file no_string_include.cpp): no message at all; the program built and printed "We have 3 apples.", as in F0-31, because another header brought std::string in. Keep the include anyway. The point of the lab is the comparison, so record honestly where your prediction was wrong. R8

Verification

Your prediction card has a filled row for every step, and Listing 1 builds and runs again at the end. university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F0-36 must report every broken listing as "compile failed as expected" and fixed.cpp with exit code 0.

Troubleshooting

  • No message appears, although you broke something → you did not save the file, or you built a different file → check the file name in the build command.
  • The message names a header file you did not write (inside the library) → read the first message that names your own file → the mistake is almost always in your file.
  • A message is too long to read → copy only the first line into your notebook, then the line with your file and line number.

Extension

Write a tiny program with exactly one mistake that produces at least three messages. Swap programs with a friend and find each other's single mistake, using only the messages.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Dev changed one line of a working program. Now the compiler prints three errors, one of them very long and full of strange words. Dev thinks he broke three things at once and wants to start the whole program again from scratch.

Evidence pack

Evidence 1 — the source, cascade.cpp:

#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main()
{
    int apples = 3;
    std::string fruit = "apples;
    std::cout << "We have " << apples << ' ' << fruit << ".\n";
    return 0;
}

Evidence 2 — the compiler's real messages from this build:

cascade.cpp:7:25: error: missing terminating " character [-Werror]
    7 |     std::string fruit = "apples;
      |                         ^
cascade.cpp:7:25: error: missing terminating " character
    7 |     std::string fruit = "apples;
      |                         ^~~~~~~~
cascade.cpp: In function 'int main()':
cascade.cpp:8:55: error: conversion from 'std::basic_ostream<char>' to non-scalar type 'std::string' {aka 'std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>'} requested
    8 |     std::cout << "We have " << apples << ' ' << fruit << ".\n";
      |     ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^~~~~~~~
cc1plus: all warnings being treated as errors

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-36/cascade.out; run record cascade.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:47:05Z; result: compile failed as expected (messages saved in cascade.out).

Questions

  1. How many separate messages that say "error" do you count? Which lines do they name?
  2. Which message is the first, and what does it say in plain words?
  3. Why does line 8, which was not changed, get an error?
  4. What is the single fix? Predict what happens after it.
  5. What would you tell Dev about starting again from scratch?

Method hints

Ignore everything after the first error for now. Go to the line and column it names, and look at each character. Then ask: if the compiler believes that line 7 never ended, how would it read line 8? Write two hypotheses ("three mistakes", "one mistake with follow-on errors") and test them against the evidence.

Mini-project

Make an "error dictionary" for yourself: for at least six different messages you met in KID102 (in this chapter and in F0-30 to F0-35), write the message's first line, the mistake that caused it, and the fix, in your own words. Include at least one follow-on error and one warning turned into an error.

Rubric: six correct entries (3 points); each entry has a real message copied exactly (1 point); explanations in your own words that a classmate understands (1 point).

Summary

  • A g++ message has a file, a line, a column, a kind (error, warning, note) and a description.
  • Read the first error first; fix it; build again.
  • The reported place is where the compiler got stuck; the mistake may be earlier.
  • One mistake can cause several follow-on errors.
  • "Did you mean …?" is a spelling guess, sometimes wrong.
  • -Wall and -Wextra turn on warnings; -Werror treats them as errors.
  • A clean build does not prove the program is right; tests and the debugger do the rest.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. File missing_semicolon.cpp; line 7; column 5; kind error; description "expected ',' or ';' before 'std'".
  2. Line 11, then line 10: the compiler reports where it got stuck, and the unfinished statement is often right before it. (Look for a missing ;, " or }.)
  3. A message caused by an earlier mistake. In Listing 3, "unused variable 'apples'" appears only because apples was misspelled on line 8. R3
  4. (b), as g++'s help says: "Treat all warnings as errors". (a) is the opposite. (c) describes -Wextra. R7
  5. The compiler matched the unknown name double_it against a similar word it knows; the real problem was that the function was defined after its call.
  6. Warnings often point at real bugs (an unused variable, = instead of ==, a variable read before it has a value); making them errors means you cannot ignore them.
  7. A missing ; at the end of the last statement before the }, most likely on line 8.
  8. Yes. The loop that never ends in F0-33 and the missing name card in F0-35 compiled without any message.

Forensic lab answer key

  • Observation: three messages say "error": two at line 7, column 25 (both "missing terminating " character"; the first carries [-Werror], so it began as a warning), and one at line 8, column 55, a long "conversion from 'std::basic_ostream<char>' to non-scalar type 'std::string'". R6
  • First message in plain words: "The text that starts at line 7, column 25 never ends: its closing quote is missing."
  • Why line 8: without the closing quote and semicolon, the compiler reads line 7 as unfinished and joins it with line 8, so it tries to put the whole printing expression into fruit. That is the long, strange message: a follow-on error.
  • Single fix: write "apples"; on line 7. Prediction: all three messages disappear and the program prints "We have 3 apples.", exactly like fixed.cpp, whose real run shows that output. R1
  • Advice for Dev: never restart because of many messages; fix the first one and build again. One character caused all three here.
  • How the evidence was made: the closing quote was deleted from line 7 of fixed.cpp; the messages are the real run R6.

Story hook

Analogy

Malik is following a rice recipe with three steps. Something goes wrong: the kitchen fills with smoke, and he has no idea which step did it. Everything happened too fast.

Now imagine Malik had a pause button for the whole kitchen. Before each step, the whole kitchen freezes. The water stops in mid-air. Malik walks around, opens every jar, reads the timer, counts the cups. Then he presses "one more step" and watches exactly what that step does. Freeze again. Look again.

With that button, finding the smoky step would be easy. He would see the moment a jar holds something it should not, or the moment the recipe tries a fourth step that does not exist.

Real kitchens have no such button. But programs do. It is called a debugger, and in this chapter you will use a real one.

What you will be able to do

  • Build a program with debugging information and start it in the debugger gdb.
  • Set a breakpoint, run to it, print variables, and continue to the next stop.
  • Step through a program line by line with next, and into a function with step.
  • Find where a loop goes one step too far, both with the debugger and with printed trace lines.
  • Read a recorded debugger session as evidence and find a bug from it.
Jargon box
Debugger
Simple words: A program that runs your program one step at a time, so you can look inside. Analogy: A pause button for the kitchen: everything freezes and you can look into every jar. Precise: A tool (here GNU gdb 15.1) that starts or attaches to a program, stops it at chosen places and shows the values of its variables (R3, R5). R3, R5, D2
Breakpoint
Simple words: A place in your program where the debugger will pause. Analogy: A sticky note on step 9: "stop here and check". Precise: A location set with the gdb command break (help text: "Set breakpoint at specified location.", R5); the program stops each time it reaches that line (R4). R4, R5, D2
Step
Simple words: Running exactly one more line of the program, then pausing again. Analogy: Doing one recipe step and freezing again. Precise: gdb's next runs one line and treats a function call as one line ("proceeding through subroutine calls"); step goes into the called function (R3, R5). R3, R5, D2
Off-by-one error
Simple words: A loop that runs one time too many or one time too few. Analogy: Stirring 21 times when the recipe said 20. Precise: A bug where a boundary is wrong by one, for example i <= size() instead of i < size(); in R1 the loop reached i = 3 for a vector of size 3. R1, R4
Trace
Simple words: Extra printed lines that show what the program is doing, step by step. Analogy: The cook saying each step out loud while cooking. Precise: Output added only for debugging, such as [trace] i = 3, which shows the order of events and the values of variables (R2). R2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows Listing 1 running under the debugger, from left to right in time. The program runs until it reaches the breakpoint, freezes, and waits while you look inside. "continue" lets it run to the next stop.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Some bugs are easy to see: the compiler points at them (F0-36). Others hide. The program builds, starts, and then does something wrong, too fast to watch. For those bugs you need to slow time down.

A debugger runs your program for you, but with a pause button. You tell it where to pause by setting a breakpoint, like a sticky note on one line: "stop here". When the program reaches that line, everything freezes. Then you can ask: what is in this jar? And that one?

From a pause you can go on in small or big steps. "Next" runs exactly one more line and freezes again. "Step" does the same, but if the line calls a function, it walks into the function with you. "Continue" runs on until the next sticky note.

The debugger does not fix anything by itself. It shows you the truth: the real values at the real moment. Your job is to compare them with what you expected. The first place where they differ is where the bug lives.

There is also a simple way without a debugger: add extra print lines that say what is happening. That is called a trace. It works everywhere, and you will try both.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

The debugger in this build is GNU gdb, version line "GNU gdb (Ubuntu 15.1-1ubuntu1~24.04.1) 15.1". It needs the program to be built with -g, which keeps the line numbers and variable names in the executable; the course flags already include -g (F0-29). R3, R5, D2

You start gdb with the program: gdb ./steps_dbg. Then you type commands. gdb's own help describes the ones we use: break "Set breakpoint at specified location."; run "Start debugged program."; print "Print value of expression EXP."; next "Step program, proceeding through subroutine calls."; step "Step program until it reaches a different source line."; continue "Continue program being debugged, after signal or breakpoint." Most have one-letter short forms, such as b, r, p, n, s and c. R5

A breakpoint such as break steps.cpp:9 stops the program each time line 9 is about to run. At each stop, print i showed the counter: 0, 1, 2, and then 3. print steps.size() showed 3, and even the condition itself could be printed: print i <= steps.size() gave true when i was 3. That is the bug: the loop condition lets i reach 3. R4

To step through code, stop at the start of main (break main) and use next. In the session for Listing 3, next moved from line 11 to line 12; step on line 12 entered double_it and showed its parameter, number=3; next twice and the program was back in main at line 13 with plates equal to 6. R3

In our sessions, gdb did not wait for a person to type. The commands were stored in a small file and gdb ran them one by one (non-interactive mode, gdb -q -batch -x steps.gdb ./steps_dbg). With set trace-commands on, gdb printed every command with a + in front, so the transcript shows what was typed and what gdb answered. At your own keyboard you type the same commands after the (gdb) prompt. R3, R4

A trace is the no-debugger method: extra output lines such as [trace] i = 3. Listing 2 printed one before each step and showed the same story as gdb: i reached 3. R2

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Debuggers and sanitizers can get in each other's way. Our first attempt at the forensic session ended with "LeakSanitizer has encountered a fatal error" and the hint "LeakSanitizer does not work under ptrace (strace, gdb, etc)". The program's own output was lost. We switched leak checking off inside gdb only, with set environment ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0, and the session worked. The runs without gdb keep every check. When a tool tells you how it fails, believe it and write it down. R9

A debugger shows you a frozen moment, but it can also change it: gdb can assign a new value to a variable while the program is paused, or stop only when a condition is true (break 9 if i == 3, a form described in gdb's help for break: "[if CONDITION]"). You will use these in later courses. R5, D2

When the program was stopped by the exception, gdb reported "Program received signal SIGABRT, Aborted." and showed a library file that is not installed on the build machine ("No such file or directory"). That is normal: the stop happened inside library code, not yours. The command backtrace lists the chain of calls that led there, so you can walk back to your own line; its help text was not saved in this build, so this last point rests on the manual. R4, D2

How the hardware actually does it

A debugger is a program that controls another program, with help from the operating system. To make a breakpoint, the debugger places a special instruction at the start of the machine code for that line. When the processor reaches it, it stops your program and hands control to the debugger, which can then read your program's memory: that is how it finds the value of i. The -g information is the map from machine code back to your line numbers and variable names. The word "ptrace" in the LeakSanitizer hint above is the name of the Linux facility that gdb uses for this control. R9, D2, D3

Not verified — check before relying on this

The exact mechanism gdb uses for breakpoints on this machine (a replaced instruction versus special processor support) was not checked in this build. Check the GDB manual (sections on breakpoints and on how gdb controls a program on Linux) and record the answer in the dossier.

Worked example

The debugger lab of this course: "find where a loop goes one step too far". We use the four questions of a detective.

  1. What did I expect? Three steps printed, then "The rice is ready.".
  2. What happened? Listing 1 printed the three steps, then stopped with std::out_of_range: "__n (which is 3) >= this->size() (which is 3)". "The rice is ready." never appeared. R1
  3. Where should I look? The message says index 3 was used on a vector of size 3. The only place that uses an index is line 9, inside the loop. So: break on line 9, and print i each time.
  4. What does the frozen program show? Stops 1 to 3: i = 0, 1, 2, and each "continue" printed one step. Stop 4: i = 3, and i <= steps.size() is true. Line 9 is about to call steps.at(3). R4

Conclusion: the condition i <= steps.size() allows one iteration too many. The valid indexes are 0 to 2, so the loop must stop when i reaches 3: i < steps.size(). Prediction for the fix: three steps, then "The rice is ready.", exit code 0. The real run of steps_fixed.cpp agreed. R6

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — steps.cpp, the loop that goes one step too far

#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    std::vector<std::string> steps = {"wash the rice", "add water", "cook until soft"};
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i <= steps.size(); ++i) {
        std::cout << "Step " << i + 1 << ": " << steps.at(i) << std::endl;
    }
    std::cout << "The rice is ready." << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • A frozen kitchen stays frozen for ever. A paused program is waiting for the debugger; if you end the debugger, the program ends too (the sessions end with kill or by letting the program finish). R4
  • In the frozen kitchen you can see everything at once. In gdb you see only what you ask for: one print per variable. You must know what to look at, which is why you form a hypothesis first. R4
  • Freezing a kitchen would not change the soup. Running under a debugger can change how a program behaves: here the leak checker refused to work under gdb until we switched it off. R9

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
gdb says it cannot find line numbers or variables.The program was built without -g.Look at the build command.Build again with -g (the course flags include it).
The program runs to the end and never stops.No breakpoint was set, or it is on a line that never runs.Set the breakpoint before run; check the line number in the source.break main is always reached.
"LeakSanitizer does not work under ptrace" and missing output.The leak checker cannot work while gdb controls the program.Read the hint lines that start with ==.set environment ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 inside gdb (R9).
next jumps over a function you wanted to see.next treats a call as one line.gdb's help: "proceeding through subroutine calls".Use step on the line with the call.
You print a variable and get a strange value.The line that sets it has not run yet: the debugger stops before the line it shows.Compare the shown line with the variable's declaration.Use next once, then print again.

Transition box

Where you came from: F0-36: bugs the compiler can see. Before that, trace tables on paper in every chapter, and the code detective of F0-08. What carries over: The method: expect, observe, compare, form hypotheses; a trace table is what a debugger shows you, filled in by the machine. What changes: You now inspect a real running program: it must be built with -g, it stops before the line shown, you see only what you ask for, and tools can interfere with each other (the sanitizer under gdb). R4, R9 What comes next: F0-38 puts everything together in a project: a guessing game with functions, a loop, decisions and a test function.

Check yourself

  1. What is a breakpoint? How do you set one on line 9 of steps.cpp?
  2. What is the difference between next and step? Use the session of Listing 3.
  3. Multiple choice. gdb stops at a breakpoint on line 10 and shows that line. Has line 10 run yet? (a) Yes (b) No (c) Only half of it
  4. Which flag must the program be built with so that gdb knows line numbers and variable names?
  5. In the session for Listing 1, what did print i <= steps.size() show at the fourth stop, and why does that prove the bug?
  6. Explain in your own words when a printed trace is enough and when a debugger is better.
  7. Apply to a new case: a loop that should add up the numbers 1 to 10 gives 45. Which breakpoint would you set, which variables would you print, and what would you look for?
  8. Why did the first forensic session lose the program's output?

Lab

Goal

The debugger lab of KID102: find where a loop goes one step too far, with gdb and with a trace, then fix it and prove the fix.

Hardware and software needed

The toolchain from F0-29 and the debugger gdb. This build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 and GNU gdb (Ubuntu 15.1-1ubuntu1~24.04.1) 15.1 on Linux x86_64, as printed by the tools (first lines of the transcripts). If your computer has a different debugger, the ideas are the same but the commands may differ; record its name and version in the dossier. R3

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Build Listing 1 with the course flags: g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined steps.cpp -o steps_dbg.
  2. Start gdb: gdb ./steps_dbg. At the (gdb) prompt, type set environment ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0, then break steps.cpp:9, then run.
  3. At each stop, type print i, write the value in a table, then type continue. Before each continue, predict what will be printed.
  4. At the stop where i is 3, type print steps.size() and print i <= steps.size(). Explain the result.
  5. Type kill and then quit. Fix line 8, rebuild, and run without gdb. Compare with your prediction.
  6. Run Listing 2 (the trace version). Which method told you more, and which was faster?
  7. Build Listing 3 and practise: break main, run, next, print cups, step, print number. Compare your screen with the recorded session.

Expected observations

Steps 2–4 match the recorded session of Listing 1 above (stops with i = 0, 1, 2, 3, and true for the last condition). Step 5: the fixed program printed this in the recorded run (file steps_fixed.cpp): R4, R6

Troubleshooting

  • "No symbol "i" in current context." → you are paused outside the loop, or not paused at all → check where gdb stopped (it shows the line).
  • The program finishes without stopping → the breakpoint was set after run, or on a different file → set it first, with the file name: break steps.cpp:9.
  • LeakSanitizer messages at the end and missing output → see the Common mistakes table.

Extension

Use a conditional breakpoint so gdb stops only at the interesting moment: break steps.cpp:9 if i == 3. Predict how many times it stops. Then use backtrace after the crash and find your own line in the list.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Chen's family timed their cooking for three days: 20, 35 and 26 minutes. Chen's program says the total was 26 minutes and the average 8 minutes a day. "We definitely cooked longer than 8 minutes!" says his mother. Chen recorded a debugger session as evidence.

Evidence pack

Evidence 1 — the source, cooking_time.cpp:

#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    std::vector<int> minutes = {20, 35, 26};
    int total = 0;
    int days = 0;
    for (int m : minutes) {
        total = m;
        days = days + 1;
    }
    std::cout << "Days: " << days << '\n';
    std::cout << "Total minutes: " << total << '\n';
    std::cout << "Average minutes per day: " << total / days << '\n';
    return 0;
}

Questions

  1. What total and average would you expect? Work them out by hand.
  2. From the session, write a table of m and total at each of the three stops. What should total have been at each stop?
  3. Which line is wrong? Write the fix.
  4. Why did the breakpoint go on line 11 and not on line 10?
  5. Write a test that would have caught this bug without a debugger.

Method hints

Compare "expected" and "observed" at every stop, not only at the end. The first stop where they differ points to the bug. Remember that gdb stops before the line it shows. State two hypotheses (for example "the input numbers are wrong" and "the total is not added up") and use the session to decide.

Mini-project

Take any program you wrote in F0-33 to F0-35 and plant one bug in it (an off-by-one condition, a reset total, or a wrong comparison). Give the program to a friend together with a one-paragraph description of the symptom. Your friend must find the bug with gdb and show you the stop where the values first went wrong.

Rubric: the bug is real and reproducible (1 point); the symptom description is accurate (1 point); the finder's table of stops shows the first wrong value (2 points); the fix is verified by a run (1 point).

Summary

  • A debugger runs your program with a pause button: breakpoints freeze it so you can look inside.
  • Build with -g; start with gdb ./program; break, run, print, next, step, continue.
  • gdb stops before the line it shows.
  • next runs a call as one line; step walks into it.
  • Find the first stop where the real values differ from what you expected.
  • A printed trace is the no-debugger method and works everywhere.
  • Tools can interfere: here LeakSanitizer had to be switched off inside gdb.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. A place where the debugger pauses the program before that line runs. break steps.cpp:9 (or b steps.cpp:9). R4, R5
  2. next runs the current line, treating a function call as one line; step walks into the called function. In the Listing 3 session, step on line 12 entered double_it with number=3. R3
  3. (b) No. gdb shows the line that will run next. (a) is the common misunderstanding behind "strange values" (Common mistakes). (c) is wrong: a line is either about to run or not.
  4. -g.
  5. $6 = true: the condition still allows the loop to run with i = 3, although valid indexes stop at 2. So the loop will try a fourth step that does not exist. R4
  6. A trace is enough when you know which values to watch and can rebuild easily; a debugger is better when you do not yet know where to look, want to look at many variables, or want to step into functions without changing the code.
  7. A breakpoint on the line that adds to the total; print the counter and the total at each stop; look for the stop where the total differs from your hand-made table (45 is 55 − 10, so suspect the last iteration is missing: an off-by-one in the condition).
  8. LeakSanitizer could not work under gdb's control ("does not work under ptrace") and stopped the program at the end with a fatal error, before its output was written. R9

Forensic lab answer key

  • Expected: total 20 + 35 + 26 = 81 minutes; average 81 / 3 = 27 minutes. Observed: total 26, average 8 (26 / 3 in whole numbers). R7
  • Table from the session: stop 1: m = 20, total = 20 (expected 20); stop 2: m = 35, total = 35 (expected 55); stop 3: m = 26, total = 26 (expected 81). The first difference is at stop 2: total always equals m. R8
  • Hypotheses: "the input numbers are wrong" is ruled out: m shows 20, 35, 26 as expected. Remaining: the total is replaced instead of added to.
  • Root cause: line 10, total = m;. Fix: total = total + m;.
  • Why line 11: gdb stops before the line it shows, so stopping at line 11 means line 10 has already run, and total shows its new value.
  • Test that would catch it: move the sum into a function int total_minutes(std::vector<int> minutes) and check it with {20, 35, 26} → 81 and {5, 5} → 10 (F0-34 style).
  • How the evidence was made: total = total + m; was changed to total = m; on purpose; the output and the session are real runs R7 and R8.

Story hook

Analogy

It is game night. Grandma says: "I am thinking of a number from 1 to 100. Guess it! I will tell you if you are too low or too high."

Leila guesses 50. "Too high." She guesses 25. "Too high." Then 12. "Too low." Seven guesses later she has it, and she says: "I can always do it in seven!"

Her brother wants to play too, but Grandma has gone to bed. "Let's teach the computer to be Grandma," says Leila. "It picks a number, it gives hints, and it counts our guesses."

That is this chapter's project. It uses everything from this course: variables, decisions, a loop, functions, a test function and the debugger mindset. And it raises a new question: how does a computer, which always follows exact steps, "think of" a number?

What you will be able to do

  • Build a complete guessing game from small functions, each with one job.
  • Write a test function for the part that gives hints, and make main refuse to start the game if a test fails.
  • Explain what a pseudo-random number generator and a seed are, and why we fix the seed for a recorded run.
  • Explain why halving the possible numbers finds any secret from 1 to 100 in at most seven guesses, using a program as proof.
  • Plan your own course project and prepare for the practical exam.
Jargon box
Pseudo-random number generator
Simple words: A recipe that produces numbers that look random. Analogy: A very long, fixed shuffled list of numbers that you start reading at some place. Precise: An algorithm that produces a sequence of numbers from a starting value (the seed); the same seed gives the same sequence, as R3 shows with seed 2026. This course uses std::mt19937 with std::uniform_int_distribution. R3, D2
Seed
Simple words: The starting number for a pseudo-random number generator. Analogy: The page where you start reading the shuffled list. Precise: The value given to a generator when it is created; with seed 2026 the game's secret was 22 in every recorded run of this build (R1, R3). R1, R3

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the recorded game. Each bar is the set of numbers that are still possible before a guess; the dot is the guess. Every hint cuts the bar about in half.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

To teach the computer to be Grandma, split her job into small jobs. One job: pick a secret number. One job: compare a guess with the secret and say "Too low.", "Too high." or "Correct!". One job: keep asking for guesses and count them. Each small job becomes a function (F0-34).

Before you trust the hint job, test it. You know the right answers: 10 against a secret of 50 must be "Too low.". A test function checks these answers by itself, every time the program starts.

Now the tricky part: picking a number. A computer follows exact steps, so it cannot really "think of" a number. Instead, it uses a recipe that makes numbers that look random. The recipe needs a starting number, called the seed. Same seed, same numbers. Different seed, different numbers.

That sounds like a weakness, but it is useful. When we record a game for this book, we choose the seed ourselves. Then everyone who runs the program gets the same secret, and our recorded guesses still work. For real play, you would let the computer choose a seed that changes every time.

And Leila's claim, "always in seven"? If you always guess the middle, each hint throws away about half of the numbers. A program can try all 100 secrets and check her claim.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

The game (Listing 1) has five functions besides main: pick_secret, hint_for, play, check_hint and test_hint_for. main runs the tests first and ends with exit code 1 if any fail, so a broken hint function can never reach the player. In the recorded run the tests reported "test_hint_for: 0 failures". R1

To pick a secret, the program creates a pseudo-random number generator, std::mt19937, from the header <random>, and gives it a seed. A second object, std::uniform_int_distribution<int> with the limits 1 and 100, turns the generator's large numbers into a number from 1 to 100. R1, D1, D2

Listing 3 proves the "same seed, same number" rule on this machine: pick_secret(2026) called twice printed "22 22". It also used std::random_device to make five different seeds; those secrets are different in every run, so the output on this page shows one example and yours will differ. R3

Why fix the seed in the game? The game reads the guesses from the keyboard, and in the recorded run they came from a file: 50, 25, 12, 18, 21, 23, 22. Those guesses only make sense for one secret. With seed 2026 the secret was 22, the game said "Correct!" on guess 7, and anyone can repeat the run and get the same lines. A run that cannot be repeated cannot be checked. R1

The play function loops while (std::cin >> guess). The loop ends when the guess is correct (return tries;) or when the input runs out, for example at the end of the file; then it prints the secret and returns 0. That second exit matters: without it, a game with no correct guess could never end. R1, R4

Listing 2 checks Leila's claim. It plays against every secret from 1 to 100, always guessing the middle, (low + high) / 2, and moving low or high after each hint. It printed "Secret 22 needs 7 guesses." and "Most guesses ever needed: 7 (first for secret 2)". So seven guesses are always enough with this method, and sometimes seven are needed. R2

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Why seven? Each guess leaves at most about half: 100, then 50, 25, 13, 7, 4, 2, 1. Seven halvings get from 100 down to one number, because 2 multiplied by itself 7 times is 128, which is more than 100, while 6 times gives 64, which is less. For 1,000 numbers it would be 10 guesses, because 2 multiplied by itself 10 times is 1,024. Listing 2 confirms the 7 for this game; changing 100 to 1000 gave "Most guesses ever needed: 10". R2, R6

The name mt19937 names a well-known generator algorithm, the "Mersenne Twister". It is fully deterministic: it keeps a block of numbers in memory and mixes them with arithmetic each time you ask for a number. It is good for games and simulations, not for secrets such as passwords; that needs a generator designed for security. D1, D2

Not verified — check before relying on this

This build checked "seed 2026 gives 22" only with one toolchain (g++ 13.3.0 and its standard library). Whether another compiler's standard library gives the same secret for the same seed was not tested: the generator and the step that maps its output to 1–100 may be specified differently. Check the random number generation clause of ISO/IEC 14882 (the C++ standard) and record in the dossier which parts are fixed by the standard. Until then, the chapter only promises "same seed, same secret, same toolchain", which is what the comment on line 6 of Listing 1 says. R1, R3, D2

How the hardware actually does it

The processor has no dice. Every instruction it runs gives the same result for the same inputs (F0-29). The generator is ordinary arithmetic on numbers stored in memory, so a fixed seed leads to a fixed series of numbers, exactly as R3 showed. R3, D3

For a seed that changes, the program asks the outside world. std::random_device asks the system for a value that is hard to predict; in R3 it gave five different seeds and so five different secrets. R3, D2

Not verified — check before relying on this

Where the operating system on the build machine gets the values for std::random_device (for example timing of hardware events, or a special processor instruction) was not checked in this build. Check the documentation of the standard library and of Linux, and record the answer in the dossier.

Worked example

Plan the game before writing it, as an engineer would. Write each job as a function with a name, inputs and an output:

  1. pick_secret(seed) → a number from 1 to 100.
  2. hint_for(guess, secret) → "Too low.", "Too high." or "Correct!". Pure: no input, no output, so it is easy to test.
  3. play(secret) → the number of guesses, or 0 if the input ran out.
  4. test_hint_for() → the number of failures, using check_hint for each case.

Then work out the test answers by hand, before running anything: 10 against 50 is too low; 90 against 50 too high; 50 against 50 correct; and an edge case, 1 against 1 correct. Then predict the recorded game with secret 22 and the guesses 50, 25, 12, 18, 21, 23, 22: too high, too high, too low, too low, too low, too high, correct, so "You found it in 7 guesses.". The real run printed exactly that. R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — game.cpp, the guessing game

#include <iostream>
#include <random>
#include <string>

// Picks the secret number between 1 and 100.
// The same seed always gives the same secret with the same toolchain.
int pick_secret(unsigned int seed)
{
    std::mt19937 generator(seed);
    std::uniform_int_distribution<int> one_to_hundred(1, 100);
    return one_to_hundred(generator);
}

// Compares a guess with the secret and returns the hint to show.
std::string hint_for(int guess, int secret)
{
    if (guess < secret) {
        return "Too low.";
    } else if (guess > secret) {
        return "Too high.";
    }
    return "Correct!";
}

// Asks for guesses until the player is right or the input runs out.
// Returns the number of guesses used, or 0 if the player never got it.
int play(int secret)
{
    int tries = 0;
    int guess = 0;
    std::cout << "I am thinking of a number from 1 to 100.\n";
    while (std::cin >> guess) {
        tries = tries + 1;
        std::string hint = hint_for(guess, secret);
        std::cout << "Guess " << tries << ": " << guess << " -> " << hint << '\n';
        if (hint == "Correct!") {
            return tries;
        }
    }
    std::cout << "No more guesses. The number was " << secret << ".\n";
    return 0;
}

// Checks one answer of hint_for. Returns 0 if it is right and 1 if it is wrong.
int check_hint(int guess, int secret, std::string expected)
{
    std::string got = hint_for(guess, secret);
    if (got == expected) {
        return 0;
    }
    std::cout << "FAIL: hint_for(" << guess << ", " << secret << ") gave \"" << got
              << "\", expected \"" << expected << "\"\n";
    return 1;
}

// The test function: answers worked out by hand. Returns the number of failures.
int test_hint_for()
{
    int failures = 0;
    failures = failures + check_hint(10, 50, "Too low.");
    failures = failures + check_hint(90, 50, "Too high.");
    failures = failures + check_hint(50, 50, "Correct!");
    failures = failures + check_hint(1, 1, "Correct!");
    std::cout << "test_hint_for: " << failures << " failures\n";
    return failures;
}

int main()
{
    if (test_hint_for() != 0) {
        return 1;
    }
    const unsigned int seed = 2026;  // fixed so that the recorded run can be repeated
    int secret = pick_secret(seed);
    int tries = play(secret);
    if (tries > 0) {
        std::cout << "You found it in " << tries << " guesses.\n";
    }
    return 0;
}

Listing 2 — halving.cpp, checking "always in seven"

#include <iostream>

// Plays the guessing game against every possible secret from 1 to 100,
// always guessing the middle of the numbers that are still possible.
int guesses_needed(int secret)
{
    int low = 1;
    int high = 100;
    int tries = 0;
    while (low <= high) {
        int guess = (low + high) / 2;
        tries = tries + 1;
        if (guess == secret) {
            return tries;
        }
        if (guess < secret) {
            low = guess + 1;
        } else {
            high = guess - 1;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main()
{
    int most = 0;
    int hardest = 0;
    for (int secret = 1; secret <= 100; ++secret) {
        int tries = guesses_needed(secret);
        if (tries > most) {
            most = tries;
            hardest = secret;
        }
    }
    std::cout << "Secret 22 needs " << guesses_needed(22) << " guesses.\n";
    std::cout << "Most guesses ever needed: " << most << " (first for secret " << hardest << ")\n";
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Grandma really thinks of a number. The program computes one from the seed; with the same seed, it always "thinks of" 22. R3
  • Grandma notices if Leila stops playing. The program only notices when the input ends; that is why play has a second way out. R1
  • Grandma might cheat or make a mistake on a bad day. A tested function gives the same hint for the same inputs every time, and if it is wrong, it is wrong every time, which is what makes tests useful. R1, R4

Lab

Goal

Build, test and play the guessing game, then prove the "seven guesses" claim and see the effect of the seed.

Hardware and software needed

The toolchain from F0-29. This build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 on Linux x86_64. R1

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Type Listing 1. Build it with the course flags and play by typing guesses; press Ctrl+D (Linux or macOS) to end the input early.
  2. Before you play, predict: what will test_hint_for print? Check.
  3. Make a file with the recorded guesses and run ./game < game.in. Compare with the recorded output.
  4. Break the test on purpose: change "Too low." to "Too small." on line 60. Predict what happens, then run.
  5. Run Listing 2. Then change 100 to 1000 in both places where the range appears and run again. Compare with your prediction from Check yourself question 8.
  6. Run Listing 3 three times. Which line changes and which does not?

Expected observations

Step 3 matches the output of Listing 1 above (secret 22, found in 7). Step 6: "Seed 2026 twice: 22 22" every time; the five other numbers change. R1, R3

Troubleshooting

  • Secret is not 22 with seed 2026 → different toolchain or standard library → record it; see the "Not verified" box in Layer 3.
  • The game waits and does nothing → it is waiting for your guess → type a number and press Enter.
  • Error about std::mt19937 → missing #include <random> (F0-36).

Extension

Add a function int count_hint(std::vector<int> guesses, int secret) that plays a whole list of guesses without the keyboard and returns the number of guesses used. Test it with the recorded guesses (expected 7).

Forensic lab

Scenario

Leila's brother Omar changed the game. He says: "The computer is cheating! I guessed 50, it said too low. 75, too low. 88, too low. All the way to 100, too low, and then it said the number was 22!" He also says: "The tests printed something, but I'll look at them later."

Evidence pack

Evidence 1 — Omar's main and hint_for (the rest is the same as Listing 1), file game_bug.cpp:

#include <iostream>
#include <random>
#include <string>

// Picks the secret number between 1 and 100.
// The same seed always gives the same secret with the same toolchain.
int pick_secret(unsigned int seed)
{
    std::mt19937 generator(seed);
    std::uniform_int_distribution<int> one_to_hundred(1, 100);
    return one_to_hundred(generator);
}

// Compares a guess with the secret and returns the hint to show.
std::string hint_for(int guess, int secret)
{
    if (guess > secret) {
        return "Too low.";
    } else if (guess < secret) {
        return "Too high.";
    }
    return "Correct!";
}

// Asks for guesses until the player is right or the input runs out.
// Returns the number of guesses used, or 0 if the player never got it.
int play(int secret)
{
    int tries = 0;
    int guess = 0;
    std::cout << "I am thinking of a number from 1 to 100.\n";
    while (std::cin >> guess) {
        tries = tries + 1;
        std::string hint = hint_for(guess, secret);
        std::cout << "Guess " << tries << ": " << guess << " -> " << hint << '\n';
        if (hint == "Correct!") {
            return tries;
        }
    }
    std::cout << "No more guesses. The number was " << secret << ".\n";
    return 0;
}

// Checks one answer of hint_for. Returns 0 if it is right and 1 if it is wrong.
int check_hint(int guess, int secret, std::string expected)
{
    std::string got = hint_for(guess, secret);
    if (got == expected) {
        return 0;
    }
    std::cout << "FAIL: hint_for(" << guess << ", " << secret << ") gave \"" << got
              << "\", expected \"" << expected << "\"\n";
    return 1;
}

// The test function: answers worked out by hand. Returns the number of failures.
int test_hint_for()
{
    int failures = 0;
    failures = failures + check_hint(10, 50, "Too low.");
    failures = failures + check_hint(90, 50, "Too high.");
    failures = failures + check_hint(50, 50, "Correct!");
    failures = failures + check_hint(1, 1, "Correct!");
    std::cout << "test_hint_for: " << failures << " failures\n";
    return failures;
}

int main()
{
    test_hint_for();  // "I will look at the test results later."
    const unsigned int seed = 2026;  // fixed so that the recorded run can be repeated
    int secret = pick_secret(seed);
    int tries = play(secret);
    if (tries > 0) {
        std::cout << "You found it in " << tries << " guesses.\n";
    }
    return 0;
}

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-38/game_bug.out; run record game_bug.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:47:12Z; exit code: 0.

Questions

  1. Is the computer cheating? What was the secret, and were the hints true?
  2. Which two lines of hint_for are wrong? Use the FAIL lines.
  3. Why did the game start although two tests failed?
  4. Why did the game end after seven guesses instead of waiting for more?
  5. Write the two fixes, and say how you would prove them.

Method hints

Read the evidence from the top: the first lines are the test results, printed before the game. Compare the expected and the observed hint for one guess by hand. State a hypothesis for each symptom and check it against the source.

Mini-project

Course project brief. Write your own small game or tool for your home, with at least three functions and one test function that runs at the start of main. Ideas: a times-table quiz, a pocket-money tracker that uses a list, or a recipe scaler. Hand in: the source code, a build log made with the course flags, one recorded run with its input file, and a half page explaining your functions and your test cases. If your program uses random numbers, fix the seed for the recorded run and say why.

Rubric: builds with no warnings under the course flags (2 points); at least three functions, each with one clear job (2 points); a test function with cases worked out by hand, including an edge case, and main stops if a test fails (2 points); a recorded run that can be repeated (2 points); a clear explanation (2 points).

Practical exam preparation. The practical exam asks you to write a short program under time limits, for example a times-table program for one number entered by the user, with a function and a test. Practise: write int times(int a, int b), a test function for it, and a loop that prints the table from 1 to 10. Time yourself, and build with the course flags so the warnings are part of the practice.

Summary

  • Build a program from small functions, each with one job; test the pure ones.
  • Run the test function first, and stop if it fails; never ignore its result.
  • A pseudo-random number generator makes numbers that look random from a seed.
  • Same seed, same numbers (checked here with one toolchain); fix the seed for recorded runs and tests.
  • Use a changing seed, such as one from std::random_device, for real play.
  • Guessing the middle halves the possibilities: at most 7 guesses for 1 to 100.
  • Every loop that reads input needs a way out when the input ends.

Forensic lab answer key

  • Not cheating: the secret was 22 (the last line), so every guess from 50 to 100 was too high; the program said "Too low." each time. The hints were false. R4

Electricity is like water in pipes (and where that breaks)
