Story hook

Analogy

Lina is watering the garden with her grandmother. The hose is connected to a tap. When Grandma opens the tap wide, water rushes out fast. When she opens it a little, the water only trickles.

Lina squeezes the end of the hose with her thumb. The opening gets narrow. Now less water gets through. Her thumb is in the way of the flow.

"What pushes the water?" Lina asks. "Pressure," says Grandma. "The water behind pushes the water in front."

Later that evening, Lina's torch will not switch on. She wonders: is there "pressure" inside a battery too? Is there a "thumb" inside the torch? This chapter says yes, a little. Then it shows where the water story stops being true.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain voltage, current and resistance with the water picture: pressure, flow and a narrow pipe.
  • Calculate a current from a voltage and a resistance with Ohm's law, using exercise numbers.
  • Explain why electricity needs a closed loop, and why an open loop has no current.
  • Name at least two places where the water picture is wrong.
  • Run a tiny C++ program that does the Ohm's-law arithmetic and predict its output.
Jargon box
Electricity
Simple words: tiny charged particles moving through a material, carrying energy to a lamp or a motor. Analogy: water moving through the pipes of a house. Precise: the flow of electric charge (here, through metal wires, where the charge carriers are electrons) driven by a voltage. D1 D2
Voltage
Simple words: how hard the battery pushes. Analogy: water pressure. Precise: the electrical potential difference between two points; it is measured in volts (V). D1
Current
Simple words: how much electricity flows past a point each second. Analogy: how much water flows through the pipe. Precise: the rate of flow of electric charge; it is measured in amperes (A, "amps"); one milliampere (mA) is one thousandth of an ampere. D1
Resistance
Simple words: how much something gets in the way of the flow. Analogy: a narrow part of the pipe (Lina's thumb on the hose). Precise: the ratio of voltage to current for a part; it is measured in ohms (Ω). D1
Circuit
Simple words: a complete loop that electricity can travel around. Analogy: a closed loop of pipe with a pump. Precise: a closed path of conductors and parts through which current can flow from one terminal of a source back to the other. D1
Battery
Simple words: a store of energy that pushes electricity around a loop. Analogy: a pump that makes pressure. Precise: one or more electrochemical cells that keep a voltage between two terminals, marked + and −. D1
Ohm's law
Simple words: a rule that links push, flow and narrowness. Analogy: more pressure gives more flow; a narrower pipe gives less flow. Precise: for a resistor, V = I × R, so I = V ÷ R. D1 D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 puts the two loops side by side. On the left is a loop of water pipe. On the right is a loop of wire. Every part on the left has a partner on the right.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Think about the water pipes in a home. Water moves when something pushes it. In a garden hose, the push comes from the pressure behind the tap. More push means more water flows.

Electricity also needs a push. A battery gives that push. We call the push voltage. A bigger voltage pushes harder.

The flow of water is how much water goes past each second. The flow of electricity is called current. When the battery pushes harder, more current flows. When something gets in the way, less current flows.

What gets in the way? In a hose, a narrow part. Lina's thumb made the hose narrow. In electricity, a part called a resistor gets in the way on purpose. How much it gets in the way is its resistance.

So we have three ideas and three partners:

  • water pressure is like voltage (the push);
  • water flow is like current (how much moves);
  • a narrow pipe is like resistance (what gets in the way).

There is one more big idea. Electricity only flows around a closed loop. The loop goes out of the battery, through the parts, and back into the battery. We call that loop a circuit. If the loop has a gap anywhere, the flow stops everywhere. A light switch makes a gap on purpose. That is how it turns a lamp off.D1

Here water and electricity are different. A broken water pipe spills water on the floor. A broken wire does not spill electricity. The flow stops. You will see this again in "Where the analogy breaks".

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Engineers measure the three ideas with units. Voltage is measured in volts, written V. Current is measured in amperes, written A. In this course, small currents are written in milliamperes, mA. One ampere is 1,000 milliamperes. Resistance is measured in ohms, written Ω.D1

The three are linked by Ohm's law. For a resistor, voltage equals current times resistance: V = I × R. We can turn it around to find the current: I = V ÷ R.D1 D2

Look at what the rule says. If you double the voltage, the current doubles. If you double the resistance, the current halves. That matches the water picture. More pressure, more flow. Narrower pipe, less flow.

You can use the law with any numbers. In this chapter we use exercise numbers. They are not taken from any real part. For example: a 6 V push across 300 Ω gives 6 ÷ 300 = 0.02 A. That is 20 mA. The worked example below does this slowly.

Note

Ohm's law is a rule for resistors. Some parts, such as the LED in the next chapter, do not follow it in a simple way. F0-40 shows how we still use it for the resistor next to the LED.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. In a metal wire, the moving charges are electrons. Electrons carry negative charge, so they drift from − towards +. Engineers still draw current flowing from + to −. That habit is called conventional current, and every diagram in this course uses it.D1 D2 Energy is delivered to a resistor as heat. The power is P = V × I, measured in watts. HW101 builds on these ideas with real measurements.D2

How the hardware actually does it

A metal wire is full of electrons that can move. Before the switch closes, they are already there, all along the wire. When the loop closes, the battery's push acts on the whole loop. Electrons all around the loop start to drift together. That is why a lamp lights straight away when you press the switch. Nothing has to travel all the way from the battery first.D1 D2

Worked example

These are exercise numbers only. They are not from any real battery or resistor.

Loop A: 6 V and 300 Ω

  1. Write the law: I = V ÷ R.
  2. Put in the numbers: I = 6 ÷ 300.
  3. Work it out: 6 ÷ 300 = 0.02. The unit is amperes, so I = 0.02 A.
  4. Change to milliamperes: multiply by 1,000. 0.02 × 1,000 = 20. So I = 20 mA.

Loop B: twice the resistance

Now use 600 Ω with the same 6 V. I = 6 ÷ 600 = 0.01 A = 10 mA. The resistance doubled, so the current halved.

Loop C: half the voltage

Now use 3 V with 300 Ω. I = 3 ÷ 300 = 0.01 A = 10 mA. The push halved, so the current halved.

Loop D: the loop is open

Same battery and resistor as Loop A, but a switch is open. There is a gap, so there is no closed loop. The current is 0 mA. Ohm's law for the resistor still holds: zero current means zero volts across the resistor.

Listing 1 below does these four sums. Its real output matches the hand results.

Code walk-through

You do not need to write C++ yet. KID102 teaches that. Here you run a given program, read it with the table, and change one number. If you have not used a compiler before, ask your teacher or parent to run the build command for you.

Listing 1 — ohms_law.cpp

// Ohm's law with made-up exercise numbers (not taken from any real part).
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Loop
{
    std::string name;
    double volts;
    double ohms;
    bool closed;
};

int main()
{
    const std::vector<Loop> loops = {
        {"A", 6.0, 300.0, true},
        {"B", 6.0, 600.0, true},
        {"C", 3.0, 300.0, true},
        {"D", 6.0, 300.0, false},
    };
    for (const Loop& loop : loops) {
        double milliamps = 0.0;
        if (loop.closed) {
            milliamps = loop.volts * 1000.0 / loop.ohms;
        }
        std::cout << "Loop " << loop.name << ": " << loop.volts << " V, "
                  << loop.ohms << " ohms, " << (loop.closed ? "closed" : "open")
                  << " -> current " << milliamps << " mA\n";
    }
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1// Ohm's law …A comment for humans. The computer skips it.It reminds us the numbers are made up.
2–4#include …Brings in tools for printing, text and lists.The program uses all three.
6–12struct Loop { … };Describes one loop: a name, volts, ohms, and whether it is closed.Like a form with four boxes to fill in.
14–15int main()The program starts here.Every C++ program has one main.
16–21const std::vector<Loop> loops = { … };A list of the four loops from the worked example.Change a number here to try your own loop.
22for (const Loop& loop : loops) {Repeats the next steps once for each loop.One rule, used four times.
23double milliamps = 0.0;Starts the current at zero.An open loop keeps this zero.
24–26if (loop.closed) { milliamps = loop.volts * 1000.0 / loop.ohms; }Only for a closed loop: current = volts × 1,000 ÷ ohms.This is Ohm's law, I = V ÷ R, already in mA.
27–29std::cout << …Prints one line about the loop.You can check the computer against your own sums.
31return 0;Tells the computer "all went well".A zero exit code means success.

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined ohms_law.cpp -o ohms_law, then run ./ohms_law.

Loop A: 6 V, 300 ohms, closed -> current 20 mA
Loop B: 6 V, 600 ohms, closed -> current 10 mA
Loop C: 3 V, 300 ohms, closed -> current 10 mA
Loop D: 6 V, 300 ohms, open -> current 0 mA

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-39/ohms_law.out; run record ohms_law.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:27:29Z; exit code: 0.

Check: Loop A says 20 mA, Loops B and C say 10 mA, and the open Loop D says 0 mA. That is the same as the worked example.R1

Where the analogy breaks

The water picture is useful. It is also wrong in some places. Here are three.

  1. Electricity needs a closed loop. Water from an open tap pours out and falls on the ground. It does not need to come back. Electricity only flows if the path goes all the way back to the battery.D1
  2. An open wire does not leak. Cut a water pipe and water sprays out. Cut a wire and nothing comes out. The current stops everywhere in the loop.D1
  3. Some parts have no pipe partner. Later courses meet parts called capacitors and inductors. They store energy in ways that no simple pipe can copy. HW101 explains them with their own pictures.D2

A fourth, gentle warning: water pressure can hurt nobody at home. The same is not true of all electricity. Wall sockets are dangerous. This university never uses them in a lab. See F0-46.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Your answer is 1,000 times too small (for example 0.02 when you expected 20)You found amperes but wrote mALook at the unit after each stepMultiply amperes by 1,000 to get milliamperes
Your answer gets bigger when the resistance gets biggerYou multiplied instead of dividedAsk: "a narrower pipe gives more flow?" That cannot be rightUse I = V ÷ R
You give a current for a loop with a gapForgot that an open loop has no currentTrace the loop with your finger from + back to −If your finger must jump a gap, the current is 0
The program prints the old numbers after you changed themYou did not build again after editingCheck the time on the program fileRun the build command again, then run the program
Transition box

Where you came from: KID101 (F0-06 and F0-10) showed that computers and robots have inputs, outputs and motors. You saw the "what". You did not see the electricity that powers them. What carries over: following exact steps, checking your answer, and the habit of asking "where does this story stop being true?". What changes: you now need units (V, A, mA, Ω) and the rule I = V ÷ R; and the closed-loop idea is new, with no easy home-life partner.D1 What comes next: F0-40 adds an LED and a switch to the loop, first in our text simulator.

Check yourself

  1. In the water picture, what stands for voltage, for current and for resistance?
  2. Use Ohm's law with exercise numbers: 6 V across 200 Ω. What is the current in mA?
  3. A loop has 3 V and 600 Ω. Which is the current? (a) 200 mA (b) 5 mA (c) 1,800 mA (d) 0.005 mA
  4. You double the resistance and keep the voltage the same. What happens to the current?
  5. A switch in the loop is open. What is the current? Why?
  6. Explain in your own words one place where the water picture is wrong.
  7. Apply it to a new case: a toy has two identical batteries in a row, which together push twice as hard as one. The resistance stays the same. What happens to the current?
  8. Edit Listing 1 so Loop B uses 1,200 ohms. Predict the new current before you run it.

Lab

Goal: run the Ohm's-law program, predict new results, and check your predictions.

Hardware and software needed: a computer with a C++ compiler. The run in this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0. No circuit parts are used in this chapter.

Safety

This lab uses only a computer. Never use a wall socket, a mains plug or anything plugged into the wall for an experiment. This university has no mains-voltage labs at any level.S1

Steps

  1. Open university/labs/F0-39/ohms_law.cpp. Read it next to the table above.
  2. Build it with the build command above. You should see no messages.
  3. Run ./ohms_law. You should see the four lines shown in the output above.
  4. On paper, invent two new loops. Use only exercise numbers. Work out each current by hand.
  5. Add your two loops to the list on lines 16–21. Build and run again.
  6. Compare. If the computer and your paper disagree, find the step that differs.

Expected observations

The first four lines are the same as in the real run above. Your new lines follow I = V × 1,000 ÷ R in mA.

Verification

Your paper answers match the program for both new loops. A loop you mark false prints 0 mA.

Troubleshooting

  • Build error near your new line → a missing comma or brace → compare with line 17 → copy its shape exactly.
  • The program prints a very long decimal → your numbers do not divide evenly → that is fine → round it on paper the same way.
  • Nothing changed → you ran the old program → build again first.

Extension

Find a resistance that gives exactly 15 mA from 6 V. Check it in the program.

Forensic lab

Scenario. Sami did the homework below. The teacher says one step is wrong. Your job is to find it, explain it and fix it.

Evidence pack (Sami's written steps; exercise numbers only):

StepSami wrote
1Loop: 6 V, 300 Ω, switch closed.
2Ohm's law: I = V ÷ R.
3I = 6 ÷ 300 = 0.02.
4So the current is 0.02 mA.
5The next loop is the same, but the switch is open. I = 6 ÷ 300 = 0.02 mA again.

Questions.

  1. Which step first goes wrong? Quote it.
  2. What should that step say?
  3. Step 5 has a second mistake. What is it?
  4. How could Sami catch both mistakes next time?

Method hints. Write the unit after every number. Ask "amperes or milliamperes?" at each step. Then trace the open loop with your finger. Compare with the real output of Listing 1, which was produced by the run, not by hand.

Mini-project

Make a two-column poster: "Water" and "Electricity". Draw the water loop and the electric loop. Add the three partners (pressure, flow, narrow pipe). Then add a red box called "Where it breaks" with two points in your own words.

Rubric: both loops closed and labelled (2); the three partners correct (1); two correct "where it breaks" points (2); no real-part numbers (1).

Summary

  • Voltage is the push, current is the flow, resistance is what gets in the way.
  • The water picture: pressure, flow and a narrow pipe.
  • Ohm's law for a resistor: V = I × R, so I = V ÷ R.
  • 1 A is 1,000 mA; write the unit after every number.
  • Electricity needs a closed loop; any gap stops the current everywhere.
  • The water picture breaks: open wires do not leak, and some parts have no pipe partner.
  • All numbers in this chapter are exercise numbers, not real parts.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Pressure stands for voltage, flow for current, and a narrow pipe for resistance.
  2. I = 6 ÷ 200 = 0.03 A = 30 mA.
  3. (b) 5 mA: 3 ÷ 600 = 0.005 A = 5 mA. (a) 200 mA comes from dividing the wrong way round (600 ÷ 3). (c) 1,800 mA comes from multiplying (3 × 600). (d) 0.005 is the right number in amperes, but with the wrong unit.
  4. The current halves. A narrower pipe lets less water through.
  5. 0 mA. There is a gap, so there is no closed loop for the current to travel around.
  6. Any one, in your words: electricity needs a full loop back to the battery; a cut wire does not spill; capacitors and inductors have no simple pipe partner.
  7. The current doubles, because the push doubles and the resistance stays the same (I = V ÷ R).
  8. 6 × 1,000 ÷ 1,200 = 5, so the program should print 5 mA for Loop B.

Forensic lab answer key

Root cause: step 4. Sami calculated 0.02 in amperes, then wrote "mA". The correct line is "0.02 A, which is 20 mA". Second mistake: step 5 used Ohm's law on an open loop. With a gap there is no current: 0 mA. Evidence: Listing 1's real output shows 20 mA for the closed 6 V, 300 Ω loop and 0 mA for the open one (R1). Prevention: write the unit after every number, and trace the loop before calculating. Wrong answers and why: "step 3 is wrong" — no, 6 ÷ 300 is 0.02; "the law should be V ÷ I" — no, that gives resistance, not current. How the evidence was made: written by the author as a deliberately broken worked calculation, in the style of the F0 forensic idea "find the wrong step"; it is not program output.

Circuits, LEDs and resistors in a simulator

Story hook

Analogy

At Kofi's home, the bathroom sink has a one-way drain. Water goes down it. It never comes back up. If you could turn the drain upside down, nothing would go through at all.

Kofi's mother also put a water saver on the kitchen tap. It makes the opening narrow. Without it, water splashes everywhere when the tap is opened wide.

Today Kofi wants to light a tiny lamp called an LED. It turns out the LED is a little like that one-way drain. It also needs a "water saver" next to it. Kofi will build it first on the computer, where nothing can break. Then, with his mother watching, he will build it with real parts.

What you will be able to do

  • Build a loop with a battery, a switch, a resistor and an LED in the course's text simulator.
  • Explain why an LED works only one way round and why it needs a resistor.
  • Calculate a resistor value from exercise numbers, labelled as pretend datasheet values.
  • Diagnose a dark LED from multimeter readings: reversed LED or missing connection.
  • Follow the safety rules for a supervised kit build.
Jargon box
LED
Simple words: a tiny lamp that lights when electricity flows through it the right way. Analogy: a one-way drain that glows when water goes through. Precise: a light-emitting diode: a diode (a one-way part) that gives off light when current flows through it in the forward direction. D1 D2
Diode
Simple words: a part that lets electricity through in one direction only. Analogy: a one-way drain. Precise: a two-terminal part that conducts current mainly from its anode to its cathode and blocks it the other way. D2
Anode and cathode
Simple words: the two legs of an LED: the one for the + side and the one for the − side. Analogy: the top and the bottom of the drain. Precise: the anode is the terminal current enters in the forward direction; the cathode is where it leaves. D2
Resistor
Simple words: a small part that gets in the way of electricity on purpose. Analogy: the water saver that makes the tap narrow. Precise: a part made to have a stated resistance, used here to limit the current through an LED. D1
Forward voltage
Simple words: the part of the battery's push that the LED needs before it lights. Analogy: the drain needs a little water pressure before it starts to flow. Precise: the voltage across a diode when it conducts in the forward direction; its value comes from the part's datasheet. D2 D3
Datasheet
Simple words: the instruction sheet a maker writes for a part, with its true numbers. Analogy: the label on a food packet that says what is inside. Precise: the manufacturer's document that states a part's ratings, limits and behaviour. D3
Simulator
Simple words: a program that pretends to be a real thing so you can try ideas safely. Analogy: practising a recipe on paper before using the stove. Precise: software that models a system's behaviour; this course uses its own small C++ text simulators. R1
Multimeter
Simple words: a tester that measures voltage, current and resistance. Analogy: a pressure gauge you can hold against any part of the pipe. Precise: a measuring instrument with several ranges; in its voltage mode its two probes show the voltage between two points. D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the loop you will build. The current leaves the battery's + side, goes through the switch, the resistor and the LED, and comes back to −.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

An LED is a tiny lamp. It is not like a normal bulb. It is a one-way part. Electricity can go through it in one direction only. Turn it around and it blocks the flow, like a drain upside down.D1

So an LED has a + leg and a − leg. The + leg is called the anode. The − leg is called the cathode. The anode must face the battery's + side.D2

An LED also needs a helper: a resistor. Without one, too much current can rush through. That can ruin the LED. The resistor is like the water saver on Kofi's tap. It keeps the flow gentle.D1

Before you touch any parts, you build the loop in a simulator. This course has its own tiny simulator, written in C++. You describe a loop in one line of text. The program tells you if the LED lights, and if the current is too high. Nothing can break inside a simulator.

Only after the simulator works do you build the real loop. A grown-up watches. You use the battery-powered kit chosen for this course, and nothing else.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

When an LED conducts, a certain voltage appears across it. This is its forward voltage. The rest of the battery's voltage appears across the resistor. So the resistor's share is: battery voltage − forward voltage.D2

Now Ohm's law from F0-39 works on the resistor alone. The current through the resistor is its voltage divided by its resistance. In a single loop, the same current flows through every part, so this is also the LED's current.D1 D2

Written as a formula: I = (Vbattery − Vforward) ÷ R. To choose a resistor for a wanted current, turn it around: R = (Vbattery − Vforward) ÷ I.

Where do the forward voltage and the largest safe current come from? From the datasheet of the exact LED in your kit. No book number and no number in this chapter replaces it.D3

Not verified — check before relying on this

Every LED, battery and resistor number in this chapter is an exercise number: "in this exercise, pretend the datasheet says the forward voltage is 2 V and the maximum current is 20 mA; pretend the battery pack gives 6 V". They are not taken from any real part. Before the kit build, an adult copies the real values from the datasheet of the LED in your kit and from the kit's battery documentation (dossier part F, document D3). The kit itself is a decision for the owner; it is not chosen yet. Which leg of your LED is the anode is also shown in its datasheet or the kit's instructions: check there, do not guess.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. A diode does not follow Ohm's law. Its current rises very steeply once the voltage across it passes a certain level. That is why an LED connected straight to a battery has almost nothing to limit its current, and why the resistor matters.D2 Our simulator uses a simpler model: a fixed forward voltage, and either "conducts" or "blocks". HW101 replaces it with the real curve and real measurements.

How the hardware actually does it

Inside an LED is a tiny piece of a special material called a semiconductor. It has two regions joined together. When current flows the forward way, energy is given off as light at the joint. The other way round, the joint blocks the current. The colour and the forward voltage depend on the material, which is why each LED's datasheet gives its own values.D2 D3

Worked example

In this exercise, pretend the datasheet says: forward voltage 2 V, maximum current 20 mA. Pretend the battery pack gives 6 V. These are not real-part numbers.

  1. The resistor's share of the push: 6 V − 2 V = 4 V.
  2. Try a 200 Ω resistor. I = 4 ÷ 200 = 0.02 A = 20 mA. That is exactly the pretend maximum. Our course rule: stay below the maximum, not at it.
  3. Try a 1,000 Ω resistor. I = 4 ÷ 1,000 = 0.004 A = 4 mA. Well below the pretend maximum. The LED lights more dimly.
  4. Try a 100 Ω resistor. I = 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 A = 40 mA. That is twice the pretend maximum. Not allowed: choose a bigger resistor.
  5. Smallest resistor for the pretend maximum: R = 4 ÷ 0.02 = 200 Ω. Anything bigger keeps the current lower.

The simulator run below shows the same three currents (20, 4 and 40 mA) for Amara's, Ben's and Chen's loops.R1

Code walk-through

The simulator reads one loop per line from a text file. Each line has five things: a name, the battery volts, the switch (1 = closed, 0 = open), the LED direction (1 = right way round, 0 = reversed) and the resistor in ohms (0 = no resistor).

Listing 1 — circuit_sim.cpp

// A tiny circuit truth model: battery, switch, resistor and LED in one loop.
// The LED numbers are PRETEND exercise numbers, not from a real datasheet.
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main()
{
    const double pretendForwardVolts = 2.0;  // "pretend the datasheet says 2 V"
    const double pretendMaxMilliamps = 20.0; // "pretend the datasheet says 20 mA"

    std::string name;
    double batteryVolts = 0.0;
    int switchClosed = 0;
    int ledForward = 0;
    double resistorOhms = 0.0;

    while (std::cin >> name >> batteryVolts >> switchClosed >> ledForward >> resistorOhms) {
        std::cout << name << ": ";
        if (switchClosed == 0) {
            std::cout << "loop open at the switch -> no current, LED dark\n";
        } else if (ledForward == 0) {
            std::cout << "LED turned the wrong way -> it blocks, no current, LED dark\n";
        } else if (batteryVolts <= pretendForwardVolts) {
            std::cout << "battery too weak to push through the LED -> LED dark\n";
        } else if (resistorOhms <= 0.0) {
            std::cout << "NO RESISTOR -> nothing limits the current: too much! (never do this)\n";
        } else {
            const double milliamps = (batteryVolts - pretendForwardVolts) * 1000.0 / resistorOhms;
            std::cout << "current " << milliamps << " mA -> LED lit";
            if (milliamps > pretendMaxMilliamps) {
                std::cout << ", but ABOVE the pretend maximum of " << pretendMaxMilliamps
                          << " mA: choose a bigger resistor";
            }
            std::cout << "\n";
        }
    }
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–2// A tiny circuit truth model …Comments describing the model.They say loudly that the LED numbers are pretend.
3–4#include …Tools for reading, printing and text.The program reads a file and prints results.
8–9const double pretendForwardVolts = 2.0; …The pretend datasheet values.For a real kit, an adult would copy the real datasheet values here.
11–15std::string name; double batteryVolts …Five labelled jars for one line of input.One jar per field of the loop description.
17while (std::cin >> name >> …)Reads one loop at a time until the file ends.Add a line to the file to test a new loop.
19–20if (switchClosed == 0)Open switch: there is a gap.No closed loop, no current (F0-39).
21–22else if (ledForward == 0)Reversed LED: it blocks.The one-way rule of a diode.
23–24else if (batteryVolts <= pretendForwardVolts)The battery's push is not more than the forward voltage.The LED needs its share before it lights.
25–26else if (resistorOhms <= 0.0)No resistor in the loop.Nothing limits the current: a loud warning.
28const double milliamps = (batteryVolts - pretendForwardVolts) * 1000.0 / resistorOhms;Current in mA from the resistor's share of the voltage.I = (Vbattery − Vforward) ÷ R, as in Layer 2.
29std::cout << "current " …Prints the current and "LED lit".You compare it with your hand sum.
30–33if (milliamps > pretendMaxMilliamps)Warns when the current is above the pretend maximum.The simulator catches the mistake before a real LED is ruined.
37return 0;Ends the program successfully.Exit code 0.

Every line matches a case from Layer 1 or the worked example.R1

Where the analogy breaks

  1. A drain does not need a full loop. Water goes down a drain and away. The LED's current must come back to the battery through wire W2. Remove W2 and the LED stays dark, even though "the drain" is the right way up.D1
  2. A drain lets a little water through at low pressure. Our simple model says an LED either blocks or conducts. A real diode's behaviour changes smoothly with voltage. The simulator's sharp "on/off" is a simplification.D2
  3. A water saver does not get warm. A resistor turns electrical energy into heat. With a big current, it can get hot. Pipes do not do that.D2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
LED dark, everything looks connectedLED reversedSimulator line "LED turned the wrong way"; on the kit, a multimeter shows the whole battery voltage across the LED (forensic lab)Turn the LED round, battery disconnected first
LED dark, LED the right way roundA gap: switch open or a wire missingTrace the loop with your finger; the multimeter shows the whole battery voltage across the gapClose the switch or add the missing wire
Simulator says "ABOVE the pretend maximum"Resistor too smallDo the worked-example sumChoose a bigger resistor
Simulator says "NO RESISTOR"The resistor was left outLook for 0 in the last fieldAlways put a resistor in series with the LED
Simulator prints nothing for your new lineA field is missing or not a numberCount the five fieldsWrite all five, separated by spaces
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-39 gave you voltage, current, resistance, the closed loop and Ohm's law. What carries over: I = V ÷ R still works for the resistor; the closed-loop rule still decides if anything flows.D1 What changes: most dangerous first: real parts can be ruined by too much current, so every real build needs a resistor and an adult; the LED is one-way and has its own forward voltage, which only its datasheet can tell you.D2 D3 What comes next: F0-41 adds buttons and switches, and shows how two switches together make AND and OR.

Check yourself

  1. Why does an LED light only one way round?
  2. What job does the resistor do in an LED loop?
  3. Pretend the datasheet says 2 V forward voltage and 20 mA maximum, and the battery gives 6 V. What current flows with 400 Ω? Is that allowed?
  4. Same pretend numbers. Which resistor is the smallest allowed? (a) 30 Ω (b) 200 Ω (c) 3 Ω (d) 400 Ω
  5. Where must real forward-voltage and maximum-current numbers come from?
  6. Explain in your own words why we build in the simulator first.
  7. Apply it to a new case: write a simulator input line for a loop named "Hana" with a 6 V battery, closed switch, reversed LED and 300 Ω. Predict the output line.
  8. Gus's 1.5 V loop stayed dark. Why, in the simulator's model?

Lab

Safety

Part B uses real parts. Do it only with an adult watching the whole time. Use only the battery-powered kit chosen for this course, designed for children. No mains electricity, nothing plugged into the wall, no LiPo batteries. Disconnect the battery pack before you add, remove or move any part. Never connect the battery's + and − together with a wire. If anything gets warm or smells, hands off and tell your adult.S1

Goal: build an LED loop in the simulator, then (supervised) with the kit, and explain each part.

Hardware and software needed: Part A: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Part B: the course kit's battery pack, one switch, one resistor, one LED and wires, as listed by the kit's instructions.

Part A — simulator (do this first)

  1. Build and run Listing 1 as shown above. You should see the seven lines of the real output.
  2. Add a line for your own loop to circuit_sim.in. Predict the output on paper.
  3. Run again. Compare with your prediction.
  4. Find, with pretend numbers, a resistor that gives between 5 mA and 15 mA. Prove it with a run.

Part B — the kit (supervised)

Safety

Adult present. Battery pack disconnected while you place parts. Connect it last, and disconnect it first when you change anything.S1

Not verified — check before relying on this

Part B was not performed in this build: no kit was available, and no kit has been chosen yet. The steps describe the kit-independent idea only. The adult checks every step against the chosen kit's own instructions and the datasheets in dossier part F (D3), including the real resistor value to use.

  1. With your adult, read the kit's instructions for the LED: which leg is the anode.
  2. Copy the real forward voltage and maximum current from the LED's datasheet. Do the worked-example sum with those numbers. Your adult checks it.
  3. Place switch, resistor and LED in one loop like Figure 1. Leave the switch open.
  4. Connect the battery pack. Close the switch. The LED should light.
  5. Disconnect the battery. Turn the LED round. Reconnect and close the switch. It should stay dark.
  6. Disconnect the battery. Put the LED back the right way.

Expected observations

Part A: the outputs shown above, plus your own lines. Part B: the LED lights only the right way round, and only with the switch closed.

Verification

Your simulator line for your kit build (with the real datasheet numbers) predicts "LED lit" with a current below the datasheet maximum, and the kit LED lights.

Troubleshooting

  • Kit LED dark → reversed LED or a gap → follow the forensic lab method below.
  • Simulator line ignored → a missing field → count five fields.
  • LED very dim → the resistor is large → that is safe; a smaller one (still above the minimum) gives more light.

Extension

Add two LEDs in a row to the simulator's idea on paper. How much push is left for the resistor? (Hint: subtract two forward voltages.)

Forensic lab

Scenario: "The LED stays dark". Three students built the loop of Figure 1. Circuit P works. In circuits Q and R the LED stays dark. Their teacher measured the voltage across each part with a multimeter. Find what is wrong in Q and in R.

Questions.

  1. Compare P with Q and R. Which readings are different?
  2. In Q, where does the whole 6 V appear? What does that tell you?
  3. In R, where does the whole 6 V appear? What does that tell you?
  4. State the fault in Q and in R, and the fix for each.
  5. How could a learner prevent each fault?

Method hints. When no current flows, there is no voltage across the resistor (Ohm's law: 0 × R = 0). The whole push then appears across the one place that blocks the loop. Make two hypotheses for each circuit, then use the readings to rule one out.

Mini-project

Write a "loop card" for your kit build: a drawing like Figure 1, the real datasheet values (copied by your adult), your resistor sum, and your simulator line with its output. Rubric: drawing is a closed loop with LED direction marked (2); sum correct and below the maximum (2); simulator line matches the build (1); sources named (1).

Summary

  • An LED is a one-way part: anode to the + side, cathode to the − side.
  • An LED needs a resistor to limit its current.
  • The resistor's share of the push is battery voltage − forward voltage.
  • I = (Vbattery − Vforward) ÷ R; stay below the datasheet maximum.
  • Real LED numbers come only from the datasheet of the LED in your kit.
  • Simulator first; the kit only with an adult, battery disconnected while wiring.
  • A dark LED: the whole battery voltage appears across the reversed LED or across the gap.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. It is a diode: a one-way part that conducts from anode to cathode and blocks the other way.
  2. It limits the current, so the LED is not ruined.
  3. (6 − 2) ÷ 400 = 0.01 A = 10 mA. Allowed: below the pretend 20 mA maximum.
  4. (b) 200 Ω: 4 ÷ 0.02 = 200. (a) 30 Ω and (c) 3 Ω give far too much current (about 133 mA and about 1,333 mA). (d) 400 Ω is allowed but is not the smallest.
  5. From the datasheet of the exact LED in your kit, never from memory or this chapter.
  6. In your words: mistakes cost nothing in the simulator; you learn the loop before real parts can be ruined or get warm.
  7. Hana 6 1 0 300. Output: Hana: LED turned the wrong way -> it blocks, no current, LED dark (the same rule as Eli's line in the real run).
  8. 1.5 V is not more than the pretend 2 V forward voltage, so the model says the battery cannot push current through the LED.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: in P the resistor has 4 V and the LED 2 V, with 20 mA. In Q and R the current is 0 mA and the resistor has 0 V. In Q the whole 6 V is across the LED; in R the whole 6 V is across wire W2. Root cause Q: the LED is reversed; it blocks, so the full push appears across it. Fix: disconnect the battery, turn the LED round. Root cause R: wire W2 is missing (a gap between the LED and the battery's − side); the full push appears across the gap. Fix: disconnect the battery, add the wire. Hypotheses ruled out: "flat battery" — no, the full 6 V is measured somewhere in Q and R; "LED broken" in R — the LED shows 0 V, so the break is elsewhere. Prevention: check LED direction against the kit's instructions; trace the loop with a finger before connecting the battery. How the evidence was made: meter.cpp with meter.in, which marks P as "none", Q as "reversed" and R as "gap"; ideal model, pretend numbers (R1).

Story hook

Analogy

In Priya's home there are two kinds of switches. The hallway light has a switch that stays where you put it. Flip it down and the light stays on. Flip it up and it stays off.

The doorbell is different. It rings only while you hold the button. When you let go, a spring pushes the button back up, and the ringing stops.

Priya's little cousin wants a "secret" lamp. It should light only if he presses two buttons at the same time. Priya wonders: how do you wire that? And how would you make one button that turns a lamp on with one press and off with the next? This chapter answers both questions.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain the difference between a switch that stays and a push button that springs back.
  • Predict when an LED lights with two switches in series (AND) or in parallel (OR).
  • Read a truth table produced by the course simulator.
  • Explain why a "toggle" light must remember the button's last state.
  • Wire and explain a button-controlled LED, in the simulator and (supervised) with the kit.
Jargon box
Switch
Simple words: a part that opens or closes a gap in a circuit. Analogy: a tap on a pipe: open lets water through, closed stops it (careful: for electricity, a "closed" switch lets current through). Precise: a component with contacts that connect (closed) or disconnect (open) a conducting path. D1
Push button
Simple words: a switch that is on only while you press it. Analogy: a doorbell button. Precise: a momentary switch: a spring returns its contacts to their rest position when released. D1
Series
Simple words: parts placed one after the other in the same loop. Analogy: two taps on the same pipe: water passes only if both are open. Precise: a connection in which the same current passes through each part in turn. D1
Parallel
Simple words: parts placed side by side, each giving the current its own path. Analogy: two pipes joined side by side: water passes if either tap is open. Precise: a connection in which the parts share the same two connection points, so current can take either path. D1
Truth table
Simple words: a table that lists every combination of inputs and the result. Analogy: a chart on the fridge: "if this and that, then …". Precise: a table giving the output of a logic function for every combination of its inputs. D4
Toggle
Simple words: change to the other state: on becomes off, off becomes on. Analogy: pressing the light switch in the hallway once more. Precise: an operation that inverts a two-state value; here it happens once per new button press. R1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the two ways to wire two switches, A and B, with one LED. On the left they are in series. On the right they are in parallel.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A switch makes a gap in the loop, or closes it. Closed means connected. Open means there is a gap. You met the gap idea in F0-39: one gap stops the current everywhere.D1

Be careful with the words. A closed water tap stops water. A closed switch lets current through. The words go the other way round. Say it slowly: closed switch, closed loop, current flows.

Some switches stay where you put them. A push button does not. A small spring pushes it back when you let go. Like the doorbell, it only connects while you press.D1

Now take two switches. Put them one after the other in the loop. That is called series. The current must pass through A and then through B. If either one is open, there is a gap. So the LED lights only when A and B are both closed. That is Priya's cousin's secret lamp.

Put them side by side instead. That is called parallel. Now the current has two roads. If A is closed, it can use A. If B is closed, it can use B. So the LED lights when A or B is closed, or both.

A truth table lists every case. With two switches there are four cases. Figure 1 and the program below show all four.D4

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Write "closed" as 1 and "open" as 0. Write "LED on" as 1 and "LED off" as 0. Then series switches behave like AND: the output is 1 only when both inputs are 1. Parallel switches behave like OR: the output is 1 when at least one input is 1. MA102 chapter F0-26 builds these truth tables with the same two light switches.D1 D4

The LED still needs its resistor, in both circuits. The switches decide whether the loop is closed. The resistor decides how much current flows when it is.D1

The second idea is the toggle light. One press turns it on. The next press turns it off. A plain wire cannot do that. Something has to remember. In the next chapter a microcontroller does the remembering. Here, our simulator does it.

A program reads a button again and again. Each reading is one "tick". If the program toggled the light at every tick where the button is down, a long press would flip it many times. So the program must remember the previous tick. It toggles only when the button was up last tick and is down now. That moment is the start of a new press.R2

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. When the metal contacts inside a real button close, they can bounce: they touch, part and touch again several times in a very short moment. A fast program could see one press as several. Programs handle this by ignoring changes for a short time after the first one; this is called debouncing.D2 How long that time should be depends on the button, so it comes from its datasheet or a measurement, not from this chapter. Our simulator's button does not bounce: each tick is clean.

How the hardware actually does it

Inside a push button are two metal contacts and a spring. Pressing pushes a metal piece across the contacts, which closes the gap. Releasing lets the spring lift it away again. A toggle switch has a lever that holds the metal piece in one of two positions until you move it.D1 The exact inside of the buttons in your kit is shown in their datasheet (D3).

Worked example

Part 1: series or parallel?

Switch A is closed (1). Switch B is open (0).

  1. Series: the current must pass A and B. B is open, so there is a gap. LED off. In logic: 1 AND 0 = 0.
  2. Parallel: the current can pass through A. LED on. In logic: 1 OR 0 = 1.

Part 2: the toggle light, tick by tick

The button readings are: up, down, down, down, up. The light starts off. Remember the last reading each time.

  1. Tick 0: up. Not a new press. Light stays off.
  2. Tick 1: down, and it was up before. New press! Toggle: light on.
  3. Tick 2: down, but it was down before. Not new. Light stays on.
  4. Tick 3: down, was down. Light stays on.
  5. Tick 4: up. Light stays on. It will go off at the next new press.

Listing 2's real output shows exactly these first five ticks.R2

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — switches_logic.cpp: the series and parallel truth table.

// Two switches and one LED: in series (one after the other) or in parallel (side by side).
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    std::cout << "A B | series LED | parallel LED\n";
    for (int a = 0; a <= 1; ++a) {
        for (int b = 0; b <= 1; ++b) {
            const bool series = (a == 1) && (b == 1);   // both must be closed
            const bool parallel = (a == 1) || (b == 1); // either one is enough
            std::cout << a << " " << b << " | "
                      << (series ? "ON " : "off") << "        | "
                      << (parallel ? "ON" : "off") << "\n";
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

1// Two switches …A comment for humans.Says what is modelled.

7–8for (int a = 0; a <= 1; ++a) and the same for bTries A = 0 and 1, and for each, B = 0 and 1.Four cases: every combination.
9const bool series = (a == 1) && (b == 1);&& means AND.Both switches must be closed.
10const bool parallel = (a == 1) || (b == 1);|| means OR.Either switch is enough.
11–13std::cout << …Prints one row of the table.Shows ON or off for each circuit.

Listing 2 — button_led.cpp: a scripted push button drives a "hold" light and a "toggle" light.

// A scripted push button, read once per tick, drives two lights:
// a "hold" light (on while pressed) and a "toggle" light (flips on each new press).
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    int tick = 0;
    int pressed = 0;
    int wasPressed = 0;
    bool toggleLight = false;

    std::cout << "tick button hold-light toggle-light\n";
    while (std::cin >> pressed) {
        const bool holdLight = (pressed == 1);
        if (pressed == 1 && wasPressed == 0) { // a NEW press: up last tick, down now
            toggleLight = !toggleLight;
        }
        wasPressed = pressed;
        std::cout << tick << "    " << (pressed == 1 ? "down" : "up  ") << "   "
                  << (holdLight ? "ON " : "off") << "        "
                  << (toggleLight ? "ON" : "off") << "\n";
        ++tick;
    }
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–2// A scripted push button …Comments.Explain the two lights.
7–10int tick = 0; int pressed = 0; int wasPressed = 0; bool toggleLight = false;Four labelled jars: the tick number, the button now, the button last tick, and the toggle light.wasPressed is the memory a plain wire does not have.
12std::cout << "tick button …";Prints the heading.Labels the columns.
13while (std::cin >> pressed)Reads the next button reading (1 = down, 0 = up) from the input file.One loop round = one tick.
14const bool holdLight = (pressed == 1);The hold light copies the button.This is what a button wired straight to an LED does.
15–17if (pressed == 1 && wasPressed == 0) { toggleLight = !toggleLight; }Only at a new press, flip the toggle light.! means NOT: on becomes off and off becomes on.
18wasPressed = pressed;Remember this tick for next time.Without this line the program forgets (see the forensic lab).
19–21std::cout << tick …Prints the tick, the button and both lights.A log you can check line by line.
22++tick;Counts up the tick.Gives each line a number.
24return 0;Ends successfully.Exit code 0.

Input button_led.in (one reading per tick): 0 1 1 1 0 0 1 0 0 1 1 0.

Where the analogy breaks

  1. The words "open" and "closed" swap. An open tap lets water flow. An open switch stops current. If you carry the tap picture too far, you will say the opposite of what you mean.D1
  2. An open switch has the push across it. Close a tap and the pipe is still full of still water. Open a switch and the battery's whole voltage appears across the gap, as F0-40's forensic lab showed. Pipes give no hint of that.D1
  3. Taps do not bounce. Turning a tap is smooth. Real button contacts can bounce, which a fast program can notice (Layer 3).D2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
"Secret lamp" lights with one button onlyButtons wired in parallel instead of seriesTrace the loop: is there a second road around one button?Put the buttons one after the other
The LED never lights in the series circuitOne switch is always open, or a gap elsewhereClose each switch alone and trace the loopFind the gap (F0-40 method)
Toggle light flickers while the button is heldThe program toggles at every "down" tickLook at a log: does it change on ticks where the button stays down?Toggle only when it was up last tick and is down now
You say "close the switch to stop the LED"Tap words used for switchesSay: closed switch = connectedOpen the switch to stop the current
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-40 built one loop with one switch, a resistor and an LED; KID101 F0-02 used light switches for bits. What carries over: closed loop or gap; a resistor with every LED; the simulator before the kit.D1 What changes: two switches together make logic (AND, OR); and a toggle needs memory, which wires alone do not have, so a program enters the story.R2 What comes next: F0-42 gives the memory and the timing job to a microcontroller that blinks an LED.

Lab

Safety

Part B uses real parts: adult supervision the whole time; only the battery-powered kit chosen for this course; no mains, nothing plugged into the wall, no LiPo batteries. Disconnect the battery pack before you change any wire. Never connect + to − directly. If anything gets warm or smells, hands off and tell your adult.S1

Troubleshooting

  • LED always on → the button is bypassed by a wire → trace the loop → remove the bypass.
  • LED never on → reversed LED or gap → use the F0-40 forensic method.
  • Simulator log shorter than expected → fewer numbers in your input → count them.

Mini-project

Design a "two-key" lamp on paper: two push buttons in series with an LED and resistor. Draw it like Figure 1, write its truth table, and write a simulator input file for Listing 1's idea with your own labels. Rubric: correct series drawing (2); correct truth table (2); clear explanation of why one button is not enough (1); no real-part numbers without a datasheet (1).

Summary

  • A switch closes or opens a gap; closed means connected.
  • A push button connects only while pressed; a spring returns it.
  • Series switches: LED on only if A AND B are closed.
  • Parallel switches: LED on if A OR B (or both) is closed.
  • A toggle light needs memory: toggle only on a new press (up before, down now).
  • Real buttons can bounce; programs can ignore changes for a short time.
  • Simulator first; kit only with an adult.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. A switch that stays keeps its position until you move it; a push button connects only while pressed and a spring returns it.
  2. No. In series the current must pass both; B open makes a gap.
  3. (c). (a) is the series (AND) answer. (b) forgets that with both open there is no road at all. (d) is the opposite of OR.
  4. Line 18: wasPressed = pressed; (used by the check on line 15).
  5. In your words: a wire only connects or not, right now; it cannot know whether the last press turned the lamp on or off. Something must remember.
  6. Parallel: either button alone should close the loop.
  7. Readings 1, 1, 0, 1. Tick 0 is a new press (up before the start): on. Tick 1 is still down: no change. Tick 2 up: no change. Tick 3 is a new press: off. It ends off.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: in Jun's log the light changes at ticks 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 10 — at every "down" tick. New presses are only at ticks 1, 6 and 9. Hypotheses: (1) the button bounces; (2) the program toggles on every down tick. The simulator's button cannot bounce (each tick is a clean scripted reading), and the program has no memory of the last tick, so (2) is proven. Fix: add int wasPressed = 0;, change the condition to pressed == 1 && wasPressed == 0, and add wasPressed = pressed; after it — exactly Listing 2. Verification: with the same input, the light changes only at ticks 1, 6 and 9 (Listing 2's real output, R2). Prevention: test with a long press in the input. How the evidence was made: button_broken.cpp is Listing 2 with the memory removed, run on the same input (R2).

Story hook

Analogy

Diego is helping his aunt bake bread. The recipe card says: "Knead for one minute. Rest for one minute. Repeat." His aunt sets a kitchen timer. Knead, beep. Rest, beep. Knead again.

Diego notices that the card never says "stop". His aunt laughs. "I stop when the dough is ready. The card would go on forever."

That evening Diego sees a tiny green light blinking on the internet box at home. On, off, on, off. "Is there a recipe card inside that box too?" he asks. Yes, there is. A small computer is following a recipe like his: turn on, wait, turn off, wait, repeat. In this chapter you write that recipe and run it in our simulator. Then, with an adult, you may try it on a real board.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a microcontroller is, using the recipe picture and precise words.
  • Describe the shape of a blink program: set up a pin, then loop forever (on, wait, off, wait).
  • Run the course's blink simulator and change the timing to make a new rhythm.
  • Calculate how many blinks happen in a given time.
  • Find the missing line in a blink program from its log.
  • Follow the supervised steps for a real board, checked against the kit's own instructions.
Jargon box
Microcontroller
Simple words: a very small computer on one chip, made to control things like lights and motors. Analogy: a cook who only knows one short recipe card and repeats it all day. Precise: an integrated circuit that contains a processor, memory for the program and data, and input/output pins on one chip. D2 D1
Pin (input/output)
Simple words: a little metal leg of the chip that the program can switch on or off, or read. Analogy: a light switch the cook can flip, or a doorbell the cook can listen to. Precise: a terminal connected to the chip's input/output circuits; as a digital output the program drives it high or low, as an input the program reads its level. D2
High and low
Simple words: "on" and "off" for a pin. Analogy: the light switch up or down (KID101 F0-02). Precise: the two voltage levels of a digital signal; the actual voltages are given in the microcontroller's datasheet. D2 D3
Program loop
Simple words: steps that repeat again and again. Analogy: "knead, rest, repeat" on the recipe card. Precise: a sequence of instructions that the processor carries out again and again; the main loop of a blink program has no end condition. D4
Millisecond (ms)
Simple words: a very short time: one second cut into a thousand parts. Analogy: a tiny tick of the kitchen timer. Precise: one thousandth of a second; 1,000 ms = 1 s. D1
Firmware
Simple words: the program that lives inside a small device. Analogy: the recipe card glued inside the cook's cupboard. Precise: software stored in a device's non-volatile memory that runs when the device starts. D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 has two parts. On the left is the blink recipe as a loop. On the right is what the LED does over time.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A microcontroller is a tiny computer on one chip. It is much smaller than a laptop. It does not have a screen or a keyboard. It has little metal legs called pins instead.D2

A program can switch a pin on or off. On is called high. Off is called low. If an LED and its resistor are connected to the pin, the LED follows the pin. Pin high, LED on. Pin low, LED off.D2

To blink the LED, the program follows a recipe. Turn the LED on. Wait a little. Turn it off. Wait a little. Do it again. Like Diego's bread, the recipe never says stop. It is a loop that runs as long as the board has power.D4

The waiting matters. Computers are very fast. Without a wait, the LED would change far too quickly for anyone to see. We measure the wait in milliseconds. A thousand milliseconds make one second.

In this chapter you run the blink recipe in our simulator first. It prints what the LED would do and when. Then, with an adult, you may try a real board from the kit.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Every blink program has the same shape, whatever the board. First, a setup step runs once. It tells the chip that the LED pin is an output. Then the main loop runs forever: set the pin high, wait, set it low, wait.D2 D4

Here is that shape as pseudocode. Pseudocode is a recipe written in plain words that looks a bit like code.

Watch out

Pseudocode — not buildable, not for any real board. The real names of the "make output", "set pin" and "wait" instructions depend on the board, its library and its toolchain. They come from the kit's documentation (D3), which is not chosen yet. Do not type this into a board's tools.

SETUP (runs once):
    make the LED pin an OUTPUT
LOOP (runs forever):
    set the LED pin HIGH      -- LED on
    wait ON_TIME milliseconds
    set the LED pin LOW       -- LED off
    wait OFF_TIME milliseconds

The simulator in Listing 1 does the same steps in ordinary C++. Instead of a real pin, it prints "LED ON" or "LED off". Instead of really waiting, it adds the wait to a pretend clock. So the run is instant, and it prints the exact time of every change.R1

One full blink takes ON_TIME + OFF_TIME. With 500 ms + 500 ms, one blink takes 1,000 ms, which is one second. The program built for a real board is called firmware. The kit's tools copy it onto the board, where it starts every time the board gets power.D2

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. A "wait" on a real microcontroller can be done in two ways. The program can count clock ticks and do nothing else until enough have passed (a busy wait). Or it can set up a hardware timer and do other work until the timer says the time is up.D2 A busy wait is the easy way to blink. It has a cost: while waiting, the program cannot read a button. Robots need the second way. RB101 and the firmware courses of F3 come back to this.

How the hardware actually does it

Inside the chip, each output pin is connected to a tiny electronic switch arrangement. When the program writes "high" into a special memory location for that pin, the switch connects the pin to the chip's supply voltage. When it writes "low", the pin is connected to the chip's ground (its − side). The LED and resistor between the pin and ground then form a closed loop only when the pin is high.D2 The pin can only give a small current; the largest allowed value is in the microcontroller's datasheet (D3). F0-44 shows why that matters for motors.

Worked example

The timing numbers below are our own exercise choices. They are not taken from any board.

How long is one blink?

ON_TIME = 500 ms, OFF_TIME = 500 ms. One blink = 500 + 500 = 1,000 ms = 1 s.

How many blinks in ten seconds?

Ten seconds = 10 × 1,000 = 10,000 ms. Blinks = 10,000 ÷ 1,000 = 10 blinks.

A faster rhythm

You want two blinks every second, with equal on and off times. One blink must take 1,000 ÷ 2 = 500 ms. Split it equally: ON_TIME = 250 ms, OFF_TIME = 250 ms.

When does the LED switch?

With 500/500 and three blinks, the LED turns on at 0, 1,000 and 2,000 ms, and off at 500, 1,500 and 2,500 ms. The total simulated time is 3,000 ms. Listing 1's real output prints these exact times.R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — blink_sim.cpp: the blink recipe in the course simulator.

// A simulated microcontroller blink: a loop that turns an LED on, waits,
// turns it off, waits. Time is a pretend clock, so nothing really sleeps.
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    const int onMs = 500;   // how long the LED stays on (exercise choice)
    const int offMs = 500;  // how long it stays off (exercise choice)
    const int blinks = 3;   // a real board would loop forever; we stop after 3

    int clockMs = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < blinks; ++i) {
        std::cout << "t=" << clockMs << " ms  LED ON\n";
        clockMs += onMs;    // "wait onMs"
        std::cout << "t=" << clockMs << " ms  LED off\n";
        clockMs += offMs;   // "wait offMs"
    }
    std::cout << "simulated time: " << clockMs << " ms for " << blinks << " blinks\n";
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–2// A simulated microcontroller blink …Comments.Say clearly that time is pretend.
3#include <iostream>Brings in printing.The "LED" is a printed line.

13std::cout << … "LED ON\n";"Set the pin high", printed with the time.Stands in for the real pin.

Until then, the simulator result above is the tested result.

Where the analogy breaks

  1. A cook notices problems; a microcontroller does not. Diego's aunt stops kneading when the dough is ready. The chip keeps blinking forever, even if the LED is missing or broken. It does exactly what the recipe says.D4
  2. The waits are far shorter and far more exact. A kitchen timer is "about a minute". A microcontroller counts its clock; how exact the timing is depends on the board's clock, which its datasheet describes (D3). The kitchen picture hides how precise this can be.D2
  3. A cook can do two things at once. Diego's aunt can listen to the radio while the dough rests. A busy-waiting program cannot do anything else while it waits (Layer 3).D2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
LED stays on all the timeThe "LED off" step is missingRead the log: only "LED ON" lines (forensic lab)Add the off step before the second wait
LED looks on all the time, but the log has both linesThe waits are far too short to seeLook at the times in the log: are they close together?Use longer ON and OFF times
On a real board, LED never lightsWrong pin, reversed LED, missing resistor or gapCheck the pin named in the kit's documentation; use the F0-40 forensic methodFix the wiring with the battery disconnected
The rhythm is twice as fast as plannedYou halved both times by mistakeAdd on + off and compare with your planRecalculate: one blink = on + off

Expected observations

Verification

The simulator's total time equals blinks × (on + off). On the board, ten blinks take about ten times one blink, as far as you can measure by hand.

Summary

  • A microcontroller is a small computer on one chip with pins.
  • A program sets an output pin high (LED on) or low (LED off).
  • Blink shape: set up once; loop forever: on, wait, off, wait.
  • One blink takes ON_TIME + OFF_TIME; 1,000 ms = 1 s.
  • The course simulator uses a pretend clock and prints each change.
  • Real-board code depends on the kit; it is not given here and is untested on hardware.
  • Every real-board step is supervised and follows the kit's documentation.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: the log has only "LED ON" lines, at 0, 1,000 and 2,000 ms; there is no "LED off" line, but the total time is still 3,000 ms. Hypotheses: (1) wiring: the LED is connected straight to the battery, so the pin cannot turn it off; (2) program: the off step is missing. The simulator has no wiring at all and still never turns the LED off, so the program is at fault (hypothesis 2 proven; hypothesis 1 is not needed to explain the evidence, though Nadia's adult may still check it). Root cause: the line that prints "LED off" (set the pin low) is missing between the two waits. Fix: insert it after clockMs += onMs;, as on line 15 of Listing 1. Verification: the fixed program prints the same log as Listing 1 (R1). Prevention: read the program against the pseudocode, one step per line. How the evidence was made: blink_broken.cpp is Listing 1 with line 15 removed, run in this build (R1).

Story hook

Analogy

When Ama walks into the kitchen at night, she does three things without thinking. Her eyes notice it is dark, so she reaches for the light. Her hand feels the table edge before she bumps into it. And when she carries a bowl of soup, she feels if it starts to tip.

Light, distance, tilt. Her body senses each one, and her brain decides what to do.

A robot cannot see, feel or balance like Ama. But it can have small parts that measure light, distance and tilt. These parts turn the world into numbers. A program reads the numbers and decides. This chapter is about those parts, the sensors, and about one tricky problem: what to do when a number keeps wobbling around the line between "dark" and "bright".

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a sensor does, with the senses picture and precise words.
  • Describe in words how a light sensor, a distance sensor and a tilt sensor work, and what their datasheets must tell you.
  • Use a threshold to turn a sensor reading into a yes/no decision.
  • Run the course's sensor simulator on a scripted table of readings.
  • Diagnose a flickering night-light from its log and fix it with two thresholds.
Jargon box
Sensor
Simple words: a part that measures something about the world and turns it into an electrical signal. Analogy: a sense, like eyes or touch. Precise: a device that converts a physical quantity (light, distance, tilt …) into an electrical signal that a circuit or program can read. D1 D2
Reading
Simple words: one number the program gets from a sensor at one moment. Analogy: one look at the thermometer. Precise: a single sampled value of a sensor's output, in units stated by its datasheet (or, in our simulator, our own made-up units). R1
Threshold
Simple words: the line you choose between "yes" and "no". Analogy: "if it is darker than this, switch on the hall light". Precise: a chosen value that a reading is compared with to make a two-way decision. R1
Noise
Simple words: small random wobbles in a sensor's numbers. Analogy: a shaky hand reading a ruler. Precise: unwanted variation in a measured signal that does not come from the quantity being measured. D2
Hysteresis
Simple words: using two lines instead of one, so a decision does not flip back and forth. Analogy: you put a jumper on when it is clearly cold and take it off only when it is clearly warm. Precise: a switching rule with separate "turn on" and "turn off" thresholds, leaving a dead zone between them. D2
Analog and digital signal
Simple words: analog is a number that can take many values; digital here means only two, yes or no. Analogy: a dimmer knob versus a light switch. Precise: an analog signal varies continuously; a digital signal has two levels (high and low, F0-42). A microcontroller turns an analog voltage into a number with an analog-to-digital converter. D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the path from the world to a decision. Three sensors feed the program. The program compares each reading with a threshold.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A sensor is a part that measures something. It is like one of your senses. A light sensor is like eyes. A distance sensor is like your hand reaching out in the dark. A tilt sensor is like the balance sense that tells you if you are leaning.D1

Each time the program asks a sensor, it gets a reading. Some readings are numbers, like "light level 52". Some are only yes or no, like "tilted: yes".

A number on its own does not tell the program what to do. So you choose a line, a threshold. For example: "if the light is below 30, it is dark". Now the program can decide.

Real sensor numbers wobble a little. This wobble is called noise. If the light is close to your line, the number may jump above and below it again and again. A night-light would flicker on, off, on, off. You will find and fix this problem in the forensic lab.D2

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Light

One kind of light sensor is a part whose resistance changes with the light that falls on it. Put it in a loop with a fixed resistor, and the voltage between them changes with the light. A microcontroller can turn that voltage into a number.D1 D2 Other light sensors are small chips that send the number directly. Which kind your kit has, and what its numbers mean, is in its datasheet.

Distance

One way to measure distance is like an echo. The sensor sends out a short pulse of sound or light. The pulse bounces off an object and comes back. The sensor measures how long the round trip took. The longer the time, the farther away the object.D2 The pulse travels there and back, so the distance is half of (speed × time). The speed and the sensor's range come from its datasheet, not from this chapter.

Tilt

A simple tilt sensor is a switch that closes or opens when it leans. Inside, a small moving part touches or leaves two contacts. So it gives a yes/no signal, like the buttons of F0-41.D1 More advanced motion sensors give numbers for how much the board is tilting; RB101 and HW302 meet them.

Not verified — check before relying on this

This chapter does not say which light, distance or tilt sensor your kit contains, what units its readings use, its range, or how it must be wired. Those come from the datasheets of the sensors in the kit chosen for this course (dossier part F, D3), which is not chosen yet. All numbers in our simulator are made up: light in "simulator units" from 0 to 100, distance in centimetres from a scripted table, tilt as 0 or 1.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. A microcontroller reads an analog voltage with an analog-to-digital converter (ADC). The ADC gives a whole number in a fixed range. How many steps that range has, and which voltage matches the top step, are in the microcontroller's datasheet.D2 D3 Every reading also carries noise. Two common defences are to average several readings and to use two thresholds (hysteresis). MA202 (F0-62) measures sensor noise properly with statistics.

How the hardware actually does it

A sensor changes something electrical when the world changes: a resistance, a voltage, a time, or whether a contact is closed. The microcontroller measures that change through one of its pins. A yes/no sensor uses a digital input pin, read as high or low (F0-42). A number sensor either uses an analog input pin with the ADC, or sends its number as a message of bits.D2 Which way your kit's sensors work is stated in their datasheets (D3).

Worked example

All numbers here are scripted exercise values in our simulator's own units.

One threshold

Rule: light below 30 means "dark". Readings: 80, 52, 31, 29, 10.

  1. 80 < 30? No → bright.
  2. 52 < 30? No → bright.
  3. 31 < 30? No → bright. Close to the line!
  4. 29 < 30? Yes → dark.
  5. 10 < 30? Yes → dark.

Why one line flickers

At dusk the readings wobble: 31, 29, 31, 28, 30, 29. With one line at 30 the decision flips: bright, dark, bright, dark, bright, dark. That is six changes in six readings.

Two lines: hysteresis

New rule: switch on only below 26; switch off only above 34. Starting off, the same wobbling readings never go below 26, so the lamp stays off. When the readings later drop to 24, it switches on once, and stays on. The forensic answer key shows this in a real run.R2

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — sensor_read.cpp: reads a scripted table of three sensors and prints decisions.

// Reading three pretend sensors from a scripted table and making decisions.
// Each input line: time in seconds, light level (0-100, simulator units),
// distance in cm, tilted (0 or 1). All values are made up for this exercise.
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    const int darkBelow = 30;      // our choice: light under 30 counts as "dark"
    const int nearBelowCm = 20;    // our choice: closer than 20 cm counts as "near"

    int seconds = 0;
    int light = 0;
    int distanceCm = 0;
    int tilted = 0;

    std::cout << "time light distance tilt | decisions\n";
    while (std::cin >> seconds >> light >> distanceCm >> tilted) {
        std::cout << seconds << " s  " << light << "   " << distanceCm << " cm   "
                  << tilted << "   | ";
        std::cout << (light < darkBelow ? "dark " : "bright ");
        std::cout << (distanceCm < nearBelowCm ? "NEAR " : "clear ");
        std::cout << (tilted == 1 ? "TILTED" : "level") << "\n";
    }
    return 0;
}

1–3// Reading three pretend sensors …Comments: the input format, and that values are made up.No real-sensor numbers are claimed.
8const int darkBelow = 30;The light threshold.Our choice for the exercise; change it and see.
9const int nearBelowCm = 20;The distance threshold.Also our choice.
11–14int seconds …; int light …; int distanceCm …; int tilted …;Four jars for one row of readings.One jar per column of the table.
16std::cout << "time light distance tilt | decisions\n";Prints the heading.Labels the columns.
17while (std::cin >> seconds >> light >> distanceCm >> tilted)Reads one row at a time from the scripted table.Like asking the sensors once per second.
18–19std::cout << seconds …Prints the raw readings.Always log what you measured before what you decided.

Where the analogy breaks

  1. Your senses fill gaps; sensors do not. Your brain mixes what you see, hear and remember. A sensor gives only its one number. If it is pointed the wrong way or covered with dust, the program still trusts it.D2
  2. Sensors sample; senses feel all the time. The program only knows the world at the moments it takes a reading. Between two readings, it knows nothing.R1
  3. Sensor errors are specific and measurable. Your eyes are "a bit tired". A sensor's noise and limits are written in its datasheet and can be measured (MA202).D2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Light flickers on and off at duskOne threshold and noisy readings near itLog the readings: are they wobbling around the line?Use two thresholds (hysteresis)
Decision is the opposite of what you wanted< and > swappedTest with one very high and one very low readingRead the comparison aloud: "light below 30 means dark"
A reading of exactly 30 gives the "wrong" answerUnclear rule at the lineTest the edge value itselfDecide on purpose: below 30, or 30 and below
Simulator stops earlyA row has three numbers instead of fourCount the numbers in the last printed row's next lineFix the input row
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-42 made a microcontroller blink an LED on a fixed rhythm; F0-41 read a button. What carries over: pins, high and low, the program loop, logs you can check line by line.D2 What changes: most dangerous first: a program now acts on what it senses, so a wrong or noisy reading leads to a wrong action; numbers replace yes/no, so you choose thresholds; and every real number belongs to a datasheet.D3 What comes next: F0-44 adds muscles: motors, and the drivers that let a small pin control them.

Lab

Safety

Part B uses real parts: an adult supervises; only the kit chosen for this course; no mains, no LiPo batteries. Power off before changing any wire. Do not look into a distance sensor's light source if your kit's sensor uses light; follow its datasheet's safety notes.S1 D3

Goal: make decisions from a scripted sensor table, choose your own thresholds, and (supervised, when a kit exists) compare with real readings.

Hardware and software needed: Part A: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Part B: the kit's microcontroller board and one sensor, with its datasheet.

Part A — simulator

  1. Build and run Listing 1 with its input. Check each decision by hand.
  2. Write your own table of six rows: walking from a bright room into a dark one towards a wall. Predict the decisions.
  3. Run with your table: ./sensor_read < my_table.in. Compare.
  4. Change darkBelow to 50. Which rows change?

Part B — a real sensor (supervised)

Not verified — check before relying on this

Untested on hardware (AH-26): no kit or sensor was available in this build. Wiring, units and the program to read the sensor come from the kit's documentation (D3); the adult checks each step there.

  1. With your adult, read the sensor's datasheet: what does it measure, in what units, over what range?
  2. Wire it as the kit documentation shows, power off. Your adult checks.
  3. Read and write down ten readings in a bright room and ten in a dim room.
  4. Type your readings into a table file for Listing 1's format (use 0 for columns you did not measure) and run the simulator on your own data.

Expected observations

Part A: the real output above, then your own. Part B: your readings wobble a little even when nothing changes. They are your measurements on your sensor, not a specification.

Verification

Every decision in your run matches your hand prediction.

Troubleshooting

  • No output rows → the input file name is wrong → check the < part of the command.
  • All "dark" → threshold too high → print the readings and compare.
  • Real readings never change → wrong pin or wiring → recheck with the documentation.

Extension

Add a fourth decision: "danger" when the reading is NEAR and TILTED at the same time (an AND, like F0-41).

Forensic lab

Scenario. Tomás built a night-light in the simulator. "At sunset it goes crazy," he says. "On, off, on, off, then it finally stays on."

Evidence pack. The real output of his program, nightlight_flicker.cpp, on a scripted table of dusk readings (one per minute):

His rule: lamp on when light is below 30, otherwise off (one threshold).

Questions.

  1. Between which minutes does the lamp change? How many changes are there?
  2. What do the readings do between minutes 3 and 10?
  3. Give two hypotheses: a broken lamp, or the rule. Which one does the evidence support?
  4. Propose a fix with two thresholds. Which minute will the lamp switch on with your fix?
  5. How would you prove your fix works?

Method hints. Draw the readings as a line on squared paper. Draw your threshold as a flat line. Count how often the readings cross it.

Mini-project

Plan the course project, the night-light, on paper: which sensor, which thresholds (two), what the LED does, and a scripted table of readings for a whole evening. Rubric: two thresholds with a dead zone (2); a table that tests the dead zone (2); a clear log prediction (1); no real-sensor numbers without a datasheet (1).

Summary

  • A sensor turns something in the world into an electrical signal; a program reads it.
  • Light, distance and tilt: a number, a number (from an echo time), a yes/no.
  • A threshold turns a number into a decision.
  • Noise near one threshold makes decisions flicker.
  • Two thresholds (hysteresis) stop the flicker.
  • Real units, ranges and wiring come only from the kit's sensor datasheets.
