Story hook

Analogy

Yusuf's family has a big water tank on the roof. A thick pipe brings the water down to the garden. The water in that pipe pushes hard enough to spin a little water wheel Yusuf built.

Yusuf is small, and the main valve is stiff. He cannot turn it alone. So his father fitted a clever valve: a little lever opens it. Yusuf pushes the little lever with one finger, and the big flow from the tank does the heavy work.

A microcontroller is like Yusuf. It is very good at deciding, but its pins are weak. A motor is like the water wheel: it needs a big flow. In this chapter you meet the "clever valve" that lets a weak pin control a strong motor. It is called a motor driver.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a motor does and how to make it turn the other way.
  • Explain why a microcontroller pin must not drive a motor directly, and what a motor driver does instead.
  • Predict the motor's direction from the four switches of an H-bridge, and spot the forbidden combination.
  • Compare a pin's current limit with a motor's needs, using clearly labelled pretend numbers.
  • Diagnose a short circuit from a driver's command log.
Jargon box
Motor
Simple words: a part that turns electricity into spinning. Analogy: a muscle; or Yusuf's water wheel. Precise: an electric machine that converts electrical energy into rotation; in a simple DC motor, reversing the current reverses the direction. D1 D2
Motor driver
Simple words: a helper circuit that lets a weak signal switch a strong motor current. Analogy: a tap opened by a small control valve. Precise: a circuit (it can be a single chip) that uses a low-current control input to switch the motor's higher current from a separate supply. D2
Transistor
Simple words: an electronic switch with no moving parts, worked by a small signal. Analogy: a tap opened by a small control valve. Precise: a semiconductor device in which a small current or voltage at one terminal controls a larger current between two others. D2
H-bridge
Simple words: four switches around a motor that let it turn either way. Analogy: four valves around the water wheel that choose which side the water enters. Precise: a circuit of four switches (in practice transistors) arranged in an H, with the motor as the crossbar; closing opposite corners drives current through the motor in one direction or the other. D2
Short circuit
Simple words: a path that lets current rush from + to − without going through anything useful. Analogy: a burst pipe straight from the tank to the drain. Precise: an unintended low-resistance connection between points at different voltages, which lets a large current flow. D1
Current limit
Simple words: the most current a part may safely give or take. Analogy: the most water a small pipe can carry before it bursts. Precise: a maximum rating stated in the part's datasheet; exceeding it can damage the part. D3

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows an H-bridge. The four switches are S1 to S4. The motor M sits in the middle. Closing S1 and S4 sends current one way. Closing S3 and S2 sends it the other way.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A motor turns electricity into spinning. It is the robot's muscle. Connect a simple motor to a battery one way, and it spins one way. Swap the two wires, and it spins the other way.D1

Can the microcontroller from F0-42 run a motor straight from a pin? No. A pin is weak. It can only give a small current, like Yusuf's finger. A motor needs a much bigger current, like the water wheel. Asking the pin to do it can damage the chip.D2 D3

So we use a motor driver. It is like Yusuf's clever valve. The pin sends a small "go" signal. The driver then lets the big current flow from the battery to the motor. The pin decides; the driver does the heavy work.D2

How does the driver choose a direction? Picture four switches around the motor, in the shape of the letter H. Close the top-left and the bottom-right, and the current crosses the motor one way. Close the other two corners, and it crosses the other way. That is an H-bridge.

There is one rule you must never break. Never close both switches on the same side. That would join the battery's + straight to its −. That is a short circuit. Parts can get hot and be ruined.D1

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A microcontroller's output pin has a current limit. The datasheet states it. A motor's datasheet states how much current it draws, and that number rises when the motor starts or is held still.D2 D3 When the second number is bigger than the first, the pin must not drive the motor.

A motor driver contains transistors. A transistor is a switch with no moving parts. A small signal at its control terminal lets a bigger current flow through it. That is the registered analogy: a tap opened by a small control valve.D2

Four transistors arranged as an H-bridge give direction control. Closing S1 and S4 makes current flow left to right through the motor. Closing S3 and S2 makes it flow right to left. Closing S1 and S2 (or S3 and S4) makes a short from + to −, so a driver's control rules must forbid it.D2

There is a second reason for a driver. A motor contains coils of wire. When the current through a coil is switched off suddenly, the coil can produce a brief high voltage. Drivers are designed to deal with this so it does not reach the microcontroller.D2 F0-39's "where the analogy breaks" warned that coils (inductors) have no simple pipe partner; here is one place where that matters.

Not verified — check before relying on this

No motor, driver or board is named, and no real current is given. The numbers in Listing 1 are pretend exercise numbers: "pretend the board datasheet says a pin may give 10 mA; pretend the motor datasheet says it wants 300 mA". The real pin limit, motor current and driver ratings come from the datasheets of the parts in the kit chosen for this course (dossier part F, D3). Whether your kit's driver has built-in protection against the forbidden switch combination is also in its datasheet; do not assume it.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. To control speed, a driver can switch the motor on and off very quickly. The motor's own inertia smooths the pulses. The share of time it is on (the duty cycle) sets the average push. This technique is called pulse-width modulation (PWM).D2 When a real H-bridge changes direction, it must make sure the switches on one side are never on together, even for a moment, during the change.D2 The forensic lab shows what happens in our model when a program forgets that.

How the hardware actually does it

Inside a simple DC motor, current flows through coils of wire that sit near magnets. The current makes the coils act like magnets too. Pushing and pulling between the coils and the magnets turns the shaft. Reversing the current reverses the push, so the shaft turns the other way.D1 D2 In the driver, transistors replace our four switches, and the motor's current comes from the battery pack, not from the microcontroller's pin.

Worked example

Part 1: does the pin need help? (pretend numbers)

In this exercise, pretend the board datasheet says a pin may give at most 10 mA, and the motor datasheet says the motor wants 300 mA.

  1. Compare: 300 mA is more than 10 mA. The pin must not drive the motor.
  2. How many times more? 300 ÷ 10 = 30. The motor wants 30 times what the pin may give.
  3. Conclusion: use a motor driver. The pin only sends the control signal.

Part 2: read the H-bridge

  1. S1 = 1, S2 = 0, S3 = 0, S4 = 1. Opposite corners, left top to right bottom: forward.
  2. S1 = 0, S2 = 1, S3 = 1, S4 = 0. The other opposite corners: backward.
  3. S1 = 1, S2 = 1, S3 = 1, S4 = 0. S1 and S2 are both closed on the left side: short circuit, whatever the others do.
  4. All 0: no path through the motor: not driven.

Listings 1 and 2 below give the same answers in real runs.R1 R2

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — driver_check.cpp: compares a pretend pin limit with a pretend motor need.

// Can a microcontroller pin run a motor by itself? PRETEND numbers only:
// real limits come from your kit's microcontroller and motor datasheets.
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    const double pretendPinMaxMilliamps = 10.0;     // "pretend the board datasheet says 10 mA"
    const double pretendMotorNeedsMilliamps = 300.0; // "pretend the motor datasheet says 300 mA"

    const double ratio = pretendMotorNeedsMilliamps / pretendPinMaxMilliamps;
    std::cout << "pin can give at most: " << pretendPinMaxMilliamps << " mA\n";
    std::cout << "motor wants:          " << pretendMotorNeedsMilliamps << " mA\n";
    std::cout << "motor wants " << ratio << " times what the pin may give\n";
    if (pretendMotorNeedsMilliamps > pretendPinMaxMilliamps) {
        std::cout << "-> use a motor driver: the pin only sends the small 'go' signal\n";
    } else {
        std::cout << "-> still check the datasheets before connecting anything\n";
    }
    return 0;
}

Listing 2 — hbridge_sim.cpp: the H-bridge truth model.

// A motor driver drawn as four switches (an "H-bridge" truth model).
//   S1 = top-left,  S2 = bottom-left,  S3 = top-right,  S4 = bottom-right.
// The motor sits in the middle, between the left side and the right side.
// Each input line: step name, then S1 S2 S3 S4 (1 = closed, 0 = open).
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main()
{
    std::string step;
    int s1 = 0;
    int s2 = 0;
    int s3 = 0;
    int s4 = 0;

    while (std::cin >> step >> s1 >> s2 >> s3 >> s4) {
        std::cout << step << ": S1=" << s1 << " S2=" << s2 << " S3=" << s3 << " S4=" << s4
                  << " -> ";
        if ((s1 == 1 && s2 == 1) || (s3 == 1 && s4 == 1)) {
            std::cout << "SHORT CIRCUIT: battery + joined straight to battery - (never allowed)\n";
        } else if (s1 == 1 && s4 == 1) {
            std::cout << "current flows left to right: motor turns FORWARD\n";
        } else if (s3 == 1 && s2 == 1) {
            std::cout << "current flows right to left: motor turns BACKWARD\n";
        } else {
            std::cout << "no path through the motor: motor not driven\n";
        }
    }
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–4// A motor driver drawn as four switches …Names the switches like Figure 1 and gives the input format.The code and the figure use the same names.
10–14std::string step; int s1 …Jars for a step name and four switch states.One line of input fills them.
16while (std::cin >> step >> s1 >> s2 >> s3 >> s4)Reads one switch setting at a time.Test many settings from one file.
17–18std::cout << step …Prints the setting.The log shows what was asked.
19–20if ((s1 == 1 && s2 == 1) || (s3 == 1 && s4 == 1))Checks the forbidden combinations first.Safety rule before anything else.
21–22else if (s1 == 1 && s4 == 1)Opposite corners: forward.Current crosses left to right.
23–24else if (s3 == 1 && s2 == 1)Other corners: backward.Current crosses right to left.
25–26elseAnything else: no path through the motor.The motor is not driven.
29return 0;Ends successfully.Exit code 0.

forward 1 0 0 1

Where the analogy breaks

  1. A transistor is not an instant valve. The "clever valve" picture hides that a transistor takes a short time to switch and has thresholds, which is why direction changes need care (Layer 3).D2
  2. Coils fight back. Turning off a water wheel's valve does not send a spike back up the pipe to Yusuf's finger in the same way. A motor's coils can produce a brief high voltage when switched off; pipes have no simple partner for this.D2
  3. Muscles get tired and tell you; motors do not. An overloaded motor draws more current and gets warm. Only measurements and datasheets tell you its limits.D2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Motor connected to a pin; the board resets or stops workingThe motor draws more than the pin may giveCompare datasheet numbers (Listing 1's sum)Use a motor driver; disconnect power first
Simulator prints "SHORT CIRCUIT"Both switches on one side closedLook at S1+S2 and S3+S4 in the logOpen all switches before closing the new pair
Motor turns the wrong wayMotor wires swapped, or wrong corner pairCheck which pair is closed for "forward"Swap the pair in the program (or the wires, power off)
Motor does not move, no shortNo opposite-corner pair is closedRead the switch states in the logClose S1+S4 or S3+S2
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-42 drove an LED from a pin; F0-43 read sensors. What carries over: pins high and low, the program loop, switches in series and parallel (F0-41), and Ohm's-law thinking about current (F0-39).D1 What changes: most dangerous first: motors move, can pinch fingers and can start unexpectedly; they need much more current than a pin can give, so a driver and a separate battery supply are needed; one wrong switch combination is a short circuit.S1 D2 What comes next: F0-45 puts sensors and motors together: a simulated robot follows a line.

Check yourself

  1. How do you make a simple DC motor turn the other way?
  2. Why must a microcontroller pin not drive a motor directly?
  3. Pretend numbers: a pin may give 5 mA; the motor wants 250 mA. How many times too much is that?
  4. Which switch setting is a short circuit? (a) S1=1 S4=1 (b) S3=1 S2=1 (c) S3=1 S4=1 (d) all open
  5. Which registered analogy describes a transistor, and where does it break?
  6. Explain in your own words what an H-bridge is for.
  7. Apply it to a new case: a fan should blow, then suck air back. Which switch pairs would you use, and what must happen between the two?

Lab

Safety

Motors move. They can pinch fingers and can start unexpectedly. Part B: an adult supervises the whole time; only the battery-powered kit chosen for this course; no mains, no LiPo batteries, no propellers. Keep fingers, hair and loose clothing away from wheels and gears. Test with the wheels lifted off the table. Disconnect the battery pack before changing any wire. If anything gets warm or smells, hands off and tell your adult.S1

Goal: predict motor direction from switch settings in the simulator, find forbidden settings, and (supervised, when a kit exists) run a motor forwards and backwards through the kit's driver.

Hardware and software needed: Part A: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Part B: the kit's microcontroller board, motor driver, motor and battery pack, with their datasheets.

Part A — simulator

  1. Build and run Listings 1 and 2. Compare with the worked example.
  2. Write all 16 settings of S1–S4 into a new input file. Predict each result.
  3. Run Listing 2 on your file. How many settings are short circuits? Check against your prediction.
  4. Change Listing 1's pretend numbers to your own pretend pair. Predict, run, compare.

Part B — a real motor through the kit's driver (supervised)

Not verified — check before relying on this

Untested on hardware (AH-26): no kit, motor or driver was available in this build. The steps are kit-independent; all wiring, control inputs and program instructions come from the kit's documentation and the driver's datasheet (D3). The adult checks each step there.

  1. With your adult, find in the driver's documentation: which inputs mean forward, backward and stop.
  2. Power off. Wire board, driver, motor and battery pack as the documentation shows. Wheels off the table.
  3. Your adult checks the wiring. Then power on.
  4. Run a program (from the kit's documentation) that goes forward, stops, then goes backward.
  5. Power off before any change.

Expected observations

Part A: 7 of the 16 settings are short circuits (count them yourself first). Part B (untested): the motor turns one way, stops, then turns the other way.

Verification

Your predictions for all 16 settings match the simulator. On the kit, direction changes only when the documented inputs change.

Troubleshooting

  • Simulator skips a line → five fields needed → count them.
  • Motor turns the wrong way → swap the forward/backward inputs in the program, or the motor wires with power off.
  • Motor hums but does not turn → wheels blocked, or the battery is weak → power off, check with your adult.

Extension

Write a safe "change direction" sequence for the simulator: forward, all open, backward. Show that no step is a short.

Forensic lab

Scenario. Mei's robot program drove forward and then tried to back up. In our simulated driver, the log flagged a problem at that moment. Find the cause.

Evidence pack. The real output of hbridge_log.cpp replaying the six commands Mei's program sent:

Questions.

  1. At what time does the problem appear? Which switches are closed?
  2. What did Mei's program want at that moment? Which switch should already have been open?
  3. Give two hypotheses: "the driver is broken" or "the program changed switches in the wrong order". Which does the evidence support?
  4. Write a safe sequence of commands for going from forward to backward.
  5. Why would this matter much more on a real driver than in our simulator?

Method hints. Compare each line with the one before. Which switches changed? Was anything closed before something else was opened?

Mini-project

Make a poster: "Why my robot needs a driver". Show Yusuf's clever valve, Figure 1's H-bridge, the forbidden settings in red with a second marker (a cross), and the pretend-number sum from Listing 1 labelled "pretend". Rubric: analogy mapped explicitly (2); H-bridge settings correct (2); forbidden settings marked by shape as well as colour (1); numbers labelled pretend (1).

Summary

  • A motor turns electricity into spinning; reversing the current reverses it.
  • A pin is weak; a motor needs much more current: use a motor driver.
  • A transistor is a tap opened by a small control valve.
  • An H-bridge: S1+S4 forward, S3+S2 backward.
  • Never close both switches on one side: short circuit.
  • Change direction by opening everything first, then closing the new pair.
  • Real ratings come only from the kit's datasheets; motors are tested with wheels lifted and an adult present.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Reverse the current through it: swap its two connections (or use an H-bridge).
  2. The motor needs more current than the pin's current limit; the pin (and the chip) can be damaged, and the motor's coils can send voltage spikes back.
  3. 250 ÷ 5 = 50 times.
  4. (c): S3 and S4 are both on the right side. (a) is forward, (b) is backward, (d) is not driven.
  5. "A tap opened by a small control valve". It breaks because a transistor takes a short time to switch and has thresholds and analog behaviour; a valve picture hides this.
  6. In your words: it lets a motor turn either way by choosing which pair of opposite switches is closed.
  7. Blow: S1+S4; suck: S3+S2 (or the other way round, depending on wiring). Between them, open all switches (and let the fan slow down) before closing the new pair.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: at 1.5s the log shows S1=1, S2=1, S3=1, S4=0 and "SHORT CIRCUIT". The wish was "backward". At 1.6s the setting is the correct backward pair (S3+S2) with S1 open. Root cause: the program closed the new pair (S2, S3) before opening S1 from the forward pair, so S1 and S2 were closed together on the left side. Hypotheses: "driver broken" is ruled out: the simulated driver is the same code that gives correct results at every other step, and the bad line has a bad command in it. Fix: forward (S1+S4) → all open → backward (S3+S2). Verification: run the fixed command list through hbridge_log.cpp; no SHORT CIRCUIT line appears. Why it matters more for real: on a real driver, a short joins battery + to − through the switches; large current flows and parts can overheat (D1, D2); our simulator only prints a warning. How the evidence was made: hbridge_log.in was written by the author with the wrong order at 1.5s, then replayed by hbridge_log.cpp in this build (R2).

A simulated robot follows a line

← F0-44 · course KID103 · catalogue · F0-46 →

Story hook

Analogy

Rosa and her little brother Leo play a game in the hallway. A long ribbon lies on the floor. It curves a little to the left, then to the right. Leo must walk along it while looking only at his feet.

"Ribbon under my feet: walk straight," Leo says. "Ribbon a bit to my right: step right. Ribbon a bit to my left: step left." He follows it all the way to the kitchen.

Then Rosa puts a sock over one of Leo's eyes for fun. He gets mixed up between left and right. He steps the wrong way, and the ribbon is gone. "I lost it!" he laughs.

Leo was doing exactly what a line-following robot does: look, decide, step, again and again. In this chapter you run that robot in our text simulator. You will also see what happens when its "eyes" are mixed up.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain how a line-following robot works: sense, decide, act, repeat.
  • Trace the robot's steering rule by hand, row by row, on a text track.
  • Run the course's line-following simulator and change the track.
  • Diagnose a robot that loses the line, from its log, and find the swapped sensors.
  • Name two ways a real robot differs from our grid robot.
Jargon box
Line follower
Simple words: a robot that drives along a line drawn on the floor. Analogy: Leo walking along the ribbon, looking at his feet. Precise: a mobile robot whose program uses downward-facing sensors to detect a line and steers to keep the line under its sensors. D2
Control loop
Simple words: look, decide, act, and do it again. Analogy: riding a bicycle and correcting your balance all the time. Precise: a repeated cycle that measures the system, compares the measurement with what is wanted, and applies a correction. D1
Feedback
Simple words: using what you sense now to choose what you do next. Analogy: Leo looks at the ribbon after every step. Precise: using a measurement of a system's output to adjust its input. D1
Error (control)
Simple words: how far you are from where you want to be. Analogy: how far the ribbon is from Leo's feet. Precise: the difference between the wanted value and the measured value; here, which side of the robot the line is on. D1 Not the same as a bug or a compiler error.
Grid world
Simple words: a pretend world made of squares, printed as text. Analogy: a floor of square tiles. Precise: a simulation in which positions are whole-number cells of a grid and the robot moves one cell per step; our track is a list of text rows. R1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the robot on the text track. It has three sensors in a row under its front: left, middle, right. Each one says 1 if it sees the line and 0 if it sees floor.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A line-following robot has sensors that look down at the floor. Each sensor can tell line from floor. Our robot has three: one on the left, one in the middle, one on the right.

The robot's program is a short rule, like Leo's. If the middle sensor sees the line, drive straight. If only the left one sees it, steer left. If only the right one sees it, steer right. If none sees it, the robot has lost the line.

The robot does this again and again. Look. Decide. Move. Look again. This repeating cycle is a control loop. Using what you see to choose what you do next is called feedback.D1

Our robot lives in a grid world made of text. The floor is dots. The line is # signs. The robot is the letter R. It drives down one row each step. At each row it can move one square left or right. The program prints every row, so you can watch its path.R1

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A control loop has three parts. It measures where the system is. It compares that with where it should be. It applies a correction. The difference between wanted and measured is called the error.D1

In our robot, the wanted state is "line under the middle sensor". The three sensors measure a rough error: line to the left, line in the middle, or line to the right. The correction is one step in the direction of the line. That is why the rule "steers back to the line".

This is the simplest kind of correction: a fixed step, whatever the size of the error. A smoother rule is possible, where a bigger error gives a bigger correction. RB101 (F9-05) and later RB202 build that idea step by step, up to the PID controller.D1

The rule depends on the sensors being where the program thinks they are. If the left and right sensors are swapped, every correction goes the wrong way. A small error becomes a bigger one, and the robot drives away from the line. That is the forensic lab.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. One common design steers with two driven wheels, one on each side. Turning the right wheel faster than the left makes the robot curve left, and the other way round.D2 Each wheel's speed is set through a motor driver (F0-44). A real robot also moves continuously: it can overshoot the line and swing back and forth. How strongly to correct is a trade-off between reacting fast and swinging. RB101's forensic lab "the robot that zig-zags" studies exactly that.D1

How the hardware actually does it

On a real robot, each line sensor is a small light sensor pointed at the floor; some designs add a small light source next to it. A dark line and a light floor reflect different amounts of light, so the sensor's reading differs, and a threshold (F0-43) turns it into "line" or "floor".D3 The program reads the sensors, decides, and sets the two motor speeds through the driver, many times per second. Which sensors your kit has, and their thresholds, come from its datasheets (D4). This chapter uses only the simulator.

Worked example

Trace the robot by hand on the first rows of the track in Listing 1. Columns are numbered from 0. The robot starts in column 4.

  1. Row 0 ....#.......: the line is in column 4. Middle sensor (column 4) sees it. Sensors 010. Go straight. Robot stays in column 4.
  2. Row 1: same. Straight.
  3. Row 2 .....#......: the line moved to column 5. Left (3) sees floor, middle (4) sees floor, right (5) sees the line. Sensors 001. Steer right: robot moves to column 5.
  4. Row 3 ......#.....: line in column 6. Robot at 5. Sensors 001 again. Steer right to column 6.
  5. Row 6 ......#..... (after the bend at row 5): robot is at column 7, line at 6. Left (6) sees it. Sensors 100. Steer left to column 6.

Check your trace against the real output below: rows 2 and 3 say "steer right", row 6 says "steer left".R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — line_follow.cpp: the line-following robot on a text grid.

// A simulated robot follows a line drawn on a text grid.
// '#' is the line. The robot drives down one row per step. It has three
// sensors (left, middle, right) that look at the row it is on.
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    std::vector<std::string> track = {
        "....#.......",
        "....#.......",
        ".....#......",
        "......#.....",
        "......#.....",
        ".......#....",
        "......#.....",
        ".....#......",
        "....#.......",
        "....#.......",
    };
    const int width = static_cast<int>(track[0].size());
    int col = 4; // the robot starts on the line

    for (std::size_t row = 0; row < track.size(); ++row) {
        const bool left = col > 0 && track[row][col - 1] == '#';
        const bool middle = track[row][col] == '#';
        const bool right = col + 1 < width && track[row][col + 1] == '#';

        std::string action = "straight";
        if (!middle && left) {
            col -= 1;            // line is to the left: steer left
            action = "steer left";
        } else if (!middle && right) {
            col += 1;            // line is to the right: steer right
            action = "steer right";
        } else if (!middle) {
            action = "LOST the line";
        }

        std::string picture = track[row];
        picture[col] = 'R';
        std::cout << picture << "  sensors " << left << middle << right << "  " << action << "\n";
    }
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–3// A simulated robot follows a line …Comments describing the world.Say what the symbols mean.
4–6#include …Tools for printing, text and lists.The track is a list of text rows.
10–21std::vector<std::string> track = { … };The track: ten rows, # is the line.Edit these rows to draw your own track.
22const int width = static_cast<int>(track[0].size());How many columns a row has.Used to stop the right sensor looking off the edge.
23int col = 4;The robot's starting column.It starts on the line.
25for (std::size_t row = 0; row < track.size(); ++row) {One step per row.The control loop: one round per row.
26const bool left = col > 0 && track[row][col - 1] == '#';Left sensor: is the cell to the left a #?col > 0 stops it looking off the left edge.
27const bool middle = track[row][col] == '#';Middle sensor.The cell under the robot.
28const bool right = col + 1 < width && …;Right sensor.Guarded against the right edge.
30std::string action = "straight";The default decision.Used when the middle sees the line.
31–33if (!middle && left) { col -= 1; … }Line only on the left: move one column left.The correction towards the line.
34–36else if (!middle && right) { col += 1; … }Line only on the right: move right.The mirror correction.
37–39else if (!middle) { action = "LOST the line"; }No sensor sees the line.The robot reports it is lost.
41–42std::string picture = track[row]; picture[col] = 'R';Copies the row and draws R at the robot's new column.A picture of the path.
43std::cout << picture << " sensors " …Prints the row, the three sensor values and the decision.A log you can trace by hand.
45return 0;Ends successfully.Exit code 0.

Every printed row has R on a # cell: the robot never lost the line.R1

Where the analogy breaks

  1. Leo can see the whole ribbon ahead; the robot cannot. Leo can look up and plan. Our robot sees only three cells in its own row. It reacts; it does not plan.R1
  2. Real robots do not move in tidy squares. Our robot jumps exactly one column. A real robot rolls, turns smoothly, can overshoot and swing, and its wheels can slip.D1 D2
  3. Leo notices when something is odd. With a sock over one eye, Leo laughed and stopped. A robot with swapped sensors keeps following its rule, even as it drives away from the line.R2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Robot steers away from the line and loses itLeft and right sensors swapped (in wiring or code)Find the first row where it steers; is the line on that side?Swap them back
Robot loses the line at a sharp bendThe line moved more than one column in one rowLook at the track: does any row jump by 2 or more?Draw gentler bends, or let the robot steer further
Program crashes or prints garbage on your own trackRows of different lengthsCount the characters in each rowMake every row the same width
Robot starts "LOST"Start column not on the lineCompare col on line 23 with row 0Set the start column to the # in row 0
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-43 turned sensor readings into decisions; F0-44 turned decisions into motion through a driver. What carries over: thresholds, if/else rules, logs you can trace, simulator first.R1 What changes: most dangerous first: now the robot's own motion changes what it senses next, so a wrong rule can make things worse at every step (the swapped-sensor robot); the program runs in a loop that never waits for a human.D1 What comes next: F0-46 collects the safety habits you need before any of this moves on a real table; RB101 (F9-05) makes the steering smoother.

Check yourself

  1. What do the three sensor values 001 mean, and what does the robot do?
  2. Name the three steps of a control loop.
  3. The robot is in column 6. The row is .....#....... Which sensors see the line, and where does the robot go?
  4. Which track would our robot fail on? (a) a straight line (b) a line that moves one column every row (c) a line that jumps three columns in one row (d) a line that bends left and then right
  5. What is the "error" in our robot?
  6. Explain in your own words why swapped sensors make the robot drive away from the line.
  7. Apply it to a new case: a robot vacuum should follow a wall on its right. It has one sensor that sees "wall near" or "wall far". Write a rule like ours.

Lab

Safety

This lab uses only the simulator: no moving parts. A real line-following robot comes later (RB101), with an adult, wheels lifted off the table for first tests, and only a battery-powered kit designed for children.S1

Goal: run the line follower, draw your own track, and find the sharpest bend it can follow.

Hardware and software needed: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). No hardware.

Steps

  1. Build and run Listing 1. Trace three rows by hand and compare.
  2. Draw your own track on squared paper: twelve rows, each the same width, one # per row.
  3. Type it into lines 10–21 (add rows if you like). Set the start column on line 23.
  4. Predict the robot's path. Build and run. Compare.
  5. Make a bend where the line jumps two columns in one row. Predict, then run.

Expected observations

On Listing 1's track, the real output above. On your track, the robot follows every bend of one column per row; a two-column jump makes it lose the line.

Verification

Your hand trace matches the program's log row by row, including where it gets lost.

Troubleshooting

  • Build error in the track → a missing comma or quote → compare with line 11.
  • Strange crash on your track → rows of different width → count characters.
  • LOST at row 0 → wrong start column → fix line 23.

Extension

Let the robot steer two columns when it is lost, towards the side where it last saw the line. Which jump can it follow now? (You need a new jar to remember the last side.)

  2. In that row, which side was the line really on? Which way did the robot steer?

Mini-project

Design a "race track" of at least fifteen rows that the robot can follow from start to finish, with at least three bends. Then make one change that makes it fail, and explain why. Rubric: track followed to the end (2); three bends (1); a failing change with a correct explanation (2); hand trace of two rows (1).

Summary

  • A line follower senses, decides and acts, again and again: a control loop.
  • Our rule: middle → straight; left only → steer left; right only → steer right; none → lost.
  • Feedback: what the robot senses now decides its next move.
  • The grid robot can follow bends of one column per row.
  • Swapped sensors turn every correction the wrong way.
  • Real robots roll, overshoot and slip; RB101 makes the steering smoother.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Left 0, middle 0, right 1: the line is to the right; the robot steers right one column.
  2. Sense (measure), decide (compare with what is wanted), act (correct); then repeat.
  3. Robot at 6: left sensor looks at column 5, which is the #. Sensors 100: steer left to column 5.
  4. (c). A jump of three columns leaves all three sensors on floor: LOST. (a), (b) and (d) move at most one column per row, which the rule handles.
  5. Which side of the middle sensor the line is on (left, none, right).
  6. In your words: the program thinks the line is on the left when it is on the right, so it steps away; the next row the line is even farther, until no sensor sees it.
  7. For example: wall far → steer right a little; wall near → steer left a little; repeat every step. (A one-sensor robot wobbles along the wall; that is fine for this answer.)

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: rows 0 and 1 are straight. In row 2 the line is in column 5 (to the right), but the log says sensors 100 and "steer left"; the robot moves to column 3. From row 3 the sensors read 000 and the robot reports "LOST the line"; in row 8 a sensor sees the line again, but the robot steers away from it once more. Hypotheses: "the track changed" is ruled out: the # cells printed in every row are the same as in Listing 1's log. "Sensors swapped" fits: in row 2 the line was on the right but the left sensor reported it. Root cause: lines 25 and 27 of line_follow_swapped.cpp read the wrong cells: left reads col + 1 and right reads col - 1. Fix: swap them back, as in Listing 1; on a real robot, check which physical sensor is wired to which input. Verification: the fixed program produces Listing 1's log (R1). Prevention: a test track whose first bend goes to the right (and another to the left), checked at the first steering row. How the evidence was made: Listing 1 with the two sensor lines deliberately swapped, run in this build (R2).

Story hook

Analogy

When Zainab cooks with her uncle, they have habits. They wash their hands first. They turn pan handles inwards, so nobody knocks them. They use oven gloves for hot trays. And her uncle is always in the kitchen when the stove is on.

Zainab does not think of these as rules any more. They are habits. She does them without being told, like brushing her teeth.

Making things with circuits and motors also needs habits. Some dangers you can see, like a spinning wheel. Some you cannot see, like a battery whose two ends are touching the same piece of metal. This chapter turns the safety rules of the whole course into habits, and gives you a small program that will not say "go" until every habit is checked.

What you will be able to do

  • State the faculty's safety rules: adult supervision, kits designed for children, simulator first, no mains, no LiPo batteries, no propellers.
  • Explain the reason behind each habit on the checklist.
  • Run the course's safety-checklist program and explain why a missing answer counts as "no".
  • Investigate a "warm battery" incident from its checklist record and say which habits would have prevented it.
  • Write your own maker checklist for the course project.
Jargon box
Supervision
Simple words: a responsible adult is with you, watching, the whole time. Analogy: Zainab's uncle staying in the kitchen while the stove is on. Precise: in this university, an adult present for every physical activity at levels L0–L2, able to stop the activity at once. S1
Mains electricity
Simple words: the electricity in the wall sockets of a building. Analogy: the high-pressure water main under the street, not the garden hose. Precise: the building's alternating-current supply from the electricity network; its voltage is dangerous, and this university has no mains-voltage labs at any level. S1 D1
LiPo battery
Simple words: a kind of rechargeable battery used in drones and some robots, which can catch fire if mistreated. Analogy: a pressure cooker: useful, but only with strict rules. Precise: a lithium polymer battery; it can catch fire if punctured, over-charged, over-discharged, short-circuited or charged unattended. It is not used in F0. S1
Short circuit
Simple words: a path that lets current rush from + to − without going through anything useful. Analogy: a burst pipe straight from the tank to the drain. Precise: an unintended low-resistance connection between points at different voltages, which lets a large current flow (defined in F0-44). D1
Checklist
Simple words: a list you go through, item by item, before you start. Analogy: checking you have every ingredient before you cook. Precise: a written list of conditions that must all be confirmed before an activity begins. R1
Fail-safe default
Simple words: if you are not sure, choose the safe answer. Analogy: if you do not know whether the stove is off, treat it as on. Precise: a design rule: when information is missing or a part fails, the system goes to its safe state; our checklist treats a missing answer as "no". R1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the safe order of work in this course. Every physical step has a gate before it: the checklist.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

In this course, some rules are never broken. An adult watches every physical activity. You use only the battery-powered kit chosen for the course, designed for children. You try every idea in the simulator first.S1

Three things are never used in this part of the university. No mains electricity: nothing from a wall socket. No LiPo batteries: the kind that can catch fire if mistreated. No propellers: they can cut skin and eyes.S1

Then come the habits. Disconnect the battery before you change any wire. Keep the table clear of metal things, drinks and loose parts. Keep fingers and hair away from wheels and gears. Test motors with the wheels in the air. If anything gets warm or smells, take your hands away and call your adult.S1 D1

A good way to build habits is a checklist. You answer every question before you start. If one answer is "no", you stop and fix it first. Pilots and surgeons use checklists. Makers do too.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Each habit has a reason. Knowing the reason helps you keep the habit when nobody is watching.

HabitReason
Adult watching, the whole timeAn adult can stop things at once and decide what to do if something goes wrong.S1
Simulator firstMistakes in the simulator cost nothing; mistakes with parts can ruin them or make them hot.S1
Battery disconnected while wiringA loose wire can touch the wrong place and make a short circuit while you work.D1
No metal objects on the tableA paperclip, key or coin can touch both battery terminals and make a short circuit.D1
No drinks on the tableSpilled liquid can connect parts that should not touch, and ruin parts.D1
Only the course kit and its batteriesThe kit is chosen for children and its parts are documented; unknown parts have unknown limits.S1 D2
Wheels lifted, hands off moving partsMotors can pinch fingers and can start unexpectedly.S1
Warm or smelly: hands off, call the adultHeat and smell are signs of too much current; the adult disconnects power.D1
Tidy up: battery out, parts awaySmall parts and batteries left out can be lost, shorted or reached by younger children.D2
Not verified — check before relying on this

This chapter gives general habits only. It gives no battery numbers, no charging rules and no storage rules, because they belong to specific products. The kit and its battery pack are not chosen yet (decision left to the owner). Before any physical lab, the adult reads the kit maker's safety instructions and the battery maker's instructions (D2), and adds their rules to the checklist.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Engineers who build machines that can hurt people use the same ideas, in more detail. One is the fail-safe default: when information is missing, the system chooses the safe state. Our checklist program does this on lines 21–22 of Listing 1: a missing answer counts as "no". Another is an interlock: a machine that will not start unless a guard is closed. Faculty F11 (security and safety-critical engineering) studies these ideas properly.R1

How the hardware actually does it

Why does a short circuit make a battery warm? A short circuit has almost no resistance, so by Ohm's law a large current flows. That current passes through the battery itself and the wires. Every part with some resistance turns electrical energy into heat, and with a large current, that heat builds up fast.D1 D3 Nothing glows or moves to warn you first. That is why the habits must come before the danger, not after.

Worked example

Elif answers the six questions of Listing 1: yes, yes, no, yes, yes, yes.

  1. Count the "no" answers: one (question 3, the table is not clear).
  2. The rule: start only if every answer is yes. One "no" means stop.
  3. The program prints "STOP: 1 check(s) not passed".
  4. Elif clears the table and runs the checklist again: six yes answers.
  5. Now the program says she may start, with her adult watching.

A second case: Ari's answer file has only five answers. The sixth question gets no answer. The program counts it as "no" and says STOP. Missing information never counts as safe.

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — safety_check.cpp: a checklist that will not say "go" until every answer is yes.

// A pre-build safety checklist. It reads one answer (y or n) per question
// and refuses to say "go" unless every answer is y.
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    const std::vector<std::string> questions = {
        "Is your adult in the room and watching?",
        "Is the battery pack disconnected while you change wires?",
        "Is the table clear of metal objects, drinks and loose parts?",
        "Are you using only the battery-powered kit chosen for this course?",
        "Has the circuit already worked in the simulator?",
        "Do you know to stop, hands off, and call your adult if anything gets warm or smells?",
    };

    int missing = 0;
    for (const std::string& question : questions) {
        std::string answer;
        if (!(std::cin >> answer)) {
            answer = "n"; // no answer counts as no
        }
        const bool ok = (answer == "y");
        if (!ok) {
            ++missing;
        }
        std::cout << (ok ? "[yes] " : "[NO]  ") << question << "\n";
    }
    if (missing == 0) {
        std::cout << "All checks passed: you may start, with your adult watching.\n";
    } else {
        std::cout << "STOP: " << missing << " check(s) not passed. Fix them first.\n";
    }
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–2// A pre-build safety checklist …Comments.State the rule: no "go" unless every answer is y.
3–5#include …Tools for reading, printing, text and lists.The questions are a list of text.
9–16const std::vector<std::string> questions = { … };The six checklist questions.Add your kit's own rules here.
18int missing = 0;Counts the "no" answers.Starts at zero.
19for (const std::string& question : questions) {Goes through the questions in order.Nothing is skipped.
20–23if (!(std::cin >> answer)) { answer = "n"; }Reads an answer; if there is none, uses "n".The fail-safe default.
24const bool ok = (answer == "y");Only an exact "y" counts as yes."maybe" or a typo counts as no.
25–27if (!ok) { ++missing; }Counts each "no".The gate needs this count.
28std::cout << (ok ? "[yes] " : "[NO] ") << question …Prints each question with its answer.A record you can show your adult.
30–34if (missing == 0) { … } else { … "STOP: " … }The gate: all yes, or stop.Figure 1's checklist step.
35return 0;Ends successfully.Exit code 0 (the program ran; the answer is in the text).

Input safety_check.in: six lines, each y.

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined safety_check.cpp -o safety_check, then ./safety_check < safety_check.in.

[yes] Is your adult in the room and watching?
[yes] Is the battery pack disconnected while you change wires?
[yes] Is the table clear of metal objects, drinks and loose parts?
[yes] Are you using only the battery-powered kit chosen for this course?
[yes] Has the circuit already worked in the simulator?
[yes] Do you know to stop, hands off, and call your adult if anything gets warm or smells?
All checks passed: you may start, with your adult watching.

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-46/safety_check.out; run record safety_check.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:27:36Z; exit code: 0.

All six answers were yes, so the gate opens.R1

Where the analogy breaks

  1. A hot stove warns you; a short circuit may not. A stove glows or a pan steams. A shorted battery can look exactly the same as a safe one until it is already warm. You cannot see current.D1
  2. Kitchen water is safe to touch; electricity is not always. The water picture of F0-39 makes electricity feel friendly. Our kit's battery is chosen to be low voltage, but mains electricity can kill. The water picture must never make you curious about a wall socket.S1
  3. Kitchen habits are learned at home; kit rules come from documents. Your uncle can show you how to hold a knife. The safe way to use a specific battery or charger is written by its maker, and only that document is the rule.D2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Battery or wire gets warmA short circuit, or too much currentAdult disconnects power first; then look for metal touching both terminals, or a missing resistorRemove the short; follow the F0-40 resistor rule; run the checklist again
Motor starts while your hand is near itTesting with power connected and wheels downWas the test step done with wheels lifted?Lift wheels; keep hands off; power on last
Checklist says STOP but you "feel ready"A "no" answer you did not noticeRead the [NO] linesFix that item; never skip the gate
Checklist says STOP with all answers yesAn answer typed as "Y" or "yes" instead of "y"Look for [NO] next to an item you meant to answer yesType exactly y; this strictness is on purpose
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-39 to F0-45 built circuits, blinked LEDs, read sensors, drove motors through a driver and followed a line, each with a safety box. What carries over: every rule from those safety boxes, now gathered into one checklist; the short circuit from F0-44; the simulator-first habit.S1 What changes: most dangerous first: you will soon build the course project and, in RB101, a moving robot, so habits must work without being reminded; and new kits bring new maker instructions that join your checklist.D2 What comes next: the KID103 project (a night-light, simulator first) and RB101 (F9-07 robot safety), which uses these habits on real robots.

Troubleshooting

  • Build error after adding a question → missing comma or quote → compare with line 10.
  • Count seems wrong → an answer typed as "Y" → only lowercase y counts.
  • Program waits forever → you ran it without < file → type answers, or add the input file.

Extension

Make the program print, for each [NO], a one-line reason taken from the Layer 2 table.

Forensic lab

Scenario: "The warm battery". During a kit session, Ravi felt the battery pack get warm. His adult disconnected it at once, and nobody was hurt. Ravi had run the checklist that morning. Here is his recorded run.

Evidence pack. (1) The real output of the checklist with the answers Ravi typed that day (safety_check_incident.cpp, the same code as Listing 1, with his answer file):

[yes] Is your adult in the room and watching?
[NO]  Is the battery pack disconnected while you change wires?
[NO]  Is the table clear of metal objects, drinks and loose parts?
[yes] Are you using only the battery-powered kit chosen for this course?
[yes] Has the circuit already worked in the simulator?
[yes] Do you know to stop, hands off, and call your adult if anything gets warm or smells?
STOP: 2 check(s) not passed. Fix them first.

Real output, copied from university/labs/F0-46/safety_check_incident.out; run record safety_check_incident.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:27:37Z; exit code: 0.

(2) The adult's note, written after the session (a story for this lab, not program output): "Ravi was moving the LED while the battery pack was still connected. A paperclip from his homework was on the table next to the battery clip. When I disconnected the pack, the paperclip was lying across both battery terminals. The LED loop itself was wired correctly."

Questions.

  1. Which checklist items were answered "no"? What did the program say?
  2. Give two hypotheses for the warm battery. Which does the evidence support?
  3. Which two habits would each have prevented this?
  4. What did Ravi do that the checklist does not allow?
  5. Suggest one change to the session (not to the program) that would make starting after a STOP harder.

Method hints. Line up the checklist record with the adult's note. For each [NO], ask: "does the note show this risk happening?" Remember F0-44's short circuit and the "How the hardware actually does it" section above.

Mini-project

Write the safety checklist for the course project (the night-light): at least eight questions, each with a reason, adapted from Listing 1 and the kit's instructions. Put it into the program and run it. Rubric: eight relevant questions (2); each with a correct reason (2); includes the faculty rules (simulator first, adult, no mains, no LiPo) (1); a real run shown to your adult (1).

Summary

  • Always: adult supervision, the course kit designed for children, simulator first.
  • Never in F0: mains electricity, LiPo batteries, propellers.
  • Habits: battery disconnected while wiring; clear table; hands and hair away from moving parts; wheels lifted for tests.
  • Warm or smelly: hands off, call your adult.
  • A checklist is a gate: any "no" means stop and fix.
  • Fail-safe default: missing information counts as "no".
  • Product-specific rules come from the kit and battery makers' instructions.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Mains electricity, LiPo batteries, propellers.
  2. A loose wire can touch the wrong place and make a short circuit while you work.
  3. Metal conducts; a coin touching both terminals is a short circuit.
  4. (b). Five answers are y; the sixth is missing and counts as "no" (fail-safe default). (a) would treat missing information as safe. (c) the program always prints a result. (d) only one answer is missing.
  5. If you are not sure, choose the safe state. Example: if you do not know whether the iron is off, treat it as on and ask an adult.
  6. In your words: you cannot see a short circuit; the battery looks normal until it is already warm, while a stove warns you by glowing or steaming.
  7. For example: "Is the buzzer the one from the course kit, wired as its instructions show?" Reason: unknown parts have unknown limits.
  8. The kit and battery makers' own instructions, read by the adult (D2).

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: two [NO] lines: "battery pack disconnected while you change wires" and "table clear of metal objects, drinks and loose parts"; the program printed "STOP: 2 check(s) not passed". Hypotheses: (1) a faulty battery; (2) a short circuit across the battery terminals. The adult's note says the paperclip was lying across both terminals and the LED loop was correct, which supports (2); a faulty battery is not needed to explain the evidence (it could be checked later with the battery maker's instructions). Root cause: a short circuit through the paperclip, made possible by a connected battery while wiring and a metal object on the table. Habits that prevent it: disconnect the battery while wiring; clear the table of metal. What Ravi did wrong: he started even though the checklist said STOP. Prevention: the adult reads the checklist output before the kit box is opened (a human gate as well as the program's). How the evidence was made: safety_check_incident.in was written by the author with "n" for questions 2 and 3 and run through the same checklist code (R1); the adult's note is a story written for this lab, not a record of a real event.

Story hook

Analogy

The restaurant on the corner has a water tank on its roof. Every morning, Rosa, the manager, checks the plumbing before the cooks arrive. A pipe runs from the tank down to the kitchen taps, and a drain pipe carries the water back to a pump that lifts it up again.

One day the kitchen tap on the ground floor gushes, but the tap on the first floor only dribbles. Tomás, the new cook, asks why. "The water on the ground floor has fallen further," says Rosa. "It has more pressure behind it. What matters is the difference in height between the tank and the tap."

Tomás then asks a second question: "How much water goes through the pipe each minute?" That is a different thing. Pressure is the push. Flow is the amount moving. Electricity has both too, and engineers keep them carefully apart. This chapter is about that push and that flow.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain charge, current and voltage with the plumbing picture and with their precise definitions and units.
  • Calculate the charge moved by a steady current, Q = I × t, and check it with a small C++ program.
  • Explain why a voltage is always measured between two points, and what "ground" means.
  • Predict the sign of a voltmeter reading from where the red and black probes are placed.
  • Diagnose a set of readings in which the probes were swapped.
Jargon box
Charge
Simple words: the "stuff" of electricity: tiny particles carry it, and it can be positive or negative. Analogy: the water itself in the restaurant's pipes. Precise: electric charge is a property of particles such as electrons (negative) and protons (positive); it is measured in coulombs (C). D2 D3
Current
Simple words: how much charge flows past a point each second. Analogy: how much water flows through a pipe each second. Precise: the rate of flow of charge, I = Q ÷ t for a steady flow; measured in amperes (A); one ampere is one coulomb per second. D2 D3
Voltage
Simple words: the push that makes charge move, measured between two points. Analogy: the difference in water pressure between two places in the plumbing. Precise: the potential difference between two points: the energy given to (or taken from) each coulomb of charge that moves between them; measured in volts (V), where one volt is one joule per coulomb. D2 D3
Potential
Simple words: the "height" of one point, compared with a chosen zero point. Analogy: how high a tap is above the basement floor. Precise: the voltage of a point measured from a chosen reference point; only differences of potential have physical meaning. D2
Ground (reference)
Simple words: the point we agree to call 0 V. Analogy: the basement floor from which every height in the building is measured. Precise: the node of a circuit chosen as the 0 V reference for all other potentials; in battery circuits it is usually the battery's − terminal by the designer's choice. D2
Conventional current
Simple words: the direction engineers draw current: from + to − outside the battery. Analogy: drawing the water's direction on the building plan. Precise: the direction positive charge would move; in metal wires the electrons actually move the opposite way, and circuit diagrams use the conventional direction. D2
Voltmeter
Simple words: a tool that shows the voltage between its two probes. Analogy: the plumber's pressure gauge with two hoses. Precise: an instrument (often one mode of a multimeter, F1-07) that displays the potential of its red probe minus the potential of its black probe. D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows a battery and three parts in one loop. Each labelled point has a potential, measured from ground. The pressure bars on the right show the same numbers as "heights". A voltmeter reads the difference between the two points its probes touch.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Everything around you is made of tiny particles. Some of them carry charge. In a metal wire, very many tiny charged particles called electrons can move. When they move together in one direction, we have an electric current.D2

Think of the restaurant's plumbing. The water is the charge. How much water passes a point each second is the current. A thin trickle is a small current. A gushing tap is a big current.

Water does not move by itself. Something must push it. In the restaurant, the height of the roof tank makes the pressure. In a circuit, a battery makes the push. That push is called voltage.D1

Here is the important part. Pressure only makes sense between two places. Rosa compares the tank with the tap. A voltage is the same: it is always measured between two points. "The voltage at point B" really means "the voltage between point B and a point we agreed to call zero". We call that zero point ground.D2

Last, the water must go round. The pump lifts it, it falls through the taps, and the drain brings it back. Charge also needs a closed loop. You met that rule in F0-39. Without a loop, there is no current.D1

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Charge and current

Charge is measured in coulombs (C). Current is the rate at which charge passes a point. For a steady current, the charge moved in a time t is Q = I × t. One ampere means one coulomb passing each second.D3 So 20 mA (0.020 A) flowing for 60 s moves 0.020 × 60 = 1.2 C. Listing 1 does this sum for four cases.

In a single loop with no branches, the same current flows through every part. Charge is not used up by a lamp or a resistor; it goes all the way round. What the parts use is energy, not charge.D2 F1-04 turns this into the junction rule for circuits with branches.

Voltage, potential and ground

Voltage is energy per charge. If one coulomb moves from one point to another and gains or loses one joule, the voltage between the points is one volt.D3 A battery gives energy to the charge that passes through it. The other parts take that energy back out, as light or heat.D2

Because voltage is a difference, we pick one point as the reference and call it ground (0 V). The voltage of any point measured from ground is its potential. The voltage between two points is then the difference of their potentials: VBC = VB − VC. In Figure 1, VB = 4.5 V and VC = 1.5 V, so VBC = 3 V.D2

The order matters. VCB = 1.5 − 4.5 = −3 V. A minus sign is not an error. It says that the first point is lower than the second.

Which way does current go?

On circuit diagrams, current is drawn leaving the battery's + terminal and returning to its − terminal. This is conventional current. In metal wires, the electrons really move the other way. Both descriptions give the same answers for every calculation in this course, so engineers keep the conventional direction.D2

Reading a voltmeter

A voltmeter shows the potential of its red probe minus the potential of its black probe.D1 Put black on ground and red on a point, and you read that point's potential. Swap the probes and the reading changes sign. F1-07 covers the multimeter in full, including how to measure current safely.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. The rule "voltages around any closed loop add up to zero" follows from voltage being a difference of potentials: walk around the loop, add each difference, and you are back at the start. In Figure 1: (6 − 4.5) + (4.5 − 1.5) + (1.5 − 0) = 6 V of drops, matching the battery's 6 V rise. This is Kirchhoff's voltage law; F1-04 uses it.D2 The idea that a potential exists at every point is a model. It holds very well for the slow, small circuits of this course. It needs care for fast-changing signals and long wires, which HW204 and HW302 meet later.

How the hardware actually does it

Inside a battery, a chemical reaction moves charge from one terminal to the other. This builds up a potential difference between the terminals. When a closed loop is connected, charge flows through the outside circuit and the reaction keeps the difference going.D1 D2 A real battery's voltage depends on its chemistry and its state of charge. The number printed on it is a nominal label. Its real behaviour is given in the maker's datasheet (D4). This chapter does not quote any real battery number.

Worked example

Exercise numbers, not measurements. Ana's LED loop draws a steady 20 mA.

  1. Convert to amperes: 20 mA = 20 ÷ 1000 = 0.020 A.
  2. In 1 s it moves Q = 0.020 × 1 = 0.020 C.
  3. In one minute (Ben's case) it moves Q = 0.020 × 60 = 1.200 C.
  4. Chidi's loop draws a quarter of that current, 5 mA. In one minute: 0.005 × 60 = 0.300 C, a quarter of the charge.
  5. Dara's motor draws 1000 mA = 1 A. In 1 s it moves 1 C: one ampere is one coulomb per second.

Now the potentials of Figure 1. Black probe on GND: A reads 6 V, B reads 4.5 V, C reads 1.5 V. Across each part (red on the higher point): part 1: 6 − 4.5 = 1.5 V; part 2: 4.5 − 1.5 = 3 V; part 3: 1.5 − 0 = 1.5 V. The three drops add to 6 V. Listing 1 and the forensic generator check both sets of numbers.R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — charge.cpp: reads a name, a current in milliamperes and a time in seconds, and prints the charge moved.

// Charge moved by a steady current: Q = I x t.
// The currents and times in charge.in are exercise numbers, not measurements.
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main()
{
    std::string name;
    double milliamps = 0.0;
    double seconds = 0.0;

    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(3);
    while (std::cin >> name >> milliamps >> seconds) {
        const double amps = milliamps / 1000.0;
        const double coulombs = amps * seconds;
        std::cout << name << ": " << milliamps << " mA for " << seconds << " s moves "
                  << coulombs << " C of charge\n";
    }
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–2// Charge moved …Says what the program computes and that the inputs are exercise numbers.Honest labelling: nothing here was measured.
3–5#include <iomanip> …Brings in printing, formatting and text.iomanip gives std::setprecision.
9–11std::string name; double milliamps …Three variables for one input line.Units are in the names, so you cannot mix mA and A by accident.
13std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(3);Prints every number with three decimals.Makes the output easy to compare with your hand sums.
14while (std::cin >> name >> milliamps >> seconds)Reads lines until the input ends.Add a line to charge.in to test your own case.
15const double amps = milliamps / 1000.0;Converts mA to A.Formulas use base units: forgetting this gives answers 1000 times too big.
16const double coulombs = amps * seconds;Q = I × t.The definition of current, turned around.
17–18std::cout << name …Prints one result line.One line per case, in the input order.
20return 0;Ends with exit code 0.The run log records it.

Input charge.in:

Ana 20 1
Ben 20 60
Chidi 5 60
Dara 1000 1

Where the analogy breaks

  1. An open pipe spills; an open wire does not. Cut a water pipe and the water pours out. Cut a wire and the current simply stops: charge does not leak out of the end into the room.D2
  2. Water moves at the speed you see; electrical effects do not. When you close a switch, the lamp lights at once, even though each electron in the wire drifts slowly. The push travels through the whole loop far faster than any single charge moves. The plumbing picture hides this.D2
  3. Real pressure comes from height; voltage comes from energy per charge. The roof tank is a helpful picture, but no part of a circuit is "higher" in space. The 4.5 V at B is about energy, not about where B sits on the table.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
A reading is negative when you expected positiveRed and black probes swappedCheck which probe is on the higher point; compare with the forensic evidence belowBlack on the reference (often GND), red on the point you want
Answer is 1000 times too bigmA used as A in a formulaWrite units next to every numberConvert first, as line 15 of Listing 1 does
"The voltage at B" means different things to two peopleNo agreed reference pointAsk: "measured from where?"Mark GND on the diagram and measure from it
You think the current is smaller after a partConfusing charge with energyMeasure the current before and after the part (F1-07): same value in a single loopRemember: parts use energy, not charge
Transition box

Where you came from: KID103 (F0-39, F0-40) gave you the water picture, the closed loop and Ohm's law with exercise numbers. MA101 gave you the algebra used here. What carries over: the plumbing picture for voltage and current, the closed-loop rule, and the habit of labelling exercise numbers.D1 What changes: most dangerous first: you now name voltage as a difference between two points, so a reading without a reference point is meaningless; you meet the coulomb and Q = I × t; current direction becomes a convention; units must be converted before every formula.D2 D3 What comes next: F1-02 links voltage and current through resistance, Ohm's law, and finds a resistance from a table of readings.

Check yourself

  1. What is the difference between current and voltage, in one sentence each?
  2. A current of 50 mA flows for 10 s. How much charge moves?
  3. Point P is at 3.3 V and point Q at 1.2 V (both measured from ground). What does a voltmeter show with red on Q and black on P? (a) 4.5 V (b) 2.1 V (c) −2.1 V (d) −4.5 V
  4. Why must a voltage always name two points?
  5. In a single loop, the current before a resistor is 8 mA. What is the current after it? Why?
  6. Explain in your own words why the roof-tank picture fails when a wire is cut.
  7. Apply to a new case: a loop has a 9 V battery and two parts. Point M, between them, is at 3 V from ground (the − terminal). What is the voltage across each part?
  8. Which way do electrons move in a wire, compared with conventional current?

Lab

Goal: compute charge from current and time with Listing 1, then predict and check voltmeter signs with the probe model.

Hardware and software needed: Part A: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Part B (optional): the course's low-voltage battery kit and multimeter, chosen by the owner.

Safety

Part A: none beyond normal computer use. Part B: learners at L1 do physical labs only with adult supervision, at low voltage, with a battery kit designed for their age. No mains electricity at any level. Never connect a battery's + and − terminals directly with a wire or with the meter's probes in a current mode. If anything gets warm or smells, disconnect the battery and tell your supervisor.S1

Part A — simulator (do this first)

  1. Build and run Listing 1 with the command above. You should see the four lines of the real output.
  2. Add a line You 15 120 to charge.in. Predict the charge on paper (15 mA for 2 minutes), then run.
  3. Build and run the forensic generator probes.cpp (same build command). Before running, write down what you expect for each line from Figure 1.
  4. Add three lines of your own to probes.in, with probes on any two of A, B, C, GND. Predict each reading, including its sign, then run.

Part B — real battery and meter (optional, supervised)

Not verified — check before relying on this

Part B was not performed in this build: no kit or meter was available, and the owner has not yet chosen them. The steps describe the idea only. The supervisor checks each step against the kit's instructions and the multimeter's user manual (dossier part F, D4), including which socket and dial position give a voltage reading.

  1. With the battery disconnected, build a loop of two or three resistors from the kit, as in Figure 1.
  2. Connect the battery. Set the meter to a voltage range, as its manual says. Black probe on the − terminal (your GND).
  3. Touch red on each junction point in turn. Write down each reading.
  4. Swap the probes on one point. Write down the reading and its sign.
  5. Disconnect the battery.

Expected observations

Part A: the real outputs shown in this chapter and your own predicted lines. Part B: potentials that fall from the + terminal towards GND, and a reading that changes sign when you swap probes. Your own measured values are your measurements: write them down with the date and the meter used.

Verification

Every line you added matches your paper prediction to the number of decimals printed. In Part B, the drops across the parts add up to the battery reading within the meter's stated accuracy (from its manual).

Troubleshooting

  • A line of your input is ignored → a field is missing or not a number → check each line has exactly the fields the program reads.
  • probes stops with an error mentioning map::at → a point name is misspelt → use only A, B, C, GND (upper case).
  • Part B shows 0 everywhere → the loop is open or the meter is in the wrong mode → trace the loop; check the dial against the manual.

Extension

Change probes.cpp so that it reads the four potentials from the first input line instead of fixing them in the code. Then describe a circuit with a 9 V battery and three parts of your choice.

Forensic lab

Scenario: "The readings that do not add up". Three learners, Mei, Omar and Priya, measured the circuit of Figure 1 and handed in their readings. Omar is worried: "My numbers are all wrong, half of them are negative." Is Omar's circuit broken? Is anyone's?

Evidence pack. The readings below were produced by the course's probe model (probes.cpp with probes.in), not by a real meter. Each line names where each probe was placed, as the learners wrote in their notebooks.

Omar (red on GND, black on A):  -6.00 V
Omar (red on B, black on A):  -1.50 V
Omar (red on C, black on B):  -3.00 V

Questions.

  1. Which of Omar's readings are negative? What do they have in common?
  2. Using Mei's readings, work out what Omar should have read with the probes the usual way round.
  3. Is Omar's circuit broken? Give the evidence.
  4. Priya measured across each part. Do her three readings agree with Mei's? Show the sum.
  5. Write a one-line rule that would have prevented Omar's worry.

Method hints. For every line, write reading = V(red) − V(black). Form two hypotheses for Omar ("circuit faulty" and "probes reversed") and test each against Mei's and Priya's numbers.

Mini-project

Make a one-page "potential map" of a circuit of your choice (exercise numbers): a drawing like Figure 1 with GND marked, a bar for each point's potential, and a table of what a voltmeter would show between six pairs of points. Check your table with probes.cpp (edit its potentials). Rubric: GND clearly marked and used (1); all six readings correct with sign (2); drops add up to the battery voltage (1); the run output attached (1).

Summary

  • Charge is measured in coulombs; current is charge per second, in amperes.
  • For a steady current, Q = I × t; convert mA to A first.
  • Voltage is energy per charge, measured between two points, in volts.
  • Ground is the point we choose as 0 V; a potential is a voltage measured from ground.
  • A voltmeter shows V(red) − V(black); swapping probes changes the sign only.
  • In a single loop the same current flows everywhere; parts use energy, not charge.
  • Conventional current goes from + to − outside the battery; electrons in metal move the other way.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Current is how much charge passes a point each second (amperes); voltage is the energy per charge between two points, the push (volts).
  2. 50 mA = 0.050 A; Q = 0.050 × 10 = 0.5 C.
  3. (c) −2.1 V: V(red) − V(black) = 1.2 − 3.3. (b) is the size with the probes the other way round. (a) and (d) add the potentials instead of subtracting them.
  4. Voltage is a difference of potential, like a difference of height: it has no meaning for one point alone, unless a reference (ground) is understood.
  5. 8 mA. In a single loop there is only one path, and charge is not used up by the resistor; only energy is taken out.
  6. In your words: water pours out of a cut pipe, but a cut wire just stops the current; nothing spills, because charge needs the closed loop to move at all.
  7. The part between + (9 V) and M (3 V) has 9 − 3 = 6 V; the part between M and the − terminal has 3 − 0 = 3 V. Together 9 V.
  8. Opposite: electrons drift from − towards + through the outside circuit; conventional current is drawn from + to −.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: all three of Omar's readings are negative, and in each one his red probe is on the lower point (GND below A, A above B, B above C). Expected values: from Mei's potentials, Omar's lines should read 6.00, 1.50 and 3.00 V: exactly his numbers without the minus sign. Conclusion: the circuit is fine; Omar placed the probes the other way round. Hypothesis "circuit faulty" is ruled out because the sizes match Mei's and Priya's readings. Priya: 1.50 + 3.00 + 1.50 = 6.00 V, equal to Mei's A-to-GND reading (Kirchhoff's voltage law). Prevention: "black on the lower point or on GND, red on the point you are asking about; a minus sign means the probes are reversed, not that the circuit is broken". How the evidence was made: probes.cpp with fixed exercise potentials A = 6, B = 4.5, C = 1.5, GND = 0, and probes.in listing the probe placements (R1).
