Story hook

Analogy

The restaurant's kitchen has two sinks. One is fed by a wide pipe. The other, added later by a hurried builder, is fed by a pipe as thin as a pencil. With the same roof tank behind both, the wide pipe fills a pot in seconds. The thin one takes ages.

Aiko, who runs the kitchen, makes a test. She opens each tap and counts how many cups fill in one minute. Then she asks Rosa to move the tank higher, so there is more pressure, and counts again. For each pipe, double the pressure gives about double the cups.

"So each pipe has its own number," Aiko says. "Pressure divided by flow. The thin pipe's number is big. The wide pipe's number is small." She has just discovered, with water, what this chapter calls resistance and Ohm's law.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain resistance with the narrow-pipe picture and with its precise definition and unit, the ohm.
  • Use Ohm's law, V = I × R, in all three forms, with correct unit prefixes (k, M, m).
  • Find a resistance from a table of voltage and current readings, by hand and with a C++ program.
  • Tell an ohmic part (straight-line V–I graph) from a non-ohmic one.
  • Diagnose a wrong resistor in a batch from test-bench readings.
Jargon box
Resistance
Simple words: how strongly a part holds back the current. Analogy: how narrow a pipe in the restaurant's plumbing is. Precise: the ratio of the voltage across a part to the current through it, R = V ÷ I; measured in ohms (Ω). D2 D3
Ohm (Ω)
Simple words: the unit of resistance. Analogy: a "narrowness number" for a pipe. Precise: one ohm is the resistance through which one volt drives one ampere (1 Ω = 1 V/A). D3
Ohm's law
Simple words: for many parts, the current is proportional to the voltage. Analogy: twice the pressure through the same pipe gives twice the flow. Precise: V = I × R with R constant; parts that obey it over their working range are called ohmic. D2
Resistor
Simple words: a part made to have a known resistance. Analogy: a pipe section deliberately made narrow. Precise: a two-terminal component manufactured with a stated nominal resistance, a tolerance and a power rating (values from its datasheet). D1 D4
Tolerance
Simple words: how far a real part may be from the number written on it. Analogy: pipes from the same shop are never exactly the same width. Precise: the maximum allowed difference between the actual and nominal value, usually given as a percentage in the datasheet. D2 D4
V–I graph
Simple words: a drawing of voltage against current for a part. Analogy: Aiko's table of pressure and cups per minute, drawn as dots. Precise: a plot of the voltage across a part against the current through it; for an ohmic part the points lie on a straight line through the origin whose slope is R. D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 plots the five exercise readings of Listing 1 for one resistor. The points sit close to one straight line through the origin. The steeper the line, the bigger the resistance. A dashed line for a 1 kΩ resistor is drawn for comparison.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Every part of a circuit holds back the current a little. Some parts hold it back a lot. How strongly a part holds back the current is its resistance.D2

In the restaurant, a narrow pipe holds back the water. A wide pipe lets it rush through. A thick copper wire is like the wide pipe. A resistor is like the pencil-thin pipe: it is made on purpose to hold back the current by a known amount.D1

Aiko found a rule. Double the pressure on the same pipe, and you get double the flow. For a resistor, the rule is the same. Double the voltage, and you get double the current. That rule is called Ohm's law.D2

Resistance is measured in ohms, written with the Greek letter Ω. A resistor of 1,000 Ω holds back the current more than a resistor of 100 Ω.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Ohm's law in three forms

For a resistor, the voltage across it and the current through it are proportional: V = I × R. You can rearrange it to I = V ÷ R or R = V ÷ I. You met the second form in F0-39; now you use all three.D2

The units fit together: one volt across one ohm drives one ampere.D3 In practice you meet prefixes. 1 kΩ (kilo-ohm) is 1,000 Ω. 1 MΩ (mega-ohm) is 1,000,000 Ω. 1 mA is 0.001 A. A useful shortcut: volts divided by kilo-ohms gives milliamperes. For example, 5 V ÷ 2.2 kΩ ≈ 2.27 mA.

Reading resistance from a graph

Plot the voltage against the current. For an ohmic part, the points lie on a straight line through the origin. The slope of that line, rise in volts over run in amperes, is the resistance (Figure 1).D2

Real readings are never perfect. Each pair gives a slightly different V ÷ I. A better estimate uses all the points at once. The least-squares slope through the origin is R = Σ(V × I) ÷ Σ(I × I): multiply each pair, add them up, and divide by the sum of the squared currents. Listing 1 computes it. This is the same "fit a line" idea you met in MA101's graphs.

Not everything obeys Ohm's law

Ohm's law is a property of some parts, not a law of nature for all of them. A diode (F1-06) has a curved V–I graph: almost no current at low voltage, then a steep rise. A lamp filament's resistance changes as it heats up.D2 For those parts, V ÷ I still gives a number at one point, but that number changes from point to point.

Nominal value and tolerance

A resistor sold as 2.2 kΩ is not exactly 2,200 Ω. The maker states a tolerance: how far the real value may be from the nominal one. The tolerance, the power rating and how the value is marked on the part all come from the maker's datasheet.D4

Not verified — check before relying on this

This chapter does not teach how resistor values are marked on the body of the part (colour bands or printed codes), because no marking standard or datasheet could be opened in this build. Before the kit lab, check the marking scheme in the datasheet of the resistors in the chosen kit (D4), or the marking standard that datasheet names. Measuring each resistor with the meter (F1-07) is a safe check either way.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. The resistance of a wire grows with its length and shrinks with its cross-section area; the material sets a constant called its resistivity. That is why long, thin wires resist more than short, thick ones, just like pipes.D2 Resistance also changes with temperature, by an amount that depends on the material; a resistor's datasheet states how much (D4). Fitting a line through the origin assumes the meter reads zero at zero current; a careful engineer also fits a line with an offset and checks that the offset is small.

How the hardware actually does it

In a metal, the moving electrons keep bumping into the vibrating atoms of the material. Each bump turns some of their energy into heat. That is resistance at the smallest scale.D2 A resistor is made from a material and a shape chosen so that the bumping adds up to the wanted value. How a particular resistor is built (a film on a ceramic body, a wire wound on a core, a tiny chip) is described in its datasheet, together with its limits (D4). The heat side of the story is F1-03.

Worked example

Exercise numbers, not measurements. Yusuf applies five voltages to one resistor and reads the currents: (1 V, 0.46 mA), (2 V, 0.92 mA), (3 V, 1.35 mA), (4 V, 1.83 mA), (5 V, 2.26 mA).

  1. First pair: R = 1 V ÷ 0.00046 A ≈ 2,173.9 Ω.
  2. Third pair: R = 3 ÷ 0.00135 ≈ 2,222.2 Ω. The single-pair values scatter by a few tens of ohms.
  3. Least-squares slope: Σ(V × I) = 1 × 0.00046 + 2 × 0.00092 + 3 × 0.00135 + 4 × 0.00183 + 5 × 0.00226 = 0.02497 V·A.
  4. Σ(I × I) = 0.00046² + 0.00092² + 0.00135² + 0.00183² + 0.00226² ≈ 1.1337 × 10−5 A².
  5. R ≈ 0.02497 ÷ 0.000011337 ≈ 2,202 Ω, close to a 2.2 kΩ resistor.
  6. Check with the other form: at 5 V, I = 5 ÷ 2,202 ≈ 2.27 mA, close to the 2.26 mA read.

Listing 1 prints the same per-pair values and 2202.5 Ω for the fit.R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — ohm_fit.cpp: computes V ÷ I for every reading and the best-fit resistance through the origin.

// Ohm's law from a table of (voltage, current) pairs.
// For each pair: R = V / I. For the whole table: the best straight line
// through the origin, R = sum(V*I) / sum(I*I) (least squares).
// The pairs in ohm_fit.in are exercise numbers, not measurements.
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main()
{
    std::string part;
    double volts = 0.0;
    double milliamps = 0.0;
    double sumVI = 0.0;
    double sumII = 0.0;

    std::cout << std::fixed;
    while (std::cin >> part >> volts >> milliamps) {
        const double amps = milliamps / 1000.0;
        std::cout << part << ": V = " << std::setprecision(2) << volts << " V, I = " << milliamps
                  << " mA, V/I = " << std::setprecision(1) << volts / amps << " ohms\n";
        sumVI += volts * amps;
        sumII += amps * amps;
    }
    if (sumII > 0.0) {
        std::cout << "best-fit resistance through the origin: " << sumVI / sumII << " ohms\n";
    }
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–4// Ohm's law from a table …States the method and that the inputs are exercise numbers.The formula in the comment is the one in Layer 2.
11–15std::string part; … double sumII = 0.0;Variables for one reading and two running sums.Sums start at zero before the loop.
17std::cout << std::fixed;Fixed-point printing.Decimals are set per number below.
18while (std::cin >> part >> volts >> milliamps)Reads one reading per line.Your own readings can be added to the file.
19const double amps = milliamps / 1000.0;mA to A.Ohm's law in base units gives ohms directly.
20–21… volts / amps …Prints V, I and R = V ÷ I for this reading.Shows the scatter of single readings.
22–23sumVI += volts * amps; sumII += amps * amps;Adds this reading to the two sums.The two sums of the least-squares formula.
25–27if (sumII > 0.0) { … sumVI / sumII … }Prints the best-fit slope.The guard avoids dividing by zero when the file is empty.

R1 2.0 0.92
R1 3.0 1.35
R1 4.0 1.83
R1 5.0 2.26

Where the analogy breaks

  1. Flow in a real pipe is not proportional to pressure. Water in a pipe becomes turbulent at high flow, and then doubling the pressure gives less than double the flow. A resistor stays proportional over its working range. The pipe picture would make you expect a curve that a resistor does not have.D2
  2. A resistor heats up; a narrow pipe barely does. The energy a resistor holds back turns into heat. F1-03 shows that this heat can damage a part.D2
  3. Pipes leak; wires need a loop. As in F1-01, charge does not spill from an open end, so "a narrow pipe with nothing after it" has no electrical meaning.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix

A resistor reads a very different value from its labelWrong part picked, or the label misreadMeasure it out of circuit with the meter (F1-07)Replace it; sort parts by measured value
Program prints no best-fit lineInput file empty or badly formattedCheck the three fields per lineFix the input
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-01 defined voltage as a difference between two points and current as charge per second; F0-39 used I = V ÷ R with exercise numbers. What carries over: the plumbing picture, unit conversion before each formula, and reading the voltage across a part with the probes the right way round.D2 What changes: most dangerous first: Ohm's law holds only for ohmic parts, so never apply it blindly to an LED or a lamp; real resistors differ from their label by their tolerance; you now estimate a value from many noisy readings instead of one.D2 D4 What comes next: F1-03 asks where the held-back energy goes: power and heat, and why a resistor can get too hot.

Check yourself

  1. State Ohm's law in its three forms.
  2. A 4.7 kΩ resistor has 9.4 V across it. What current flows?
  3. You want 10 mA from a 5 V supply through one resistor. Which value? (a) 50 Ω (b) 500 Ω (c) 2 Ω (d) 0.5 Ω
  4. A part gives 1 V at 1 mA and 2 V at 5 mA. Is it ohmic? Explain.
  5. On a V–I graph (V up, I across), which line is the bigger resistance: the steeper or the flatter?
  6. Explain in your own words why the best-fit slope is better than the value from one reading.
  7. Apply to a new case: a heating wire has 12 V across it and 3 A through it. What is its resistance? If the voltage dropped to 6 V and the wire were ohmic, what current would flow?
  8. Why does a resistor marked 2.2 kΩ not read exactly 2,200 Ω on a meter?

Lab

Goal: estimate a resistance from a table of readings with Listing 1, then (optionally, supervised) from your own measurements.

Hardware and software needed: Part A: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Part B (optional): the course kit's battery or low-voltage supply, two or three resistors, and the course multimeter, as chosen by the owner.

Safety

Part A: none beyond normal computer use. Part B: adult supervision; low-voltage battery kit only; no mains. Disconnect the battery before changing any part. Measure resistance only with the battery disconnected (F1-07). If a part gets warm, disconnect and tell your supervisor.S1

Part A — the fit program

  1. Build and run Listing 1. You should see the five lines and the best-fit value shown above.
  2. Replace the last reading by R1 5.0 2.80 (a deliberately bad reading). Predict whether the fit goes up or down, then run.
  3. Restore the file. Add five readings for a second part called R2 that you invent for a 1 kΩ resistor. Note: the program fits all lines together. Change the program so it prints a separate fit for each part name (hint: a std::map from name to the two sums).

Part B — your own readings (optional, supervised)

Not verified — check before relying on this

Part B was not performed in this build: no kit, supply or meter was available, and none has been chosen. How to set the chosen meter to measure voltage and current, and which current range is safe, must be taken from its user manual (D4). F1-07 explains the general method; do F1-07's simulator lab first if you have not measured current before.

  1. Measure the resistor with the battery disconnected (resistance mode). Write the value down.
  2. Build battery → resistor → back, with the meter in series in current mode as F1-07 shows. Read the current.
  3. Move the meter to voltage mode, across the resistor. Read the voltage.
  4. Repeat with a different battery voltage if the kit offers one. Put your readings into ohm_fit.in and run.

Expected observations

Part A: the real output above; with the bad reading, the fit moves towards a smaller resistance (more current for the same voltage). Part B: your fitted value is close to the resistance you measured directly, within the tolerance the datasheet gives. Your numbers are your measurements, labelled with date and meter.

Verification

Your modified program prints one fit per part, and for each part the fit agrees with a hand calculation from two of its readings to within the scatter of the readings.

Troubleshooting

  • Fit is wildly off → one reading in A instead of mA → check the units column.
  • Compiler error about std::map → missing #include <map>.
  • Part B current reads zero → the meter is not in series, or its current fuse is open (F1-07 forensic lab).

Extension

Fit a line with an offset, V = R × I + V0, using the two-unknowns least-squares formulas, and check that V0 is close to zero for the exercise data.

Forensic lab

Scenario: "The batch with a stranger in it". A box of resistors, all labelled 2.2 kΩ, is checked on a test bench before use. The bench applies the same voltage to each part and records the current. Lin, who runs the bench, says two parts "feel wrong". Which ones, and what are they really?

Questions.

  1. What current should a 2.2 kΩ resistor draw at 5 V? Which parts differ?
  2. Compute R = V ÷ I for each odd part.
  3. Both odd values are related to 2.2 kΩ in a simple way. How? What kind of mix-up could cause that?
  4. Could tolerance explain the odd parts? Why or why not?
  5. What would you change in the stores or the bench process to catch this earlier?

Method hints. Start from the expected current for the label. Ask whether each difference is small (a few percent, tolerance) or a whole factor. Form at least two hypotheses for the cause and say what evidence would separate them.

Mini-project

Write sort_parts.cpp: it reads labelled resistors with a bench voltage and current, computes each resistance, and prints "ok", "check tolerance" or "WRONG PART (about N times the label)". Test it on bench.out's numbers. Rubric: correct resistance (2); clear thresholds stated in a comment, with the tolerance taken as an input number rather than invented (1); test run shown (1); one-paragraph explanation with the pipe analogy (1).

Summary

  • Resistance is V ÷ I, measured in ohms (Ω); 1 Ω = 1 V/A.
  • Ohm's law: V = I × R, I = V ÷ R, R = V ÷ I, for ohmic parts.
  • Volts divided by kilo-ohms gives milliamperes.
  • On a V–I graph an ohmic part is a straight line through the origin; its slope is R.
  • Use many readings and a best-fit slope, not one reading.
  • Diodes and lamps are not ohmic.
  • Real resistors differ from their label by up to their tolerance (from the datasheet).

Answers to Check yourself

  1. V = I × R; I = V ÷ R; R = V ÷ I.
  2. I = 9.4 V ÷ 4.7 kΩ = 2 mA.
  3. (b) 500 Ω: 5 ÷ 0.010 = 500. (a) 50 Ω gives 100 mA, ten times too much (a decimal-place slip). (d) 0.5 Ω comes from 5 ÷ 10, using mA as if it were A. (c) 2 Ω comes from 10 ÷ 5, the formula upside down.
  4. No: 1 V ÷ 1 mA = 1 kΩ, but 2 V ÷ 5 mA = 400 Ω. The ratio changes, so the V–I graph is not a straight line through the origin.
  5. The steeper line: more volts are needed for the same current.
  6. In your words: every reading has a small error; the fit uses all readings so the errors partly cancel, and one bad reading has less effect.
  7. R = 12 ÷ 3 = 4 Ω. If ohmic, at 6 V: I = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 A. (A real heating wire changes resistance with temperature, so a measurement would be needed.)
  8. Because of its tolerance: the maker allows the real value to differ from the nominal value by a stated amount (datasheet), and the meter has its own accuracy too.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: expected current 5 V ÷ 2.2 kΩ ≈ 2.273 mA; R1, R2, R4 and R6 match. R3 draws 22.727 mA and R5 draws 0.227 mA. Values: R3 = 5 ÷ 0.022727 ≈ 220 Ω; R5 = 5 ÷ 0.000227 ≈ 22 kΩ. Pattern: each is the label divided or multiplied by exactly 10: the same digits with the wrong multiplier, which points to parts from the neighbouring drawers (220 Ω and 22 kΩ) mixed into the 2.2 kΩ box. Tolerance ruled out: tolerance is a small percentage, not a factor of 10. Fix and prevention: remove R3 and R5; measure a sample from each box on arrival; keep neighbouring values in clearly separated stores. How the evidence was made: bench.cpp with bench.in listing the true values 2200, 2200, 220, 2200, 22000, 2200 Ω (R1).

Story hook

Analogy

In the restaurant's back room there is a hand mill for grinding spices. Kwame turns the handle slowly and the mill grinds a little. When the dinner rush starts, he turns it fast and hard. Soon his arms ache and the mill's iron body is warm to the touch.

"It is not only how hard you push," says Aiko. "It is how hard you push and how fast the handle goes round. Both together decide how much work you do each minute." And the faster the work, the more of it ends up as warmth in the mill.

Electric parts are the same. Push (voltage) times flow (current) tells you how fast energy is delivered. In a resistor, almost all of that energy becomes heat. Too much, too fast, and a part can scorch the board it sits on. This chapter shows you how to calculate it before anything gets hot.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain power as the rate of energy transfer, in watts, with the mill picture and precisely.
  • Calculate power with P = V × I, P = I² × R and P = V² ÷ R, and choose the convenient form.
  • Compare the power in a part with its power rating, using exercise numbers labelled as such.
  • Calculate energy from power and time, E = P × t.
  • Diagnose "the hot resistor" from a schematic and meter readings.
Jargon box
Energy
Simple words: the ability to do work, such as making light, movement or heat. Analogy: the total effort Kwame spends at the mill during a shift. Precise: a quantity measured in joules (J); in a circuit, each coulomb moved through a voltage V transfers V joules. D2 D3
Power
Simple words: how fast energy is delivered or used. Analogy: how hard and how fast Kwame turns the mill at this moment. Precise: the rate of energy transfer, P = E ÷ t; in a part with voltage V across it and current I through it, P = V × I; measured in watts (W), one watt being one joule per second. D2 D3
Dissipation
Simple words: electrical energy turning into heat inside a part. Analogy: the mill's iron body getting warm. Precise: the conversion of electrical power into heat in a resistive part; for a resistor all of P = I² × R is dissipated. D2
Power rating
Simple words: the most power a part may take without damage, as its maker says. Analogy: the mill's sign "do not turn faster than this". Precise: the maximum continuous power dissipation stated in a part's datasheet, under the conditions the datasheet states. D4
Short circuit
Simple words: a path with almost no resistance straight across a source. Analogy: a burst pipe that lets the tank empty at once. Precise: an unintended low-resistance connection between two points at different potentials, which lets a large current flow; the current is limited only by the source's internal resistance and the wiring. D1 D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows a power budget for the LED loop of F0-40 (exercise numbers: 6 V battery, LED taking 2 V, 200 Ω resistor, 20 mA). The battery delivers power; the resistor and the LED take it. The two shares add up to the battery's total.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A battery stores energy. When current flows, the battery hands that energy to the parts in the loop. A lamp turns it into light. A motor turns it into movement. A resistor turns it into heat.D1 D2

Power tells you how fast the energy is handed over. Think of Kwame at the spice mill. A strong push turned slowly is not much work per minute. A gentle push turned fast is not much either. A strong push turned fast is a lot. In a circuit, the push is the voltage and the speed of flow is the current. Multiply them and you get the power.D2

Power is measured in watts (W). A small LED loop uses a few hundredths of a watt. That is why we often use milliwatts (mW): one thousandth of a watt.

Here is the important safety idea. Every part has a limit, written by its maker. If a resistor must turn too much power into heat, it gets hot. It can scorch the board or burn a finger. So engineers calculate the power first, and pick a part that can take it.D4

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Why P = V × I

Voltage is energy per coulomb (F1-01). Current is coulombs per second. Multiply them: (joules per coulomb) × (coulombs per second) = joules per second. That is power, in watts.D2 D3 So for any part, the power is the voltage across it times the current through it.

Three forms for a resistor

For a resistor, Ohm's law lets you replace V or I:

  • P = V × I (works for any part);
  • P = I × R × I = I² × R (handy when you know the current);
  • P = V × (V ÷ R) = V² ÷ R (handy when you know the voltage).

All three give the same number for a resistor. Listing 1 computes all three, as a check. Note the squares: doubling the current through a resistor gives four times the power.D2

Energy over time

Energy is power multiplied by time: E = P × t. A resistor taking 0.08 W for 60 s turns 0.08 × 60 = 4.8 J into heat.D3 A battery's maker states how much it can deliver in its datasheet; that is what decides how long a circuit can run (D4).

Power budget

Energy is not created or lost in a circuit: the power the source delivers equals the total power taken by the parts.D2 In Figure 1, 120 mW = 80 mW + 40 mW. Writing such a budget is a quick check on any calculation.

Power rating and margin

Each resistor's datasheet states a power rating. Running a part near its rating makes it hot. Engineers keep a margin: they choose a part whose rating is comfortably above the calculated power.D2 How much margin a project uses is a design rule that the team writes down. In this course's exercises, the "pretend rating" is an exercise number; the real rating comes from the datasheet (D4).

Not verified — check before relying on this

Real resistors are sold with several power ratings, and the rating can depend on the surrounding temperature. No datasheet could be opened in this build, so this chapter quotes no real rating. Before the kit lab, the supervisor copies the rating of the kit's resistors and any temperature conditions from their datasheet (D4).

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. A part's temperature rises until the heat it loses to its surroundings equals the power it dissipates. How much it rises per watt depends on its size, its leads, the board and the air around it; datasheets describe this with a thermal resistance or with a derating curve that lowers the allowed power at higher temperatures.D2 D4 The same idea, scaled up, is why processors need heat sinks and why GPU and server chapters care about power (HW301).

How the hardware actually does it

In a resistor, the moving charges lose energy in collisions with the atoms of the material (F1-02). That energy makes the atoms vibrate more strongly, which is what "hotter" means.D2 The heat then leaves through the part's body and leads into the board and the air. A bigger body has more surface to lose heat from, which is one reason higher-rated resistors are physically larger. Their exact sizes and ratings are in the maker's datasheet (D4).

Worked example

Exercise numbers, not real-part values. Each resistor in Listing 1's input has a pretend rating of 0.25 W.

  1. Kiri: 4 V across 200 Ω. I = 4 ÷ 200 = 0.02 A. P = 4 × 0.02 = 0.08 W. Check: I² × R = 0.0004 × 200 = 0.08 W. 0.08 ÷ 0.25 = 32 % of the pretend rating.
  2. Lars: 4 V across 1,000 Ω. P = V² ÷ R = 16 ÷ 1,000 = 0.016 W, 6.4 % of the rating.
  3. Musa: 7 V across 100 Ω. I = 0.07 A. P = 7 × 0.07 = 0.49 W, almost twice the pretend rating. This part would overheat.
  4. Nadia: 12 V across 1,000 Ω. P = 144 ÷ 1,000 = 0.144 W, 57.6 % of the rating.
  5. Energy for Kiri over one minute: E = 0.08 × 60 = 4.8 J of heat.

Notice Musa's case: the resistor is only ten times smaller than Lars's, with a bit more voltage, but the power is thirty times larger. Power grows with the square of voltage for a fixed resistance.R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — power.cpp: power in a resistor three ways, compared with a pretend rating.

// Power in a resistor three ways: P = V x I = I x I x R = V x V / R.
// Each line of power.in: a name, the voltage across the resistor (V),
// its resistance (ohms) and the pretend power rating of the part (W).
// All numbers are exercise numbers, not values from a real datasheet.
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main()
{
    std::string name;
    double volts = 0.0;
    double ohms = 0.0;
    double ratingWatts = 0.0;

    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);
    while (std::cin >> name >> volts >> ohms >> ratingWatts) {
        const double amps = volts / ohms;
        const double pVI = volts * amps;
        const double pIIR = amps * amps * ohms;
        const double pVVR = volts * volts / ohms;
        std::cout << name << ": I = " << amps << " A, P = " << pVI << " W (V*I), " << pIIR
                  << " W (I*I*R), " << pVVR << " W (V*V/R)";
        if (pVI > ratingWatts) {
            std::cout << " -> ABOVE the pretend rating of " << ratingWatts << " W";
        } else {
            std::cout << " -> " << std::setprecision(1) << 100.0 * pVI / ratingWatts
                      << " % of the pretend rating" << std::setprecision(4);
        }
        std::cout << "\n";
    }
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–4// Power in a resistor three ways …States the formulas and the input format; flags pretend numbers.No real datasheet values hide in the code.
11–14std::string name; double volts …Variables for one input line.Each case has its own rating, as real parts would.
16std::setprecision(4)Four decimals.Small powers like 0.0160 W stay visible.
18const double amps = volts / ohms;Ohm's law for the current.F1-02.
19–21pVI, pIIR, pVVRThe three power formulas.Agreement is a self-check of the algebra.
22–23std::cout << name …Prints the current and the three powers.You compare them with your hand sums.
24–25if (pVI > ratingWatts)Flags a part above its rating.The check you must do before building.
27–28100.0 * pVI / ratingWattsOtherwise prints the percentage of the rating used.Shows how much margin is left.

Nadia 12 1000 0.25

Where the analogy breaks

  1. A tired person slows down; a resistor does not. Kwame stops when his arms ache. A resistor keeps taking the same power as long as the voltage stays, until it fails. Nothing in the part protects itself.D2
  2. Narrow water pipes do not warm up noticeably. In the registered pipe picture (guide 8.1), a narrow pipe only slows the flow. In a resistor, all the held-back energy becomes heat. The pipe picture alone would never warn you about a hot part.
  3. An LED is not a resistor. P = V × I works for the LED, but I² × R and V² ÷ R do not, because the LED does not obey Ohm's law (F1-06).D2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Power comes out a million times too bigmA used as A in I² × R (the error is squared)Write units; 20 mA² is not 400 A²Convert to amperes first
Wrong power for a resistor in a loop with an LEDUsed the supply voltage instead of the voltage across the resistorAsk: "the voltage between which two points?" (F1-01)Use VR = Vsupply − VLED
Resistor is hot, circuit "works"Value too small, or rating too lowMeasure current and voltage across it; compute P; forensic labCorrect value; part with enough rating
Battery empties quicklyA short circuit or a too-small resistance draws a large currentMeasure the current in series (F1-07)Remove the short; add or increase the series resistor
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-01 (voltage as energy per charge, current as charge per second) and F1-02 (Ohm's law). What carries over: V, I and R, with voltage always measured across the part you are asking about; Ohm's law for resistors only.D2 What changes: most dangerous first: a wrong value can now cause heat and damage, not only a wrong number; power grows with the square of current or voltage; every part has a maker's rating you must check before building.D2 D4 What comes next: F1-04 connects several resistors in series and in parallel, and shows how voltage and current, and therefore power, are shared.

Check yourself

  1. What is power, and what is its unit?
  2. A resistor has 3 V across it and 15 mA through it. What power does it dissipate?
  3. The current through a resistor is doubled. The power becomes: (a) the same (b) twice (c) four times (d) half.
  4. A 100 Ω resistor carries 50 mA. Compute the power with I² × R, then check with V × I.
  5. Why does a short circuit across a battery waste a lot of power, even though the "load" has almost no resistance?
  6. Explain in your own words why we compare a part's power with its datasheet rating before building.
  7. Apply to a new case: a 5 V supply feeds a 1 kΩ resistor for one hour. How much energy becomes heat?
  8. In Figure 1, which part takes the most power, and why?

Lab

Goal: calculate and check resistor power for several designs with Listing 1, then choose safe values for an LED loop.

Hardware and software needed: Part A: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Part B (optional): the kit's battery, resistors and LED, and the course meter, chosen by the owner.

Safety

Part B: adult supervision, low-voltage battery kit only, no mains. Calculate the power of every resistor before connecting the battery. Never touch a part to test if it is hot; if you smell burning or see discolouring, disconnect the battery and wait. Never connect the battery's terminals together.S1

Part A — simulator

  1. Build and run Listing 1. You should see the four lines above.
  2. Add a case for a 9 V supply with a 2 V LED and a 330 Ω resistor (exercise numbers). Work out the voltage across the resistor first, predict the power, then run.
  3. Find, for a 9 V supply and a 2 V LED, the smallest resistor that keeps the power under a pretend 0.25 W rating and the current under a pretend 20 mA. Which limit decides?

Part B — kit check (optional, supervised)

Not verified — check before relying on this

Part B was not performed in this build; no kit was available and none is chosen. Replace every pretend number with the values from the datasheets of the kit's battery, resistors and LED (D4) before building.

  1. With the real datasheet numbers, compute the resistor's power for your LED loop. Write it next to the rating.
  2. Build the loop (battery last). Measure the voltage across the resistor and the current (F1-07). Compute P from your readings.
  3. Compare measured and predicted power. Disconnect the battery.

Expected observations

Part A: the outputs shown, plus your cases; in step 3 the 20 mA current limit is reached long before the 0.25 W power limit (check it). Part B: measured power close to your prediction, well below the rating.

Verification

For each case, the three formulas in the output agree, and a power budget (source = sum of parts) balances within rounding.

Troubleshooting

  • Power far too large → you used the supply voltage instead of the resistor's share.
  • Your hand sum disagrees by 1,000 or 1,000,000 → unit conversion of mA (squared in I² × R).
  • Part B: LED dark → see F0-40's forensic method (reversed LED or gap).

Extension

Add a column to Listing 1 for energy in one hour, and a "margin" input: flag any part above a chosen fraction of its rating.

Forensic lab

Scenario: "The hot resistor". A small indicator board has three identical LED channels. After an hour of testing, Sofia notices a burnt smell and a brown mark on the board next to channel 2. Its LED is also much brighter than the others. The schematic for every channel is: 9 V supply → resistor marked 1 kΩ on the schematic → LED → ground. Sofia measured each channel with the supply on, without touching any part.

CH1: across resistor 7.00 V, across LED 2.00 V, channel current 7.00 mA
CH2: across resistor 7.00 V, across LED 2.00 V, channel current 70.00 mA

Questions.

  1. Which readings are the same in all channels, and which differ?
  2. What current does the schematic predict for each channel?
  3. From channel 2's readings, compute the resistance actually fitted.
  4. Compute the power in channel 2's resistor and in a correct channel's resistor. Compare both with a pretend rating of 0.25 W.
  5. Name the root cause, the fix, and one check that would have caught it before the board was powered.

Method hints. Voltages alone cannot tell the channels apart here: why not? Use the current. State two hypotheses (wrong resistor; faulty LED) and decide which the evidence supports.

Mini-project

Write a "power budget" sheet for a circuit with a supply, two resistors and an LED in one loop (exercise numbers). For each part: voltage, current, power, pretend rating and margin; then the total. Check it with Listing 1 (or your extended version). Rubric: budget balances (2); each power computed with an appropriate formula (1); the riskiest part identified with a reason (1); run output attached (1).

Summary

  • Power is the rate of energy transfer, in watts: 1 W = 1 J/s.
  • For any part, P = V × I, with V the voltage across that part.
  • For a resistor, also P = I² × R = V² ÷ R; all its power becomes heat.
  • Doubling current or voltage on a resistor gives four times the power.
  • Energy is power times time: E = P × t.
  • Source power equals the sum of the parts' powers (the power budget).
  • Check every part's power against its datasheet rating, with margin, before building.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: all three channels show 7.00 V across the resistor and 2.00 V across the LED; only the current differs: 7.00 mA in channels 1 and 3, 70.00 mA in channel 2. (In this ideal model the voltages are fixed by the supply and the LED, so they cannot reveal the fault; the current does.) Prediction: 7 V ÷ 1 kΩ = 7 mA. Fitted value: 7 V ÷ 0.070 A = 100 Ω, ten times smaller than the schematic. Power: channel 2: 7 × 0.070 = 0.49 W, about twice the pretend 0.25 W rating, hence the heat and the brown mark; correct channels: 7 × 0.007 = 0.049 W, about a fifth of the rating. The LED also carries ten times its designed current, which explains its brightness and puts it at risk. Ruled out: "faulty LED" — its voltage matches the others and the extra current is exactly explained by a 100 Ω resistor. Fix: power off, replace the resistor with the 1 kΩ part, inspect the LED and the board. Prevention: measure each resistor before fitting, or measure each channel's current at first power-on with a current-limited supply. How the evidence was made: hot_resistor.cpp with hot_resistor.in giving the fitted values 1000, 100, 1000 Ω (R1).

Story hook

Analogy

The restaurant is growing. Rosa wants water in two new places: a vegetable sink and a dishwasher. The plumber, Mr Okafor, offers two ways to connect them.

"Way one: one pipe goes through the vegetable sink's narrow tap, and then on through the dishwasher's narrow valve. All the water passes both, one after the other. Way two: the pipe splits in two. Some water goes to the sink, some to the dishwasher, and the two streams join again in the drain."

Rosa thinks. "In way one, if someone closes the sink tap, the dishwasher gets nothing. In way two, each one works on its own." Mr Okafor nods. "And in way two, the building draws more water in total." Rosa has just compared series and parallel connections. This chapter does the same with resistors, and gives you the rules to calculate both.

What you will be able to do

  • Recognise series and parallel connections on a circuit diagram.
  • Calculate the equivalent resistance of resistors in series and in parallel.
  • Apply the loop rule (voltages) and the junction rule (currents) to check every answer.
  • Design a voltage divider and predict its output.
  • Diagnose a divider whose output sags when a device is connected (loading).
Jargon box
Series
Simple words: parts connected one after another, so the same current passes through all of them. Analogy: Mr Okafor's way one: one pipe through the sink tap and then the dishwasher valve. Precise: components connected end to end with no branch between them, so they carry the same current; their voltages add. D2
Parallel
Simple words: parts connected side by side between the same two points, so they share the same voltage. Analogy: way two: the pipe splits, feeds both, and joins again. Precise: components connected between the same two nodes, so they have the same voltage; their currents add. D2
Node
Simple words: a meeting point of wires. Analogy: a pipe joint where several pipes meet. Precise: a point (or a set of points joined by wire) in a circuit, which has one potential. D2
Equivalent resistance
Simple words: one resistor that would do the same job as a group. Analogy: one pipe that lets through the same flow as a whole set of pipes. Precise: the single resistance that draws the same current from a source as the network it replaces; series: R1 + R2; parallel: 1 ÷ (1/R1 + 1/R2). D2
Kirchhoff's laws
Simple words: two bookkeeping rules: voltages round a loop add to zero; currents into a joint equal currents out. Analogy: water going round the building ends where it started; water into a pipe joint equals water out. Precise: the voltage law: the sum of potential differences around any closed loop is zero; the current law: the sum of currents into any node equals the sum out. D2
Voltage divider
Simple words: two resistors in series that give a smaller voltage from their middle point. Analogy: a tap halfway down a pipe gives part of the full pressure. Precise: a series pair R1, R2 across Vin whose junction has Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2) when nothing draws current from the junction. D2
Loading
Simple words: when connecting something to a circuit changes the circuit's voltages. Analogy: opening an extra tap halfway down a pipe lowers the pressure there. Precise: the change in a circuit's behaviour caused by the current drawn by a connected load; a load across R2 of a divider forms R2 ∥ Rload and lowers Vout. D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the same two resistors, 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ, on the same 9 V supply, first in series and then in parallel. The numbers are the ones Listing 1 printed.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

There are two simple ways to connect two parts. In series, they sit one after the other in a single path. All the current must pass through both. If one is removed, the path is broken and everything stops.D1

In parallel, the path splits into branches. Each part sits on its own branch, between the same two meeting points. Each branch gets the full push of the battery. If one branch is broken, the others keep working.D1

Think of Mr Okafor's pipes. Two narrow taps in series make the water's path harder: less water flows. Two narrow taps in parallel give the water two ways through: more water flows in total. Resistors behave the same way. In series, the total resistance goes up. In parallel, it goes down.D2

Two bookkeeping rules help you check your sums. Round any loop, the battery's push is all used up by the parts. And at any meeting point, the current coming in equals the current going out.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Series

Resistors in series carry the same current I. By Ohm's law, V1 = I × R1 and V2 = I × R2. Kirchhoff's voltage law says these add up to the supply: V = V1 + V2 = I × (R1 + R2). So the pair behaves like one resistor Req = R1 + R2.D2 The larger resistor takes the larger share of the voltage.

Parallel

Resistors in parallel have the same voltage V across them. Their currents are I1 = V ÷ R1 and I2 = V ÷ R2. Kirchhoff's current law at the node says the supply current is I = I1 + I2 = V × (1/R1 + 1/R2). So 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2.D2 For two resistors this can be written Req = R1 × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2). The result is always smaller than the smaller resistor. The smaller resistor takes the larger share of the current.

Engineers often write "∥" for "in parallel with": 1 kΩ ∥ 2 kΩ ≈ 667 Ω.

The voltage divider

Two resistors in series across a supply give, at their middle node, Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2), where R2 is the one between the middle and ground.D2 Two equal resistors give half the supply. Dividers are everywhere: sensors (HW302) and the inputs of logic chips (HW102) meet them.

Loading

The divider formula assumes nothing draws current from the middle node. If you connect a device with resistance RL there, it sits in parallel with R2. The lower half becomes R2 ∥ RL, which is smaller, so Vout drops. If RL is much larger than R2, the drop is small. If RL is close to R2 or smaller, the drop is large.D2 The forensic lab is about exactly this, and F1-07 shows that a meter itself is a load.

Power in combinations

In series, the larger resistor dissipates more (P = I² × R with the same I). In parallel, the smaller resistor dissipates more (P = V² ÷ R with the same V).D2 Check each part against its rating (F1-03).

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Not every network reduces to series and parallel steps; a bridge of five resistors does not. For those, engineers write Kirchhoff's current law at every node with the unknown node potentials and solve the equations (nodal analysis); circuit simulators do this automatically.D2 Seen from its output, any network of resistors and sources behaves like one source in series with one resistance (the Thévenin equivalent); for a divider that resistance is R1 ∥ R2, which is why a load must be large compared with it.D2

How the hardware actually does it

A wire joining parts has a very small resistance, so all points along it have almost the same potential: that is why a node can be treated as one point.D2 On a breadboard, the rows of holes are joined underneath by metal strips, so parts plugged into one row are in the same node. Which holes are joined on the kit's breadboard is shown in its documentation (D4); check it before wiring, because a part placed along a strip instead of across it is shorted out.

Worked example

Exercise numbers. A 9 V supply, R1 = 1 kΩ, R2 = 2 kΩ.

  1. Series. Req = 1 + 2 = 3 kΩ. I = 9 V ÷ 3 kΩ = 3 mA. V1 = 3 mA × 1 kΩ = 3 V. V2 = 3 mA × 2 kΩ = 6 V. Check: 3 + 6 = 9 V.
  2. Parallel. I1 = 9 ÷ 1 kΩ = 9 mA. I2 = 9 ÷ 2 kΩ = 4.5 mA. Total 13.5 mA. Req = 9 V ÷ 13.5 mA ≈ 0.667 kΩ. Check: 1 × 2 ÷ (1 + 2) = 0.667 kΩ, smaller than 1 kΩ.
  3. Divider. With R2 = 2 kΩ at the bottom, Vout = 9 × 2 ÷ 3 = 6 V: the series V2 again.
  4. Very unequal parallel. 1 kΩ ∥ 100 kΩ on 6 V: 6 mA + 0.06 mA = 6.06 mA, Req ≈ 990 Ω. The big resistor hardly changes anything.
  5. Loading. A divider of two 10 kΩ resistors on 6 V gives 3 V. Connect a 10 kΩ load to the middle: the bottom becomes 10 ∥ 10 = 5 kΩ, so Vout = 6 × 5 ÷ 15 = 2 V.

Listing 1 and the forensic generator print these numbers.R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — network.cpp: two resistors in series or parallel, with Kirchhoff checks.

// Two resistors and one supply, connected in series (S) or in parallel (P).
// Prints the equivalent resistance, every voltage and current, and checks
// the two loop rules: voltages around a loop add up to the supply (series)
// and currents into a junction equal the currents out (parallel).
// All values in network.in are exercise numbers.
#include <cmath>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main()
{
    char how = ' ';
    double supply = 0.0;
    double r1 = 0.0;
    double r2 = 0.0;

    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(3);
    while (std::cin >> how >> supply >> r1 >> r2) {
        if (how == 'S') {
            const double req = r1 + r2;
            const double amps = supply / req;
            const double v1 = amps * r1;
            const double v2 = amps * r2;
            std::cout << std::setprecision(0) << "series   " << r1 << " + " << r2
                      << std::setprecision(3) << ": Req = " << req << " ohms, I = "
                      << amps * 1000.0 << " mA, V1 = " << v1 << " V, V2 = " << v2 << " V";
            std::cout << (std::fabs(v1 + v2 - supply) < 1e-9 ? "  [V1 + V2 = supply: ok]\n"
                                                              : "  [loop rule FAILED]\n");
        } else if (how == 'P') {
            const double req = 1.0 / (1.0 / r1 + 1.0 / r2);
            const double i1 = supply / r1;
            const double i2 = supply / r2;
            const double total = supply / req;
            std::cout << std::setprecision(0) << "parallel " << r1 << " | " << r2
                      << std::setprecision(3) << ": Req = " << req << " ohms, I1 = "
                      << i1 * 1000.0 << " mA, I2 = " << i2 * 1000.0 << " mA, total = "
                      << total * 1000.0 << " mA";
            std::cout << (std::fabs(i1 + i2 - total) < 1e-12 ? "  [I1 + I2 = total: ok]\n"
                                                             : "  [junction rule FAILED]\n");
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

Every line passes its Kirchhoff check and matches the worked example.R1

Where the analogy breaks

  1. Real pipes split unevenly for many reasons. In plumbing, bends, height and turbulence change how water splits. For ideal resistors in parallel, the split follows exactly I = V ÷ R for each branch. The pipe picture suggests more uncertainty than the rule has.D2
  2. An extra open tap in a building may not change the pressure much; a load on a divider can. A building's mains water often has a strong supply behind it. A divider made of large resistors is a "weak" source: a modest load can pull its voltage down a lot (loading). Do not trust the pipe intuition here; calculate.
  3. Wires are not "pipes with a little resistance" in every case. We treat a node as one point. For fast signals and long wires that is no longer exact (HW204).

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Parallel result larger than either resistorAdded the resistances instead of their reciprocalsSanity check: parallel is always smaller than the smallestUse 1 ÷ (1/R1 + 1/R2)
Divider output too lowSomething connected to the middle loads itMeasure with and without the load (forensic lab)Smaller divider resistors, or a load with higher resistance
Divider gives Vin − expectedR1 and R2 swappedWhich resistor goes to ground?Put R2 between the output and ground
A part has 0 V across it on the breadboardBoth its legs are in the same connected row: it is shortedCheck the breadboard's connection pattern (D4)Place the part across two different rows
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-01 to F1-03: voltage between two points, Ohm's law for one resistor, power. What carries over: Ohm's law applied to each part on its own, with that part's own voltage and current; power checks against ratings.D2 What changes: most dangerous first: connecting anything to a circuit can change it (loading), so a measured or designed voltage holds only for the circuit as it is; you now reason about whole networks with two conservation rules, Kirchhoff's voltage and current laws; parallel combinations always lower the resistance and raise the supply current.D2 What comes next: F1-05 adds a new part, the capacitor, whose voltage cannot jump, and uses a resistor with it to make time delays.

Check yourself

  1. In series, what is the same for every part? In parallel?
  2. Find Req for 470 Ω and 330 Ω in series, and in parallel.
  3. Three equal 3 kΩ resistors in parallel have Req = (a) 9 kΩ (b) 3 kΩ (c) 1 kΩ (d) 0.33 kΩ.
  4. A divider has R1 = 3 kΩ (top) and R2 = 1 kΩ (bottom) on 12 V. What is Vout?
  5. In Figure 1's parallel circuit, which resistor dissipates more power? Compute both.
  6. Explain in your own words why a load on a divider lowers its output.
  7. Apply to a new case: a string of four identical lamps in series on a supply; one breaks. What happens, and why? What would happen in parallel?
  8. Use Kirchhoff's current law: 20 mA enter a node; one branch carries 12 mA out. What does the other carry?

Lab

Goal: predict and check series, parallel and divider circuits with Listing 1, and measure loading.

Hardware and software needed: Part A: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Part B (optional): the kit's battery, breadboard and resistors, and the course meter, chosen by the owner.

Safety

Part B: adult supervision, low-voltage battery kit only, no mains. Calculate currents and powers before connecting (parallel branches add current). Disconnect the battery before rewiring. Never place a wire or a meter in current mode directly across the battery.S1

Part A — simulator

  1. Build and run Listing 1. You should see the five lines above, each with "ok".
  2. Add three lines of your own (at least one parallel pair of very different values). Predict Req and the currents first, then run.
  3. Build and run divider_load.cpp (same build command). Predict each output from Layer 2 before you look.
  4. Extend Listing 1 with a third letter, D, that prints a divider's output for a given supply, R1 and R2.

Part B — breadboard (optional, supervised)

Not verified — check before relying on this

Part B was not performed in this build; no kit, breadboard or meter was available or chosen. The breadboard's connection pattern, the meter's settings and the resistor values come from the kit's and meter's documentation (D4).

  1. Build a divider from two equal resistors. Measure Vout with the meter (voltage mode).
  2. Add a third resistor from the output to ground (the "load"). Measure again and compare with your prediction.
  3. Build two resistors in parallel; measure each branch current and the total (F1-07 method).

Expected observations

Part A: the outputs shown, and your D lines agreeing with the formula. Part B: totals that follow Kirchhoff's laws within the meter's accuracy, and a divider output that drops when the load is added.

Verification

Your added lines print "ok" for both checks, and your D option reproduces the forensic generator's first line (3.00 V from 6 V and two 10 kΩ resistors).

Troubleshooting

  • "rule FAILED" printed → an input value is zero or negative → check the line.
  • Part B divider reads the full supply → the bottom resistor is not connected to ground.
  • Part B reading lower than predicted even without load → the meter's own input resistance loads a high-value divider (F1-07).

Extension

Write a function that reduces a list of resistors in series, and another for a list in parallel; use them to find Req of (1 kΩ ∥ 1 kΩ) in series with 500 Ω, and check by hand.

Forensic lab

Scenario: "The divider that sags". A board makes a 3 V reference from a 6 V supply with two 10 kΩ resistors. Three different sensor modules, A, B and C, can be plugged into the reference point. Elif reports: "With sensor A the reference is fine. With B it is wrong, and with C it is far too low."

Evidence pack. Readings produced by the course's divider model (divider_load.cpp), not by a real board.

sensor-A: divider output 2.99 V, supply current 0.30 mA
sensor-B: divider output 2.00 V, supply current 0.40 mA

Questions.

  1. What does the divider give with nothing plugged in? Does that match the design?
  2. Why does the supply current increase when B or C is plugged in?
  3. From B's reading, work out the resistance of the bottom half, and then B's own input resistance.
  4. Do the same for C.
  5. Propose two different fixes, and say what each costs (power, parts).

Method hints. Compare "nothing" with each sensor. Hypotheses: "the divider resistors changed" or "the sensor draws current". Which readings separate them? Use Vout = 6 × Rlow ÷ (10 kΩ + Rlow) and solve for Rlow.

Mini-project

Design a divider that gives 2 V from 5 V and stays within 5 % when loaded by a 100 kΩ device (exercise numbers). Show your calculation for the loaded and unloaded outputs, check it with your extended Listing 1, and state the divider's own current and power. Rubric: unloaded output correct (1); loaded output within 5 % and shown (2); power stated (1); run shown (1).

Summary

  • Series: same current; voltages add; Req = R1 + R2.
  • Parallel: same voltage; currents add; 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2; Req is smaller than the smallest.
  • Kirchhoff's voltage law: voltages round a loop sum to zero. Current law: in = out at every node.
  • Divider: Vout = Vin × R2 ÷ (R1 + R2), with no load.
  • A load in parallel with R2 lowers Vout: loading.
  • Check every combination with the two laws and every part with its rating.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Series: the current. Parallel: the voltage.
  2. Series: 470 + 330 = 800 Ω. Parallel: 470 × 330 ÷ 800 ≈ 193.9 Ω.
  3. (c) 1 kΩ: 1/R = 3 × (1/3 kΩ) = 1/(1 kΩ). (a) is the series answer. (b) forgets that more branches lower R. (d) inverts the wrong number.
  4. 12 × 1 ÷ (3 + 1) = 3 V.
  5. The 1 kΩ: 9² ÷ 1,000 = 0.081 W; the 2 kΩ: 81 ÷ 2,000 = 0.0405 W. With the same voltage, the smaller resistor takes more current and more power.
  6. In your words: the load is a second path to ground from the middle node, in parallel with the bottom resistor, so the bottom half has less resistance and gets a smaller share of the supply.
  7. In series, the only path is broken, so all four lamps go out. In parallel, each lamp has its own branch with the full voltage, so the other three stay lit.
  8. 20 − 12 = 8 mA out of the node through the other branch.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: nothing plugged: 3.00 V, 0.30 mA (design value 6 × 10 ÷ 20 = 3 V). A: 2.99 V. B: 2.00 V and 0.40 mA. C: 0.50 V and 0.55 mA. The supply current grows because each sensor adds a second path to ground. B: 2 = 6 × Rlow ÷ (10 kΩ + Rlow) gives Rlow = 5 kΩ; 10 kΩ ∥ RB = 5 kΩ gives RB = 10 kΩ. C: 0.5 = 6 × Rlow ÷ (10 kΩ + Rlow) gives Rlow ≈ 909 Ω; 10 kΩ ∥ RC ≈ 909 Ω gives RC ≈ 1 kΩ. A's input resistance is large compared with 10 kΩ (the model used 1 MΩ). Root cause: loading: sensors B and C have input resistances comparable with or smaller than the divider's resistors. The hypothesis "divider resistors changed" is ruled out because the unloaded reading is exactly the design value. Fixes: use much smaller divider resistors (more current and power wasted in the divider, check ratings), or put a buffer stage between divider and sensor (a later course topic), or choose sensors with high input resistance. How the evidence was made: divider_load.cpp with divider_load.in: open, 1 MΩ, 10 kΩ, 1 kΩ (R1).

Story hook

Analogy

In the restaurant's basement there is an odd little tank. Across its middle is a stretchy rubber wall. Water can flow in on one side and push the rubber, and the same amount of water is pushed out on the other side. But no water ever crosses the wall.

When Rosa opens the supply, water rushes in at first. As the rubber stretches, it pushes back harder and harder. The flow slows down, and at last it stops: the rubber's push equals the supply's pressure. If the inlet pipe is narrow, the filling takes longer. If the tank is bigger, it takes longer too.

Hamid, the night cook, uses the tank as a timer: "When the gauge reaches the red mark, the bread is ready." The electric version of that tank is called a capacitor. With a resistor, it makes a timer, and a timer is the first step towards a blinking light and, much later, towards the clock of a processor.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a capacitor stores, and why its voltage cannot jump instantly.
  • Use Q = C × V and the unit farad with its prefixes (µF, nF).
  • Predict the charging curve of a resistor–capacitor (RC) circuit and the time constant τ = R × C.
  • Compare a step-by-step simulation with the formula, using a C++ program.
  • Diagnose a timer that runs too slowly from a logged charging curve.
Jargon box
Capacitor
Simple words: a part that stores charge on two plates that do not touch. Analogy (proposed): the basement tank with a stretchy rubber wall. Precise: a two-terminal component made of two conductors separated by an insulator; when a voltage V is applied, charges +Q and −Q collect on the two sides, with Q = C × V. D2
Capacitance
Simple words: how much charge a capacitor holds for each volt. Analogy (proposed): how big and how stretchy the tank's rubber wall is. Precise: C = Q ÷ V, measured in farads (F); one farad is one coulomb per volt; practical values use µF (10−6 F), nF (10−9 F) and pF (10−12 F). D2 D3
RC circuit
Simple words: a resistor and a capacitor together, used to make a delay. Analogy (proposed): the rubber-wall tank filled through a narrow pipe. Precise: a circuit in which a capacitor charges or discharges through a resistance, so its voltage changes gradually rather than at once. D2
Time constant (τ)
Simple words: the "speed setting" of an RC circuit: bigger means slower. Analogy (proposed): how long the tank takes to fill most of the way. Precise: τ = R × C, in seconds when R is in ohms and C in farads; after one τ a charging capacitor has covered 1 − e−1 ≈ 63.2 % of the way to the supply voltage. D2 R1
Exponential curve
Simple words: a curve that changes fast at first and then slower and slower. Analogy: the tank fills quickly at first, then creeps towards full. Precise: here V(t) = Vs × (1 − e−t/τ), where e ≈ 2.718 is the base of natural logarithms; in each further τ the remaining gap shrinks by the same factor e−1 ≈ 0.368. D2
Polarised capacitor
Simple words: a capacitor with a + leg and a − leg that must not be swapped. Analogy: a tank whose rubber wall may only be pushed from one side. Precise: a capacitor type (for example an electrolytic) that is designed to be used with one terminal always positive; its datasheet gives the polarity marking and the maximum voltage. D1 D4

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the voltage on a capacitor charging through a resistor from a 5 V supply (exercise values: 10 kΩ and 100 µF, so τ = 1 s). The curve rises quickly, then flattens. The marks show the voltage after one, two and three time constants.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A capacitor is made of two metal plates with an insulator between them. Current cannot pass through the insulator. But when a battery is connected, charge piles up on one plate and leaves the other. The capacitor is "charged".D1 D2

Think of Hamid's tank with the rubber wall. Water flows in on one side and out on the other, but none crosses the wall. The more the wall stretches, the harder it pushes back. Charging slows down as the capacitor fills, and stops when its push equals the battery's.

Put a resistor in the way, and charging takes time. A bigger resistor means a narrower pipe: slower. A bigger capacitor means a bigger tank: slower too. Multiply the two and you get the circuit's time constant, its "speed setting".D2

That is how you can build a timer without a computer. Wait until the capacitor's voltage reaches a mark, then do something. In F1-08 you will use that idea to blink an LED.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Charge and voltage: Q = C × V

A capacitor's charge is proportional to its voltage: Q = C × V. The constant C is its capacitance, in farads. One farad is one coulomb per volt, which is very large; real parts are often in microfarads (µF) or nanofarads (nF).D2 D3 Example: a 100 µF capacitor at 5 V holds Q = 0.0001 × 5 = 0.0005 C.

Why the voltage cannot jump

To change the voltage, you must move charge, and moving charge takes current over time. Current is charge per second, so the capacitor's voltage changes at a rate of I ÷ C volts per second.D2 With a resistor limiting the current, the voltage cannot change instantly. That is the property every timing circuit uses.

Charging through a resistor

Connect supply Vs, resistor R and an empty capacitor in series. At the start, the capacitor has 0 V, so the whole supply is across R and the current is Vs ÷ R. As the capacitor charges, its voltage Vc rises, the resistor's share Vs − Vc shrinks, and so does the current. The result is the exponential curve of Figure 1:D2

Vc(t) = Vs × (1 − e−t/τ), with τ = R × C.

Ohms times farads gives seconds, so τ is a time.D3 After 1 τ the capacitor reaches about 63 % of Vs; after 3 τ about 95 %; after 5 τ about 99 %. These percentages are pure arithmetic of the formula, and Listing 1 prints them.R1

Discharging

A charged capacitor connected across a resistor alone discharges along the mirror curve: Vc(t) = V0 × e−t/τ. After 1 τ, about 37 % of the starting voltage is left.D2

Using the curve as a timer

To know when the capacitor reaches a voltage Vx, solve the formula for t: t = τ × ln(Vs ÷ (Vs − Vx)), where ln is the natural logarithm (a calculator key). For Vx = 63.2 % of Vs, this gives t = τ. F1-08 uses the same idea with two thresholds to make a blinker.

Note

Maths you need here. ex and ln(x) are inverse operations, just as squaring and square root are. MA101 covers powers and logarithms of 2; e is another base, and your calculator or std::exp and std::log in C++ compute them. You do not need to derive the curve at L1; you need to use it and check it.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. The exponential comes from a simple rule: at every instant, the rate of rise of Vc is proportional to the remaining gap, (Vs − Vc) ÷ (R × C). Listing 1 applies exactly this rule in tiny time steps (Euler's method, MA302) and lands on the formula's values within a few millivolts. Real capacitors are not ideal: they have a tolerance, a small leakage current through the insulator, a maximum voltage and, for some types, a capacitance that changes with voltage or temperature. All of these come from the datasheet (D4) and change how accurate an RC timer can be.D2

How the hardware actually does it

A capacitor's plates are often thin metal foils or films, rolled or stacked with an insulating layer between them. Larger plate area and a thinner insulator give more capacitance.D2 Inside chips, every wire and every transistor gate also has a little capacitance. Charging those tiny capacitances through the resistance of transistors is why signals take time to change, the propagation delay of F1-15, and why faster clocks need more power (HW301). Which capacitor types the kit contains, and their polarity marks and voltage ratings, are in the kit's datasheets (D4).

Worked example

Exercise values. Vs = 5 V, R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 µF.

  1. τ = R × C = 10,000 Ω × 0.0001 F = 1 s.
  2. Starting current: 5 V ÷ 10 kΩ = 0.5 mA.
  3. At t = 1 s: Vc = 5 × (1 − e−1) = 5 × (1 − 0.3679) ≈ 3.16 V.
  4. At t = 3 s: Vc = 5 × (1 − e−3) = 5 × (1 − 0.0498) ≈ 4.75 V.
  5. When does it reach 2.5 V (half)? t = 1 × ln(5 ÷ 2.5) = ln 2 ≈ 0.693 s.
  6. Charge stored when full: Q = 100 µF × 5 V = 500 µC = 0.0005 C.
  7. Replace C by 1,000 µF: τ becomes 10 s. Every time on the curve is ten times longer.

Listing 1 prints 3.162 V (step by step) and 3.161 V (formula) at 1 s, and 4.751 V at 3 s.R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — rc_charge.cpp: charges a capacitor in 1 ms steps and compares with the formula every 0.5 s.

// Charging a capacitor through a resistor from a fixed supply.
// Two ways: (1) step by step: in each small time step dt the current
// I = (Vs - Vc) / R adds charge I * dt, so Vc rises by I * dt / C;
// (2) the formula Vc(t) = Vs * (1 - e^(-t / (R * C))).
// R, C and Vs are exercise numbers: 10 kilo-ohms, 100 microfarads, 5 V.
#include <cmath>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    const double supply = 5.0;
    const double ohms = 10000.0;
    const double farads = 100e-6;
    const double tau = ohms * farads;
    const double dt = 0.001;

    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(3);
    std::cout << "tau = R * C = " << tau << " s\n";
    std::cout << "   t (s)   step-by-step (V)   formula (V)   percent of supply\n";
    double vc = 0.0;
    const int stepsPerPrint = 500;
    for (int k = 0; k <= 10 * stepsPerPrint; ++k) {
        if (k % stepsPerPrint == 0) {
            const double t = k * dt;
            const double formula = supply * (1.0 - std::exp(-t / tau));
            std::cout << std::setw(8) << t << std::setw(19) << vc << std::setw(14) << formula
                      << std::setw(17) << std::setprecision(1) << 100.0 * formula / supply
                      << std::setprecision(3) << "\n";
        }
        const double amps = (supply - vc) / ohms;
        vc += amps * dt / farads;
    }
    return 0;
}

12–14supply = 5.0; ohms = 10000.0; farads = 100e-6;The circuit's values in base units.100e-6 is 100 µF written in farads.
15const double tau = ohms * farads;τ = R × C.1 s for these values.
16const double dt = 0.001;Time step: 1 ms.Small compared with τ, so the steps follow the curve closely.
21double vc = 0.0;The capacitor starts empty.Initial condition.
23for (int k = 0; k <= 10 * stepsPerPrint; ++k)5,000 steps of 1 ms: 5 s.Covers 5 τ.
24–29if (k % stepsPerPrint == 0) { … std::exp(-t / tau) … }Every 500 steps, prints t, the simulated Vc, the formula and the percentage.Puts the two methods side by side.
31const double amps = (supply - vc) / ohms;Current now: the resistor's share of the voltage over R.Ohm's law on the resistor (F1-02).

Where the analogy breaks

  1. The guide's registry warns that capacitors have no simple pipe equivalent. The rubber-wall tank is a proposed picture. It gets "no flow through, push-back grows" right, but a real capacitor has no moving wall: the charges sit on plates and the "push-back" is the electric field between them.D2
  2. A rubber wall stretches unevenly and can tear slowly; an ideal capacitor is exactly linear. Q = C × V is a straight line. Real parts depart from it in ways their datasheets describe, not in the way rubber does.
  3. Current seems to "go through" a capacitor while it charges. In the tank, water clearly does not cross the wall. In a circuit, a meter in series with a charging capacitor shows a current, and charge leaves one plate as it arrives on the other. The analogy makes this look stranger than it is.D2

Transition box

Where you came from: F1-01 to F1-04: steady currents and voltages in resistor networks; nothing depended on time. What carries over: Ohm's law for the resistor at every instant; the definition of current as charge per second; series connection (R and C share one current).D2 What changes: most dangerous first: some capacitors are polarised and have a voltage rating, so wiring them backwards or overvolting them can damage them; circuits now have time: values change, so a single reading needs a time stamp; the maths uses exponentials and logarithms.D1 D2 What comes next: F1-06 meets the diode and the LED, the part your blinker will drive; F1-08 combines an RC circuit with thresholds into a blinker.

Check yourself

  1. What does a capacitor store, and what is its capacitance?
  2. Compute τ for R = 47 kΩ and C = 10 µF.
  3. After one time constant, a capacitor charging from 0 V towards 9 V is at about: (a) 9 V (b) 5.7 V (c) 3.3 V (d) 4.5 V.
  4. Why can a capacitor's voltage not jump instantly when it is charged through a resistor?
  5. A 220 µF capacitor at 6 V: how much charge does it hold?
  6. Explain in your own words why the charging gets slower as the capacitor fills.
  7. Apply to a new case: you want an RC circuit to reach about 95 % of the supply after 6 s, with R = 20 kΩ. Which C?
  8. Predict: in Listing 1, what happens to the "step-by-step" column if dt is changed to 0.1 s (and stepsPerPrint to 5, so it still prints every 0.5 s)? Then change it and run.

Lab

Goal: predict RC charging times, check them with Listing 1, and (optionally, supervised) measure a real RC circuit against the prediction, as the HW101 lab "RC timing measured against prediction" asks.

Hardware and software needed: Part A: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Part B (optional): the kit's battery, a resistor, a capacitor, a push button or switch, the course meter and a stopwatch, as chosen by the owner.

Safety

Part B: adult supervision; low-voltage battery kit only; no mains. Check a polarised capacitor's + and − marking against its datasheet before connecting, and never exceed its rated voltage. Discharge the capacitor through a resistor (not a bare wire) before handling or rewiring. Disconnect the battery to rewire. If a capacitor gets warm, bulges or hisses, disconnect and step back; your supervisor handles it.S1 D1

Part A — simulator

  1. Build and run Listing 1. You should see the table above.
  2. Change C to 220 µF. Predict τ and the voltage at 1 s, then run.
  3. Add a discharge phase: after 5 s, switch the supply to 0 V and continue for another 5 s. Check that after one more τ the voltage is about 37 % of where it started.
  4. Answer Check-yourself question 8 by running the program with dt = 0.1 and stepsPerPrint = 5.

Part B — real RC timing (optional, supervised)

Not verified — check before relying on this

Part B was not performed in this build: no kit, meter or capacitor was available, and the kit is not chosen. The values of R and C, the capacitor's tolerance, polarity and voltage rating come from the datasheets (D4). A meter connected across the capacitor draws a little current and can change the curve for large resistors (F1-07); the chosen meter's input resistance is in its manual (D4).

  1. From the datasheet values, compute τ and the predicted voltage at 1 τ, 2 τ and 3 τ. Choose R and C so that τ is several seconds, so you can read the meter by eye.
  2. Wire battery → switch → R → C → back, with the meter (voltage mode) across C, and the capacitor discharged.
  3. Close the switch and start the stopwatch together. Read the meter at each predicted time. Write down every reading with its time.
  4. Open the switch, discharge the capacitor through a resistor, and repeat twice.
  5. Find the time at which the reading crossed 63 % of the battery voltage. That is your measured τ.

Expected observations

Part A: the real output above and your modified runs. Part B: a curve with the shape of Figure 1; a measured τ close to R × C, differing by an amount that the parts' tolerances and the meter's loading can explain. Label every number as "measured on (date) with (meter)".

Verification

Your measured τ, averaged over three runs, lies within the range allowed by the tolerances of R and C (from their datasheets). If not, explain why using the troubleshooting list.

Troubleshooting

  • Voltage jumps at once to the supply → the resistor is bypassed or missing.
  • Voltage rises far slower than predicted → capacitor value 10× or a unit confusion (forensic lab).
  • Voltage stops well below the supply → meter loading or leakage (Layer 3; F1-07).
  • Readings differ between runs → the capacitor was not fully discharged before starting.

Extension

Fit τ from all your readings, not just the 63 % point: compute ln(Vs ÷ (Vs − Vc)) for each reading and fit a straight line through the origin against t (the method of F1-02). Its slope is 1 ÷ τ.

Forensic lab

Scenario: "The blink that is ten times too slow". Rui built a timer from the design R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 µF on a 5 V supply. The design promises τ = 1 s. "It works, but everything happens about ten times too slowly," Rui says. A data logger recorded the capacitor voltage after switch-on.

Questions.

  1. What voltage is 63.2 % of 5 V? At what time does the log reach it?
  2. What is the measured τ? How does it compare with the design?
  3. Assuming R is correct, what capacitance was fitted?
  4. Give two possible ways this mistake could happen in the workshop, and one test that tells them apart from a wrong resistor.
  5. How would you prevent it next time?

Method hints. Use the 63 % rule, then check with a second point (for example 86.5 % at 2 τ). Hypotheses: "C is wrong" or "R is wrong". A resistor can be measured with power off (F1-07); what would that measurement show in each case?

Mini-project

This is the first half of the HW101 course project (an RC blinker). Choose R and C (exercise values, or kit values from datasheets) so that a capacitor charging from 0 V reaches 3 V from a 5 V supply in 0.5 s. Show the calculation with ln, check it with a modified Listing 1, and write a prediction table for the voltage every 0.1 s. Rubric: correct formula and τ (2); simulated crossing within 1 % of 0.5 s (1); prediction table (1); clear note of which values are exercise or datasheet values (1).

Summary

  • A capacitor stores charge: Q = C × V; capacitance is in farads (µF, nF in practice).
  • Its voltage cannot jump; it changes as charge flows in or out.
  • Charging through R: Vc = Vs × (1 − e−t/τ); discharging: V0 × e−t/τ.
  • τ = R × C; after 1 τ about 63 %, after 3 τ about 95 %, after 5 τ about 99 %.
  • Time to reach Vx: t = τ × ln(Vs ÷ (Vs − Vx)).
  • Step-by-step simulation and the formula agree when the step is small.
  • Polarised capacitors: correct polarity and voltage rating, from the datasheet.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Charge (equal and opposite on its two plates). Capacitance is charge per volt, C = Q ÷ V, in farads.
  2. τ = 47,000 × 0.00001 = 0.47 s.
  3. (b) 5.7 V: 9 × 0.632 ≈ 5.69 V. (a) is "full", which needs about 5 τ. (c) 3.3 V is the 37 % left in a discharge. (d) 4.5 V is half, reached at about 0.69 τ.
  4. Its voltage is Q ÷ C, and charge can only arrive at the rate the current allows; the resistor limits the current, so the voltage changes gradually.
  5. Q = 0.000220 × 6 = 0.00132 C (1.32 mC).
  6. In your words: the fuller it is, the closer its voltage is to the supply, so less voltage is left across the resistor, so less current flows, so it fills more slowly.
  7. About 95 % at 3 τ, so τ = 2 s; C = τ ÷ R = 2 ÷ 20,000 = 100 µF.
  8. With dt = 0.1 s (a tenth of τ), each step uses the current at the start of the step, which is too large for the rest of the step, so the step-by-step column runs ahead of the formula. Forensic lab answer key

Observation: 63.2 % of 5 V is 3.16 V; the log shows 3.16 V at t = 10 s. Second check: 86.5 % (4.32 V) at 2 τ appears at t = 20 s. Measured τ: 10 s, ten times the design's 1 s. Fitted C: τ ÷ R = 10 ÷ 10,000 = 0.001 F = 1,000 µF. Possible causes: a 1,000 µF part taken from the neighbouring drawer, or a marking misread (a factor of ten). A wrong resistor (100 kΩ) would give the same τ; measuring R with power off (F1-07) separates the two: it reads 10 kΩ here. Prevention: check each part's marking against its datasheet and measure R before fitting; record the predicted τ on the build sheet and check the first run against it. How the evidence was made: blink_log.cpp with blink_log.in = 1000 (µF), R = 10 kΩ, supply 5 V, formula Vs × (1 − e−t/τ) sampled every 2 s (R1).
