Story hook

Analogy

The restaurant's drain pipe has a small flap valve inside. Water flowing out to the street pushes the flap open. If water ever tried to flow back in, it would push the flap shut. Mr Okafor, the plumber, says it is the most important part in the basement.

The flap is a little stiff. A trickle with almost no pressure does not open it. But once the pressure passes a certain level, it swings wide open, and then even a tiny extra push lets a lot more water through. "That is why there is a narrow section after it," says Mr Okafor. "Otherwise a big push would send a flood."

In F0-40 you met the LED as a one-way part that needs a resistor. Now you will see why, with the curve that describes the flap's stiffness, and you will calculate exactly how much current your LED gets.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a diode does, with the flap-valve picture and its precise V–I behaviour.
  • Identify anode and cathode on the symbol, and forward and reverse bias.
  • Calculate the series resistor for an LED with the simple fixed-voltage model, and judge when that model is good enough.
  • Solve an LED loop with a curve model in C++, and compare the two models.
  • Diagnose uneven brightness in LEDs that share one resistor.
Jargon box
Diode
Simple words: a part that lets current through one way and blocks it the other way. Analogy (proposed): the one-way flap valve in the restaurant's drain. Precise: a two-terminal semiconductor device that conducts readily when its anode is more positive than its cathode (forward bias) and passes only a tiny current in the opposite direction (reverse bias), up to its breakdown voltage. D2
Anode and cathode
Simple words: the diode's two ends: current goes in at the anode and out at the cathode. Analogy: the inlet and outlet side of the flap. Precise: in the forward direction, conventional current enters the anode and leaves the cathode; the symbol's triangle points from anode to cathode, towards the bar. D2
Forward voltage
Simple words: the voltage across a diode when it conducts. Analogy: the pressure needed to hold the flap open. Precise: the voltage across a forward-biased diode at a stated current; it changes only a little over a wide range of current, and its value for a given part comes from the datasheet. D2 D4
LED
Simple words: a diode that gives off light when current flows forward. Analogy: a flap valve that glows while water flows through it. Precise: a light-emitting diode; its colour and forward voltage depend on its semiconductor material, and its brightness rises with forward current up to the datasheet's maximum. D1 D2
I–V curve
Simple words: a graph of how much current flows at each voltage. Analogy: a chart of flow against pressure for the stiff flap. Precise: the plot of current against voltage for a part; a resistor's is a straight line (F1-02), a diode's is nearly flat and then rises very steeply. D2
Breakdown (reverse)
Simple words: what happens if you push a diode backwards too hard: it suddenly conducts and can be destroyed. Analogy: the flap torn off by too much back-pressure. Precise: the reverse voltage above which reverse current rises sharply; the datasheet gives the maximum reverse voltage, which for LEDs can be low. D2 D4

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the I–V curve of the course's model LED (pretend parameters, the same as Listing 1) together with the "load line" of a 220 Ω resistor on 5 V. The LED's operating point is where the two meet.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A diode is a one-way part. Current can flow through it in one direction, from the anode to the cathode. In the other direction, it blocks.D2 On a circuit drawing, the diode is a triangle pointing at a bar. The triangle shows the way current may go.

An LED is a diode that glows. You met it in F0-40. Like Mr Okafor's flap, it needs a certain push before it opens. Below that push, almost no current flows and the LED is dark. Above it, the current rises very quickly.D1 D2

That fast rise is the danger. A little more voltage gives a lot more current, and too much current destroys the LED. So we never connect an LED straight to a battery. A resistor in series limits the current, just like the narrow section after the flap.D1

Turned the wrong way, an LED stays dark. Pushed backwards too hard, it can be damaged too. The datasheet says how much backward push it can take.D4

Layer 2 — the student explanation

The diode's I–V curve

For a resistor, current is proportional to voltage (F1-02). For a diode, the forward current grows exponentially with voltage. A common model is I = Is × (eV/Vn − 1), where Is is a tiny current and Vn a small voltage that depend on the device.D2 Because the curve is so steep, the voltage across a conducting diode changes only a little while the current changes a lot. That nearly constant voltage is the forward voltage.

In reverse, the model gives I ≈ −Is: practically nothing. Listing 1's last line shows −1.000e−18 A at −5 V. A real diode also has a reverse breakdown voltage, which this model does not include; its maximum reverse voltage is in the datasheet.D2 D4

The simple model and the series resistor

For design, engineers often replace the curve by a constant forward voltage VF from the datasheet. Then Kirchhoff's voltage law (F1-04) gives the resistor's share: VR = Vs − VF, and the current is I = (Vs − VF) ÷ R. To choose R for a wanted current: R = (Vs − VF) ÷ I.D2 This is F0-40's formula, now justified.

How good is it? Listing 1 solves the loop both ways. With 220 Ω on 5 V, the curve model gives 14.27 mA and the simple model (pretend VF = 2 V) gives 13.64 mA, about 5 % apart. With 1 Ω, the curve gives 2,875 mA and the simple model 3,000 mA: both say "destroyed", and that is the point. The simple model is good for choosing a resistor; it is useless for predicting what happens with no resistor.R1

Load line

The resistor gives a second relation: I = (Vs − V) ÷ R. Drawn on the LED's I–V graph, it is a straight line, the load line. The circuit must satisfy both, so it sits where they cross (Figure 1).D2 A bigger R makes the line lower and the current smaller.

Power and limits

The LED's power is P = VF × I (F1-03). The datasheet gives the maximum forward current and often a recommended operating current; stay below the maximum with margin.D4 Remember the resistor's power too: (Vs − VF) × I.

LEDs in parallel

Two LEDs in parallel have the same voltage. Because their curves are steep, a tiny difference between the two parts means a large difference in current. If they share one resistor, one LED can take most of the current.D2 The usual rule: give each LED its own resistor. The forensic lab shows this.

Not verified — check before relying on this

All LED numbers in this chapter (Is, Vn, the 2 V "simple" forward voltage) are pretend exercise values. Real forward voltages, maximum currents, maximum reverse voltages and how the anode is marked on the part differ by colour, material and maker. Before the kit lab, copy them from the datasheet of the LED in the chosen kit (D4).

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. A diode's forward voltage at a fixed current falls as it gets warmer; if two parallel LEDs share a resistor, the one taking more current heats more, its voltage drops, and it takes even more current. This positive feedback is why parallel LEDs without individual resistors are a known reliability problem.D2 Ordinary silicon diodes are used to let current through only one way, for example to protect a circuit if a battery is inserted backwards, or to turn alternating current into one-direction current (rectification).D2 Neither topic is needed for this course's labs.

How the hardware actually does it

A diode is a crystal of semiconductor with two regions joined together: one treated so it has spare electrons (n-type), one so it has missing electrons, "holes" (p-type). At the junction, a thin zone forms that blocks current. A forward voltage narrows that zone and lets charges cross; a reverse voltage widens it.D2 In an LED, electrons and holes meeting at the junction give off their energy as light; the material decides the colour and the forward voltage.D2 The same p–n junctions are the building blocks of the transistor in F1-09.

Worked example

Exercise numbers. A 5 V supply, an LED with pretend VF = 2 V and a pretend maximum current of 20 mA.

  1. Wanted current with margin: 14 mA. R = (5 − 2) ÷ 0.014 ≈ 214 Ω. Choose the next value you have above it, for example 220 Ω.
  2. Simple model check: I = 3 ÷ 220 ≈ 13.6 mA. Below 20 mA.
  3. Curve model (Listing 1): 14.27 mA at 1.860 V. Still below 20 mA; the simple model was about 5 % low.
  4. Resistor power: (5 − 1.86) × 0.01427 ≈ 0.045 W. LED power: 1.86 × 0.01427 ≈ 0.027 W.
  5. With 100 Ω instead: simple model 30 mA, curve model 31.0 mA. Both above the pretend maximum: not allowed.

These numbers come from the run below.R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — led_model.cpp: solves an LED and resistor loop with the curve model (by bisection) and with the simple model.

// An LED in series with a resistor, solved two ways.
// Curve model: I = Is * (e^(V / Vn) - 1), with PRETEND parameters
// Is = 1e-18 A and Vn = 0.05 V (exercise values, not from a datasheet).
// The loop needs (Vs - V) / R = I(V); we find V by bisection.
// Simple model: the LED always takes a fixed pretend 2 V.
#include <cmath>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>

double ledAmps(double volts)
{
    const double is = 1e-18;
    const double vn = 0.05;
    return is * (std::exp(volts / vn) - 1.0);
}

double solveLedVolts(double supply, double ohms)
{
    double low = 0.0;
    double high = supply;
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; ++i) {
        const double mid = 0.5 * (low + high);
        const double resistorAmps = (supply - mid) / ohms;
        if (ledAmps(mid) > resistorAmps) {
            high = mid;
        } else {
            low = mid;
        }
    }
    return 0.5 * (low + high);
}

int main()
{
    const double supply = 5.0;
    const double pretendFixedVolts = 2.0;
    const double resistors[] = {1000.0, 470.0, 220.0, 100.0, 1.0};

    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(3);
    std::cout << "supply " << supply << " V\n";
    std::cout << "      R (ohms)   LED V (curve)   I curve (mA)   I simple (mA)\n";
    for (const double ohms : resistors) {
        const double v = solveLedVolts(supply, ohms);
        const double curveMilliamps = (supply - v) / ohms * 1000.0;
        const double simpleMilliamps = (supply - pretendFixedVolts) / ohms * 1000.0;
        std::cout << std::setprecision(0) << std::setw(14) << ohms << std::setprecision(3)
                  << std::setw(16) << v << std::setw(15) << curveMilliamps
                  << std::setw(16) << simpleMilliamps << "\n";
    }
    std::cout << "reversed LED at -5 V: I = " << std::scientific << ledAmps(-5.0) << " A\n";
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–5// An LED in series …States both models and that the parameters are pretend.No real-part number in the code.
10–15double ledAmps(double volts)The curve model I = Is × (eV/Vn − 1).One function, used for every resistor.
17–31double solveLedVolts(double supply, double ohms)Finds the LED voltage where LED current equals resistor current, by halving an interval 100 times.Bisection: always converges here because one current rises and the other falls with V.
23–28resistorAmps = …; if (ledAmps(mid) > resistorAmps) { high = mid; } else { low = mid; }If the LED would take more than the resistor gives, the voltage must be lower.The crossing of curve and load line in Figure 1.
35–37supply = 5.0; pretendFixedVolts = 2.0; resistors[] = {…}The cases to solve.Includes a 1 Ω "no real resistor" case.

Real output, copied from university/labs/F1-06/led_model.out; run record led_model.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:40:49Z; exit code: 0.

The curve model's voltage moves only from 1.785 V to 1.899 V while the current grows almost tenfold: the "nearly constant forward voltage" in numbers.R1

Where the analogy breaks

  1. A flap valve opens at one pressure; a diode has no sharp opening point. The current grows smoothly and exponentially. "Forward voltage" is the voltage at a stated current, not a switch-on threshold.D2
  2. A flap valve holds back any back-pressure until it breaks; a diode leaks a tiny reverse current and can break down at a voltage the datasheet states. For some LEDs that voltage is small; the flap picture would make you over-confident.D2 D4
  3. A valve does not make light. The glow of an LED comes from the junction physics, not from flow "rubbing" anything. And unlike a valve, a conducting LED also turns part of its power into heat.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
LED darkReversed, or a gap in the loopMeter across the LED shows the whole supply voltage in both cases; check direction against the datasheet marking (F0-40 forensic method)Turn it round, or close the gap, battery disconnected
LED flashes brightly once and never lights againNo series resistor, or one far too smallCalculate I with the simple modelReplace the LED; always use R = (Vs − VF) ÷ I
Two parallel LEDs: one bright, one dimShared resistor; slightly different curvesMeasure each LED's current (forensic lab)One resistor per LED
Calculated current noticeably different from measuredSimple model's VF differs from the real one at this currentMeasure V across the LEDRecalculate with the measured VF
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-02 to F1-05: parts with straight-line (resistors) or time-dependent (capacitors) behaviour; F0-40's LED rule of thumb. What carries over: Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop, Ohm's law for the resistor, power checks against ratings.D2 What changes: most dangerous first: a diode's current rises exponentially, so without a limiting resistor it can destroy itself in an instant; Ohm's law no longer applies to the part itself; direction matters; real values come only from the datasheet, and a model is a choice you must justify.D2 D4 What comes next: F1-07 teaches you to measure all of this safely with a multimeter, including the current through your LED.

Check yourself

  1. On the diode symbol, which end is the anode, and which way does conventional current flow when it conducts?
  2. A 9 V supply, an LED with (pretend) VF = 2 V, wanted current 10 mA. Which resistor?
  3. Why does an LED need a series resistor? (a) To make it brighter (b) Because its current rises very steeply with voltage (c) Because it only works on alternating current (d) To protect the battery from reverse current.
  4. In Listing 1's output, by how much does the LED voltage change when the current goes from 3.2 mA to 31.0 mA?
  5. Why is the simple model useless for the 1 Ω case, even though it gives a number?
  6. Explain in your own words what the load line is and why the operating point is where it crosses the curve.
  7. Apply to a new case: three LEDs (pretend VF = 2 V each) in series on 9 V with 10 mA wanted. Which resistor? What if the supply were 5 V?
  8. Why should parallel LEDs each have their own resistor?

Lab

Goal: choose and verify an LED's series resistor, first in the simulator, then (optionally, supervised) on a breadboard: the HW101 lab "LED current limiting".

Hardware and software needed: Part A: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Part B (optional): the kit's battery, breadboard, LEDs and resistors, and the course meter, chosen by the owner.

Safety

Part B: adult supervision; low-voltage battery kit only; no mains. Never connect an LED to the battery without a series resistor. Calculate the current first and check it against the datasheet maximum. Disconnect the battery to rewire. Do not stare into a bright LED at close range; follow any eye-safety note in its datasheet.S1 D4

Part A — simulator

  1. Build and run Listing 1. You should see the table above.
  2. Add 330 Ω and 150 Ω to the resistors list. Predict each current with the simple model, then run and compare with the curve model.
  3. Change the supply to 3 V. Predict which resistors still light the LED usefully, then run. Why does the gap between the models grow?
  4. Change is in ledAmps to 4e-18 (a "different batch"). How much does the 220 Ω current change? (This prepares the forensic lab.)

Part B — breadboard (optional, supervised)

Not verified — check before relying on this

Part B was not performed in this build: no kit, LED or meter was available, and the kit is not chosen. Every value (VF, maximum current, anode marking, battery voltage) comes from the datasheets of the kit's parts (D4).

  1. From the datasheet, choose a current below the maximum and compute R. Pick the nearest larger resistor you have.
  2. Build battery → R → LED (anode towards R) → back. Connect the battery last.
  3. Measure the voltage across the LED and across R (F1-07). Compute the current from VR ÷ R.
  4. Measure the current directly with the meter in series (F1-07). Compare.
  5. Try two larger resistors. Record brightness (by eye) and current.

Expected observations

Part A: outputs as shown and your added rows; at 3 V the currents are much smaller and the models differ more (the resistor's share of the voltage is small, so VF errors matter more). Part B: the measured V across the LED close to its datasheet VF; the two current measurements agree within the meter's accuracy.

Verification

Your measured current is below the datasheet maximum and within about 10 % of your simple-model prediction; if not, recompute with the measured VF and explain.

Troubleshooting

  • LED dark → reversed or a gap (Common mistakes).
  • A row shows inf or -nan → a resistor of 0 Ω divides by zero (a quick test of that change in this build printed exactly that; it is not kept as a listing); use a small positive value, as the 1 Ω row does.
  • Very dim LED at 3 V → the supply barely exceeds VF; that is expected.

Extension

Add a function that, given a wanted current, finds R using the curve model (bisection on R), and compare with the simple model's R.

Forensic lab

Scenario: "One bright, one dim". To save a part, Noor wired two LEDs in parallel and fed them through one 150 Ω resistor from 5 V. Both LEDs have the same label, but one is bright and the other dim. Noor measured the currents.

Evidence pack. Produced by the course's LED model (two_leds.cpp) with hidden pretend curve parameters for the two LEDs (in the answer key), not by real LEDs.

Questions.

  1. Check Kirchhoff's current law with the three currents.
  2. What is the same for both LEDs, and what differs?
  3. If both LEDs were identical, what would each current be?
  4. Explain why a small difference between the parts gives such a large difference in current.
  5. Propose the fix and check, with the simple model and pretend VF = 1.8 V, which resistor each LED needs for about 10 mA.

Method hints. Parallel parts share their voltage (F1-04). Look at Figure 1: how much current changes for a small change in voltage near the operating point? Hypotheses: "the dim LED is damaged" or "the parts differ slightly". What would distinguish them?

Mini-project

For the HW101 course project, your blinker will drive an LED. Write a one-page "LED drive sheet": supply voltage, LED datasheet values (or labelled pretend values), chosen current with margin, resistor value, resistor and LED power, and a table comparing simple-model and curve-model currents from a modified Listing 1. Rubric: correct resistor with margin (2); powers computed (1); model comparison shown (1); every number labelled as datasheet, pretend or measured (1).

Summary

  • A diode conducts from anode to cathode and blocks the other way, up to its breakdown voltage.
  • Its forward current rises exponentially with voltage; the voltage stays nearly constant while the current changes a lot.
  • An LED is a diode that emits light; it always needs a current limit.
  • Simple model: I = (Vs − VF) ÷ R; R = (Vs − VF) ÷ I.
  • The operating point is where the diode curve meets the resistor's load line.
  • Give each parallel LED its own resistor.
  • Every real LED number comes from its datasheet.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. The anode is the triangle's flat side; the cathode is the bar. Conventional current flows from anode to cathode, the way the triangle points.
  2. R = (9 − 2) ÷ 0.010 = 700 Ω; choose the nearest larger value available.
  3. (b). (a) A resistor makes it dimmer, not brighter. (c) LEDs work on steady current. (d) The resistor limits forward current; it does not stop reverse current.
  4. From 1.785 V to 1.899 V: about 0.11 V for almost ten times the current.
  5. With 1 Ω, almost nothing limits the current; the real result depends on the battery's internal resistance, the wires and the LED's damage, none of which the simple model contains. Both models agree only that the current is far above any safe value.
  6. In your words: the load line is every combination of LED voltage and current that the resistor and supply allow; the LED's curve is every combination the LED allows; the circuit must obey both at once, so it sits where they cross.
  7. Series LEDs add their forward voltages: 3 × 2 = 6 V; R = (9 − 6) ÷ 0.010 = 300 Ω. With 5 V the supply is less than the 6 V the string needs, so the LEDs stay dark.
  8. Because parallel LEDs share one voltage and their steep curves differ slightly, a shared resistor lets one LED take most of the current; separate resistors set each current independently.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: resistor current 21.337 mA = LED A 4.267 mA + LED B 17.069 mA (current law holds). Both LEDs share 1.799 V; B takes four times A's current. If identical: each would take half, about 10.7 mA. Explanation: on a steep exponential curve, the same voltage gives very different currents if the curves are shifted even slightly; the model's Is for B is four times A's, a shift of only Vn × ln 4 ≈ 0.07 V along the voltage axis. Ruled out: "A is damaged" — A conducts normally and the currents add up exactly; a damaged LED would show an abnormal voltage or no current. Fix: one resistor per LED. With the simple model and pretend VF = 1.8 V: R = (5 − 1.8) ÷ 0.010 = 320 Ω each; small differences between the LEDs then change their currents only slightly, because most of the voltage is across the resistors. How the evidence was made: two_leds.cpp with two_leds.in = Is(A) 1e−18 A, Is(B) 4e−18 A, Vn 0.05 V; supply 5 V, 150 Ω (R1).

Story hook

Analogy

Mr Okafor, the plumber, carries two tools into the restaurant's basement. The first is a pressure gauge with two little hoses. He touches one hose to a joint in the pipe and the other to the drain, and the needle shows the difference in pressure. Nothing has to be taken apart, and almost no water leaves the pipe.

The second tool is a flow meter. To use it, he must close the valve, cut the pipe open and fit the meter into the gap, so that all the water passes through it. "Never," he warns his apprentice Ines, "fit the flow meter straight across the tank's outlet and the drain. It has almost no resistance. The whole tank would empty through it in one rush, and the meter would burst."

A multimeter is both tools in one box, plus a third: a tester for how narrow a pipe is. Used the right way, it tells you the truth about a circuit. Used the wrong way, it can lie to you or even get damaged. This chapter is about using it the right way.

What you will be able to do

  • Measure voltage with the meter in parallel with the part, and read the sign correctly.
  • Measure current with the meter in series, and explain why it must never go across a source.
  • Measure resistance with the power off and the part isolated.
  • Estimate how much a meter disturbs the circuit it measures (loading and burden), with a C++ model.
  • Diagnose a meter whose current fuse has opened, from a notebook of readings.
Jargon box
Multimeter
Simple words: one meter that can measure voltage, current and resistance. Analogy (proposed): the plumber's pressure gauge, flow meter and pipe tester in one box. Precise: a test instrument with selectable modes and ranges (at least voltage, current and resistance), connected through two probes to sockets chosen for the mode; the exact sockets, ranges and limits are given in its user manual. D1 D4
Voltmeter (in parallel)
Simple words: the voltage mode: probes touch the two ends of a part. Analogy: the pressure gauge's two hoses on two joints. Precise: a voltage measurement is made with the meter connected in parallel with the part; an ideal voltmeter draws no current; a real one has a large but finite input resistance. D2
Ammeter (in series)
Simple words: the current mode: you open the loop and let the current pass through the meter. Analogy: the flow meter fitted into the cut pipe. Precise: a current measurement is made with the meter in series, so the circuit's current flows through the meter's small internal (shunt) resistance; an ideal ammeter has zero resistance. D2
Ohmmeter
Simple words: the resistance mode: the meter sends its own small current through a part. Analogy: testing how narrow a pipe is after taking it out of the building. Precise: a resistance measurement in which the meter applies a known small current or voltage from its own battery; it is valid only with the circuit unpowered, and the part should be isolated from parallel paths. D1 D2
Input resistance
Simple words: how much the voltmeter itself resists current; bigger is better. Analogy: how little water the gauge's hoses let through. Precise: the resistance a voltmeter presents between its probes; it appears in parallel with the measured part and causes loading (F1-04); its value is given in the meter's manual. D2 D4
Burden (shunt) resistance
Simple words: the small resistance inside the meter in current mode. Analogy: the slight narrowing the flow meter adds to the pipe. Precise: the series resistance an ammeter adds to the circuit; the voltage across it (the burden voltage) slightly reduces the current being measured. D2
Fuse
Simple words: a weak link that breaks on purpose when the current is too high. Analogy: a pipe section designed to burst first, safely, before anything else does. Precise: a protective device that opens the circuit when its current exceeds its rating for long enough; meters usually protect their current inputs with fuses whose ratings are in the manual. D1 D4

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the three ways of connecting a meter. Voltage: across the part, with the circuit working. Current: in series, with the loop opened and the meter fitted into the gap. Resistance: the part out of the circuit, with no power at all.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A multimeter is a box with a dial, a display and two probes, one red and one black. The dial chooses what you measure.D1

To measure voltage, you touch the probes to the two ends of a part, while the circuit is on. The meter sits beside the part. It is like Mr Okafor's pressure gauge: it compares two points and takes almost nothing from the circuit.D1 D2

To measure current, you must open the loop and put the meter into the gap. All the current then flows through the meter. It is like fitting the flow meter into a cut pipe. On many meters, you also move the red probe to a different socket for current. The manual says which.D1 D4

Here is the golden rule. In current mode, the meter has almost no resistance. Never touch its probes straight across a battery. A huge current would flow through it, and its fuse would blow, or worse.D1

To measure resistance, switch the circuit off and take the part out. The meter uses its own tiny battery to test the part. If the circuit is still on, the reading is wrong, and the meter can be harmed.D1

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Voltage: parallel, and the loading error

A voltmeter shows V(red) − V(black), as in F1-01. It is connected in parallel with the part, so it adds a path for current: its input resistance Rm. For an ideal meter Rm would be infinite. For a real one it is large, and it is listed in the manual.D2 D4

When the part's own resistance is small compared with Rm, the effect is negligible. When it is comparable, the meter loads the circuit exactly as a sensor loaded the divider in F1-04, and the reading is too low. Listing 1 shows this: on a divider of two 1 MΩ resistors, a meter with Rm = 1 MΩ (pretend) reads 2.000 V instead of 3.000 V.R1

Current: series, burden, and the fuse

An ammeter goes in series and adds its small burden resistance Rs to the loop. That lowers the current a little: I = V ÷ (R + Rs). The error matters only when the circuit's own resistance is small.D2 In Listing 1, a 10 Ω burden in a 100 Ω loop reduces the reading by 9.1 %; a 0.1 Ω burden by 0.1 %.

Because Rs is small, putting an ammeter across a source (in parallel) makes a near short circuit (F1-03). The current is limited only by the source's internal resistance and Rs. That is why current inputs are fused: the fuse opens to protect the meter.D1 D2 A meter with an open fuse reads 0 in current mode, whatever the circuit does: a classic trap, and the forensic lab.

Resistance: power off, part isolated

An ohmmeter drives its own small current through the part and measures the voltage. Any other source in the circuit would add to or fight with that current, so the circuit must be unpowered.D2 Other parts in parallel with the one you test give you the parallel combination (F1-04), not the part's own value; lift one leg of the part, or take it out. Capacitors should be discharged first (F1-05).

Ranges, resolution and accuracy

A meter shows a limited number of digits. The smallest step it can show on a range is its resolution. How close the reading is to the truth is its accuracy, which the manual states, often as a percentage of the reading plus a number of digits.D4 When you do not know the size of a voltage or current, start on the highest range and work down, unless the meter selects ranges by itself (the manual says).D1 A display such as "OL" means "over the limit of this range" on many meters; check what yours shows.

Not verified — check before relying on this

No real multimeter or manual was available in this build. The input resistance (1 MΩ, 10 MΩ), burden resistances (0.1, 1, 10 Ω), the 400 mA range and the 500 mA fuse used in this chapter's programs are pretend exercise values, not values of any product. The real meter's input resistance, burden voltage, fuse ratings, socket layout, overload display, accuracy and safety category come from the chosen meter's user manual (D4). The meter itself is a decision for the owner.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Inside, a digital multimeter measures a voltage with an analog-to-digital converter (F1-08, HW302). For current it measures the small voltage across its shunt; for resistance it passes a known current and measures the voltage; for voltage it divides the input down with a high-resistance divider, which is what sets the input resistance.D2 Every measurement disturbs the system a little. An engineer's habit is to ask, for each reading, "how much did my instrument change what I measured?", and to estimate it, as Listing 1 does. Changing signals add a further question: is the meter fast enough? That leads to the oscilloscope and the logic analyser in later courses (HW204).

How the hardware actually does it

The current shunt is a resistor of very small, precisely known value. The meter reads the voltage across it and divides by its resistance: Ohm's law used backwards.D2 The fuse is a short piece of conductor that melts when too much current heats it, opening the path (F1-03's I² × R heating used on purpose).D1 The values of the shunts and the fuses, and how to replace a fuse safely, are in the meter's manual (D4); a replaced fuse must match the manual's rating exactly.

Worked example

Exercise values.

  1. Voltmeter loading. Divider: 6 V, R = 100 kΩ top and bottom; meter Rm = 1 MΩ across the bottom. Bottom becomes 100 kΩ ∥ 1 MΩ = 100,000 × 1,000,000 ÷ 1,100,000 ≈ 90.9 kΩ. Reading = 6 × 90.9 ÷ (100 + 90.9) ≈ 2.857 V, about 4.8 % low.
  2. Same divider with Rm = 10 MΩ: bottom ≈ 99.0 kΩ; reading ≈ 2.985 V, 0.5 % low.
  3. Ammeter burden. 1 V across 100 Ω: true current 10 mA. With Rs = 1 Ω: 1 ÷ 101 ≈ 9.901 mA, 1 % low.
  4. Ammeter across a source (do not do this). 6 V battery with pretend internal resistance 0.5 Ω, meter Rs = 0.1 Ω: I = 6 ÷ 0.6 = 10 A. Power in the meter's shunt: 10² × 0.1 = 10 W. Any small fuse opens.

Listing 1 prints cases 1–3; the forensic generator models case 4.R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — meter_effect.cpp: how much a voltmeter's input resistance and an ammeter's burden change the reading.

// How a meter changes what it measures (ideal model, exercise numbers).
// Part 1: a voltmeter with input resistance Rm across the bottom resistor
// of a divider (6 V, two equal resistors R). The meter is in parallel
// with that resistor, so the bottom becomes R || Rm.
// Part 2: an ammeter with internal resistance Rs placed in series with a
// 100 ohm resistor on a 1 V supply.
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>

double parallel(double a, double b)
{
    return 1.0 / (1.0 / a + 1.0 / b);
}

int main()
{
    const double supply = 6.0;
    const double dividerResistors[] = {1e3, 1e5, 1e6, 1e7};
    const double meterInputs[] = {1e6, 1e7};

    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(3);
    std::cout << "Part 1: voltmeter on a divider (true answer always 3.000 V)\n";
    for (const double rm : meterInputs) {
        for (const double r : dividerResistors) {
            const double bottom = parallel(r, rm);
            const double reading = supply * bottom / (r + bottom);
            std::cout << "  Rm = " << std::setw(12) << std::setprecision(0) << rm
                      << "  R = " << std::setw(10) << r << std::setprecision(3)
                      << "  reading = " << reading << " V  error = "
                      << std::setprecision(1) << 100.0 * (reading - 3.0) / 3.0 << " %"
                      << std::setprecision(3) << "\n";
        }
    }

    const double ammeterSupply = 1.0;
    const double load = 100.0;
    const double shunts[] = {0.1, 1.0, 10.0};
    const double trueMilliamps = ammeterSupply / load * 1000.0;
    std::cout << "Part 2: ammeter in series (true answer without meter " << trueMilliamps
              << " mA)\n";
    for (const double rs : shunts) {
        const double reading = ammeterSupply / (load + rs) * 1000.0;
        std::cout << "  Rs = " << std::setw(5) << std::setprecision(1) << rs
                  << " ohms  reading = " << std::setprecision(3) << reading << " mA  error = "
                  << std::setprecision(1) << 100.0 * (reading - trueMilliamps) / trueMilliamps
                  << " %" << std::setprecision(3) << "\n";
    }
    return 0;
}

Rule of thumb from the run: the voltmeter error is about 1 % or less when the circuit's resistance is about a hundred times smaller than Rm; the ammeter error is about 1 % or less when the burden is about a hundred times smaller than the loop's resistance.R1

Where the analogy breaks

  1. A pressure gauge on a water pipe takes no water at all; a voltmeter does take a little current. That small current is the loading error of Listing 1, and it can be large in high-resistance circuits.D2
  2. Cutting a water pipe is a big job; opening a circuit loop is easy, and so is forgetting to close it. After a current measurement the loop must be restored; with the meter removed and the gap left open, nothing works.
  3. A plumber's pipe tester does not need the water off; an ohmmeter needs the power off. The ohmmeter injects its own current, and any live source corrupts the reading.D2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Current mode reads 0, circuit clearly worksMeter's current fuse is openMeasure the same current in a known-good setup; check continuity of the fuse as the manual describesSupervisor replaces the fuse with exactly the rating in the manual
"OL" or a flash when measuring currentMeter in current mode across a sourceLook at where the probes areDisconnect at once; measure current only in series
Voltage reading too low in a high-value dividerMeter loadingCompare with Listing 1's estimateNote the error, or use a meter with higher input resistance
Resistance reading jumps or is nonsenseCircuit still powered, or other parts in parallelIs the battery disconnected? Is one leg lifted?Power off, isolate the part
Voltage mode reads nothingRed probe still in the current socketCheck the sockets against the manualMove the probe back for voltage
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-01 to F1-06: predicting voltages, currents and resistances with Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's laws and models. What carries over: V(red) − V(black) (F1-01); series and parallel and loading (F1-04); power and short circuits (F1-03).D2 What changes: most dangerous first: a meter in current mode across a source makes a short circuit, so where you place the probes now has physical consequences; every reading is disturbed a little by the instrument; and real numbers enter your work for the first time, so each one needs a date, an instrument and an accuracy.D1 D2 What comes next: F1-08 asks what a signal is when voltages change over time, how a digital circuit decides "high" or "low", and finishes the RC blinker.

Check yourself

  1. How is a meter connected to measure voltage? To measure current?
  2. Why must the power be off when you measure resistance?
  3. A learner puts the meter, set to current, directly across a battery. What happens? (a) It shows the battery's voltage (b) It shows a small current (c) A very large current flows, the fuse may open (d) Nothing, the meter is protected so it is fine to do.
  4. From Listing 1's output: a meter with Rm = 10 MΩ on a divider of two 1 MΩ resistors reads what, and how big is the error?
  5. Why does an ammeter with a larger burden resistance read a smaller current?
  6. Explain in your own words why "the meter changes what it measures" and when it matters.
  7. Apply to a new case: you measure 1.4 kΩ across a 2.2 kΩ resistor still soldered on a board. What is the most likely reason?
  8. Your meter reads 0 mA in series with a lit LED. List two hypotheses and a test for each.

Lab

Goal: estimate meter errors with Listing 1, then (optionally, supervised) measure voltage, current and resistance on a low-voltage circuit correctly.

Hardware and software needed: Part A: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Part B (optional): the kit's battery, breadboard, resistors and an LED, and the course multimeter with its manual, as chosen by the owner.

Safety

Low voltage only: the kit's battery. Never measure mains or anything plugged into the wall, at any level of this university. Adult supervision for every Part B step. Before each measurement, check the dial and the sockets against the manual. Never put the meter in current mode across a battery or any part; measure current only in series. Measure resistance only with the battery disconnected. Use the probes by their insulated handles. If the meter shows an overload, smells or gets warm, disconnect at once.S1 D4

Part A — simulator

  1. Build and run Listing 1. You should see the twelve lines above.
  2. Add a 100 MΩ meter to meterInputs. Predict the error on the 1 MΩ divider, then run.
  3. Build and run the forensic generator meter_log.cpp (same command, input meter_log.in). Read it before the forensic questions.
  4. Write meter_check.in lines for a correct measuring sequence (voltage across battery, across resistor, current in series) and run meter_log.cpp with it. Every reading should be sensible.

Part B — real measurements (optional, supervised)

Not verified — check before relying on this

Part B was not performed in this build: no meter or kit was available, and neither is chosen. Dial positions, sockets, ranges, fuse ratings and the overload display depend on the chosen meter and are taken from its manual (D4). The supervisor checks every step against it.

  1. Battery disconnected: measure each resistor (resistance mode). Record value, range and date.
  2. Build battery → resistor → LED → back (F1-06 resistor). Voltage mode: measure across the battery, the resistor and the LED. Check that the two parts add up to the battery (F1-04).
  3. Battery disconnected: open the loop between battery and resistor. Set current mode and move the red probe to the current socket as the manual says. Put the meter in the gap. Connect the battery and read the current.
  4. Disconnect the battery, move the red probe back to the voltage socket, close the loop.
  5. Compare the measured current with VR ÷ R from step 2.

Expected observations

Part A: the real outputs; with 100 MΩ the 1 MΩ divider error drops to about 0.5 %. Part B: the two current values agree within the meter's stated accuracy; the voltages add up around the loop.

Verification

A measurement record with every reading's mode, range, date and meter, where each value is consistent with your F1-06 prediction, or the difference is explained with loading, burden or tolerance.

Troubleshooting

  • Current reads 0 → fuse open or probe in the wrong socket (forensic lab).
  • Voltage reads negative → probes reversed (F1-01).
  • Resistance reads lower than the label on a board → parallel paths; lift a leg.
  • Readings drift on a capacitor → it is charging or discharging through the meter (F1-05).

Extension

Add to Listing 1 a third experiment: the meter's input resistance across a charging capacitor (F1-05). How does the final voltage change? (Hint: the capacitor now charges towards a divided voltage.)

Forensic lab

Scenario: "The meter that stopped reading current". Ines measured an LED circuit (6 V battery, 1 kΩ resistor, LED) and copied every display into her notebook. "After step 4 the current is always zero, but when I measure voltages the circuit is fine. Is my LED broken?"

Evidence pack. Ines's notebook as replayed by the course's meter model (meter_log.cpp with her steps in meter_log.in). The model meter is our own, not a real product; its pretend range and fuse values are in the program's comments.

step 1  mode V  probes battery           display: 6.00 V
step 2  mode V  probes resistor          display: 4.00 V
step 3  mode A  probes in-series         display: 4.00 mA
step 4  mode A  probes battery           display: OL
step 5  mode A  probes in-series         display: 0.00 mA
step 6  mode V  probes resistor          display: 4.00 V
step 7  mode A  probes in-series         display: 0.00 mA

Questions.

  1. Which readings are as expected from the circuit? Check them with Ohm's law (pretend LED voltage 2 V).
  2. What was different about step 4? Why does the display show "OL"?
  3. Step 6 says 4.00 V across the resistor. What current does that imply? Why does step 7 show 0.00 mA?
  4. Name the root cause, and say why "the LED is broken" is ruled out.
  5. What must Ines and her supervisor do now, and what habit prevents it next time?

Method hints. Separate "what the circuit does" (voltage readings) from "what the meter does" (current readings). Write two hypotheses and find the reading that distinguishes them.

Mini-project

Write a one-page "measurement card" for the chosen meter (or, until it is chosen, a template with blanks): how to set voltage, current and resistance; which socket for each; the input resistance, burden and fuse ratings copied from the manual; and three rules in your own words. Then use Listing 1 with the real input resistance to state the largest circuit resistance for which your voltage readings stay within 1 %. Rubric: every number traced to the manual or marked blank (2); correct connection rules (1); Listing 1 run with the real value (1); clear rules (1).

Summary

  • Voltage: meter in parallel, circuit powered; reading = V(red) − V(black).
  • Current: meter in series, loop opened; never across a source.
  • Resistance: power off, part isolated; the meter supplies its own current.
  • A voltmeter's input resistance loads high-resistance circuits; an ammeter's burden lowers low-resistance currents.
  • Current inputs are fused; an open fuse reads 0 in current mode.
  • Every real reading needs mode, range, date, instrument and accuracy.
  • No mains, ever; supervised, low-voltage kits only.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Voltage: in parallel with the part (probes on its two ends). Current: in series (loop opened, meter in the gap).
  2. The ohmmeter uses its own small current; another source would add to it and give a wrong reading, and could damage the meter.
  3. (c). (a) is what voltage mode would show. (b) is wrong because nothing limits the current except tiny resistances. (d) is wrong: the fuse is a last line of protection, not permission.
  4. 2.857 V, an error of −4.8 %.
  5. The burden is in series with the circuit, so the total resistance is larger and the current is smaller: I = V ÷ (R + Rs).
  6. In your words: to measure, the meter must join the circuit, as a parallel path (voltage) or a series resistance (current); it matters when the meter's resistance is not very different from the circuit's.
  7. Other parts on the board are in parallel with it; the meter shows the combination (smaller than either). Lift one leg and measure again.
  8. Hypothesis 1: the meter's fuse is open; test: measure a known current, or check the fuse as the manual says. Hypothesis 2: the red probe is in the voltage socket; test: look at the sockets. (A third: the meter is not really in series but beside a wire that still carries the current; test: trace the loop.)

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: steps 1–3 are as expected: battery 6.00 V; resistor 4.00 V (6 − 2 V LED); current 4.00 mA (4 V ÷ 1 kΩ, minus a negligible burden). In step 4 Ines put the meter, in current mode, with its probes on the battery terminals: "OL" means the current was above the range. With the model's pretend 0.5 Ω battery resistance and 0.1 Ω shunt, about 10 A flowed, far above the pretend 500 mA fuse, which opened. Steps 5–7: every current reading is 0.00 mA, but step 6 shows 4.00 V across the resistor, which means 4 mA is flowing when the loop is closed without the meter. Root cause: the meter's current fuse opened at step 4; the meter, not the circuit, is faulty. "LED broken" is ruled out by step 6 (the loop conducts and the LED takes its 2 V share). Action: stop using current mode; the supervisor replaces the fuse with exactly the rating in the manual (D4) and checks the meter on a known circuit. Prevention: current only in series; before connecting in current mode, say aloud "where does the current come from and where does it go?". How the evidence was made: meter_log.cpp with meter_log.in (steps 1–7), ideal model with pretend values (R1).

Story hook

Analogy

In the restaurant kitchen there are two ways news reaches Aiko. The oven has a thermometer with a needle. It can point anywhere: a bit warmer, a bit cooler, any value in between. The pass has a bell. When a dish is ready, a cook rings it. The bell is either ringing or not.

The thermometer tells Aiko much more, but she must look closely, and a shaky needle is hard to read. The bell tells her only one thing, yet she hears it clearly even when the kitchen is noisy. Kemal, the new waiter, once rang the bell three times by accident because his hand trembled on the rope. The cooks thought three dishes were ready.

Electronics uses both kinds of signal. Analog signals are like the thermometer. Digital signals are like the bell. This chapter shows how a circuit turns one into the other, why a trembling hand fools a simple bell, and how a capacitor and two thresholds make a light blink on its own: the HW101 course project.

What you will be able to do

  • Tell an analog signal from a digital one, and give an example of each.
  • Convert an analog voltage into a 1-bit and a 3-bit digital value with a threshold and with equal steps.
  • Explain why digital signals tolerate noise, and how a single threshold can still be fooled.
  • Use hysteresis (two thresholds) to clean a noisy signal.
  • Predict the blink period of an RC relaxation oscillator and check it against a simulation.
Jargon box
Signal
Simple words: a voltage that changes over time to carry information. Analogy: any message reaching Aiko: the needle's position or the bell's ringing. Precise: a quantity, here a voltage, whose variation in time represents information. D2
Analog signal
Simple words: a signal that can take any value in a range. Analogy (proposed): the oven thermometer's needle. Precise: a signal whose value varies continuously and whose exact value carries the information. D2 D3
Digital signal
Simple words: a signal that is read as one of a few values, usually just HIGH or LOW. Analogy (proposed): the order bell: ringing or not. Precise: a signal interpreted as one of a finite set of levels, in binary logic two (1 and 0), each corresponding to a range of voltages. D2 D3
Threshold
Simple words: the line between "counts as LOW" and "counts as HIGH". Analogy: how hard the rope must be pulled before the bell rings. Precise: the input voltage at which a digital input's interpretation changes; real logic families specify ranges guaranteed to be read as LOW or HIGH in their datasheets. D2 D4
Noise
Simple words: unwanted wiggles added to a signal. Analogy: Kemal's trembling hand on the bell rope. Precise: unwanted random or interfering variations superimposed on a signal. D2
Hysteresis
Simple words: using two thresholds: a higher one to switch on, a lower one to switch off. Analogy: the bell only rings after a firm pull, and only resets after the rope is fully let go. Precise: a property of a circuit whose switching threshold depends on its present state; a Schmitt trigger has an upper threshold for rising inputs and a lower one for falling inputs. D2
Sampling and quantisation
Simple words: reading an analog voltage at moments in time and rounding it to one of a fixed set of steps. Analogy: Aiko writing down the thermometer every few minutes, to the nearest mark. Precise: sampling takes values at discrete times; quantisation maps each value to one of 2n codes for an n-bit converter (an analog-to-digital converter, ADC). D2
Oscillator
Simple words: a circuit that keeps switching back and forth on its own. Analogy: a kitchen timer that rings, resets itself and rings again. Precise: a circuit that produces a periodic output without a periodic input; a relaxation oscillator does it by charging and discharging a capacitor between two thresholds. D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows one analog signal sampled twelve times, and the 1-bit digital view of each sample with a threshold at 2.5 V. Figure 2, further down, shows the course project's blinker: a capacitor voltage moving between two thresholds and the output switching each time.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A signal is a voltage that changes to carry a message. Some signals can be any value. A light sensor's voltage creeps up slowly as the room gets brighter. That is an analog signal, like the oven thermometer.D2

Other signals are read as just two values: HIGH or LOW, 1 or 0. That is a digital signal, like the order bell. Computers use digital signals everywhere. A bit, which you met in KID101, travels on a wire as HIGH or LOW.D3

How does a circuit decide? It uses a threshold. Above the line, it reads HIGH. Below, it reads LOW. A little wobble on the wire does not matter, as long as the voltage stays clearly on one side. That is why digital signals are so reliable.D2

But a slow, shaky signal near the line can cross it several times. Then one real event looks like many, just as Kemal's trembling hand rang the bell three times. The cure is to use two lines: one to switch on and a lower one to switch off. That trick is called hysteresis.D2

The same two-line trick, with a capacitor, makes a light blink all by itself. You will build that, first in the simulator.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

From analog to digital

Turning an analog voltage into numbers takes two steps. Sampling takes its value at chosen moments. Quantisation rounds each value to one of a fixed number of steps. With n bits there are 2n steps: 1 bit gives 2 (a single threshold), 3 bits give 8.D2 Listing 1 does both for a smooth wave: for a 0–5 V range and 3 bits, each step is 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625 V wide, and a sample of 3.147 V becomes code 5 (101 in binary, MA102), because 3.147 ÷ 0.625 = 5.03.R1

Something is always lost. Between samples you do not know what happened, and within a step all voltages look the same. More bits and faster sampling lose less. HW302 (F1-64) studies analog-to-digital converters properly.

Logic levels and noise margin

Real digital inputs do not use one sharp line. Their datasheets guarantee that voltages below one level are read as LOW and voltages above a higher level as HIGH; in between, the result is not guaranteed. Outputs are guaranteed to be lower than the LOW limit or higher than the HIGH limit. The gap between what an output guarantees and what an input needs is the noise margin: noise smaller than that cannot flip a bit.D2

Not verified — check before relying on this

This chapter gives no real logic-level voltages: they differ between logic families and supply voltages, and no datasheet could be opened in this build. The 2.5 V threshold and the 2 V / 3 V Schmitt thresholds in the programs are exercise values. Real input and output levels, and real Schmitt-trigger thresholds, come from the datasheet of the part chosen for the kit (D4).

Hysteresis

A slow input near a single threshold, with a little noise on it, can cross the threshold several times. Each crossing is a new edge. A counter connected to it counts too many events: the forensic lab. A Schmitt trigger input uses two thresholds. A rising input must pass the upper one to become HIGH; a falling input must pass the lower one to become LOW. Noise smaller than the gap between them cannot cause extra edges.D2

The RC blinker: a relaxation oscillator

Now combine F1-05 and hysteresis. Take a Schmitt-trigger inverter: its output is HIGH when its input is LOW, and LOW when its input is HIGH. Connect a resistor from its output back to its input, and a capacitor from its input to ground.D2

  1. Start: the capacitor is empty, the input LOW, so the output is HIGH. The capacitor charges towards Vdd through R.
  2. When Vc passes the upper threshold VT+, the output switches LOW. Now the capacitor discharges towards 0 V through R.
  3. When Vc falls below the lower threshold VT−, the output switches HIGH again. Repeat forever.

Each half is a piece of the RC curve. Using F1-05's "time to reach a voltage" formula, the HIGH time (charging from VT− to VT+) is tH = R × C × ln((Vdd − VT−) ÷ (Vdd − VT+)), and the LOW time (discharging from VT+ to VT−) is tL = R × C × ln(VT+ ÷ VT−). With exercise values Vdd = 5 V, VT+ = 3 V, VT− = 2 V and R × C = 1 s, both are ln 1.5 ≈ 0.4055 s, a period of 0.811 s. An LED with its own series resistor (F1-06) on the output blinks at that rate. Listing 2 simulates it.R1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. The blink period depends on R, C and the two thresholds. Real Schmitt thresholds vary from part to part and with supply voltage and temperature, within limits the datasheet states; so do R and C within their tolerances. An engineer therefore predicts a range of periods, not one number, and checks the measured period against that range.D2 D4 The first cycle is longer, because the capacitor starts from 0 V instead of from VT−: Listing 2 shows 0.9163 s, which is τ × ln(5 ÷ 2). The same "a capacitor charging to a threshold" idea, at nanosecond scale inside chips, sets gate delays (F1-15) and limits clock speeds (F1-18).

How the hardware actually does it

A digital input is built from transistors (F1-09) arranged so that their output switches sharply when the input crosses a voltage near the middle of the supply. A Schmitt trigger adds internal feedback that shifts the switching point depending on the present output, which creates the two thresholds.D2 An analog-to-digital converter compares the input with reference voltages to produce its code; its resolution and speed are in its datasheet. HW102 builds gates from transistors, and HW302 studies converters.

Worked example

Exercise values.

  1. 3-bit code. Range 0–5 V, 8 steps of 0.625 V. A sample of 4.268 V: 4.268 ÷ 0.625 = 6.83, so code 6 (110). A sample of 0.732 V: 1.17, so code 1 (001). A sample of 4.915 V: 7.86, so code 7 (111).
  2. 1-bit. Threshold 2.5 V: 1.853 V gives 0; 3.147 V gives 1.
  3. Blinker HIGH time. tH = 1 s × ln((5 − 2) ÷ (5 − 3)) = ln 1.5 = 0.4055 s.
  4. Blinker LOW time. tL = 1 s × ln(3 ÷ 2) = 0.4055 s. Period 0.811 s, about 1.23 blinks per second.
  5. First HIGH period (from 0 V to 3 V): 1 s × ln(5 ÷ 2) = 0.9163 s.
  6. Slower blink. Double C: every time doubles: period 1.622 s.

Listings 1 and 2 print these values.R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — digitize.cpp: one analog wave, seen as voltages, as 1-bit values and as 3-bit codes.

// One analog signal, seen three ways.
// The analog value: a smooth wave between 0 V and 5 V (exercise numbers).
// A 1-bit digital view: HIGH if the value is above one threshold (2.5 V).
// A 3-bit view: the 0..5 V range cut into 8 equal steps, codes 0 to 7.
#include <cmath>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <numbers>

int main()
{
    const double fullScale = 5.0;
    const double threshold = 2.5;
    const int levels = 8;
    const int samples = 12;

    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(3);
    std::cout << " sample   analog (V)   1-bit   3-bit code   code in binary\n";
    for (int k = 0; k < samples; ++k) {
        const double phase = 2.0 * std::numbers::pi * (k + 0.5) / samples;
        const double volts = 2.5 - 2.5 * std::cos(phase);
        const int bit = volts > threshold ? 1 : 0;
        int code = static_cast<int>(volts / fullScale * levels);
        if (code > levels - 1) {
            code = levels - 1;
        }
        std::cout << std::setw(7) << k << std::setw(13) << volts << std::setw(8) << bit
                  << std::setw(13) << code << "              " << ((code >> 2) & 1)
                  << ((code >> 1) & 1) << (code & 1) << "\n";
    }
    return 0;
}

8#include <numbers>Gives std::numbers::pi (C++20).No hand-typed value of π.
12–15fullScale = 5.0; threshold = 2.5; levels = 8; samples = 12;The range, the 1-bit threshold, the 3-bit steps, the number of samples.Exercise values.
20–21phase = …(k + 0.5)…; volts = 2.5 - 2.5 * std::cos(phase);The analog signal at sample k: a smooth wave from 0 V up to 5 V and back.The half-sample offset keeps every sample away from exactly 2.5 V, where rounding would decide the bit.
22const int bit = volts > threshold ? 1 : 0;1-bit conversion.One threshold.

27–29((code >> 2) & 1) …Prints the code's three bits.Shifts and masks from MA102.

Listing 2 — relaxation.cpp: the course project's blinker as a simulation, with the predicted times.

// An RC blinker with no microcontroller: a model of a Schmitt-trigger
// relaxation oscillator. The output is HIGH (5 V) or LOW (0 V). The
// capacitor charges toward the output through R. When Vc rises above the
// upper threshold the output goes LOW; when Vc falls below the lower
// threshold the output goes HIGH again. Thresholds, R and C are exercise
// numbers, not values from a real part's datasheet.
#include <cmath>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    const double vdd = 5.0;
    const double upper = 3.0;
    const double lower = 2.0;
    const double ohms = 10000.0;
    const double farads = 100e-6;
    const double tau = ohms * farads;
    const double dt = 0.0001;

    const double predictedHigh = tau * std::log((vdd - lower) / (vdd - upper));
    const double predictedLow = tau * std::log(upper / lower);
    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);
    std::cout << "predicted: HIGH for " << predictedHigh << " s, LOW for " << predictedLow
              << " s, period " << predictedHigh + predictedLow << " s\n";

    double vc = 0.0;
    bool high = true;
    double lastSwitch = 0.0;
    int switches = 0;
    for (long k = 1; k <= 60000; ++k) {
        const double out = high ? vdd : 0.0;
        vc += (out - vc) / ohms * dt / farads;
        const double t = k * dt;
        if (high && vc > upper) {
            high = false;
        } else if (!high && vc < lower) {
            high = true;
        } else {
            continue;
        }
        ++switches;
        std::cout << "t = " << t << " s  output -> " << (high ? "HIGH (LED on) " : "LOW  (LED off)")
                  << "  time since last switch " << t - lastSwitch << " s\n";
        lastSwitch = t;
    }
    std::cout << "switches in 6 s: " << switches << "\n";
    return 0;
}

21–22predictedHigh = tau * std::log(…); predictedLow = …The formulas of Layer 2.The prediction is computed before the simulation runs.

Every half-period after the first is 0.4055 s, equal to the prediction to four decimals; the first is 0.9163 s, as Layer 3 explains.R1

Where the analogy breaks

  1. A bell is either ringing or silent; a digital wire is always at some voltage. "HIGH" and "LOW" are interpretations of ranges of an analog voltage. Between the guaranteed ranges, a real input's reading is undefined, which a bell has no equivalent for.D2
  2. Aiko can glance at the thermometer whenever she likes; a sampled system sees only its samples. If the signal changes faster than the sampling, the samples can tell a completely wrong story (HW302 explains aliasing).D2
  3. A trembling hand is one kind of noise; electrical noise has many sources (other wires, motors, the circuit's own parts), and hysteresis helps only with noise smaller than the gap between the thresholds.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
A counter counts several events for one press or one slow riseNoise crossing a single thresholdLog the input samples near the threshold (forensic lab)Hysteresis (Schmitt input), or a software rule that needs a clear rise and a clear fall
Blinker never blinks; output stuckOrdinary inverter without hysteresis, or thresholds outside the capacitor's rangeMeasure Vc: does it settle between the thresholds?Use a Schmitt-trigger part (datasheet)
Blink period differs from predictionReal thresholds, R or C differ from the values usedMeasure the half-periods and compare with a predicted rangeRecompute with datasheet ranges; adjust R
3-bit codes look shifted by oneRounding versus truncation in the conversionCheck a value right at a step boundaryDocument which rule your converter uses
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-01 to F1-07: voltages and currents as continuous quantities, the RC curve, and measuring with a meter; MA102: bits and binary. What carries over: every digital signal is still a voltage that obeys Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws; RC timing from F1-05; LED drive from F1-06.D2 What changes: most dangerous first: a digital input near its threshold can produce wrong or extra bits, so "it is digital, so it is clean" is false without margins and hysteresis; signals are now functions of time, so a meter is often too slow and later courses use oscilloscopes and logic analysers; information becomes numbers through sampling and quantisation, which always lose something.D2 What comes next: HW102 begins with F1-09 The transistor as a switch: the part that makes HIGH and LOW inside every gate.

Check yourself

  1. Give one example of an analog signal and one of a digital signal from everyday life.
  2. With a 0–5 V range and 3 bits, which code does 2.0 V give? Write it in binary.
  3. Why can a digital signal ignore small noise? (a) Digital wires have no noise (b) Small noise does not move the voltage across the threshold region (c) Digital circuits filter all noise (d) Noise only affects analog meters.
  4. What is hysteresis, and what problem does it solve?
  5. In Listing 2, why is the first HIGH period longer than the others?
  6. Explain in your own words how a capacitor and two thresholds make a light blink without a computer.
  7. Apply to a new case: with Vdd = 5 V, VT+ = 3 V, VT− = 2 V, what R × C gives a period of 2 s?
  8. Predict: in Listing 2, make the thresholds 3.5 V and 1.5 V. Is the period longer or shorter? Compute it, then run.

Lab

Goal: convert an analog signal to digital, and predict, simulate and (optionally, supervised) measure the period of an RC blinker: the HW101 lab "RC timing measured against prediction", and the core of the course project.

Hardware and software needed: Part A: a computer with a C++ compiler (this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Part B (optional): the kit's battery, breadboard, a Schmitt-trigger part, a resistor and capacitor for the timer, an LED with its resistor, the course meter and a stopwatch, as chosen by the owner.

Safety

Part B: adult supervision; low-voltage battery kit only; no mains. Check the chip's supply pins and orientation against its datasheet before connecting power; a chip inserted backwards can get hot. Respect polarised capacitors (F1-05) and LED resistors (F1-06). Disconnect the battery before rewiring.S1 D4

Part A — simulator

  2. Change Listing 1 to 4 bits (16 levels). Predict the code of 3.147 V, then run.
  3. In Listing 2, double C. Predict the half-period, then run.

Part B — the real blinker (optional, supervised)

Its pin connections, supply range, threshold ranges and output current limit must come from its datasheet (D4). An integrated timer chip could be used instead, with a different formula from its own datasheet; this chapter does not give that formula because no datasheet was opened.

  1. From the datasheet, copy the supply range and the minimum and maximum of both thresholds. Compute the shortest and longest predicted period for your R and C (with their tolerances).
  2. Choose R × C so the period is a few seconds, easy to time by eye.
  3. Build: Schmitt inverter powered as the datasheet shows; R from output to input; C from input to ground; LED and its resistor from the output to ground.
  4. Connect the battery. Time ten blinks with the stopwatch. Divide by ten.
  5. Optional: with the meter on Vc, watch it move between two values; write them down.

Expected observations

Part A: the outputs shown; 3.147 V becomes code 10 (1010) with 4 bits; doubling C doubles both half-periods. Part B: a blinking LED whose measured period lies inside your predicted range; a meter on Vc may be too slow to follow it exactly (F1-07).

Verification

Simulation: every half-period after the first equals the prediction to the printed precision. Real circuit: the measured period, averaged over ten blinks, lies inside the predicted range from datasheet tolerances. If not, say which assumption failed.

Troubleshooting

  • LED always on or always off → no hysteresis (ordinary inverter), wrong pins, or the capacitor not connected.
  • Blinks far too fast or slow → unit error in C (F1-05 forensic lab).
  • Simulation prints no switches → thresholds outside 0–Vdd, or upper below lower.

Extension

Make the HIGH and LOW times different by giving the charge and discharge paths different resistances (in the simulator: use one R when the output is HIGH and another when LOW). Derive the new formulas and check them with a run.

Questions.

  1. Find every place where the counter saw a rising edge. What happened between them?
  2. How big are the wiggles near the threshold (compare neighbouring samples)?
  3. Is the sensor really reporting three openings? What evidence decides it?
  4. Propose a fix with two thresholds. Which thresholds would give one count for this log? Check with the samples.

Method hints. Mark the samples above and below 2.5 V. Hypotheses: "three real events" or "one slow, noisy event". A real event should end with a clear return to LOW; does the log show that between the counts?

Mini-project

HW101 course project: an RC timer that blinks an LED without a microcontroller. Deliver: (1) a prediction sheet with the formulas, your R, C, thresholds (datasheet values or labelled exercise values), the predicted half-periods and the predicted range from tolerances; (2) a simulation with a modified Listing 2 and its real output; (3) if the kit is available, supervised, the circuit built and the period measured over ten blinks, with date and instruments; (4) a one-page comparison of prediction, simulation and measurement. Rubric (default project rubric of guide 11.5): correctness and tests 35 %; engineering quality 20 %; measurement and evidence 20 %; documentation 15 %; presentation 10 %.

Summary

  • Analog signals take any value; digital signals are read as one of a few levels, usually two.
  • Sampling and quantisation turn analog into numbers; n bits give 2n codes.
  • Thresholds and noise margins let digital signals ignore small noise.
  • Slow, noisy inputs near one threshold create extra edges; hysteresis cures this.
  • A Schmitt inverter, R and C make a relaxation oscillator: tH = RC ln((Vdd − VT−) ÷ (Vdd − VT+)), tL = RC ln(VT+ ÷ VT−).
  • Real thresholds and parts vary: predict a range, then measure.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Examples: analog: a thermometer, a dimmer's brightness, a microphone's voltage; digital: a light switch's on/off, a doorbell pressed or not, a bit on a computer wire.
  2. 2.0 ÷ 0.625 = 3.2, so code 3, binary 011.
  3. (b). (a) and (c) are false: digital wires do carry noise, and nothing filters all of it. (d) is false: large enough noise flips digital bits too.
  4. Two thresholds: a higher one to switch to HIGH and a lower one to switch back to LOW. It stops noise near a single threshold from producing extra edges.
  5. The capacitor starts empty at 0 V, so the first charge goes from 0 V to 3 V instead of from 2 V to 3 V: τ × ln(5 ÷ 2) = 0.9163 s instead of 0.4055 s.
  6. In your words: the output charges the capacitor until it reaches the upper threshold, which flips the output; then the capacitor discharges until the lower threshold flips it back; the LED follows the output.
  7. Period = 2 × RC × ln 1.5 = 0.811 × RC, so RC = 2 ÷ 0.811 ≈ 2.47 s (for example 24.7 kΩ with 100 µF).
  8. Longer: tH = ln((5 − 1.5) ÷ (5 − 3.5)) = ln(2.333) ≈ 0.847 s; tL = ln(3.5 ÷ 1.5) ≈ 0.847 s; period ≈ 1.69 s with RC = 1 s. The thresholds are further apart, so each half takes longer.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: rising edges at ms 13 (2.69 V), ms 15 (2.59 V) and ms 18 (3.10 V). Between them the signal dipped just below 2.5 V (1.96 V at ms 14, 2.48 V at ms 17) while still rising on average. Neighbouring samples differ by up to about 0.7 V: the wiggle is comparable to the distance from the threshold. Conclusion: one slow, noisy rise, not three events: the signal never returns to a clear LOW (it stays above 1.96 V after ms 12 and ends at 4.55 V). Fix: hysteresis with an upper threshold of 3.0 V and a lower threshold of 2.0 V: the first sample above 3.0 V (3.21 V at ms 16) counts once, and the signal never falls below 2.0 V afterwards. Verified by bounce_fixed.cpp on the same samples:

samples: 30, events counted with hysteresis: 1

Testing: generate logs with larger noise, faster and slower rises, and several real openings separated by clear LOW periods; check that the count equals the number of real openings each time.
