Story hook

Analogy

Mateo runs the pass, the counter between the kitchen and the dining room. Four stations put plates on it: grill, soup, salad and dessert. Only one plate can go through the hatch at a time. Mateo looks at the order number on the ticket and slides that station's plate through.

Above the stations hangs a ticket board with four lamps. When a new order arrives, the board lights exactly one lamp, the one for the station that must cook it. The other three stay dark.

Mateo is doing two jobs that every computer does billions of times: choosing one of several inputs by a number, and turning a number into "this one, and no other". In hardware these jobs have names: the multiplexer and the decoder.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a multiplexer and a decoder do, with their truth tables and symbols.
  • Build a 2-to-1 multiplexer from four NAND gates, and a 4-to-1 multiplexer as a tree of 2-to-1 multiplexers.
  • Build a 2-to-4 decoder with an enable input from NOT and AND gates.
  • Design a combinational circuit from a word description, via its truth table.
  • Write a one-hot probe testbench, and use it to find swapped select lines (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Combinational circuit
Simple words: a circuit whose outputs depend only on its inputs right now, with no memory. Analogy: the pass: what goes through depends only on the plates and the ticket in front of Mateo, not on yesterday's orders. Precise: a digital circuit without feedback or storage, whose outputs are a Boolean function of its current inputs (after the outputs settle, F1-15). Circuits with memory are sequential (HW201). D2
Multiplexer (mux)
Simple words: a circuit that chooses one of several inputs and passes it to the output. Analogy: Mateo sliding one station's plate through the hatch. Precise: a combinational circuit with 2n data inputs, n select inputs and one output, whose output equals the data input whose index is the binary number on the select inputs. D2 D1
Select input
Simple words: the input that says which choice to make, written as a binary number. Analogy: the order number on the ticket. Precise: the control inputs of a multiplexer or decoder; with n select bits there are 2n choices. D2
Decoder
Simple words: a circuit that turns a binary number into one active line out of many. Analogy: the ticket board lighting exactly one station lamp. Precise: a combinational circuit with n inputs and 2n outputs, of which exactly the output whose index equals the input number is 1 (when enabled). D2
Enable
Simple words: an on/off input that lets a circuit work or keeps all its outputs off. Analogy: the main switch of the ticket board: when it is off, no lamp lights. Precise: an input that, when inactive, forces a decoder's outputs to their inactive value (here 0) regardless of the other inputs. D2 R1
One-hot
Simple words: a group of wires where exactly one is 1. Analogy: one lit lamp on the ticket board. Precise: an encoding in which exactly one bit of a group is 1; a decoder's outputs are one-hot when enabled. D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the multiplexer symbol and the four NANDs inside a 2-to-1 multiplexer.

Figure 2 builds a bigger multiplexer from smaller ones. This "tree" idea is how the forensic lab's circuit is built.

Figure 3 shows a decoder. Each output gate recognises one select pattern.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A multiplexer is a chooser. It has several data inputs and one output. A small number, the select, says which input to pass on. With one select wire you can choose between two inputs. With two select wires you can count 00, 01, 10, 11, so you can choose between four.

A decoder works the other way round. It takes a small number and lights exactly one of its outputs. With two input wires it has four outputs. Input 10 is the number two, so output number two lights up.

Both are made of gates you already know. A decoder output is an AND gate that only says 1 for its own number. A multiplexer is a set of AND-like gates, one per input, with an OR to collect the one that was let through.

These two parts are everywhere inside a computer. A computer's memory uses a decoder to find the one box an address points to. Its calculator uses a multiplexer to choose which answer to keep.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Combinational design from a description

A combinational circuit has no memory: its outputs are a function of its present inputs. Designing one follows a fixed recipe: write the truth table from the word description, write a sum-of-products formula (one AND term per row with output 1), simplify if you can, then build it from gates. Multiplexers and decoders are the first useful products of this recipe. D2

The multiplexer

A 2-to-1 multiplexer has data inputs d0, d1, a select input s and output y. Its description is "y = d0 when s = 0, y = d1 when s = 1". The sum-of-products formula is y = (d0 AND NOT s) OR (d1 AND s). Each AND term is a gate that lets one input through only when it is selected; the OR collects them. D2 W1

Turning AND-OR into NAND-NAND is De Morgan's law again: (x AND y) OR (z AND w) = NAND(NAND(x, y), NAND(z, w)). So the mux is g2 = NAND(d0, ns), g3 = NAND(d1, s), and y = NAND(g2, g3), plus g1 to make ns = NOT s: four NANDs, Figure 1. W1 R1

Bigger multiplexers come from smaller ones. A 4-to-1 mux needs two select bits s1 s0. In the tree of Figure 2, the first level uses s0 to choose within each pair (d0 or d1, d2 or d3), and the second level uses s1 to choose between the pairs. The select number s1 s0 is read as a binary number, so 10 chooses d2. That costs 3 × 4 = 12 NANDs. W1 R2

The decoder

A 2-to-4 decoder has two inputs s1 s0 and four outputs y0 to y3. Output yk is 1 exactly when s1 s0 is the binary number k. Each output is one AND term of the truth table: y2 = s1 AND NOT s0, for example. With an enable input en, each AND gets a third input en, so all outputs are 0 when en = 0. The outputs are one-hot when enabled: exactly one is 1. D2 R1

Decoders and multiplexers are close relatives. A multiplexer can be built from a decoder whose outputs gate each data input, followed by an OR. Conversely, the AND terms inside a multiplexer are a decoder. D2 W1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Two properties make multiplexers important in design. First, any Boolean function of n inputs can be built from a 2n-to-1 multiplexer: put the function's truth-table outputs on the data inputs as constants and the function's inputs on the select lines. Second, a multiplexer is how hardware implements "choose", the hardware version of if and switch; in F1-14 the ALU chooses its result with one. D2 W1

The tree in Figure 2 is not the only structure. A wide AND-OR (one AND term per input, as in the formula) has fewer levels of gates, which matters for speed (F1-15); a tree reuses one small tested block. Choosing between them is an early example of the size-versus-speed trade-offs of real design. D2

Not verified — check before relying on this

The course book D1 names its own multiplexer and demultiplexer chips and gives them fixed interfaces. Those names and pin lists were not opened in this build, so this chapter uses its own names (mux2, mux4, dec2to4). Check D1 before mapping these modules onto the book's projects.

How the hardware actually does it

Inside a memory chip, an address is decoded so that one row of storage cells is selected; inside a processor, multiplexers choose which register's value goes to the adder and which result is written back. You will meet both again: the register file and memory in HW201, and the datapath in HW202. Real chips may build multiplexers from transmission gates (pairs of transistors used as pass switches) instead of NANDs; that is a transistor-level choice the logic function does not see. D2

Worked example

From a description to a circuit

Description: "A buzzer at the pass sounds when the selected station's plate is ready. There are two stations, the select s picks one, and r0, r1 are 1 when that station's plate is ready." Truth table rows with output 1:

sr1r0buzzAND term
0011NOT s AND NOT r1 AND r0
0111NOT s AND r1 AND r0
1101s AND r1 AND NOT r0
1111s AND r1 AND r0

The first two terms combine to (NOT s AND r0), because r1 can be either value. The last two combine to (s AND r1). So buzz = (r0 AND NOT s) OR (r1 AND s): exactly a 2-to-1 multiplexer with d0 = r0 and d1 = r1. A description that says "choose by a number" usually becomes a multiplexer. W1

Trace the tree

Inputs d = d3 d2 d1 d0 = 0 1 0 0 (only d2 is 1), select s1 s0 = 10. m0 uses s0 = 0 and passes d0 = 0 (lo = 0). m1 uses s0 = 0 and passes d2 = 1 (hi = 1). m2 uses s1 = 1 and passes hi = 1. Output y = 1 = d2. The probe run of Listing 3 prints "d2" in the row for select 1 0. W1 R2

Code walk-through

One new piece of Verilog: buses. wire [3:0] d declares four wires d[3], d[2], d[1], d[0] under one name, and d[s] in a testbench picks the wire whose index is the number s.

Listing 1 — mux_decoder.v

// Multiplexers and a decoder, built from gates.

// 2-to-1 multiplexer from four NANDs: y = s ? d1 : d0
module mux2(input wire d0, input wire d1, input wire s, output wire y);
    wire ns, t0, t1;
    nand g1(ns, s, s);         // ns = NOT s
    nand g2(t0, d0, ns);       // 0 only when d0 is chosen and is 1
    nand g3(t1, d1, s);        // 0 only when d1 is chosen and is 1
    nand g4(y, t0, t1);
endmodule

// 4-to-1 multiplexer from three 2-to-1 multiplexers: s = 2'b10 chooses d[2]
module mux4(input wire [3:0] d, input wire [1:0] s, output wire y);
    wire lo, hi;
    mux2 m0(.d0(d[0]), .d1(d[1]), .s(s[0]), .y(lo));
    mux2 m1(.d0(d[2]), .d1(d[3]), .s(s[0]), .y(hi));
    mux2 m2(.d0(lo),   .d1(hi),   .s(s[1]), .y(y));
endmodule

// 2-to-4 decoder with enable: exactly one output is 1 when en is 1
module dec2to4(input wire [1:0] s, input wire en, output wire [3:0] y);
    wire n0, n1;
    not g0(n0, s[0]);
    not g1(n1, s[1]);
    and g2(y[0], en, n1,   n0);
    and g3(y[1], en, n1,   s[0]);
    and g4(y[2], en, s[1], n0);
    and g5(y[3], en, s[1], s[0]);
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
4–5module mux2(input wire d0, input wire d1, input wire s, output wire y); wire ns, t0, t1;The 2-to-1 mux and its three inside wires.Names match Figure 1.
6nand g1(ns, s, s);ns = NOT s.The NOT from F1-11.
7–8nand g2(t0, d0, ns); nand g3(t1, d1, s);Each is 0 only when its input is selected and is 1.The two AND terms, in NAND form.
9nand g4(y, t0, t1);y is 1 if either term let a 1 through.The OR, in NAND form (De Morgan).
13–14module mux4(input wire [3:0] d, input wire [1:0] s, output wire y);Four data wires as one bus, two select wires as one bus.Buses keep the port list short.
15–16mux2 m0(.d0(d[0]), .d1(d[1]), .s(s[0]), .y(lo));First level: pairs chosen by s[0].Figure 2, left column.
17mux2 m2(.d0(lo), .d1(hi), .s(s[1]), .y(y));Second level, chosen by s[1].The high select bit picks the pair.
21–24not g0(n0, s[0]); not g1(n1, s[1]);Inverted select bits.Verilog's built-in not and and primitives are used here for readability; each could be replaced by NANDs (F1-11).
25–28and g2(y[0], en, n1, n0); …One three-input AND per output.Each output recognises one number; en is in every term.

Listing 2 — tb_mux_decoder.v (exhaustive test of all three blocks)

// Testbench: every input combination of mux2, mux4 and dec2to4.
module tb_mux_decoder;
    reg d0, d1, s1;
    reg [3:0] d;
    reg [1:0] s;
    reg en;
    wire y2, y4;
    wire [3:0] yd;
    integer i;
    integer errors = 0;

    mux2    m2(.d0(d0), .d1(d1), .s(s1), .y(y2));
    mux4    m4(.d(d), .s(s), .y(y4));
    dec2to4 dc(.s(s), .en(en), .y(yd));

    initial begin
        for (i = 0; i < 8; i = i + 1) begin            // mux2: 3 inputs, 8 rows
            {s1, d1, d0} = i[2:0];
            #1;
            if (y2 !== (s1 ? d1 : d0)) errors = errors + 1;
        end
        for (i = 0; i < 64; i = i + 1) begin           // mux4: 6 inputs, 64 rows
            {s, d} = i[5:0];
            #1;
            if (y4 !== d[s]) errors = errors + 1;
        end
        $display("en s1 s0 | y3 y2 y1 y0");
        for (i = 0; i < 8; i = i + 1) begin            // decoder: 3 inputs, 8 rows
            {en, s} = i[2:0];
            #1;
            $display(" %b  %b  %b |  %b  %b  %b  %b", en, s[1], s[0], yd[3], yd[2], yd[1], yd[0]);
            if (yd !== (en ? (4'b0001 << s) : 4'b0000)) errors = errors + 1;
        end
        if (errors == 0) $display("ALL PASS (80 vectors: mux2 8, mux4 64, dec2to4 8)");
        else $display("FAIL: %0d of 80 vectors wrong", errors);
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
17–21{s1, d1, d0} = i[2:0]; … (s1 ? d1 : d0)All 8 rows of the 2-to-1 mux, compared with Verilog's choice operator ? :.The reference is written as "if s1 then d1 else d0".
22–26{s, d} = i[5:0]; … if (y4 !== d[s])All 64 combinations of 4 data bits and 2 select bits.d[s] is the definition of a mux in one expression.
28–33{en, s} = i[2:0]; … (4'b0001 << s)All 8 decoder rows; the expected output is 0001 shifted left by s, or 0000 when disabled.The shift makes a one-hot pattern (F0-25 taught shifts).
34–35ALL PASS (80 vectors ...)The verdict: 8 + 64 + 8 vectors.Every input combination of every block.

Listing 3 — tb_mux4_probe.v (one-hot probe)

// Testbench: one-hot probe of a 4-to-1 multiplexer. Only input d[k] is 1;
// for each select value, which k comes out?
module tb_mux4_probe;
    reg [3:0] d;
    reg [1:0] s;
    wire y;
    integer k, j;
    integer errors = 0;

    mux4 dut(.d(d), .s(s), .y(y));

    initial begin
        $display("select s1 s0 | output is 1 when the only 1 is on input ...");
        for (j = 0; j < 4; j = j + 1) begin
            s = j[1:0];
            $write("         %b  %b |", s[1], s[0]);
            for (k = 0; k < 4; k = k + 1) begin
                d = 4'b0001 << k;
                #1;
                if (y === 1'b1) $write(" d%0d", k);
                if (y !== d[s]) errors = errors + 1;
            end
            $write("   (expected d%0d)\n", j);
        end
        if (errors == 0) $display("ALL PASS (16 probes)");
        else $display("FAIL: %0d of 16 probes wrong", errors);
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
14–16for (j = 0; j < 4; ...) s = j[1:0];For each select value…One output row per select value.
17–21d = 4'b0001 << k; … if (y === 1'b1) $write(" d%0d", k);…puts a 1 on exactly one data input k at a time, and prints k if the output follows it.A one-hot probe tells you which input is really connected for each select value: an exact map, not only pass/fail.
23$write(" (expected d%0d)\n", j);Prints what the row should say.Puts the expectation next to the observation.

Where the analogy breaks

  • Mateo moves a plate; a multiplexer copies a value. The unselected inputs keep their values and the selected one is not "used up". Many multiplexers can read the same input at once. D2
  • Mateo takes time to read the ticket and can be distracted; a mux has no attention. It responds to every change of any input, selected or not, after a gate delay. It never "waits for the ticket". D2
  • The ticket board could light no lamp by mistake and a cook would notice; a decoder with a fault is silent. Only a test (like Listing 2's 8 rows) finds an output that never lights.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Select 01 gives d2 and select 10 gives d1 (real output in the forensic lab).The select bits are swapped between the tree levels.One-hot probe (Listing 3).First level uses s[0], second level s[1].
The mux output is inverted.The OR stage was built as AND-NOT, or the final NAND is missing.Compare the full truth table: every row flipped.NAND-NAND form, as Listing 1.
Two decoder outputs are 1 at once.An AND term is missing a NOT (for example s0 instead of n0).Print all four outputs for each input (Listing 2's table).Each output must use every select bit, inverted where its number has a 0.
Decoder outputs not all 0 when en = 0.en missing from some AND terms.Check the en = 0 rows of the table.Add en to every term.
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-11 built every single gate from NAND. What carries over: NAND-NAND form via De Morgan, structural Verilog, exhaustive testbenches. What changes: you now design blocks with many inputs from a word description (truth table → sum of products → gates), use buses, and build big blocks from small tested ones; tests now report which input is connected (probes), not only pass/fail. What comes next: F1-13 applies the same recipe to arithmetic: the half adder and the full adder. D2

Check yourself

  1. How many select bits does an 8-to-1 multiplexer need? How many outputs does a 3-to-8 decoder have?
  2. Write the sum-of-products formula of a 2-to-1 mux.
  3. In a 2-to-4 decoder with en = 1 and s1 s0 = 11, which outputs are 1?
  4. Which statement is correct? (a) A mux can only pass a 1. (b) A decoder's outputs are one-hot when enabled. (c) A 4-to-1 mux needs four select bits. (d) A combinational circuit remembers its last input.
  5. Explain in your own words why a 4-to-1 mux tree needs s0 on the first level and s1 on the second.
  6. Apply it to a new case: build a 4-to-1 mux from a 2-to-4 decoder, four AND gates and one OR gate. Write the formula for y.
  7. Predict what the probe of Listing 3 prints if m2 used s[0] and both m0 and m1 used s[1]. Then compare with the forensic evidence.

Lab

Goal

Build an 8-to-1 multiplexer as a tree of 2-to-1 multiplexers and a 3-to-8 decoder, and test both exhaustively.

Hardware and software needed

No hardware. Icarus Verilog 12.0 (R1, R2). Untested on hardware.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-12; confirm ALL PASS in mux_decoder.out and mux4_probe.out.
  2. Write mux8 with ports input wire [7:0] d, input wire [2:0] s, output wire y, from two mux4 and one mux2. Decide on paper which select bit each level uses.
  3. Write dec3to8 with input wire [2:0] s, input wire en, output wire [7:0] y.
  4. Extend Listing 2: 211 = 2048 rows for mux8 (8 data + 3 select bits) and 16 rows for the decoder.
  5. Write a probe like Listing 3 for mux8 (8 × 8 = 64 probes).

Expected observations

The given blocks print the decoder table and ALL PASS (R1), and the probe prints d0, d1, d2, d3 down the diagonal (R2). Your mux8 probe should print d0 to d7 down the diagonal.

Verification

ALL PASS for 2048 + 16 vectors and 64 probes.

Troubleshooting

  • Probe shows the right inputs in the wrong rows. Select bits swapped between levels (see the forensic lab).
  • The probe never shows d4 to d7. The inner loop over k still stops at 4; for mux8 it must run to 8.
  • Rows look shuffled. In {s, d} = i[10:0]; the leftmost part of the concatenation takes the highest bits of i; check that the 3 select bits and 8 data bits add up to 11 and are in the order you meant.

Extension

Implement XOR of three inputs with one 8-to-1 mux whose data inputs are constants (Layer 3), and test it.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Priya built a sound board: four buttons choose one of four sounds through a 4-to-1 multiplexer. Sounds 0 and 3 play correctly; buttons 1 and 2 play each other's sound. Her friend says one of the sound files must be mislabelled. Find the real cause.

Evidence pack

Priya's multiplexer file and the real output of the probe testbench (Listing 3) run on it, with the correct mux2 of Listing 1.

// Forensic evidence: the 4-to-1 multiplexer from Priya's sound board, exactly as handed in.

    wire lo, hi;
    mux2 m0(.d0(d[0]), .d1(d[1]), .s(s[1]), .y(lo));
    mux2 m1(.d0(d[2]), .d1(d[3]), .s(s[1]), .y(hi));
    mux2 m2(.d0(lo),   .d1(hi),   .s(s[0]), .y(y));
endmodule

Questions

  1. Which select values give the wrong input, and which input do they give?
  2. State two hypotheses: one about the data wiring (the "mislabelled file") and one about the select wiring. Which observation decides?
  3. Which lines of Listing 4 are wrong, and how?
  4. Why are selects 00 and 11 still correct?
  5. Write the fix and the test that proves it.

Method hints

Write the select values in binary next to the inputs they produced. Look for a pattern in the bits, not in the numbers. Then trace one wrong row through Figure 2 with Priya's select connections.

Mini-project

Design a "kitchen display selector": a 2-bit station number chooses which of four 4-bit order counts appears on one 4-bit display. Build it from four mux4 instances (one per bit) and write an exhaustive or probe-style testbench.

Rubric (5 points): truth-table description in words (1); correct structural module with buses (1); test proving every station shows its own count (2); one paragraph explaining why a 4-bit choice needs four multiplexers (1).

Summary

  • Combinational circuits have no memory; design them via truth table → sum of products → gates.
  • A 2n-to-1 multiplexer chooses one data input by an n-bit select number.
  • A 2-to-1 mux is (d0 AND NOT s) OR (d1 AND s): four NANDs.
  • Bigger muxes are trees of smaller ones; the low select bit goes to the first level.
  • An n-to-2n decoder makes one output 1 (one-hot) for each input number; an enable can turn all outputs off.
  • A one-hot probe maps which input is really connected for each select value.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. 3 select bits (2 × 2 × 2 = 8); 8 outputs.
  2. y = (d0 AND NOT s) OR (d1 AND s).
  3. Only y3.
  4. (b). (a) A mux passes whatever value the selected input has, 0 or 1. (c) Four inputs need two select bits. (d) That would be a sequential circuit.
  5. Any answer that says: the select number s1 s0 means 2 × s1 + s0; inputs d0, d1 differ only in s0 and so do d2, d3, so s0 must choose within pairs; s1 then chooses the pair.
  6. y = (y0 AND d0) OR (y1 AND d1) OR (y2 AND d2) OR (y3 AND d3), where y0–y3 are the decoder outputs for the select bits (enable tied to 1).
  7. It would print d0 for 00, d2 for 01, d1 for 10 and d3 for 11: exactly the forensic evidence.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: select 0 1 gives d2 and select 1 0 gives d1; selects 0 0 and 1 1 are correct (FAIL 4 of 16 probes, R3). Hypotheses: (1) data inputs d1 and d2 are swapped (a "mislabelled file"); (2) the select bits are swapped. Under (1), the one-hot probe would still show each select value picking one input, and swapping the data would also be fixed by relabelling; but the wrong rows are exactly those whose two select bits differ (01 and 10), the signature of swapped select bits. The source decides it: data wiring in Listing 4 lines 4–5 matches Listing 1. Root cause: Listing 4, lines 4–6: m0 and m1 use s[1] and m2 uses s[0]; the levels' select bits are swapped. Why 00 and 11 survive: swapping two equal bits changes nothing. Fix: m0 and m1 use s[0], m2 uses s[1], as Listing 1; the probe then prints the diagonal and ALL PASS (R2). Prevention: a one-hot probe or an exhaustive test with d[s] as the reference. How the evidence was made: Listing 1's mux4 with the select bits of the two levels exchanged, run with Listing 3 in this build. Wrong answers: "the sound files are mislabelled" (relabelling would only hide the fault; the data wiring is correct); "mux2 is broken" (it passes its own 8-row test in R1).

Story hook

Analogy

The kitchen counts finished plates on a row of small flip boards. Each board shows only an empty side or a full side: 0 or 1. Hana is in charge of the board on the right. When a plate is finished, she flips her board.

If her board was already full, it cannot show "2". So she flips it back to empty and sends a runner with a token to the next board on the left. That board's cook adds the token to whatever arrives there.

Hana's rule is all of binary addition: "write the last digit here, carry one to the left". In this chapter you turn that rule into gates. One board with two inputs is a half adder. A board that also takes the runner's token is a full adder.

What you will be able to do

  • Add binary numbers by hand, column by column, with carries.
  • Derive the half adder (XOR for the sum, AND for the carry) from its truth table.
  • Build a full adder from two half adders and an OR gate, and from nine NAND gates.
  • Test both full adders exhaustively against ordinary addition in a simulator.
  • Spot a testbench width mistake that makes 1 + 1 + 1 look like 1.
  • Find a missing carry term in a full adder from its truth-table output (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Sum bit and carry bit
Simple words: when you add one column, the sum bit is the digit you write down and the carry bit is what you pass to the next column. Analogy: Hana's board after the flip (sum) and the runner's token (carry). Precise: for inputs whose total in one column is T (0 to 3), the sum bit is T mod 2 and the carry bit is T div 2 (integer division). W1 D3
Half adder
Simple words: a circuit that adds two bits and gives a sum bit and a carry bit. Analogy: one board with no runner arriving. Precise: a combinational circuit with inputs a, b and outputs s = a XOR b and c = a AND b, so that 2c + s = a + b. D2 R1
Full adder
Simple words: a circuit that adds three bits: two digits and a carry coming in. Analogy: a board whose cook also takes the runner's token. Precise: a combinational circuit with inputs a, b, cin and outputs s = a XOR b XOR cin and cout = (a AND b) OR (cin AND (a XOR b)), so that 2·cout + s = a + b + cin. D2 R1
Carry in, carry out (cin, cout)
Simple words: the carry arriving from the column to the right, and the carry leaving to the column to the left. Analogy: the token the runner brings, and the token sent on. Precise: the carry input and carry output of a full adder; chaining cout of one bit to cin of the next makes a multi-bit adder (F1-14). D2
Expression width (Verilog)
Simple words: how many bits Verilog uses to work out an expression. Analogy: a board that only has room for one digit: a total of 3 is written as 1 and the rest is lost. Precise: Verilog sizes an expression from its operands and its context; adding three 1-bit values in a 1-bit context keeps only the low bit. The run width_demo shows it. D5 R3

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the half adder. Look at its truth table: the two outputs, read as a 2-bit number c s, are the sum of a and b.

Figure 2 is the full-adder circuit, the required diagram for this topic. It is two half adders in a row with an OR gate collecting their carries.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Adding binary numbers works like adding decimal numbers. You start at the right and add one column at a time. In binary a column can only hold 0 or 1. So 1 + 1 is "0, carry 1", the same way 5 + 5 in decimal is "0, carry 1".

A half adder adds one column with two bits. The digit you write down is 1 when exactly one bit is 1. That is XOR. The carry is 1 only when both bits are 1. That is AND. Two gates, and a machine can add.

But most columns have three things to add: two digits and the carry from the right. A full adder handles all three. It adds the two digits with one half adder, then adds the carry with a second half adder. If either step made a carry, it sends one carry to the left.

Line up four full adders and you can add four-bit numbers. That is the next chapter.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

One column of binary addition

In a column, the total T of the bits being added is 0, 1, 2 or 3. The sum bit is T mod 2 and the carry bit is T div 2. Writing T in binary gives both at once: 2 = 10 (carry 1, sum 0), 3 = 11 (carry 1, sum 1). This is ordinary place value from F0-21. W1

The half adder

With two inputs, T = a + b. The truth table in Figure 1 shows s is 1 exactly when a and b differ: s = a XOR b. The carry is 1 only for a = b = 1: c = a AND b. So a half adder is one XOR and one AND. Its outputs satisfy 2c + s = a + b for all four rows. W1 R1 D2

The full adder

A full adder adds a, b and a carry in cin. Its sum is 1 when an odd number of the three inputs are 1: s = a XOR b XOR cin. Its carry out is 1 when at least two inputs are 1. D2 W1

Figure 2 builds it from parts you have. Half adder 1 adds a and b, giving s1 = a XOR b and c1 = a AND b. Half adder 2 adds s1 and cin, giving s = s1 XOR cin and c2 = s1 AND cin. The carry out is c1 OR c2. Why OR and not another adder? If c1 = 1 then a = b = 1, so s1 = 0 and c2 = 0. The two carries are never 1 together, so OR is enough. W1 R1

In the NAND-only style of F1-11, a full adder needs nine NANDs. Two four-NAND XORs make the sum, and they share inside wires with the carry: the first XOR's t1 = NAND(a, b) and the second XOR's t4 = NAND(x1, cin) are exactly the inverted carry terms, so cout = NAND(t1, t4) costs one more gate. Listing 1 contains both versions, and the testbench checks both against ordinary addition. W1 R1 D1

Testing arithmetic

A full adder has three inputs, so an exhaustive test has 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 rows. The reference is plain arithmetic: the 2-bit number {cout, s} must equal a + b + cin. Here a trap waits. Verilog works out an expression width from the operands; three 1-bit values added in a 1-bit context give a 1-bit answer, so 1 + 1 + 1 prints as 1. Storing the total in a 32-bit integer first gives 3. The run width_demo shows both lines, and Listing 2 uses the integer. R3 D5

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

The carry-out formula can be written in several equivalent ways. "At least two of three" is the majority function: cout = (a AND b) OR (a AND cin) OR (b AND cin). Figure 2 uses (a AND b) OR (cin AND (a XOR b)), which reuses the XOR already needed for the sum. The terms a AND b ("this column generates a carry by itself") and a XOR b ("this column passes an incoming carry on") get names, generate and propagate, in the faster adders of F1-15. D2 W1

Gate counts depend on what you count. Our structural full adder uses 2 XOR, 2 AND and 1 OR. The NAND-only version uses 9 NANDs. Yosys, given the one-line behavioural adder and asked for NAND cells, reports 7 NAND and 5 NOT cells: 12 NAND-equivalents in our counting, more than the hand design, as with the XOR in F1-11. R1 R4 D6

Not verified — check before relying on this

The course book D1 builds a half adder and a full adder as two of its arithmetic chips, with its own pin names. Those names and the book's exact constructions were not opened in this build. The nine-NAND construction here was designed and tested in this build (R1); whether it matches any book's figure is unverified.

How the hardware actually does it

Every processor's arithmetic unit contains adders built from full-adder logic or from faster relatives of it. The ideas of this chapter, a sum bit and a carry bit per column, survive unchanged; what changes in fast designs is how quickly the carry reaches the left end, which F1-15 measures in simulation. Chip designers also use full-adder cells built directly from transistors rather than from separate gates; the function is the same. D2

Worked example

Add 0111 + 0011 by hand

That is 7 + 3. Work right to left, writing T (the column total), the sum bit and the carry out.

Column (place value)abcinTscout
0 (1)110201
1 (2)111311
2 (4)101201
3 (8)001110

Reading the sum bits from column 3 down to column 0: 1010 = 8 + 2 = 10. And 7 + 3 = 10. Each row of this table is one row of the full-adder truth table printed by the run of Listing 2. W1 R1

Check the carries never collide

Row a = 1, b = 1, cin = 1: half adder 1 gives s1 = 0, c1 = 1. Half adder 2 adds s1 = 0 and cin = 1: s = 1, c2 = 0. cout = 1 OR 0 = 1, s = 1: total 3. Row a = 0, b = 1, cin = 1: s1 = 1, c1 = 0; then s = 0, c2 = 1; cout = 1. In no row are c1 and c2 both 1. W1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — adders.v

// Half adder and full adder, built from gates.

module half_adder(input wire a, input wire b, output wire s, output wire c);
    xor g1(s, a, b);           // sum bit: 1 when exactly one input is 1
    and g2(c, a, b);           // carry bit: 1 when both inputs are 1
endmodule

// A full adder from two half adders and an OR gate.
module full_adder(input wire a, input wire b, input wire cin,
                  output wire s, output wire cout);
    wire s1, c1, c2;
    half_adder h1(.a(a),  .b(b),   .s(s1), .c(c1));
    half_adder h2(.a(s1), .b(cin), .s(s),  .c(c2));
    or g3(cout, c1, c2);
endmodule

// The same full adder from nine NAND gates only.
module full_adder_nand(input wire a, input wire b, input wire cin,
                       output wire s, output wire cout);
    wire t1, t2, t3, x1, t4, t5, t6;
    nand g1(t1, a, b);         // g1..g4: x1 = a XOR b (the four-NAND XOR of F1-11)
    nand g2(t2, a, t1);
    nand g3(t3, b, t1);
    nand g4(x1, t2, t3);
    nand g5(t4, x1, cin);      // g5..g8: s = x1 XOR cin
    nand g6(t5, x1, t4);
    nand g7(t6, cin, t4);
    nand g8(s, t5, t6);
    nand g9(cout, t1, t4);     // cout = (a AND b) OR (x1 AND cin)
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
3–6xor g1(s, a, b); and g2(c, a, b);The half adder of Figure 1, with Verilog's built-in xor and and gate primitives.Two gates; output port first, as with nand.
9–11module full_adder(input wire a, input wire b, input wire cin, ...); wire s1, c1, c2;The full adder and its three inside wires.Names match Figure 2.
12–13half_adder h1(.a(a), .b(b), .s(s1), .c(c1));
half_adder h2(.a(s1), .b(cin), .s(s), .c(c2));		Two half-adder instances in a row.Reuse of a tested block.
14or g3(cout, c1, c2);Collects the two carries.OR is enough because c1 and c2 are never both 1 (Worked example).
18–20module full_adder_nand(...); wire t1, t2, t3, x1, t4, t5, t6;The NAND-only full adder.Same ports, so the same testbench checks it.
21–24nand g1(t1, a, b); … nand g4(x1, t2, t3);x1 = a XOR b with the four-NAND XOR of F1-11.t1 = NAND(a, b) is kept for the carry.
25–28nand g5(t4, x1, cin); … nand g8(s, t5, t6);s = x1 XOR cin, again four NANDs.t4 = NAND(x1, cin) is kept for the carry.
29nand g9(cout, t1, t4);cout = NAND(NAND(a, b), NAND(x1, cin)) = (a AND b) OR (x1 AND cin).De Morgan once more; one extra gate makes the carry.

Listing 2 — tb_adders.v

// Testbench: all 8 input rows of both full adders, checked against ordinary addition.
module tb_adders;
    reg a, b, cin;
    wire s, cout, s9, cout9;
    integer i;
    integer expected;                      // 32 bits wide, so 1 + 1 + 1 can be 3
    integer errors = 0;

    full_adder      fa(.a(a), .b(b), .cin(cin), .s(s),  .cout(cout));
    full_adder_nand fn(.a(a), .b(b), .cin(cin), .s(s9), .cout(cout9));

    initial begin
        $display("a b cin | cout s | a+b+cin | 9-NAND cout s");
        for (i = 0; i < 8; i = i + 1) begin
            {a, b, cin} = i[2:0];
            #1;
            expected = a + b + cin;
            $display("%b %b  %b  |  %b   %b |    %0d    |       %b    %b",
                     a, b, cin, cout, s, expected, cout9, s9);
            if ({cout, s}   !== expected[1:0]) errors = errors + 1;
            if ({cout9, s9} !== expected[1:0]) errors = errors + 1;
        end
        if (errors == 0) $display("ALL PASS (16 checks: 8 rows x 2 designs)");
        else $display("FAIL: %0d of 16 checks wrong", errors);
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
6integer expected;A 32-bit variable for the reference total.Avoids the width trap (run width_demo).
9–10full_adder fa(...); full_adder_nand fn(...);Both designs on the same inputs.Two independent designs checked against one reference.
14–15{a, b, cin} = i[2:0];All 8 input rows.Exhaustive for three inputs.
17expected = a + b + cin;Ordinary addition, 0 to 3.The reference model: arithmetic, not gates.
20–21if ({cout, s} !== expected[1:0]) ...Joins cout and s into a 2-bit number and compares with the low 2 bits of the total.2·cout + s = a + b + cin is the definition of a full adder.

Listing 3 — width_demo.v (the testbench trap)

// Demonstration of a testbench trap: Verilog sizes an expression by its operands.
module width_demo;
    reg a = 1'b1, b = 1'b1, cin = 1'b1;     // three 1-bit values, all 1
    integer wide;                          // a 32-bit variable

    initial begin
        $display("a + b + cin printed directly:        %0d", a + b + cin);
        wide = a + b + cin;
        $display("a + b + cin stored in an integer:    %0d", wide);
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule

Where the analogy breaks

  • Hana flips her board and then the runner leaves; in a full adder there is no "then". The sum and carry are both computed by gates reacting at the same time; only signal delay orders them (F1-15). D2
  • A runner can carry more than one token; a carry is one bit. The most any column of a full adder can pass on is a single 1, because 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 = binary 11. The analogy suggests tokens could pile up; in binary addition they cannot. W1
  • Boards count plates that exist; an adder's bits mean whatever the program says. The same bits can be a count, a negative number in two's complement (F0-24) or part of a letter; the adder does not know. D2

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Carry out wrong only in rows 011 and 101 (real output in the forensic lab).The carry ignores the incoming carry: the term (a XOR b) AND cin is missing.List the failing rows; what do they have in common?cout = c1 OR c2, as Figure 2.
The testbench prints "a+b+cin = 1" for 1 + 1 + 1 (real output of width_demo).The reference was computed at 1-bit width.Print the reference on its own.Store it in an integer first (Listing 2, line 17).
Sum wrong in every row with cin = 1.The second half adder takes a or b instead of s1.Compare the rows with cin = 0 (correct) and cin = 1.Feed s1 into half adder 2.
cout right, s inverted in every row.XNOR used instead of XOR (or an extra NOT).Every s value flipped is the signature.Use XOR.
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-12 designed choosing circuits from truth tables; F0-21 taught binary place value. What carries over: the truth-table recipe, NAND-only construction, exhaustive tests. What changes: the outputs now mean a number, so the reference model in the testbench is arithmetic (a + b + cin), and you must watch the width of that arithmetic; correctness has an algebraic form, 2·cout + s = a + b + cin. What comes next: F1-14 chains full adders into a multi-bit adder and builds an ALU around it. D2

Check yourself

  1. Add 1011 + 0110 in binary by hand. Check in decimal.
  2. Which gates form a half adder, and which output does each make?
  3. For a = 1, b = 0, cin = 1, give s1, c1, s, c2 and cout in Figure 2.
  4. Which formula is a correct carry out of a full adder? (a) a AND b AND cin (b) a XOR b XOR cin (c) (a AND b) OR (cin AND (a XOR b)) (d) a OR b OR cin
  5. Explain in your own words why the OR gate in Figure 2 never has to deal with two carries at once.
  6. Apply it to a new case: a "full subtractor" computes a − b − bin with a difference bit and a borrow out. Write its truth table (8 rows).
  7. Predict what width_demo would print on its first line if a, b and cin were declared reg [1:0] (2 bits each, all equal to 1). Then try it.

Lab

Goal

Build a full adder three ways (two half adders, nine NANDs, and the majority formula), prove all three equal ordinary addition, and compare their gate counts.

Hardware and software needed

No hardware. Icarus Verilog 12.0 (R1); Yosys 0.33 for gate counts (R4). Untested on hardware.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-13; confirm adders.out ends with ALL PASS (16 checks).
  2. Add a module full_adder_maj whose carry is (a AND b) OR (a AND cin) OR (b AND cin), using and and or primitives.
  3. Add it to the testbench as a third design and change the check count.
  4. Count the gates of each version by hand and write a small table.
  5. Optional: synthesise full_adder_maj with the Yosys command of Listing 4 (change the file and top names) and compare.

Expected observations

The given designs print the table in the Code walk-through, with the a+b+cin column going 0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, and ALL PASS (R1). Your third design must agree in all 8 rows.

Verification

ALL PASS for 24 checks (8 rows × 3 designs).

Troubleshooting

  • Your reference column shows 0 or 1 only. The width trap: see Listing 3.
  • A three-input or gate seems missing. The and, or, nand primitives accept more than two inputs (Listing 1 of F1-12 uses a three-input and).
  • "FAIL: 2 of 24". Look at which design and rows fail; compare with the forensic lab's signature.

Extension

Build the full subtractor of question 6 and test it against a − b − bin computed in an integer.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Kofi's full adder passes six of eight rows. "Two wrong out of eight is close enough for a first try," he says, and wants to use it in his 4-bit adder. Before he does, find exactly what is missing and predict what it would do to 4-bit sums.

Evidence pack

Kofi's file and the real output of the unchanged testbench (Listing 2). The testbench also checks a NAND version; Kofi did not write one, so the file includes a stand-in (lines 11–15) that is known to be correct.

Listing 5 — fa_bad.v (evidence)

// Forensic evidence: Kofi's full adder, exactly as handed in.
module full_adder(input wire a, input wire b, input wire cin,
                  output wire s, output wire cout);
    wire s1, c1;
    xor g1(s1, a, b);
    xor g2(s, s1, cin);
    and g3(c1, a, b);
    assign cout = c1;          // carry out
endmodule

// Kofi's file did not include a NAND version; this copy keeps the testbench unchanged.
module full_adder_nand(input wire a, input wire b, input wire cin,
                       output wire s, output wire cout);
    assign {cout, s} = a + b + cin;
endmodule

Questions

  1. Which rows fail, and which output is wrong in them?
  2. What do the failing rows have in common? State two hypotheses.
  3. Which line of Listing 5 is the root cause? Write the missing term.
  4. Predict one 4-bit sum that a ripple adder made of Kofi's full adders would get wrong, and one it would get right.
  5. Why is "six of eight rows" not "close enough" for an adder?

Method hints

Compare Kofi's cout column with the 9-NAND column next to it, row by row. Then use the Worked example's question: when must a carry come from cin rather than from a and b?

Mini-project

Write a one-page "adder datasheet" for your full adder: symbol, truth table, the circuit of Figure 2 redrawn, the 9-NAND circuit drawn from Listing 1, gate counts for three designs, and the simulator output that proves each.

Rubric (5 points): correct table and formulas (1); both circuits drawn with wire names matching your code (2); counts with a sentence on what is being counted (1); real outputs attached (1).

Summary

  • One binary column: sum = total mod 2, carry = total div 2.
  • Half adder: s = a XOR b, c = a AND b.
  • Full adder: s = a XOR b XOR cin; cout = (a AND b) OR (cin AND (a XOR b)), "at least two of three".
  • A full adder is two half adders and an OR; the two carries never collide.
  • NAND-only: 9 gates, because the carry reuses the XORs' inside wires.
  • Test arithmetic against arithmetic, and compute the reference at a wide enough width.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. 1011 + 0110 = 10001 (columns from the right: 1+0 = 1; 1+1 = 0 carry 1; 0+1+1 = 0 carry 1; 1+0+1 = 0 carry 1; final carry 1). Decimal: 11 + 6 = 17 = 16 + 1.
  2. XOR makes the sum bit; AND makes the carry bit.
  3. s1 = 1, c1 = 0; s = 1 XOR 1 = 0, c2 = 1 AND 1 = 1; cout = 0 OR 1 = 1. Total 2 = binary 10.
  4. (c). (a) is 1 only when all three are 1, missing the two-of-three rows. (b) is the sum bit, not the carry. (d) is 1 whenever any input is 1.
  5. Any answer that says: c1 = 1 only when a = b = 1; then s1 = 0, so half adder 2 adds 0 + cin and cannot carry; so c1 and c2 are never both 1.
  6. a b bin | d bout: 000 | 0 0; 001 | 1 1; 010 | 1 1; 011 | 0 1; 100 | 1 0; 101 | 0 0; 110 | 0 0; 111 | 1 1.
  7. It would print 3: the operands are now 2 bits wide, so the sum is worked out at 2 bits and 3 = binary 11 fits. (Check it with your own run; the run is the evidence.)

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: rows a b cin = 0 1 1 and 1 0 1 fail: Kofi's cout is 0 where the reference total is 2 and the 9-NAND column shows 1. The sum column is correct in every row (R2). Common factor: in both failing rows exactly one of a, b is 1 and cin is 1: the carry must come from cin. Hypotheses: (1) the carry ignores cin; (2) the sum is wrong and the reference misreads it. The sum column matches the 9-NAND stand-in in all rows, which rules out (2). Root cause: Listing 5, line 8: assign cout = c1; uses only a AND b; the term (a XOR b) AND cin (c2 in Figure 2) and the OR are missing. Effect on 4-bit sums: any addition where a carry must pass through a column with exactly one 1 goes wrong, for example 0001 + 0011 (1 + 3): column 1 has a = 0, b = 1, cin = 1, so the carry is lost and the result is 0000 instead of 0100 (4). Additions with no carry chain through such a column, such as 0001 + 0010, stay right. Why six of eight is not enough: an adder must be right for every input; a program cannot avoid the failing rows. Fix: add and g4(c2, s1, cin); and or g5(cout, c1, c2);; rerun: ALL PASS. How the evidence was made: Listing 1's full adder rewritten without the second carry term, run with Listing 2 in this build. Wrong answers: "the testbench reference is wrong" (the 9-NAND stand-in agrees with the reference in all 8 rows).

Story hook

Analogy

The counting boards of F1-13 now stand in a row of four, each with its own cook. Tunde, on the right, adds first and sends his runner left. Each cook waits for the runner from the right before writing a final digit. The token travels down the row, one station at a time.

Next to the row stands Ines's prep station. It has several tools: the counting row, a slicer, a grater, a peeler. A dial on the front, set by the head chef's order ticket, decides which tool's result is placed on the plate. The dial has eight positions, and a small panel of four lamps reports facts about the result: "the plate is empty", "the result is negative", and two more about the counting row.

The row is a ripple-carry adder. Ines's station is an ALU, the arithmetic logic unit at the heart of every processor. In this chapter you build both and test them until you trust them.

What you will be able to do

  • Build an N-bit ripple-carry adder from full adders and explain why it is correct for every input.
  • Subtract with the same adder, using two's complement: a − b = a + NOT b + 1.
  • Design an ALU with eight operations, a result multiplexer and four status flags (zero, negative, carry, overflow), and explain each flag.
  • Test the ALU against a reference model: exhaustively at 4 bits, with edge cases and pseudo-random vectors at 16 bits.
  • Locate a faulty carry connection in a 4-bit adder from its test vectors ("the adder that is wrong for 7 + 1").
Jargon box
Ripple-carry adder
Simple words: a multi-bit adder made by chaining full adders, each passing its carry to the next. Analogy: the row of counting boards, with the runner's token travelling from right to left. Precise: an N-bit adder of N full adders in which the carry out of bit i is the carry in of bit i + 1; the carry may have to pass ("ripple") through every bit. D2 R1
ALU (arithmetic logic unit)
Simple words: the part of a processor that does arithmetic and logic on two numbers, choosing the operation from a code. Analogy: Ines's prep station with its tools and the selector dial. Precise: a combinational circuit with two N-bit operands, an operation code (opcode) and an N-bit result plus status flags; it computes several functions and selects one with a multiplexer. D2 D1
Opcode (operation code)
Simple words: a small binary number that says which operation the ALU should do. Analogy: the dial position on Ines's station. Precise: the select input of the ALU's result multiplexer and of any operation-specific logic; this chapter's ALU uses a 3-bit code with eight operations. W1
Status flags (Z, N, C, V)
Simple words: extra one-bit outputs that report facts about the result: is it zero, is it negative, did the addition carry out, did it overflow? Analogy: the four lamps on the station's panel. Precise: Z = 1 when every result bit is 0; N = the top bit of the result (its sign in two's complement); C = the carry out of the top bit for ADD and SUB; V = 1 when a signed (two's complement) ADD or SUB gives a result outside the range of N bits. D2 R3
Overflow (signed)
Simple words: the true answer is too big or too small to fit, so the bits show a wrong signed number. Analogy: a four-board row asked to show a count that needs five boards, read as a signed count. Precise: in N-bit two's complement, the representable range is −2N−1 to 2N−1 − 1; a signed sum outside that range overflows; this happens exactly when the carry into the top bit differs from the carry out of it. D2 W1 R3
Reference model
Simple words: a second, simpler description of what the answer should be, used to check the circuit. Analogy: the head chef's recipe card that the tasting checks against. Precise: an independent implementation of the specification (here, integer arithmetic in the testbench) whose outputs are compared with the design under test for every applied vector. D1 D2
Pseudo-random test vectors
Simple words: test inputs that look random but come from a formula, so the same list appears every run. Analogy: a tasting list drawn by lottery, but from a lottery whose draw can be repeated exactly. Precise: inputs produced by a deterministic generator from a fixed seed; used when exhaustive testing is too large; the run is repeatable because the seed is fixed. D5 R4

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 chains four full adders. Bit 0 is on the right, as in written numbers, so the carry runs right to left.

Figure 2 is the ALU built in this chapter. The adder does ADD and SUB; the gates do the logic operations; a multiplexer, driven by the opcode, chooses the result.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

You add long numbers one column at a time, starting on the right, and each column may pass a carry to the next. A ripple-carry adder does exactly that with one full adder per column. The carry "ripples" from right to left, like a row of people passing a token.

Subtraction does not need a new machine. In F0-24 you learned two's complement: to make −b, flip all bits of b and add 1. So a − b is a + (flipped b) + 1. The adder adds a and the flipped b, and the extra 1 enters as the first carry. One adder, two jobs.

An ALU puts the adder next to some plain gates (AND, OR, XOR, NOT) and a multiplexer. The opcode picks which answer leaves the ALU. Next to the answer, four flags report facts: is the answer zero, is it negative, did the adder carry out of the top, and did a signed answer overflow?

Layer 2 — the student explanation

The ripple-carry adder and why it is correct

An N-bit ripple-carry adder joins N full adders: bit i adds ai, bi and the carry ci, producing si and ci+1, with c0 = cin. Each full adder guarantees 2·ci+1 + si = ai + bi + ci (F1-13). Multiply that equation for bit i by 2i and add the equations for all bits: every inside carry appears once on each side and cancels. What remains is 2N·cout + s = a + b + cin, where s, a and b are read as N-bit numbers. So the adder is correct for every input, as long as every full adder is. W1 D2

The run of Listing 2 checks this for all 512 input combinations of the 4-bit adder (16 × 16 values of a and b, times 2 values of cin) against plain integer addition, and prints ALL PASS. R1

Subtraction with the same adder

In N-bit two's complement, −b is represented by NOT b + 1. So a − b = a + NOT b + 1. The ALU feeds the adder with b XOR sub on every bit, where sub = 1 for subtraction: XOR with 1 flips a bit and XOR with 0 leaves it (F1-11). The "+ 1" enters as the adder's carry in, also equal to sub. One control wire turns the adder into a subtractor. D2 W1

Four flags

The status flags describe the result. Z (zero) is the NOR of all result bits. N (negative) is the top result bit, which is the sign in two's complement. C (carry) is the carry out of the top bit for ADD and SUB: for unsigned addition, C = 1 means the true sum did not fit in N bits. For subtraction in our ALU, C = 1 means no borrow was needed (a ≥ b as unsigned numbers): 7 − 7 gives C = 1, 5 − 7 gives C = 0, as the run shows. D2 R3

V (overflow) is about signed numbers. Adding two positive numbers must not give a negative result, and adding two negative numbers must not give a positive one. Both failures happen exactly when the carry into the top bit differs from the carry out of it, so V = cout XOR cmsb. In 4 bits, 7 + 1 = 1000, which is −8 as a signed number: the run prints V = 1 and N = 1 for it. The same bits, read as unsigned, are a correct 8 (C = 0). The adder does not know which reading you mean; the flags let the program decide. D2 W1 R3

The ALU

Our ALU has a 3-bit opcode: 000 ADD, 001 SUB, 010 AND, 011 OR, 100 XOR, 101 NOT a, 110 pass a, 111 pass b. All operations are computed at the same time; the result multiplexer keeps one. This is the combinational design of F1-12 at a larger scale: an 8-to-1 multiplexer per result bit. C and V are forced to 0 for the logic operations, so they only report on arithmetic. W1 R3

Testing an ALU

The testbench (Listing 4) contains a reference model: plain integer arithmetic and Verilog's bitwise operators, with no gates. For every vector it computes the expected result and all four flags, and compares. At 4 bits there are 16 × 16 × 8 = 2,048 combinations, so the test is exhaustive. At 16 bits there are 216 × 216 × 8 = 235 = 34,359,738,368 combinations, too many to run here, so the testbench uses 7 hand-picked edge cases and 200,000 pseudo-random test vectors from a fixed seed. A random test can miss a fault; the edge cases target the places where faults hide (all ones + 1, the most negative number − 1). W1 R3 R4

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Three design questions turn this teaching ALU into a real one. First, speed: the ripple-carry adder's worst case grows with N, which F1-15 measures; real ALUs use faster adder structures. Second, the operation set: real instruction sets add shifts, comparisons ("set if less than"), and sometimes multiplication in separate units. Third, the flag conventions: which flags exist, what C means after a subtraction, and which instructions update flags at all are defined by each instruction set architecture, not by the adder. D2

Not verified — check before relying on this

Real instruction set architectures differ in their flags: some have no flags register, and some define the carry after subtraction as a borrow (the opposite of our C). This chapter does not state any real architecture's rule. Check the architecture manual named in HW202 (F1-23) before comparing our flags with a real processor.

Not verified — check before relying on this

The course book D1 has its own ALU with its own control bits and output flags, built as a project in its hardware simulator. That design and its HDL were not opened in this build; this chapter's ALU is our own design, tested here (R3, R4). Do not assume its opcodes, flags or interface match the book's. The course card's practical exam ("design and test a 4-bit ALU in the simulator") and project ("a tested 16-bit ALU") are set in this course's Verilog form; the owner may later choose the book's simulator instead (decision recorded in NOTES).

How the hardware actually does it

In a processor, the ALU sits in the datapath between the register file and the place where results are written back (F1-24 in HW202). The opcode is not chosen by a person: the control unit derives it from the instruction being executed. The flags go to a status register (on architectures that have one), where later conditional branch instructions read them. The adder, the logic gates and the result multiplexer are the same kinds of block you built here, made of CMOS gates (F1-10). Yosys maps the 4-bit ripple-carry adder onto 28 NAND and 20 NOT cells, four copies of the 7 + 5 cells it used for one full adder in F1-13. D2 R5 D6

Worked example

7 + 1 in 4 bits, carry by carry

a = 0111, b = 0001, cin = 0.

Bitaibicarry insicarry out
011c0 = 00c1 = 1
110c1 = 10c2 = 1
210c2 = 10c3 = 1
300c3 = 11cout = 0

Result 1000 = 8, cout = 0. Every carry is 1: 7 + 1 is a carry chain through three bits, which is why it is a good test vector. As unsigned numbers, 8 is correct (C = 0). As signed 4-bit numbers, 7 + 1 should be +8, which does not fit (the range is −8 to +7), and 1000 reads as −8. The carry into bit 3 is 1 and the carry out is 0; they differ, so V = 1. The ALU run prints y=8 Z=0 N=1 C=0 V=1. W1 R3

5 − 7 in 4 bits

  1. NOT 7 = NOT 0111 = 1000. Add 0101 + 1000 + 1 (the carry in).
  2. 0101 + 1000 = 1101; plus 1 = 1110. cout = 0.
  3. 1110 as a signed 4-bit number: −8 + 4 + 2 = −2. And 5 − 7 = −2. N = 1, Z = 0.
  4. C = 0: a borrow was needed (5 < 7 unsigned). V = 0: −2 is in range. The run prints y=e ... N=1 C=0 V=0 (e is hex for 1110). W1 R3

Code walk-through

Two new pieces of Verilog appear. A parameter (#(parameter N = 4)) makes a module's width adjustable, like a template argument in C++. A generate loop (generate for ...) places one full adder per bit at elaboration time; it is not a loop that runs in time. D5

Listing 1 — rca4.v (the 4-bit adder of Figure 1, written out by hand; it uses full_adder.v, the gate-level full adder of F1-13, in the same folder)

// A 4-bit ripple-carry adder: four full adders, each carry feeding the next.
module rca4(input wire [3:0] a, input wire [3:0] b, input wire cin,
            output wire [3:0] s, output wire cout);
    wire c1, c2, c3;                       // carries between the bits
    full_adder fa0(.a(a[0]), .b(b[0]), .cin(cin), .s(s[0]), .cout(c1));
    full_adder fa1(.a(a[1]), .b(b[1]), .cin(c1),  .s(s[1]), .cout(c2));
    full_adder fa2(.a(a[2]), .b(b[2]), .cin(c2),  .s(s[2]), .cout(c3));
    full_adder fa3(.a(a[3]), .b(b[3]), .cin(c3),  .s(s[3]), .cout(cout));
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
2–3module rca4(input wire [3:0] a, input wire [3:0] b, input wire cin, output wire [3:0] s, output wire cout);4-bit inputs and sum, a carry in and a carry out.cin lets the same block do the "+1" of subtraction.
4wire c1, c2, c3;The three carries between bits.Names match Figure 1.
5–8full_adder fa0(..., .cin(cin), ..., .cout(c1)); … fa3(..., .cin(c3), ..., .cout(cout));Four full adders; each one's carry out is the next one's carry in.The ripple. Line 8 is where the forensic lab's fault lives.

Listing 2 — tb_rca4.v

// Testbench: a short list of named test vectors, then all 512 input combinations.
module tb_rca4;
    reg [3:0] a, b;
    reg cin;
    wire [3:0] s;
    wire cout;
    integer i, expected;
    integer errors = 0;
    reg [8:0] vec [0:7];                   // {cin, a, b} for the named vectors

    rca4 dut(.a(a), .b(b), .cin(cin), .s(s), .cout(cout));

    initial begin
        vec[0] = {1'b0, 4'd1, 4'd1};   vec[1] = {1'b0, 4'd3, 4'd1};
        vec[2] = {1'b0, 4'd7, 4'd1};   vec[3] = {1'b0, 4'd4, 4'd4};
        vec[4] = {1'b0, 4'd4, 4'd0};   vec[5] = {1'b0, 4'd9, 4'd6};
        vec[6] = {1'b0, 4'd15, 4'd1};  vec[7] = {1'b1, 4'd5, 4'd2};
        $display(" a + b + cin | expected | got (cout s) | check");
        for (i = 0; i < 8; i = i + 1) begin
            {cin, a, b} = vec[i];
            #1;
            expected = a + b + cin;
            $display("%2d + %2d + %0d  |    %2d    |   %2d (%b %b) | %s", a, b, cin,
                     expected, {cout, s}, cout, s, ({cout, s} === expected[4:0]) ? "ok" : "WRONG");
        end
        for (i = 0; i < 512; i = i + 1) begin
            {cin, a, b} = i[8:0];
            #1;
            expected = a + b + cin;
            if ({cout, s} !== expected[4:0]) errors = errors + 1;
        end
        if (errors == 0) $display("ALL PASS (512 of 512 input combinations)");
        else $display("FAIL: %0d of 512 input combinations wrong", errors);
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule

Listing 3 — alu.v

// An N-bit ALU: a ripple-carry adder for ADD and SUB, gates for the logic operations,
// a multiplexer to choose the result, and four status flags.
//
// op  operation        op  operation
// 000 ADD  a + b       100 XOR  a ^ b
// 001 SUB  a - b       101 NOT  ~a
// 010 AND  a & b       110 PASS a
// 011 OR   a | b       111 PASS b

module adder_n #(parameter N = 4)
    (input wire [N-1:0] a, input wire [N-1:0] b, input wire cin,
     output wire [N-1:0] s, output wire cout, output wire c_msb);
    wire [N:0] c;                          // c[i] is the carry into bit i
    assign c[0] = cin;
    genvar i;
    generate
        for (i = 0; i < N; i = i + 1) begin : bitslice
            full_adder fa(.a(a[i]), .b(b[i]), .cin(c[i]), .s(s[i]), .cout(c[i+1]));
        end
    endgenerate
    assign cout = c[N];                    // carry out of the top bit
    assign c_msb = c[N-1];                 // carry into the top bit (for overflow)
endmodule

module alu #(parameter N = 4)
    (input wire [N-1:0] a, input wire [N-1:0] b, input wire [2:0] op,
     output reg [N-1:0] y,
     output wire zero, output wire negative, output wire carry, output wire overflow);
    wire sub = (op == 3'b001);
    wire [N-1:0] b_in = b ^ {N{sub}};      // SUB: invert every bit of b ...
    wire [N-1:0] sum;
    wire c_out, c_msb;
    adder_n #(N) add(.a(a), .b(b_in), .cin(sub), .s(sum), .cout(c_out), .c_msb(c_msb));
                                           // ... and add 1 through the carry-in
    always @* begin                        // the result multiplexer
        case (op)
            3'b000, 3'b001: y = sum;
            3'b010: y = a & b;
            3'b011: y = a | b;
            3'b100: y = a ^ b;
            3'b101: y = ~a;
            3'b110: y = a;
            default: y = b;
        endcase
    end

    wire arith = (op == 3'b000) | (op == 3'b001);
    assign zero     = ~|y;                 // NOR of all result bits
    assign negative = y[N-1];              // the top bit (two's complement sign)
    assign carry    = arith & c_out;
    assign overflow = arith & (c_out ^ c_msb);
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–8Comment block with the opcode table.Documents the eight operations.The specification lives next to the code.
10–12module adder_n #(parameter N = 4) (... output wire c_msb);An N-bit adder with an extra output: the carry into the top bit.c_msb is needed for the overflow flag.
13–14wire [N:0] c; assign c[0] = cin;N + 1 carry wires; c[0] is the carry in.c[i] is the carry into bit i.
15–20generate for (i = 0; i < N; i = i + 1) begin : bitslice … full_adder fa(...)Places N full adders, bit i joined to c[i] and c[i+1].Listing 1 for any width; bitslice names the copies.
21–22assign cout = c[N]; assign c_msb = c[N-1];The carry out of, and into, the top bit.C and V flags.
29–30wire sub = (op == 3'b001); wire [N-1:0] b_in = b ^ {N{sub}};sub is 1 only for SUB; {N{sub}} repeats it N times, so every bit of b is XORed with sub.Flips b for subtraction (two's complement step 1).
33adder_n #(N) add(..., .cin(sub), ...);The adder, with carry in = sub.Adds the "+1" (step 2).
35–45always @* begin case (op) ... endcase endChooses y from the opcode.A behavioural description of the result multiplexer: always @* re-evaluates whenever an input changes, so this is combinational, not a stored value. A synthesis tool turns it into multiplexer gates. D5
47wire arith = (op == 3'b000) | (op == 3'b001);1 for ADD and SUB.C and V only mean something for arithmetic.
48–51assign zero = ~|y; … assign overflow = arith & (c_out ^ c_msb);The four flags. ~|y is NOR of all bits of y.Z, N, C, V exactly as defined in Layer 2.

Listing 4 — tb_alu.v (reference-model testbench for any width)

// Testbench for the N-bit ALU: a reference model computes every expected result and flag.
// N = 4: all 2048 combinations. Larger N: edge cases plus 200000 pseudo-random vectors.
module tb_alu;
    parameter N = 4;
    reg [N-1:0] a, b;
    reg [2:0] op;
    wire [N-1:0] y;
    wire zero, negative, carry, overflow;
    integer i, seed, errors, checks;

    alu #(N) dut(.a(a), .b(b), .op(op), .y(y), .zero(zero), .negative(negative),
                 .carry(carry), .overflow(overflow));

    // Reference model: ordinary integer arithmetic, no gates.
    task check;
        reg [N:0] full;
        reg [N-1:0] ry;
        reg rc, rv;
        integer sa, sb, sr;
        begin
            sa = $signed(a);
            sb = $signed(b);
            rc = 0; rv = 0; sr = 0;
            case (op)
                3'b000: begin full = {1'b0, a} + {1'b0, b};      sr = sa + sb; end
                3'b001: begin full = {1'b0, a} + {1'b0, ~b} + 1; sr = sa - sb; end
                3'b010: full = {1'b0, a & b};
                3'b011: full = {1'b0, a | b};
                3'b100: full = {1'b0, a ^ b};
                3'b101: full = {1'b0, ~a};
                3'b110: full = {1'b0, a};
                default: full = {1'b0, b};
            endcase
            ry = full[N-1:0];
            if (op == 3'b000 || op == 3'b001) begin
                rc = full[N];
                rv = (sr > (2 ** (N - 1)) - 1) || (sr < -(2 ** (N - 1)));
            end
            checks = checks + 1;
            if (y !== ry || zero !== (ry == 0) || negative !== ry[N-1] ||
                carry !== rc || overflow !== rv) begin
                errors = errors + 1;
                if (errors <= 5)
                    $display("MISMATCH op=%b a=%h b=%h: got y=%h ZNCV=%b%b%b%b, expected y=%h ZNCV=%b%b%b%b",
                             op, a, b, y, zero, negative, carry, overflow,
                             ry, (ry == 0), ry[N-1], rc, rv);
            end
        end
    endtask

    task show;                              // print one named example
        begin
            #1;
            check;
            $display("op=%b a=%h b=%h -> y=%h  Z=%b N=%b C=%b V=%b", op, a, b, y,
                     zero, negative, carry, overflow);
        end
    endtask

    initial begin
        errors = 0; checks = 0; seed = 102;
        $display("ALU width N = %0d", N);
        op = 3'b000; a = 7;  b = 1;  show;     // 7 + 1
        op = 3'b000; a = {N{1'b1}}; b = 1; show; // all ones + 1
        op = 3'b001; a = 5;  b = 7;  show;     // 5 - 7
        op = 3'b001; a = 7;  b = 7;  show;     // 7 - 7
        op = 3'b001; a = {1'b1, {(N-1){1'b0}}}; b = 1; show; // most negative - 1
        op = 3'b010; a = 12; b = 10; show;     // 1100 AND 1010
        op = 3'b100; a = 12; b = 10; show;     // 1100 XOR 1010
        if (N <= 8) begin
            for (i = 0; i < (8 << (2 * N)); i = i + 1) begin
                {op, a, b} = i;
                #1;
                check;
            end
        end else begin
            for (i = 0; i < 200000; i = i + 1) begin
                a = $random(seed);
                b = $random(seed);
                op = $random(seed);
                #1;
                check;
            end
        end
        if (errors == 0) $display("ALL PASS (%0d vectors)", checks);
        else $display("FAIL: %0d of %0d vectors wrong", errors, checks);
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
4parameter N = 4;The width, 4 unless changed on the command line.The 16-bit run uses -P tb_alu.N=16.
15–49task check;The reference model and the comparison, as a reusable task.Called for every vector.
21–22sa = $signed(a);Reads the bits of a as a signed number.Needed for the overflow check.
25–26full = {1'b0, a} + {1'b0, b}; / ... + {1'b0, ~b} + 1Adds at N + 1 bits, so the carry out is kept in full[N].The width lesson of F1-13, applied.
37rv = (sr > (2 ** (N - 1)) - 1) || (sr < -(2 ** (N - 1)));Overflow: the true signed result is outside the N-bit range.Defines V from the range, independently of the circuit's c_out XOR c_msb.
40–46if (y !== ry || zero !== (ry == 0) || ...)Compares the result and all four flags; prints up to five mismatches.A failing run shows concrete examples.
63–69op = 3'b000; a = 7; b = 1; show; …Seven named examples, printed.The edge cases of the Worked example.
70–75for (i = 0; i < (8 << (2 * N)); ...) {op, a, b} = i;For N ≤ 8: every combination (8 × 22N).Exhaustive at 4 bits: 2,048 vectors.
77–83a = $random(seed); …For larger N: 200,000 pseudo-random vectors from seed 102.Repeatable; the same vectors every run. D5

Where the analogy breaks

  • Cooks wait politely for the runner; full adders do not wait. Every full adder computes immediately from whatever its carry input currently is, and corrects itself when a new carry arrives. Until the last carry settles, the outputs can be wrong for a moment (F1-15). D2
  • Ines uses one tool at a time; the ALU uses all of them every time. All operations are computed in parallel and the multiplexer discards all but one. That costs power but no extra time for the choice. D2
  • The lamp "negative" in a kitchen means the count is below zero; the N flag is only the top bit. For unsigned numbers, N = 1 means "large", not "negative". The flags report bits; the program decides what they mean. W1

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
7 + 1 = 0; 4 + 0 = 12; 1 + 1 correct (real output in the forensic lab).A wrong wire on the carry into bit 3.Compute got − expected for each failing vector: it is always ±8 (bit 3).Connect bit 3's carry in to c3.
Subtraction off by one (5 − 7 = −3).b inverted but carry in left at 0.Check a − 0: it gives a − 1.cin = sub.
V wrong for SUB only.Overflow computed from the original b's sign instead of the carries.Compare V for 0x8 − 1 (must be 1) and 0x7 − 0xF.V = c_out XOR c_msb.
Testbench passes but carry flag never checked.Reference computed at N bits, so the carry is lost.Print full[N].Compute at N + 1 bits (Listing 4, lines 25–26).
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-13 built one full adder; F1-12 built multiplexers; F0-24 taught two's complement. What carries over: full adders, the mux as "choose", exhaustive tests against arithmetic. What changes: circuits are now parameterised by width and built by generate loops; the same bits are read two ways (unsigned and signed), so you need flags; and exhaustive testing stops being possible at 16 bits, so you test with edge cases and pseudo-random vectors against a reference model. What comes next: F1-15 adds time: how long the carry takes to ripple, and what happens if you read the result too early. D2

Check yourself

  1. How many full adders does a 16-bit ripple-carry adder need, and how many carry wires run between them?
  2. Write the steps of 6 − 3 in 4 bits using a + NOT b + 1. Give the result and C.
  3. In 4 bits, which additions overflow as signed numbers? (a) 3 + 4 (b) 5 + 4 (c) −8 + 7 (d) −1 + −1
  4. Why does the testbench compute full with N + 1 bits?
  5. Explain in your own words why the ripple-carry adder is correct for all inputs if each full adder is.
  6. Apply it to a new case: add an operation 'SLT' (set to 1 if a < b as signed numbers, else 0) to the ALU. Which existing signals can you use?
  7. Predict the four flags for ADD of 0xF + 0x1 in 4 bits, then check against the run.
  8. Why is 7 + 1 a better test vector than 1 + 1 for a 4-bit adder?

Lab

Goal

Build, from your own full adder, a 4-bit ALU that passes the exhaustive reference-model test, then show that the same testbench catches a fault you plant.

Hardware and software needed

No hardware. Icarus Verilog 12.0 (R1, R3, R4); Yosys 0.33 (R5). Untested on hardware.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-14 and read rca4.out, alu4.out and alu16.out: all end with ALL PASS.
  2. Copy alu.v to my_alu.v and replace the always @* multiplexer with gates: one 8-to-1 mux per bit, built from your mux2 of F1-12.
  3. Run the 4-bit test: iverilog -g2012 -Wall -o my tb_alu.v full_adder.v my_alu.v && vvp -n my.
  4. Plant a fault: change the carry in of the adder from sub to 1'b0. Predict which operations and flags fail, then run.
  5. Remove the fault and run the 16-bit test with -P tb_alu.N=16.

Expected observations

The given ALU passes 2,055 vectors at 4 bits and 200,007 at 16 bits (R3, R4). With the planted fault, the testbench should print MISMATCH lines for SUB only, with results one less than expected; record your own output.

Verification

Your gate-level ALU prints ALL PASS at 4 and 16 bits, and the planted fault is detected. This is the practical exam task of HW102 at 4 bits.

Troubleshooting

  • "MISMATCH" only in flags, result correct. Check which flag differs in the printed line: Z N C V are printed in that order.
  • The 16-bit run takes a long time. 200,000 vectors take several seconds in a simulator; reduce the count while debugging, then restore it.
  • "Unknown module type: full_adder". Add full_adder.v to the command line.

Extension

Add the SLT operation of question 6 by giving it an opcode of your choice (replace "pass b"), extend the reference model, and test exhaustively.

Forensic lab

Scenario: the adder that is wrong for 7 + 1

A student's calculator circuit shows 7 + 1 = 0. "Adding 1 works," they say, "I tried 1 + 1." Their teacher asks for the test-vector report and the adder file. From the test vectors alone, locate the faulty carry connection; then confirm in the file.

Evidence pack

The test-vector report from the unchanged testbench (Listing 2), run on the student's adder:

 4 +  4 + 0  |     8    |    0 (0 0000) | WRONG

15 +  1 + 0  |    16    |    8 (0 1000) | WRONG

The student's file (read it only after answering questions 1–3):

Listing 5 — rca4_bad.v (evidence)

// Forensic evidence: the 4-bit adder from the "7 + 1" bug report, exactly as handed in.
module rca4(input wire [3:0] a, input wire [3:0] b, input wire cin,
            output wire [3:0] s, output wire cout);
    wire c1, c2, c3;                       // carries between the bits
    full_adder fa0(.a(a[0]), .b(b[0]), .cin(cin), .s(s[0]), .cout(c1));
    full_adder fa1(.a(a[1]), .b(b[1]), .cin(c1),  .s(s[1]), .cout(c2));
    full_adder fa2(.a(a[2]), .b(b[2]), .cin(c2),  .s(s[2]), .cout(c3));
    full_adder fa3(.a(a[3]), .b(b[3]), .cin(s[2]), .s(s[3]), .cout(cout));
endmodule

Questions

  1. For each WRONG line, compute got − expected. Which single bit is wrong in every case?
  2. State at least two hypotheses that would make that bit wrong (for example, a faulty full adder in bit 3; a wrong carry into bit 3). Which vectors rule out the faulty full adder?
  3. For each failing vector, work out the true carry c3 and the sum bit s2. What do you notice?
  4. Find the faulty line in Listing 5 and write the fix.
  5. Explain why 1 + 1 passes and why 384 of 512 combinations fail.

Method hints

Work from the outputs inward: the wrong bit tells you which full adder's output is wrong; then ask which of its three inputs (a3, b3, carry in) could be wrong. Compare the carry in it should have received with nearby wires.

Mini-project

This is the start of the course project: a tested 16-bit ALU. Using your gate-level ALU from the lab, write a short design document: the opcode table, the flag definitions, Figure 2 redrawn for your design, the test strategy (edge cases you chose and why, the random seed, the vector count) and the real output of your 16-bit run.

Rubric (5 points): opcode table and flag definitions consistent with the code (1); diagram matches the module structure (1); at least six edge cases with a reason for each (1); 16-bit run ALL PASS with the command shown (1); one paragraph on what a random test cannot prove (1).

Summary

  • A ripple-carry adder chains N full adders; the carry passes from bit to bit.
  • It is correct for every input because the full-adder equations sum to 2N·cout + s = a + b + cin.
  • Subtraction: a − b = a + NOT b + 1; one control signal both flips b and sets the carry in.
  • Flags: Z (all zero), N (top bit), C (carry out, unsigned), V (carry into top XOR carry out, signed overflow).
  • An ALU computes all operations and selects one with a multiplexer driven by the opcode.
  • Test against a reference model: exhaustively when small, with edge cases and seeded random vectors when large.
  • A fault shows its location in the test vectors: the same wrong bit in every failure points to one full adder's inputs.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. 16 full adders; 15 carry wires between them (plus cin into bit 0 and cout out of bit 15).
  2. NOT 0011 = 1100. 0110 + 1100 = 1 0010; plus the carry in 1: 0110 + 1100 + 1 = 1 0011. Result 0011 = 3, C = 1 (no borrow, 6 ≥ 3).
  3. (b) and nothing else. 5 + 4 = 9 > 7. (a) 7 fits. (c) −1 fits. (d) −2 fits; the carry out is 1 but that is not overflow (C = 1, V = 0).
  4. To keep the carry out in full[N]; at N bits it would be lost and the C flag could not be checked (the width trap of F1-13).
  5. Any answer that says: each full adder satisfies 2·carry out + sum = its three inputs; weighting bit i by 2i and adding all bits, each inside carry is counted once as an output and once as an input, so they cancel, leaving the whole-number equation.
  6. Compute a − b with the adder (sub = 1) and use its flags: a < b as signed numbers exactly when N XOR V = 1 for that subtraction (the sign bit is right when there is no overflow and flipped when there is). Output 0…01 when N XOR V = 1, else 0. Prove it in your extension with the exhaustive test.
  7. 0xF + 0x1 = 1 0000: y = 0, Z = 1, N = 0, C = 1, V = 0 (−1 + 1 = 0 in signed terms, in range). The run prints y=0 Z=1 N=0 C=1 V=0.
  8. 7 + 1 makes the carry ripple through bits 0, 1 and 2 into bit 3, so it exercises every carry connection; 1 + 1 only uses the carry from bit 0 to bit 1.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: 7 of the 8 named vectors are wrong; only 1 + 1 is right. got − expected is −8 for 7 + 1, 4 + 4, 15 + 1 and 5 + 2 + 1, and +8 for 3 + 1, 4 + 0 and 9 + 6 (in 9 + 6 and 15 + 1 the change in bit 3 also changes the carry out). Every failure is in bit 3 (worth 8), with cout following from it. 384 of 512 combinations fail (R2). Hypotheses: (1) the bit-3 full adder is faulty; (2) its carry in is wrong; (3) its a3/b3 inputs are miswired. For 4 + 0 the true carry into bit 3 is 0 and a3 = b3 = 0, yet s3 = 1: bit 3 is adding a 1 that is not there, so its carry in is wrong (2), not its data inputs (3); and the same bit-3 adder gives correct results whenever c3 and s2 agree, which argues against (1). Pattern: in every failing vector the true c3 differs from s2 (the sum bit of bit 2), and the result is exactly what bit 3 gives if its carry in is s2: for 7 + 1, s2 = 0 while c3 = 1; for 4 + 0, s2 = 1 while c3 = 0. In 1 + 1, s2 = c3 = 0, so it passes. Over all inputs, s2 ≠ c3 in 384 of 512 cases. Root cause: Listing 5, line 8: .cin(s[2]) instead of .cin(c3): the carry into bit 3 is wired to the neighbouring sum wire. Fix: .cin(c3); rerun: ALL PASS (R1). Prevention: include long-carry vectors (7 + 1, 15 + 1) in every adder test, and run the exhaustive test, not only a few hand-picked sums. How the evidence was made: Listing 1 with the carry in of bit 3 changed from c3 to s[2], run with Listing 2 in this build. Wrong answers: "adding 1 is broken" (1 + 1 is right, and failures also occur with b = 0, as in 4 + 0); "the full adder in bit 3 is broken" (with the correct carry in, the same full adder passes in R1).
