Story hook

Analogy

In the kitchen of F1-14, the head chef has started ringing a bell. At every ring, a waiter collects whatever is on the counting row and carries it to the dining room. The bell rings at a steady pace, no matter what the cooks are doing.

Most of the time this works. But Ravi notices something odd on busy nights: some orders arrive at the tables with the wrong count. They are always the orders where the runner's token had to travel all the way down the row. The waiter took the plate before the last cook had finished.

Nobody made a mistake in the recipe. The recipe needs time, and the bell did not wait for it. Every real circuit has the same problem. In this chapter you measure how long gates take, find the slowest path, and see what happens when a result is read too early.

What you will be able to do

  • Define propagation delay and explain why a circuit's output is only correct after it has settled.
  • Find the critical path of a circuit by counting gate delays, and predict the worst-case delay of an N-bit ripple-carry adder.
  • Simulate gates with delays and read a timing diagram, including wrong intermediate values.
  • Explain a glitch (hazard) in a multiplexer and remove it with a covering term.
  • Diagnose results that are wrong only for long carry chains as a timing fault, not a logic fault (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Propagation delay
Simple words: the time from an input changing to the output reaching its new, final value. Analogy: the time between an order arriving and the plate being finished on the counter. Precise: the maximum time from a change at a circuit's input until its output is stable at the new value; for a path through several gates it is the sum of the gate delays along the path. D2
Contamination delay
Simple words: the shortest time before an output can start to change after an input changes. Analogy: how soon the first cook can touch the plate after the order arrives. Precise: the minimum time from an input change until any output begins to change; together with the propagation delay it bounds when an output may be changing. D2
Critical path
Simple words: the slowest route from any input to any output. Analogy: the order that has to visit every station in the row. Precise: the path through a combinational circuit with the largest sum of gate delays; it sets the circuit's propagation delay. D2
Settle
Simple words: to stop changing and show the final answer. Analogy: the moment the last cook puts down the spoon. Precise: a combinational output has settled when, after an input change, no further change will happen until the inputs change again; before that it may show wrong intermediate values. W1 R2
Glitch (hazard)
Simple words: a short wrong pulse on an output that should not have changed. Analogy: a plate that briefly disappears from the counter while two cooks swap places, then comes back. Precise: an unwanted transient on a combinational output caused by different path delays; a static-1 hazard is a momentary 0 on an output whose correct value stays 1. D2 R3
Timing diagram
Simple words: a picture of signals changing over time, one row per signal. Analogy: the kitchen's order log with a time for every step. Precise: a plot of signal values against time; high and low levels for single bits, and labelled segments for multi-bit values (buses). D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 is a timing diagram of the 4-bit ripple-carry adder from F1-14, rebuilt with a delay on every gate. a = 1111 is fixed and b changes from 0 to 1, so the carry must travel through every bit. Read the carries going up like stairs.

Figure 2 shows a different timing effect. Both data inputs of a multiplexer are 1, so its output should stay 1 when the select changes. The plain four-NAND multiplexer of F1-12 dips to 0 for one unit.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Until now, gates answered instantly. Real gates do not. When an input changes, the transistors inside need a little time to switch and to charge the wires they drive. Only then does the output change. That little time is the gate's delay.

A signal that passes through many gates collects many delays. In a ripple-carry adder, the carry may have to pass through every bit, one after the other. So a wide adder can take much longer than a narrow one for the same kind of sum.

While the carry is still travelling, the sum bits show wrong numbers. In Figure 1 the adder says 12, then 8, and only then the right answer. If another circuit reads the sum too early, it gets a wrong number, even though every gate is wired correctly.

The cure is patience, or speed. Either wait long enough for the slowest case, or build a faster adder. Engineers do both: they find the slowest path and design around it.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Delay of a gate and of a path

A gate's propagation delay is the time from an input change until its output is stable at the new value. In CMOS the delay comes from charging and discharging the capacitance of the wires and gate inputs that the output drives, through the resistance of the transistors that are on (F1-09, Layer 3). The delay of a path is the sum of the delays of the gates along it. The contamination delay is the opposite bound: the shortest time before an output can begin to change. D2

In this chapter we use a model: every NAND gate takes exactly 1 time unit. Verilog writes this as nand #1. The simulator then moves every output change 1 unit later than the input change that caused it. Real gates have different delays for different gate types, loads and directions of change; the model keeps only the idea. D5 R1

The critical path of a ripple-carry adder

The critical path is the slowest path from any input to any output. In the nine-NAND full adder of F1-13, a change on cin reaches cout through two NANDs (g5, then g9), and reaches s through three (g5, then g6 or g7, then g8). For an N-bit ripple-carry adder whose carry must travel the whole way, the carry into bit N−1 arrives after 2(N−1) units, and that bit's sum needs 3 more: 2(N−1) + 3 = 2N + 1 units. The carry out arrives at 2N. So the worst case grows in proportion to N. W1

The simulation agrees. With a = all ones and b changing from 0 to 1, the last output change comes after 9, 17 and 33 units for 4, 8 and 16 bits: 2N + 1 each time. With a = 0, the same change of b settles after 4 units at every width, because no carry has to travel. Delay depends on the data, but a design must allow for the worst case. R1 W1

Wrong values before the output settles

Figure 1 shows the 4-bit case unit by unit: the carries rise at 102, 104, 106 and 108, and the sum passes through 1100 and 1000 before it settles at 0000 (with cout = 1) at 109. A combinational output is only meaningful after it has settled. Between the input change and the end of the propagation delay, it may show any value. R2 D2

Glitches

A glitch is a short wrong pulse on an output that should not change at all. Figure 2's multiplexer computes y = NAND(NAND(d0, NOT s), NAND(d1, s)). When s falls, the term with s turns off after one delay, but the term with NOT s turns on only after two (NOT s itself needs a delay). For one unit neither term holds y at 1. Adding the term NAND(d0, d1) as a third input of the output NAND "covers" the gap: when d0 = d1 = 1 it holds y at 1 whatever s does. In Boolean algebra the extra term changes nothing (it is the consensus term d0 AND d1), but in time it removes the hazard. D2 R3 W1

Reading results at a deadline

In a computer, a combinational block's output is read by the next stage at fixed moments, set by a clock (F1-18 in HW201). If the time between readings is shorter than the critical path, results with long carry chains are read before they settle. The forensic lab shows exactly this: an 8-bit adder read 8 units after its inputs change gives correct sums for short carry chains and wrong ones for long chains. Read at 20 units, longer than its 17-unit worst case, every sum is right. R4 R5

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Because the ripple-carry delay grows in proportion to N, fast adders compute the carries differently. A carry-lookahead adder computes, for each bit, whether it generates a carry (a AND b) or propagates one (a XOR b), the two terms named in F1-13, and combines them for groups of bits in parallel, so the carry into a far bit does not wait for every bit before it. Prefix adders push the same idea further; their delay grows much more slowly with N, at the cost of more gates. D2

Timing analysis in industry is not done by simulating all inputs. Static timing analysis tools add up the documented delays of every cell along every path, for worst-case and best-case conditions, and report paths that are too slow (setup violations) or too fast (hold violations, where contamination delay matters). HW201 introduces setup and hold with flip-flops. D2

Not verified — check before relying on this

This chapter contains no real gate delay. "1 time unit per NAND" is our model's choice, and the numbers 9, 17 and 33 are counts of those units from our simulation. Real delays depend on the manufacturing process, supply voltage, temperature and load, and are given in the datasheet of a named part or in a cell library's timing data. If you build an adder from real logic chips, take the delay from that part's datasheet (AH-21), or measure it and label it as your measurement.

How the hardware actually does it

On a chip, every gate output drives the capacitance of the wires and the gates it is connected to; switching means moving charge through transistors that are on. More load, longer wires and weaker transistors mean longer delays. This is why designers care about how many gates hang on one output and how far signals travel, and why the clock speed of a processor is limited by the slowest path between its storage elements. A processor splits long paths into stages with storage in between, which is pipelining (F1-26 in HW202). D2

Worked example

Predict the settle time of a 4-bit adder, then check

Model: 1 unit per NAND; the nine-NAND full adder of F1-13. Input change: b0 from 0 to 1 at time 100, with a = 1111.

  1. Bit 0: t1 = NAND(a0, b0) falls at 101; cout0 = NAND(t1, t4) rises at 102. So c1 rises at 102.
  2. Each further bit has the carry in on g5 and the carry out on g9: 2 units per bit. c2 at 104, c3 at 106, c4 (cout) at 108.
  3. Bit 3's sum: c3 arrives at 106; g5, then g7, then g8: s3 settles at 109.
  4. Formula: 2N + 1 = 2 × 4 + 1 = 9 units after the change, so at 109.

The run of Listing 2 prints the carries rising at 102, 104, 106, 108 and the last sum change at 109 (Figure 1), and Listing 1's run prints "4-bit 9". W1 R1 R2

Which sums go wrong if you read early?

An 8-bit adder is read 8 units after the inputs change. The carry reaches bit k after about 2k units, and a sum bit needs a little more. So a sum is safe only if its carry chain is short. 15 + 1: the carry passes bits 0 to 3 into bit 4, about 8 units, plus the sum delay, too late; the reading shows 8 instead of 16. 2 + 3: no long chain; correct. Predict the others before reading the forensic evidence. W1 R4

Code walk-through

New Verilog: a delay on a gate, nand #1 g1(...), and $monitor, which prints a line every time one of its values changes. $time is the current simulation time. D5

Listing 1 — delay_adder.v

// The 9-NAND full adder of F1-13, now with a delay: every NAND takes 1 time unit
// to change its output after an input changes ("#1"). The unit is our model's own,
// not nanoseconds of any real chip.
module full_adder_d(input wire a, input wire b, input wire cin,
                    output wire s, output wire cout);
    wire t1, t2, t3, x1, t4, t5, t6;
    nand #1 g1(t1, a, b);
    nand #1 g2(t2, a, t1);
    nand #1 g3(t3, b, t1);
    nand #1 g4(x1, t2, t3);
    nand #1 g5(t4, x1, cin);
    nand #1 g6(t5, x1, t4);
    nand #1 g7(t6, cin, t4);
    nand #1 g8(s, t5, t6);
    nand #1 g9(cout, t1, t4);
endmodule

// An N-bit ripple-carry adder made of those full adders.
module adder_d #(parameter N = 4)
    (input wire [N-1:0] a, input wire [N-1:0] b, input wire cin,
     output wire [N-1:0] s, output wire cout);
    wire [N:0] c;
    assign c[0] = cin;
    genvar i;
    generate
        for (i = 0; i < N; i = i + 1) begin : bitslice
            full_adder_d fa(.a(a[i]), .b(b[i]), .cin(c[i]), .s(s[i]), .cout(c[i+1]));
        end
    endgenerate
    assign cout = c[N];
endmodule

1–3Comment: the time unit is our model's own.States the model honestly in the file.Numbers from this run are model units.
4–5module full_adder_d(...)The nine-NAND full adder of F1-13, renamed.Same logic, now with delays.
7–15nand #1 g1(t1, a, b); …Each NAND changes its output 1 unit after its inputs change.#1 is the delay; without it every gate would react in zero time.
19–31module adder_d #(parameter N = 4) … generate …An N-bit ripple-carry adder from those full adders.The same structure as adder_n in F1-14.

Listing 2 — tb_ripple_delay.v (settle times for 4, 8 and 16 bits)

// Testbench: how long until 4-, 8- and 16-bit ripple-carry adders settle?
// Case "long carry": a = all ones, b changes from 0 to 1 (the carry ripples through every bit).
// Case "no carry":   a = 0,        b changes from 0 to 1 (only bit 0 changes).
module tb_ripple_delay;
    reg [15:0] a, b;
    wire [3:0]  s4;
    wire [7:0]  s8;
    wire [15:0] s16;
    wire c4, c8, c16;
    integer last4, last8, last16, t0;

    adder_d #(4)  add4 (.a(a[3:0]), .b(b[3:0]), .cin(1'b0), .s(s4),  .cout(c4));
    adder_d #(8)  add8 (.a(a[7:0]), .b(b[7:0]), .cin(1'b0), .s(s8),  .cout(c8));
    adder_d #(16) add16(.a(a),      .b(b),      .cin(1'b0), .s(s16), .cout(c16));

    always @(s4 or c4)   last4  = $time;   // remember when each output last changed
    always @(s8 or c8)   last8  = $time;
    always @(s16 or c16) last16 = $time;

    task measure(input [15:0] new_a, input [255:0] label);
        begin
            a = new_a; b = 0;
            #200;                           // let everything settle first
            t0 = $time;
            b = 1;                          // the change we time
            #200;
            $display("%0s: settled after  4-bit %0d   8-bit %0d   16-bit %0d time units",
                     label, last4 - t0, last8 - t0, last16 - t0);
            $display("    results: 4-bit %b_%h  8-bit %b_%h  16-bit %b_%h",
                     c4, s4, c8, s8, c16, s16);
        end
    endtask

    initial begin
        measure(16'hFFFF, "long carry (all ones + 1)");
        measure(16'h0000, "no carry   (0 + 1)       ");
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule

20–33task measure(...)Sets a, waits 200 units to settle, records t0, changes b to 1, waits, prints last change − t0.The settle time of each adder for that input change.
35–38measure(16'hFFFF, ...); measure(16'h0000, ...);The long-carry case and the no-carry case.Worst case versus best case.

Listing 3 — tb_carry_trace.v (the data of Figure 1)

// Testbench: watch the carries of a 4-bit ripple-carry adder change, one by one.
// a = 1111 stays fixed; b changes from 0000 to 0001 at time 100.
module tb_carry_trace;
    reg [3:0] a, b;
    wire [3:0] s;
    wire cout;

    adder_d #(4) dut(.a(a), .b(b), .cin(1'b0), .s(s), .cout(cout));

    initial begin
        a = 4'b1111; b = 4'b0000;
        #100;
        $display("time | carries c4 c3 c2 c1 | sum s3..s0");
        $monitor("%4t |          %b  %b  %b  %b |   %b", $time,
                 dut.c[4], dut.c[3], dut.c[2], dut.c[1], s);
        b = 4'b0001;                       // the change, at time 100
        #50;
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule

Listing 4 — glitch_mux.v and Listing 5 — tb_glitch.v

// The four-NAND 2-to-1 multiplexer of F1-12, with 1 time unit of delay per NAND,
// and a "covered" version with one extra NAND that holds the output steady.
module mux2_d(input wire d0, input wire d1, input wire s, output wire y);
    wire ns, t0, t1;
    nand #1 g1(ns, s, s);
    nand #1 g2(t0, d0, ns);
    nand #1 g3(t1, d1, s);
    nand #1 g4(y, t0, t1);
endmodule

module mux2_covered(input wire d0, input wire d1, input wire s, output wire y);
    wire ns, t0, t1, t2;
    nand #1 g1(ns, s, s);
    nand #1 g2(t0, d0, ns);
    nand #1 g3(t1, d1, s);
    nand #1 g5(t2, d0, d1);    // extra term: 0 whenever d0 and d1 are both 1
    nand #1 g4(y, t0, t1, t2); // a three-input NAND
endmodule

// Testbench: both data inputs are 1, so the right answer is 1 whatever s is.
// Watch both multiplexers while s changes from 1 to 0.
module tb_glitch;
    reg d0, d1, s;
    wire y_plain, y_covered;

    mux2_d       m1(.d0(d0), .d1(d1), .s(s), .y(y_plain));
    mux2_covered m2(.d0(d0), .d1(d1), .s(s), .y(y_covered));

    initial begin
        d0 = 1; d1 = 1; s = 1;
        #10;
        $display("time | s | plain: ns t0 t1 y | covered y");
        $monitor("%4t | %b |         %b  %b  %b %b |     %b", $time, s,
                 m1.ns, m1.t0, m1.t1, y_plain, y_covered);
        s = 0;                                 // the change, at time 10
        #10;
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule

L5: 11–12d0 = 1; d1 = 1; s = 1; #10;Both data inputs 1; settle.The correct output is 1 for either s.

Where the analogy breaks

  • A waiter can see that a plate is not finished; a reading circuit cannot. Nothing in a combinational output says "not settled yet"; a wrong intermediate value looks exactly like a right one. That is why timing must be guaranteed by design, not checked at run time. D2
  • Cooks work at different speeds from day to day; our model's gates all take exactly 1 unit. Real delays vary between gate types, chips, temperatures and supply voltages; the model hides all of that (Layer 3). D2
  • A plate that disappears for a moment is a nuisance; a glitch can be read. If a later circuit happens to read during the glitch, it gets the wrong value, so glitches matter wherever an output is used without waiting for it to settle.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Some sums wrong, only for long carry chains; exhaustive logic test passes (real output in the forensic lab).Result read before it settles.Compare failing vectors' carry-chain lengths; rerun with a longer wait.Wait at least the critical-path delay, or use a faster adder.
All delays print as 0.Gates written without #1, so the model has no delay.Look for # after the gate type.Add the delay to every gate.
Timing numbers look like nanoseconds.A `timescale line, or a habit, labels model units as real time.Check the file and the claim.Write "time units" and say where real delays come from (Layer 3 box).
A testbench reads outputs with #0 or no wait and gets old values.The outputs have not settled yet.Print with $monitor to see when they change.Wait longer than the worst case before checking.
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-14 built and tested an adder and an ALU as pure logic, where outputs appear instantly. What carries over: the circuits, their truth tables and their tests are unchanged. What changes: correctness now has a second condition: the right value at the right time. Outputs pass through wrong values before they settle, the worst case depends on the longest path, and the data decide how long a particular input takes. What comes next: HW201 starts with F1-16 (latches and flip-flops): circuits with memory, read at clock edges, where the timing you measured here sets how fast the clock may tick. D2

Check yourself

  1. Define propagation delay in one sentence.
  2. In the 1-unit-per-NAND model, what is the worst-case settle time of a 32-bit ripple-carry adder made of nine-NAND full adders?
  3. Why does adding 0 + 1 settle faster than 15 + 1 in a 4-bit ripple adder?
  4. Which statement is correct? (a) A glitch means the logic is wrong. (b) A combinational output can show wrong values before it settles. (c) The critical path is the path with the fewest gates. (d) Model time units are nanoseconds.
  5. Explain in your own words why the covering term removes the glitch in Figure 2 but does not change the truth table.
  6. Apply it to a new case: a 16-bit adder is read 25 units after its inputs change. Using the 2N + 1 model, will it always be correct? Name one sum that would be read wrong.
  7. Predict: in Listing 2, what would the long-carry settle time be for a 12-bit adder? Then add a 12-bit instance and run it.

Lab

Goal

Measure the settle time of ripple-carry adders of several widths in simulation, compare with the 2N + 1 prediction, and find the shortest safe reading time for an 8-bit adder.

Hardware and software needed

No hardware. Icarus Verilog 12.0 (R1–R5). All times are model units; untested on hardware.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-15 and read ripple_delay.out.
  2. Add 2-bit and 12-bit instances to Listing 2; predict their long-carry settle times with 2N + 1; run.
  3. Make a table: N, predicted, measured. Plot it on paper.
  4. Run the reading test with different waits: iverilog -g2012 -Wall -o s -P tb_sample.WAIT=12 tb_sample.v delay_adder.v && vvp -n s, then 16, 17, 18.
  5. Find the smallest WAIT that passes, and explain it with the critical path.

Expected observations

Long-carry settle times of 9, 17 and 33 units for 4, 8 and 16 bits, and 4 units for the no-carry case (R1). Reading after 8 units fails 3 of 8 vectors (R4); after 20 units all pass (R5). Record your own WAIT results; the eight vectors in Listing 6 do not include every worst case, so explain whether your smallest passing WAIT is safe for every input.

Verification

Your measured times equal 2N + 1 for every width you tried, and your chosen WAIT is at least the worst-case settle time of the 8-bit adder (not only of the eight test vectors).

Troubleshooting

  • Settle time printed as a huge or negative number. The output never changed after t0, so last still holds an old time; check that the input change really changes the sum.
  • Different results from the same command. Should not happen: the simulation is deterministic. Check that you edited and compiled the file you think you did.
  • The glitch does not appear. The gate delays were removed or made unequal; the glitch needs the NOT path to be slower than the direct path.

Extension

Build a 4-bit carry-lookahead carry unit from generate and propagate signals (D2, title only) with 1-unit gates, and compare its worst-case carry-out time with the ripple adder's 8 units.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Elif's team connected the 8-bit adder of Listing 1 to a display that reads the sum at a fixed moment after the inputs change. Some customers see wrong totals. The adder passed the exhaustive logic test in F1-14's style, so the team suspects the display. Find the real cause from the evidence.

Evidence pack

The reading testbench (Listing 6, the "display") and its real output with the reading moment used by the team.

Listing 6 — tb_sample.v (evidence)

// Testbench: an 8-bit ripple-carry adder whose result is read WAIT time units
// after the inputs change, the way a later circuit with a fixed deadline would read it.
module tb_sample;
    parameter WAIT = 8;
    reg [7:0] a, b;
    wire [7:0] s;
    wire cout;
    integer i, expected, wrong;
    reg [15:0] vec [0:7];

    adder_d #(8) dut(.a(a), .b(b), .cin(1'b0), .s(s), .cout(cout));

    initial begin
        vec[0] = {8'd2,   8'd3};   vec[1] = {8'd85,  8'd170};
        vec[2] = {8'd100, 8'd27};  vec[3] = {8'd3,   8'd1};
        vec[4] = {8'd15,  8'd1};   vec[5] = {8'd127, 8'd1};
        vec[6] = {8'd255, 8'd1};   vec[7] = {8'd64,  8'd64};
        a = 0; b = 0; wrong = 0;
        #100;
        $display("result read %0d time units after the inputs change", WAIT);
        $display("  a  +   b  | expected | read | check");
        for (i = 0; i < 8; i = i + 1) begin
            {a, b} = vec[i];
            #(WAIT);
            expected = a + b;
            $display("%3d + %3d  |   %3d    | %3d  | %s", a, b, expected, {cout, s},
                     ({cout, s} === expected[8:0]) ? "ok" : "WRONG");
            if ({cout, s} !== expected[8:0]) wrong = wrong + 1;
            #100;                              // back to rest before the next vector
            a = 0; b = 0;
            #100;
        end
        if (wrong == 0) $display("ALL PASS (8 vectors)");
        else $display("FAIL: %0d of 8 vectors read wrong", wrong);
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule

100 +  27  |   127    | 127  |    ok
  3 +   1  |     4    |   4  |    ok
 15 +   1  |    16    |   8  | WRONG
127 +   1  |   128    | 120  | WRONG
255 +   1  |   256    | 248  | WRONG
 64 +  64  |   128    | 128  |    ok
FAIL: 3 of 8 vectors read wrong

Real output, copied from university/labs/F1-15/sample_early.out; run record sample_early.log: Icarus Verilog version 12.0 (stable) (); vvp from the same package; 2026-10-09T18:49:00Z; exit code: 0.

Questions

  1. Which sums are wrong, and by how much? Write each wrong reading and the right sum in binary.
  2. What do the wrong sums have in common that the right ones do not? (Think about carries.)
  3. State two hypotheses: a logic fault in the adder, and a timing fault in the reading. Which evidence rules out the logic fault?
  4. Using the 2N + 1 model, what is the earliest safe reading time for this 8-bit adder? Is 8 enough?
  5. Propose two different fixes and say what each costs.

Method hints

For each vector, write a and b in binary and mark the columns where a carry is created and passed on; count the length of the longest chain. Compare with how far a carry can travel in 8 units (2 units per bit).

Mini-project

Write a one-page "timing report" for your 16-bit ALU from F1-14: rebuild its adder with 1-unit NAND gates, measure the worst-case settle time of ADD in simulation, state the critical path in words, and recommend a minimum reading time with a safety margin you justify.

Rubric (5 points): correct critical path described (1); simulation measurement with the command and output shown (1); comparison with a prediction (1); reasoned margin, labelled as model units (1); one sentence on what would change on real hardware and where its numbers would come from (1).

Summary

  • Gates take time: the propagation delay is the time until an output is stable after an input change.
  • A path's delay is the sum of its gate delays; the critical path is the slowest one.
  • A ripple-carry adder's worst case grows in proportion to its width: 2N + 1 units in our model (measured 9, 17, 33 for 4, 8, 16 bits).
  • Before it settles, an output may show wrong values; in Figure 1 the adder shows 12 and 8 before 16.
  • Glitches come from unequal path delays; a covering (consensus) term removes the multiplexer's glitch without changing its truth table.
  • A result read before it settles is wrong only for slow inputs: that is the signature of a timing fault.
  • Model time units are not real delays; real numbers come from a named part's datasheet or a measurement.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. The time from an input change until the output is stable at its new value (the maximum over the circuit's paths).
  2. 2 × 32 + 1 = 65 units.
  3. 0 + 1 changes only bit 0 and creates no carry chain; 15 + 1 creates a carry that must pass through bits 0–3, 2 units per bit, before the top sum bit and cout are final.
  4. (b). (a) A glitch is a timing effect; the logic can be correct (Figure 2's mux passes its truth-table test). (c) It is the slowest path, usually the one with the most gate delays. (d) They are our model's units.
  5. Any answer that says: the extra term d0 AND d1 is 1 whenever both data inputs are 1, which is exactly the case where the select change opens a gap; it holds y at 1 through the gap. In every steady state it is already implied by the other two terms (consensus), so the truth table is unchanged.
  6. Worst case 2 × 16 + 1 = 33 units > 25, so no. Any sum whose carry ripples through most bits, for example 0xFFFF + 1, would be read before it settles.
  7. 2 × 12 + 1 = 25 units (check with your own run).

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: 15 + 1 reads 8 (should be 16), 127 + 1 reads 120 (should be 128), 255 + 1 reads 248 (should be 256); the other five are right (R4). In each wrong case the reading is 8 too small: when it is read, bits 0–2 already show their final 0s, but the carry has not yet passed bit 3, so bit 3 and the bits above it still show their old values (for 15 + 1, 00001000 instead of 00010000). Common factor: the three wrong sums have carry chains of 4, 7 and 8 bits (from bit 0 upward); the right ones have no chain longer than 2 bits (3 + 1 has a 2-bit chain; 85 + 170 and 64 + 64 have none that ripples from bit 0 upward through several bits, and 100 + 27 has no carry at all). Hypotheses: (1) a logic fault in the adder; (2) the result is read before it settles. The same adder and vectors read after 20 units are all correct (R5), and its logic is the tested nine-NAND design; that rules out (1). Root cause: the reading moment (WAIT = 8, Listing 6 line 4) is shorter than the adder's worst-case settle time, 2 × 8 + 1 = 17 units (R1 measured 17). Fixes: read later (WAIT ≥ 17, with a margin; costs speed), or use a faster adder such as carry-lookahead (costs gates). Prevention: derive the reading time from the critical path, and test with the worst-case vectors (all ones + 1), not only typical sums. How the evidence was made: Listing 6 with its default WAIT of 8 units, on the delay-model adder of Listing 1, in this build. Wrong answers: "the display is broken" (with WAIT = 20 the same display reads correctly); "the adder has a wiring fault like F1-14's" (the wrong vectors are exactly the long carry chains, and the logic passes every vector when read late).

Story hook

Analogy

It is the busiest hour in the restaurant. Waiters call orders through the serving hatch, the window between the dining room and the kitchen. Chef Ama has a problem: an order is spoken once, and then the waiter is gone. If nobody writes it down, the kitchen forgets it.

So the kitchen keeps a ticket rail. Each order is clipped to the rail and stays there after the waiter leaves. But a new trouble appears. Waiters keep changing tickets while the cooks are reading them, and a cook starts a dish from a half-changed slip.

Ama's fix is a small bell. Tickets on the rail may be swapped only at the moment the bell rings. Between rings, the rail stands still and every cook reads the same thing. This chapter builds both ideas in hardware: the open hatch (a latch) and the ticket rail swapped at the bell (a flip-flop).

What you will be able to do

  • Explain why the circuits of HW102 cannot remember, and how feedback gives a circuit memory.
  • Trace an SR latch made of two NOR gates through set, reset, hold and the forbidden input, and check your trace against a simulation.
  • Tell a D latch from a D flip-flop by reading a timing diagram.
  • Build an edge-triggered flip-flop from two latches and verify it in a logic simulator.
  • Diagnose a description that accidentally creates a latch (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Combinational circuit
Simple words: a circuit whose outputs depend only on its inputs right now. Analogy: a cook who answers "what goes with fish?" the same way every time, with no notebook. Precise: a circuit without memory: after the propagation delay, its outputs are a fixed function of its current inputs (the gates, adders and multiplexers of HW102). D1
Sequential circuit
Simple words: a circuit whose outputs also depend on what happened before. Analogy: a kitchen with a ticket rail: what it cooks next depends on the tickets already clipped there. Precise: a circuit with memory: its outputs depend on its current inputs and on its stored state, which records information about past inputs. D1
Feedback (in a circuit)
Simple words: an output wired back to an input of the same circuit. Analogy: two cooks who each keep repeating what the other one just said. Precise: a connection that forms a loop from a gate's output back to its own input, directly or through other gates; feedback is what lets a circuit hold a value. (The robotics and control courses use "feedback" for a different idea: measuring a result and correcting towards a target.) D1
Latch
Simple words: a one-bit memory that can change whenever its control input says "open". Analogy: the serving hatch: while it is open, the newest plate is what you see; when it closes, the last plate stays in view. Precise: a level-sensitive storage element: while its enable (or clock) input is at the active level the output follows the data input ("transparent"); otherwise the output holds. D1
SR latch
Simple words: a latch with a Set button and a Reset button. Analogy: a "table taken" sign with two levers: one flips it to taken, the other to free. Precise: a latch made of two cross-coupled NOR (or NAND) gates, with inputs S (set, makes Q = 1) and R (reset, makes Q = 0); S = R = 1 is not allowed. D1 D3
D latch
Simple words: a latch with one data input D and one enable input. Analogy: the serving hatch with one plate slot. Precise: a latch whose output Q follows D while the enable input is 1 and holds its last value while the enable input is 0; it avoids the forbidden input of the SR latch. D1
Flip-flop
Simple words: a one-bit memory that changes only at one instant: the clock's edge. Analogy: a ticket clip on the rail that may be swapped only when the bell rings. Precise: an edge-triggered storage element; a D flip-flop copies D to Q at the active edge of its clock (here the rising edge) and holds Q at all other times. D1 D2
Clock edge
Simple words: the moment a clock signal changes, from 0 to 1 (rising) or from 1 to 0 (falling). Analogy: the instant the bell rings, not the time between rings. Precise: a transition of the clock signal; a rising-edge-triggered flip-flop samples its input at the 0-to-1 transition. Clocks themselves are the subject of F1-18. D1
Timing diagram
Simple words: a picture of signals as lines that go up and down over time. Analogy: a strip showing, minute by minute, which tickets were on the rail. Precise: a plot of signal values (horizontal axis: time) used to show the order of events; in this course they are drawn from real simulation runs. D1
Testbench (see "Logic simulator, testbench", HW102)
Simple words: a pretend world written in code that pokes a circuit and watches what it does. Analogy: a practice service with fake orders before the restaurant opens. Precise: a simulation-only module that drives a design's inputs, observes its outputs and (ideally) checks them; it is not itself hardware. D4 D5
Unknown value (x)
Simple words: the simulator's way of saying "this could be 0 or 1; I cannot tell". Analogy: a ticket clip before anyone has clipped a ticket. Precise: in Verilog simulation a 1-bit signal has four values: 0, 1, x (unknown) and z (not driven); storage starts as x until something sets it. D4 R1
Metastability
Simple words: a storage element caught exactly halfway between 0 and 1 for a while. Analogy: a coin that lands on its edge and wobbles before it falls. Precise: a state in which a bistable element's output lingers between the two valid levels for an unpredictable time, caused by inputs that change too close to the sampling instant or by S and R released together. D1
Inferred latch
Simple words: a latch you did not ask for, created because your description forgot a case. Analogy: a cook who, when an order is missing, keeps serving the previous one. Precise: a latch that a synthesis tool creates from a hardware description in which some output is not assigned on every path through the logic, so the description implies "keep the old value". D1 R3

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the smallest memory there is: two NOR gates, each feeding its output into the other's input. The loop is the memory. The table beside it lists what each input pair does.

Figure 2 is the most important picture of the chapter. The same data signal d drives a D latch and a D flip-flop. The latch copies d for as long as the clock is high, so short wiggles of d pass straight through. The flip-flop looks at d only at the rising edges (dashed lines) and ignores everything in between.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Every circuit you built in HW102 had a short memory: none at all. Change the inputs of an adder, and a moment later the old answer is gone. That is fine for adding, but a computer must also remember: which instruction comes next, what number is in a register, which letter you just typed.

The trick is to make a circuit talk to itself. Take two gates and feed each one's output into the other one's input. Now they hold each other in place, like two friends leaning back to back. Push one of them once, and they settle into the new position and stay there. That loop is a one-bit memory.

A latch is such a loop with a door in front of it. While the door is open, whatever you put in goes straight through, like plates through the open serving hatch. When the door closes, the last plate stays.

A flip-flop is stricter. It takes a new value only at one instant: the moment the bell rings, which in a computer is the clock edge. Everything that happens between rings is ignored. Computers use flip-flops almost everywhere because then every part of the machine changes at the same moments, in step.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Memory needs feedback

A combinational circuit computes its outputs from its present inputs only; its gates form no loops D1. A sequential circuit has feedback: some output returns to an input. Its outputs then depend on the present inputs and on a stored state D1. Every memory element in this course, from the latch to the DRAM cell of F1-20, is a way of holding state.

The SR latch

In Figure 1, gate g1 computes Q = NOT(R OR Qn) and gate g2 computes Qn = NOT(S OR Q) D1. Remember that a NOR gate outputs 1 only when both its inputs are 0 (F1-10).

  • Set (S = 1, R = 0): g2 has a 1 input, so Qn = 0. Then g1 sees R = 0 and Qn = 0, so Q = 1.
  • Hold (S = 0, R = 0): each gate's output is decided by the other gate's output. Q = 1 keeps Qn = 0, and Qn = 0 keeps Q = 1. The latch remembers.
  • Reset (S = 0, R = 1): the mirror image: Q = 0, Qn = 1.
  • Forbidden (S = 1, R = 1): both gates have a 1 input, so Q = Qn = 0. The outputs are no longer opposites. Worse, if S and R return to 0 at the same instant, both gates see two 0 inputs and both switch to 1, then both see a 1 and switch to 0, and so on.

Listing 2's simulation shows all four cases, with a delay of one time unit per gate. You can watch the set ripple through the gates (Qn falls at t = 6, Q rises at t = 7) and the forbidden release make the latch oscillate from t = 30 to the end of the run R1. In a real circuit the two gates are never exactly equal, so the loop falls to one side after a while; which side, and when, cannot be predicted. That is metastability D1. The simulator, with its perfectly equal delays, oscillates forever instead: a model, not the real behaviour.

The D latch

The forbidden input is a trap, so designers add two gates in front of the SR latch: S becomes "D AND enable", and R becomes "NOT D AND enable" D1. Now S and R can never both be 1. While enable = 1, Q follows D: the latch is transparent. While enable = 0, both S and R are 0 and the latch holds. That is the D latch. Listing 3 describes it in Verilog by its behaviour rather than its gates.

The D flip-flop

A transparent latch has a weakness. Suppose its output feeds logic that feeds back into its own input, as in the counter of F1-17. While the latch is open, a new value can race around the loop several times. The flip-flop fixes this: it captures D only at the rising clock edge and holds Q for the whole rest of the period D1 D2.

One classic construction uses two D latches in a row (Listing 5). The first, the master, is open while the clock is 0. The second, the slave, is open while the clock is 1. The two are never open at the same time. When the clock rises, the master closes, holding the value D had just before the edge, and the slave opens and passes that value to Q. Until the next rising edge nothing new can get through D1. The run of Listing 6 checks that this two-latch flip-flop and the one-line behavioural flip-flop of Listing 4 agree at every edge R2.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

An edge-triggered flip-flop is only edge-triggered if its input is stable around the edge. Its data sheet gives a setup time (D stable before the edge), a hold time (D stable after it) and a clock-to-Q delay (how long Q takes to change) D1. F1-18 uses these three to compute how fast a clock may run. If D changes inside the setup-and-hold window, the flip-flop can become metastable, exactly like the SR latch released from S = R = 1 D1.

Why do almost all designs use flip-flops and not latches? Timing analysis of a flip-flop design is simple: each path goes from one edge to the next. With latches, a signal may pass through several open latches in one phase, so the analysis must follow it across phases. Latch-based designs exist, but they are a specialist technique D1.

The simulator matters too. Verilog is simulated as a sequence of events. Listing 4 uses the non-blocking assignment q <= d: all flip-flops that share an edge read their inputs first and update afterwards, as real flip-flops do D4. F1-21 shows what goes wrong with the other kind of assignment. Simulators also start every stored value as x (unknown). The x at the start of Figure 2 is not a bug: it is the honest answer before any clock edge or reset has stored something D4 R2.

Not verified — check before relying on this

Real setup times, hold times, clock-to-Q delays and the probability that a flip-flop stays metastable longer than a given time are properties of a specific part or chip process. This build opened no data sheet, so the chapter gives no numbers. Before using any value, read it from the data sheet of the named part (or the timing library of the chip process) and record it in the dossier (AH-21).

How the hardware actually does it

In silicon, the NOR gates of Figure 1 are made of transistors used as switches, as in F1-09 and F1-10. Many chips build their storage elements from a pair of cross-coupled inverters (the same loop with no S and R inputs) plus switches that open and close with the clock; F1-20 meets the same loop again inside an SRAM cell D1. A processor contains a very large number of flip-flops: its registers (F1-17), its program counter and the boundaries between pipeline stages in HW202 D1. All of them listen to the same clock, which is why the clock network gets its own chapter (F1-18).

Worked example

Tracing the SR latch by hand

Each NOR gate takes 1 time unit. At t = 5, S becomes 1 while Q and Qn are still unknown.

  1. g2 sees S = 1. A NOR with any 1 input gives 0, whatever the other input is. One unit later, at t = 6, Qn = 0.
  2. g1 now sees R = 0 and Qn = 0, so its output becomes 1 one unit later: t = 7, Q = 1.
  3. At t = 10, S returns to 0. g2 sees S = 0 and Q = 1: output stays 0. g1 sees 0 and 0: output stays 1. Nothing changes. The latch holds 1.
  4. At t = 25, S = R = 1: both outputs fall to 0 (t = 26).
  5. At t = 30, both inputs return to 0. Each gate sees 0, 0 and switches to 1 at t = 31. Then each sees a 1 and switches to 0 at t = 32. The pattern repeats every 2 time units.

Compare with the recorded output of Listing 2 below: rows t = 6, 7, 26, 31, 32 are exactly these steps R1.

Predicting a latch and a flip-flop

Use Figure 2. The clock has period 20 and rises at 10, 30, 50 and so on. Between t = 10 and t = 20 the clock is high. d falls at t = 15 and rises at t = 18.

  • Latch: open while clk = 1, so q_latch falls at 15 and rises at 18. It shows the wiggle.
  • Flip-flop: at the edge t = 10, d = 1 (it rose at 5), so q_ff = 1 until the next edge. At t = 30, d = 0 (it fell at 27), so q_ff = 0. The wiggle at 15–18 never reaches q_ff.

The run prints "t=10 rising edge: d was 1" and "t=30 rising edge: d was 0", matching this prediction R2.

Code walk-through

This course describes circuits in Verilog and simulates them with Icarus Verilog, a free logic simulator; F1-21 teaches you to read Verilog properly. For now, read each listing with its table. Every listing was compiled and run in this build by the lab script run.sh in university/labs/F1-16/, which also turns the simulation's value-change file into a text timing diagram with the university's small Python tool wave.py (in the same folder) D5.

Listing 1 — sr_latch.v

// An SR latch made of two cross-coupled NOR gates.
// Each gate has a delay of 1 time unit, so the simulator shows the order of events.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module sr_latch (
    input  wire s,      // set: make q = 1
    input  wire r,      // reset: make q = 0
    output wire q,
    output wire qn      // normally the opposite of q
);
    nor #1 g1 (q, r, qn);   // q  = NOT (r OR qn)
    nor #1 g2 (qn, s, q);   // qn = NOT (s OR q)
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–2// An SR latch made of ...Comments.Say what the module is and why delays are used.
3`timescale 1ns/1nsSets the simulation time unit.Every #1 means one unit; the unit has no hardware meaning here.
4–9module sr_latch ( input wire s, ... output wire qn );Declares a hardware block with two inputs and two outputs.A module is a part with pins, not a function that runs.
10nor #1 g1 (q, r, qn);A NOR gate named g1: output q, inputs r and qn, delay 1.The first output listed is the gate's output.
11nor #1 g2 (qn, s, q);The second NOR: output qn, inputs s and q.q and qn each appear as an input of the other gate: the feedback loop.
12endmoduleEnds the description.—

Listing 2 — sr_latch_tb.v (testbench)

// Testbench: set, hold, reset, hold, then the forbidden input S = R = 1 and its release.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module sr_latch_tb;
    reg  s = 0;
    reg  r = 0;
    wire q;
    wire qn;

    sr_latch dut (.s(s), .r(r), .q(q), .qn(qn));

    initial begin
        $display("time  S R | Q Qn   (x = unknown)");
        $monitor("%4t  %b %b | %b %b", $time, s, r, q, qn);
        #5 s = 1;           // set
        #5 s = 0;           // hold: the latch remembers 1
        #5 r = 1;           // reset
        #5 r = 0;           // hold: the latch remembers 0
        #5 s = 1; r = 1;    // forbidden: both inputs active
        #5 s = 0; r = 0;    // release both at the same instant
        #10 $finish(0);
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
3module sr_latch_tb;A module with no pins: the testbench.It exists only in simulation.
4–7reg s = 0; reg r = 0; wire q; wire qn;regs are values the testbench sets; wires carry the latch's outputs.The testbench drives inputs and watches outputs.
9sr_latch dut (.s(s), .r(r), .q(q), .qn(qn));Places one latch ("device under test") and connects its pins by name.Like wiring a part onto a board.
12–13$display(...); $monitor(...);Prints a heading, then a line every time any listed signal changes.Gives the event-by-event table of the output.
14–19#5 s = 1; ... #5 s = 0; r = 0;Waits 5 units, changes an input, and so on: set, hold, reset, hold, forbidden, release.The four rows of Figure 1's table, in order.
20#10 $finish(0);Ends the simulation 10 units later.Without it the oscillation would run forever.

Listing 3 — d_latch.v

// A D latch: while en = 1 the output follows d ("transparent"); while en = 0 it holds.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module d_latch (
    input  wire en,
    input  wire d,
    output reg  q
);
    always @(en or d)
        if (en)
            q = d;
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
3–7module d_latch ( input wire en, input wire d, output reg q );Pins: enable, data, output. output reg means q is set inside a behaviour block.In Verilog, reg does not by itself mean "a register in hardware".
8always @(en or d)Re-evaluates whenever en or d changes.A level-sensitive behaviour.
9–10if (en) q = d;When en = 1, q takes d. When en = 0, nothing is assigned, so q keeps its value."Keep the old value" is exactly what makes this a latch. The forensic lab shows the same pattern created by accident.

Listing 4 — d_flipflop.v

// A D flip-flop: q takes the value of d only at the rising edge of clk.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module d_flipflop (
    input  wire clk,
    input  wire d,
    output reg  q
);
    always @(posedge clk)
        q <= d;
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
8always @(posedge clk)Runs only at a rising edge (posedge) of clk.This single word makes the behaviour edge-triggered.
9q <= d;Non-blocking assignment: q takes the value d had at the edge.The standard way to describe a flip-flop D4.

Listing 5 — ms_flipflop.v

// A master-slave D flip-flop built from two D latches.
// The master is open while clk = 0, the slave while clk = 1,
// so q can only change just after clk rises.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module ms_flipflop (
    input  wire clk,
    input  wire d,
    output wire q
);
    wire m;   // the master latch's output
    d_latch master (.en(~clk), .d(d), .q(m));
    d_latch slave  (.en(clk),  .d(m), .q(q));
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
10wire m;The wire between the two latches.m holds the master's value.
11d_latch master (.en(~clk), .d(d), .q(m));The master latch, open while clk = 0 (~ is NOT).It follows d during the low half of the period.
12d_latch slave (.en(clk), .d(m), .q(q));The slave latch, open while clk = 1, copying m to q.When clk rises the master closes and the slave opens: q changes only then.

Listing 6 — latch_vs_ff_tb.v (testbench for Listings 3–5)

// Testbench: the same d drives a D latch (enabled by clk), an edge-triggered
// D flip-flop, and a master-slave flip-flop made of two latches.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module latch_vs_ff_tb;
    reg  clk = 0;
    reg  d = 0;
    wire q_latch;
    wire q_ff;
    wire q_ms;
    integer errors = 0;

    d_latch     u1 (.en(clk), .d(d), .q(q_latch));
    d_flipflop  u2 (.clk(clk), .d(d), .q(q_ff));
    ms_flipflop u3 (.clk(clk), .d(d), .q(q_ms));

    always #10 clk = ~clk;          // one clock period = 20 time units

    // d changes at awkward moments: some while clk is high, some while it is low
    initial begin
        $dumpfile("latch_vs_ff.vcd");
        $dumpvars(0, latch_vs_ff_tb);
        #5  d = 1;      // t = 5:  clk is low
        #10 d = 0;      // t = 15: clk is high, the latch passes this change through
        #3  d = 1;      // t = 18
        #9  d = 0;      // t = 27
        #8  d = 1;      // t = 35
        #20 d = 0;      // t = 55: clk is high
        #3  d = 1;      // t = 58
        #4  d = 0;      // t = 62: clk is low
        #13 d = 1;      // t = 75
        #20 d = 0;      // t = 95
        #22 d = 1;      // t = 117
        #3  d = 0;      // t = 120
        #40 $finish(0);
    end

    // after every rising edge, both flip-flops must hold the value d had at that edge
    reg d_at_edge;
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        d_at_edge = d;
        #2;
        $display("t=%0t rising edge: d was %b -> q_ff = %b, q_ms = %b, q_latch = %b",
                 $time - 2, d_at_edge, q_ff, q_ms, q_latch);
        if (q_ff !== d_at_edge || q_ms !== d_at_edge)
            errors = errors + 1;
    end

    initial begin
        #158;
        if (errors == 0)
            $display("RESULT: PASS (both flip-flops captured d at every rising edge)");
        else
            $display("RESULT: FAIL (%0d mismatches)", errors);
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
12–14d_latch u1 (...); d_flipflop u2 (...); ms_flipflop u3 (...);Three parts, all fed by the same clk and d.A fair side-by-side comparison.
16always #10 clk = ~clk;Flips clk every 10 units: period 20, rising at 10, 30, 50, ...The testbench's clock generator.
20–21$dumpfile(...); $dumpvars(0, latch_vs_ff_tb);Records every signal change into a value-change (VCD) file.Figure 2 and the text diagram below are drawn from this file.
22–34#5 d = 1; ... #40 $finish(0);Changes d at the times written in the comments.Some changes fall while clk is high, to show the latch's transparency.
38–46always @(posedge clk) begin d_at_edge = d; #2; ... endAt each rising edge, remembers d, waits 2 units, prints all outputs and counts mismatches.The self-check: both flip-flops must equal d at the edge.
48–54#158; if (errors == 0) $display("RESULT: PASS ...")Prints the verdict near the end.The lab script requires "RESULT: PASS" here.

Build and run command (the one actually used): iverilog -g2005 -Wall -o latch_vs_ff.vvp latch_vs_ff_tb.v d_latch.v d_flipflop.v ms_flipflop.v && vvp -n latch_vs_ff.vvp

Where the analogy breaks

  • The bell is not a person deciding. Chef Ama can choose when to ring. A clock edge comes from a clock signal at regular times (F1-18), and every flip-flop connected to it reacts, whether or not anything useful changed.
  • A ticket can be read halfway through being clipped; a flip-flop's output can be neither 0 nor 1. A half-clipped ticket still has readable words on it. A metastable flip-flop has an output voltage between the two valid levels, and logic reading it may see 0 in one place and 1 in another D1.
  • The hatch has no "forbidden" position. Nothing bad happens if two waiters push plates at once. The SR latch does have one: S = R = 1 breaks the rule that Q and Qn are opposites, as the run shows R1.
  • A rail holds many tickets; a flip-flop holds one bit. To hold a number you need one flip-flop per bit, side by side: a register (F1-17).

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
Outputs show x at the start of the run (Listing 2, t = 0; Figure 2 until t = 10).Nothing has stored a value yet; storage starts unknown.Check whether the x disappears after the first edge or set.Expected at power-up. If it must not be unknown, add a reset (F1-17).
Q and Qn are both 0, then flicker every time unit (Listing 2, t = 26–40).S = R = 1, then both released together.Look for the row where S and R are both 1.Never drive S = R = 1; use a D latch or flip-flop instead.
A combinational block "remembers" an old value (forensic lab).An output is not assigned in every case, so a latch is inferred.Synthesis log says "Latch inferred"; simulation shows a held value.Assign a default at the top of the block, or cover every case.
Short glitches on the data line appear on the output.A latch was used where a flip-flop was needed.Timing diagram: does the output change while the clock is high?Use always @(posedge clk) and <=.
Transition box

Where you came from: HW102 built combinational circuits, ending with propagation delay in F1-15: outputs follow inputs after a delay, and forget them. What carries over: gates, truth tables and delays; a latch is built from the same NOR and NAND gates, and its behaviour is traced with the same delay reasoning D1. What changes: outputs now depend on the past; the order of events matters; storage can start unknown; some input combinations are forbidden; and a description can create memory by accident. What comes next: F1-17 puts flip-flops side by side to make registers, counters and shift registers, all moving together on one clock.

Check yourself

  1. Which of these is a sequential circuit? (a) a 4-bit adder (b) a multiplexer (c) an SR latch (d) a decoder.
  2. In Figure 1, S = 0 and R = 1. What are Q and Qn, and why?
  3. Explain in your own words why a loop of two gates can remember a bit but a single gate cannot.
  4. A D latch has enable = 1 from t = 0 to t = 10. D changes from 0 to 1 at t = 4 and back to 0 at t = 7. What is Q at t = 8? What would an edge-triggered flip-flop clocked at t = 0 and t = 10 show at t = 8?
  5. Why is S = R = 1 forbidden for the NOR SR latch? Give two reasons, one from the table and one from the run.
  6. Apply it to a new case: in Listing 5, someone connects both latches to clk (no ~). What does the circuit become, and why?
  7. Predict, then run: in Listing 6, add #2 d = 1; #2 d = 0; changes around t = 92–96 (clk is high then). Which outputs change? Run the lab to check.
  8. True or false: in Verilog, an output reg always becomes a flip-flop in hardware. Explain.

Lab

Goal

Simulate an SR latch, a D latch and two kinds of D flip-flop, and prove from the timing diagram which one is edge-triggered.

Hardware and software needed

No hardware. A computer with Icarus Verilog and Python 3. The runs in this chapter used the versions printed in their run records: "Icarus Verilog version 12.0 (stable)" and "Python 3.13.16" (as printed by the tools) R1 R2. Yosys is used in the forensic lab ("Yosys 0.33") R3.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use: this lab is simulation only.

Steps

  1. From the repository root, run the whole lab: university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-16. It writes a .out and a .log file for every step.
  2. Open sr_latch.out. Before reading it, write your own predicted table for t = 0 to 40 using the Worked example. Then compare row by row.
  3. Run one step by hand, inside university/labs/F1-16: iverilog -g2005 -Wall -o latch_vs_ff.vvp latch_vs_ff_tb.v d_latch.v d_flipflop.v ms_flipflop.v, then vvp -n latch_vs_ff.vvp. You should see the eight "rising edge" lines and RESULT: PASS.
  4. Draw the diagram: python3 -I wave.py latch_vs_ff.vcd 2/1 160 clk d q_latch q_ff q_ms. Mark with a pencil every place where q_latch changes but q_ff does not.
  5. Edit latch_vs_ff_tb.v as in question 7 and repeat steps 3–4.

Expected observations

The SR latch output matches Figure 1's table and oscillates after the simultaneous release R1. q_ff and q_ms are identical and change only at rising edges; q_latch also changes inside high clock phases R2.

Verification

The testbench prints RESULT: PASS (both flip-flops captured d at every rising edge), and run_lab.sh exits with status 0. Your marked diagram shows at least two places where only the latch changed.

Troubleshooting

  • Unknown module type: d_latch → you compiled the testbench without the design files → list every .v file on the iverilog command line.
  • The simulation never ends → a $finish line was deleted, and the clock generator runs forever → put it back, or stop with Ctrl+C.
  • wave.py prints a KeyError → the signal name is not in the VCD file → use the names declared in the testbench (clk, d, q_latch, q_ff, q_ms).

Extension

Write sr_nand.v: an SR latch from two NAND gates. Its inputs are active-low (0 means "do it"). Find its forbidden input with a testbench, and explain the difference from the NOR version.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Sam wrote a three-input selector for a classroom display. The specification says: y = a when sel = 0, b when sel = 1, c when sel = 2, and 0 when sel = 3. The display sometimes shows a 1 when sel = 3. Sam says "the simulator must be broken, my code has no flip-flops". Find out what is really going on.

Evidence pack

Sam's description (Listing 7), the run of the self-checking testbench mux_tb.v (it tries all 32 input patterns in counting order and prints the sel = 3 rows and every wrong row), and the relevant line of the synthesis tool's log.

Listing 7 — mux_bug.v (evidence)

// Forensic evidence: a 3-input selector written by Sam.
// Specification: y = a when sel = 0, b when sel = 1, c when sel = 2, and 0 when sel = 3.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module mux_bug (
    input  wire [1:0] sel,
    input  wire       a,
    input  wire       b,
    input  wire       c,
    output reg        y
);
    always @(*) begin
        if (sel == 2'd0)
            y = a;
        else if (sel == 2'd1)
            y = b;
        else if (sel == 2'd2)
            y = c;
    end
endmodule

11always @(*) beginA block re-evaluated whenever any input it reads changes.Meant to describe combinational logic.
12–17if (sel == 2'd0) y = a; else if ... else if (sel == 2'd2) y = c;Assigns y for sel = 0, 1 and 2.Read the specification again and compare.

Questions

  1. Which rows are wrong? What do they have in common, apart from sel = 3?
  2. The testbench tries patterns in counting order, so each sel = 3 row comes right after a sel = 2 row with the same a, b and c. Use that fact: where does the wrong 1 come from?
  3. State two hypotheses (for example "the simulator is broken" and one about the description) and say what evidence would separate them.
  4. What does the synthesis tool's message say about the hardware Sam's text describes?
  5. Give the fix, and a rule or test that would have caught the mistake before the display was built.

Method hints

Compare the code with the specification line by line: for every value of sel, ask "what is y assigned?". Then read the evidence for something that behaves like memory. Grade yourself with the forensic rubric of guide section 11.2.

Mini-project

Build a toggle flip-flop: a circuit with inputs clk and t whose output q flips (0 to 1, or 1 to 0) at a rising edge when t = 1 and holds when t = 0. Use Listing 4's flip-flop plus one gate. Write a self-checking testbench that prints RESULT: PASS, draw its timing diagram with wave.py, and explain in three sentences why a latch in place of the flip-flop would not work (hint: think about the loop while the latch is open).

Rubric (10 points): correct design (3); testbench checks at least 8 edges and both t values (3); timing diagram included and explained (2); latch explanation correct (2).

Summary

  • Combinational circuits have no memory; sequential circuits store state, and storing needs feedback.
  • Two cross-coupled NOR gates form an SR latch: set, reset, hold; S = R = 1 is forbidden.
  • A D latch is transparent while enabled and holds while not; it removes the forbidden input.
  • A D flip-flop copies D only at the clock edge; two latches open on opposite clock levels make one.
  • Real flip-flops need D stable around the edge (setup and hold) or they can become metastable.
  • Simulators start storage as x; a timing diagram from a real run is the best evidence of behaviour.
  • An output left unassigned in some case of a combinational block creates an inferred latch.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. (c). The adder, multiplexer and decoder are combinational: their outputs depend only on present inputs. The SR latch has feedback and stores a bit.
  2. Reset: g1 has input R = 1, so Q = 0; g2 then sees S = 0 and Q = 0, so Qn = 1. Q = 0, Qn = 1.
  3. A good answer: a single gate's output is decided by its present inputs only. In a loop, each gate's output is one of the other gate's inputs, so the pair can stay in either of two self-consistent states with no outside input holding them; that remembered choice is the bit.
  4. Latch: transparent the whole time, so Q followed D: at t = 8, Q = 0 (D fell at 7). Flip-flop: it sampled D at t = 0 (D = 0) and will sample again at t = 10, so at t = 8 it still shows 0, but for a different reason; with D = 1 at t = 0 it would show 1 the whole time, ignoring the change at 7.
  5. From the table: it gives Q = Qn = 0, so the outputs are no longer opposites. From the run: releasing both inputs together makes the simulated latch oscillate (t = 30–40), and a real one can become metastable.
  6. Both latches are open at the same time (while clk = 1) and closed at the same time, so d passes straight through both while clk is high: the circuit becomes a single transparent latch, not an edge-triggered flip-flop.
  7. q_latch shows the extra pulse because clk is high; q_ff and q_ms do not change, because no rising edge occurs during the pulse. (If your edit moved d at a rising edge, the flip-flops would change there.)
  8. False. reg only means "assigned inside a behaviour block". Listing 3 is a latch, Listing 4 a flip-flop, and Listing 7 shows a reg that becomes an inferred latch; with every case assigned (mux_fixed.v) the same kind of reg is pure combinational logic.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: exactly 4 of 32 patterns fail, all with sel = 3 and c = 1; y is 1 instead of 0 R3. Hypotheses: (1) the simulator is broken; (2) the description stores a value. In counting order each failing row follows a sel = 2 row with the same c, where y = c = 1 was correct; at sel = 3 nothing assigns y, so y keeps 1. The fixed description, run with the same simulator, passes all 32 patterns R4, which rules out (1). Root cause: Listing 7, lines 12–17: no assignment to y when sel = 3. In an always @(*) block that means "keep the old value", which is the behaviour of a latch. The synthesis tool confirms it: "Latch inferred for signal `\mux_bug.\y'" R3. Fix: assign a default first (y = 1'b0; at the top of the block, as in mux_fixed.v) or add a final else y = 1'b0;; after the fix the tool reports 0 inferred latches R4. Prevention: a coding rule "every combinational block assigns every output first", a testbench that tries every input pattern in more than one order, and a check that the synthesis log contains no "Latch inferred" lines. How the evidence was made: the correct selector with its default assignment deleted, simulated and synthesized in this build. Wrong answers: "the simulator is broken" (the fixed version passes in the same simulator); "a flip-flop is involved" (there is no clock; the stored value is level-sensitive, a latch).
