Story hook

Analogy

At the restaurant door stands a "take a number" machine. Each guest pulls a ticket, and a display over the counter shows whose turn it is. Every time the kitchen's bell rings and a table is free, the display moves on by one: 7, 8, 9.

Inside, the ticket rail has grown. It no longer holds one slip but a row of four clips, and all four are swapped together when the bell rings. Along the pass, finished plates sit on a short conveyor. At every ring, each plate slides one place towards the dining room, and a new plate enters at the kitchen end.

Kofi, the new waiter, asks: "Why does everything move at the bell, and never in between?" Because then nobody ever sees a half-changed display, a half-swapped row, or two plates in one place. In this chapter you build all three machines from flip-flops: the row of clips (a register), the number display (a counter) and the conveyor (a shift register).

What you will be able to do

  • Build a register with load and reset from D flip-flops, and say which input wins when several are active.
  • Design a synchronous counter as "a register plus an adder that feeds it", with enable and wrap-around.
  • Explain why a ripple counter passes through wrong values, using a real simulation trace.
  • Trace a shift register bit by bit.
  • Diagnose "the counter skips" from a timing diagram (the course's forensic lab).
Jargon box
Register (hardware)
Simple words: a row of flip-flops that store one number together. Analogy: a row of ticket clips on the rail, all swapped at the same ring of the bell. Precise: n D flip-flops sharing one clock, storing an n-bit value; extra inputs (load or enable, reset) decide whether a clock edge stores new data, clears, or keeps the value. The CPU registers named by instructions (HW202, "Register (CPU)") are built this way. D1 D2
Load (enable)
Simple words: the input that says "store the new value at the next edge". Analogy: the cook's nod that says "yes, swap my ticket at this ring". Precise: a control input of a register: at a clock edge, if load = 1 the register takes its data input, otherwise it keeps its value. D1
Reset (synchronous and asynchronous)
Simple words: the input that clears a register to a known value, usually 0. Analogy: wiping the rail clean before service. Precise: a synchronous reset acts only at a clock edge; an asynchronous reset acts at once, without waiting for the clock. D1
Counter
Simple words: a register that adds 1 to itself at each clock edge. Analogy: the "take a number" display at the door. Precise: a sequential circuit whose state steps through a fixed sequence, usually binary 0, 1, 2, ..., 2n − 1 and then wraps to 0. D1
Synchronous counter
Simple words: a counter in which all bits change at the same clock edge. Analogy: all digits of the display flip at the same ring. Precise: a counter whose flip-flops share one clock; the next value is computed by combinational logic (an incrementer) from the current value. D1
Ripple counter
Simple words: a counter in which each bit's change triggers the next bit, one after another. Analogy: a line of cooks who each start only when the neighbour has finished. Precise: a counter in which only the lowest flip-flop is clocked by the clock and each other flip-flop is clocked by the output of the one before it; the bits change at different times. D1
Wrap-around
Simple words: after the biggest number, the counter goes back to 0. Analogy: the display after 99 shows 00. Precise: arithmetic modulo 2n: in 4 bits, 15 + 1 = 0 (see MA102). W1
Shift register
Simple words: a register whose bits move one place at each clock edge. Analogy: the plate conveyor on the pass. Precise: a chain of flip-flops in which each flip-flop's input is the previous one's output; a serial input enters at one end at each edge. D1
Glitch
Simple words: a short wrong value that appears while signals are changing. Analogy: the display flashing a wrong number for a blink before it settles. Precise: a brief unintended value on a signal, caused by inputs or bits that change at slightly different times. D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows a 4-bit register. It is nothing more than four D flip-flops from F1-16, side by side, all connected to the same clock. A small selector in front of each one chooses what it stores: the new data, zero, or its own old value.

Figure 2 compares two ways to count. On the left, a synchronous counter: a register whose input is its own output plus one, computed by an incrementer (the adder of F1-14 with one input fixed at 1). On the right, a ripple counter: a chain in which each bit is clocked by the bit before it.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

One flip-flop remembers one bit. A number needs several bits, so you put several flip-flops in a row and connect them all to the same clock. That row is a register. At each clock edge, every flip-flop in the row stores its new bit at the same moment, so the number changes in one clean step.

Sometimes you want the register to keep its number. So each flip-flop gets a small chooser in front: "new number" or "my old number". A wire called load controls the chooser. Another wire called reset forces everything to zero, so the register never starts as a mystery.

Now feed the register's output into an adder that adds 1, and feed the adder's answer back into the register. At every clock edge the number grows by one: 0, 1, 2, 3. That is a counter, like the "take a number" display. When it reaches the biggest number its bits can hold, it wraps around to 0.

A shift register is a row of flip-flops where each one copies its neighbour. At each edge every bit moves one place, like plates sliding along the conveyor.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Registers with load and reset

A register of n bits is n D flip-flops sharing a clock D1 D2. On its own, a D flip-flop stores something at every edge. To make "keep" possible, a 2-input multiplexer (F1-12) in front of each flip-flop selects D or the flip-flop's own Q, controlled by load D1. A synchronous reset adds one more choice, the constant 0, and is checked first. Listing 1 writes all of this in five lines; the order of the if statements is the priority: reset, then load, then keep R1.

An asynchronous reset clears the flip-flop immediately, without waiting for an edge D1. In Verilog you write it by adding the reset to the event list: always @(posedge clk or posedge reset), as the ripple counter of Listing 4 does. Both kinds exist in real designs; within one design, pick one style and use it consistently.

Synchronous counters

A synchronous counter is a register plus an incrementer: next = count + 1 D1. Every flip-flop sees the same clock, so all bits change together, one flip-flop delay after the edge. Between edges the incrementer has a whole clock period to compute the next value. That is the time budget studied in F1-18.

Two extras make counters useful. An enable input lets the counter pause (enable = 0 means "keep"). A wrap output (Listing 2, line 11) is 1 during the cycle in which the next edge will take the counter from 15 back to 0; a second counter can use it as its own enable, which is how a two-digit display counts 00 to 99 D1. In 4 bits, 15 + 1 wraps to 0 because only the lowest four bits of 16 (binary 10000) are kept W1.

Ripple counters

A cheaper design uses no adder at all. Bit 0 toggles at every clock edge. Bit 1 toggles whenever bit 0 falls from 1 to 0, bit 2 whenever bit 1 falls, and so on D1. This counts correctly, but slowly and untidily: when the count goes from 7 (0111) to 8 (1000), bit 0 falls first, which then makes bit 1 fall, which makes bit 2 fall, which makes bit 3 rise. With a flip-flop delay of 1 time unit, the real run of Listing 4 passes through 6, 4 and 0 before it reaches 8 R2. Those short wrong values are glitches. Any circuit that reads the counter at the wrong moment, or decodes "count = 0", can be fooled. That is why designs that must be read reliably use synchronous counters.

Shift registers

In a shift register, flip-flop k takes the output of flip-flop k − 1 at each edge, and a serial input enters at bit 0 D1. Listing 3 writes this as q <= {q[2:0], serial_in}: keep the lower three bits, move them up, and put the new bit at the bottom. After four edges, four bits that arrived one at a time sit side by side. This is how a serial line (one wire, one bit per clock) becomes a parallel number; HW204 meets it again in input and output devices.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Why "one clock" is a design rule. In a synchronous design, every flip-flop is clocked by the same clock, and all logic between flip-flops is combinational. Then the behaviour can be reasoned about one cycle at a time: at each edge, every register takes the value its input logic computed during the previous cycle D1. The testbench in Listing 5 relies on exactly this: its models (lines 39–41) compute the next state from the current state, once per edge, and the hardware must agree R1. Clocking a flip-flop from another flip-flop's output, as the ripple counter does, breaks this rule; synthesis and timing tools then treat each such output as a separate clock, and analysis gets harder D1.

Counters are the smallest finite state machines. A counter's state is its value; its next-state logic is "+1". F1-19 generalises this: any next-state logic, any outputs.

Edge or level? In Verilog, the event list of an always block decides what kind of storage you describe. @(posedge clk) describes edge-triggered flip-flops; a list of levels such as @(clk) or @(en or d) describes something that reacts to every change D3. The forensic lab of this chapter is about exactly that difference.

Not verified — check before relying on this

How long the in-between values of a real ripple counter last depends on the flip-flop delays of the actual part or chip, which this build cannot measure. The 1-time-unit delay in Listing 4 is an exercise value. For a real part, take the propagation delays from its data sheet (AH-21) and record them in the dossier.

How the hardware actually does it

The program counter of a processor is a register with load, increment and reset, exactly the kind of circuit in this chapter; F1-21 reads one, and the course project builds it for HW202 D2. The processor's registers (the ones instructions name) are registers in this sense too, grouped into a register file with read and write ports D1. Counters appear wherever hardware must measure time or count events, for example a timer that raises an interrupt every N clock cycles (F1-42) D1. Shift registers sit behind serial links, where bits arrive one at a time and are collected into bytes.

Worked example

Following the register, the counter and the shift register

Listing 5 drives the three parts with the inputs in its table below. Predict each row before you read the output.

  1. Cycle 0: reset = 1. The register and the counter become 0 at the edge. The shift register has no reset: it shifts in the first serial bit, 1, so q_shift = xxx1 (three unknown bits remain).
  2. Cycle 2: load = 1 and d = 9, so the register becomes 9 (1001). The counter, enabled, goes 1 → 2.
  3. Cycles 4 and 5: enable = 0, so the counter stays at 3. The register keeps 9 because load = 0.
  4. Cycle 6: load = 1, d = 6: the register becomes 6.
  5. Shift register: the serial bits are 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0 (the binary number 10110010, left bit first). After cycle 3 the register shows the first four bits in order: 1011. After cycle 7 it shows the next four: 0010.
  6. Cycle 17: count = 15 with enable = 1, so wrap = 1. At the next edge (cycle 18) the count wraps to 0 W1.

Every prediction appears in the recorded output, and the testbench's own models agree at all 20 cycles R1.

The ripple counter from 7 to 8

Start: count = 0111. Rising clock edge at t = 150; each flip-flop takes 1 time unit.

  1. t = 151: bit 0 toggles 1 → 0. Count = 0110 = 6. Bit 0 fell, so bit 1 is triggered.
  2. t = 152: bit 1 toggles 1 → 0. Count = 0100 = 4. Bit 2 is triggered.
  3. t = 153: bit 2 toggles 1 → 0. Count = 0000 = 0. Bit 3 is triggered.
  4. t = 154: bit 3 toggles 0 → 1. Count = 1000 = 8. Done, 4 time units after the edge.

The run prints exactly the lines t = 151, 152, 153, 154 with counts 6, 4, 0, 8 R2. A synchronous counter would go from 7 straight to 8.

Code walk-through

All listings live in university/labs/F1-17/ and were run in this build by run.sh with Icarus Verilog; the timing diagrams were drawn from the simulations' VCD files by the university's wave.py tool D4.

Listing 1 — register4.v

// A 4-bit register: four D flip-flops that share one clock.
// On a rising clock edge: reset wins, otherwise load copies d, otherwise q holds.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module register4 (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       reset,   // synchronous: acts only at a rising edge
    input  wire       load,
    input  wire [3:0] d,
    output reg  [3:0] q
);
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (reset)
            q <= 4'd0;
        else if (load)
            q <= d;
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
8–9input wire [3:0] d, output reg [3:0] q4-bit buses: [3:0] means bits 3 down to 0.One register stores the whole number.
11always @(posedge clk) beginActs only at rising edges.Four flip-flops, one clock.
12–13if (reset) q <= 4'd0;Reset first: clear to 0. 4'd0 is "4-bit decimal 0".Synchronous reset: only at an edge.
14–15else if (load) q <= d;Otherwise, load stores d.The selector of Figure 1.
16endNo final else: q keeps its value.In a clocked block, "keep" is what a flip-flop does anyway; no latch is created.

Listing 2 — counter4.v

// A 4-bit synchronous counter: all four flip-flops share one clock.
// On a rising clock edge: reset wins, otherwise enable adds 1 (15 + 1 wraps to 0).
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module counter4 (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       reset,
    input  wire       enable,
    output reg  [3:0] count,
    output wire       wrap      // 1 while count = 15 and enable = 1: the next edge wraps
);
    assign wrap = enable && (count == 4'd15);

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (reset)
            count <= 4'd0;
        else if (enable)
            count <= count + 4'd1;
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
9, 11output wire wrap; assign wrap = enable && (count == 4'd15);Combinational output: 1 when the next edge will wrap.Lets counters be chained.
13–18always @(posedge clk) ... else if (enable) count <= count + 4'd1;At each rising edge: reset, or add 1 when enabled.count + 4'd1 is the incrementer of Figure 2; 4-bit arithmetic wraps 15 + 1 to 0.

Listing 3 — shift4.v

// A 4-bit shift register: on each rising edge every bit moves one place to the left
// and serial_in enters on the right.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module shift4 (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       serial_in,
    output reg  [3:0] q
);
    always @(posedge clk)
        q <= {q[2:0], serial_in};
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
9–10always @(posedge clk) q <= {q[2:0], serial_in};{ , } joins bits: the old bits 2..0 move up one place, the new bit enters at bit 0.Because <= reads the old q, every bit moves exactly one place per edge.

Listing 4 — ripple4.v

// A 4-bit ripple counter: each flip-flop toggles when the bit to its right falls
// from 1 to 0. Only bit 0 sees the real clock. Each flip-flop has a delay of 1 time unit.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module ripple4 (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       reset,     // asynchronous: clears at once
    output reg  [3:0] count
);
    always @(posedge clk or posedge reset)
        if (reset) count[0] <= 1'b0; else count[0] <= #1 ~count[0];
    always @(negedge count[0] or posedge reset)
        if (reset) count[1] <= 1'b0; else count[1] <= #1 ~count[1];
    always @(negedge count[1] or posedge reset)
        if (reset) count[2] <= 1'b0; else count[2] <= #1 ~count[2];
    always @(negedge count[2] or posedge reset)
        if (reset) count[3] <= 1'b0; else count[3] <= #1 ~count[3];
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
9–10always @(posedge clk or posedge reset) ... count[0] <= #1 ~count[0];Bit 0 toggles at each rising clock edge, 1 time unit later; reset clears it at once.Asynchronous reset; #1 models the flip-flop delay.
11–16always @(negedge count[0] ...) ... count[1] <= #1 ~count[1]; (and so on)Each higher bit toggles when the bit below falls (negedge).Each bit is clocked by its neighbour: the ripple.

Listing 5 — regs_tb.v (testbench for Listings 1–3)

// Self-checking testbench for register4, counter4 and shift4.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module regs_tb;
    reg        clk = 0;
    reg        reset = 1;
    reg        load = 0;
    reg  [3:0] d = 4'd0;
    reg        enable = 0;
    reg        serial_in = 0;
    wire [3:0] q_reg;
    wire [3:0] count;
    wire       wrap;
    wire [3:0] q_shift;
    integer    errors = 0;
    integer    cycle;
    reg  [3:0] model_reg;    // what each part should hold, computed by the testbench
    reg  [3:0] model_count;
    reg  [3:0] model_shift;
    reg  [7:0] bits = 8'b1011_0010;   // serial input, sent left bit first

    register4 r (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .load(load), .d(d), .q(q_reg));
    counter4  c (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .enable(enable), .count(count), .wrap(wrap));
    shift4    s (.clk(clk), .serial_in(serial_in), .q(q_shift));

    always #5 clk = ~clk;    // rising edges at 5, 15, 25, ...

    initial begin
        $display("cycle reset load  d  | q_reg | enable count wrap | in q_shift");
        model_shift = 4'bxxxx;
        for (cycle = 0; cycle < 20; cycle = cycle + 1) begin
            // change the inputs half a period before the rising edge
            reset     = (cycle == 0);
            load      = (cycle == 2 || cycle == 6);
            d         = (cycle == 2) ? 4'd9 : 4'd6;
            enable    = (cycle != 4 && cycle != 5);
            serial_in = (cycle < 8) ? bits[7 - cycle] : 1'b0;
            @(posedge clk);
            // the models: exactly the rules written in the modules' comments
            if (reset) model_reg = 4'd0; else if (load) model_reg = d;
            if (reset) model_count = 4'd0; else if (enable) model_count = model_count + 4'd1;
            model_shift = {model_shift[2:0], serial_in};
            #1;
            $display("%5d   %b    %b   %2d  |  %2d   |   %b     %2d    %b  |  %b  %b",
                     cycle, reset, load, d, q_reg, enable, count, wrap, serial_in, q_shift);
            if (q_reg !== model_reg || count !== model_count)
                errors = errors + 1;
            if (cycle >= 3 && q_shift !== model_shift)
                errors = errors + 1;
            #3;
        end
        if (errors == 0)
            $display("RESULT: PASS (20 cycles, all three parts match their rules)");
        else
            $display("RESULT: FAIL (%0d mismatches)", errors);
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
16–19reg [3:0] model_reg; ... reg [7:0] bits = 8'b1011_0010;Model values and the serial bits to send.The testbench computes the right answer independently.
21–23register4 r (...); counter4 c (...); shift4 s (...);The three parts under test.One clock for all.
30–36for (cycle = 0; cycle < 20; ...) begin reset = ...; load = ...; ...Sets each cycle's inputs half a period before the edge.Inputs never change at an edge: no races in the simulation.
37–41@(posedge clk); if (reset) model_reg = 4'd0; ...At the edge, updates the models with the same rules as the comments in Listings 1–3.An independent statement of what the hardware must do.
42–48#1; $display(...); if (q_reg !== model_reg ...) errors = errors + 1;Waits 1 unit for the flip-flops, prints a row, compares. The shift register is checked from cycle 3, once all four bits are known.!== also treats x as a mismatch.
51–55if (errors == 0) $display("RESULT: PASS ...") ...The verdict.The lab script requires PASS.

Where the analogy breaks

  • The "take a number" display could skip if the staff wanted; a counter cannot choose. A counter follows its next-state logic exactly. When it skips, the logic or the clocking is wrong (forensic lab), never a decision.
  • Plates on a conveyor are not copied; bits in a shift register are. At each edge each flip-flop copies its neighbour's old value. The last bit falls off the end and is lost unless something stores it.
  • A row of ticket clips can be swapped one clip at a time; a register's bits change together. In a synchronous design all bits change at the same edge. Only the ripple counter, which breaks that rule, shows bits changing one after another R2.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
The counter shows every second number (forensic lab).The always block reacts to both clock edges.Timing diagram: does count change on falling edges too?Use @(posedge clk).
Bits of q_shift are x for the first cycles (Listing 5 output, cycles 0–2).The shift register has no reset.The x bits disappear one per edge.Expected; add a reset if the first values matter.
A decoder fed by a ripple counter fires briefly at the wrong count.Glitches while the ripple settles (t = 151–153 in Listing 6's run).Print every change, not just values at edges.Use a synchronous counter, or read the count only at clock edges.
The register loads when reset is also 1.The if order puts load before reset.Add a test cycle with reset = load = 1 at the same edge.Check reset first.
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-16 built single flip-flops; F1-14 built adders. What carries over: the flip-flop's rule (store at the edge, hold otherwise) and the adder, unchanged; a counter is literally an adder feeding a register D1. What changes: you now reason in clock cycles, one row per edge, instead of in gate delays; and the order of control inputs (reset, load, enable) becomes part of the design. What comes next: F1-18 asks how fast the clock may tick before the adder in the loop cannot keep up.

Check yourself

  1. A 6-bit counter is at 63 and enabled. What is its value after the next edge? After 5 more edges?
  2. In Listing 1, reset = 1 and load = 1 at the same edge, with d = 12. What does q become, and which line decides it?
  3. Explain in your own words why a synchronous counter never shows the value 4 between 7 and 8, but a ripple counter can.
  4. A shift register like Listing 3 starts at 0000 and receives the bits 1, 1, 0, 1 (in that order). Write q after each of the four edges.
  5. Which is the best description of the wrap output of Listing 2? (a) 1 when count = 0 (b) 1 when count = 15, whatever enable is (c) 1 when the next edge will take the count from 15 to 0 (d) 1 for one time unit after the count wraps.
  6. Apply it to a new case: design (in words or Verilog) a counter that counts 0 to 9 and then returns to 0. What must change in Listing 2?
  7. Predict, then run: in Listing 5, change line 35 to enable = (cycle % 2 == 0);. What count does the run show at cycle 19? Run the lab to check.

Lab

Goal

Simulate a register, a synchronous counter, a shift register and a ripple counter, and check each against your own predictions and the testbench's model.

Hardware and software needed

No hardware. Icarus Verilog and Python 3; the recorded runs used "Icarus Verilog version 12.0 (stable)" and "Python 3.13.16", as printed by the tools R1 R3.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Write your predicted table for Listing 5 (cycle, q_reg, count, wrap, q_shift) on paper, using the Worked example.
  2. Run the lab from the repository root: university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-17.
  3. Compare regs.out with your table. Mark every row where you were wrong and find out why.
  4. Open ripple.out and find every transition where more than one line appears for one clock edge. List the in-between values.
  5. Make the change of question 7, rerun, and check your prediction.

Expected observations

RESULT: PASS (20 cycles, all three parts match their rules); the ripple counter shows in-between values at 1→2, 3→4, 5→6, 7→8 and the other transitions where several bits change R1 R2.

Verification

The self-checking testbench passes and run_lab.sh exits with status 0. For your own change in step 5, the testbench's models are updated by the same rule, so it must still print PASS: if it does not, your edit changed the hardware, not just the inputs.

Troubleshooting

  • Every row is a mismatch after your edit → inputs now change at the edge itself → keep input changes before @(posedge clk), as lines 31–36 do.
  • count stays x → the counter was never reset → keep reset = 1 for the first cycle.
  • wrap never becomes 1 → the run is shorter than 16 enabled cycles → lengthen the loop.

Extension

Chain two counters into a two-digit decimal counter (00 to 99): the ones digit counts 0–9 (question 6), and its "about to wrap" output enables the tens digit. Write a testbench that checks 120 cycles.

Forensic lab

Scenario: "The counter skips"

Ana built the ticket-number display for the restaurant door. Guests complain that it jumps: 1, 3, 5, 7. Ana insists that her counter "adds exactly 1 each time". The display reads the counter once just after every rising edge of the clock. You have her code, the display's log and a timing diagram from the simulator.

Evidence pack

Listing 7 — counter_skip.v (Ana's counter, evidence)

// Forensic evidence: Ana's 4-bit counter for the ticket-number display.
// It was meant to add 1 at every rising edge of clk, exactly like counter4.v.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module counter_skip (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       reset,
    input  wire       enable,
    output reg  [3:0] count,
    output wire       wrap
);
    assign wrap = enable && (count == 4'd15);

    always @(clk) begin
        if (reset)
            count <= 4'd0;
        else if (enable)
            count <= count + 4'd1;
    end
endmodule

13–18always @(clk) begin if (reset) ... else if (enable) count <= count + 4'd1; endCompare word by word with Listing 2, lines 13–18.The evidence you need is in one line.

Questions

  1. From the display log: by how much does the shown number grow per edge? Is it the same at every edge?
  2. From the timing diagram: at which instants does count change? Count the changes in one clock period.
  3. State at least two hypotheses (for example "the adder adds 2", "the display reads twice", "the counter is triggered by more than the rising edge") and say which evidence rules each one in or out.
  4. Find the line in Listing 7 that causes the fault, and explain the mechanism using the words "edge" and "level".
  5. Give the fix and a test that would have caught this before the display was installed.

Method hints

Measure on the diagram: the clock period is 10 units; how far apart are two changes of count? Then compare Listing 7 with Listing 2 character by character. A good answer quotes times and values from the evidence.

Mini-project

Build the first part of the course project: a program counter for the HW202 CPU. It is an 8-bit register with three controls, in priority order: reset (to 0), load (a jump address) and inc (add 1). Write it in Verilog, plus a self-checking testbench with at least 10 steps, including the wrap from 255 to 0 and all three controls active at once. F1-21 shows a reference program counter: build yours first, then compare.

Rubric (10 points): correct priority (3); testbench covers reset, load, inc, hold and wrap (3); testbench is self-checking and prints PASS or FAIL (2); a timing diagram of 10 edges with two sentences of explanation (2).

Summary

  • A register is n flip-flops on one clock; load chooses "new value" or "keep", reset forces a known value.
  • The order of control checks is the priority: Listing 1 checks reset, then load.
  • A synchronous counter is a register plus an incrementer; all bits change at the same edge.
  • 4-bit counting wraps from 15 to 0; a wrap output lets counters be chained.
  • A ripple counter clocks each bit from the previous one and passes through wrong in-between values.
  • A shift register moves every bit one place per edge and turns serial bits into a parallel number.
  • Describe flip-flops with @(posedge clk): reacting to the clock's level makes a counter step twice per period.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. 63 + 1 = 64 does not fit in 6 bits (largest 63), so it wraps to 0. Five more edges: 5.
  2. q becomes 0: line 12 checks reset first, so the else if (load) on line 14 is never reached.
  3. A good answer: in a synchronous counter all bits are flip-flops on the same clock edge and their new values were computed before the edge, so they change together from 0111 to 1000. In a ripple counter each bit waits for the bit before it to change, so for a short time some bits are new and some old: 0110, 0100, 0000.
  4. 0001, 0011, 0110, 1101.
  5. (c). (a) confuses "after wrap" with "about to wrap"; (b) forgets that a paused counter (enable = 0) will not wrap; (d) describes a pulse, but wrap is a level that lasts the whole cycle before the edge.
  6. Replace the "+1" rule: if count = 9 (and enabled), the next value is 0, otherwise count + 1. For example count <= (count == 4'd9) ? 4'd0 : count + 4'd1;. The wrap output should test count = 9.
  7. From cycle 0 the counter is reset; enabled cycles after that are 2, 4, ..., 18, nine edges, so count = 9 at cycle 19 (cycles with odd numbers keep the value). The model in the testbench follows the same inputs, so the run still prints PASS.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: from edge 3 on, the display grows by 2 per edge (3, 5, 7, ..., 15, then 1), and the testbench reports 8 of 8 checked edges wrong R4. In the timing diagram count changes every 5 time units, at the rising edges (15, 25, ...) and also at the falling edges (20, 30, ...): two changes per 10-unit clock period. Hypotheses: (1) the adder adds 2: ruled out, because the diagram shows single steps of 1 (1, 2, 3, 4, ...); (2) the display reads twice per edge: ruled out, because the log has exactly one line per edge and the diagram, which records the counter itself, shows the extra changes; (3) the counter is triggered by both clock edges: confirmed by the diagram. Root cause: Listing 7, line 13, always @(clk): the block runs at every change of clk's level, rising and falling, so the counter adds 1 twice per period. The edge condition posedge is missing. Fix: always @(posedge clk), as in Listing 2; the same testbench then passes, one step per edge R3. Prevention: a self-checking testbench that compares each value with the previous one (as display_tb.v does); a coding rule "every clocked block has posedge clk"; reading a timing diagram, not only values at edges. How the evidence was made: counter4.v with posedge removed from line 13, simulated in this build. Wrong answers: "the clock is too fast" (the counter steps cleanly on every half period; it is not missing values, it is making extra ones); "the display is broken" (the diagram records the counter, not the display).

Story hook

Analogy

Rosa is the expediter tonight. Her job is to ring the pass bell at a steady beat. At every ring, each cook hands the dish in front of them to the next station and starts on the one they just received.

The owner wants more dishes per hour, so he tells Rosa to ring faster. For a while it works. Then the soup station starts passing on pots that are still cold. The slowest job in the kitchen, chopping and simmering the soup, cannot finish between two rings any more. Nobody did anything wrong at the soup station. The bell simply came too soon.

A digital circuit has exactly this bell: the clock. This chapter measures it, shows how to work out how fast it may ring, and lets you watch, in a real simulation, what happens when it rings too fast.

What you will be able to do

  • Convert between clock period and clock frequency, with units.
  • Compute the minimum clock period of a path from clock-to-Q delay, logic delay and setup time, and say whether a given clock works.
  • Make slower rhythms from one clock with a counter, and explain why a clock enable is usually better than a new clock.
  • Diagnose a counter that fails because its clock is too fast for its logic (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Clock (signal)
Simple words: a signal that goes 0, 1, 0, 1 at a steady beat and tells flip-flops when to store. Analogy: the pass bell, rung at a steady beat. Precise: a periodic digital signal whose edges (here the rising edges) trigger the flip-flops of a synchronous circuit. D1
Clock period
Simple words: the time from one rising edge to the next. Analogy: the time between two rings of the bell. Precise: the duration T of one cycle of the clock, measured in seconds (often ns). D1 W1
Clock frequency
Simple words: how many clock cycles happen in one second. Analogy: rings per second. Precise: f = 1 / T, measured in hertz (Hz, cycles per second); 1 MHz is 106 Hz and 1 GHz is 109 Hz. W1
Duty cycle
Simple words: the share of each period in which the clock is 1. Analogy: how long the bell's hammer stays up compared with the whole beat. Precise: high time divided by period, written as a percentage; the clocks in this chapter's simulations are 50 % (equal high and low halves). D1
Setup time
Simple words: how long before the edge a flip-flop's input must already be steady. Analogy: the dish must be on the pass a moment before the ring, not during it. Precise: the minimum time before the active clock edge during which D must be stable for the flip-flop to sample it reliably. D1
Hold time
Simple words: how long after the edge the input must stay steady. Analogy: nobody may snatch the dish off the pass in the instant of the ring. Precise: the minimum time after the active clock edge during which D must remain stable. D1
Clock-to-Q delay
Simple words: how long a flip-flop takes to show its new value after the edge. Analogy: the moment a cook needs to pick up the handed-over dish. Precise: the delay from the active clock edge to the flip-flop's output Q becoming valid. D1
Critical path
Simple words: the slowest route signals must travel before the result is ready. Analogy: the soup station: the longest job between two rings. Precise: the path between two clocked elements with the longest total delay; it sets the minimum clock period (see also F1-15 and HW202). D1
Slack
Simple words: how much time is left over in a clock period after the slowest work is done. Analogy: the seconds the soup cook can rest before the ring. Precise: clock period minus the time the path needs; negative slack means the path fails timing. D1 W1
Clock enable
Simple words: a signal that tells flip-flops "this edge counts" or "skip this edge". Analogy: a card held up at some rings that says "the dessert station works on this ring only". Precise: a control input that makes clocked elements update only on edges where it is 1, so slow parts of a design can share the main clock. D1
Clock skew
Simple words: the clock edge reaching different flip-flops at slightly different times. Analogy: cooks far from the bell hear the ring a little later. Precise: the difference in arrival time of the same clock edge at two clocked elements, caused by the clock distribution wiring. D1
Oscillator
Simple words: the part that makes the clock's steady beat in the first place. Analogy: Rosa's metronome. Precise: a circuit that produces a periodic signal; digital systems derive their clocks from one, often multiplied or divided on the chip. D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 names the parts of a clock signal: the period, the rising and falling edges, and the high and low halves.

Figure 2 is the key idea of the chapter: the timing budget. A value leaves one flip-flop at a rising edge, travels through logic, and must arrive at the next flip-flop before the next rising edge, with time to spare for that flip-flop's setup time.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A clock in a computer is not a watch with hands. It is a wire whose value goes up and down, 0, 1, 0, 1, very steadily. Every time it goes up, every flip-flop that listens to it stores its new value at the same instant.

Between two ticks, the gates of the circuit do their work: adding, comparing, choosing. The answer must be ready before the next tick, because that tick is when the answer is stored.

So how fast can the clock go? Only as fast as the slowest job allows. If one adder needs a little more time than the gap between ticks, the flip-flop after it stores an old or half-finished answer. Nothing smokes, nothing beeps. The circuit simply computes the wrong thing.

The number of ticks per second is the clock frequency. The time between ticks is the clock period. When one goes up, the other goes down.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Period and frequency

Frequency and period are reciprocals: f = 1 / T W1. With powers of ten (MA101) this is quick: 1 MHz means 106 cycles per second, so T = 10−6 s = 1 µs = 1,000 ns; 100 MHz gives 10 ns; 1 GHz gives 1 ns. Listing 1 prints this table from the formula R1. Keep the units in every step: most mistakes in clock arithmetic are a lost factor of 1,000.

The timing budget

Look at one path in Figure 2. At a rising edge the launching flip-flop's output changes after its clock-to-Q delay. The new value travels through combinational logic, which takes the logic delay you met in F1-15. It must then be stable at the capturing flip-flop's input for the setup time before the next edge D1. So, for every path:

T ≥ tclock-to-Q + tlogic + tsetup D1

The path with the largest sum is the critical path; it sets the smallest period and therefore the highest frequency of the whole circuit D1. The difference between the period and what the path needs is the slack. Positive slack: the path works. Negative slack: the capturing flip-flop samples a value that is still changing.

There is a second rule, for the hold time: after an edge, a flip-flop's input must not change too soon. The fastest path from one flip-flop to the next must take longer than the hold time D1. Unlike the setup rule, the clock period does not appear in it, so slowing the clock does not fix a hold problem D1.

What "too fast" looks like

Listing 4 is the counter of F1-17 with a deliberately slow incrementer: its result appears 7 time units after its input changes. The flip-flops in a simulation are ideal (no clock-to-Q, no setup), so the budget is simply T ≥ 7. With a period of 10 the counter works R3. With a period of 6 it is too fast, and the forensic lab shows the result R4.

Slower rhythms: dividers and enables

Often part of a design should act less often: a display refreshed every few cycles, a timer that ticks every N cycles. Listing 2 shows two ways. The bits of a counter are themselves slower square waves: bit 0 has twice the period of the clock, bit 1 four times R2. Using such a bit as a clock for other flip-flops is possible, but it creates a second clock whose edges come a clock-to-Q delay after the main one, which brings back the problems of the ripple counter D1. The usual alternative is a clock enable: keep one clock everywhere, and generate a one-cycle pulse (here tick, every 5 cycles) that tells the slow part "this edge counts" D1. The register's load input from F1-17 is exactly such an enable.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Skew. The clock reaches flip-flops through wires and buffers, so the same edge arrives at slightly different times: clock skew. If the capturing flip-flop's clock is late, the setup budget gains time but the hold budget loses it, and the other way round D1. Chip designers build balanced distribution networks to keep skew small, and timing tools include it in their checks.

Static timing analysis. Real designs have very many paths. Tools add up the delays of every path from the cell library's data and report the worst slack for setup and hold, without simulating any input values D1. A simulation such as Listing 5 only shows the paths that particular inputs happen to exercise; this is why timing is checked by analysis, and function by simulation.

Several clocks. Larger systems have several clocks (a processor's core clock, a memory clock, a slow peripheral clock). A signal that crosses from one clock domain to another can change at any moment relative to the receiving clock, so it can violate setup or hold and cause metastability (F1-16). The classic remedy for a single control bit is a synchronizer: two flip-flops in a row on the receiving clock, which gives the first one a full cycle to settle D1. Multi-bit values need more care (handshakes or special queues).

Power. Every clock edge charges and discharges wire and transistor capacitance, so a circuit's switching power grows with its clock frequency D1. Turning off the clock to idle parts (clock gating) saves power, and must be done with special cells, not with an ordinary AND gate on the clock, which can create glitches D1.

Not verified — check before relying on this

How a real board makes its clock (a quartz crystal oscillator, an on-chip phase-locked loop that multiplies the frequency, spread-spectrum clocking) and every real number about it (frequencies, accuracy, jitter, lock time) depend on the named part. This build opened no data sheet and gives no values. For a real board, read the oscillator's data sheet and the processor's reference manual (clock chapter) and record the values in the dossier (AH-21). To see your own computer's clock, look in its documentation or its operating system's hardware report and write your own number here: ________.

How the hardware actually does it

In a chip, one clock signal must reach a very large number of flip-flops at almost the same instant. It is distributed through a tree (or a grid) of buffers designed to keep skew small, and it is one of the chip's largest consumers of power for that reason D1. The clock frequency printed on a processor's box is the result of the timing budget of its critical paths, at the voltage and temperature the maker specifies; HW202 shows how pipelining shortens the logic between flip-flops so that the clock can run faster D1 D2.

Worked example

Will this path run at 100 MHz?

Exercise A (made-up values, not a real part): clock-to-Q = 1.5 ns, logic = 6.0 ns, setup = 1.0 ns.

  1. Minimum period: 1.5 + 6.0 + 1.0 = 8.5 ns.
  2. Maximum frequency: 1 / 8.5 ns. Since 1 / (1 ns) = 1,000 MHz, f = 1,000 / 8.5 MHz ≈ 117.6 MHz.
  3. 100 MHz has T = 10 ns. Slack = 10 − 8.5 = +1.5 ns: the path works.
  4. At 125 MHz, T = 8 ns. Slack = 8 − 8.5 = −0.5 ns: it fails.
  5. Exercise B speeds the logic up to 4.0 ns: 1.5 + 4.0 + 1.0 = 6.5 ns, about 153.8 MHz.

Listing 1 computes the same numbers W1 R1.

The simulated counter

In Listing 4, the flip-flops are ideal and the incrementer takes 7 units, so the minimum period is 7 units. A period of 10 leaves slack +3; a period of 6 leaves slack −1. Listing 1's last line prints "TOO FAST (slack -1.0 ns)" for the 6-unit clock R1. (The simulation's time unit is set to 1 ns by its `timescale line, but these are exercise values, not the speed of any real adder.)

Dividing by 5 with an enable

Listing 2's counter five goes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 0, ... At the edge where five = 4, tick becomes 1 for one cycle. So tick rises once every 5 cycles; with a 10-unit clock, every 50 units. The testbench measures exactly 50 R2.

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — clock_math.cpp (C++, from SP101)

// Clock arithmetic: period = 1 / frequency, and the timing budget of one clock cycle.
// All delays below are exercise values chosen for this chapter, not data of real parts.
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Path
{
    std::string name;
    double clkToQ;   // ns: flip-flop output settles after the edge
    double logic;    // ns: slowest path through the logic between two flip-flops
    double setup;    // ns: input must be stable this long before the next edge
};

int main()
{
    // 1. Frequency to period: period in seconds = 1 / frequency in hertz.
    const std::vector<double> frequencies = {1.0, 1.0e3, 1.0e6, 100.0e6, 1.0e9};
    std::printf("%14s  %16s\n", "frequency (Hz)", "period (ns)");
    for (double f : frequencies) {
        std::printf("%14.0f  %16.3f\n", f, 1.0e9 / f);
    }

    // 2. Timing budget: the clock period must be at least clkToQ + logic + setup.
    const std::vector<Path> paths = {
        {"chapter simulation (ideal flip-flops, 7 ns adder)", 0.0, 7.0, 0.0},
        {"exercise A", 1.5, 6.0, 1.0},
        {"exercise B (logic made faster)", 1.5, 4.0, 1.0},
    };
    std::printf("\n%-50s %9s %14s\n", "path", "min period", "max frequency");
    for (const Path& p : paths) {
        const double minPeriodNs = p.clkToQ + p.logic + p.setup;
        const double maxFreqMHz = 1000.0 / minPeriodNs;   // 1 / ns = 1000 MHz
        std::printf("%-50s %6.1f ns %10.1f MHz\n", p.name.c_str(), minPeriodNs, maxFreqMHz);
    }

    // 3. Does a 6 ns clock work for the chapter simulation? (the forensic lab)
    const double periodNs = 6.0;
    const double needNs = paths[0].clkToQ + paths[0].logic + paths[0].setup;
    std::printf("\nperiod %.1f ns, path needs %.1f ns: %s (slack %.1f ns)\n", periodNs, needNs,
                periodNs >= needNs ? "OK" : "TOO FAST", periodNs - needNs);
    return 0;
}

Listing 2 — divider.v

// Slower rhythms from one clock.
// div2 and div4 are the two lowest bits of a counter: they toggle at half and a
// quarter of the clock's rate. tick is a one-cycle pulse every 5 clock cycles: the
// rest of the design keeps using clk and does its slow work only when tick = 1.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module divider (
    input  wire clk,
    input  wire reset,
    output wire div2,
    output wire div4,
    output reg  tick
);
    reg [1:0] bits;
    reg [2:0] five;      // counts 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 0, ...

    assign div2 = bits[0];
    assign div4 = bits[1];

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (reset) begin
            bits <= 2'd0;
            five <= 3'd0;
            tick <= 1'b0;
        end else begin
            bits <= bits + 2'd1;
            five <= (five == 3'd4) ? 3'd0 : five + 3'd1;
            tick <= (five == 3'd4);
        end
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
13–17reg [1:0] bits; ... assign div2 = bits[0]; assign div4 = bits[1];A 2-bit counter; its two bits are brought out.Counter bits are slower square waves.
14, 26reg [2:0] five; ... five <= (five == 3'd4) ? 3'd0 : five + 3'd1;A counter from 0 to 4, then back to 0. a ? b : c means "if a then b else c".Counting to N − 1 divides by N.
27tick <= (five == 3'd4);tick is 1 for the one cycle after five was 4.A clock enable: one pulse every 5 cycles.

Listing 3 — divider_tb.v

// Measure the period of div2 and div4 and the spacing of tick pulses, in time units.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module divider_tb;
    reg     clk = 0;
    reg     reset = 1;
    wire    div2;
    wire    div4;
    wire    tick;
    integer last2 = -1;
    integer last4 = -1;
    integer lastt = -1;
    integer p2 = 0;
    integer p4 = 0;
    integer pt = 0;

    divider dut (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .div2(div2), .div4(div4), .tick(tick));

    always #5 clk = ~clk;        // clock period 10 time units

    initial begin
        $dumpfile("divider.vcd");
        $dumpvars(0, divider_tb);
        #12 reset = 0;
        #200;
        $display("clk  period = 10 time units");
        $display("div2 period = %0d time units", p2);
        $display("div4 period = %0d time units", p4);
        $display("tick pulses every %0d time units", pt);
        if (p2 == 20 && p4 == 40 && pt == 50)
            $display("RESULT: PASS (periods 2, 4 and 5 times the clock period)");
        else
            $display("RESULT: FAIL");
        $finish(0);
    end

    // measure from one rising edge of each signal to the next
    always @(posedge div2) begin if (last2 >= 0) p2 = $time - last2; last2 = $time; end
    always @(posedge div4) begin if (last4 >= 0) p4 = $time - last4; last4 = $time; end
    always @(posedge tick) begin if (lastt >= 0) pt = $time - lastt; lastt = $time; end
endmodule

37–39always @(posedge div2) begin if (last2 >= 0) p2 = $time - last2; last2 = $time; endRecords the time between two rising edges of each output.Measures periods instead of trusting the design.
29–32if (p2 == 20 && p4 == 40 && pt == 50) ... PASSChecks 2×, 4× and 5× the clock period.A self-checking test.

Listing 4 — slow_adder_counter.v

// A counter whose "+1" logic is slow: the adder's result appears 7 time units after
// its input changes (an exercise value, not the delay of any real part).
// The flip-flops copy next into count at every rising edge of clk.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module slow_adder_counter (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       reset,
    output reg  [3:0] count
);
    wire [3:0] next;
    assign #7 next = count + 4'd1;     // the slow combinational path

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (reset)
            count <= 4'd0;
        else
            count <= next;
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
10–11wire [3:0] next; assign #7 next = count + 4'd1;The incrementer; its result appears 7 units after count changes.The #7 models a slow combinational path.
13–18always @(posedge clk) ... count <= next;The register stores whatever next shows at the edge.If next is not ready yet, the old value is stored.

Listing 5 — clock_speed_tb.v

// Run the slow-adder counter with a clock period chosen at compile time
// (-DPERIOD=10 or -DPERIOD=6) and check it against a model that adds exactly 1
// at every rising edge.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module clock_speed_tb;
    reg        clk = 0;
    reg        reset = 1;
    wire [3:0] count;
    integer    edge_no = 0;
    integer    errors = 0;
    reg  [3:0] model = 4'd0;     // what count should be

    slow_adder_counter dut (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .count(count));

    always #(`PERIOD / 2) clk = ~clk;      // first rising edge at PERIOD / 2

    initial begin
        $dumpfile("clock_speed.vcd");
        $dumpvars(0, clock_speed_tb);
        $display("clock period = %0d time units, adder delay = 7 time units", `PERIOD);
        #(2 * `PERIOD + 1) reset = 0;      // two rising edges with reset = 1
    end

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (reset)
            model = 4'd0;
        else
            model = model + 4'd1;
        #1;
        edge_no = edge_no + 1;
        if (count !== model) begin
            $display("edge %2d at t=%3t: count = %2d   <-- should be %0d", edge_no, $time - 1, count, model);
            errors = errors + 1;
        end else begin
            $display("edge %2d at t=%3t: count = %2d", edge_no, $time - 1, count);
        end
        if (edge_no == 12) begin
            if (errors == 0)
                $display("RESULT: PASS (count went up by 1 at every edge)");
            else
                $display("RESULT: FAIL (%0d of 12 edges wrong)", errors);
            $finish(0);
        end
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
15always #(`PERIOD / 2) clk = ~clk;The period is a compile-time macro, set with -DPERIOD=10 or -DPERIOD=6.The same testbench tests two clock speeds.
21#(2 * `PERIOD + 1) reset = 0;Holds reset for two edges.Gives the slow incrementer time to settle after reset.
24–36always @(posedge clk) begin ... model = model + 4'd1; #1; ... if (count !== model) ...A model counter adds exactly 1 per edge; each edge's count is compared with it.The definition of "correct".
37–43if (edge_no == 12) ... RESULT ...Verdict after 12 edges.PASS for period 10 is required by the lab script.

Where the analogy breaks

  • Rosa can wait for a slow cook; a clock never waits. A clock does not know whether the logic has finished. Correctness depends entirely on the designer choosing a period longer than the critical path.
  • A cook with a cold pot knows it; a flip-flop does not. A flip-flop that samples a value still changing gives no error signal. It stores something, maybe the old value, maybe the new one, maybe (for a while) neither: a metastable level D1.
  • Everyone hears the bell at once; clock edges arrive at slightly different times. Skew is the gap the analogy hides D1.

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
A result is off by a factor of 1,000.ns, µs and ms mixed, or MHz and GHz.Write units at every step.Convert everything to seconds and hertz first.
A counter advances only every second edge (forensic lab, clock_fast.out).Clock period shorter than the critical path.Compare the edge times with the time the logic's output changes.Longer period, faster logic, or split the logic over two cycles.
A design works at a slow clock but fails in a way that slowing the clock does not cure.Hold violation (a path too fast), not setup.Timing report: check the hold slack.Add delay to the short path (timing tools do this).
A "divided clock" makes flip-flops change a little after the main clock edge.Counter output used as a clock.Timing diagram around the edges.Use one clock and a clock enable (Listing 2's tick).
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-15 measured propagation delay through gates, and F1-17 built counters on a shared clock. What carries over: delays add along a path, exactly as in F1-15; the flip-flop's rule (store at the edge) is unchanged D1. What changes: delay is no longer just "how long until the output is right" but a budget that must fit inside one clock period; a too-fast clock fails silently, and hold problems cannot be fixed by slowing down. What comes next: F1-19 uses the clock and registers to build finite state machines, where "one edge = one step" becomes the whole design method.

Check yourself

  1. Convert: a 250 MHz clock has what period in ns? A 4 ns period is what frequency?
  2. A path has clock-to-Q 2 ns, logic 9 ns and setup 1 ns. What is the highest clock frequency for this path? What is the slack at 50 MHz?
  3. Which change can fix a setup violation? (a) a faster clock (b) a slower clock (c) a longer hold time (d) more logic on the path.
  4. Explain in your own words why a hold violation is not fixed by slowing the clock.
  5. Apply it to a new case: a design has a 100 MHz clock and needs a pulse every 1 µs to update a display. With Listing 2's method, what must the counter count to?
  6. Predict, then run: in Listing 5's experiment, which periods between 6 and 10 make the counter correct? Try -DPERIOD=8 by hand (see the Lab) and check.
  7. Why does the simulation of the too-fast clock give a neat, repeatable wrong answer, while a real circuit might not?

Lab

Goal

Find, by calculation and by simulation, the fastest clock for the slow-adder counter, and build a clock enable.

Hardware and software needed

No hardware. g++, Icarus Verilog and Python 3. Recorded runs used "g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0", "Icarus Verilog version 12.0 (stable)" and "Python 3.13.16", as printed by the tools R1 R2.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. Run the whole lab: university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-18. Check that clock_math.out, divider.out and clock_ok.out look like the outputs above.
  2. From the budget rule, predict the smallest even period that works for Listing 4 (the macro divides the period by 2, so use even numbers).
  3. In university/labs/F1-18, test periods 8, then your prediction: iverilog -g2005 -Wall -DPERIOD=8 -o test.vvp clock_speed_tb.v slow_adder_counter.v && vvp -n test.vvp.
  4. Draw the diagram of each run: python3 -I wave.py clock_speed.vcd 1/1 80 clk reset count next. Mark the slack before each edge.
  5. Change Listing 2 so that tick comes every 3 cycles; update the testbench's expected value and rerun.

Expected observations

Period 10 passes with 3 units of slack R3; period 6 fails R4. Your own runs of other periods should agree with the budget rule T ≥ 7. The divider run measures periods 20 and 40 and a tick every 50 units R2.

Verification

For each period you tried, the testbench verdict matches the sign of the slack you computed. run_lab.sh exits with status 0.

Troubleshooting

  • macro PERIOD undefined → you forgot -DPERIOD=... → add it to the iverilog command.
  • An odd period behaves strangely → `PERIOD / 2 is integer division, so 7 becomes a period of 6 → use even periods.
  • count stays x → reset released before next settled → keep line 21 as it is.

Extension

Split the slow incrementer into two halves of 4 units each with a register between them (a two-stage pipeline). What is the new minimum period, and what new problem appears in the count? (HW202 answers this in detail.)

Forensic lab

Scenario: "Fast clock, slow count"

To make the restaurant's order counter "faster", Theo shortened its clock period from 10 to 6 units. Now the counter falls behind: after twelve edges it shows 5 instead of 10. Theo suspects the reset. Find the real cause.

Questions

  1. At which edges is count wrong, and by how much does it grow per edge on average?
  2. For the edges at t = 21 and t = 27: what value did next have just before each edge? When did next last change?
  3. State at least two hypotheses (reset, the adder's logic, the clock period) and the evidence for or against each.
  4. Compute the slack of the incrementer path for periods 6 and 10, and connect it to the evidence.
  5. Propose two different fixes, and say how you would verify each one.
  6. Why might real hardware with the same fault behave less neatly than this simulation?

Method hints

Read the diagram one edge at a time: "edge at t = ..., next shows ..., so count becomes ...". Then compare the time between a change of count and the next change of next with the period.

Mini-project

Design a stopwatch display driver in Verilog: one 10-unit system clock, a tick enable every 10 cycles (one "tenth"), and a decimal counter 0–9 that advances only on ticks. Write a self-checking testbench for 250 clock cycles and draw the timing diagram of the first 40 cycles. Explain in one paragraph why you used an enable rather than a divided clock.

Rubric (10 points): correct tick spacing measured by the testbench (3); counter advances only on ticks and wraps 9 → 0 (3); diagram and explanation (2); one clock only, no counter output used as a clock (2).

Summary

  • A clock is a steady 0/1 signal; flip-flops act on its rising edges.
  • f = 1 / T: 100 MHz ↔ 10 ns, 1 GHz ↔ 1 ns. Keep units in every step.
  • Every path needs T ≥ clock-to-Q + logic delay + setup; the worst path is the critical path.
  • Slack = T minus what the path needs; negative slack means wrong values are stored, silently.
  • Hold violations come from paths that are too fast; slowing the clock does not fix them.
  • Make slow rhythms with a counter and a clock enable, not with extra clocks.
  • Skew, clock domains and power make clocks a design topic of their own; timing is checked by analysis, function by simulation.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. T = 1 / (250 × 106 Hz) = 4 × 10−9 s = 4 ns. And 4 ns gives 250 MHz: the same pair.
  2. Minimum period 2 + 9 + 1 = 12 ns, so fmax = 1,000 / 12 MHz ≈ 83.3 MHz. At 50 MHz, T = 20 ns, slack = 20 − 12 = +8 ns.
  3. (b). A faster clock (a) makes it worse; hold time (c) is a separate constraint and a property of the flip-flop; more logic (d) lengthens the path.
  4. A good answer: a hold violation happens when new data from the same clock edge reaches the next flip-flop too soon after that edge. Both events are caused by the same edge, so the time between them does not depend on when the next edge comes; changing the period does not move them apart.
  5. 1 µs / 10 ns = 100 cycles, so the counter counts 0 to 99 and raises tick once every 100 cycles.
  6. The rule is T ≥ 7. With even periods, 8 and 10 work and 6 fails. (Period 8 leaves slack 1.) Your run of -DPERIOD=8 should print RESULT: PASS.
  7. The simulator's flip-flops and delays are ideal and exact: a value is either there or not at the edge time. A real flip-flop whose input changes within its setup window can store either value or become metastable for a while, and real delays vary with voltage, temperature and each chip, so the failures can be irregular D1.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: from edge 4 (t = 21) every edge is wrong; count reaches only 5 after 12 edges, half the expected rate: it changes every 12 units, every second edge R4. In the diagram, next changes at 10, 22, 34, 46, 58: always one unit after an edge (21, 33, 45, 57). Just before the edge at t = 21, next still showed 1 (it last changed at 10, and the new value 2 appears at 22), so the edge stored 1 again; at t = 27, next = 2, so count became 2. Hypotheses: (1) reset is wrong: ruled out, reset ends at t = 13 and the first count after it is correct (edge 3); (2) the adder computes the wrong value: ruled out, next always equals count + 1, just late; (3) the clock period is shorter than the incrementer's delay: confirmed. Root cause: the incrementer needs 7 units (Listing 4, line 11), the clock gives 6: slack 6 − 7 = −1 unit (Listing 1 prints "TOO FAST (slack -1.0 ns)") R1. Every edge that follows a change of count arrives before next has settled, so the register stores the old value and the counter stalls for one cycle. Fixes: go back to a period ≥ 7 (period 10 passes, R3); or make the logic faster; or keep the fast clock and split the work across two cycles (a pipeline). Verify each with the same self-checking testbench and with the budget calculation. Prevention: compute the slack of every path before choosing a clock (static timing analysis in real tools). Real hardware: a real flip-flop whose input is changing inside its setup window could store old, new, or a metastable level, so the failure could be irregular, not this neat every-second-edge pattern D1. How the evidence was made: the correct design and testbench, compiled with -DPERIOD=6 instead of 10. Wrong answers: "reset is held too long" (count is correct at edge 3); "the counter skips" (the opposite: it repeats values; compare with the counter that skips in F1-17).

Story hook

Analogy

Every order in the restaurant has a status card on the board: ordered, cooking, plating, served. Mei, the expediter, follows a small rule card. "At each ring of the bell, look at the order's status and at what is happening. If it is cooking and the timer has run six rings, move it to plating. Otherwise leave it where it is."

Mei never needs to remember the whole history of the order. The status card says everything that matters. And the board tells the waiters what to do: an order at plating means "come to the pass now".

That is a finite state machine: a handful of named situations, one of which is current, a rule for moving between them at each clock edge, and outputs decided by the current situation. Traffic lights, vending machines, and the control unit of a processor are all built this way. In this chapter you design them from a description in words, the way the course's practical exam asks.

What you will be able to do

  • Turn a description in words into states, a state diagram, a state table and Verilog.
  • Explain the three parts of a state machine: next-state logic, state register and output logic.
  • Tell a Moore machine from a Mealy machine and say when each answers.
  • Build and test a traffic-light controller with a self-checking testbench that checks safety rules.
  • Diagnose a state machine whose state register is too narrow for its states (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Finite state machine (FSM)
Simple words: a circuit that is always in one of a few named situations and moves between them by rules. Analogy: the order's status card and Mei's rule card. Precise: a sequential circuit with a finite set of states, a state register holding the current state, next-state logic that computes the next state from the current state and inputs, and output logic. D1
State
Simple words: the situation the machine is in right now. Analogy: the word on the status card. Precise: the value held in the state register; it summarises everything about past inputs that the machine needs for its future behaviour. D1
State diagram
Simple words: a drawing with a circle for each state and an arrow for each move. Analogy: the flow chart pinned beside the order board. Precise: a directed graph whose nodes are states and whose edges are transitions, labelled with the input conditions that cause them (and, for Mealy machines, the outputs). D1
State table
Simple words: the same information as the diagram, written as a table. Analogy: Mei's rule card. Precise: a table listing, for each current state and input combination, the next state (and outputs). D1
Next-state logic
Simple words: the part that decides where to go next. Analogy: Mei reading her rule card. Precise: combinational logic computing the next state from the current state and the inputs; it is stored into the state register at the clock edge. D1
Moore machine
Simple words: a state machine whose outputs depend only on the state. Analogy: the waiters look only at the status card, not at what Mei is hearing. Precise: an FSM whose outputs are a function of the current state alone; outputs change only after a clock edge. D1
Mealy machine
Simple words: a state machine whose outputs also look at the inputs right now. Analogy: a waiter who reacts to the status card and to the customer's wave at the same time. Precise: an FSM whose outputs are a function of the current state and the current inputs; it can respond in the same cycle, at the cost of outputs that follow input changes between edges. D1
State encoding
Simple words: the bit pattern chosen for each state. Analogy: a numbered status card instead of a word. Precise: an assignment of binary codes to states; binary encoding uses ⌈log2(number of states)⌉ flip-flops, one-hot encoding uses one flip-flop per state. D1 W1
Illegal state
Simple words: a bit pattern in the state register that is not one of your states. Analogy: a status card with a word that is not on the rule card. Precise: a code the state register can hold but the design never meant to use; robust designs define a safe next state for it. D1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the shape of every state machine in this course: a state register (flip-flops from F1-17), combinational next-state logic in front of it, and combinational output logic after it.

Figure 2 is the state diagram of the Worked example: a machine that watches a stream of bits and says "found" when the last three bits were 1, 0, 1.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Many machines around you do things in steps. A traffic light goes green, then yellow, then red, and waits. A washing machine fills, washes, rinses, spins. Each step is a state, a situation the machine is in.

A finite state machine remembers only which state it is in now. That is its whole memory. At every clock tick it looks at its state and at its inputs (is a car waiting? has the timer run out?) and decides the next state. Then its outputs, like which lamps are on, follow from the state.

You can draw it: one circle per state and one arrow per move, with the reason written on the arrow. If you can draw it, you can build it from the parts you already know: flip-flops to hold the state, and gates to decide the next state and the outputs.

The nice part is that "finite" means you can check every case. A traffic light with six states has only six situations to think about, and you can make sure none of them ever shows green both ways.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Three parts

An FSM has a state register of k flip-flops, next-state logic and output logic (Figure 1) D1. At each rising edge the register stores the next state; during the following cycle the logic computes the new next state and the outputs. A counter (F1-17) is the simplest FSM: its next-state logic is "+1" and its outputs are the state itself.

Moore and Mealy

In a Moore machine, outputs depend only on the state, so they change only just after a clock edge and stay steady for the whole cycle D1. In a Mealy machine, outputs depend on the state and the present inputs D1. A Mealy machine can therefore react within the same cycle in which an input arrives, and often needs fewer states, but its outputs can change (or glitch) whenever its inputs change. Both machines in this chapter are Moore machines: their outputs are decoded from the state only. The 101 detector, for example, says "found" during the cycle after the final 1 has been stored R1; a Mealy version could say it during the same cycle the final 1 is on the input.

From words to hardware: the method

This is the method the course's practical exam tests ("design an FSM from a word description"). It follows the usual textbook steps D1 D2:

  1. Inputs and outputs. List them, with their meaning and timing ("sampled at the rising edge").
  2. States. Ask: what must the machine remember about the past to decide the future? Each distinct answer is a state. Name states by what they remember ("S10: the last two bits were 1, 0").
  3. Diagram. From every state, draw exactly one arrow for every input combination. Missing arrows are missing decisions.
  4. Table. Write the diagram as a state table and check it row by row against the words.
  5. Encoding. Choose codes. With n states, binary encoding needs ⌈log2 n⌉ bits: 4 states need 2 bits, 6 states need 3 W1. Check the register is wide enough for every code.
  6. Verilog. Write three blocks: next-state logic (always @(*) with a default), state register (always @(posedge clk) with reset), output logic.
  7. Test. Write a testbench that compares with an independent model, or checks properties that must always hold ("never green both ways").

States that last several cycles

A traffic light stays green for many clock cycles. Rather than one state per cycle, the design adds a small counter, timer, that counts cycles spent in the current state and is cleared whenever the state changes (Listing 3, line 49). The next-state logic then reads "if timer ≥ 5 and a car is waiting, go to yellow" D1. Strictly, the timer is part of the state (the full state is "state, timer"), but splitting it this way keeps the diagram readable.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Encoding choices. Binary encoding uses the fewest flip-flops. One-hot encoding (one flip-flop per state, exactly one of them 1) uses more flip-flops but often simpler, faster next-state and output logic; synthesis tools may re-encode a state machine they recognise D1 D3. Gray-style encodings, where neighbouring states differ in one bit, are used when a state value is read by another clock domain (F1-18).

Illegal states. A 3-bit register for 6 states can hold 8 codes; codes 6 and 7 are illegal states. They should never occur, but a design that will run unattended should still say what happens if one does: Listing 3's default sends any unknown code to an all-red state D1. The forensic lab shows a worse problem: a register too narrow to hold some legal codes at all.

Verification by properties. A traffic light's specification is mostly about what must never happen. The testbench in Listing 4 checks three safety properties at every cycle instead of comparing with a fixed expected sequence R2. Industrial flows go further: formal tools prove such properties for all input sequences rather than the ones a testbench tries D1.

The processor connection. The control unit of a simple processor is an FSM whose inputs are the instruction's opcode and whose outputs are the control signals of the datapath; HW202 builds one (F1-25) D2 D4.

Not verified — check before relying on this

The traffic light here is a teaching example with made-up timings (6, 4, 2 and 1 clock cycles). Real traffic signals follow national road-traffic rules and standards (for example on minimum yellow and all-red times) and safety-critical engineering rules (SS402). This build opened none of them, and nothing in this chapter is a specification for real signals.

How the hardware actually does it

An FSM in silicon is exactly Figure 1: a few flip-flops plus gates. When the synthesis tool reads Listing 3, the state register becomes three flip-flops with a reset, and the case statements become gates (F1-21 shows such a report) D3. State machines are everywhere in hardware that talks to the outside world: the controller of a serial link, the logic that answers a bus request, the sequencing inside a memory controller D1. In HW204 and the driver courses you will read device data sheets that describe a device's behaviour as states; the drivers you write mirror those state machines in software.

Worked example

From words: the 101 detector

Words: "One input bit in is sampled at each rising edge. Output found must be 1 during the cycle after the last three sampled bits were 1, 0, 1. Overlaps count: 10101 contains the pattern twice."

  1. What must be remembered? How much of the pattern has been seen so far: nothing (S0), "1" (S1), "1, 0" (S10), or the whole "1, 0, 1" (S101).
  2. Arrows. From S0: a 1 starts the pattern (S1); a 0 does not (S0). From S1: a 0 continues (S10); another 1 is still a usable first bit (S1). From S10: a 1 completes the pattern (S101); a 0 breaks it, and "0, 0" contains no useful start (S0). From S101: its last bit is a 1, so it can start the next pattern: input 0 gives "1, 0" (S10) and input 1 gives "1" (S1). This last pair of arrows is what makes overlaps count.
  3. Table:
StateMeaningin = 0in = 1found
S0 (00)nothing usefulS0S10
S1 (01)last bit 1S10S10
S10 (10)last bits 1, 0S0S1010
S101 (11)last bits 1, 0, 1S10S11
  1. Encoding: 4 states need 2 bits (22 = 4) W1; codes in brackets above.
  2. Trace on the bits 1, 0, 1, 0, 1: S0 → S1 → S10 → S101 (found) → S10 → S101 (found). Two detections, overlapping.

Listing 1 is this table in Verilog, and its run on 20 bits agrees with a direct check of the last three bits at every cycle R1.

The traffic light

Words: "A main road (NS) and a side road (EW) cross. NS is green by default. When a car waits on EW (sensor car_ew) and NS has been green for at least 6 cycles, NS goes yellow for 2 cycles, then both roads are red for 1 cycle, then EW is green for 4 cycles, yellow for 2, all red for 1, and NS is green again. After reset, both roads are red."

States: NS_GREEN, NS_YELLOW, ALL_RED_1, EW_GREEN, EW_YELLOW, ALL_RED_2. Six states need 3 bits W1. Figure 3 shows the diagram; Listing 3 is the Verilog.

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — seq101.v

// Moore state machine: found = 1 when the last three input bits were 1, 0, 1.
// Overlaps count: in 10101 the pattern is found twice.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module seq101 (
    input  wire clk,
    input  wire reset,
    input  wire in,
    output wire found
);
    localparam S0 = 2'd0,      // nothing useful seen yet
               S1 = 2'd1,      // last bit was 1
               S10 = 2'd2,     // last two bits were 1, 0
               S101 = 2'd3;    // last three bits were 1, 0, 1

    reg [1:0] state;
    reg [1:0] next;

    always @(*) begin
        case (state)
            S0:      next = in ? S1   : S0;
            S1:      next = in ? S1   : S10;
            S10:     next = in ? S101 : S0;
            default: next = in ? S1   : S10;     // S101
        endcase
    end

    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (reset)
            state <= S0;
        else
            state <= next;
    end

    assign found = (state == S101);
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
10–13localparam S0 = 2'd0, S1 = 2'd1, S10 = 2'd2, S101 = 2'd3;Names for the four state codes.Readable code; the encoding is in one place.
15–16reg [1:0] state; reg [1:0] next;The 2-bit state register and the next-state value.2 bits hold 4 codes.
18–25always @(*) begin case (state) S0: next = in ? S1 : S0; ...Next-state logic: one line per row of the state table.Every state assigns next for both inputs, so no latch is inferred (F1-16).
23default: next = in ? S1 : S10; // S101The last state, written as default.Covers every code the register can hold.
27–32always @(posedge clk) ... state <= next;The state register, with synchronous reset to S0.One step per clock edge.
34assign found = (state == S101);Output logic from the state only.That makes this a Moore machine.

Listing 2 — seq101_tb.v

// Feed a fixed bit string into seq101 and compare found with a direct check of the
// last three bits.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module seq101_tb;
    reg         clk = 0;
    reg         reset = 1;
    reg         in = 0;
    wire        found;
    reg  [19:0] bits = 20'b1010_1100_1011_0101_0010;   // sent left bit first
    reg  [2:0]  last3 = 3'b000;
    integer     i;
    integer     errors = 0;

    seq101 dut (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .in(in), .found(found));

    always #5 clk = ~clk;

    initial begin
        @(posedge clk);
        #1 reset = 0;
        $display(" i in last3 found");
        for (i = 19; i >= 0; i = i - 1) begin
            in = bits[i];
            @(posedge clk);
            last3 = {last3[1:0], in};
            #1;
            if (found)
                $display("%2d  %b   %b    %b  <- 101", 19 - i, in, last3, found);
            else
                $display("%2d  %b   %b    %b", 19 - i, in, last3, found);
            if (found !== (last3 == 3'b101))
                errors = errors + 1;
        end
        if (errors == 0)
            $display("RESULT: PASS (found = 1 exactly when the last three bits were 101)");
        else
            $display("RESULT: FAIL (%0d mismatches)", errors);
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
9–10reg [19:0] bits = 20'b1010_1100_1011_0101_0010; reg [2:0] last3The 20 test bits (underscores only group digits) and a 3-bit history.The history is the independent model.
22–26in = bits[i]; @(posedge clk); last3 = {last3[1:0], in}; #1;Applies one bit per cycle, shifts it into the history at the edge, then waits.A shift register as a reference (F1-17).
31–32if (found !== (last3 == 3'b101)) errors = errors + 1;found must be 1 exactly when the history is 101.Checks the definition, not a hand-written list.
