Listing 3 — traffic_light.v

// Traffic light for a crossing of a main road (north-south, NS) and a side road
// (east-west, EW). A Moore state machine: the lights depend only on the state.
// The side road gets green only when a car is waiting there (sensor car_ew = 1).
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module traffic_light (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       reset,
    input  wire       car_ew,     // 1 while a car waits on the side road
    output reg  [1:0] ns,         // light of the main road
    output reg  [1:0] ew,         // light of the side road
    output reg  [2:0] state
);
    // light colours
    localparam RED = 2'd0, YELLOW = 2'd1, GREEN = 2'd2;
    // states
    localparam NS_GREEN  = 3'd0,
               NS_YELLOW = 3'd1,
               ALL_RED_1 = 3'd2,
               EW_GREEN  = 3'd3,
               EW_YELLOW = 3'd4,
               ALL_RED_2 = 3'd5;
    // how many clock cycles each state lasts (at least)
    localparam T_GREEN_NS = 4'd6, T_GREEN_EW = 4'd4, T_YELLOW = 4'd2, T_ALL_RED = 4'd1;

    reg [3:0] timer;      // clock cycles spent in the current state
    reg [2:0] next;

    // next-state logic (combinational)
    always @(*) begin
        next = state;                                  // default: stay
        case (state)
            NS_GREEN:  if (timer >= T_GREEN_NS - 1 && car_ew) next = NS_YELLOW;
            NS_YELLOW: if (timer >= T_YELLOW - 1)   next = ALL_RED_1;
            ALL_RED_1: if (timer >= T_ALL_RED - 1)  next = EW_GREEN;
            EW_GREEN:  if (timer >= T_GREEN_EW - 1) next = EW_YELLOW;
            EW_YELLOW: if (timer >= T_YELLOW - 1)   next = ALL_RED_2;
            ALL_RED_2: if (timer >= T_ALL_RED - 1)  next = NS_GREEN;
            default:   next = ALL_RED_1;               // unknown code: go to a safe state
        endcase
    end

    // state register and timer (sequential)
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (reset) begin
            state <= ALL_RED_2;
            timer <= 4'd0;
        end else begin
            state <= next;
            timer <= (next == state && timer != 4'd15) ? timer + 4'd1 : 4'd0;
        end
    end

    // output logic (combinational, from the state only: Moore)
    always @(*) begin
        ns = RED;
        ew = RED;
        case (state)
            NS_GREEN:  ns = GREEN;
            NS_YELLOW: ns = YELLOW;
            EW_GREEN:  ew = GREEN;
            EW_YELLOW: ew = YELLOW;
            default:   ;                               // all-red states
        endcase
    end
endmodule

Listing 4 — traffic_tb.v

// Self-checking testbench for a traffic light: compile with -DDUT=traffic_light
// (or with the forensic evidence, -DDUT=traffic_bug). It prints one line per clock
// cycle and checks three safety rules at every cycle.
`timescale 1ns/1ns
module traffic_tb;
    reg        clk = 0;
    reg        reset = 1;
    reg        car_ew = 0;
    wire [1:0] ns;
    wire [1:0] ew;
    wire [2:0] state;
    integer    cycle;
    integer    errors = 0;
    reg  [1:0] ns_before = 2'd0;
    reg  [1:0] ew_before = 2'd0;

    `DUT dut (.clk(clk), .reset(reset), .car_ew(car_ew), .ns(ns), .ew(ew), .state(state));

    always #5 clk = ~clk;

    function [7:0] colour;            // one letter per light: R, Y or G
        input [1:0] light;
        colour = (light == 2'd0) ? "R" : (light == 2'd1) ? "Y" : (light == 2'd2) ? "G" : "?";
    endfunction

    initial begin
        $display("cycle car_ew state  NS EW");
        for (cycle = 0; cycle < 40; cycle = cycle + 1) begin
            reset  = (cycle < 2);
            // cars arrive on the side road in cycles 4-13 and 27-31
            car_ew = (cycle >= 4 && cycle <= 13) || (cycle >= 27 && cycle <= 31);
            @(posedge clk);
            #1;
            $write("%5d    %b     %0d    %s  %s", cycle, car_ew, state, colour(ns), colour(ew));
            // rule 1: never green or yellow on both roads at once
            if (ns != 2'd0 && ew != 2'd0) begin
                $write("   <-- both roads open");
                errors = errors + 1;
            end
            // rule 2: a green light may only turn into yellow (never straight to red)
            if ((ns_before == 2'd2 && ns == 2'd0) || (ew_before == 2'd2 && ew == 2'd0)) begin
                $write("   <-- green went straight to red");
                errors = errors + 1;
            end
            // rule 3: a road may turn green only after a cycle in which both were red
            if (!reset && ((ns == 2'd2 && ns_before != 2'd2 && ew_before != 2'd0) ||
                           (ew == 2'd2 && ew_before != 2'd2 && ns_before != 2'd0))) begin
                $write("   <-- green without an all-red cycle first");
                errors = errors + 1;
            end
            $write("\n");
            ns_before = ns;
            ew_before = ew;
        end
        if (errors == 0)
            $display("RESULT: PASS (40 cycles, no safety rule broken)");
        else
            $display("RESULT: FAIL (%0d safety rule violations)", errors);
        $finish(0);
    end
endmodule
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
17`DUT dut (...);The design's name comes from -DDUT=....The same safety test runs on the forensic evidence.
21–24function [7:0] colour; ...Turns a light code into a letter R, Y or G.Readable output.
29–31reset = (cycle < 2); car_ew = ...;Reset for two cycles; cars in cycles 4–13 and 27–31.Exercises both "car waiting" and "no car".
35–50three if blocksRule 1: never both roads open. Rule 2: green never goes straight to red. Rule 3: green only after an all-red cycle.Safety properties checked at every cycle.
52–53ns_before = ns; ew_before = ew;Remembers this cycle's lights for the next cycle's checks.Rules 2 and 3 compare two cycles.

Where the analogy breaks

  • Mei can improvise; an FSM cannot. If something happens that the rule card does not mention, Mei uses common sense. An FSM does exactly what its next-state logic says, including for inputs and states nobody thought about. That is why Step 3 of the method demands an arrow for every input in every state.
  • The status card holds a word; the state register holds bits. A word cannot be "too long for the card" without someone noticing. A state code that does not fit in the register is silently cut, as the forensic lab shows R3.
  • One order, one card; one machine, one state. Mei tracks many orders at once with many cards. One FSM is in exactly one state at a time; many orders would need many FSMs (or a bigger state).

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
States are skipped or reached from nowhere (forensic lab).State register narrower than the state codes.Read compiler warnings; print the state each cycle; count codes vs bits.Width ⌈log2 n⌉ at least; declare widths once.
The machine "remembers" in odd ways between edges.Next-state block without a default: an inferred latch.Synthesis log "Latch inferred" (F1-16).next = state; at the top of the block.
The output is one cycle later than expected.A Moore machine answers after the edge.Trace the diagram cycle by cycle.Expected; use a Mealy output if the same-cycle answer is required.
The pattern is not found when patterns overlap (10101 gives one detection).Wrong arrows out of the final state.Trace 10101 by hand.From S101 go to the state that matches the useful tail (S1 or S10).
The machine is stuck after power-up.No reset, or reset to an illegal code.The first lines of the trace.Reset to a legal, safe state.
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-17 built counters (FSMs with "+1" as their only rule) and F1-18 fixed the rhythm with the clock. What carries over: one register on one clock, one step per edge, and combinational logic between edges that must finish within the period D1. What changes: the next-state rule is now any logic you design from a description in words, so the hard part moves from building to specifying: naming states, covering every input in every state, and testing properties. What comes next: F1-20 stores not one state but many words, in SRAM and DRAM memory cells.

Check yourself

  1. Name the three parts of an FSM and say which of them are combinational.
  2. An FSM has 9 states. How many flip-flops does binary encoding need? One-hot?
  3. Is the traffic light of Listing 3 a Moore or a Mealy machine? Point to the lines that decide it.
  4. Trace the 101 detector (Figure 2) on the input bits 1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1. In which cycles is found = 1?
  5. Explain in your own words why the arrows leaving S101 do not both go back to S0.
  6. Apply it to a new case: design (states, diagram, table) a Moore machine with input coin that sets output open to 1 for one cycle after it has seen two coins (two cycles with coin = 1, not necessarily one after the other), and then starts again.
  7. Predict, then run: if car_ew stays 0 for the whole test (edit line 31 of Listing 4), which states will the run show after reset? Does the test still pass?

Lab

Goal

Build a traffic-light state machine from its word description and prove with a self-checking testbench that it never breaks three safety rules.

Hardware and software needed

No hardware. Icarus Verilog ("Icarus Verilog version 12.0 (stable)" in the recorded runs) R2.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use. (This simulated controller must never be used for real traffic: see the unverified box in Layer 3.)

Steps

  1. Cover Listing 3. From the words in Worked example 2, draw your own diagram and state table.
  2. Write your own my_light.v with the same ports as Listing 3 (module name my_light).
  3. Test it with the course testbench: iverilog -g2005 -Wall -DDUT=my_light -o my.vvp traffic_tb.v my_light.v && vvp -n my.vvp.
  4. Fix your design until it prints RESULT: PASS with no compiler warnings. Then compare with Listing 3.
  5. Run the official lab: university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-19.

Expected observations

For the reference design: after reset (state 5, all red), NS green from cycle 2; when cars arrive at cycle 4, NS stays green until it has been green 6 cycles, then yellow at cycle 8, all red at 10, EW green at 11–14, and so on; RESULT: PASS (40 cycles, no safety rule broken) R2.

Verification

The milestone of this lab is the testbench's three safety rules at every one of 40 cycles, plus your own extra test with a different car pattern (for example cars only in cycles 20–25). No compiler warnings.

Troubleshooting

  • "green went straight to red" → a missing yellow state, or a wrong arrow → compare your table with the words.
  • A compiler warning about port widths → your state output is not 3 bits wide → read the forensic lab before you ignore it.
  • NS never turns yellow → the condition needs both timer and car_ew; check the timer is cleared on every state change and counts otherwise.

Extension

Add a pedestrian button: when pressed, the next all-red phase lasts 3 cycles instead of 1. Add a fourth safety rule to the testbench.

Forensic lab

Scenario: "The yellow that never came"

Kofi had an older four-state traffic light without all-red phases. He added ALL_RED_1 and ALL_RED_2 and renumbered the states. In the simulator the side road's light jumps from green straight to red, and the main road turns green in the same cycle. Kofi says "the testbench is too strict". Find out what is wrong.

Questions

  1. Which states does the run show? Which of the six states never appear?
  2. After reset, the reference design is in state 5. Which state is Kofi's design in, and what lights does that state show?
  3. Read the compiler's warning. What does it tell you about the width of Kofi's state signal?
  4. State two hypotheses ("the testbench is too strict"; something in the design) and the evidence that decides.
  5. Explain the mechanism: what happens to the codes 4 (EW_YELLOW) and 5 (ALL_RED_2) when they are stored in Kofi's register?
  6. Give the fix and a rule that prevents this kind of error.

Method hints

List the codes that appear in the "state" column. Convert 4 and 5 to binary and keep only the bits Kofi's register can hold. Then open traffic_bug.v and compare its declarations with Listing 3, lines 11 and 26.

Mini-project

Design an FSM from a word description (practice for the course's practical exam). A vending machine accepts one input coin (1 = a coin arrived this cycle) and one input cancel. After three coins it sets vend = 1 for one cycle and starts again. If cancel is 1, it sets refund = 1 for one cycle (only if at least one coin was inserted) and starts again. Coin and cancel never arrive in the same cycle. Deliver: states with meanings, diagram, table, Verilog, and a self-checking testbench with at least 30 cycles that includes cancel with zero coins.

Rubric (10 points): states and table complete, an arrow for every input in every state (3); Verilog in three blocks with reset and default (2); testbench self-checking with an independent model or properties (3); the zero-coin cancel case handled and tested (2).

Summary

  • An FSM is a state register plus next-state logic plus output logic, all on one clock.
  • Moore outputs depend on the state only; Mealy outputs also on the current inputs.
  • Method: inputs and outputs → what must be remembered (states) → diagram with every arrow → table → encoding → three Verilog blocks → self-checking test.
  • n states need ⌈log2 n⌉ bits in binary encoding; check the register width.
  • Long-lasting states use a timer counter that is cleared on every state change.
  • Give every block a default and every illegal code a safe next state.
  • Test safety properties at every cycle, not only a fixed expected trace.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Next-state logic (combinational), state register (sequential: flip-flops), output logic (combinational).
  2. Binary: 4 flip-flops (23 = 8 is too few, 24 = 16 is enough). One-hot: 9.
  3. Moore: the output block (lines 54–64) reads only state, never car_ew.
  4. States after each bit: S1, S1, S10, S101 (found), S1, S10, S101 (found). found = 1 after the 4th and the 7th bit.
  5. A good answer: the last bit of a found pattern is a 1, which is also a possible first bit of the next pattern. Going back to S0 would forget it, and overlapping patterns like 10101 would be found only once.
  6. States: IDLE (no coin), ONE (one coin seen), OPEN (output open = 1). IDLE: coin → ONE, else IDLE. ONE: coin → OPEN, else ONE. OPEN: coin → ONE (that coin counts as the first of the next pair), else IDLE. Output open = 1 only in OPEN. (Choosing "OPEN → IDLE always" is also acceptable if your description says coins during OPEN are ignored; say which.)
  7. After reset: ALL_RED_2, then NS_GREEN forever (the timer stops at 15 and NS waits for a car). No rule is broken, so the test still passes; but it no longer exercises the EW states, which is why the official test includes cars.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: only states 0–3 appear; after reset the machine shows state 1 (NS yellow) instead of 5 (all red); from state 3 (EW green) it jumps to state 0 (NS green): EW goes green → red with no yellow and NS goes red → green with no all-red cycle, at cycles 8 and 37 R3. The compiler warns: "Port 6 (state) of traffic_bug expects 2 bits, got 3" R3. Hypotheses: (1) the testbench is too strict: ruled out, because the reference design passes the same testbench R2 and the violations are real safety problems; (2) the design cannot hold some states: confirmed. Root cause: traffic_bug.v still declares the old 2-bit widths: output reg [1:0] state and reg [1:0] next (Listing 3 has [2:0] on lines 11 and 26). Six states need 3 bits. Storing 4 (binary 100) keeps only 00, so EW_YELLOW becomes NS_GREEN; storing 5 (101) keeps 01, so the reset state ALL_RED_2 becomes NS_YELLOW. Fix: widen both declarations to [2:0]; the testbench then passes, as the reference does. Prevention: treat every compiler warning as an error (the lab script does this for its own designs); derive register widths from the number of states in one place; print the state in every testbench; check that every state appears at least once in a test (state coverage). How the evidence was made: Listing 3 with the two width declarations changed back to [1:0] and the module renamed, run with the unchanged testbench. Wrong answers: "the timer is wrong" (the timer works; the yellow state cannot exist at all); "the default branch is missing" (it is there, but codes 6 and 7 are not the problem: the register cannot hold codes 4 and 5).

Story hook

Yuki has recently started as a cook in a busy restaurant. On her first evening she notices something odd. The waiters never shout "make something nice with fish". They clip small tickets to a rail above the stove, and every ticket uses the same few words in the same order: an action, then where to put the result, then what to use. "GRILL 2 salmon", "PLATE 4 from-grill". The head chef reads each ticket and does exactly what it says, nothing more.

Yuki asks why the tickets are so strict. The head chef laughs. "Because then anyone can write them. The waiters, the owner, the new tablet system at the front desk. They all write the same language, and I never have to guess." Later Yuki learns that the restaurant across the street has a bigger kitchen with two stoves, but uses the very same ticket language. A waiter can move from one restaurant to the other and keep writing tickets the same way.

A processor works like that head chef. The list of words it understands, and the exact way each one is written, is called its instruction set architecture. This chapter is about that language: what is in it, how it is written as bits, and why three real families of processors chose different languages.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what an instruction set architecture (ISA) is and why it separates software from the hardware that runs it.
  • Encode and decode instructions of the university's 16-bit teaching ISA, U16, by hand: opcode, register fields and signed immediate.
  • Write a short U16 program in assembly and in machine code, assemble it and run it.
  • Compare real x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V machine code produced by real compilers, and point out fixed-length and variable-length encodings in it.
  • Diagnose a hand-encoded program that never stops by decoding its machine words field by field.
Jargon box
Instruction set architecture (ISA)
Simple words: the complete list of commands a processor understands, and the exact rules for writing each one. Analogy: the restaurant's ticket language that every waiter writes and the head chef reads. Precise: the interface between software and hardware: the instructions, their encodings, the registers and memory model visible to programs, and what each instruction does to that visible state. Different hardware designs can implement the same ISA. D1 D2
Instruction
Simple words: one command for the processor, such as "add these two numbers". Analogy: one ticket on the rail. Precise: one operation defined by the ISA, stored in memory as a binary pattern that the processor fetches, decodes and executes. D1
Machine code
Simple words: instructions written as the bit patterns the processor really reads. Analogy: the ticket written in the kitchen's short codes. Precise: the binary encoding of a program's instructions as defined by an ISA. D1
Assembly language
Simple words: machine code written with short words and numbers so people can read it. Analogy: the ticket read aloud: "grill two salmon". Precise: a textual form of machine instructions, one line per instruction, using mnemonics such as add and register names; an assembler translates it into machine code. D1 D3
Opcode
Simple words: the part of an instruction that says which command it is. Analogy: the action word at the start of a ticket. Precise: the field of an instruction encoding that selects the operation; in U16 it is bits 15–12. D1 R1
Register (CPU)
Simple words: a tiny, very fast storage place inside the processor that holds one value. Analogy: the chef's hands and cutting board. Precise: a named storage element that is part of the ISA's visible state; instructions name registers as sources and destinations. U16 has eight 16-bit registers, r0 to r7, and r0 always reads as 0. D1 R1 (The registers built from flip-flops in F1-17 are how hardware implements them.)
Immediate
Simple words: a small number written inside the instruction itself. Analogy: "add 2 pinches of salt": the 2 is on the ticket, not fetched from a shelf. Precise: a constant operand encoded in an instruction field; U16 stores it as a 6-bit two's-complement number, so it ranges from −32 to 31. D1 R1
Program counter (PC)
Simple words: the number that says which instruction comes next. Analogy: the clip on the ticket rail that marks the next ticket. Precise: a register holding the address of the instruction being fetched; it normally advances to the next instruction, and branches change it. D1
Assembler
Simple words: a program that turns assembly text into machine code. Analogy: the front-desk tablet that turns a spoken order into the kitchen's short codes. Precise: a translator from assembly language to machine code that also resolves labels into addresses or offsets. D3

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows where the ISA sits. Above it are programs and compilers; below it are the many possible circuits that can carry it out. Everything above the line only needs to know the ISA; everything below the line only needs to obey it.

Figure 2 zooms into one instruction word of U16. Sixteen bits are cut into fields. The first four bits always hold the opcode; what the other twelve bits mean depends on the opcode.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A processor cannot understand English, or C++, or even "add five numbers". It understands a short, fixed list of tiny commands. Each command does one small thing: add two numbers, copy a number from memory, jump back to an earlier command. That list, together with the exact way each command is written, is the processor's language.

Think of the restaurant tickets. The head chef understands perhaps a dozen action words. A whole dinner for a big table is many tickets, each with one action. The waiter's job is to break a wish ("a birthday dinner for six") into those simple tickets. In a computer, the compiler is that waiter: it breaks your C++ into simple instructions.

Every instruction is stored as a row of bits. A few bits say which command it is; other bits say which registers to use, or hold a small number. The processor reads the bits, works out the command, and does it. Then it moves on to the next one, marked by a pointer called the program counter.

The best part of having a fixed language is freedom below it. A small, cheap processor and a huge, fast one can understand exactly the same instructions. They carry them out in different ways, like a small kitchen and a big kitchen reading the same tickets.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

What an ISA defines

An instruction set architecture is the part of a computer's design that a programmer, a compiler writer or an operating system writer must know. It defines the instructions, how each is encoded in binary, the registers that programs can name, how memory is addressed, and the effect of every instruction on that visible state. D1 D2 It deliberately leaves out how the effect is achieved: how many steps an addition takes inside, whether instructions overlap, how big the caches are. Those choices belong to the microarchitecture, the particular hardware design that implements the ISA. D1

This split is why one compiled program can run on a whole family of processors from different years: they implement the same ISA with different microarchitectures. D1 It is also why the next six chapters can build three very different U16 machines (single-cycle, pipelined, superscalar models) and run the same programs on all of them with the same answers.

U16: the university's teaching ISA

Real ISAs have hundreds of pages of rules. To learn the ideas, this course uses a tiny ISA designed for it, called U16, in the spirit of the small teaching machines in "The Elements of Computing Systems" and the MIPS and RISC-V subsets in the Patterson and Hennessy and Harris and Harris textbooks. D1 D2 D3 Everything about U16 is defined by our own code in Listing 1, so every statement about U16 in this course can be checked against a program that really ran. R1

  • Words and registers. Every instruction and every data value is 16 bits. There are eight registers, r0 to r7. Register r0 always reads 0, and writing to it has no effect; this gives programs a free constant zero. R1
  • Memory. Instructions live in an instruction memory; data lives in a separate data memory of 256 words, addressed by word number. Keeping the two apart (a "Harvard" arrangement) keeps the datapath of F1-24 simple. R1 D1
  • Load/store. Only lw (load word) and sw (store word) touch data memory. Arithmetic works only on registers. This is the load/store style used by RISC-V and ARM64; x86-64 also allows memory operands in arithmetic instructions, as you will see in the real compiler output below. D1 R3
  • Twelve instructions. add, sub, and, or, slt (set if less than) work on two registers; addi adds an immediate; lw and sw move data; beq and bne branch when two registers are equal or not equal; out sends a register to an output port; halt stops. R1

Encoding: from fields to a 16-bit word

Every U16 instruction has a 4-bit opcode in bits 15–12. R-type instructions then hold three 3-bit register numbers: the destination rd and the sources rs and rt. I-type instructions replace rt and the unused bits by a 6-bit signed immediate. Three bits are enough to name eight registers, because 23 = 8. Six bits in two's complement give the range −32 to 31 (F0-24). R1

Encoding is shifting each field into place and combining with OR; decoding is shifting back and masking, exactly the masks and shifts of F0-25. Lines 31–57 of Listing 1 do this. For example, add r3, r3, r4 has op = 1, rd = 3, rs = 3, rt = 4, so the word is (1 << 12) | (3 << 9) | (3 << 6) | (4 << 3) = 4096 + 1536 + 192 + 32 = 5856 = 0x16E0, which is what the lab run printed. R1

Branches use PC-relative offsets: bne r2, r0, loop stores the distance from the instruction after the branch to the label, not the label's address. In the sum program, the branch is at address 7 and loop is at address 3, so the offset is 3 − (7 + 1) = −5. R1 Real ISAs also use PC-relative branches, which lets code run correctly wherever it is placed in memory. D1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Designing an ISA is a series of trade-offs that every later chapter will feel. D1 D2

  • Fixed versus variable length. Fixed-length instructions (U16's 16 bits; ARM64's 32 bits) make fetch and decode simple: the next instruction always starts a fixed distance away. Variable-length instructions (x86-64) can be denser but make finding instruction boundaries harder. RISC-V's base instructions are 32 bits, and an optional compressed extension adds 16-bit forms; the real RISC-V output in this chapter's lab contains both lengths. D4 D5 D6 R3
  • Field positions. U16 keeps rs in the same bits in every format, so the register file can start reading it before the opcode is fully decoded. RISC-V is designed with the same idea of keeping register fields in fixed places. D6 D2
  • Immediate width. Six bits are cheap but small: U16 needs two instructions to build the constant 50 (the forensic program of F1-27 does exactly that). Real ISAs offer wider immediates and special instructions to build large constants. D1
  • The zero register. U16's r0, like RISC-V's x0, always reads zero; it turns "copy" into add rd, rs, r0 and "unconditional branch" into beq r0, r0, label, so the ISA needs fewer opcodes. D6 R1
  • Unused encodings. Opcodes 12–15 are unused in U16. Our machine treats them as halt (line 93 of Listing 1); a real ISA specifies what happens, usually an exception for an undefined instruction, which the operating system handles (F1-42). D1
Not verified — check before relying on this

Register counts and widths of the real ISAs (for example how many general-purpose registers x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V programs can name) are not quoted in this chapter, because no manual could be opened in this build. The register names that appear in the lab's real disassembly (edi, eax on x86-64; w0, x1 on ARM64; a0, a5 on RISC-V) are evidence that those names exist, not a complete list. Check: Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual, Volume 1 (basic execution environment); Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile (A64 registers); The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I (programmers' model of the base integer ISA).

How the hardware actually does it

In hardware, decoding is wiring plus a little logic. The four opcode bits drive a decoder (F1-12) whose outputs become control signals; the three register fields go straight to the address inputs of the register file built from the registers of F1-17; the immediate bits go through a sign-extension circuit that copies bit 5 into the upper bits. D1 D2 Nothing "reads" the instruction the way you read a sentence: the bits are electrical signals that steer multiplexers and select ALU operations, all in parallel. F1-24 draws that datapath and F1-25 builds its control unit in Verilog.

Worked example

Task. Encode addi r2, r2, -1 and bne r2, r0, loop (at address 7, with loop at address 3) by hand, then decode the word 0xA43B to check.

  1. addi: fields. op = 6 (0110), rd = 2 (010), rs = 2 (010), imm = −1.
  2. Immediate in 6-bit two's complement. +1 is 000001; invert to 111110; add 1 to get 111111. So −1 = 111111.
  3. Join the fields. 0110 010 010 111111 → regroup into nibbles: 0110 0100 1011 1111 = 0x64BF.
  4. bne: fields. op = 10 (1010), rd = 2 (010), rs = 0 (000), offset = 3 − (7 + 1) = −5.
  5. −5 in 6 bits. +5 = 000101; invert: 111010; add 1: 111011.
  6. Join. 1010 010 000 111011 → 1010 0100 0011 1011 = 0xA43B.
  7. Decode check. 0xA43B: top nibble 1010 = 10 = bne; next three bits 010 = r2; next 000 = r0; last six 111011: bit 5 is 1, so the value is 59 − 64 = −5. Target = 7 + 1 + (−5) = 3. Correct.

Both words match the listing printed by the real run of Listing 2 (addresses 6 and 7). R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — u16.h: the whole U16 ISA in one header. It is long because it also contains the assembler and the machine used by the next six chapters; this chapter focuses on sections 1, 2, 4 and 5.

// u16.h - U16, the university's 16-bit teaching instruction set (HW202, chapter F1-23).
// One header holds the whole ISA: encoding, decoding, control signals, an assembler,
// a disassembler and a machine that executes one instruction per call (single-cycle).
// Later labs (F1-24 to F1-29) include this same file, so every chapter uses one ISA.
#pragma once
#include <array>
#include <cstdint>
#include <istream>
#include <sstream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

namespace u16
{

// ---- 1. Opcodes: the 4 high bits of every instruction word ----------------------------
enum Op : unsigned { HALT = 0, ADD, SUB, AND, OR, SLT, ADDI, LW, SW, BEQ, BNE, OUT };
const std::array<const char*, 12> kNames = {"halt", "add", "sub", "and", "or", "slt",
                                            "addi", "lw", "sw", "beq", "bne", "out"};

// ---- 2. Instruction formats -------------------------------------------------------------
//  R-type  | op:4 | rd:3 | rs:3 | rt:3 | 000 |      add sub and or slt
//  I-type  | op:4 | rd:3 | rs:3 |   imm:6     |      addi lw sw beq bne  (imm is signed)
//  X-type  | op:4 | rd:3 |  000000000        |      out halt
struct Fields
{
    unsigned op, rd, rs, rt;
    int imm;  // sign-extended from 6 bits: -32 .. 31
};

inline Fields decode(std::uint16_t w)
{
    Fields f{};
    f.op = (w >> 12) & 0xFu;
    f.rd = (w >> 9) & 0x7u;
    f.rs = (w >> 6) & 0x7u;
    f.rt = (w >> 3) & 0x7u;
    f.imm = static_cast<int>(w & 0x3Fu);
    if (f.imm & 0x20) {
        f.imm -= 64;  // bit 5 is the sign bit of the 6-bit two's-complement field
    }
    return f;
}

inline bool isRType(unsigned op) { return op >= ADD && op <= SLT; }
inline bool isIType(unsigned op) { return op >= ADDI && op <= BNE; }

inline std::uint16_t encodeR(unsigned op, unsigned rd, unsigned rs, unsigned rt)
{
    return static_cast<std::uint16_t>((op << 12) | (rd << 9) | (rs << 6) | (rt << 3));
}

inline std::uint16_t encodeI(unsigned op, unsigned rd, unsigned rs, int imm)
{
    const unsigned field = static_cast<unsigned>(imm) & 0x3Fu;  // keep the low 6 bits
    return static_cast<std::uint16_t>((op << 12) | (rd << 9) | (rs << 6) | field);
}

// ---- 3. Control signals: what the control unit (F1-25) sets for each opcode -------------
enum class Alu { Add, Sub, And, Or, Slt };
const std::array<const char*, 5> kAluNames = {"add", "sub", "and", "or", "slt"};

struct Control
{
    bool regWrite;   // write the result into register rd
    bool aluSrcImm;  // ALU input B is the immediate (1) or the second register read (0)
    bool readRdAsB;  // second register read port uses field rd (1) or field rt (0)
    bool memRead;    // load: read data memory
    bool memWrite;   // store: write data memory
    bool memToReg;   // value written to rd comes from memory (1) or from the ALU (0)
    bool branchEq;   // beq: take the branch when the ALU result is zero
    bool branchNe;   // bne: take the branch when the ALU result is not zero
    bool out;        // out: send the second register read to the output port
    bool halt;       // halt: stop the machine
    Alu alu;         // which operation the ALU performs
};

inline Control control(unsigned op)
{
    Control c{false, false, false, false, false, false, false, false, false, false, Alu::Add};
    switch (op) {
    case ADD: c.regWrite = true; c.alu = Alu::Add; break;
    case SUB: c.regWrite = true; c.alu = Alu::Sub; break;
    case AND: c.regWrite = true; c.alu = Alu::And; break;
    case OR:  c.regWrite = true; c.alu = Alu::Or;  break;
    case SLT: c.regWrite = true; c.alu = Alu::Slt; break;
    case ADDI: c.regWrite = true; c.aluSrcImm = true; break;
    case LW: c.regWrite = true; c.aluSrcImm = true; c.memRead = true; c.memToReg = true; break;
    case SW: c.aluSrcImm = true; c.readRdAsB = true; c.memWrite = true; break;
    case BEQ: c.readRdAsB = true; c.branchEq = true; c.alu = Alu::Sub; break;
    case BNE: c.readRdAsB = true; c.branchNe = true; c.alu = Alu::Sub; break;
    case OUT: c.readRdAsB = true; c.out = true; break;
    default: c.halt = true; break;  // HALT and the unused opcodes 12..15 stop the machine
    }
    return c;
}

inline std::uint16_t aluCompute(Alu op, std::uint16_t a, std::uint16_t b)
{
    switch (op) {
    case Alu::Add: return static_cast<std::uint16_t>(a + b);  // wraps modulo 2^16
    case Alu::Sub: return static_cast<std::uint16_t>(a - b);
    case Alu::And: return static_cast<std::uint16_t>(a & b);
    case Alu::Or:  return static_cast<std::uint16_t>(a | b);
    case Alu::Slt: return static_cast<std::int16_t>(a) < static_cast<std::int16_t>(b) ? 1 : 0;
    }
    return 0;
}

// ---- 4. Disassembler: machine word -> text ----------------------------------------------
inline std::string disasm(std::uint16_t w)
{
    const Fields f = decode(w);
    std::ostringstream s;
    if (f.op >= kNames.size()) {
        s << "(unused opcode " << f.op << ")";
        return s.str();
    }
    s << kNames[f.op];
    if (isRType(f.op)) {
        s << " r" << f.rd << ", r" << f.rs << ", r" << f.rt;
    } else if (f.op == LW || f.op == SW) {
        s << " r" << f.rd << ", " << f.imm << "(r" << f.rs << ")";
    } else if (isIType(f.op)) {
        s << " r" << f.rd << ", r" << f.rs << ", " << f.imm;
    } else if (f.op == OUT) {
        s << " r" << f.rd;
    }
    return s.str();
}

// ---- 5. Assembler: text -> machine words --------------------------------------------
// Syntax: one instruction per line; "label:" before it is optional; ';' starts a comment.
// ".data 7 3 9" puts words into data memory from address 0. A line that is a hexadecimal
// word such as "0x1234" is taken as machine code as it stands (write your own encodings).
struct Program
{
    std::vector<std::uint16_t> code;
    std::vector<std::uint16_t> data;
    std::vector<std::string> errors;
};

inline std::string clean(std::string s)
{
    const auto semi = s.find(';');
    if (semi != std::string::npos) {
        s.erase(semi);
    }
    for (char& ch : s) {
        if (ch == ',' || ch == '(' || ch == ')' || ch == '\t') {
            ch = ' ';
        }
    }
    return s;
}

inline int parseReg(const std::string& t, bool& ok)
{
    if (t.size() == 2 && t[0] == 'r' && t[1] >= '0' && t[1] <= '7') {
        return t[1] - '0';
    }
    ok = false;
    return 0;
}

inline Program assemble(std::istream& in)
{
    Program p;
    std::vector<std::string> lines;
    std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>> labels;
    std::string line;
    int pc = 0;
    // Pass 1: remember where every label is.
    while (std::getline(in, line)) {
        lines.push_back(line);
        std::istringstream ls(clean(line));
        std::string tok;
        if (!(ls >> tok)) {
            continue;
        }
        if (tok.back() == ':') {
            labels.emplace_back(tok.substr(0, tok.size() - 1), pc);
            if (!(ls >> tok)) {
                continue;
            }
        }
        if (tok != ".data") {
            ++pc;
        }
    }
    auto findLabel = [&labels](const std::string& name, bool& ok) {
        for (const auto& [label, addr] : labels) {
            if (label == name) {
                return addr;
            }
        }
        ok = false;
        return 0;
    };
    // Pass 2: encode every instruction.
    for (std::size_t n = 0; n < lines.size(); ++n) {
        std::istringstream ls(clean(lines[n]));
        std::vector<std::string> t;
        for (std::string tok; ls >> tok;) {
            t.push_back(tok);
        }
        if (!t.empty() && t[0].back() == ':') {
            t.erase(t.begin());
        }
        if (t.empty()) {
            continue;
        }
        bool ok = true;
        const int here = static_cast<int>(p.code.size());
        if (t[0] == ".data") {
            for (std::size_t i = 1; i < t.size(); ++i) {
                p.data.push_back(static_cast<std::uint16_t>(std::stoi(t[i], nullptr, 0)));
            }
            continue;
        }
        if (t[0].rfind("0x", 0) == 0) {
            p.code.push_back(static_cast<std::uint16_t>(std::stoul(t[0], nullptr, 16)));
            continue;
        }
        unsigned op = 0;
        while (op < kNames.size() && t[0] != kNames[op]) {
            ++op;
        }
        std::uint16_t word = 0;
        if (op == kNames.size()) {
            ok = false;
        } else if (isRType(op) && t.size() == 4) {
            const int rd = parseReg(t[1], ok), rs = parseReg(t[2], ok), rt = parseReg(t[3], ok);
            word = encodeR(op, rd, rs, rt);
        } else if ((op == LW || op == SW) && t.size() == 4) {   // lw rd, imm(rs)
            const int rd = parseReg(t[1], ok), rs = parseReg(t[3], ok);
            word = encodeI(op, rd, rs, std::stoi(t[2]));
        } else if (op == ADDI && t.size() == 4) {
            const int rd = parseReg(t[1], ok), rs = parseReg(t[2], ok);
            word = encodeI(op, rd, rs, std::stoi(t[3]));
        } else if ((op == BEQ || op == BNE) && t.size() == 4) { // offset = target - (pc + 1)
            const int rd = parseReg(t[1], ok), rs = parseReg(t[2], ok);
            const int target = findLabel(t[3], ok);
            word = encodeI(op, rd, rs, target - (here + 1));
        } else if (op == OUT && t.size() == 2) {
            word = encodeR(op, parseReg(t[1], ok), 0, 0);
        } else if (op == HALT && t.size() == 1) {
            word = 0;
        } else {
            ok = false;
        }
        if (!ok) {
            p.errors.push_back("line " + std::to_string(n + 1) + ": cannot assemble: " + lines[n]);
        }
        p.code.push_back(word);
    }
    return p;
}

// ---- 6. The machine: state plus one step (fetch, decode, execute, memory, write back) ------
struct Step
{
    int pc;                // address of the instruction executed
    std::uint16_t word;    // the instruction word fetched
    Fields f;              // its fields
    Control c;             // the control signals for it
    std::uint16_t a, b;    // register values read (port A = rs, port B = rt or rd)
    std::uint16_t aluOut;  // ALU result
    bool taken;            // branch taken?
    int nextPc;            // address of the next instruction
    bool wrote;            // did it write a register?
    std::uint16_t value;   // value written to rd (or sent to the output port)
};

struct Machine
{
    std::array<std::uint16_t, 8> reg{};
    std::array<std::uint16_t, 256> mem{};
    std::vector<std::uint16_t> code;
    std::vector<std::uint16_t> output;
    int pc = 0;
    bool halted = false;
    std::string fault;

    explicit Machine(const Program& p) : code(p.code)
    {
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < p.data.size() && i < mem.size(); ++i) {
            mem[i] = p.data[i];
        }
    }

    Step step()
    {
        Step s{};
        s.pc = pc;
        if (pc < 0 || pc >= static_cast<int>(code.size())) {
            fault = "pc " + std::to_string(pc) + " is outside the program";
            halted = true;
            return s;
        }
        s.word = code[static_cast<std::size_t>(pc)];                 // fetch
        s.f = decode(s.word);                                        // decode
        s.c = control(s.f.op);
        s.a = reg[s.f.rs];
        s.b = reg[s.c.readRdAsB ? s.f.rd : s.f.rt];
        const std::uint16_t aluB = s.c.aluSrcImm ? static_cast<std::uint16_t>(s.f.imm) : s.b;
        s.aluOut = aluCompute(s.c.alu, s.a, aluB);                   // execute
        s.value = s.aluOut;
        if (s.c.memRead || s.c.memWrite) {                           // memory
            if (s.aluOut >= mem.size()) {
                fault = "data address " + std::to_string(s.aluOut) + " is outside memory";
                halted = true;
                return s;
            }
            if (s.c.memRead) {
                s.value = mem[s.aluOut];
            } else {
                mem[s.aluOut] = s.b;
            }
        }
        if (s.c.out) {
            output.push_back(s.b);
            s.value = s.b;
        }
        s.taken = (s.c.branchEq && s.aluOut == 0) || (s.c.branchNe && s.aluOut != 0);
        s.nextPc = s.taken ? pc + 1 + s.f.imm : pc + 1;
        if (s.c.regWrite && s.f.rd != 0) {                           // write back
            reg[s.f.rd] = s.value;                                   // r0 always stays 0
            s.wrote = true;
        }
        if (s.c.halt) {
            halted = true;
            s.nextPc = pc;
        }
        pc = s.nextPc;
        return s;
    }
};

}  // namespace u16

Listing 2 — asm_listing.cpp: assemble a program from standard input, print every word in hex and in binary split into fields, then run it.

// F1-23 Listing 2: assemble a U16 program, show every machine word field by field, run it.
#include <bitset>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include "u16.h"

int main()
{
    const u16::Program p = u16::assemble(std::cin);
    for (const std::string& e : p.errors) {
        std::cout << "error: " << e << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "addr  word    op   rd  rs  rest    meaning\n";
    for (std::size_t a = 0; a < p.code.size(); ++a) {
        const std::uint16_t w = p.code[a];
        const std::string bits = std::bitset<16>(w).to_string();
        std::printf("%4zu  0x%04X  %s %s %s %s  %s\n", a, static_cast<unsigned>(w),
                    bits.substr(0, 4).c_str(), bits.substr(4, 3).c_str(),
                    bits.substr(7, 3).c_str(), bits.substr(10, 6).c_str(),
                    u16::disasm(w).c_str());
    }
    u16::Machine m(p);
    long steps = 0;
    while (!m.halted && steps < 10000) {
        m.step();
        ++steps;
    }
    for (const std::uint16_t v : m.output) {
        std::cout << "out: " << static_cast<std::int16_t>(v) << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "instructions executed: " << steps << '\n';
    if (!m.halted) {
        std::cout << "stopped: step limit of 10000 reached (the program did not halt)\n";
    }
    if (!m.fault.empty()) {
        std::cout << "fault: " << m.fault << '\n';
    }
    return p.errors.empty() ? 0 : 1;
}

The program it reads (asm_listing.in) adds five numbers stored in data memory:

; sum.s - add the five numbers stored at data addresses 0..4 and output the sum
        .data 7 3 9 4 6
        addi r1, r0, 0      ; r1 = address of the next number
        addi r2, r0, 5      ; r2 = how many numbers are left
        addi r3, r0, 0      ; r3 = running sum
loop:   lw   r4, 0(r1)      ; r4 = memory[r1]
        add  r3, r3, r4     ; sum = sum + r4
        addi r1, r1, 1      ; move to the next address
        addi r2, r2, -1     ; one number fewer to go
        bne  r2, r0, loop   ; repeat while r2 is not 0
        out  r3             ; send the sum to the output port
        halt

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined asm_listing.cpp -o asm_listing, then ./asm_listing < asm_listing.in.

Real ISAs: the same function in three machine languages

Listing 3 — add3.cc, compiled (not run) for x86-64, ARM64 and RISC-V, then disassembled with each target's objdump. The second column of each output is the machine code in hexadecimal.

// F1-23 Listing 3: one tiny C++ function, compiled for three real ISAs to compare encodings.
int add3(int a, int b, int c)
{
    return a + b + c;
}

long sum(const long* p, long n)
{
    long s = 0;
    for (long i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        s += p[i];
    }
    return s;
}

Read the byte columns. In the x86-64 output, instructions take 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 bytes (c3 is one byte, 66 0f 1f 44 00 00 six). Every ARM64 instruction is four bytes. The RISC-V output mixes four-byte words such as 00b506b3 with two-byte compressed ones such as 9d2d. R3 Notice also that x86-64 adds a value straight from memory (add (%rdi),%rax), while ARM64 and RISC-V first load it into a register (ldr, ld) and then add: the load/store style of U16. R3 The x86 output is in AT&T syntax, the GNU tools' default; F1-31 also shows Intel syntax. C1

Watch out

These objects were compiled and disassembled only. Nothing here was executed on an ARM64 or RISC-V processor: the build container has no such machine and no user-mode emulator (the logs say "not executed"). The U16 program, by contrast, really ran on the U16 machine of Listing 1.

Where the analogy breaks

  • A chef understands meaning; a processor only matches bits. A head chef would notice a ticket that says "grill 2 ice cream" and ask. A processor decodes 0x6481 as addi r2, r2, 1 without any idea that you meant −1. The forensic lab is exactly this failure. R2
  • A ticket language can grow overnight; an ISA cannot change freely. Old programs depend on every encoding, so ISAs are extended (new opcodes, new optional extensions) rather than changed, and unused encodings are reserved for that. D1 D6
  • "Different kitchens, same tickets" hides a cost. Two processors with the same ISA give the same results but not the same speed; how fast a program runs depends on the microarchitecture, which is the subject of the rest of this course. D1

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: a loop never ends. Cause: a negative immediate encoded as positive (for example 000001 instead of 111111). How to find it: disassemble the words and compare each with the intended instruction. Fix: encode negatives in two's complement in the field width. (Forensic lab, R2.)
  • Symptom: a branch lands one instruction off. Cause: offset counted from the branch itself instead of from the next instruction. How to find it: compute target = address + 1 + offset by hand. Fix: offset = target − (address + 1).
  • Symptom: the assembler reports "cannot assemble" for addi r1, r0, 40. Cause: 40 does not fit in −32…31. How to find it: check immediate ranges first. Fix: build the constant in two steps (addi r1, r0, 31 then addi r1, r1, 9). Note that the shown assembler masks the value to 6 bits silently in encodeI; the extension task asks you to add a range check.
  • Symptom: a result that should be stored is always 0. Cause: writing to r0. How to find it: look for rd = r0 in the disassembly. Fix: use another register (see the forensic lab of F1-24).
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-21 and F1-19 described hardware as registers and state machines, and SP101 taught C++ as statements and functions. What carries over: binary, hex, two's complement and masks (MA102); registers as stored state; the idea that a machine follows exact steps. What changes: the "steps" are now a fixed instruction list with exact bit encodings; a wrong bit is a different instruction, not a typo the machine can notice; and the same instructions can be run by very different hardware. D1 What comes next: F1-24 builds the datapath that fetches, decodes and executes these U16 instructions, one per clock cycle.

Check yourself

  1. Which of these is part of an ISA, and which belongs to the microarchitecture? (a) the encoding of add; (b) the number of pipeline stages; (c) which registers a program can name; (d) the size of the cache.
  2. Decode 0x7840 into U16 assembly.
  3. Encode sub r5, r1, r2 as a hex word.
  4. What is the largest and smallest immediate U16's addi can hold, and why?
  5. A beq at address 12 has offset −4. Which address does it jump to when taken?
  6. Explain in your own words why having an ISA lets the same program run on a small and a large processor.
  7. Apply it to a new case: in the real outputs, the x86-64 ret is c3, while ARM64's is d65f03c0. Which ISA has fixed-length instructions, and what does that make easier for the hardware?
  8. Predict, then run: if you change addi r2, r0, 5 to addi r2, r0, 0 in the sum program, what will it output and how many instructions will run? (Hint: the loop body runs before the first test.)

Lab

Goal. Write a U16 program in assembly and in hand-encoded machine code, run both, and compare real compiler output for three real ISAs.

Hardware and software needed. No special hardware. g++ (this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0); for step 5, the cross compilers aarch64-linux-gnu-g++ and riscv64-linux-gnu-g++ with their objdump (versions in the run logs). Lab folder: university/labs/F1-23; run everything with university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-23 from the repository root.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use.

Steps.

  1. Run the lab. Check that asm_listing.out matches the output above (out: 29, 30 instructions).
  2. Write max.s: put four numbers in .data, find the largest with lw, slt and beq, and out it. Run ./asm_listing < max.s (build the tool once with the command shown above).
  3. Hand-encode your max.s into hex words in a file max.hex (one 0x.... per line, data still in a .data line). Do the encoding on paper first.
  4. Run the hex file. Its listing must show exactly the same words as step 2's listing. Any difference is an encoding mistake: decode the word to find it.
  5. Look at real_x86.out, real_arm64.out and real_riscv64.out. For each, count the bytes of every instruction in add3, and find the instruction that returns.

Expected observations. Steps 2–4: identical word listings and the same output value. Step 5: x86-64 lengths vary, ARM64 lengths are all 4 bytes, RISC-V lengths are 2 or 4 bytes (as in the real outputs above). R3

Verification. run_lab.sh finishes with exit status 0; your two listings are identical; your program outputs the maximum for at least three different data sets, including one where the maximum is the first number and one where it is the last.

Troubleshooting.

  • "cannot assemble" → wrong operand count, a register above r7, or a label typo → read the line number in the message.
  • The program outputs a wrong maximum only when the largest number is last → the loop exits one step early → trace it with the datapath tool of F1-24.
  • "stopped: step limit" → a branch offset or sign error → decode the branch word by hand.

Extension. (1) Add a range check to encodeI so that an immediate outside −32…31 is reported as an error instead of silently masked. (2) Write add3 with four parameters and see, in the real outputs, which registers each ISA uses for the fourth argument.

Forensic lab

Scenario. Amara wrote a multiplication program directly in U16 machine code: 6 × 7 by adding 6 seven times. It should print 42. Instead the machine runs until the step limit and prints nothing. She is sure her loop is right "because the assembly in the comments is right".

Evidence pack. Amara's file and the real output of running it with Listing 2 (R2):

; multiply.hex - Amara's hand-encoded program: 6 x 7 by repeated addition (should output 42)
0x6206  ; addi r1, r0, 6
0x6407  ; addi r2, r0, 7
0x6600  ; addi r3, r0, 0
0x16C8  ; loop: add r3, r3, r1
0x6481  ; addi r2, r2, -1
0xA43D  ; bne r2, r0, loop
0xB600  ; out r3
0x0000  ; halt

addr  word    op   rd  rs  rest    meaning
   0  0x6206  0110 001 000 000110  addi r1, r0, 6
   1  0x6407  0110 010 000 000111  addi r2, r0, 7
   2  0x6600  0110 011 000 000000  addi r3, r0, 0
   3  0x16C8  0001 011 011 001000  add r3, r3, r1
   4  0x6481  0110 010 010 000001  addi r2, r2, 1

Questions.

  1. Observation: compare the comment on each line with the disassembly column. Which line differs?
  2. Hypotheses: give two possible causes for "never halts" (for example a wrong branch offset, or a counter that never reaches zero). Which column of the evidence tests each one?
  3. Root cause: decode the faulty word field by field and explain what the machine really does in the loop.
  4. Fix: give the correct hex word and show its encoding.
  5. Prevention: suggest a check that would catch this class of mistake before running.

Method hints. Trust the bits, not the comments. Decode each word in Figure 2's layout. Then ask: does the loop counter move towards zero?

Mini-project

Design an extra instruction. U16 has four unused opcodes (12–15). Propose one new instruction that would make the sum or multiply programs shorter (for example a shift, or a load with post-increment). Write: its format and encoding, its exact effect, a program that uses it, and the changes needed in encodeI/disasm/control/Machine::step. Implement it in a copy of u16.h and show a run.

Rubric. Encoding fully specified and unambiguous (3). Effect defined for every case, including r0 as destination (2). Working run with output (3). One paragraph on the trade-off: what the ISA gains and what it costs the hardware (2).

Summary

  • An ISA is the contract between software and hardware: instructions, encodings, registers, memory and effects.
  • The microarchitecture is how one design implements the ISA; many designs can share one ISA.
  • U16 has 16-bit instructions with a 4-bit opcode, 3-bit register fields and a 6-bit signed immediate.
  • Encoding is shifting fields into place; decoding is shifting and masking; immediates use two's complement.
  • Branches store PC-relative offsets: target = address + 1 + offset in U16.
  • Real compiler output shows variable-length x86-64, fixed 4-byte ARM64, and mixed 2- and 4-byte RISC-V encodings.
  • The processor decodes bits, not intentions: a wrong bit is a different, valid instruction.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. (a) and (c) are ISA: software depends on them. (b) and (d) are microarchitecture: they change speed, not results. A common wrong answer puts the cache in the ISA because programs "use" it; programs get the same results whatever its size.
  2. 0x7840 = 0111 100 001 000000: op 7 = lw, rd = 4, rs = 1, imm = 0 → lw r4, 0(r1) (address 3 of the sum program).
  3. op 2, rd 5, rs 1, rt 2: 0010 101 001 010 000 → 0010 1010 0101 0000 = 0x2A50.
  4. 31 (011111) and −32 (100000): a 6-bit two's-complement field has 26 = 64 values, half of them negative.
  5. 12 + 1 + (−4) = 9. Answering 8 forgets that the offset counts from the next instruction.
  6. Good answers mention: programs are compiled to the ISA's instructions; any processor that implements the ISA executes them with the same effects; the processors differ only in how (and how fast) they do it.
  7. ARM64: every instruction is 4 bytes, so the next instruction's address is always known, and fetch can take whole aligned words and decode several in parallel without first finding where each starts. x86-64 instructions vary in length (1 byte for c3).
  8. The body runs once with r2 = 0, then addi r2, r2, -1 makes r2 = −1, which is not 0, so the loop continues with r2 counting down from −1. It would need about 65,535 more iterations to come back to 0, and it keeps loading from rising addresses: the run stops with a fault when r1 reaches 256 ("data address 256 is outside memory"). Predict, then run it: the point is that "loop body first, test last" loops need a check before entering.

Forensic lab answer key

Root cause. Address 4 holds 0x6481, which decodes as addi r2, r2, 1 (immediate field 000001 = +1), while the comment says −1. The counter goes 7, 8, 9, …, so bne r2, r0 keeps branching. It would only reach 0 after wrapping around 16 bits, tens of thousands of iterations later; the 10,000-step limit stops it first.

Evidence. The listing line "4 0x6481 0110 010 010 000001 addi r2, r2, 1" against the comment "addi r2, r2, -1"; "stopped: step limit of 10000 reached"; no "out:" line.

Fix. −1 in six bits is 111111, so the word is 0110 0100 1011 1111 = 0x64BF. With that word the same program is cpu.in of F1-24, whose real run outputs 42.

How the fault was made. The Lab Engineer encoded the correct program and replaced the immediate field of the fourth word by the magnitude 1 instead of its two's complement.

Wrong answers and why. "The branch offset is wrong": 0xA43D decodes to bne r2, r0, -3, and 5 + 1 − 3 = 3 is the loop start, correct. "The add is wrong": it does not affect termination. Prevention: always assemble from text, or at least run the disassembler over hand-written words and diff it against the intended assembly.

Story hook

At six in the morning, before any guest arrives, Daniel walks Yuki through the empty kitchen. "Follow one ticket," he says. "It always takes the same path." He points: the ticket rail, where the next ticket is taken down. The pass, where someone reads it and calls out what each station must do. The cutting boards beside the stove, where the ingredients for this dish are laid out. The stove itself, where something is combined or cooked. The hatch to the pantry, used only when the ticket needs something stored or fetched. And finally the shelf by the stove where the result is put down, ready for the next ticket that needs it.

"Every ticket walks this road," Daniel says. "Some skip the pantry hatch. Some only move the clip on the rail. But the road is always the same." Yuki draws the road on the back of a menu. It is the same drawing you will make in this chapter, with one change of words: the kitchen becomes a datapath.

What you will be able to do

  • Name the parts of a single-cycle datapath (program counter, instruction memory, register file, sign extension, ALU, data memory, multiplexers) and what each does.
  • Trace any U16 instruction through the datapath, writing down the value on every important wire.
  • Explain why a single-cycle design needs a clock period long enough for the slowest instruction.
  • Run a program you wrote in U16 machine language on the simulated CPU and read its trace.
  • Diagnose a program whose result is always zero from a datapath trace.
Jargon box
Datapath
Simple words: the parts of the processor that hold, move and change data, connected by wires. Analogy: the road one ticket takes through the kitchen: rail, cutting boards, stove, pantry hatch, shelf. Precise: the collection of functional units (ALU, register file, memories, adders, multiplexers) and the connections between them that carry out instructions, steered by control signals. D1 D2
Register file
Simple words: the block that holds all the registers, with doors to read two of them and write one. Analogy: the row of cutting boards beside the stove, each with a number. Precise: an array of registers with (here) two read ports, addressed by register numbers from the instruction, and one write port enabled by a control signal. D1 R1
ALU (arithmetic logic unit)
Simple words: the calculator part: it adds, subtracts, compares and combines bits. Analogy: the stove, where ingredients are combined. Precise: a combinational circuit that computes one of several operations on two inputs, chosen by its operation input (built in F1-14). D2
Multiplexer (mux)
Simple words: a switch that picks one of several inputs to pass on. Analogy: the cook choosing whether the stove gets an ingredient from the board or a measured spoonful written on the ticket. Precise: a combinational selector whose select input, driven by a control signal, chooses which data input reaches the output (F1-12). D2
Sign extension
Simple words: making a short signed number longer without changing its value. Analogy: writing "−1" on a big label instead of a small one: same value, bigger space. Precise: copying the sign bit of an n-bit two's-complement value into all higher bits of a wider word; U16 extends its 6-bit immediate to 16 bits. D1 R1
Single-cycle processor
Simple words: a processor that does a whole instruction in one tick of the clock. Analogy: one cook who walks every ticket along the entire road before taking the next ticket. Precise: a design in which every instruction completes in one clock cycle, so the clock period must cover the longest path through the datapath. D1 D2
Critical path
Simple words: the slowest route signals must travel before the result is ready. Analogy: the longest walk any ticket needs. Precise: the longest combinational delay between two clocked elements; it sets the minimum clock period (F1-15, F1-18). D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 is the U16 single-cycle datapath. It is drawn from left to right in five regions that the next chapters will turn into pipeline stages: instruction fetch (IF), instruction decode and register read (ID), execute (EX), memory access (MEM) and write back (WB). Solid lines carry data; dashed lines carry control signals from the control unit (F1-25).

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Every instruction goes through the same few steps. First the processor fetches it: it looks at the program counter, the bookmark that says which instruction is next, and reads that instruction from memory. Then it decodes it: it splits the bits into the command and the register numbers, and reads the registers the command needs.

Next it executes: the ALU, the processor's calculator, adds or subtracts or compares. If the instruction is a load or a store, the processor then goes to data memory, the pantry, to fetch or put away a value. Last, it writes back the answer into a register, like putting a finished dish on the shelf.

Some instructions skip steps. An add never visits data memory. A store does not write a register. A branch only decides where the bookmark goes next. But the road is always the same, and little switches called multiplexers decide which turnings an instruction takes.

In the simplest processor, all of this happens in one tick of the clock. That is easy to understand, but slow: the tick must be long enough for the longest trip, even when the instruction is short.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

The parts and the wires

The textbook way to build a processor is to first collect the parts each instruction needs, then join them with wires and multiplexers so that every instruction can share them. D1 D2 For U16 the parts are:

  • PC, a 16-bit register (F1-17) holding the address of the current instruction, and an adder that computes PC + 1 (U16 addresses count whole instructions, not bytes). R1
  • Instruction memory: given the PC, it outputs the 16-bit instruction word. D1
  • Register file with two read ports and one write port. Read port A is always addressed by field rs. Read port B is addressed by rt for R-type instructions and by rd for sw, beq, bne and out, which read the register named in that field; a multiplexer controlled by ReadRdAsB chooses. R1
  • Sign extension of the 6-bit immediate to 16 bits. D1
  • ALU with operations add, sub, and, or and slt. A multiplexer controlled by AluSrcImm chooses whether the second ALU input is register B or the immediate. R1
  • Data memory: the ALU result is the address; register B is the data to store. R1
  • Write-back multiplexer controlled by MemToReg: the value written to rd is either the ALU result or the word read from memory; RegWrite decides whether anything is written at all. D1 R1
  • Next-PC logic: for beq/bne the ALU subtracts the two registers; if the zero test matches the branch type, the next PC is PC + 1 + imm, otherwise PC + 1. R1

One instruction, step by step

Lines 292–337 of Listing 1 in F1-23 (Machine::step) are this datapath written in C++, one region after the other: line 301 fetches, lines 302–306 decode and read the registers, line 307 runs the ALU, lines 309–320 access memory, lines 325–326 choose the next PC, and lines 327–330 write back. R1 Listing 1 of this chapter calls step once per cycle and prints the values on the main wires. Take lw r4, 0(r1) at cycle 9 of the trace: A = r1 = 1, the immediate is 0, so the ALU computes 1 + 0 = 1; data memory reads address 1, which holds 3; MemToReg selects the memory value, and r4 becomes 3. R1

The column B in the trace may show a value even for addi. That is not a bug: the register file always reads both ports, because it cannot know in advance whether the value will be needed; the AluSrcImm multiplexer then ignores it. Real datapaths behave the same way: reading is cheap and done in parallel, and multiplexers throw away what is not needed. D1 R1

Why "single-cycle" is slow

In a single-cycle design, all state (PC, registers, data memory) is updated at one clock edge, and between two edges the signals must ripple all the way from the PC through instruction memory, register file, ALU and data memory to the write-back multiplexer. The clock period must therefore be at least the delay of the slowest instruction's path, the load in a typical design, even though an add or a branch finishes earlier. D1 D2 Every instruction pays for the worst one. F1-26 fixes this by cutting the road into stages.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

  • Harvard versus unified memory. U16 has separate instruction and data memories, so one cycle can fetch an instruction and access data at once. With one shared memory, a single-cycle design would need two memory accesses in the same cycle for a load; textbook designs avoid this by assuming separate instruction and data memories (in real processors: separate instruction and data caches in front of one main memory, F1-33). D1 D2
  • Register file timing. The register file is read combinationally during the cycle and written at the clock edge. That is why the instruction can read r3 and write r3 in the same instruction (add r3, r3, r4): it reads the old value during the cycle and the new value appears after the edge (F1-16). D2
  • Word addressing. U16 counts addresses in 16-bit words, so the next instruction is at PC + 1. Byte-addressed ISAs add the instruction size instead; the real RISC-V output in F1-23 shows instructions at byte offsets 0, 2, 6, 8 and so on. R2
  • Multi-cycle alternative. Between single-cycle and pipelined designs lies the multi-cycle design: one instruction at a time, but split into several shorter cycles, so a short instruction uses fewer cycles. It reuses one ALU and one memory across cycles. This course skips it and goes straight to pipelining; D1 and D2 treat it. D1 D2

How the hardware actually does it

Everything in Figure 1 is built from parts you met in HW102 and HW201. The PC and the registers are banks of D flip-flops (F1-16, F1-17) that change only at a clock edge (F1-18). The register file's read ports are multiplexers that pick one register's outputs by number; its write port is a decoder that enables exactly one register. The memories are arrays of storage cells (F1-20). The ALU is the circuit of F1-14, and the adders are ripple-carry or faster adders. Between two clock edges nothing is "stepped": all these circuits compute at once, and the slowest chain of gates sets how soon the next edge may come (F1-15). D2 D3 The simulator steps through the regions in order only because C++ runs line by line; the hardware does them as one wave of signals.

Worked example

Task. Trace bne r2, r0, -5 at address 7 when r2 = 4 (cycle 8 of the trace).

  1. IF. PC = 7. Instruction memory outputs 0xA43B. PC + 1 = 8.
  2. ID. op = 10 (bne), rd = 2, rs = 0, imm = −5. Control sets ReadRdAsB = 1, so read port B uses rd = r2. Port A reads r0 = 0, port B reads r2 = 4. Sign extension turns 111011 into 1111 1111 1111 1011 = −5.
  3. EX. ALU op = sub (control, F1-25). A − B = 0 − 4 = −4. Not zero. Branch adder: 8 + (−5) = 3.
  4. MEM. MemRead = MemWrite = 0: nothing happens.
  5. WB. RegWrite = 0: no register changes.
  6. Next PC. BranchNe = 1 and the ALU result is not zero, so the next PC is the branch target, 3.

The trace line for cycle 8 shows A = 0, B = 4, ALU = −4, next PC 3, "(branch taken)", matching every step. R1 The order of subtraction (A − B = r0 − r2) does not matter for equality, which is all bne needs.

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — datapath.cpp: the datapath tracer. It reuses the U16 machine from F1-23 (Listing 1 there) and prints one line per clock cycle.

// F1-24 Listing 1: run a U16 program one instruction at a time and print what every part
// of the single-cycle datapath did: fetch, decode, register read, ALU, memory, write back.
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>
#include "../F1-23/u16.h"

int main()
{
    const u16::Program p = u16::assemble(std::cin);
    if (!p.errors.empty()) {
        std::cout << p.errors.front() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    u16::Machine m(p);
    std::cout << "cyc  PC  word    instruction        A(rs)  B     ALU    memory      write back"
                 "    next PC\n";
    for (int cycle = 1; !m.halted && cycle <= 60; ++cycle) {
        const u16::Step s = m.step();
        char mem[32] = "-";
        if (s.c.memRead) {
            std::snprintf(mem, sizeof mem, "read [%u]", static_cast<unsigned>(s.aluOut));
        } else if (s.c.memWrite) {
            std::snprintf(mem, sizeof mem, "write [%u]", static_cast<unsigned>(s.aluOut));
        }
        char wb[32] = "-";
        if (s.wrote) {
            std::snprintf(wb, sizeof wb, "r%u = %d", s.f.rd, static_cast<std::int16_t>(s.value));
        } else if (s.c.out) {
            std::snprintf(wb, sizeof wb, "OUT %d", static_cast<std::int16_t>(s.value));
        }
        std::printf("%3d %3d  0x%04X  %-17s %5d %5d %6d    %-10s  %-12s %3d%s\n", cycle, s.pc,
                    static_cast<unsigned>(s.word), u16::disasm(s.word).c_str(),
                    static_cast<std::int16_t>(s.a), static_cast<std::int16_t>(s.b),
                    static_cast<std::int16_t>(s.aluOut), mem, wb, s.nextPc,
                    s.taken ? "  (branch taken)" : "");
    }
    std::cout << "registers:";
    for (std::size_t r = 0; r < m.reg.size(); ++r) {
        std::cout << " r" << r << '=' << static_cast<std::int16_t>(m.reg[r]);
    }
    std::cout << '\n';
    return m.fault.empty() ? 0 : 1;
}

LinesCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–5comments, includesUses ../F1-23/u16.h, the one ISA definition.The tracer and every later model run the same machine.
9–14assemble, Machine m(p)Assembles standard input; stops on the first error; creates the machine with the program and data loaded.Data memory starts with the .data words; registers start at 0.
15–16header lineColumn titles: cycle, PC, word, instruction, A, B, ALU, memory, write back, next PC.One column per important wire of Figure 1.
17–18for (int cycle = 1; ...), m.step()One loop pass = one clock cycle = one instruction; at most 60.That equality is the definition of single-cycle.
19–24mem textDescribes the MEM region: read, write or nothing, with the address.The address always comes from the ALU.
25–30wb textDescribes the WB region: which register got which value, or the output port.Only instructions with RegWrite (and rd ≠ r0) change a register.
31–35std::printf(...)Prints the cycle's values; values are shown as signed 16-bit numbers.Casting to std::int16_t shows 0xFFFC as −4.
37–42register dump, returnPrints all eight registers; the exit status is 0 unless the machine faulted.The final state is the program's result.

Listing 2 — cpu.cpp: the U16 computer without the trace, for running whole programs.

// F1-24 Listing 2: the U16 computer. Load a program (assembly or raw machine words),
// run it until HALT, print what it sent to the output port and how many instructions ran.
#include <iostream>
#include "../F1-23/u16.h"

int main()
{
    const u16::Program p = u16::assemble(std::cin);
    for (const std::string& e : p.errors) {
        std::cout << "error: " << e << '\n';
    }
    u16::Machine m(p);
    long executed = 0;
    while (!m.halted && executed < 100000) {
        m.step();
        ++executed;
    }
    for (const std::uint16_t v : m.output) {
        std::cout << "out: " << static_cast<std::int16_t>(v) << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "halted: " << (m.halted ? "yes" : "no (step limit)") << ", instructions executed: "
              << executed << '\n';
    if (!m.fault.empty()) {
        std::cout << "fault: " << m.fault << '\n';
    }
    return (p.errors.empty() && m.fault.empty()) ? 0 : 1;
}

Its input, cpu.in, is a program written directly in U16 machine language (6 × 7 by repeated addition). The comments are for people; the machine reads only the hex words:

; multiply.hex - 6 x 7 by repeated addition, written directly in U16 machine language
0x6206  ; addi r1, r0, 6     r1 = 6 (the number to add)
0x6407  ; addi r2, r0, 7     r2 = 7 (how many times)
0x6600  ; addi r3, r0, 0     r3 = 0 (the product so far)
0x16C8  ; add  r3, r3, r1    loop: r3 = r3 + r1
0x64BF  ; addi r2, r2, -1    r2 = r2 - 1
0xA43D  ; bne  r2, r0, -3    back to the add while r2 != 0
0xB600  ; out  r3            output the product
0x0000  ; halt

out: 42
halted: yes, instructions executed: 26
