Where the analogy breaks

  • The kitchen road is walked; the datapath is not. A ticket moves from station to station over time. In a single-cycle datapath, all regions work at the same moment on the same instruction, as one wave of electrical signals settling. D2
  • Cooks look at what they need; the register file reads everything it is pointed at. Port B reads a register even for addi, and the multiplexer discards it (column B in the trace). Nothing in hardware "decides not to look". R1
  • A shelf keeps whatever you put on it; register r0 does not. Writes to r0 are discarded, by design (forensic lab). R3

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: a result stays 0. Cause: destination r0. How to find it: the trace's write-back column shows "-" for an instruction that should write. Fix: use r1–r7. (Forensic lab.)
  • Symptom: a load returns the wrong element. Cause: the address register was not advanced, or advanced before the load. How to find it: compare the "read [n]" addresses in the trace with the intended ones. Fix: order lw and addi correctly.
  • Symptom: confusion about why B is non-zero for addi. Cause: reading the B column as "used". How to find it: check AluSrcImm in the control table of F1-25. Fix: remember that multiplexers choose; the register file always reads.
  • Symptom: "pc ... is outside the program" fault. Cause: a missing halt, so execution runs off the end. How to find it: the last trace line's next PC equals the program length. Fix: end every program with halt.
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-23 defined U16's instructions as bit patterns; HW201 gave you registers, clocks and memory cells. What carries over: every encoding rule; registers that update at a clock edge; combinational logic that settles between edges. D2 What changes: the ISA's abstract "effect" becomes concrete wires and multiplexers; the instruction's fields now drive hardware directly; and timing matters: the slowest instruction sets the clock. D1 What comes next: F1-25 builds the control unit that sets the dashed signals of Figure 1, first as a table and then in Verilog.

Check yourself

  1. List the five regions of Figure 1 in order and name one part in each.
  2. For sw r3, 2(r1) with r1 = 10 and r3 = 7: what is on ALU input A, ALU input B, the ALU output, and which memory address receives which value?
  3. Which multiplexer chooses between the ALU result and the memory data, and which instructions select memory data?
  4. Why does add r3, r3, r4 work in one cycle even though it reads and writes r3?
  5. A single-cycle U16 needs, in a made-up example, 850 delay units for lw but only 600 for add. What is the clock period, and what does an add cost?
  6. Explain in your own words why the register file reads port B even for addi.
  7. Apply it to a new case: you add an instruction jr rs (jump to the address in register rs). Which new path and which new multiplexer input does Figure 1 need?
  8. Predict, then run: in the trace of the sum program, how many cycles show a memory read? Check against the output.

Lab

Goal. Complete and run the simulated CPU on a program you wrote in U16 machine language, and verify it with the datapath trace.

Hardware and software needed. No hardware; g++ (this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Folder university/labs/F1-24; run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-24 from the repository root.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use.

Steps.

  1. Run the lab. Check cpu.out shows out: 42 and datapath.out ends with r3 = 29.
  2. Complete the CPU. U16 has no shift instruction. In a copy of ../F1-23/u16.h, add SLL as opcode 12 (R-type: rd = rs shifted left by the low 4 bits of rt): add it to Op and kNames, to Alu/kAluNames/aluCompute, to control and to isRType. Point a copy of cpu.cpp at your header.
  3. Write a program in machine language (hex words only) that computes 5 × 8 with your new instruction, and run it with your cpu.
  4. Trace it with a copy of datapath.cpp using your header. For the shift instruction, write down A, B, ALU and write-back by hand before you look.
  5. Run the original sum program on your new CPU. It must still print 29 (regression test).

Expected observations. The unmodified lab output matches the outputs above. With your extension: your program outputs 40; the trace line of the shift shows ALU = A shifted by B; the sum program still outputs 29.

Verification. Exit status 0 from both programs; your hand prediction matches the trace line; the regression test passes.

Troubleshooting.

  • Your new opcode prints as (unused opcode 12) → kNames still has 12 entries → enlarge the array and add the name.
  • The machine halts at your instruction → control falls into default → add a case for it.
  • Wrong product → the shift amount uses the wrong bits → mask B with 0xF before shifting.

Extension. Add jr rs (see Check yourself 7) and use it to write a "function" that is called from two places in a program.

Forensic lab

Scenario. Kofi wrote a U16 program that counts how many of four numbers are below 5. The data are 3, 8, 1, 6, so the answer is 2. His program prints 0 every time. He suspects the slt instruction is broken in the simulator.

Evidence pack. Kofi's program and the real datapath trace of running it (R3):

; count_below.s - Kofi's program: count how many of the four numbers are below 5 (should output 2)
        .data 3 8 1 6
        addi r1, r0, 0      ; r1 = address
        addi r2, r0, 4      ; r2 = numbers left
        addi r6, r0, 5      ; r6 = the limit, 5
loop:   lw   r4, 0(r1)      ; r4 = memory[r1]
        slt  r5, r4, r6     ; r5 = 1 if r4 < 5, else 0
        add  r0, r0, r5     ; count = count + r5
        addi r1, r1, 1
        addi r2, r2, -1
        bne  r2, r0, loop
        out  r0             ; output the count
        halt

Questions.

  1. Observation: in the cycles where slt runs, what does the write-back column show? And for the add that follows?
  2. Hypotheses: state at least two (a broken slt; a wrong limit; a wrong destination register). Which columns test each?

Mini-project

Your program in your CPU's machine language (the course project in miniature). Write, in U16 machine code only, a program that outputs the first eight Fibonacci numbers (0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13) with out, using a loop. Submit the hex file with a comment per word, the real output of cpu, and the trace of the first loop iteration annotated with the region (IF/ID/EX/MEM/WB) that produced each column.

Rubric. Correct output from a real run (4). Every word commented with its assembly and fields (2). Annotated trace (2). One paragraph explaining which instruction would set the clock period in a single-cycle U16 and why (2).

Summary

  • A datapath is the set of units and wires that carry out instructions; control signals steer it.
  • U16's datapath: PC and +1 adder, instruction memory, register file (2 reads, 1 write), sign extension, ALU, data memory, multiplexers, branch adder.
  • The five regions IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB describe every instruction; some instructions use only some regions.
  • The register file reads both ports every cycle; multiplexers pick what is used.
  • Writes to r0 are discarded, by design.
  • In a single-cycle design the clock period must cover the slowest instruction, so fast instructions wait.
  • The simulator really ran a program written in U16 machine language (output 42).

Answers to Check yourself

  1. IF (PC, instruction memory, +1 adder), ID (register file, sign extension, control), EX (ALU, branch adder), MEM (data memory), WB (write-back multiplexer).
  2. A = r1 = 10; B (after the AluSrcImm multiplexer) = the immediate 2; ALU output 12; address 12 receives 7, which comes from read port B with ReadRdAsB = 1 (it reads rd = r3). A common mistake is to think the ALU adds r3.
  3. The MemToReg multiplexer in WB; only lw selects memory data.
  4. The register file is read during the cycle and written at the clock edge at its end, so the old r3 is read and the new r3 appears for the next instruction.
  5. 850 units, because one period must fit the slowest instruction; every add also takes 850 units, wasting 250.
  6. Good answers say: the register numbers are wired straight from the instruction bits; reading both ports costs no extra time; whether B is used is decided later by the AluSrcImm multiplexer, so reading always is simpler than deciding first.
  7. A path from read port A (the value of rs) to the next-PC multiplexer, which needs a third input (PC + 1, branch target, register value) and a control signal to select it.
  8. Five: one lw per loop iteration (cycles 4, 9, 14, 19, 24).

Forensic lab answer key

Root cause. add r0, r0, r5 uses r0 as the counter. In U16, r0 always reads 0 and writes to it are discarded (line 327 of u16.h: write back only if rd != 0). The count is computed and thrown away every time, and out r0 prints 0.

Evidence. slt works: cycles 5, 11, 17, 23 show ALU = 1, 0, 1, 0 and "r5 = 1", "r5 = 0"… (3 < 5, 8 < 5 false, 1 < 5, 6 < 5 false). The add r0, r0, r5 lines show ALU = 1 in cycles 6 and 18 but the write-back column is "-". The final register dump shows r0 = 0; r3, which Kofi probably meant, was never used.

Fix. Initialise a real counter (addi r3, r0, 0) before the loop, use add r3, r3, r5 and out r3. Verified pattern: this is the structure of the F1-27 forensic program, whose real runs output the correct count.

How the fault was made. The Lab Engineer wrote the correct program with r3 as the counter and replaced r3 by r0 in the add and out lines (and removed the counter's initialisation).

Wrong answers and why. "slt is broken": its results are right in the trace. "The limit is wrong": r6 = 5 in cycle 3. Prevention: the assembler could warn when an instruction with RegWrite names r0 as its destination.

Story hook

At the restaurant, one person never cooks. Amina stands at the pass, between the ticket rail and the stations. She takes each ticket, reads the action word, and calls out: "Grill, on! Pantry, nothing for this one! Shelf, put it on board three!" She does not touch the food. She only turns each ticket into a set of short commands for the stations, and she does it the same way every time for the same action word.

One evening a new expediter takes over. He has a small mistake in his habits: on "STORE" tickets, he also shouts "put it on a board!". The pantry gets the right box, but a cook also drops a copy of the box's shelf number on a cutting board, on top of the ingredient that was there. Nobody notices until a dish comes out wrong much later. In this chapter you will build Amina for U16, test her against a table, and then find the new expediter's mistake.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a control unit does and why it is combinational logic in a single-cycle processor.
  • Derive the control signals of any U16 instruction from what the instruction must do.
  • Read and simulate a control unit written in Verilog, and compare it with a reference table automatically.
  • Compare hardwired and microprogrammed control at concept level.
  • Diagnose a faulty control unit from a test-bench table and predict the program bug it causes.
Jargon box
Control unit
Simple words: the part of the processor that reads the instruction's command and switches the datapath to do it. Analogy: Amina at the pass, calling out what each station must do for this ticket. Precise: logic that maps the instruction's opcode (and sometimes other fields) to the control signals that drive multiplexer selects, write enables and ALU operation inputs. D1 D2
Control signal
Simple words: a wire that tells one part of the datapath what to do right now. Analogy: one call such as "pantry, nothing for this one". Precise: a one-bit (or few-bit) signal such as RegWrite or AluSrcImm that selects a multiplexer input, enables a write or selects an ALU operation. D1
Write enable
Simple words: a signal that allows a storage element to change at the next clock edge. Analogy: permission to put something on a board. Precise: an input of a register, register file or memory that must be 1 for a write to happen at the clock edge; RegWrite and MemWrite are write enables. D2
Hardwired control
Simple words: control built directly as logic gates. Analogy: an expediter who knows every call by heart. Precise: a control unit implemented as combinational logic (or a finite state machine) generated from the signal table. D1
Microprogrammed control
Simple words: control that reads its calls from a small built-in table of steps. Analogy: an expediter who looks up each action word in a binder of call sequences. Precise: a control unit in which each instruction selects a sequence of microinstructions stored in a control memory; each microinstruction's bits are the control signals for one step. D1 D4
Test bench
Simple words: a piece of Verilog that tests another piece by giving it inputs and printing its outputs. Analogy: a practice evening where every action word is tried once. Precise: a non-synthesisable HDL module that instantiates the design under test, drives its inputs and observes its outputs in simulation (F1-21). D2 R2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the control unit as a box between the instruction's opcode and the datapath. Four wires go in; eleven control outputs (one of them three bits wide) come out. A small piece of extra logic combines two of them with the ALU's zero test to choose the next PC.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

The datapath from the last chapter has many little switches: which value goes into the ALU, whether memory is read, whether a register is written. Something has to set all those switches for every instruction. That something is the control unit.

The control unit looks only at the command part of the instruction, the opcode. For each opcode it has a fixed answer: "for an add, write a register, use the register value, do not touch memory". For a store: "do not write a register, do write memory". It is like a lookup table: same command in, same switch settings out, every time.

Because it is a fixed table, it can be built from ordinary logic gates. You can also write it in a hardware language like Verilog, test every input, and compare the result with the table you wrote by hand. If one entry is wrong, programs will go wrong in strange ways, often far from where the mistake is.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Deriving the signals

Each control signal answers one yes/no question about the instruction, and the answer follows from the instruction's meaning. D1 D2 For U16 (Listing 1, whose output is the reference table):

  • RegWrite — does the instruction change a register? Yes for add, sub, and, or, slt, addi, lw; no for sw, branches, out, halt.
  • AluSrcImm — is the ALU's second input the immediate? Yes for addi, lw, sw (address = register + offset).
  • ReadRdAsB — does read port B need the register named in the rd field? Yes for sw (the value to store), beq/bne (the second register to compare) and out.
  • MemRead / MemWrite — only lw reads data memory; only sw writes it.
  • MemToReg — does the written value come from memory? Only for lw.
  • ALU op — sub for sub, beq and bne (equality is "difference is zero"), the named operation for and/or/slt, and add otherwise.
  • BranchEq / BranchNe / Out / Halt — one instruction each (and Halt for the unused opcodes).

R1 In the single-cycle design these outputs depend only on the current opcode, never on earlier instructions, so the control unit is combinational logic: a truth table with 4 inputs and 12 output bits. D2

Values that do not matter

For some instructions a signal's value has no effect. When RegWrite is 0, MemToReg could be 0 or 1: nothing is written anyway. Textbooks mark such entries as "don't care" (X), which lets a logic designer pick whichever value makes the circuit smaller. D1 D2 U16's reference table writes 0 in those places, so the C++ table and the Verilog can be compared exactly; the Watch out box below explains why write enables can never be "don't care".

Watch out

Write enables (RegWrite, MemWrite) and anything that changes the PC are never "don't care". A wrong 1 there changes state that a later instruction will read. The forensic lab is this mistake.

Testing hardware against a table

Listing 2 describes the same table in Verilog, with a case statement on the opcode inside an always @(*) block, which describes combinational logic (F1-21). D2 Listing 3, the test bench, applies all 16 opcodes and prints the outputs in the same column layout as Listing 1. The lab script turns Listing 1's output into numbers and compares the two tables with diff. For the reference design the real result is "no differences … for all 16 opcodes". R2 With only 16 possible inputs, this test is exhaustive: it proves the Verilog equals the table, not merely that it "seems to work".

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

  • Two-level decoding. Textbook MIPS and RISC-V designs split control in two: a main decoder produces a short "ALU op class" from the opcode, and a separate ALU decoder combines that class with function fields of R-type instructions to pick the exact ALU operation. This keeps each decoder small. U16 has no function field, so one level is enough. D1 D2
  • From table to gates. Synthesis tools turn the table into gates automatically. Yosys turned Listing 2 into 30 generic cells (AND, OR, NOT, multiplexer and similar) in this build. That number belongs to yosys's generic cell library and this exact Verilog, not to any real chip. R3
  • Hardwired versus microprogrammed. A hardwired unit is the gate circuit itself. A microprogrammed unit stores, for each instruction, a sequence of control words in a small memory and steps through them; it was attractive for complex instructions that need many steps, because changing behaviour meant changing the stored table, not the gates. Single-cycle and pipelined designs for simple ISAs such as U16 use hardwired control. D1 D4
  • Control in a pipeline. In F1-26 the signals are computed in ID and then travel with the instruction through pipeline registers, so each stage uses the signals of the instruction currently in it, not of the newest one. D1
Not verified — check before relying on this

Whether any particular commercial processor uses microcode, and for which instructions, is not stated here: no vendor manual could be opened in this build. Check the vendor's own architecture or optimisation manual for the named product before making such a claim (for x86-64: the Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual and the vendor's optimisation reference manual).

How the hardware actually does it

The four opcode bits fan out to a small network of gates. One way to picture it: a 4-to-16 decoder (F1-12) produces one line per opcode, and each control output is an OR of the lines of the opcodes that need it; RegWrite, for example, is the OR of the lines for opcodes 1–7. Synthesis then simplifies that network. D2 D3 The outputs reach the datapath's multiplexer select inputs and write enables. Because control is combinational, its delay adds to the critical path of F1-24: the multiplexers cannot settle before their select signals do.

Worked example

Task. Derive the control row for sw rd, imm(rs) and check it against the real table.

  1. What does sw do? memory[R[rs] + imm] = R[rd]. No register changes.
  2. RegWrite = 0 (no register changes).
  3. AluSrcImm = 1 (the ALU adds the immediate to compute the address); ALU op = add.
  4. ReadRdAsB = 1 (the value to store is in the register named by rd, read through port B).
  5. MemRead = 0, MemWrite = 1.
  6. MemToReg = 0 (don't care, since RegWrite = 0; the reference writes 0).
  7. BranchEq = BranchNe = Out = Halt = 0.

Row 8 of the real output reads "8 sw 0 1 1 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 add": identical. R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — control_table.cpp: prints the control table from u16::control() (lines 59–96 of u16.h in F1-23), the same function every simulator in this course uses.

// F1-25 Listing 1: print the U16 control unit as a truth table (one row per opcode).
// The table comes from u16::control(), the function the simulators use, so the table
// and the simulators can never disagree.
#include <cstdio>
#include "../F1-23/u16.h"

int main()
{
    std::printf("op  name  RegWr AluImm RdAsB MemRd MemWr MemToReg BrEq BrNe Out Halt ALU\n");
    for (unsigned op = 0; op < 16; ++op) {
        const u16::Control c = u16::control(op);
        const char* name = op < u16::kNames.size() ? u16::kNames[op] : "-";
        std::printf("%2u  %-5s %5d %6d %5d %5d %5d %8d %4d %4d %3d %4d %s\n", op, name,
                    c.regWrite, c.aluSrcImm, c.readRdAsB, c.memRead, c.memWrite, c.memToReg,
                    c.branchEq, c.branchNe, c.out, c.halt,
                    u16::kAluNames[static_cast<std::size_t>(c.alu)]);
    }
    return 0;
}

Listing 2 — control.v: the same control unit in Verilog.

// F1-25 Listing 2: the U16 control unit as combinational hardware (Verilog).
// Input: the 4-bit opcode. Outputs: the control signals of Listing 1, same names.
// alu encodes 0 = add, 1 = sub, 2 = and, 3 = or, 4 = slt.
module control (
    input  wire [3:0] op,
    output reg        reg_write, alu_imm, rd_as_b, mem_read, mem_write, mem_to_reg,
    output reg        br_eq, br_ne, out_en, halt,
    output reg  [2:0] alu
);
    always @(*) begin
        // defaults: do nothing, ALU adds
        {reg_write, alu_imm, rd_as_b, mem_read, mem_write, mem_to_reg} = 6'b000000;
        {br_eq, br_ne, out_en, halt} = 4'b0000;
        alu = 3'd0;
        case (op)
            4'd1:  begin reg_write = 1; alu = 3'd0; end                    // add
            4'd2:  begin reg_write = 1; alu = 3'd1; end                    // sub
            4'd3:  begin reg_write = 1; alu = 3'd2; end                    // and
            4'd4:  begin reg_write = 1; alu = 3'd3; end                    // or
            4'd5:  begin reg_write = 1; alu = 3'd4; end                    // slt
            4'd6:  begin reg_write = 1; alu_imm = 1; end                   // addi
            4'd7:  begin reg_write = 1; alu_imm = 1; mem_read = 1; mem_to_reg = 1; end // lw
            4'd8:  begin alu_imm = 1; rd_as_b = 1; mem_write = 1; end      // sw
            4'd9:  begin rd_as_b = 1; br_eq = 1; alu = 3'd1; end           // beq
            4'd10: begin rd_as_b = 1; br_ne = 1; alu = 3'd1; end           // bne
            4'd11: begin rd_as_b = 1; out_en = 1; end                      // out
            default: halt = 1;                                             // halt, 12..15
        endcase
    end
endmodule
LinesCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
4–9module control (...)Declares a 4-bit input and the output signals; alu is 3 bits.The module's ports are Figure 1's wires.
10always @(*)Re-evaluate whenever any input changes.Describes combinational logic, not a clocked register.
12–14defaultsSet every output to 0 and the ALU to add first.Every path assigns every output, so synthesis infers no unwanted latch (F1-21).
15–28case (op)One line per opcode sets the signals that must be 1.The table rows, written as hardware.
27default: halt = 1;Opcodes 0 and 12–15 halt.Matches u16::control's default.

Listing 3 — control_tb.v: the test bench.

// F1-25 Listing 3: test bench. Applies every opcode 0..15 and prints the outputs in the
// same columns as Listing 1, so the two tables can be compared line by line with diff.
module control_tb;
    reg  [3:0] op;
    wire reg_write, alu_imm, rd_as_b, mem_read, mem_write, mem_to_reg;
    wire br_eq, br_ne, out_en, halt;
    wire [2:0] alu;
    integer i;
    control dut (.op(op), .reg_write(reg_write), .alu_imm(alu_imm), .rd_as_b(rd_as_b),
                 .mem_read(mem_read), .mem_write(mem_write), .mem_to_reg(mem_to_reg),
                 .br_eq(br_eq), .br_ne(br_ne), .out_en(out_en), .halt(halt), .alu(alu));
    initial begin
        for (i = 0; i < 16; i = i + 1) begin
            op = i;
            #1;  // let the combinational logic settle
            $display("%2d %5d %6d %5d %5d %5d %8d %4d %4d %3d %4d %0d", op, reg_write,
                     alu_imm, rd_as_b, mem_read, mem_write, mem_to_reg, br_eq, br_ne,
                     out_en, halt, alu);
        end
        $finish;
    end
endmodule

Where the analogy breaks

  • Amina thinks; the control unit does not. An expediter can notice an odd ticket and ask. The control unit maps every 4-bit pattern to outputs, including unused ones; there is no judgement, only the table. R1
  • Calls happen one after another; control signals are all valid at once. Amina calls stations in turn. All control outputs are produced in parallel and must be stable before the clock edge. D2
  • A wrong call is usually noticed at once in a kitchen. A wrong control bit often produces no visible symptom until a later instruction reads the damaged state (forensic lab).

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: synthesis warns about an inferred latch, or simulation shows outputs keeping old values. Cause: some case branch does not assign every output. How to find it: look for outputs not set in a branch. Fix: assign defaults at the top of the always block (lines 12–14).
  • Symptom: a register changes after a store. Cause: RegWrite = 1 for sw. How to find it: diff the test-bench table against the reference. Fix: correct the row. (Forensic lab.)
  • Symptom: branches go the wrong way. Cause: ALU op for branches set to add instead of sub, so the zero test is wrong. How to find it: the ALU column for beq/bne rows. Fix: sub.
  • Symptom: diff reports every line different. Cause: column order or formatting differs, not the logic. How to find it: compare one line by eye. Fix: make the test bench print exactly the reference layout.
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-24 built the datapath with its multiplexers and write enables; F1-21 taught you to read Verilog. What carries over: the datapath unchanged; truth tables from MA102; Verilog's always @(*) and case. What changes: you now write hardware whose correctness is checked against a specification table by an exhaustive test; a single wrong bit is a silent data-corruption bug. D2 What comes next: F1-26 cuts the datapath into five stages so that five instructions are in flight at once; the control signals will then travel with each instruction.

Check yourself

  1. Write the control row (all signals) for lw and explain each value.
  2. Why is the U16 control unit combinational and not a state machine?
  3. Which signal values are "don't care" for beq, and which are definitely not?
  4. What does the diff step prove that running two or three programs would not?
  5. In Figure 1, write the Boolean expression for "take branch" and evaluate it for bne when the ALU result is 0.
  6. Explain in your own words the difference between hardwired and microprogrammed control.
  7. Apply it to a new case: you add sll (shift left, R-type) as opcode 12. Write its control row.
  8. Predict, then run: if line 24 of Listing 2 (beq) set alu = 3'd0 (add) instead of sub, which lines would diff report, and what would happen to beq r1, r2, ... when r1 = 3 and r2 = −3?

Lab

Goal. Simulate the U16 control unit in Verilog, prove it equal to the reference table, then extend it consistently in C++ and Verilog.

Hardware and software needed. No hardware. g++ 13.3.0, Icarus Verilog 12.0 (iverilog, vvp), Yosys 0.33, as printed in the run logs. Folder university/labs/F1-25; run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-25.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use. (This lab only simulates; nothing is programmed into a device.)

Steps.

  1. Run the lab. Confirm control_diff.out says "no differences".
  2. Add sll as opcode 12 in a copy of u16.h (as in the F1-24 lab) and in a copy of control.v (ALU code 5 for shift). Update the awk mapping in your copy of run.sh.
  3. Re-run and get "no differences" again.
  4. Deliberately break one bit in your Verilog copy, run, and read the diff output. Restore it.
  5. Look at control_synth.out before and after your change: how many cells did your instruction add?

Expected observations. Step 1 as shown above. Step 3: "no differences". Step 4: exactly one line differs, the row of the opcode you changed.

Verification. The exhaustive comparison reports no differences for all 16 opcodes with your extension; your extended CPU still runs the sum program of F1-23 to 29.

Troubleshooting.

  • iverilog reports "Unable to bind wire/reg/memory" → a port name in the test bench does not match the module → compare names.
  • Every diff line differs → column widths in $display do not match → copy the format string exactly.
  • The ALU column differs only for your new row → awk does not know the new ALU name → add it to the mapping.

Extension. Rewrite Listing 2 without case: one assign per output, written as a Boolean expression of the four opcode bits. Prove it equal with the same diff.

Forensic lab

Scenario. Bo edited the control unit "to tidy it up". Afterwards, a program that saves a running total to memory and then keeps adding to it gives totals that jump to strange values right after each save. Bo says the store instruction "definitely works, the memory has the right value".

Evidence pack. Bo's control unit (control_bug.v), the real test-bench output and the real comparison with the reference table (R4):

// F1-25 forensic: a colleague's edited U16 control unit as combinational hardware (Verilog).
// Input: the 4-bit opcode. Outputs: the control signals of Listing 1, same names.
// alu encodes 0 = add, 1 = sub, 2 = and, 3 = or, 4 = slt.
module control (
    input  wire [3:0] op,
    output reg        reg_write, alu_imm, rd_as_b, mem_read, mem_write, mem_to_reg,
    output reg        br_eq, br_ne, out_en, halt,
    output reg  [2:0] alu
);
    always @(*) begin
        // defaults: do nothing, ALU adds
        {reg_write, alu_imm, rd_as_b, mem_read, mem_write, mem_to_reg} = 6'b000000;
        {br_eq, br_ne, out_en, halt} = 4'b0000;
        alu = 3'd0;
        case (op)
            4'd1:  begin reg_write = 1; alu = 3'd0; end                    // add
            4'd2:  begin reg_write = 1; alu = 3'd1; end                    // sub
            4'd3:  begin reg_write = 1; alu = 3'd2; end                    // and
            4'd4:  begin reg_write = 1; alu = 3'd3; end                    // or
            4'd5:  begin reg_write = 1; alu = 3'd4; end                    // slt
            4'd6:  begin reg_write = 1; alu_imm = 1; end                   // addi
            4'd7:  begin reg_write = 1; alu_imm = 1; mem_read = 1; mem_to_reg = 1; end // lw
            4'd8:  begin reg_write = 1; alu_imm = 1; rd_as_b = 1; mem_write = 1; end // sw
            4'd9:  begin rd_as_b = 1; br_eq = 1; alu = 3'd1; end           // beq
            4'd10: begin rd_as_b = 1; br_ne = 1; alu = 3'd1; end           // bne
            4'd11: begin rd_as_b = 1; out_en = 1; end                      // out
            default: halt = 1;                                             // halt, 12..15
        endcase
    end
endmodule

Questions.

  1. Observation: which opcode's row differs, and in which column?
  2. Hypotheses: list two explanations for "totals jump after a save" (for example a wrong store address, or a register being overwritten). Which one does the diff support?
  3. Root cause: with this bit set, what does sw r3, 0(r1) do to r3? (Use Figure 1 of F1-24: what value reaches the write-back multiplexer when MemToReg = 0?)
  4. Fix: which line of control_bug.v must change, and how?
  5. Prevention: what should run automatically before any edit to the control unit is accepted?

Method hints. Compare tables first, programs second. Then follow the one wrong signal through the datapath to see which state it changes.

Mini-project

A microprogrammed U16, on paper. Design a microprogrammed control for a multi-cycle U16 where each instruction takes 3–5 steps (fetch, decode, execute, memory, write back). Write the microinstruction format (which control bits it has), and the microprogram for add, lw, sw and beq. Then write one page comparing it with Listing 2: size, ease of change, and speed.

Rubric. Microinstruction format complete and consistent with Figure 1 of F1-24 (3). Four correct microprograms (4). Comparison argued with the table and synthesis numbers from this lab (3).

Summary

  • The control unit maps each opcode to the control signals of the datapath.
  • In a single-cycle design it is combinational: a truth table with 4 inputs for U16.
  • Each signal is derived from what the instruction must do; some entries are "don't care", write enables never are.
  • The Verilog control unit was simulated and compared exhaustively with the C++ reference: no differences.
  • Yosys turned it into a small number of generic gates (30 cells in this build).
  • Microprogrammed control stores control words in a memory; hardwired control is the logic itself.
  • A wrong control bit corrupts state silently; exhaustive table comparison finds it immediately.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. RegWrite 1 (writes rd), AluSrcImm 1 (address = rs + imm), ReadRdAsB 0 (port B not needed; reading rt is harmless), MemRead 1, MemWrite 0, MemToReg 1 (value comes from memory), BranchEq/BranchNe/Out/Halt 0, ALU add. Matches row 7 of the real table.
  2. Its outputs depend only on the current opcode, not on anything that happened before, and the whole instruction finishes in one cycle, so there is no state to remember.
  3. Don't care: MemToReg (RegWrite = 0, so nothing is written) and MemRead (the loaded value is never used, in this simple model without caches). Definitely not don't care: RegWrite = 0 and MemWrite = 0 (write enables), ALU op = sub and AluSrcImm = 0 (the ALU must compare the two registers), ReadRdAsB = 1, BranchEq = 1. A common error is to call AluSrcImm "don't care" because the immediate is needed anyway: it is, but in the branch adder, and it must not reach the ALU.
  4. That the Verilog equals the specification for every possible opcode. Programs exercise only the instructions they contain, and only in the states they reach.
  5. take = (BranchEq AND zero) OR (BranchNe AND NOT zero). For bne with ALU result 0: zero = 1, so (0 AND 1) OR (1 AND 0) = 0: not taken (the registers were equal).
  6. Good answers say: hardwired control is the gate circuit computing the signals directly; microprogrammed control looks up stored control words, one per step, so behaviour can be changed by changing the stored table, at the cost of a lookup per step.
  7. RegWrite 1, AluSrcImm 0, ReadRdAsB 0, MemRead 0, MemWrite 0, MemToReg 0, branches/Out/Halt 0, ALU = the new shift operation.
  8. One line, row 9 (ALU 1 versus 0). Then beq would add: 3 + (−3) = 0, so zero = 1 and the branch would be taken although the registers differ. Running the diff would show the line before any program misbehaved.

Forensic lab answer key

Root cause. In control_bug.v line 23, the sw row sets reg_write = 1. A store therefore also writes register rd. With MemToReg = 0 the written value is the ALU result, which for sw is the address (rs + imm). So sw r3, 0(r1) stores r3 correctly in memory, then overwrites r3 with the address. The next additions start from that address: "the total jumps".

Evidence. The diff shows exactly one differing line: opcode 8, second column (RegWrite) 0 in the reference, 1 in Bo's version. Memory receives the right value (MemWrite and the data path are unchanged), which is why Bo saw a correct value in memory.

Fix. Remove reg_write = 1; from the 4'd8 line, as in Listing 2. Verify with the same diff ("no differences").

How the fault was made. The Lab Engineer copied Listing 2 and added reg_write = 1; to the sw line (and changed the header comment); run.sh generated the evidence with the same test bench.

Wrong answers and why. "The store address is wrong": AluSrcImm and ALU op for sw are unchanged, and memory holds the right value. "The add is broken": add's row matches. Prevention: run the exhaustive table comparison in continuous integration on every change to the control unit.

Story hook

On a quiet Monday the restaurant has one cook on the line, Tomás. He takes a ticket, reads it, preps the ingredients, cooks, plates, and only then takes the next ticket. Every dish is perfect, and the queue of tickets grows longer and longer.

On Friday the owner tries something new. Five people stand in a row of stations: one takes tickets off the rail, one reads them and lays out ingredients, one cooks, one fetches from the pantry, one plates. Every time a small bell rings, each dish slides one station to the right. No single dish is ready any sooner; in fact each dish now waits a little at every hand-over. But once the row is full, a finished plate comes out at every bell. The queue of tickets shrinks.

Then the owner notices two things. The pantry station is the slowest, so the bell can only ring as fast as the pantry allows. And at the start of the evening, the first plate still takes five bells. This chapter is about that row of stations, the pipeline, and about the honest arithmetic of how much faster it really is.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain pipelining with the precise words throughput, latency, stage and pipeline register.
  • Draw a pipeline diagram (instructions against clock cycles) for a short program and count its cycles.
  • Calculate the speed-up of a pipeline from stage delays, including the slowest stage, register overhead and fill time.
  • Name the three kinds of hazard that stop a pipeline from reaching one instruction per cycle.
  • Diagnose why a pipeline is less than "five times faster" from timing evidence.
Jargon box
Pipelining
Simple words: working on several instructions at once, each at a different step. Analogy: five kitchen stations in a row; at every bell each dish moves one station on. Precise: an implementation technique in which the execution of an instruction is split into stages, and successive instructions overlap, one per stage. D1 D2
Pipeline stage
Simple words: one step of the instruction's journey, done in one clock cycle. Analogy: one station in the row. Precise: one part of the datapath between two pipeline registers; the classic five are IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB. D1
Pipeline register
Simple words: a set of storage cells between two stages that holds one instruction's values for the next stage. Analogy: the tray at the hand-over between two stations. Precise: a clocked register (IF/ID, ID/EX, EX/MEM, MEM/WB) that captures the outputs of one stage, including the instruction's control signals, at each clock edge. D1 D2
Throughput
Simple words: how many jobs finish per unit of time. Analogy: plates out of the kitchen per hour. Precise: the rate of completed instructions, for example instructions per cycle or per second. D1
Latency
Simple words: how long one job takes from start to finish. Analogy: the time from a ticket's arrival to its plate leaving. Precise: the time from the start to the completion of one instruction; pipelining does not reduce it and usually increases it slightly. D1
CPI (cycles per instruction)
Simple words: on average, how many clock ticks each instruction costs. Analogy: bells per plate, averaged over the evening. Precise: total clock cycles divided by instructions executed; an ideal scalar pipeline approaches 1. D1
Hazard
Simple words: a situation where the next instruction cannot go ahead in the next cycle. Analogy: a station that cannot start because it is missing something. Precise: a condition that prevents the next instruction from executing in its designated cycle; the kinds are structural, data and control hazards. D1 D3

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 is a pipeline diagram: time runs to the right in clock cycles, instructions run downwards. Each instruction occupies one stage per cycle and moves one stage to the right at every clock edge. The diagonal band shows five instructions in flight at once from cycle 5. This is the "five-stage pipeline" diagram required for this chapter; the hazards that break its neat staircase are drawn in F1-27.

Figure 2 shows what makes the overlap possible: four pipeline registers cut the datapath of F1-24 into five stages. Each register holds everything the next stage needs about its instruction, including the control signals computed in ID.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A processor that does one whole instruction at a time leaves most of its parts idle. While the ALU is adding, the part that fetches instructions has nothing to do. Pipelining puts every part to work at the same time, each on a different instruction.

Picture the row of kitchen stations again. At every bell, every dish moves one station along. While dish 3 is being cooked, dish 4 is being prepared and dish 5 is being read. No single dish gets faster. But plates come out much more often, one per bell once the row is full.

There is a catch. The bell can only ring as fast as the slowest station. If the pantry needs more time than the stove, everyone waits for the pantry. And at the very start, the row is empty: the first plate still needs five bells. So a five-station row is less than five times faster, and the lab will tell you exactly how much less.

There is a second catch. Sometimes a dish needs something that the dish in front of it has not finished yet. Then the row has to wait. Those waits are called hazards, and the next two chapters are all about them.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Stages and pipeline registers

The five regions of the single-cycle datapath become five stages: IF (fetch), ID (decode and register read), EX (ALU operation or address calculation), MEM (data memory access) and WB (write back to the register file). D1 D2 Between stages, pipeline registers capture each stage's results at the clock edge, so in the next cycle the following stage works on them while the earlier stage starts on the next instruction. D1 Everything an instruction needs later must travel with it in these registers: its operand values, its destination register number and its control signals. If the control signals were not carried along, the MEM stage would use the signals of the instruction currently in ID, a different instruction. D1

Counting cycles

With k stages and no hazards, the first instruction finishes after k cycles and then one more finishes every cycle, so n instructions take k + (n − 1) cycles. D1 For the five-stage pipeline that is n + 4. Listing 2's real runs agree: six instructions (five addi and halt) take 10 cycles, and the 30 executed instructions of the sum program take 34 cycles in the ideal mode. R1 R2 The CPI is cycles divided by instructions: 34 / 30 ≈ 1.13, which approaches 1 as programs get longer.

From cycles to time

Fewer cycles per instruction is only half the story; the length of a cycle matters too. Execution time = instructions × CPI × clock period. D1 Pipelining raises CPI from 1 (single-cycle) to a bit more than 1 but shortens the clock period, because one cycle now only has to cover one stage. The period is set by the slowest stage plus the delay of the pipeline register, so unbalanced stages and register overhead keep the speed-up below the number of stages. D1 D2 Listing 3 computes this for made-up stage delays.

Why real pipelines do not reach CPI = 1

The ideal count assumes each instruction can always enter the next stage. Three kinds of hazard break that assumption: structural hazards (two instructions need the same hardware in the same cycle), data hazards (an instruction needs a result that an earlier instruction has not yet written) and control hazards (the pipeline does not yet know which instruction comes after a branch). D1 D3 U16 avoids the classic structural hazard by having separate instruction and data memories, so IF and MEM never compete. Data hazards are F1-27; control hazards are F1-27 and F1-28. In the ideal mode of Listing 2 the model ignores all of them, which is why its diagrams look perfect.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

  • Speed-up formula. With stage delays d1…dk, register overhead r and n instructions, single-cycle time is n·Σd and pipelined time is (k + n − 1)·(max d + r). For large n the speed-up tends to Σd / (max d + r), which equals k only if all stages are equal and r = 0. D1 R3
  • Deeper pipelines. Splitting stages further shortens the period but adds register overhead per stage and makes every hazard cost more cycles (a branch resolved in stage 10 wastes more fetches than one resolved in stage 3). There is therefore a depth beyond which performance falls. D3
  • Register-file timing trick. Textbook five-stage pipelines write the register file in the first half of a cycle and read it in the second half, so an instruction in ID can read a value being written by an instruction in WB in the same cycle. The model in Listing 1 uses this rule. D1 R1
  • A model, not a circuit. Listing 1 does not simulate pipeline registers gate by gate. It executes the program with the U16 machine and then computes, from stated rules, the cycle in which each instruction enters each stage. This is a standard way to study timing; the next step would be a cycle-accurate HDL pipeline, a good mini-project for HW201 graduates. R1

How the hardware actually does it

A pipeline register is a bank of flip-flops (F1-16) clocked by the same clock as every other register (F1-18). At each rising edge, all four pipeline registers capture their inputs at once; between edges, the combinational logic of each stage computes from the values its left-hand register holds. D2 So "an instruction moves one stage right" really means "the values describing it are copied from one register to the next at the edge". To hold an instruction in place (a stall), the hardware disables the write of a pipeline register and inserts a "do nothing" instruction, a bubble, into the next stage; to cancel one (a flush), it clears that instruction's control signals to zero so it changes no state. D1 The model shows stalls as lower-case stage names and flushes as xx.

Worked example

Task. Using Listing 3's stage delays (IF 200, ID 100, EX 200, MEM 250, WB 100, register overhead 20, in made-up delay units, du), compare 1,000 instructions on the single-cycle and pipelined machines.

  1. Single-cycle period. All stages in one cycle: 200 + 100 + 200 + 250 + 100 = 850 du.
  2. Pipelined period. The slowest stage plus the register: 250 + 20 = 270 du.
  3. Single-cycle time. 1,000 × 850 = 850,000 du.
  4. Pipelined cycles. 5 + (1,000 − 1) = 1,004 cycles; time 1,004 × 270 = 271,080 du.
  5. Speed-up. 850,000 / 271,080 ≈ 3.14.
  6. Limit for very long programs. 850 / 270 ≈ 3.15. Not 5, because MEM is slower than the average stage and every cycle pays the register overhead.

The real run of Listing 3 prints the same numbers in its 1000 row (271080 and 3.14). R3

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — pipe.h: the five-stage timing model used in this chapter and the next two.

// pipe.h - a timing model of the classic five-stage pipeline for U16 programs (F1-26).
// Stages: IF (fetch), ID (decode + register read), EX (ALU), MEM (data memory), WB (write
// back). The program is first executed by the U16 machine (u16.h); the model then works out,
// for every executed instruction, the cycle in which it enters each stage, using the rules
// written next to each line below. It is a model of timing, not a gate-level circuit.
#pragma once
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include "../F1-23/u16.h"

namespace pipe
{

struct Config
{
    bool dataHazards;    // false = pretend no instruction ever waits for another's result
    bool forwarding;     // true = results are passed straight from EX/MEM to a later EX
    bool branchPenalty;  // true = taken branches are found in EX; wrong fetches are flushed
};

struct Row
{
    std::string text;    // the instruction, as disassembled
    int ifc = 0, id = 0, ex = 0, mem = 0, wb = 0;  // cycle of entry into each stage
    bool flushed = false;                           // fetched on the wrong path, then cancelled
    int lastCycle = 0;                              // flushed rows: last cycle drawn
};

struct Result
{
    std::vector<Row> rows;  // executed instructions and flushed wrong-path fetches, in order
    int instructions = 0, cycles = 0, dataStalls = 0, branchLost = 0;
};

// Registers an instruction reads (r0 never causes a hazard: it is always 0).
inline std::vector<unsigned> sources(const u16::Fields& f)
{
    const u16::Control c = u16::control(f.op);
    std::vector<unsigned> s;
    if (u16::isRType(f.op) || u16::isIType(f.op)) {
        s.push_back(f.rs);
    }
    if (u16::isRType(f.op)) {
        s.push_back(f.rt);
    }
    if (c.readRdAsB) {
        s.push_back(f.rd);
    }
    s.erase(std::remove(s.begin(), s.end(), 0u), s.end());
    return s;
}

inline Result schedule(const u16::Program& prog, const Config& cfg, long maxSteps = 5000)
{
    u16::Machine m(prog);
    std::vector<u16::Step> trace;
    while (!m.halted && static_cast<long>(trace.size()) < maxSteps) {
        trace.push_back(m.step());
    }
    Result r;
    std::vector<Row> done;      // executed instructions only (for hazard look-ups)
    int nextFetch = 1;          // earliest cycle the next instruction may enter IF
    for (const u16::Step& s : trace) {
        Row x;
        x.text = u16::disasm(s.word);
        x.ifc = nextFetch;
        const Row* prev = done.empty() ? nullptr : &done.back();
        x.id = std::max(x.ifc + 1, prev ? prev->ex : 0);        // ID is free when prev left it
        int ex = std::max(x.id + 1, prev ? prev->ex + 1 : 0);   // one instruction per stage
        const int exNoHazard = ex;
        if (cfg.dataHazards) {
            for (const unsigned reg : sources(s.f)) {
                for (std::size_t k = done.size(); k-- > 0;) {     // newest earlier writer of reg
                    const u16::Step& p = trace[k];
                    if (!(p.c.regWrite && p.f.rd == reg)) {
                        continue;
                    }
                    const Row& w = done[k];
                    if (!cfg.forwarding) {
                        ex = std::max(ex, w.wb + 1);   // read in ID during WB's cycle or later
                    } else if (p.c.memRead) {
                        ex = std::max(ex, w.mem + 1);  // a load's value exists after MEM
                    } else {
                        ex = std::max(ex, w.ex + 1);   // an ALU value exists after EX
                    }
                    break;
                }
            }
        }
        r.dataStalls += ex - exNoHazard;
        x.ex = ex;
        x.mem = x.ex + 1;
        x.wb = x.mem + 1;
        nextFetch = std::max(x.ifc + 1, x.id);  // the next instruction enters IF as x leaves it
        r.rows.push_back(x);
        done.push_back(x);
        if (cfg.branchPenalty && s.taken) {
            // Fetch went on with pc+1, pc+2...; the branch is resolved at the end of EX, so
            // those fetches are cancelled and the target is fetched in the next cycle.
            int f = nextFetch, id = x.ex;
            for (int k = 1; f <= x.ex; ++k) {
                Row w;
                const std::size_t a = static_cast<std::size_t>(s.pc + k);
                w.text = a < prog.code.size() ? u16::disasm(prog.code[a]) : "(past the end)";
                w.flushed = true;
                w.ifc = f;
                w.id = std::max(f + 1, id);
                w.lastCycle = x.ex;
                r.rows.push_back(w);
                f = std::max(f + 1, w.id);
                id = w.id + 1;
            }
            // without the flush the next instruction would enter ID at max(nextFetch+1, x.ex);
            // now it enters ID at x.ex + 2
            r.branchLost += x.ex + 2 - std::max(nextFetch + 1, x.ex);
            nextFetch = x.ex + 1;
        }
    }
    r.instructions = static_cast<int>(done.size());
    r.cycles = done.empty() ? 0 : done.back().wb;
    return r;
}

// Draw rows [0, maxRows) as a pipeline diagram. A stage name in capitals is the cycle an
// instruction enters that stage; lower case means it is still there (stalled); "xx" marks
// cycles of a fetch that was flushed.
inline void draw(const Result& r, std::size_t maxRows)
{
    const std::size_t n = std::min(maxRows, r.rows.size());
    int last = 0;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        last = std::max(last, r.rows[i].flushed ? r.rows[i].lastCycle : r.rows[i].wb);
    }
    std::printf("%-20s", "cycle:");
    for (int c = 1; c <= last; ++c) {
        std::printf("%3d", c);
    }
    std::printf("\n");
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        const Row& x = r.rows[i];
        std::printf("%-20s", (x.flushed ? "  (flushed) " + x.text : x.text).c_str());
        for (int c = 1; c <= last; ++c) {
            const char* cell = "  .";
            if (x.flushed) {
                cell = (c >= x.ifc && c <= x.lastCycle) ? " xx" : "  .";
            } else if (c == x.ifc) { cell = " IF"; }
            else if (c > x.ifc && c < x.id) { cell = " if"; }
            else if (c == x.id) { cell = " ID"; }
            else if (c > x.id && c < x.ex) { cell = " id"; }
            else if (c == x.ex) { cell = " EX"; }
            else if (c == x.mem) { cell = " ME"; }
            else if (c == x.wb) { cell = " WB"; }
            std::printf("%s", cell);
        }
        std::printf("\n");
    }
}

inline void summary(const Result& r)
{
    std::printf("instructions %d, cycles %d, CPI %.2f, data-stall cycles %d, "
                "cycles lost to taken branches %d\n",
                r.instructions, r.cycles,
                r.instructions ? static_cast<double>(r.cycles) / r.instructions : 0.0,
                r.dataStalls, r.branchLost);
}

}  // namespace pipe

Listing 2 — pipeline.cpp: draw the diagram for a program in a chosen mode.

// F1-26 Listing 2: draw the pipeline diagram of a U16 program and count its cycles.
//   pipeline [ideal|stall|forward] [rows]   (program on standard input; default: ideal 12)
#include <cstdlib>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include "pipe.h"

int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
    const std::string mode = argc > 1 ? argv[1] : "ideal";
    const std::size_t rows = argc > 2 ? static_cast<std::size_t>(std::atoi(argv[2])) : 12;
    pipe::Config cfg{false, false, false};               // ideal: nothing ever waits
    if (mode == "stall") {
        cfg = pipe::Config{true, false, true};           // hazards, no forwarding
    } else if (mode == "forward") {
        cfg = pipe::Config{true, true, true};            // hazards, with forwarding
    } else if (mode != "ideal") {
        std::cout << "unknown mode " << mode << '\n';
        return 2;
    }
    const u16::Program p = u16::assemble(std::cin);
    if (!p.errors.empty()) {
        std::cout << p.errors.front() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    const pipe::Result r = pipe::schedule(p, cfg);
    std::cout << "mode: " << mode << '\n';
    pipe::draw(r, rows);
    pipe::summary(r);
    std::cout << "single-cycle machine: " << r.instructions << " cycles (one long cycle each)\n";
    return 0;
}

Listing 3 — stage_time.cpp: time for n instructions, single-cycle versus pipelined, from stage delays (input stage_time.in).

// F1-26 Listing 3 (forensic evidence): how long do N instructions take on a single-cycle
// machine and on a five-stage pipeline, given the delay of each stage? Delays are read from
// standard input in made-up "delay units" (du); they describe no real chip.
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    std::vector<std::string> names;
    std::vector<int> delay;
    int latch = 0;  // extra delay of the pipeline register between two stages
    std::string name;
    int d = 0;
    while (std::cin >> name >> d) {
        if (name == "latch") {
            latch = d;
        } else {
            names.push_back(name);
            delay.push_back(d);
        }
    }
    int sum = 0, slowest = 0;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < delay.size(); ++i) {
        std::printf("stage %-4s %4d du\n", names[i].c_str(), delay[i]);
        sum += delay[i];
        slowest = std::max(slowest, delay[i]);
    }
    const int single = sum;               // one long cycle must fit every stage in a row
    const int piped = slowest + latch;    // the clock must fit the slowest stage + its latch
    const long stages = static_cast<long>(delay.size());
    std::printf("single-cycle clock period %d du; pipelined clock period %d du (slowest stage "
                "%d + latch %d)\n", single, piped, slowest, latch);
    std::printf("%10s %16s %16s %9s\n", "N instr", "single-cycle du", "pipelined du", "speed-up");
    for (const long n : {1L, 5L, 10L, 100L, 1000L, 1000000L}) {
        const long t1 = n * single;
        const long t2 = (stages + n - 1) * piped;  // fill the pipe, then one result per cycle
        std::printf("%10ld %16ld %16ld %9.2f\n", n, t1, t2, static_cast<double>(t1) / t2);
    }
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • A dish is a physical thing; an instruction is a set of values. Nothing travels: at each clock edge every pipeline register copies new values in. Two "copies" of an instruction's data can exist at once in different registers (its result in EX/MEM and again in MEM/WB). D2
  • Kitchen stations can be a little early or late; pipeline stages cannot. All stages move at the same clock edge. A station that finishes early still waits for the edge; there is no "sliding along when ready". D1
  • A cook can see the dish ahead; a stage sees only its own register. If a dish needs something from the one in front, a cook would shout. Hardware needs explicit extra wires (forwarding) and detection logic for that, which F1-27 adds. D1

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: expecting "5 stages = 5× faster". Cause: ignoring the slowest stage, register overhead and fill time. How to find it: compute Σd / (max d + r). Fix: use the formula; balance stages. (Forensic lab.)
  • Symptom: thinking pipelining makes each instruction faster. Cause: mixing up latency and throughput. How to find it: in the run, the first addi still needs 5 cycles. Fix: say "more instructions per second", never "faster instructions".
  • Symptom: a diagram with two instructions in the same stage in the same cycle. Cause: forgetting that each stage holds one instruction. How to find it: check every column has each stage name at most once. Fix: shift the later instruction right.
  • Symptom: counting n × 5 cycles. Cause: treating the pipeline as single-cycle with five steps. Fix: n + 4 for the ideal five-stage pipeline.
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-24 and F1-25: one instruction at a time, all control signals from the current opcode. What carries over: the same datapath parts, the same control table and the same U16 programs, which give the same results. R2 What changes: five instructions are in flight at once; each needs its own copy of values and control signals in pipeline registers; time is now cycles × a shorter period; and instructions can interfere with each other (hazards). D1 What comes next: F1-27 turns the hazards on, measures what they cost, and removes most of the cost with forwarding.

Check yourself

  1. Define throughput and latency for a pipeline, and say which one pipelining improves.
  2. How many cycles do 20 independent instructions take in the ideal five-stage pipeline? And 1?
  3. Why must control signals travel through the pipeline registers?
  4. Stage delays 150, 150, 150, 150, 150 du with register overhead 10 du. What is the speed-up limit for long programs?
  5. Name the three kinds of hazard and give a one-line example of each.
  6. Explain in your own words why a single instruction is not faster in a pipeline.
  7. Apply it to a new case: a designer splits MEM (250 du) into two stages of 125 du each, making six stages. Using Listing 3's other numbers, what are the new clock period and the new limit speed-up?
  8. Predict, then run: with stage_time.in as given, for which smallest n in the table is the pipeline faster than the single-cycle machine? Check against the output.

Lab

Goal. Draw pipeline diagrams with the model, check them by hand, and explore how stage balance changes the speed-up.

Hardware and software needed. No hardware; g++ 13.3.0 as recorded. Folder university/labs/F1-26; run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-26.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use.

Steps.

  1. Run the lab; compare pipeline.out and sum_ideal.out with the outputs above.
  2. On paper, draw the ideal diagram of the multiply program (../F1-24/cpu.in) for its first 8 executed instructions. Then run ./pipeline ideal 8 < ../F1-24/cpu.in (build as shown) and compare.
  3. Verify the formula: the multiply program executes 26 instructions; predict its ideal cycle count, then read the summary line.
  4. Edit stage_time.in: make the five stages equal while keeping the same total (170 each). Predict the limit speed-up, run, compare.
  5. Try a six-stage design (Check yourself 7) by adding a line to stage_time.in.

Expected observations. Step 3: 26 + 4 = 30 cycles. Step 4: 850 / 190 ≈ 4.47 for long runs, better than 3.15, still below 5 because of the register overhead.

Verification. Your hand-drawn diagram matches the model row for row; your predicted cycle counts and speed-ups match the program output to two decimals.

Troubleshooting.

  • "unknown mode" → the mode must be ideal, stall or forward.
  • The diagram is cut off → the second argument limits rows; pass a larger number.
  • stage_time prints nothing useful → the input file must have "name number" pairs, one per line.

Extension. Add a "multi-cycle" column to stage_time.cpp: one instruction at a time, but each instruction only uses the cycles of the stages it needs (assume a period of the slowest stage). Use the instruction mix of the sum program (count how many of each kind ran).

Forensic lab

Scenario. A student team pipelined their teaching CPU into five stages and wrote in their report: "our CPU is now five times faster". Their teacher, Ms Okafor, timed a single instruction from fetch to write back on the old and the new design: it took longer on the new one. The team says the measurement must be wrong.

Evidence pack. The team's stage delays (stage_time.in, shown above as the input of Listing 3) and the real output of Listing 3 for those delays (R3, shown above in the code walk-through).

Questions.

  1. Observation: what speed-up does the evidence show for n = 1, 5, 1000 and 1,000,000?
  2. Hypotheses: list at least two reasons a five-stage pipeline could fall short of 5× (consider the clock period and the number of cycles).
  3. Root cause: which two effects explain the long-run limit? And which quantity (latency or throughput) did Ms Okafor measure?
  4. Fix: suggest two design changes that would raise the long-run speed-up, and estimate one of them with Listing 3.
  5. Prevention: how should the team state the speed-up in their report so that it is true?

Method hints. Separate "cycles" from "time per cycle". Find the stage that sets the clock. Then look at what fraction of a five-instruction run is filling the pipeline.

Mini-project

Your own pipeline diagram generator. Write a small C++ program that reads a list of stage delays and an instruction count and prints, as text, the pipeline diagram of the first 8 instructions with real times (in du) at the top instead of cycle numbers, for both the single-cycle and the pipelined machine. Use it to explain, in one paragraph with numbers, why the first instruction finishes later in the pipelined machine.

Rubric. Program builds with the course flags and runs (3). Diagram correct for the given delays (3). Paragraph uses throughput, latency and clock period correctly (2). One test with unequal and one with equal stages (2).

Summary

  • Pipelining overlaps instructions: each stage works on a different instruction every cycle.
  • Pipeline registers between stages hold each instruction's values and control signals.
  • Ideal cycle count: k + n − 1; for five stages, n + 4 (real run: 30 instructions, 34 cycles).
  • Throughput improves; the latency of one instruction does not.
  • The clock period is the slowest stage plus register overhead, so speed-up is below the number of stages.
  • Short programs gain little or lose, because of pipeline fill.
  • Structural, data and control hazards keep CPI above 1; the next chapters measure and reduce them.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Throughput: instructions completed per unit time; latency: time for one instruction from start to end. Pipelining improves throughput; latency stays the same or grows slightly (register overhead).
  2. 20 + 4 = 24 cycles; 1 instruction: 5 cycles.
  3. Different stages hold different instructions in the same cycle; each stage must use the signals of its own instruction, so the signals are stored with the instruction as it moves.
  4. Σd / (max d + r) = 750 / 160 ≈ 4.69. Balanced stages get close to 5, but the overhead keeps it below.
  5. Structural: one memory used by IF and MEM in the same cycle. Data: add r3, r3, r4 right after lw r4, .... Control: the instruction after a bne is fetched before the branch is decided.
  6. Good answers say: the instruction still passes through all the same steps, plus a register hand-over at each stage; pipelining only lets other instructions use the idle stages at the same time.
  7. Slowest stage is now IF or EX at 200 du, so the period is 220 du; the sum is still 850 du; limit 850 / 220 ≈ 3.86 (better than 3.15). With six stages, fill takes 5 extra cycles instead of 4.
  8. n = 5: 4250 versus 2430 du (speed-up 1.75). For n = 1 the pipeline is slower (850 versus 1350).

Forensic lab answer key

Root cause. Two effects. (1) The clock period is set by the slowest stage (MEM, 250 du) plus the register overhead (20 du), so even for very long runs the speed-up is 850 / 270 ≈ 3.15, not 5. (2) For short runs, filling the pipeline dominates: five instructions take 5 + 4 = 9 cycles of 270 du = 2,430 du, compared with 4,250 du single-cycle (1.75×); a one-instruction test is slower (0.63×).

Evidence. Listing 3's real output: periods 850 and 270; speed-ups 0.63 (n = 1), 1.75 (n = 5), 3.14 (n = 1000), 3.15 (n = 1,000,000). Ms Okafor measured latency: one instruction now takes 5 × 270 = 1,350 du instead of 850 du (the n = 1 row). Her measurement is right, and so is a throughput gain: 1.75× for five instructions, 3.15× in the limit. The team's mistake is the claim "5×", not the pipeline.

Fix. Balance the stages (for example split MEM, or move work out of it), reduce register overhead, and benchmark with long programs. Balanced 170-du stages give 850 / 190 ≈ 4.47 (lab step 4).

How the evidence was made. The Lab Engineer chose delays with one slow stage and ran Listing 3; no fault was injected into code, the "fault" is the team's claim.

Wrong answers and why. "Hazards": the delay model has none, and the shortfall appears anyway. "The pipeline needs more stages": more stages without balancing do not move the slowest stage. Prevention: report speed-up with the formula, the measured n and both clock periods, never as "k stages = k×".
