Story hook

The five-station row from the last chapter works beautifully for a while. Then a ticket arrives: "make the sauce", and right behind it, "pour the sauce over the fish". The sauce is still on the stove when the fish reaches the plating station. The plating cook stands there, waiting. Behind her, every station waits too.

Daniel, the head chef, watches for a few minutes. Then he changes one rule. "Don't wait for the sauce to be bottled and put on the shelf. As soon as it leaves the stove, hand the pot straight across the counter to whoever needs it." The waiting shrinks to almost nothing.

Almost. One kind of ticket still causes a pause: anything that needs an ingredient from the pantry. The pantry runner comes back one bell too late for the very next station, however fast the hand-over is. Daniel's fix for that is cleverer still: he reorders the tickets so that something else is cooked in that gap. This chapter is about those waits (hazards), the hand-over (forwarding), and the reordering trick. Its forensic lab is the course's classic: the slow loop.

What you will be able to do

  • Identify read-after-write data hazards in a U16 or real assembly sequence and say which stages are involved.
  • Explain forwarding (bypassing): which values are forwarded, from where, to where, and when it cannot help.
  • Calculate stall cycles with and without forwarding, and the cost of taken branches, from a pipeline diagram.
  • Remove a load-use stall by reordering instructions, and prove that the result is unchanged.
  • Diagnose "the slow loop": find the load-use hazard from a pipeline diagram and the assembly.
Jargon box
Data hazard (read after write, RAW)
Simple words: an instruction needs a result that an earlier instruction has not finished writing. Analogy: the fish reaches plating while the sauce is still on the stove. Precise: a dependence in which instruction j reads a register that an earlier instruction i writes, and j would read it in the pipeline before i has written it. D1 D3
Stall (bubble)
Simple words: making an instruction wait a cycle, with an empty slot moving down the pipeline instead. Analogy: a station that does nothing for one bell while the rest of the row moves on. Precise: holding an instruction (and those behind it) in place for a cycle while a no-operation, the bubble, is inserted into the next stage. D1
Forwarding (bypassing)
Simple words: giving a result straight to the next instruction that needs it, before it is written into the register. Analogy: handing the pot across the counter instead of bottling the sauce and shelving it first. Precise: extra datapath paths and multiplexers that deliver a result from the EX/MEM or MEM/WB pipeline register to the ALU inputs of a later instruction in EX, selected by a forwarding unit that compares register numbers. D1 D2
Load-use hazard
Simple words: using a value loaded from memory in the very next instruction. Analogy: the pantry runner comes back one bell too late for the next station. Precise: a RAW hazard where the producer is a load whose value exists only at the end of MEM, so a dependent instruction immediately after it must stall one cycle even with forwarding. D1 R1
Control hazard (branch hazard)
Simple words: not knowing which instruction comes next until a branch is decided. Analogy: the next ticket depends on a guest's answer that has not come back yet. Precise: a hazard caused by fetching instructions after a branch before the branch outcome and target are known; wrongly fetched instructions must be flushed. D1
Flush
Simple words: cancelling instructions that were started by mistake. Analogy: throwing away dishes started for the wrong ticket. Precise: turning instructions already in early pipeline stages into bubbles (their control signals set to zero) so they change no state. D1
Instruction scheduling
Simple words: putting instructions in a different order so the pipeline waits less, without changing the result. Analogy: cooking something else while the pantry runner is away. Precise: reordering independent instructions (by a compiler or by hardware) to separate producers from consumers, preserving all data dependences. D1 D3

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the three cases you must be able to recognise in a pipeline diagram: a stall without forwarding, the same pair with forwarding, and the load-use case where even forwarding needs one bubble.

Figure 2 shows the hardware that makes Figure 1b possible: two extra paths into the ALU's input multiplexers, chosen by a forwarding unit, and a hazard detection unit that inserts the bubble of Figure 1c.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

In a pipeline, instructions overlap. That is the whole point. But sometimes an instruction needs the answer of the one right before it. In a pipeline, that answer is not written down yet when the next instruction wants to read it. This clash is called a hazard.

The simple fix is to wait. The second instruction stops for a few ticks until the first one has written its answer. The pipeline does not break, but it gets slower: empty slots, called bubbles, travel down the row.

The clever fix is forwarding. The answer exists as soon as the ALU has computed it, even before it is written into the register. So the hardware adds a short-cut wire that hands the fresh answer straight to the next instruction. Most waits disappear.

One wait stays: when the answer comes from memory. A value from memory arrives one step later than an ALU answer, so the very next instruction is still too early. The trick then is to put a different, useful instruction in between. Compilers do this all the time.

Branches cause a different problem. The pipeline fetches the next instructions before it knows whether the branch jumps. If it guessed wrong, it throws those instructions away. That costs cycles too.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

When does a RAW hazard happen?

In the five-stage pipeline, an instruction reads its source registers in ID and writes its destination in WB, three stages later. D1 If instruction i writes register r and one of the next instructions reads r, the reader's ID may come before i's WB. With the register file written in the first half of a cycle and read in the second half, a reader whose ID is in the same cycle as the writer's WB is safe; anything earlier is a hazard. D1 For adjacent instructions that means two stall cycles, for instructions two apart one stall cycle, and from three apart none. The real run of the sum program without forwarding shows exactly this: add r3, r3, r4 right after lw r4 shows ID id id EX, two stall cycles. R1

Write-after-read and write-after-write orderings cannot cause trouble in this simple pipeline, because instructions read in ID and write in WB in program order; they matter in the out-of-order processors of F1-29. D3

Forwarding

An ALU result exists at the end of EX, two cycles before WB. Forwarding sends it from the EX/MEM pipeline register directly to the ALU inputs of the next instruction, and from MEM/WB to the instruction after that. D1 D2 The forwarding unit's rule, in words: "if the instruction in EX/MEM writes a register (RegWrite = 1), its destination is not r0, and it equals a source of the instruction now in EX, select the EX/MEM value for that input; otherwise, check MEM/WB the same way; otherwise use the value read in ID". The newer producer (EX/MEM) wins when both match. D1 In the model, forwarding is line 86 of pipe.h: the reader's EX may start one cycle after the producer's EX. R1

The load-use hazard

A load's value exists only at the end of MEM, one stage later than an ALU result. An instruction immediately after the load reaches EX in the same cycle the load is in MEM, too early even for forwarding: the arrow in Figure 1c would point backwards in time. So the hazard detection unit stalls the dependent instruction for one cycle, then the value is forwarded from MEM/WB. D1 The model encodes this as line 84 of pipe.h. In the sum loop with forwarding, the only remaining data stall is exactly this one, once per iteration: 5 stall cycles in 5 iterations. R1

Scheduling away the stall

If an independent instruction is placed between the load and its use, the bubble is filled with useful work. In the sum loop, the two addi instructions do not depend on r4, so they can move up between lw and add (reordered.s). The result must not change, and the real runs on the U16 computer prove it: both versions output 29. R2 With forwarding, the reordered loop has no data stalls at all: 42 cycles instead of 47. R2 Compilers perform this kind of instruction scheduling for the pipelines they target. D1 D3

Control hazards

The model's pipeline keeps fetching the next instructions in order (it predicts "not taken") and decides branches at the end of EX. When a branch is taken, the two instructions fetched after it are flushed and the target is fetched in the next cycle: two lost cycles per taken branch. D1 R1 In the diagrams these are the rows marked (flushed), with xx cells. The sum loop's branch is taken four times, so 8 cycles are lost in every version. Deciding branches earlier (in ID) would halve that, at the cost of extra comparison hardware and new hazards in ID; predicting better is F1-28. D1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

  • Accounting identity. In the model, total cycles = instructions + 4 + data-stall cycles + branch cycles, and every real run satisfies it: 30 + 4 + 20 + 8 = 62, 30 + 4 + 5 + 8 = 47, 30 + 4 + 0 + 8 = 42. Checking the identity is a quick test of any hand-drawn diagram. R1 R2
  • Stores. A sw needs its data value in MEM, not EX, so a design can forward a load's result to a following store without a stall. The model is conservative and treats the store's data like an ALU input; the textbooks discuss the refinement. D1 R1
  • Interlocks versus exposed delays. The hardware stall for load-use is called an interlock. Some early pipelined ISAs instead made the delay part of the ISA: the instruction after a load must not use its result, and the compiler fills the slot. That leaks the microarchitecture into the ISA (F1-23), which later implementations then have to carry. D3
  • Forwarding costs. Each forwarding path adds wires and a wider multiplexer at the ALU inputs, on the critical path of EX. Deep or wide pipelines need many more paths, one reason they are expensive. D3

How the hardware actually does it

The forwarding unit is a few comparators: 3-bit equality checks between the source fields carried in ID/EX and the destination fields in EX/MEM and MEM/WB, gated by those registers' RegWrite bits and a "not r0" check. Their outputs are the select inputs of the ALU input multiplexers in Figure 2. D1 D2 The hazard detection unit compares the sources of the instruction in ID with the destination of a load in ID/EX (MemRead = 1). On a match it does three things in the same cycle: it keeps the PC and IF/ID from loading (so the same instructions are fetched and decoded again), and it writes zeros into the control fields of ID/EX, which turns that slot into a bubble. A flush works the same way for the wrongly fetched instructions after a taken branch. D1 All of it is combinational logic plus write enables on pipeline registers: no instruction "waits" in any active sense.

Worked example

Task. Predict the cycles of the sum loop's first iteration without forwarding, then check against the real diagram.

  1. lw r4, 0(r1) (4th instruction): IF 4, ID 5, EX 6, MEM 7, WB 8.
  2. add r3, r3, r4 reads r4. Without forwarding it may read r4 in ID no earlier than r4's WB cycle 8. It enters ID in cycle 6, stalls in cycles 7 and 8, enters EX in cycle 9: two stall cycles.
  3. addi r1, r1, 1 does not read r4. It was fetched in cycle 6 but must wait in IF while add holds ID: IF 6, ID 9, EX 10.
  4. addi r2, r2, -1: IF 9, ID 10, EX 11, MEM 12, WB 13.
  5. bne r2, r0, loop reads r2, written in WB at cycle 13. It enters ID at cycle 11, stalls in 12 and 13, enters EX at 14: two more stall cycles. The branch is resolved at the end of cycle 14; the target lw is fetched in cycle 15.

The real run shows the same cells: add "IF ID id id EX", the first addi "IF if if ID", bne "IF ID id id EX", and two flushed fetches. R1 With forwarding, step 2 becomes one stall (load-use), step 5 becomes zero (ALU result forwarded from EX/MEM), and the iteration is 3 cycles shorter.

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — hazards.cpp: runs the model of F1-26 (pipe.h) on one program twice, without and with forwarding.

// F1-27 Listing 1: the same U16 program through the pipeline model twice: without
// forwarding (wait for write back) and with forwarding. Program on standard input.
//   hazards [rows]   (default 10 diagram rows)
#include <cstdlib>
#include <iostream>
#include "../F1-26/pipe.h"

int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
    const std::size_t rows = argc > 1 ? static_cast<std::size_t>(std::atoi(argv[1])) : 10;
    const u16::Program p = u16::assemble(std::cin);
    if (!p.errors.empty()) {
        std::cout << p.errors.front() << '\n';
        return 1;
    }
    std::cout << "== without forwarding: a reader waits until the writer's WB cycle ==\n";
    const pipe::Result slow = pipe::schedule(p, pipe::Config{true, false, true});
    pipe::draw(slow, rows);
    pipe::summary(slow);
    std::cout << "== with forwarding: results go straight from EX or MEM to the next EX ==\n";
    const pipe::Result fast = pipe::schedule(p, pipe::Config{true, true, true});
    pipe::draw(fast, rows);
    pipe::summary(fast);
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • A cook can see the sauce is not ready; hardware must compare numbers. Hazard detection is not seeing: it is equality checks on 3-bit register numbers. Two instructions that touch the same memory word through different registers are not detected this way at all (in this pipeline, memory accesses happen in order in MEM, so it does not matter). D1
  • Handing a pot across is free; forwarding is not. Every path costs wires and multiplexer delay on the critical path. D3
  • Reordering tickets could change a dinner; reordering instructions must not change results. Only independent instructions may move. In the sum loop, moving add above lw would add the old r4: a wrong answer, not a faster one.

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: a hand-drawn diagram with forwarding still shows two stalls for ALU-to-ALU dependences. Cause: forgetting the EX/MEM path. How to find it: compare with the model's forward-mode output. Fix: an ALU result can be used in the next cycle's EX.
  • Symptom: a diagram with zero stalls after a load used immediately. Cause: forwarding "backwards in time". How to find it: draw the arrow; it must point right or straight down. Fix: one bubble.
  • Symptom: a reordered program prints a different answer. Cause: a moved instruction depended on one it jumped over. How to find it: list each instruction's sources and destination; check every pair that changed order. Fix: move only independent instructions. Always rerun the program (R2) after scheduling.
  • Symptom: counting r0 as a dependence. Cause: r0 is never written, so it never creates a hazard (line 51 of pipe.h drops it). Fix: ignore r0 sources.
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-26: the ideal pipeline, n + 4 cycles. What carries over: the five stages, the pipeline registers, the diagram format and the timing model. What changes: instructions now interfere: results must be forwarded or waited for, loads cost a bubble when used at once, and taken branches flush work. Program order and register numbers decide performance, so the same algorithm can run at very different CPIs. D1 R1 What comes next: F1-28 attacks the remaining branch cycles by predicting branches.

Check yourself

  1. In addi r1, r0, 5 followed by add r2, r1, r1, how many stall cycles are there (a) without forwarding, (b) with forwarding?
  2. Same question for lw r1, 0(r2) followed by add r3, r1, r1.
  3. Why does a dependence through r0 never stall?
  4. Which pipeline registers can forward to the EX stage, and which one wins when both hold r1?
  5. Explain in your own words why the load-use stall cannot be removed by forwarding.
  6. Apply it to a new case: in lw r4, 0(r1), lw r5, 1(r1), add r6, r4, r5, how many stall cycles with forwarding? Why?
  7. How many cycles are lost to a taken branch in the model, and why that number?
  8. Predict, then run: with forwarding, how many cycles does the multiply program ../F1-24/cpu.in take? (Count its executed instructions, data stalls and taken branches first.)

Lab

Goal. Measure what hazards cost in the model, remove stalls by scheduling, and prove the results unchanged.

Hardware and software needed. No hardware; g++ 13.3.0 as recorded. Folder university/labs/F1-27; run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-27.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use.

Steps.

  1. Run the lab. Compare the summaries with the table above.
  2. Draw the first loop iteration of the sum program with forwarding by hand, then compare with the model.
  3. Predict the multiply program's cycles with forwarding (Check yourself 8). Run ./hazards 12 < ../F1-24/cpu.in and compare.
  4. Write your own loop that copies 5 numbers from data addresses 0–4 to 10–14 (lw, then sw). Measure it, then schedule it to remove stalls, and prove with cpu that memory 10–14 holds the same values (add lw+out at the end).
  5. Record the accounting identity (instructions + 4 + stalls + branch cycles) for every run you make.

Expected observations. Step 1 matches the table. Step 3: 26 instructions, the add/addi/bne dependences are all forwarded, 6 taken branches × 2 = 12 branch cycles, so 26 + 4 + 0 + 12 = 42 cycles; check it.

Verification. Every summary satisfies the identity; your scheduled copy loop gives the same memory contents as the original, shown by real cpu output.

Troubleshooting.

  • The identity does not hold in your hand count → you probably counted a stall twice (one instruction's stall also delays the next, but is counted once).
  • Your copy loop's stores write the wrong place → the offset in sw is relative to the base register; check sw rX, 10(r1).
  • Diagrams too wide → print fewer rows; the summary still counts everything.

Extension. Change pipe.h (in a copy) so that branches are resolved in ID instead of EX: taken branches then cost one cycle, but a branch that needs a value computed by the instruction right before it must stall. Measure both effects on the sum loop.

Forensic lab — "The slow loop"

Scenario. Leila maintains a sensor program on a small pipelined U16 core with forwarding. It counts how many of eight readings are above 50. A colleague says the core "should do this loop at about one instruction per cycle", but the profile shows far more cycles than instructions. Leila has the assembly and a pipeline diagram recorded by the timing model.

Evidence pack. The program (forensic.s) and the real pipeline diagrams and summaries (R3). Use the second diagram: the core has forwarding.

; count_big.s - count how many of the eight readings are larger than 50 (expected output: 3)
        .data 12 75 40 51 9 50 88 23
        addi r1, r0, 0      ; r1 = address of the next reading
        addi r2, r0, 8      ; r2 = readings left
        addi r3, r0, 0      ; r3 = count
        addi r6, r0, 31     ; r6 = 50, built in two steps
        addi r6, r6, 19     ;   (an immediate holds at most 31)
loop:   lw   r4, 0(r1)      ; r4 = reading
        slt  r5, r6, r4     ; r5 = 1 if 50 < reading
        add  r3, r3, r5     ; count = count + r5
        addi r1, r1, 1
        addi r2, r2, -1
        bne  r2, r0, loop
        out  r3
        halt

Questions.

  1. Observation: in the forwarding diagram, which instruction has a lower-case id cell in the loop, and in which cycle? How many data-stall cycles does the summary report, and how many loop iterations are there?
  2. Hypotheses: give two candidate causes of the extra cycles (for example the branch, an ALU-to-ALU dependence, a load-use dependence). Which ones does the evidence support, and how many cycles does each explain?
  3. Root cause: name the instruction pair that causes the data stalls, and explain why forwarding cannot remove them.
  4. Fix: reorder the loop so the data stalls disappear without changing the result. Say how you would prove the result is unchanged.
  5. Prevention: what would make this kind of stall visible before a profile is needed?

Method hints. Use the identity: cycles = instructions + 4 + stalls + branch cycles. Split the extra cycles into data and branch parts first. Then find the instruction with the lower-case cell and look at the instruction directly above it.

Mini-project

Be the compiler. Take the U16 multiply and Fibonacci programs you wrote earlier (F1-24). For each, (1) list every RAW dependence with its distance in instructions; (2) predict stalls without and with forwarding; (3) schedule the code to minimise cycles with forwarding; (4) run the model and the computer to confirm cycles and unchanged output.

Rubric. Dependence list complete and correct (3). Predictions match the model (3). Scheduled versions faster and still correct, with real outputs (3). One paragraph on which stalls cannot be removed, and why (1).

Summary

  • A RAW data hazard occurs when an instruction reads a register before an earlier instruction has written it.
  • Without forwarding, an adjacent dependence costs two stall cycles in the five-stage pipeline.
  • Forwarding passes results from EX/MEM and MEM/WB straight to the ALU inputs; ALU-to-ALU dependences then cost nothing.
  • A load used by the next instruction still costs one bubble: the load-use hazard.
  • Scheduling independent instructions between a load and its use removes that bubble; the result must be re-checked (both versions output 29).
  • Taken branches cost two cycles in the model (resolved in EX, two fetches flushed).
  • Cycles = instructions + 4 + stall cycles + branch cycles in every real run.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. (a) 2 (add's ID must wait for addi's WB); (b) 0 (EX/MEM forwarding).
  2. (a) 2; (b) 1 (load-use bubble). Answering 0 for (b) is the "forwarding backwards in time" mistake.
  3. r0 always reads 0 and is never written, so no instruction produces a newer r0 for a later one to wait for.
  4. EX/MEM (from the previous instruction) and MEM/WB (from the one before that). EX/MEM wins: it holds the most recent value of r1 in program order.
  5. Good answers say: the loaded value only exists at the end of MEM; the next instruction's EX starts in that same cycle; forwarding moves values forward in time, never backwards; so one cycle must pass.
  6. One stall. add uses r5, loaded by the instruction right before it (load-use, 1 bubble); r4 was loaded two instructions earlier and arrives in time through MEM/WB forwarding.
  7. Two cycles: the branch is resolved at the end of EX, by which time two later instructions have been fetched in order; both are flushed, and the target is fetched in the next cycle.
  8. 26 executed instructions; dependences add r3,r3,r1 → none from a load, addi r2 → bne forwarded; 6 taken branches × 2 = 12; so 26 + 4 + 0 + 12 = 42 cycles.

Forensic lab answer key

Root cause. In the loop, slt r5, r6, r4 uses r4 immediately after lw r4, 0(r1): a load-use hazard. With forwarding, it costs one bubble per iteration. The diagram shows slt as "IF ID id EX" in cycles 7–10 (the id in cycle 9), and the summary reports 8 data-stall cycles for 8 iterations.

Evidence. Forwarding summary: 55 instructions, 81 cycles, 8 data-stall cycles, 14 branch cycles. Identity: 55 + 4 + 8 + 14 = 81. The 14 branch cycles are 7 taken branches × 2 (the eighth time the loop exits). So the "extra" 22 cycles split into 8 (load-use) and 14 (branches); the ALU-to-ALU dependences (slt → add, addi r2 → bne) cost nothing with forwarding. (The first diagram, without forwarding, has 50 stall cycles: that core would be much slower, but Leila's core forwards.)

Fix. Move addi r1, r1, 1 between the load and the slt (forensic_fixed.s). Real runs: with forwarding, 73 cycles and 0 data-stall cycles (R3); the U16 computer prints out: 3 for both versions (answer_forensic, answer_forensic_fixed), so the result is unchanged.

How the fault was made. The Lab Engineer wrote the loop in the natural "load, then use" order; no other change. The evidence is the model's real output.

Wrong answers and why. "The branch is the problem": it costs 14 cycles, which a predictor (F1-28) could reduce, but the question asks about the stall marked in the diagram, and the 8 data-stall cycles are exactly the load-use count. "Forwarding is broken": ALU-to-ALU pairs show no stall. Prevention: let the compiler schedule for the pipeline; review hot loops with a pipeline model or with the processor's documented latencies.

Story hook

Every evening at the restaurant, the same regular, Mr Haddad, sits at table seven. When the waiter brings him the menu, the kitchen already knows: grilled vegetables, every time. So the grill cook starts the vegetables the moment Mr Haddad sits down, long before the waiter comes back with the order. On most evenings the plate is ready almost as soon as the order arrives.

Once a month, Mr Haddad surprises everyone and orders soup. The half-grilled vegetables go to the staff meal, and the soup is started late. Nobody minds: one wasted start a month is a small price for being early on all the other evenings.

But when a new guest sits at table seven, a guest who orders something different each time, the grill cook's habit backfires every other evening. The kitchen learns to stop guessing for that table. A processor faces the same choice at every branch, millions of times a second. This chapter is about how it guesses, how it learns, and how to tell from evidence when guessing is going wrong.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain why a pipeline must guess the outcome of a branch, and what a wrong guess costs.
  • Simulate static and dynamic predictors (always not taken, always taken, 1-bit, 2-bit saturating counter) on a branch outcome sequence and count mispredictions.
  • Calculate the cycles lost to mispredictions and their effect on CPI.
  • Describe the hardware tables behind prediction (branch history table, branch target buffer) at concept level.
  • Diagnose a loop that became slow because its data changed from sorted to unsorted.
Jargon box
Branch prediction
Simple words: guessing which way a branch will go before it is known, so the pipeline can keep going. Analogy: starting Mr Haddad's vegetables before he orders. Precise: a technique by which the processor chooses the next fetch address after a branch before the branch is resolved, and recovers (flushes) if the guess was wrong. D1 D2
Misprediction penalty
Simple words: the cycles thrown away when a guess is wrong. Analogy: the half-grilled vegetables plus the late soup. Precise: the number of cycles lost between fetching down the wrong path and resuming at the correct one; 2 cycles for a taken branch in the model of F1-27. D1 R1
Static prediction
Simple words: a fixed guessing rule that never changes. Analogy: "always start vegetables at table seven". Precise: a prediction that does not depend on run-time history, for example always not taken, or "backward branches taken, forward branches not taken". D1 D2
Dynamic prediction
Simple words: guessing based on what the branch did recently. Analogy: the cook remembering what table seven ordered last time. Precise: prediction using state updated at run time with each branch's actual outcome. D1
2-bit saturating counter
Simple words: a tiny counter from 0 to 3 that moves up when the branch is taken and down when it is not; 2 and 3 mean "guess taken". Analogy: the cook changes the habit only after being surprised twice in a row. Precise: a predictor state machine with four states (strongly/weakly not taken, weakly/strongly taken) that must mispredict twice in a row to change its prediction from a strong state. D1 D2
Branch history table (BHT)
Simple words: a small memory of predictors, one slot per branch (roughly). Analogy: a notebook with one line per table: "usually vegetables", "unpredictable". Precise: a table of prediction state (for example 2-bit counters) indexed by low-order bits of the branch's address; different branches can share an entry (aliasing). D1 D2
Branch target buffer (BTB)
Simple words: a memory that remembers where a branch jumped to last time. Analogy: knowing not only that table seven orders, but which dish. Precise: a cache indexed by the fetch address that supplies a predicted target address, so that a predicted-taken branch can be followed in the fetch stage before decoding. D2
Speculative execution
Simple words: doing work before knowing it is needed, and undoing it if not. Analogy: cooking for an order that has not arrived yet. Precise: executing instructions down a predicted path before the prediction is confirmed, without allowing them to change architectural state until it is (F1-29). D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 is the 2-bit saturating counter as a state machine (F1-19). Each arrow is labelled with the actual branch outcome that causes it. Notice that from either "strong" state, one surprise only weakens the guess; a second surprise is needed to flip it.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A branch is a fork in the road: "if this is true, go there; otherwise carry on". In a pipeline, the next instructions must be fetched before the branch has been worked out. So the processor has to guess which way the fork goes.

If the guess is right, nothing is lost. If it is wrong, the instructions started on the wrong road are thrown away, and the right ones are started late. That costs a few clock ticks each time.

The simplest guess never changes: for example "always carry on". Better guessers remember. A branch at the end of a loop jumps back almost every time, so "it jumped last time, it will jump again" is usually right. An even better guesser waits for two surprises in a row before changing its mind, so one odd case, like the loop's last turn, does not fool it twice.

Guessing only works when there is a pattern. If a branch depends on data that looks random, no memory helps, and the processor loses time on about half of those branches. Sometimes the fix is in the data, sometimes in the code.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

What prediction must achieve

In the five-stage model, a branch is resolved at the end of EX; the two instructions fetched behind it are flushed if the fetch went the wrong way, costing 2 cycles. R1 With the model's fixed rule "predict not taken", every taken branch is a misprediction. The cost in cycles is mispredictions × penalty, and the CPI contribution is that divided by the instruction count. D1 For the reordered sum loop of F1-27: 4 taken branches × 2 = 8 cycles, so 42 cycles in total; with a perfect predictor, 34 cycles (R1). The gap grows with the penalty, and longer pipelines resolve branches later, so better prediction matters more as pipelines get deeper. D2 R1

Static prediction

Static schemes need no memory. "Always not taken" is free to implement: keep fetching in order. "Always taken" needs the target address early. "Backward taken, forward not taken" uses the sign of the branch offset: loops branch backwards and are usually taken. D1 D2 On a loop branch that is taken three times and then not taken (Listing 1's pattern), "always taken" is right 30 of 40 times and "always not taken" only 10 of 40 times. R1

Dynamic prediction: 1-bit and 2-bit

A 1-bit predictor remembers the last outcome and predicts it again. On a loop it mispredicts twice per loop execution: on the exit (it predicted taken) and on the first iteration of the next execution (it remembers the exit). D1 The real run agrees: 20 mispredictions out of 40, pattern X..XX..XX..X. R1

A 2-bit saturating counter (Figure 1) changes its prediction only after two consecutive surprises from a strong state. On the same loop it mispredicts once per loop execution, on the exit. D1 D2 The run shows 12 mispredictions: one per execution for ten executions, plus two at the start while the counter warms up from "strongly not taken". R1 Over this short run "always taken" (10) still beats it, because the warm-up is a larger share of 40 branches; over a long run the counter converges to one miss per loop exit, the same as "always taken" on this pattern, while also adapting to branches that are mostly not taken, which "always taken" cannot.

Data-dependent branches

Some branches depend on data: if (value >= 128). If the data are sorted, the outcomes form long runs (N…N then T…T) and any dynamic predictor is nearly perfect. If the same values arrive in random order, the outcomes look random and a 2-bit counter is right only about as often as chance allows. The forensic lab measures exactly this with the same 64 values: 2 mispredictions sorted, 34 unsorted. R2 Two remedies exist: change the data order, or remove the branch. Compilers can turn a simple if into a conditional select instruction with no branch at all; the real x86-64 and ARM64 output in F1-31 does this for maxOf (cmovge, csel), while the RISC-V output in the same lab uses a branch. R3

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

  • Tables and aliasing. Real predictors keep many counters in a branch history table indexed by low bits of the branch address. Two branches with the same low bits share a counter and can disturb each other (aliasing). D1 D2
  • Correlation. The outcome of one branch often depends on recent outcomes of others (if (x > 0) …; if (x > 5) …). Correlating or two-level predictors index their counters with a global history register of recent outcomes, combined with address bits; tournament predictors choose between a local and a global predictor per branch. D2
  • Targets. Predicting "taken" is useless without the target. A branch target buffer, looked up with the fetch address, supplies it in IF. Function returns are predicted with a return address stack, because one return instruction goes back to many call sites. D2
  • Recovery. Instructions fetched after a predicted branch must not change registers or memory until the prediction is confirmed. In the five-stage pipeline they cannot reach WB before the branch resolves in EX, so flushing is enough; in out-of-order machines (F1-29) a reorder buffer holds speculative results. D2
Not verified — check before relying on this

The organisation, size and accuracy of the branch predictor in any real processor are not stated here, and no measurement of the build container's own predictor was possible (the perf tool printed a kernel-tools version error in this container, so hardware branch-miss counters could not be read). To study a real CPU, use the vendor's optimisation reference manual for that exact model, and measure with perf stat on a machine where it works; record the tool version and machine (AH-23).

How the hardware actually does it

Each 2-bit counter is two flip-flops and a little logic: an incrementer and decrementer that saturate, exactly the state machine of Figure 1 (F1-19). A branch history table is a small memory array of such counters, read in the fetch stage with bits of the PC and written when the branch resolves (F1-20). D1 D2 Prediction happens in IF, before the instruction is even decoded, so the hardware must find out "is this a branch, and where does it go?" from tables looked up with the address alone; that is the BTB's job. When the branch resolves and disagrees, the flush logic of F1-27 cancels the younger instructions and the PC is loaded with the correct address. D2

R1 A 1-bit predictor from "not taken" would give X..XX..X: also 4 wrong in these eight, but it keeps paying 2 per loop execution from then on, against the counter's 1.

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — predictor.cpp: four predictors on a nested-loop branch, plus the pipeline model with and without a perfect predictor.

// F1-28 Listing 1: four branch predictors on the branch of a nested loop, and what the
// mispredictions cost in a five-stage pipeline that finds branches in EX (2 lost cycles).
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include "../F1-26/pipe.h"

struct Predictor
{
    std::string name;
    int state;   // meaning depends on kind
    int kind;    // 0 always not taken, 1 always taken, 2 one-bit, 3 two-bit counter

    bool predict() const
    {
        switch (kind) {
        case 0: return false;
        case 1: return true;
        case 2: return state == 1;          // 1 = "taken last time"
        default: return state >= 2;         // 0,1 predict not taken; 2,3 predict taken
        }
    }

    void update(bool taken)
    {
        if (kind == 2) {
            state = taken ? 1 : 0;
        } else if (kind == 3) {
            state = taken ? (state < 3 ? state + 1 : 3) : (state > 0 ? state - 1 : 0);
        }
    }
};

int main()
{
    // The inner loop's closing branch: taken 3 times, then not taken (loop exit), 10 times.
    std::vector<bool> outcomes;
    for (int outer = 0; outer < 10; ++outer) {
        for (int inner = 0; inner < 4; ++inner) {
            outcomes.push_back(inner < 3);
        }
    }
    std::printf("branch outcomes (T taken, N not taken), first 12: ");
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < 12; ++i) {
        std::printf("%c", outcomes[i] ? 'T' : 'N');
    }
    std::printf(" ... (%zu in total)\n", outcomes.size());
    std::printf("%-22s %8s %14s %9s %18s\n", "predictor", "branches", "mispredictions",
                "accuracy", "cycles lost (x2)");
    std::vector<Predictor> ps = {{"always not taken", 0, 0}, {"always taken", 0, 1},
                                 {"1-bit (last outcome)", 0, 2}, {"2-bit counter", 0, 3}};
    for (Predictor& p : ps) {
        int wrong = 0;
        std::string trace;
        for (const bool t : outcomes) {
            const bool guess = p.predict();
            if (guess != t) {
                ++wrong;
            }
            if (trace.size() < 12) {
                trace += guess == t ? '.' : 'X';
            }
            p.update(t);
        }
        const double acc = 100.0 * (outcomes.size() - wrong) / outcomes.size();
        std::printf("%-22s %8zu %14d %8.1f%% %18d   first 12: %s\n", p.name.c_str(),
                    outcomes.size(), wrong, acc, 2 * wrong, trace.c_str());
    }
    // The same idea inside the pipeline model: the sum loop of F1-23 with forwarding.
    std::istringstream sum(
        ".data 7 3 9 4 6\n addi r1, r0, 0\n addi r2, r0, 5\n addi r3, r0, 0\n"
        "loop: lw r4, 0(r1)\n addi r1, r1, 1\n addi r2, r2, -1\n add r3, r3, r4\n"
        " bne r2, r0, loop\n out r3\n halt\n");
    const u16::Program prog = u16::assemble(sum);
    const pipe::Result guessNotTaken = pipe::schedule(prog, pipe::Config{true, true, true});
    const pipe::Result perfect = pipe::schedule(prog, pipe::Config{true, true, false});
    std::printf("reordered sum loop, forwarding, predict not taken: ");
    pipe::summary(guessNotTaken);
    std::printf("reordered sum loop, forwarding, perfect prediction: ");
    pipe::summary(perfect);
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined predictor.cpp -o predictor.

Where the analogy breaks

  • A cook guesses per guest; a predictor guesses per table entry. Entries are chosen by address bits, so two unrelated branches can share one "notebook line" and confuse each other (aliasing). D1
  • Wasted vegetables are visible; wasted instructions must be invisible. A wrongly started instruction may never change registers or memory. The hardware guarantees that the architectural result is the same as without guessing; only time is lost. D2
  • A cook can ask the guest; the processor cannot ask the program. The only information is the address and the history of outcomes. That is why rearranging data or code can matter more than a cleverer predictor (forensic lab).

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: a 2-bit trace by hand differs from the program. Cause: letting the counter go beyond 0 or 3. How to find it: check each state stays in 0–3. Fix: saturate.
  • Symptom: "the 2-bit counter is worse than always-taken, so it is useless". Cause: judging from a short run that includes warm-up. How to find it: count mispredictions per loop execution after the first. Fix: compare steady states, and remember branches that are mostly not taken.
  • Symptom: blaming the predictor for a slow loop whose branch is perfectly regular. Cause: the cost is elsewhere (for example load-use stalls). How to find it: use the identity of F1-27 to split stalls from branch cycles. Fix: fix the larger term first.
  • Symptom: confusing "taken" with "true". Cause: compilers often invert conditions; a C++ if whose condition is true may compile to a branch that is not taken. How to find it: read the assembly (F1-31). Fix: reason about the branch instruction, not the source line.
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-27: taken branches flush two instructions in the five-stage pipeline. What carries over: the pipeline, the flush mechanism, the accounting identity, and the finite state machines of F1-19. What changes: the processor now predicts instead of always assuming "not taken", learns from history, and performance depends on the pattern of branch outcomes in your data. D1 R2 What comes next: F1-29 goes further: issue several instructions per cycle and execute them out of order, which makes prediction even more important.

Check yourself

  1. Why must a pipelined processor predict branches at all?
  2. A loop branch is taken 99 times then not taken once, and the loop runs many times. How many mispredictions per loop execution for (a) always not taken, (b) 1-bit, (c) 2-bit in steady state?
  3. With a 2-cycle penalty and the numbers of question 2(c), how many cycles are lost per loop execution?
  4. Which predictor is best for a branch that is taken only 5 % of the time, and why?
  5. What is a branch target buffer for, and why is "predict taken" useless without it?
  6. Explain in your own words why sorting data can make a loop faster even though it does the same work.
  7. Apply it to a new case: if (x % 2 == 0) on x = 0, 1, 2, 3, … gives T N T N … . How does a 2-bit counter do? What predictor could do better?
  8. Predict, then run: change Listing 1 so the inner loop has 9 iterations instead of 4. Predict the mispredictions of each predictor, then run it.

Lab

Goal. Measure predictors on branch patterns and connect mispredictions to pipeline cycles.

Hardware and software needed. No hardware; g++ 13.3.0 as recorded. Folder university/labs/F1-28; run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-28.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use.

Steps.

  1. Run the lab; check predictor.out and forensic.out match the outputs on this page.
  2. Do Check yourself 8: change line 39's inner < 4 to inner < 9 (and line 40's inner < 3 to inner < 8), predict, run.
  3. Add a fifth predictor kind: "backward taken, forward not taken" needs a direction; give every outcome list a direction flag and implement it.
  4. Add the alternating pattern T N T N … (Check yourself 7) and measure all predictors on it.
  5. For each experiment, write the cycles lost at 2 per misprediction and the CPI change for a loop body of 5 instructions.

Expected observations. Step 2: always-taken 10 mispredictions (one exit per execution); 1-bit 20; 2-bit 12 (warm-up 2 + 10); always-not-taken 80. Step 4: the 2-bit counter is right only about half the time or worse, depending on its start state.

Verification. Your hand predictions match the program's counts; your new predictor's numbers can be checked by hand on the first 12 outcomes using the X/. trace.

Troubleshooting.

  • The "first 12" trace is shorter than 12 → your outcome list is shorter; it prints at most 12.
  • Accuracy above 100 % or negative → integer arithmetic mixing size_t and int; compute in double.
  • Pipeline lines unchanged after editing the outcome list → they use their own program (lines 69–80), by design.

Extension. Implement a tiny global-history predictor: keep the last 2 outcomes of the branch in a 2-bit history and use it to choose one of four 2-bit counters. Test it on the alternating pattern; explain the result.

Forensic lab

Scenario. Priya's monitoring job loops over 64 sensor values every minute and counts those at or above 128. Yesterday it was fast. Today, with "the same values", it is noticeably slower on the pipelined core. Nobody changed the code. The upstream team says they "only stopped sorting the data before sending it, to save time".

Evidence pack. The branch outcomes of if (value >= 128) for both days, with a 2-bit counter's mispredictions, produced by the Lab Engineer's model from the real values (R2):

// F1-28 forensic evidence: the branch "if (value >= 128)" inside a loop over 64 values,
// predicted by a 2-bit counter, once for yesterday's data and once for today's data.
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

static int run(const char* label, const std::vector<int>& values)
{
    int counter = 0, wrong = 0;   // 2-bit counter: 0,1 predict not taken; 2,3 predict taken
    std::printf("%-10s outcomes: ", label);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < values.size(); ++i) {
        const bool taken = values[i] >= 128;
        const bool guess = counter >= 2;
        wrong += guess != taken;
        counter = taken ? (counter < 3 ? counter + 1 : 3) : (counter > 0 ? counter - 1 : 0);
        if (i < 40) {
            std::printf("%c", taken ? 'T' : 'N');
        }
    }
    std::printf("...  mispredictions %d of %zu\n", wrong, values.size());
    return wrong;
}

int main()
{
    std::vector<int> today;
    std::uint32_t x = 12345;                 // fixed seed: the same "random" data every run
    for (int i = 0; i < 64; ++i) {
        x = x * 1103515245u + 12345u;        // a linear congruential generator
        today.push_back(static_cast<int>((x >> 16) % 256));
    }
    std::vector<int> yesterday = today;      // same values ...
    for (std::size_t i = 1; i < yesterday.size(); ++i) {   // ... sorted (insertion sort)
        for (std::size_t j = i; j > 0 && yesterday[j - 1] > yesterday[j]; --j) {
            std::swap(yesterday[j - 1], yesterday[j]);
        }
    }
    int below = 0;
    for (const int v : today) {
        below += v < 128;
    }
    std::printf("64 values, %d of them below 128 (the same values on both days)\n", below);
    const int w1 = run("yesterday", yesterday);
    const int w2 = run("today", today);
    std::printf("cycles lost at 2 per misprediction: yesterday %d, today %d\n", 2 * w1, 2 * w2);
    return 0;
}

Questions.

  1. Observation: describe the outcome strings for each day. Are the counts of T and N the same?
  2. Hypotheses: list two possible causes of the slowdown (more work, a predictor problem). Which evidence rules out "more work"?
  3. Root cause: explain from Figure 1 why the 2-bit counter does well yesterday and badly today.
  4. Fix: give two different fixes (one in the data, one in the code) and say how you would verify each.
  5. Prevention: what should the upstream team have checked before changing the data order?

Method hints. Count first (same values?), then look at runs of equal letters. A predictor that learns from history needs history that repeats.

Mini-project

A branch predictor bake-off. Generate four outcome sequences of at least 1,000 branches each: a nested loop, a sorted data branch, an unsorted data branch, and an alternating branch. Implement at least three predictors (including the 2-bit counter and one of your own design). Present a table of mispredictions and cycles lost, and a one-page recommendation: which predictor would you put in a small pipelined U16 core, and why?

Rubric. Sequences generated reproducibly from a fixed seed (2). Three predictors implemented and tested on hand-checked short cases (3). Table from real runs (2). Recommendation argued from the numbers, including hardware cost (3).

Summary

  • A pipeline fetches before branches resolve, so it must predict; wrong guesses cost the misprediction penalty.
  • Static predictors use fixed rules; dynamic predictors learn from each branch's history.
  • A 1-bit predictor misses twice per loop execution; a 2-bit saturating counter misses once in steady state.
  • In the model, perfect prediction would cut the reordered sum loop from 42 to 34 cycles.
  • Data-dependent branches are predictable only if the data have patterns: 2 versus 34 mispredictions for the same 64 values, sorted versus unsorted.
  • Branch-free code (conditional select) avoids the problem for simple cases.
  • Real predictors use tables, histories and target buffers; their details come only from vendor documents and measurement.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Because the next instructions are fetched before the branch is resolved; without a prediction the pipeline would have to stop fetching (stall) at every branch.
  2. (a) 99 (every taken iteration); (b) 2 (the exit, and the first iteration of the next execution); (c) 1 (the exit only).
  3. 1 × 2 = 2 cycles per loop execution.
  4. A dynamic predictor (2-bit) or static "not taken": both are right about 95 % of the time; "always taken" would be wrong 95 % of the time. The 2-bit counter also adapts if the behaviour changes.
  5. It gives the predicted target address in the fetch stage; without a target, the processor cannot fetch from the taken path until the branch is decoded and its target computed, so predicting "taken" would save nothing.
  6. Good answers say: the work is the same, but with sorted data the branch outcomes come in long runs, which a history-based predictor learns, so few fetches are wasted; unsorted data make outcomes look random and many fetches are flushed.
  7. From state 0: N, then 1, … it oscillates between states 0 and 1 (or 1 and 2) and is wrong about half the time. A predictor that uses the previous outcome of this branch as history (global or local history, Extension) can learn "after T comes N" and be almost always right.
  8. Pattern 8 × T then N, ten times: always-not-taken 80, always-taken 10, 1-bit 20, 2-bit 12. Check against your run.

Forensic lab answer key

Root cause. The same 64 values (37 below 128 on both days: the first output line) arrive sorted yesterday and unsorted today. Sorted, the outcomes are 37 N then 27 T: the 2-bit counter misses only twice, when it switches at the boundary. Unsorted, the outcomes alternate irregularly (TNNTNTNNTTTN…), the counter keeps being pushed between states, and it misses 34 of 64. At 2 cycles each that is 68 lost cycles versus 4.

Evidence. "64 values, 37 of them below 128 (the same values on both days)" rules out more work; "mispredictions 2 of 64" versus "34 of 64"; the outcome strings show long runs versus short runs.

Fix. Data: sort upstream again (if sorting costs less than the misses, which must be measured). Code: remove the branch, for example count += (value >= 128);, which compilers can turn into a compare-and-set or conditional select without a branch; verify by reading the assembly (F1-31) and re-measuring.

How the evidence was made. The Lab Engineer generated 64 values with a fixed linear congruential generator, sorted a copy with insertion sort, and ran the same 2-bit counter on both. The "slowdown" is the model's misprediction count, not a time measured on hardware.

Wrong answers and why. "There are more values today": the count line says otherwise. "The predictor is broken": it is nearly perfect yesterday. Prevention: treat data order as part of the performance contract; benchmark with realistic data orders before changing them.

Story hook

The restaurant has grown. On busy nights one cook at each station is not enough, so Amina hires a second grill cook and a second sauce cook. Now two tickets can move through the stations side by side. On the first busy night it works beautifully for a table of eight ordering eight separate salads. Then a table orders a soup that needs a stock, which needs roasted bones, which need the oven first. The second cooks stand around: every step waits for the one before it.

So Amina changes the rule. Cooks no longer take tickets strictly in order. They look along the rail and start any dish whose ingredients are ready, while the soup's long chain simmers. At the pass, though, Amina still sends plates out in ticket order, so the guests never notice the shuffle in the kitchen.

Modern processors do both of these things: they have several "cooks" per stage, and they work on whatever is ready. This chapter explains the ideas, measures them in a small model, and then shows them in a real program on the build machine, where the same additions run faster when written with four running sums instead of one.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain superscalar issue and out-of-order execution, and why both are limited by dependences between instructions.
  • Find the dependency chains in a short instruction sequence and estimate its best possible cycle count.
  • Calculate IPC (instructions per cycle) from a model run and compare machines.
  • Describe register renaming, the reorder buffer and in-order commit at concept level.
  • Diagnose a real loop whose speed is limited by one dependency chain, using its disassembly.
Jargon box
Superscalar
Simple words: a processor that can start more than one instruction in the same clock cycle. Analogy: two grill cooks working side by side. Precise: a processor that issues several instructions per cycle to several execution units; the maximum number is its issue width. D1 D2
Issue width
Simple words: how many instructions can start per cycle at most. Analogy: how many cooks stand at the station. Precise: the maximum number of instructions the issue logic can send to execution units in one cycle. D2
IPC (instructions per cycle)
Simple words: how many instructions finish per clock tick, on average. Analogy: plates out per bell. Precise: instructions completed divided by cycles; the reciprocal of CPI (F1-26). Above 1 is possible only on a superscalar processor. D1
Instruction-level parallelism (ILP)
Simple words: how many instructions in a program could run at the same time because they do not need each other's results. Analogy: eight separate salads versus one soup chain. Precise: the potential overlap among instructions of a single thread, limited by data dependences, control dependences and resources. D2
Dependency chain
Simple words: a line of instructions where each one needs the result of the one before. Analogy: bones → stock → soup. Precise: a path in the data-dependence graph; the longest path (sum of latencies) bounds the run time from below, however many units there are. D2
Out-of-order execution
Simple words: running instructions as soon as their inputs are ready, not strictly in program order. Analogy: cooks starting any dish whose ingredients are ready. Precise: dynamic scheduling in which instructions wait in a window (reservation stations or an issue queue) and are dispatched when their operands are available, while results are committed in program order. D1 D2
Register renaming
Simple words: giving each new result its own hidden register, so instructions that only reuse a register name stop blocking each other. Analogy: a fresh labelled pot per ticket instead of everyone sharing "pot 10". Precise: mapping architectural registers to a larger set of physical registers at decode, which removes write-after-read and write-after-write (name) dependences and leaves only true read-after-write dependences. D2
Reorder buffer (ROB)
Simple words: a queue that remembers the program order so results can be made official in that order. Analogy: Amina's ticket rail at the pass: plates leave in ticket order, whenever they were cooked. Precise: a circular buffer of in-flight instructions in program order; an instruction commits (updates architectural state) only when it reaches the head and has completed, which gives precise exceptions and lets mispredicted work be discarded. D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the two sum programs of Listing 1 as dependence graphs. On the left, every addition feeds the next one: a single chain. On the right, the additions alternate between two sums, so there are two chains of half the length that can run side by side.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A faster processor can try two tricks. The first is to do two or more instructions at the same moment, like two cooks at one station. The second is to not wait in line: if the next instruction is stuck waiting for something, start a later one that is ready.

Both tricks only help when instructions do not need each other. If every step needs the answer of the step before, extra cooks stand idle. Ten people cannot boil one egg faster.

So the shape of a program matters. Adding up a list into one total makes a long chain: each addition waits for the last. Adding into four separate totals and combining them at the end makes four short chains, and the processor can work on all four at once. The answer is the same; the speed is not.

The processor keeps a strict list of the program's order, and only makes results official in that order. That way, even though the work inside is shuffled, the program sees exactly what it asked for.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

From one instruction per cycle to several

The pipeline of F1-26 can at best finish one instruction per cycle: CPI 1, IPC 1. A superscalar processor fetches, decodes and issues several instructions per cycle, with several execution units. D1 D2 In Listing 1, sixteen independent additions (sequence A) take 16 cycles on a 1-wide machine and 8 cycles on a 2-wide one: IPC 2.00. R1 More width costs more hardware: more register file ports, more forwarding paths, and dependence checks between every pair of instructions issued together. D2

Dependences set the limit

Sequence B loads eight values and adds each into one running sum. The model gives loads and floating-point adds 3 cycles of latency. The eight additions form one chain of 8 × 3 = 24 cycles; with the first load, 27 cycles is the best any machine can do. The model agrees: 27 cycles on the 2-wide machine, in order or out of order. R1 Width does not help a chain. This is the most important idea in the chapter: the longest dependency chain bounds the time. D2

In order versus out of order

Sequence C has two chains (Figure 1). A 2-wide in-order machine still takes 30 cycles, because it must stop at the first instruction that is not ready, even when later instructions could go. An out-of-order machine with a window of 8 instructions takes 18 cycles: it issues loads and the other chain's additions while one chain waits. R1 Out-of-order execution finds the parallelism that the code's shape allows; it cannot invent parallelism that is not there (B stays at 27). D2

Sequence D, with four sums, takes 20 cycles out of order, not fewer than C. R1 Once the chains are short enough, another limit binds: only 2 instructions issue per cycle, and D has 19 instructions, two more combining additions than C. Every speed-up runs into the next bottleneck.

Keeping the program's meaning

Instructions may execute out of order, but the program must see results as if they ran in order. The reorder buffer holds instructions in program order; each one commits, making its result official, only when it reaches the head and has finished. D2 If an older instruction faults, or a branch was mispredicted (F1-28), everything younger in the buffer is discarded. This is how speculative execution stays invisible to the program, apart from time. D2

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

  • Name dependences and renaming. Listing 1's out-of-order model refuses to issue an instruction that would overwrite a register an older, waiting instruction still needs (lines 34–42). Those write-after-read and write-after-write conflicts are about names, not data. Real out-of-order cores rename architectural registers onto a larger physical register file, so only true read-after-write dependences remain. D2
  • The pieces. A typical textbook out-of-order core has: a front end (fetch with branch prediction, decode, rename); an issue queue or reservation stations, where instructions wait for operands; execution units; a result bus that wakes up waiting instructions; and the reorder buffer for in-order commit. D2
  • Memory ordering. Loads and stores also need ordering checks: a load may not take a value from memory if an older store to the same address has not happened yet. Load/store queues track this. D2
  • Limits. Window size, issue width, number of units of each kind, branch mispredictions and cache misses (F1-33) all cap IPC. Static alternatives exist: VLIW machines leave scheduling to the compiler. D1 D2
  • Floating point and reordering. Floating-point addition is not associative under rounding, so a compiler may not turn one running sum into four on its own unless told that reassociation is allowed. The real disassembly below shows GCC 13.3.0 at -O2 kept the single chain in sumOne. D3 R3
Not verified — check before relying on this

This chapter does not state the issue width, window or reorder-buffer size, or floating-point add latency of any real processor, including the build machine (the run log records only "Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz", which does not name the core design). The model's 3-cycle latencies are invented for teaching. Hardware event counters could not be read: perf printed "perf not found for kernel 6.18.44-fc" in the container. Before quoting real numbers, take them from the vendor's optimisation manual for the exact model and confirm with measurements.

How the hardware actually does it

Everything here is built from the parts of F1-20 and F1-21. The rename table is a small register file indexed by architectural register number whose entries are physical register numbers; a free list hands out unused physical registers. D2 Each waiting instruction in the issue queue stores the tags of the physical registers it needs; when a unit finishes, it broadcasts its tag, and comparators in every queue entry mark matching operands ready. That broadcast-and-compare logic grows with width × window size, which is one reason real windows and widths are finite. D2 The reorder buffer is a circular queue with head and tail pointers, written at rename and read at commit (F1-19 counters). None of this changes the ISA: the same U16 or x86-64 program runs unchanged, faster or slower (F1-23).

Worked example

Task. Estimate the best cycle count of sequence C (two sums) by hand, then compare with the model.

  1. Chains. Each sum receives four additions: chain length 4 × 3 = 12 cycles. The final combining addition adds 3: 15 cycles of chain after the first value is available.
  2. First load. The first addition cannot start before its load finishes: 3 cycles. Lower bound from dependences: about 3 + 15 = 18 cycles.
  3. Issue limit. 17 instructions at 2 per cycle need at least 9 cycles to issue: not binding here.
  4. Model. The out-of-order run gives 18 cycles, IPC 0.94: the machine reached the dependence bound. R1
  5. In order. The 2-wide in-order run gives 30 cycles: it waits at every addition whose load or earlier addition is not done, even when the other chain could proceed. R1

The same reasoning for B gives 3 + 8 × 3 = 27 cycles, which is what every 2-wide machine in the model achieved. R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — ilp.cpp: a small issue model with configurable width and in-order or out-of-order issue.

// F1-29 Listing 1: how many cycles do three small instruction sequences take on three
// model machines: 1-wide in-order, 2-wide in-order, and 2-wide out-of-order with a window
// of 8 instructions? Latencies are model values (load 3 cycles, fadd 3, addi 1), not the
// values of any real CPU.
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Instr
{
    std::string text;
    int dest, src1, src2;  // register numbers; -1 = none
    int latency;           // cycles until the result can be used
};

// Returns the cycle at which every instruction has finished.
static int simulate(const std::vector<Instr>& prog, int width, bool outOfOrder, int window)
{
    std::vector<int> readyAt(16, 0);          // cycle at which each register's value is ready
    std::vector<int> issued(prog.size(), -1); // cycle at which each instruction issued
    std::size_t next = 0;                     // oldest instruction not yet issued
    int finish = 0;
    for (int cycle = 1; next < prog.size(); ++cycle) {
        int slots = width;
        const std::size_t end = outOfOrder ? std::min(prog.size(), next + window) : prog.size();
        for (std::size_t i = next; i < end && slots > 0; ++i) {
            if (issued[i] >= 0) {
                continue;
            }
            const Instr& in = prog[i];
            const bool ready = (in.src1 < 0 || readyAt[in.src1] <= cycle) &&
                               (in.src2 < 0 || readyAt[in.src2] <= cycle);
            // an out-of-order machine must also not overwrite a register an older,
            // not-yet-issued instruction still has to read or write (renaming would fix this)
            bool clash = false;
            for (std::size_t k = next; k < i && outOfOrder; ++k) {
                if (issued[k] < 0 && (prog[k].src1 == in.dest || prog[k].src2 == in.dest ||
                                      prog[k].dest == in.dest)) {
                    clash = true;
                }
            }
            if (!ready || clash) {
                if (!outOfOrder) {
                    break;  // in-order: nobody may overtake the oldest waiting instruction
                }
                continue;
            }
            issued[i] = cycle;
            if (in.dest >= 0) {
                readyAt[in.dest] = cycle + in.latency;
            }
            finish = std::max(finish, cycle + in.latency - 1);
            --slots;
        }
        while (next < prog.size() && issued[next] >= 0) {
            ++next;
        }
    }
    return finish;
}

int main()
{
    // r1 = pointer, values loaded into r2..r9, running sums in r10..r13
    auto sums = [](int accumulators) {     // load 8 values, fadd each into one of the sums
        std::vector<Instr> p;
        for (int i = 0; i < 8; ++i) {
            const int acc = 10 + i % accumulators;
            p.push_back({"lw", 2 + i, 1, -1, 3});
            p.push_back({"fadd", acc, acc, 2 + i, 3});
        }
        for (int a = 1; a < accumulators; ++a) {   // combine the partial sums at the end
            p.push_back({"fadd", 10, 10, 10 + a, 3});
        }
        return p;
    };
    std::vector<Instr> independent;
    for (int i = 0; i < 16; ++i) {         // sixteen adds that do not depend on each other
        independent.push_back({"addi", 2 + i % 12, 0, -1, 1});
    }
    const std::vector<Instr> chain = sums(1), twoAcc = sums(2), fourAcc = sums(4);
    std::printf("%-34s %6s %18s %18s %18s\n", "sequence", "instr", "1-wide in-order",
                "2-wide in-order", "2-wide out-of-order");
    const std::vector<std::pair<std::string, const std::vector<Instr>*>> all = {
        {"A: 16 independent adds", &independent},
        {"B: 8 x (load, fadd) into ONE sum", &chain},
        {"C: 8 x (load, fadd) into TWO sums", &twoAcc},
        {"D: 8 x (load, fadd) into FOUR sums", &fourAcc}};
    for (const auto& [name, prog] : all) {
        const int n = static_cast<int>(prog->size());
        const int c1 = simulate(*prog, 1, false, 1);
        const int c2 = simulate(*prog, 2, false, 1);
        const int c3 = simulate(*prog, 2, true, 8);
        std::printf("%-34s %6d %8d (IPC %.2f) %8d (IPC %.2f) %8d (IPC %.2f)\n", name.c_str(), n,
                    c1, static_cast<double>(n) / c1, c2, static_cast<double>(n) / c2, c3,
                    static_cast<double>(n) / c3);
    }
    return 0;
}

Listing 2 — accum.cc: the same idea on the real build machine. It is the evidence for the forensic lab, so its outputs appear there.

// F1-29 Listing 2 (forensic evidence): add up 2^20 doubles with one running sum and with
// four running sums, and time both on the machine it runs on. Built with -O2 by run.sh.
#include <algorithm>
#include <chrono>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

__attribute__((noinline)) double sumOne(const std::vector<double>& v)
{
    double s = 0.0;
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) {
        s += v[i];
    }
    return s;
}

__attribute__((noinline)) double sumFour(const std::vector<double>& v)
{
    double s0 = 0.0, s1 = 0.0, s2 = 0.0, s3 = 0.0;
    std::size_t i = 0;
    for (; i + 4 <= v.size(); i += 4) {
        s0 += v[i];
        s1 += v[i + 1];
        s2 += v[i + 2];
        s3 += v[i + 3];
    }
    for (; i < v.size(); ++i) {
        s0 += v[i];
    }
    return (s0 + s1) + (s2 + s3);
}

template <typename F>
static double medianMs(F f, const std::vector<double>& v, double& result)
{
    std::vector<double> ms;
    for (int rep = 0; rep < 21; ++rep) {
        const auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        result = f(v);
        const auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        ms.push_back(std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(t1 - t0).count());
    }
    std::sort(ms.begin(), ms.end());
    return ms[ms.size() / 2];
}

int main()
{
    std::vector<double> v(1 << 20);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) {
        v[i] = static_cast<double>(i % 1000) * 0.5;  // halves: every partial sum is exact
    }
    double r1 = 0.0, r4 = 0.0;
    const double t1 = medianMs(sumOne, v, r1);
    const double t4 = medianMs(sumFour, v, r4);
    std::printf("one running sum : result %.1f, median of 21 runs %.3f ms\n", r1, t1);
    std::printf("four running sums: result %.1f, median of 21 runs %.3f ms\n", r4, t4);
    std::printf("ratio one/four: %.2f\n", t1 / t4);
    return r1 == r4 ? 0 : 1;
}

Build command (from run.sh): g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror accum.cc -o accum, then objdump -d --no-show-raw-insn -M intel -C for the two functions.

Where the analogy breaks

  • Cooks can taste and improvise; units cannot. Each execution unit does one kind of operation with a fixed latency; the scheduling is mechanical, done every cycle by comparators. D2
  • A kitchen can always hire more cooks. Hardware cost grows faster than width: every extra issue slot needs more register ports, more bypass paths and more comparisons. D2
  • Guests never see a dish thrown away; programs never see a squashed instruction's result, but they can see its timing. That side channel of speculative execution is a security topic beyond this course (F2-47).

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: expecting a 4-wide processor to run any loop 4 times faster. Cause: ignoring dependency chains. How to find it: draw the graph; find the longest chain. Fix: shorten chains (more accumulators, tree reductions) where correctness allows.
  • Symptom: splitting a floating-point sum changes the last digits. Cause: rounding depends on the order of additions. How to find it: compare with values whose sums are exact (Listing 2 uses halves for this reason). Fix: decide whether the change is acceptable; document it.
  • Symptom: a model run shows no gain from out-of-order execution. Cause: the window is too small, or all instructions are in one chain. How to find it: vary window on line 94. Fix: none needed: that is the lesson.
  • Symptom: a timing comparison flips between runs. Cause: noise on a shared machine. How to find it: repeat; use medians, as Listing 2 does. Fix: report the spread and the machine, never a single number (AH-23).
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-28: a pipeline guessing branches to keep instructions flowing. What carries over: hazards, stalls and the idea that a result must not be used before it exists. What changes: several instructions per cycle and a dynamic order; performance now depends on the shape of the dependence graph, not only on instruction counts. D2 R1 What comes next: F1-30 adds a different kind of parallelism: several whole cores, each running its own instruction stream.

Check yourself

  1. What is the difference between superscalar and out-of-order? Can a processor be one without the other?
  2. Why does sequence B take 27 cycles on every 2-wide machine in the model?
  3. What does the reorder buffer guarantee, and why is that needed?
  4. What kinds of dependence does register renaming remove, and which kind remains?
  5. Sequence A has IPC 2.00 on the 2-wide machines. What would you predict on a 4-wide out-of-order machine? What could stop it?
  6. Explain in your own words why four running sums can be faster than one, even though the number of additions is the same.
  7. Apply it to a new case: computing a product of 8 numbers, p *= x[i]. Draw the dependence graph and propose a faster form.
  8. Predict, then run: change line 94 to a window of 2 instead of 8. Predict the effect on C and D, then run.

Lab

Goal. Measure the effect of width, issue order and code shape in the model, and observe the same effect on the real build machine.

Hardware and software needed. No hardware; g++ 13.3.0 and GNU objdump 2.42 as recorded. Folder university/labs/F1-29; run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-29.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use.

Steps.

  1. Run the lab. Check ilp.out matches this page exactly; accum.out will show different times on your machine.
  2. Add a 4-wide out-of-order column to line 92–97 (width 4, window 16). Predict A, B, C, D first.
  3. Change the load latency on line 70 from 3 to 10 (a cache miss, F1-33). Which sequences suffer most in order? Out of order?
  4. Add sequence E: eight sums. Does it beat D? Explain with the issue limit.
  5. Run accum five times (rerun the lab). Record the ratio each time, with your machine's CPU model.

Expected observations. Step 2: A reaches 4 cycles; B stays near 27. Step 3: in-order times grow sharply; out-of-order times grow less where loads are independent. Step 4: little or no gain. Step 5: the ratio stays above 1 but varies between runs.

Verification. Every model number can be checked by the hand method of the worked example: max(dependence bound, instructions ÷ width).

Troubleshooting.

  • The model never finishes → an instruction can never become ready; check source register numbers are below 16.
  • accum exits with code 1 → the two sums differ: you changed the data so the sums are no longer exact.
  • Ratio below 1 → background load on the machine; rerun; report the spread.

Extension. Add renaming to the model: delete the clash check (lines 34–42) and give each result a fresh register. Measure C and D again and explain the difference.

Forensic lab

Scenario. Jonas maintains a statistics tool. A colleague submits a change that replaces a tidy summing loop with an "ugly" one using four separate sums. Jonas is about to reject it, but the colleague says it runs faster. Jonas thinks this is impossible: it does the same number of additions, and the compiler optimises both with -O2 anyway. He asks you to decide with evidence.

Evidence pack. Listing 2 above; its run on the build machine; and the disassembly of both functions produced from the same binary.

Questions.

  1. Observation: are the results equal? Which version ran faster in this run, and by how much? What do you need to know before generalising?
  2. Hypotheses: list three possible explanations (fewer instructions, memory effects, dependency chains). How would you test each with the evidence here?
  3. Root cause: find the hot loop in each disassembly. Which register carries the sum in sumOne? How many registers carry sums in sumFour's main loop?
  4. Fix: should the change be accepted? Under what conditions on the data and rounding?
  5. Prevention: how should a team record such a performance claim so that it can be checked later?

Method hints. Look for addsd (add scalar double) and its destination register. A loop whose every addition writes and reads the same register is one chain.

Mini-project

Dependence-graph analyser. Extend Listing 1 so it prints, for any sequence, the length of the longest dependency chain (in cycles), the issue bound (instructions ÷ width), and the model's actual cycles. Write five sequences of your own (including a tree reduction of 8 values) and present a table that shows which bound binds for each. Add a one-page note relating your findings to Listing 2's real timing.

Rubric. Longest-chain computation correct on hand-checked cases (3). Five sequences with predictions written before running (3). Table from real runs (2). Clear, honest link to the real timing, with machine and spread recorded (2).

Summary

  • Superscalar processors issue several instructions per cycle; IPC can exceed 1.
  • Out-of-order processors issue whatever is ready within a window, and commit in program order through a reorder buffer.
  • Register renaming removes name dependences; true read-after-write dependences remain.
  • The longest dependency chain bounds the time: in the model, one sum takes 27 cycles on any 2-wide machine; two sums take 18 out of order.
  • Once chains are short, other limits bind: four sums gave 20 cycles, not fewer.
  • On the build machine, four running sums ran faster than one in the logged run, and the disassembly shows why: one xmm0 chain versus four registers.
  • Real widths, windows and latencies must come from vendor documents and measurement.
