Answers to Check yourself

  1. Superscalar = several instructions issued per cycle; out-of-order = issue order differs from program order. Yes: a 2-wide in-order machine is superscalar but not out-of-order (Listing 1's middle column); a 1-wide machine could issue out of order.
  2. Its eight additions form one chain of 8 × 3 cycles, after a first load of 3 cycles: 27 cycles is the dependence bound, and width cannot shorten a chain.
  3. That results become architectural state in program order; needed for precise exceptions and to discard work after a mispredicted branch.
  4. Write-after-read and write-after-write (name dependences); read-after-write (true dependence) remains.
  5. About 4 cycles (IPC 4.00), if the machine has four units able to do the adds and enough register ports; the model's 12-register reuse could create name clashes without renaming.
  6. Good answers say: one sum makes every addition wait for the previous one's latency; four sums make four independent chains whose additions can be in flight at the same time; the total work is equal but the longest chain is about a quarter as long.
  7. A single chain of 8 multiplications; a tree form multiplies pairs (4 independent), then pairs of results (2), then the final one: chain length 3 multiplications instead of 8 (rounding caveats as for sums).
  8. With a window of 2, the out-of-order machine sees too few instructions to find the other chain, so C and D move towards the in-order numbers. Check against your run.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation. Both results are 261820800.0 (exact, because every value is a multiple of 0.5). In the run shown above, the four-sum version took less time; the exact milliseconds and the printed ratio change with every rerun, and in this build session the ratio stayed between about 1.4 and 1.6. One machine, one session: do not generalise without measuring on the target. R2

Root cause. In sumOne, the hot loop (addresses 14c0–14d2) is two addsd xmm0, … per iteration: every addition reads and writes xmm0, so each must wait for the previous one's latency. The compiler unrolled by two but kept one chain, because reassociating floating-point additions would change rounding. In sumFour, the hot loop (1528–154a) adds into xmm0, xmm2, xmm1 and xmm3: four independent chains that an out-of-order core can overlap. Instruction count per element is similar, so "fewer instructions" does not explain it. R3

Ruling out memory. Both versions read the same 8 MB array in the same order, once per repetition; memory traffic is the same. A stronger test: rerun with a smaller array that fits in cache (F1-33); if the gap persists, the chain is the cause.

Fix and prevention. Accept the change if the small rounding differences of reordering are acceptable for the tool (document it), or use a compiler option that permits reassociation for that function. Record the claim with the machine, compiler, options, median and spread, and keep the benchmark in the repository so it can be rerun.

Wrong answers and why. "The compiler made them identical": the disassembly shows otherwise. "Four sums do fewer additions": both do 220 additions plus a handful. "It is a cache effect": both access the same data in the same order.

Story hook

Analogy

Amina is the head chef of a busy restaurant. Whatever is on her cutting board she can use at once. The shelves beside the stove hold a few dozen jars; the long shelf along the wall holds more; the back room holds more still. Everything else lives in the big pantry at the end of a long corridor.

One evening the new kitchen helper, Kofi, is sent to the pantry for a single jar of saffron. Amina waits, knife in hand, until he comes back. The dish cannot continue without it. Later the same evening, Kofi is sent to fetch forty sacks of rice for tomorrow. Nobody waits for any single sack; what matters is how many sacks per minute the corridor can carry, and whether several helpers can walk it at the same time.

Those are two different questions about the same corridor: how long until the first thing arrives? and how much arrives per minute once deliveries are flowing? Engineers call them latency and bandwidth, and a processor asks both of them billions of times a second.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain latency and bandwidth with their units, and why a program can be limited by either one.
  • Measure the load latency of your own machine for working sets of growing size with a pointer-chasing program, and read the plateaus of the curve.
  • Measure read bandwidth with independent loads and explain why it is far higher than "one block per latency".
  • Apply Little's law to compute how many bytes must be in flight to reach a given bandwidth.
  • Diagnose a latency benchmark that was fooled by a predictable access pattern.
Jargon box
Latency
Simple words: how long you wait from asking for something until it arrives. Analogy: the time of one round trip of the helper to the pantry. Precise: the time between issuing a memory request (for example a load) and the moment its data can be used; measured in seconds (ns) or in processor clock cycles. D1 D2
Bandwidth
Simple words: how much data arrives per second once it is flowing. Analogy: how many sacks per minute the corridor can carry. Precise: the rate of data transfer, in bytes per second (GB/s = 109 bytes per second in this course); also called throughput when it describes a measured rate. D2 D3
Memory hierarchy
Simple words: several layers of storage, from tiny and fast to huge and slow. Analogy: cutting board, shelves by the stove, shelf along the wall, back room, pantry, warehouse across town. Precise: the organisation of a computer's storage into levels (registers, caches, main memory, storage) in which each level is larger, slower and cheaper per byte than the one above it, and holds copies of data used by the level above. D1 D2
Cache
Simple words: a small fast memory that keeps copies of data you used recently. Analogy: the shelves near the stove. Precise: a small, fast memory, managed by hardware, that holds copies of blocks of main memory so that later accesses to them are served quickly; F1-33 explains its organisation. D1 D2
Working set
Simple words: the data a program keeps using during one phase of its work. Analogy: the jars a dish needs this evening. Precise: the set of memory locations (or its size in bytes) that a program accesses repeatedly during an interval of time; whether it fits in a cache level decides that level's hit rate. D1
Little's law
Simple words: to keep stuff arriving fast while each trip is slow, many trips must be under way at once. Analogy: forty sacks per minute with a five-minute walk means two hundred sacks must be on the way at any moment. Precise: in a steady system, the average number of items in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends inside; for memory, bytes in flight = bandwidth × latency. D3
Memory-level parallelism
Simple words: several memory requests waiting at the same time instead of one after another. Analogy: several helpers walking the corridor together. Precise: the number of outstanding memory accesses a processor can have at once; it needs independent addresses, because a load whose address depends on another load cannot start until that load returns. D3
Prefetching
Simple words: fetching data before it is asked for, by guessing what comes next. Analogy: a helper who notices you take jars from left to right and brings the next one early. Precise: starting a memory transfer before the program's own access, either by instructions in the program (software prefetch) or by hardware that detects patterns such as fixed strides (hardware prefetch). D1 D3

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 is the memory hierarchy drawn as the restaurant. Each level up is smaller and faster; each level down is larger and slower. The figure has no numbers on purpose: sizes and times belong to a named product's documents, or to your own measurement in the lab.

Figure 2 shows why latency and bandwidth are different questions. On the left, each request waits for the one before it: the corridor carries one jar per round trip. On the right, several independent requests overlap: the trip still takes as long, but many jars are on their way at once.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A processor works on numbers that sit in its registers, its cutting board. When it needs a number that is not there, it must ask memory for it. If the number is on a nearby shelf (a cache), it comes back quickly. If it is only in the pantry (main memory), the processor waits for a long walk.D1

Why not make the whole pantry as fast as the shelf by the stove? Because fast storage is expensive and takes room, and big storage is slower to search and further away. So computers use a little fast memory and a lot of slow memory, and keep copies of the things you use most in the fast part.D2

The waiting time for one trip is the latency. The amount delivered per second once many trips are under way is the bandwidth. A program that needs one thing before it can know what to ask for next (like following clues on a treasure hunt) feels every trip's latency. A program that asks for many things at once (like a long shopping list) can use the bandwidth.D3

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Why memory is slower than the processor

F1-20 showed the two cell types: an SRAM cell holds a bit in a small loop of transistors and can be read quickly; a DRAM cell holds a bit as charge on a capacitor, is much smaller, and must be read through a slower sense-and-restore process and refreshed.D2 D5 Because DRAM cells are small and cheap, main memory is built from DRAM, and because SRAM is fast, caches are built from SRAM.D2 Main memory also sits outside the processor chip, on a bus driven by a memory controller, which adds the time of crossing chips and of the controller's scheduling.D3

There is a second, more general reason. A larger memory needs more address decoding, longer wires and more cells per data line, so for the same technology a larger memory is slower than a smaller one.D2 This is why the hierarchy of Figure 1 exists: no single memory is both large and fast, so the designer builds several levels and relies on programs reusing the same data (F1-34 calls this locality).D1 D2

Two different measures

Latency is the time from issuing a request until its data can be used. Bandwidth is the rate at which data is delivered, in bytes per second.D2 They are linked but not the same: a wide road with a long journey has high bandwidth and high latency. If only one request is outstanding at a time, the rate is at most one block per latency. For 64-byte blocks and a latency of 100 ns that is 64 bytes per 100 ns, which is 0.64 GB/s, whatever the road could carry (exercise numbers; Listing 3 prints the same sum).R3

Little's law

Little's law says that in a steady system the average number of items inside equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends inside.D3 For memory: bytes in flight = bandwidth × latency. To read 10 GB/s from a memory with 100 ns latency, 10 bytes per ns × 100 ns = 1,000 bytes must be on their way at every moment, about sixteen 64-byte blocks (exercise numbers, checked by Listing 3).R3 If the hardware can only keep a few requests outstanding, or the program cannot generate independent addresses, the full bandwidth is out of reach.D3

Dependent and independent loads

A load whose address is computed from the value of another load cannot start until that load has returned. Following a linked list is the standard example: p = p->next again and again. Such a chain exposes the full latency of every step, which is exactly why benchmarks use it to measure latency (Listing 1).D1 D3 Summing an array is the opposite: every address is known in advance (a + i), so the processor's out-of-order core (F1-29) and the hardware prefetchers can have many loads in flight, and the measured rate approaches the bandwidth (Listing 2).D3

Working sets and plateaus

If a program's working set fits in a cache level, almost all of its accesses are served by that level after the first pass, and its time per access stays flat as the working set grows, until the set no longer fits. Plotting time per access against working-set size therefore shows plateaus separated by steps, one plateau per level.D1 Listing 1 draws that curve for the machine it runs on. The positions of the steps are evidence about your machine's caches; the sizes the operating system reports are another (F1-33). Neither is a datasheet.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Outstanding misses. To overlap misses, a cache must keep accepting requests while earlier misses are pending (a "non-blocking" or "lockup-free" cache) and must track each pending miss until its data returns.D3 The number of misses a core can keep in flight is a design limit; by Little's law it caps the bandwidth one core can draw at roughly (outstanding misses × block size) ÷ latency. The measured multi-thread bandwidth in F1-39 rises with the number of threads on this build's machine, which is consistent with a per-core limit, but the build did not verify the limit's value for this CPU.

Not verified — check before relying on this

How many outstanding L1 data-cache misses one core of the build container's processor can track, and how many its hardware prefetchers add, were not checked. The documents to check are the processor vendor's optimisation reference manual for the exact model (the model string is in every .log of this chapter) and the Hennessy–Patterson chapter on memory hierarchy design (D3).

Prefetching changes what you measure. Hardware prefetchers detect simple patterns, such as accesses to consecutive blocks, and fetch ahead.D3 A latency benchmark whose chain visits blocks in address order therefore measures something closer to bandwidth than latency. Listing 1 shuffles the visiting order to defeat this; the forensic lab shows what happens without the shuffle.

Virtual memory joins the curve. Each load also needs its virtual address translated. Once the working set spans more pages than the translation cache (the TLB, F1-38) covers, the random chain also pays for page-table walks, so the largest working sets in Listing 1 measure DRAM latency plus translation cost.D1 F1-38 separates the two.

Measurement discipline. Build with optimisation and without sanitizers (sanitizers add work to every access); warm up before timing; make the result observable (the checksum) so the compiler cannot delete the loop; use a monotonic clock (std::chrono::steady_clock); repeat and report the spread; and name the machine. On a shared virtual machine, other tenants and the hypervisor add noise, so one run is a sample, not a property of the processor.D6 S1

How the hardware actually does it

A load first checks the L1 data cache. On a miss, the request goes to the next level, and so on; at the last cache level a miss becomes a request to the memory controller, which turns it into DRAM commands for the right channel, bank, row and column (F1-39).D2 D3 The data comes back as a whole block (a cache line, F1-33), is installed in the caches on the way, and the waiting load completes.D2 Meanwhile an out-of-order core keeps executing instructions that do not depend on the load; when nothing independent is left, the core stalls.D3 In F1-27 the "memory" stage of the five-stage pipeline took one cycle; that was a simplification valid only when the access hits in the first-level cache.

The build container reports an Intel Xeon processor (model string in the logs) running as a virtual machine with four CPUs. Its cache sizes appear in F1-33's cache_info.out as the kernel reports them. Nothing in this chapter is a specification of that processor: every time below was measured on the build container, once, and labelled so.

Worked example

Exercise numbers first. A memory system has 100 ns latency and the program wants 10 GB/s.

  1. Units: 10 GB/s = 10 × 109 bytes per 109 ns = 10 bytes per ns.
  2. Little's law: bytes in flight = 10 bytes/ns × 100 ns = 1,000 bytes.
  3. In 64-byte blocks: 1,000 ÷ 64 = 15.6, so about 16 block requests must be outstanding at all times.
  4. With only one request outstanding: 64 bytes per 100 ns = 0.64 GB/s.
  5. If the latency halves to 50 ns with the same 10 GB/s goal, only 500 bytes (7.8 blocks) need to be in flight (case C).

Listing 3 prints exactly these numbers from littles.in.R3 Then run.sh feeds it the measured numbers of this build's largest working set: the last line of Listing 1's random-chain output (latency) and of Listing 2's output (bandwidth). The result, in the second output block of Listing 3, says how many blocks the build container must have had in flight during Listing 2 if both measurements describe the same memory: about thirty. That is an inference from two measurements on one machine, not a hardware fact.R1 R3

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — chase.cc: the pointer-chasing latency benchmark. Each node fills one 64-byte block; the chain visits all nodes in a shuffled order, so each load's address is the value the previous load returned.

// Pointer chasing: the average time of ONE load whose address depends on the load before it,
// for working sets of growing size. Each node fills one 64-byte block so every load touches
// a new block. Mode "random" links the nodes in a shuffled cycle; mode "sequential" links
// node i to node i+1 (a pattern the hardware can predict). Numbers are measurements, not specs.
#include <chrono>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <random>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct alignas(64) Node
{
    std::size_t next;
    char pad[64 - sizeof(std::size_t)];
};

// Choose a visiting order (shuffled, or 0, 1, 2, ... for "sequential"), then link the nodes
// in that order; the last links back to the first, so the links form ONE cycle through all n.
std::vector<Node> makeChain(std::size_t n, bool random)
{
    std::vector<std::size_t> order(n);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        order[i] = i;
    }
    if (random) {
        std::mt19937_64 rng(12345);
        for (std::size_t i = n - 1; i > 0; --i) {
            std::uniform_int_distribution<std::size_t> pick(0, i - 1);
            std::swap(order[i], order[pick(rng)]);
        }
    }
    std::vector<Node> nodes(n);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        nodes[order[i]].next = order[(i + 1) % n];
    }
    return nodes;
}

int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
    const bool random = !(argc > 1 && std::string(argv[1]) == "sequential");
    const std::size_t loads = 4'000'000;
    std::printf("mode: %s chain, %zu dependent loads per size\n",
                random ? "random" : "sequential", loads);
    std::printf("%14s %12s\n", "working set", "ns per load");
    std::size_t sink = 0;
    for (std::size_t bytes = 4 * 1024; bytes <= 256u * 1024 * 1024; bytes *= 2) {
        const std::vector<Node> nodes = makeChain(bytes / sizeof(Node), random);
        std::size_t p = 0;
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < nodes.size(); ++i) {  // warm-up: touch every node once
            p = nodes[p].next;
        }
        const auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        for (std::size_t i = 0; i < loads; ++i) {
            p = nodes[p].next;  // the next address is known only after this load returns
        }
        const auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        sink += p;
        const double ns = std::chrono::duration<double, std::nano>(t1 - t0).count() / loads;
        std::printf("%10zu KiB %12.2f\n", bytes / 1024, ns);
    }
    std::printf("(checksum %zu)\n", sink);
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
13–17struct alignas(64) NodeA node is the index of the next node plus padding to 64 bytes, aligned to 64.Every load lands in a different 64-byte block, so no two loads share a cache line.
22–32order, std::mt19937_64 rng(12345)Makes the visiting order 0, 1, 2… and, in random mode, shuffles it with a fixed seed.A fixed seed makes every run visit the same order, so runs are comparable.
33–36nodes[order[i]].next = order[(i + 1) % n];Links each node to the next one in the visiting order; the last links to the first.The links always form one single cycle through all nodes, so the chase never gets stuck in a small loop.
42const bool random = …Chooses the mode from the command line.The same program produces both runs of the forensic lab.
48for (… bytes = 4 * 1024; … bytes *= 2)Working sets from 4 KiB to 256 MiB, doubling.Doubling gives evenly spaced points on a logarithmic axis.
51–53warm-up loopWalks the whole chain once before timing.The first touch of each page costs extra (F1-38); it must not be counted as latency.
54–58p = nodes[p].next;Four million dependent loads between two clock readings.Because each address is the previous result, the loads cannot overlap: time per load = latency.
59, 63sink += p; … checksumUses the final value.Without it the optimiser could delete the loop as having no effect.
60–61duration<double, std::nano>Divides elapsed nanoseconds by the number of loads.The average includes a tiny loop overhead; small working sets show it.

Listing 2 — bandwidth.cc: independent loads. It sums 64-bit numbers, re-reading the block until 4 GiB have been read for each block size.

// Read bandwidth: sum a block of 64-bit numbers again and again, for blocks of growing size.
// The loads are independent of each other, so the hardware may have many in flight at once.
// Numbers are measurements on the machine that ran this program, not specifications.
#include <chrono>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    const std::size_t totalBytes = 4ull * 1024 * 1024 * 1024;  // read 4 GiB in total per size
    std::printf("%14s %12s\n", "block size", "GB/s read");
    std::uint64_t sink = 0;
    for (std::size_t bytes = 16 * 1024; bytes <= 512u * 1024 * 1024; bytes *= 4) {
        std::vector<std::uint64_t> data(bytes / sizeof(std::uint64_t), 1);
        const std::size_t repeats = totalBytes / bytes;
        const auto t0 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        for (std::size_t r = 0; r < repeats; ++r) {
            std::uint64_t sum = 0;
            for (const std::uint64_t x : data) {
                sum += x;
            }
            sink += sum;
        }
        const auto t1 = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
        const double ns = std::chrono::duration<double, std::nano>(t1 - t0).count();
        std::printf("%10zu KiB %12.2f\n", bytes / 1024, double(repeats * bytes) / ns);
    }
    std::printf("(checksum %llu)\n", static_cast<unsigned long long>(sink));
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
12totalBytes = 4ull * 1024 * 1024 * 1024Reads the same total for every size.Small blocks are re-read many times, so each line takes a similar time and the clock's resolution is not an issue.
15bytes *= 4Block sizes 16 KiB … 256 MiB.Covers sizes that fit in each reported cache level and sizes that do not.
21–23for (const std::uint64_t x : data) sum += x;Reads every element in order.The addresses do not depend on loaded values, so many loads can be in flight; the compiler may also use vector instructions (F1-29).
28double(repeats * bytes) / nsBytes per nanosecond, which is GB/s.1 byte/ns = 109 bytes/s: decimal gigabytes, as the unit rule of guide 13.3 asks to state.

Build command: g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror bandwidth.cc -o bandwidth, then ./bandwidth.

Listing 3 — littles.cpp: Little's law as a calculator.

// Little's law for memory: bytes that must be "in flight" = bandwidth x latency.
// Each input line: a name, a latency in nanoseconds and a bandwidth in GB/s (1 GB = 10^9 bytes).
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main()
{
    std::string name;
    double latencyNs = 0.0;
    double gigabytesPerSecond = 0.0;
    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(1);
    while (std::cin >> name >> latencyNs >> gigabytesPerSecond) {
        const double bytesPerNs = gigabytesPerSecond;           // 1 GB/s = 1 byte per ns
        const double bytesInFlight = bytesPerNs * latencyNs;    // Little's law
        const double linesInFlight = bytesInFlight / 64.0;      // 64-byte blocks
        const double oneAtATime = 64.0 / latencyNs;             // GB/s with one block in flight
        std::cout << name << ": " << latencyNs << " ns x " << gigabytesPerSecond << " GB/s = "
                  << bytesInFlight << " bytes in flight = " << linesInFlight
                  << " blocks of 64 B; one block at a time would give " << std::setprecision(2)
                  << oneAtATime << " GB/s\n" << std::setprecision(1);
    }
    return 0;
}
LineCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
13while (std::cin >> name >> latencyNs >> gigabytesPerSecond)Reads one case per line.Add your own machine's numbers as a new line.
14bytesPerNs = gigabytesPerSecondUnit conversion: 1 GB/s is exactly 1 byte per ns.Keeps the law in consistent units.
15bytesInFlight = bytesPerNs * latencyNsLittle's law.The number the hardware must sustain.
16–17/ 64.0, 64.0 / latencyNsConverts to 64-byte blocks; computes the one-at-a-time rate.Shows how far a dependent chain is from the bandwidth.

Where the analogy breaks

  1. Distance is time, not metres. The pantry is "far" because of how DRAM is read, how many chips and controllers lie in between and how big it is, not mainly because of the length of the wires a signal travels.D2 D3 A kitchen helper's walk time grows with metres; memory latency does not follow a simple distance rule.
  2. The chef does not choose what goes on the shelves. Caches fill automatically, block by block, and evict by a fixed policy (F1-33). Amina decides which jars to keep near the stove; a program can only influence the caches indirectly, through the order of its accesses.D1
  3. Helpers fetch whole trays, not jars. Memory always moves a whole block (64 bytes on this build's machine) even when the program wanted 8 bytes; a helper bringing one jar has no such rule. This is why the order of accesses matters so much (F1-34).D1

Common mistakes and debugging

SymptomCauseHow to find itFix
The benchmark reports 0 ns or impossibly small timesThe compiler removed the loop because its result was never usedDisassemble (objdump -d, F1-31): the timed loop is missingUse the result (the checksum) as Listings 1 and 2 do
"Memory latency" stays low even for huge working setsThe chain visits blocks in a predictable order; prefetchers fetch aheadRun ./chase sequential and compare (forensic lab)Shuffle the visiting order
Times ten or more times slower than a colleague'sBuilt with -O0 or with sanitizersRead the build command in the .logTime only -O2 builds without sanitizers; test correctness with the sanitizer build separately
Numbers jump between runsOther programs, frequency changes, a shared virtual machineRepeat five or more times; look at the spreadReport the median and the range; name the machine (AH-23)
Bandwidth 7 % lower than "expected"GB versus GiB confusionCheck the units of both numbersThis course's GB/s is 109 bytes per second; GiB is 230 bytes
Not verified — check before relying on this

On the build container, the latency curve of Listing 1 starts its long climb at working sets of a few MiB, far below the L3 size the virtual machine reports (F1-33). Possible explanations: the L3 is shared with other virtual machines on the same host; translation (TLB) misses grow with the working set; the reported L3 size describes the host processor's whole cache, not the part this guest can use. None of these was verified in this build. To check on your own machine: run the F1-38 TLB lab, and read the vendor documentation for your processor model.

Transition box

Where you came from: HW202 built a CPU whose memory stage (F1-24, F1-27) answered in one cycle, and F1-30 put several cores on one chip.D2 What carries over: the load and store instructions, the pipeline, out-of-order execution (F1-29) and the habit of reading the assembly a compiler produced. What changes: a load now takes anywhere from a few cycles to hundreds of nanoseconds depending on where its data is, so the order in which a program touches memory can matter more than the number of instructions; and every performance number is a measurement on a named machine, not a constant.D1 R1 What comes next: F1-33 opens a cache and shows how an address picks its place in it: lines, sets and ways.

Check yourself

  1. Define latency and bandwidth, each with a unit.
  2. A memory has 80 ns latency. A program follows a linked list whose nodes are each in a different 64-byte block, never in cache. Roughly how many GB/s does it read? (a) 0.8 (b) 80 (c) 6.4 (d) 0.08
  3. Using Little's law: to stream 20 GB/s from a memory with 100 ns latency, how many 64-byte blocks must be in flight?
  4. Explain in your own words why Listing 1 links nodes in a shuffled order.
  5. Why does Listing 1 put each node in its own 64-byte block instead of packing 8-byte nodes together?
  6. Predict, then run: if you change Listing 2 to read only every eighth element (one per 64-byte block) of the 256 MiB block, will the GB/s it prints (bytes the program asked for) go up, down or stay the same? Run it to check.
  7. Apply to a new case: a robot's control program walks a tree of obstacles (each node points to its children) once per control cycle. Which of the two measures, latency or bandwidth, limits it, and what change to the data layout would help?
  8. Why is a time measured on a cloud virtual machine not a property of "the processor"?

Lab

Goal

Measure the latency curve and the read bandwidth of your own computer, and explain their shape with the memory hierarchy (card lab, first half: "results, not spec numbers").

Hardware and software needed

A computer running Linux with g++ (this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0) or clang++. No special hardware. A laptop on battery may change its clock speed; plug it in.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use. The programs allocate up to 256 MiB; close large applications first on a machine with little memory.

Steps

  1. Copy chase.cc, bandwidth.cc, littles.cpp and littles.in from university/labs/F1-32/.
  2. Build the timing programs with -O2 (commands above). Run ./chase random five times and ./bandwidth five times; keep every output.
  3. For each working-set size, write down the median of the five latency values. Draw the curve with a logarithmic x axis (by hand or with any tool).
  4. Mark the steps. Run university/labs/F1-33/cache_info.sh (or read /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cache/) and write the reported sizes next to the steps.
  5. Add a line with your own largest-set latency and bandwidth to littles.in and run Listing 3.

Expected observations

On the build container (measured, one session, shown above): a flat region under 2 ns, a step after 32 KiB, a second plateau, a rise after 1 MiB and a long climb to a few hundred nanoseconds at 256 MiB; bandwidth highest for small blocks and lowest for the largest. Your numbers will differ: they are your measurements, labelled with your machine and date.

Verification

(1) Your five runs agree within a spread you report. (2) Each step you marked lies within one doubling of a cache size reported by your operating system, or you wrote down why not. (3) Your Little's-law line gives a number of blocks in flight greater than one.

Troubleshooting

  • All latencies the same → the build used -O0 or the chain is sequential → check the command and the first output line.
  • The program is killed → not enough memory → lower the largest size in line 48 and record that you did.
  • Very noisy results → background load or power saving → close programs, plug in, repeat, report median and range.

Extension

Add a third mode to chase.cc that runs two independent chains interleaved in one loop (p = nodes[p].next; q = nodes[q].next;). Predict the time per load, then measure: what does it tell you about memory-level parallelism?

Mini-project

Write a one-page "memory passport" of your computer: the latency curve (median of five runs, with range), the bandwidth table, the cache sizes the OS reports, a Little's-law estimate of blocks in flight, and three sentences explaining the curve's shape. Every number carries its machine, tool, version and date (AH-23). Rubric: curve and table complete with spread (2); steps matched to reported sizes or the mismatch explained (1); Little's law applied correctly (1); measurements labelled as measurements (1).

Summary

  • Latency is the wait for one request; bandwidth is the delivery rate once requests flow.
  • Memory is a hierarchy because no single memory is both large and fast; SRAM caches sit in front of DRAM main memory.
  • Dependent loads (pointer chasing) expose latency; independent loads can overlap and approach bandwidth.
  • Little's law: bytes in flight = bandwidth × latency.
  • A latency-versus-working-set curve has plateaus and steps that hint at cache sizes.
  • Predictable access orders let prefetchers hide latency; benchmarks must defeat them to measure it.
  • Every time in this chapter is a measurement on the build container, not a specification.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Latency: time from request to usable data (ns or cycles). Bandwidth: data delivered per unit time (bytes per second, here GB/s = 109 B/s).
  2. (a) 0.8 GB/s: one 64-byte block per 80 ns = 64 ÷ 80 = 0.8 bytes/ns. (b) confuses ns with GB/s; (c) is 64 ÷ 10; (d) is off by ten.
  3. 20 bytes/ns × 100 ns = 2,000 bytes = 31.25, so about 32 blocks (Listing 3, case B).
  4. In address order, the hardware prefetchers can predict the next block and fetch it early, so the time measured is no longer the full latency; shuffling makes the next address unpredictable.
  5. Packed 8-byte nodes would put eight nodes in one block; seven of every eight loads would then hit in the cache because a whole block arrives at once, and the benchmark would not measure the latency of a miss.
  6. The GB/s the program asks for goes down (in this build's F1-34 stride table, the 256 MiB row falls from stride 1 to stride 8), because each 8-byte request now drags a whole 64-byte block from memory: the memory still moves blocks, but the program uses only one eighth of each.
  7. Latency: each child's address comes from loading its parent, a dependent chain. Storing the tree in an array in the order it is visited (for example breadth-first, children next to each other) lets the prefetcher and independent loads help.
  8. Because the machine is shared and virtualised: other tenants, the hypervisor and clock changes affect it; the number belongs to that machine at that time, with that tool and version (AH-23).

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: up to 32 KiB both runs are under about 2 ns per load; from 1–2 MiB on, the random chain climbs to a few hundred ns while the sequential chain stays in the single or low double digits. Hypotheses: (H1) Rafael's machine has much faster DRAM — ruled out, it is the same machine and the same run session; (H2) the sequential chain lets the hardware prefetch the next blocks, so most loads hit in a cache — consistent: the only difference between the runs is the order of the links (line 26 of Listing 1); (H3) the sequential chain also crosses pages in order, so translation is cheaper — possible as a contributor. Conclusion: Leila's random chain measures load latency; Rafael's measures how well prefetching hides it. Prevention: "Latency was measured with a randomly ordered pointer chain, each node in its own 64-byte block, on machine X with toolchain Y on date Z." How the evidence was made: chase.cc run with argument sequential (identity order) and random (fixed-seed shuffle) by run.sh (R1).

Story hook

Analogy

Amara runs the evening shift in a busy restaurant building. The head chef works on the ground floor; the pantry, the cold room, the dish-washing room and the till are spread around the building. Everything moves through one service corridor with a lift at the end.

Every trolley that enters the corridor carries a label with a room number: "pantry, shelf 16" or "till, drawer 2". The doorkeeper at each door reads the label and opens only if the number belongs to their room. If two trolleys try to enter the corridor at the same time, Amara lets one in and makes the other wait.

One evening a new cold-room door is fitted, and its sign says it owns rooms 3000 to 30FF. The till's door, further along, still says 3080 to 3087. That night, some deliveries to the till arrive half-frozen. Nobody broke anything on purpose. Two doors answered the same label. This chapter is about corridors like that one, the labels, the doorkeepers, and what goes wrong when two of them disagree.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what an address bus, a data bus and control signals carry, and why one shared bus allows only one transfer at a time.
  • Read a memory map and decode, by hand and in code, which device answers a given address.
  • Compute the peak transfer rate of a bus from its width and its transfer rate, and say why the real rate is lower.
  • Explain bus masters, arbitration and why a second master (a DMA engine) makes the CPU wait.
  • Diagnose an address-decoding overlap from a decoder table and a read log (the forensic lab).
Jargon box
Bus
Simple words: the paths that carry information between the parts of a computer (defined first in F0-05; this chapter adds detail). Analogy: the service corridor and its lift. Precise: a set of connections that carries addresses, data and control signals between the processor, memory and devices; on a shared bus only one sender may drive the data lines at a time. D1 D2
Address bus
Simple words: the wires that say where a value should go or come from. Analogy: the room-and-shelf label on a trolley. Precise: the group of signals that carries the address of a transfer; with n address lines, 2n distinct addresses can be named. D1 W1
Data bus
Simple words: the wires that carry the value itself. Analogy: the trolley's load. Precise: the group of signals that carries the data of a transfer; its width (for example 8, 32 or 64 bits) is how many bits move in one transfer. D1
Control signals
Simple words: the extra wires that say what kind of transfer this is and when it is valid. Analogy: the "deliver" or "collect" stamp on the trolley, and the bell that says "now". Precise: signals such as read/write, a clock or strobe that marks valid data, and handshake or error signals; the exact set belongs to each bus's specification. D2
Address decoder
Simple words: the circuit that checks an address and wakes up the one device it belongs to. Analogy: the doorkeeper who reads the label. Precise: combinational logic that compares (part of) the address with each device's window and asserts that device's select (chip-select) signal. D1
Memory map
Simple words: the table that says which address range belongs to which device. Analogy: the building's floor plan with room numbers. Precise: the assignment of address ranges (windows) to memories and device registers in an address space; addresses outside every window are holes. D1
Bus master and arbitration
Simple words: a master is a part that may start transfers; arbitration decides which master goes next. Analogy: Amara deciding which trolley enters the corridor first. Precise: a bus master (in newer documents: an initiator or requester) drives addresses and starts transactions; an arbiter grants the bus to one requesting master at a time by a policy such as fixed priority or round-robin. D2
Bus contention
Simple words: two senders talking on the same wires at once. Analogy: two doors answering the same label. Precise: two drivers enabled on the same line at the same time; with push-pull outputs it can damage parts, with open-drain lines the result is the AND of the senders; either way the value is wrong. D1
Bandwidth (of a bus)
Simple words: how many bytes the bus can move each second at most. Analogy: how many trolleys per minute the corridor can take, times their load. Precise: peak bandwidth = width in bytes × transfers per second; the sustained rate is lower because of arbitration, address phases, wait states and protocol overhead. D2 W1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the smallest useful system: one CPU, one memory and two devices on one shared bus. The address decoder looks at the address lines and raises exactly one select line.

Figure 2 draws the same memory map as a strip of addresses. The forensic lab of this chapter is a strip where two windows overlap.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A computer is a building full of rooms. The CPU is the head chef. Memory is the pantry. The screen, the keyboard and the timer are other rooms. They all need to pass things to each other, and they do it through the same corridor: the bus.

Every delivery has two parts. The label says where it goes: that is the address. The trolley's load is the value: that is the data. A third stamp says "deliver" (write) or "collect" (read). At each door a doorkeeper, the address decoder, reads the label and opens only for its own rooms.

The corridor is narrow. Only one trolley fits at a time. If two cooks want to send something at the same moment, someone has to decide who goes first. That someone is the arbiter. Later in this course you will meet faster buildings with many private corridors, one per room. The labels and the doorkeepers stay the same.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Three groups of signals

A classic parallel bus has three groups of signals D1 D2. The address bus carries the address of the transfer. The data bus carries the value. The control signals say whether this is a read or a write and mark the moment when address and data are valid (a clock edge, or a strobe on asynchronous buses). With n address lines, 2n addresses can be named: 16 lines give 216 = 65,536 addresses, 32 lines give 232 = 4,294,967,296 W1.

A transaction is one complete transfer. For a write, the master puts the address, the data and "write" on the bus, and the selected device stores the data. For a read, the master puts the address and "read" on the bus, and the selected device puts its data on the data lines for the master to latch D1. The bus itself does not know whether the address belongs to memory or to a device. That is the job of the decoder.

Address decoding and the memory map

The address decoder compares the address with each device's window and asserts that device's select line D1. The list of windows is the memory map. In Listing 1 the map is RAM at 0x0000–0x0FFF, an LED register at 0x2000–0x2003 and a timer at 0x3000–0x300F. A write to 0x0010 lands in RAM. A write to 0x2000, issued by exactly the same kind of instruction, lands in the LED register. A read of 0x1800 finds no window and ends as a bus error (run R1, cycle 6). This is the root of memory-mapped I/O, the subject of F1-41: to the CPU, a device register is "only an address".

Real decoders rarely compare every bit. A window whose size is a power of two and whose base is a multiple of that size can be decoded from the high address bits alone: the window 0x3000–0x300F is "the top twelve bits of a 16-bit address equal 0x300" W1. Cheap decoders that ignore some bits make the same device appear at several addresses (aliases). That is legal, but a driver writer must know it D1.

One sender at a time

Many devices are connected to the same data lines, so they must not all drive them. Devices that are not selected leave the lines alone: their outputs are tri-state (disconnected) or open-drain (only able to pull low) D1. If two devices drive the lines at once, that is bus contention. With push-pull outputs, one pulls up while the other pulls down, which is an electrical fault; with open-drain lines the result is the AND of the two values. Either way the value read is wrong D1. The forensic lab shows the AND case.

Masters and arbitration

A bus master may start transactions. The CPU is one. A DMA engine (F1-44) is another: it moves data between a device and memory without the CPU D2. When two masters want the shared bus in the same cycle, an arbiter grants it to one, using a policy such as fixed priority or round-robin D2. Listing 2 models round-robin: with the CPU wanting 6 transfers and the DMA engine 4, the bus is busy for 10 cycles, and each master waits 4 cycles (run R2). Nothing is lost, but the two masters' work is serialised.

How fast is a bus?

The peak bandwidth of a bus is its width in bytes times the number of transfers per second D2. An exercise bus that is 32 bits (4 bytes) wide and makes one transfer per clock at 100 MHz peaks at 4 × 100,000,000 = 400,000,000 bytes per second W1. The sustained rate is lower: an address phase may cost a cycle, a slow device may add wait states, and arbitration costs time D2. These are exercise numbers, not the specification of any real bus.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Analogy first: the single corridor became a road network with junctions, toll gates and private lanes. The labels on the trolleys did not change.

Hierarchies of buses. Real systems do not hang every device on one bus. A fast connection joins the CPU cores, their caches and the memory controllers; bridges connect slower I/O buses below it D2. A bridge forwards a transaction from one side to the other when the address belongs to a window behind it, so the decoder of Figure 1 becomes a tree of decoders. You will see one such tree in QEMU's PCI listing in F1-45, where a PCI bridge owns a "memory range" and forwards it to bus 1.

From shared parallel buses to point-to-point links. Many wide parallel wires switching together are hard to run fast: they must all arrive within the same time window (skew), and every extra device adds electrical load. Modern external connections such as PCI Express use point-to-point serial lanes with the clock embedded in the data stream, and send transactions as packets with headers instead of using separate address wires D3 D2. The ideas of this chapter survive the change: there is still an address, a decoder (routing), a read/write distinction, and the possibility of a transaction no one claims.

Split and posted transactions. A simple bus holds the bus for the whole read, from address to data. Faster buses split a read into a request and a later completion, so the bus can carry other traffic in between; writes may be posted, meaning the master does not wait for the target to finish D3. Posted writes are one reason why device drivers sometimes read a register back after writing it: the read cannot complete until earlier writes on the same path have arrived. The details belong to each bus's ordering rules, which F1-45 names.

Not verified — check before relying on this

The exact ordering rules for posted writes, reads and completions (which may pass which) are defined in the PCI Express Base Specification's chapter on transaction ordering, and differently for on-chip interconnects such as the Arm AMBA protocols. This build could not open either document. Check the ordering section of the specification for the bus you are using before relying on "a read flushes earlier writes" in a driver.

On-chip interconnects. Inside a system-on-chip, CPU cores, GPUs, DMA engines and peripherals meet on an on-chip interconnect, often with several independent channels for addresses, write data, read data and responses, so that reads and writes can be in flight at once. The memory map of such a chip lives in its technical reference manual (TRM), and a Linux or devicetree description repeats it. Chapter F1-41 prints the real memory maps of three QEMU machines.

How the hardware actually does it

At the electrical level a bus line is a wire with a voltage: high for 1, low for 0 (F1-08). A master changes its address and data outputs, and the control signals mark when receivers should sample them, often on a clock edge (F1-18) D1. The decoder is ordinary combinational logic built from the gates of HW102: comparators feeding AND gates, one output per device D1. Shared lines need outputs that can let go: a tri-state buffer has an extra enable input and, when disabled, neither pulls up nor down D1. An open-drain output can only pull down; a pull-up resistor makes the line high when nobody pulls, which is why two senders produce the AND of their bits. You will meet open-drain lines again in I2C (F1-47), where this "AND" is used on purpose.

Worked example

Decode four addresses with the toy map

Map: RAM 0x0000–0x0FFF (size 0x1000), LEDS 0x2000–0x2003 (size 4), TIMER 0x3000–0x300F (size 0x10).

  1. 0x0010: 0x0010 ≥ 0x0000 and 0x0010 − 0x0000 = 0x0010 < 0x1000, so RAM, offset 0x010.
  2. 0x2000: RAM fails (0x2000 − 0 is not < 0x1000). LEDS: 0x2000 − 0x2000 = 0 < 4, so LEDS, offset 0.
  3. 0x3004: TIMER: 0x3004 − 0x3000 = 4 < 0x10, so TIMER, offset 4.
  4. 0x1800: not in any window, so a bus error.

Run R1 printed exactly these four results (cycles 1, 3, 4 and 6) R1.

Bandwidth with overhead

Exercise bus: 4 bytes wide, 100 million cycles per second. If every transfer needs one address cycle and one data cycle, only half the cycles move data: 4 × 50,000,000 = 200,000,000 bytes per second, half the peak. If the CPU and a DMA engine share the bus and the DMA engine uses 4 of every 10 cycles (as in run R2), the CPU is left with 60 % of whatever the bus delivers W1.

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — bus_decode.cpp: a shared bus, a decoder and a made-up memory map.

// F1-40 Listing 1: a tiny shared bus with an address decoder.
// The "CPU" issues read and write transactions; the decoder picks the one
// device whose address window contains the address. A made-up memory map.
#include <cstdint>
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Device
{
    std::string name;
    std::uint32_t base;            // first address of the window
    std::uint32_t size;            // number of byte addresses in the window
    std::vector<std::uint8_t> cells;
};

struct Bus
{
    std::vector<Device> devices;
    int cycle = 0;

    Device* decode(std::uint32_t addr)
    {
        for (Device& d : devices) {
            if (addr >= d.base && addr - d.base < d.size) {
                return &d;
            }
        }
        return nullptr;            // nobody answers: a bus error
    }

    void write(std::uint32_t addr, std::uint8_t data)
    {
        ++cycle;
        Device* d = decode(addr);
        if (d == nullptr) {
            std::printf("cycle %2d  WRITE addr=0x%04X data=0x%02X  -> BUS ERROR (no device)\n",
                        cycle, addr, data);
            return;
        }
        d->cells[addr - d->base] = data;
        std::printf("cycle %2d  WRITE addr=0x%04X data=0x%02X  -> %-6s offset 0x%03X\n",
                    cycle, addr, data, d->name.c_str(), addr - d->base);
    }

    int read(std::uint32_t addr)
    {
        ++cycle;
        Device* d = decode(addr);
        if (d == nullptr) {
            std::printf("cycle %2d  READ  addr=0x%04X            -> BUS ERROR (no device)\n",
                        cycle, addr);
            return -1;
        }
        const std::uint8_t v = d->cells[addr - d->base];
        std::printf("cycle %2d  READ  addr=0x%04X data=0x%02X  <- %-6s offset 0x%03X\n",
                    cycle, addr, v, d->name.c_str(), addr - d->base);
        return v;
    }
};

int main()
{
    Bus bus;
    bus.devices.push_back({"RAM", 0x0000, 0x1000, std::vector<std::uint8_t>(0x1000)});
    bus.devices.push_back({"LEDS", 0x2000, 0x0004, std::vector<std::uint8_t>(0x0004)});
    bus.devices.push_back({"TIMER", 0x3000, 0x0010, std::vector<std::uint8_t>(0x0010)});

    std::printf("memory map: RAM 0x0000-0x0FFF, LEDS 0x2000-0x2003, TIMER 0x3000-0x300F\n");
    bus.write(0x0010, 0x2A);       // store a value in RAM
    bus.read(0x0010);              // load it back
    bus.write(0x2000, 0x05);       // same kind of write, but it lands on the LED register
    bus.write(0x3004, 0x64);       // a timer register
    bus.read(0x3004);
    bus.read(0x1800);              // a hole in the map
    std::printf("total bus cycles: %d (one transaction per cycle on this shared bus)\n",
                bus.cycle);
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used, by run_lab.sh): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined bus_decode.cpp -o bus_decode

LinesCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
9–15struct DeviceA device has a name, a window (base, size) and some byte cells.A window is all the decoder needs to know about a device.
17–20struct BusThe bus holds the device list and a cycle counter.One counter for everyone: a shared bus does one transaction per cycle here.
22–30decode()Returns the first device whose window contains the address, or nullptr.addr - d.base < d.size is the window test; written this way it cannot overflow.
32–44write()Counts a cycle, decodes, stores the byte at the offset, prints the transaction.The same code path serves RAM and the LED register: the bus does not care.
46–59read()Counts a cycle, decodes, returns the byte or −1 for a bus error.A hole in the map is an error, not a zero.
65–67push_back(...)Builds the memory map of Figure 1.The map is data, not code: decoders are configured, not rewritten.
70–75six transactionsWrite and read RAM, write the LEDs, write and read the timer, read a hole.Cycle 3 is the key line: a "store" that turns on lights.

Listing 2 — bus_arbiter.cpp: two masters, one bus, round-robin arbitration.

// F1-40 Listing 2: two bus masters share one bus. Each cycle the arbiter grants
// the bus to exactly one requester (round-robin), so the other one waits.
#include <cstdio>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Master
{
    std::string name;
    int wanted;      // transactions this master still has to do
    int done = 0;
    int waited = 0;  // cycles spent requesting but not granted
};

int main()
{
    std::vector<Master> m{{"CPU", 6}, {"DMA", 4}};
    int last = 1;    // index of the master granted last time
    int cycle = 0;
    while (m[0].done < m[0].wanted || m[1].done < m[1].wanted) {
        ++cycle;
        const bool req0 = m[0].done < m[0].wanted;
        const bool req1 = m[1].done < m[1].wanted;
        int grant = -1;
        if (req0 && req1) {
            grant = (last == 0) ? 1 : 0;   // both ask: take turns
        } else if (req0) {
            grant = 0;
        } else {
            grant = 1;
        }
        last = grant;
        ++m[grant].done;
        const int other = 1 - grant;
        const bool other_req = (other == 0) ? req0 : req1;
        if (other_req) {
            ++m[other].waited;
        }
        std::printf("cycle %2d  request CPU=%d DMA=%d  grant=%s%s\n", cycle, req0 ? 1 : 0,
                    req1 ? 1 : 0, m[grant].name.c_str(), other_req ? "  (other waits)" : "");
    }
    for (const Master& x : m) {
        std::printf("%s: %d transactions, %d cycles waiting\n", x.name.c_str(), x.done, x.waited);
    }
    std::printf("bus busy for %d cycles: the work of both masters is serialised\n", cycle);
    return 0;
}

Real output, copied from university/labs/F1-40/bus_arbiter.out; run record bus_arbiter.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:34:06Z; exit code: 0.

LinesCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
7–13struct MasterHow many transactions a master wants, has done, and how long it waited.Waiting time is the cost of sharing.
17–18last, cycleRemembers who had the bus last.Round-robin needs memory of the last grant.
21–32grant logicIf both request, grant the one that did not go last; otherwise grant the only requester.Exactly one grant per cycle: the arbiter is what prevents contention.
33–39bookkeepingCounts the grant and the other master's wait.Run R2 shows 4 waiting cycles for each master.
42–45summaryPrints totals.10 cycles for 10 transactions: sharing serialises, it does not add capacity.

Where the analogy breaks

  • A corridor can hold a queue; a simple shared bus holds one transfer. In the restaurant, trolleys can line up inside the corridor. On a simple shared bus, a waiting master holds its request outside; nothing is "in the corridor" except the current transfer. Split-transaction and packet-based links (Layer 3) do keep several transfers in flight D3.
  • Doorkeepers do not take time to think; decoders do. The analogy hides that decoding and driving long wires take time, which limits how fast a shared parallel bus can run. This is one reason modern links are point-to-point (Layer 3) D2.
  • Two trolleys collide; two bus drivers combine. When two doors answer at once, the restaurant gets two deliveries. On open-drain lines you get one value, the AND of both, and nothing tells you it happened unless the hardware detects it (run R3) R3.

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: a read returns a value that is the AND (or a mix) of two expected values. Cause: overlapping windows, so two devices answer. Find it: list every window with its last address (base + size − 1) and sort by base; any window that starts before the previous one ends is an overlap (forensic lab). Fix: correct the size or the base in the decoder table.
  • Symptom: a device appears at several addresses. Cause: partial decoding (some address bits ignored). Find it: write a value at one address and read it back at others. Fix: usually none needed, but never place another device in the alias range.
  • Symptom: off-by-one window: the last register of a device is unreachable, or one byte beyond it answers. Cause: confusing size with last address (0x10 bytes from 0x3000 end at 0x300F, not 0x3010). Find it: test the first and last address of every window and the first address after it. Fix: store base and size, compute last = base + size − 1 in one place.
  • Symptom: "bandwidth is lower than the bus width times the clock". Cause: that number is the peak; address phases, wait states and other masters take cycles. Find it: count cycles per useful transfer, as in the worked example. Fix: none; quote sustained rates from measurements, labelled as such.
Transition box

Where you came from: F1-24 and F1-30 showed the CPU's datapath and its cores, and F0-05 drew the computer as a kitchen map with "corridors" between the parts. What carries over: binary addresses, hexadecimal, combinational logic (a decoder is a comparator plus gates), and the clock that marks when signals are valid D1. What changes: the CPU is no longer alone: other masters share the bus and make it wait; addresses can belong to devices instead of memory; and a wrong address no longer means "a wrong value" but possibly "the wrong device" D2. What comes next: F1-41 uses the memory map to talk to devices: registers that look like memory but do not behave like it.

Check yourself

  1. Name the three groups of bus signals and what each carries.
  2. How many distinct addresses can 20 address lines name? Show the calculation.
  3. With the toy map, which device answers 0x300F, and which answers 0x3010?
  4. A 64-bit wide exercise bus makes 200 million transfers per second. What is its peak bandwidth in bytes per second? Which of these is the sustained rate: (a) exactly the peak, (b) at most the peak, (c) twice the peak?
  5. Explain in your own words why two devices must never drive the same data lines at the same time.
  6. Apply to a new case: a board adds a UART at 0x2002–0x2009. Which existing window does it overlap, and at which addresses?
  7. Predict, then run: change the order of push_back calls in Listing 1 so that a device whose window covers 0x0000–0x3FFF comes first. What will every transaction print? Run it and compare.
  8. Why does the arbiter in Listing 2 make the total cycle count equal to the sum of both masters' transactions?

Lab

Goal

Extend the toy bus with a new device, prove with a test that no two windows overlap, and measure (in cycles) how arbitration slows the CPU down.

Hardware and software needed

No hardware. A computer with a C++20 compiler; the Lab Engineer used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 through university/labs/run_lab.sh.

Safety

None beyond normal computer use.

Steps

  1. From the repository root run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F1-40. You should see no output; then open university/labs/F1-40/bus_decode.out and compare it with the output shown above.
  2. Copy bus_decode.cpp to my_bus.cpp in the same folder. Add a device "UART", 0x2100, 0x0008. Add a write to 0x2104 and a read from 0x2108. Predict both results before you run.
  3. Write a function bool overlaps(const Bus&) that sorts the windows by base and checks that each window's base is greater than the previous window's last address. Call it at the start of main and print the result.
  4. Make the check fail on purpose by changing the UART's base to 0x2002. Run again.
  5. In bus_arbiter.cpp, give the CPU 20 transactions and the DMA engine 20. Then change the policy to "the CPU always wins". Record the waiting cycles of each master for both policies.

Expected observations

Step 2: the write lands in UART offset 4; the read from 0x2108 is a bus error (the window ends at 0x2107). Step 3 prints "no overlap"; step 4 prints an overlap between LEDS and UART. Step 5: with round-robin both masters wait; with fixed priority the CPU never waits and the DMA engine waits until the CPU is done.

Verification

Your overlap check returns false for the original map and true for the map of the forensic lab (bus_overlap.cpp). Your programs build with the flags of run_lab.sh with no warnings and no sanitizer reports.

Troubleshooting

  • Sanitizer error "heap-buffer-overflow" in write(): the cells vector is smaller than the window size. Make cells exactly size bytes.
  • A read of the last address of a window is a bus error: your window test uses <= with the size instead of <, or you computed last = base + size.
  • The arbiter loop never ends: a master was granted but its done counter was not increased.

Extension

Add wait states: give each device a number of cycles per access (RAM 1, TIMER 3) and count total cycles. Then make the decoder ignore address bit 8 and show the timer appearing at an alias address.

Forensic lab

Scenario

Ravi's team added a UART to a small board. Since then, characters read from the UART are wrong: an 'A' (0x41) arrives as '@' (0x40), and the timer's registers sometimes read strangely. The hardware engineer says "the UART chip works on another board". You get the decoder table and a short read log captured by the bus model the team uses for testing.

Evidence pack

The decoder table and the read log, produced by bus_overlap.cpp (run R3). In this model every register of a device reads as one fixed byte: TIMER 0x64, UART 0x41, LEDS 0x05.

decoder table:
  RAM   base=0x0000 size=0x1000  last=0x0FFF
  LEDS  base=0x2000 size=0x0004  last=0x2003
  TIMER base=0x3000 size=0x0100  last=0x30FF
  UART  base=0x3080 size=0x0008  last=0x3087
READ 0x2000  selected=LEDS       data=0x05
READ 0x3004  selected=TIMER      data=0x64
READ 0x3080  selected=TIMER+UART data=0x40  <-- CONTENTION: more than one device drove the bus
READ 0x3081  selected=TIMER+UART data=0x40  <-- CONTENTION: more than one device drove the bus
READ 0x30F0  selected=TIMER      data=0x64

Real output, copied from university/labs/F1-40/bus_overlap.out; run record bus_overlap.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:34:07Z; exit code: 0.

Questions

  1. Which reads are wrong, and what value did each of them return instead of the expected one?
  2. Show, bit by bit, how 0x40 can come from 0x64 and 0x41.
  3. Which line of the decoder table is the root cause? Use the board notes in the source comment.
  4. Propose the fix and the test that would have caught this before the board shipped.
  5. Why did the UART "work on another board"?

Method hints

Compute the last address of every window and look for windows whose ranges intersect. Then check which reads fall into the intersection. Form at least two hypotheses (a faulty UART; a decoding problem) and say which evidence rules each in or out.

Mini-project

Write a "memory map linter": a program that reads a text file of name base size lines and reports overlaps, windows not aligned to their size (for power-of-two sizes), holes, and the total mapped bytes. Test it with the toy map, the forensic map and a map of your own design with at least six devices.

Rubric (10 points): correct overlap detection with the overlapping range printed (3); alignment check (2); a test file for each rule, including one that passes all rules (3); clear output a teammate can act on (2).

Summary

  • A bus carries addresses (where), data (what) and control signals (read or write, and when).
  • n address lines name 2n addresses; the memory map assigns windows of them to memories and devices.
  • The address decoder selects exactly one device per transfer; addresses in no window are holes and end as bus errors.
  • Only one sender may drive shared data lines; two at once is contention, and the value read is wrong.
  • Masters start transfers; an arbiter grants the shared bus to one master at a time, so masters wait for each other.
  • Peak bandwidth = width × transfers per second; sustained bandwidth is lower.
  • Modern links are point-to-point and packet-based, but addresses, routing and "nobody answered" remain.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Address bus: where (the address). Data bus: what (the value). Control: the kind of transfer (read or write) and when the signals are valid (clock or strobe), plus handshakes.
  2. 220 = 1,048,576 addresses (each extra line doubles the count: 210 = 1,024, and 1,024 × 1,024 = 1,048,576).
  3. 0x300F: TIMER, offset 0xF (the last byte of its window). 0x3010: nobody; it is a hole, so a bus error.
  4. 8 bytes × 200,000,000 = 1,600,000,000 bytes per second peak. (b): the sustained rate is at most the peak. (a) ignores address phases, wait states and arbitration; (c) is impossible: no protocol overhead adds capacity.
  5. Any answer that says: both would try to set the same wire to their own values; the receiver then reads a value that belongs to neither (or, with push-pull outputs, the parts fight electrically); so the bus allows one driver at a time, enforced by the decoder (one select) and the arbiter (one master).
  6. LEDS (0x2000–0x2003). The overlap is 0x2002–0x2003.
  7. Every transaction (including 0x1800, which was a hole) is decoded to that first device, because decode() returns the first match. The bus errors disappear; the LED and timer writes go to the big device instead. The run confirms it if you print the device name.
  8. Because exactly one transaction happens per cycle and no cycle is wasted when someone requests: the arbiter only decides the order, not the amount of work.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation: reads of 0x3080 and 0x3081 select TIMER+UART and return 0x40; reads of 0x2000, 0x3004 and 0x30F0 are normal (R3). Bits: 0x64 = 0110 0100, 0x41 = 0100 0001; AND = 0100 0000 = 0x40, so the value is the open-drain AND of both devices. Hypotheses: (1) a faulty UART: ruled out, because reads that select only the UART would be needed to show that, and the only UART reads are the contended ones; the chip also works on another board. (2) A decoding overlap: confirmed, the TIMER window is 0x3000–0x30FF (size 0x100) and contains the UART window 0x3080–0x3087. Root cause: the TIMER line of the decoder table has size 0x0100; the board notes say 0x3000–0x300F, so the size must be 0x0010. Fix: set the size to 0x0010; rerun: 0x3080 then selects UART alone and returns 0x41, and 0x30F0 becomes a hole. Prevention: the overlap check from the lab, run on every decoder table at build time. Why it worked elsewhere: the other board's map had no device inside the oversized timer window. How the evidence was made: Listing 1's map with a UART added and the timer's size deliberately set to 0x100. Wrong answers: "the UART sends the wrong bit 0" (it is never read alone); "the timer is broken" (0x3004 reads correctly).

Prereqs

Goals
Explain the GPU as a hall of many helpers; write, launch and check kernels; use the thread hierarchy and memory spaces; time kernels correctly; achieve coalesced access and measure bandwidth.

  1. F6-01 Many hands make light work: what a GPU is (exemplar in section 14)

  6. F6-06 Measuring time correctly: events, warm-up, median of many runs
  7. F6-07 What is my GPU? Device query and the vendor's documentation

E1 (harness, device report, SAXPY bit-exact), E2 (copy kernels, strides, offsets, pinned memory).

Q; M; F; P: write, check and time a kernel from a specification on the lab GPU.

The GPU benchmark harness (C++ with a CUDA back end and a slot for HIP), used by every later F6–F8 lab.

Track E: E1, E2; 13.2 topics 1–2; 13.4 measurement protocol.

What makes a robot

Story hook

Amara is learning to ride a bicycle in the park. Her uncle walks next to her. At first she wobbles a lot.

Then something changes. Amara starts to notice things. She sees the path bend. She feels the bicycle lean a little to the left.

Each time, she decides what to do. "Lean back a little. Turn the handlebars a bit." Then her arms and legs do it.

Notice, decide, do. Notice, decide, do. She does this again and again, many times each minute, without thinking about it.

"You are riding!" her uncle shouts. Amara laughs. She did not know it yet, but she had just shown him how a robot works.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what makes a machine a robot, using three words: sense, think, act.
  • Sort machines from everyday life into "robot" and "not a robot", and give a reason.
  • Point to the sense, think and act parts in a tiny robot program.
  • Predict what a simulated robot will do when you change one number.
  • Find the bug in a robot that bumps into a wall, from its printed log.
Jargon box
Robot
Simple words: a machine that notices the world, decides what to do, and then moves or changes something, again and again. Analogy: a body with senses, a brain and muscles. Precise: a machine that measures its surroundings with sensors, computes a decision with a program, and acts on the world with actuators, in a repeating loop. D2
Sense–think–act
Simple words: the three jobs a robot does over and over: notice, decide, do. Analogy: Amara noticing the bend, deciding to steer, and steering. Precise: a way to describe a robot's work as a repeating cycle of measuring (sense), computing a decision (think) and commanding its actuators (act). D2
Sensor
Simple words: a part that lets a robot notice something, like light or distance. Analogy: your eyes, ears and skin. Precise: a device that measures a physical quantity and turns it into a signal or number the robot's computer can read. D2
Actuator
Simple words: a part that makes the robot move or change something. Analogy: your muscles. Precise: a device that turns a command from the computer into motion or another physical effect; an electric motor is one example. D2
Simulator
Simple words: a program that pretends to be the robot and its world, so you can test safely. Analogy: practising bicycle balance on a game screen before the real park. Precise: software that computes how a model of a robot and its surroundings would behave, step by step, so programs can be tested without real hardware. In this course, the simulators are tiny C++ programs written by this university. R1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the three jobs of a robot as a circle. Amara's bicycle ride is drawn above it, so you can match each part.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Your body has three kinds of parts that work together. Your senses notice things. Your brain decides. Your muscles move. A robot has the same three kinds of parts.

A robot's senses are called sensors. A sensor might notice light, a bump, or how far away a wall is. A robot's brain is a computer running a program. A robot's muscles are called actuators. The robots in this course use electric motors as their muscles.

Here is the important part. A robot does not sense once and then stop. It senses, thinks and acts, and then it does it all again. It keeps going round the circle in Figure 1, like Amara on her bicycle.

Why does it need to go round again? Because the world changes. When the robot moves, the wall gets closer. The line on the floor bends. If the robot never looked again, it would not notice.

So what is not a robot? Think of a toaster with a timer. It heats the bread for a fixed time. It does not look at the bread. It does not notice if the bread is already brown. It acts, but it does not sense and decide. So most people would not call it a robot.

Now imagine a cleaning robot that rolls across a floor. When it bumps a chair, a bump sensor notices. Its program decides to turn. Its motors turn it. Then it does it all again. That fits sense, think, act.

Some machines are in between. Imagine a door that opens when you walk up to it. It senses you and acts. But it only does one tiny thing. People argue about whether that is a robot. That is fine! In this course, we will ask a clear question: does it sense, think and act, again and again?

You learned in F0-10 that robots are computers with muscles. In this chapter you add the senses and the circle. In the next chapters you will meet each part closely.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Robotics books describe a robot as a machine with three groups of parts. Sensors measure the world. A computer runs a program that turns measurements into decisions. Actuators turn decisions into motion. D2

The program runs these three jobs in a loop. Each time round the loop, the program reads the sensors, decides, and sends commands to the actuators. The action changes the robot's position, so the next sensor reading is different. D2 D1

This "act, then measure again" idea is called feedback. You will meet it properly in F9-05. The listing in this chapter already shows it in a tiny way: the robot measures the wall every step, so it stops at the right place. R1

In this course the robot and its world live inside a simulator. A simulator is a program that pretends to be the robot and the world. Our simulators are tiny C++ programs that this university wrote and ran. They print what happens, step by step, as text. R1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Engineers do not always split a robot into exactly three neat boxes. Big robots run many loops at once. A fast inner loop might keep a motor at the right speed. A slower outer loop might plan a path across a room. Each loop still senses, decides and acts. You will see loops inside loops in later courses, starting with RB202. D1 D2

How the hardware actually does it

In a real small robot, a sensor is an electronic part that changes a voltage when the thing it measures changes. A small computer called a microcontroller reads that voltage as a number. The program compares the number with a rule and decides. Then the computer switches power to a motor through a motor driver, because the computer's own pins cannot power a motor directly. D4 D2 You will see the parts of real kits in later courses (RB201). The exact parts of any kit come from its own datasheets, never from memory.

Worked example

Let us be the robot from the listing, by hand. A corridor has squares numbered 0, 1, 2 and so on. A wall stands at square 10. The robot starts at square 0. Its rule is: "If the wall is 2 squares away or closer, stop. Otherwise roll forward one square."

  1. Step 1. Sense: the wall is 10 − 0 = 10 squares away. Think: is 10 two or less? No. Act: move to square 1.
  2. Step 2. Sense: 10 − 1 = 9 squares. Think: no. Act: move to square 2.
  3. Steps 3 to 8 work the same way. After step 8 the robot stands on square 8.
  4. Step 9. Sense: 10 − 8 = 2 squares. Think: is 2 two or less? Yes. Act: stop.
  5. Step 10. Sense: still 2. Think: yes. Act: stay stopped.

So the robot stops at square 8, two squares before the wall. The program run below agrees, step by step. R1

Try one change in your head. What if the rule said "3 squares or closer"? Then step 8 would see 10 − 7 = 3 and stop. The robot would stop on square 7.

Code walk-through

You do not need to know C++ yet. KID102 teaches it. Here you read the program like a recipe and change numbers. Every line is explained in the table.

Listing 1 — sense_think_act.cpp

// F9-01 Listing 1: a robot in a corridor that senses, thinks and acts.
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    const int wall = 10;   // the wall stands at square 10 of the corridor
    int position = 0;      // the robot starts at square 0

    for (int step = 1; step <= 10; ++step) {
        int distance = wall - position;   // SENSE: how far away is the wall?
        bool tooClose = distance <= 2;    // THINK: is the wall close?
        if (tooClose) {
            std::cout << "step " << step << ": wall is " << distance
                      << " squares away -> stop\n";   // ACT: stay still
        } else {
            position = position + 1;                  // ACT: roll forward
            std::cout << "step " << step << ": wall is " << distance
                      << " squares away -> forward to square " << position << '\n';
        }
    }
    return 0;
}
