Where the analogy breaks

  • A robot has no common sense. Amara knows a puddle is not a wall. Our robot only knows the one number its rule looks at. If a box appears in the corridor, Listing 1 does not notice it, because its "sensor" only measures the wall. R1
  • A robot senses only what its sensors measure. Your eyes see colour, shape and movement at once. A real sensor measures one kind of thing, in its own way, with small errors. You will see these errors in F9-02. D3
  • A robot's loop runs in steps. Your body feels balance all the time. A computer program reads its sensors at separate moments, one loop round after another. Between two readings it does not know what changed. D1
  • A robot does not learn by itself in this course. Amara gets better with practice. Our robots do exactly what the program says, every time. If the rule is wrong, the robot repeats the same mistake until a person fixes the program.

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: the robot drives into the wall (the log says "BUMP"). Cause: the robot sensed once, before the loop, and never looked again. How to find it: look at the distance in the log. If it never changes while the robot moves, the sensing is not inside the loop. Fix: move the sensing line inside the loop. The forensic lab below shows this from a real run. R2
  • Symptom: the robot never moves at all. Cause: the stop rule is too wide, for example "stop if the wall is 20 squares away or closer" in a corridor of 10. How to find it: the first log line already says "stop". Fix: make the number in the rule smaller than the starting distance.
  • Symptom: you call a machine a robot because it moves. Cause: looking only at the "act" part. How to find it: ask "what does it sense, and does that change what it does?" Fix: check all three jobs and the loop.
  • Symptom: the program does not build after you edit it. Cause: a missing ; or brace. How to find it: read the first error message; it names a line. Fix: compare your line with the listing. F0-36 shows how to read such messages calmly.
Transition box

Where you came from: KID101 showed that a computer follows exact steps (F0-01), has inputs and outputs (F0-06), and that robots are computers with muscles (F0-10). What carries over: the robot's brain is still a computer that follows exact steps; sensors are inputs and motors are outputs. D5 What changes: the steps now repeat in a loop, and each round depends on what the sensors just measured, so the world itself becomes part of the program's story. D2 What comes next: F9-02 looks closely at the "sense" part: how a light sensor sees a line, and why its readings wobble.

Check yourself

  1. Name the three jobs a robot does, in order.
  2. Which part of the body matches a robot's actuators? (a) eyes (b) brain (c) muscles (d) skin
  3. A toaster heats bread for a set time and then pops it up. Is it a robot in this course's sense? Give your reason.
  4. A robot lawn mower turns when it bumps into a fence. Name its sense, think and act parts.
  5. Explain in your own words why a robot must sense again after it moves.
  6. In Listing 1, which line is the "think" part?
  7. Apply it to a new case: change line 11 to distance <= 4. On which square will the robot stop?
  8. Why do we test robots in a simulator first?

Lab

Goal. Run the corridor robot, predict how one change moves its stopping square, and check your prediction.

Hardware and software needed. A computer with a C++ compiler, set up by your teacher or parent. This build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; another recent compiler is fine. No robot hardware. No computer? Do the paper version: draw 11 squares, put a coin on square 0, and be the robot, following the rule step by step.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use. This lab is simulator only.

Steps.

  1. Copy sense_think_act.cpp from the course folder university/labs/F9-01.
  2. Build and run it with the build command shown in the code walk-through, or ask your adult helper to run university/labs/run_lab.sh university/labs/F9-01. You should see ten lines, ending with two "stop" lines.
  3. Write down your prediction: if line 6 says const int wall = 15;, where will the robot stop? (Hint: the loop only runs 10 times.)
  4. Make the change and run again. Compare with your prediction.
  5. Put line 6 back to 10. Change line 11 to distance <= 4. Predict, run and compare.

Expected observations. With the original program the last two lines say the wall is 2 squares away and the robot stops, as in the output above. R1 With wall = 15 the loop ends before the robot gets close, so it never stops: ten steps are not enough.

Verification. Your written prediction matches the printed stopping square for both changes. If not, find the step where your hand-worked version and the log first differ.

Troubleshooting.

  • Nothing prints → the program was built but not run → run the file the compiler made (./sense_think_act).
  • An error about a missing ; → a semicolon was deleted while editing → compare your line with the listing.
  • The robot stops on a different square than you predicted → you counted the distance from the wrong square → redo the worked example with the new number.

Extension. Change the loop to run 15 times (line 9). With wall = 15, where does the robot stop now? Then make the robot go two squares per step (line 16). Does it still stop safely? Try it and explain.

Forensic lab

Scenario. Kenji copied the corridor robot and "tidied" it. Now his robot drives straight into the wall. He sent you his program and the log it printed. Your job: find out why, from the evidence.

Evidence pack. Kenji's program, sensed_once.cpp:

// F9-01 forensic evidence: the same robot, but with one line moved.
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    const int wall = 10;   // the wall stands at square 10 of the corridor
    int position = 0;      // the robot starts at square 0

    int distance = wall - position;       // SENSE (now outside the loop)
    for (int step = 1; step <= 12; ++step) {
        bool tooClose = distance <= 2;    // THINK: is the wall close?
        if (tooClose) {
            std::cout << "step " << step << ": wall is " << distance
                      << " squares away -> stop\n";
        } else if (position + 1 >= wall) {
            std::cout << "step " << step << ": wall is " << distance
                      << " squares away -> forward... BUMP! hit the wall at square "
                      << wall << '\n';
        } else {
            position = position + 1;
            std::cout << "step " << step << ": wall is " << distance
                      << " squares away -> forward to square " << position << '\n';
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

Questions.

  1. Observation: what number does the log say for the wall distance at each step? What happens to the robot's square at the same time?
  2. Hypotheses: write two possible reasons for the bump before you look at the code.
  3. Root cause: which line of Kenji's program is in the wrong place? Prove it with the log.
  4. Fix: what change makes the robot stop safely? How would you check your fix?
  5. Prevention: what could Kenji check in every robot log to catch this early?

Method hints. Compare two columns of the log: the distance and the square. In a working robot, if one goes up, the other must go down. Then compare Kenji's program with Listing 1, line by line, around the loop.

Mini-project

The robot spotter's poster. Find six machines at home, at school or in a story. For each, draw it and write its sense, think and act parts, or say which part is missing. Decide: robot or not a robot? Give one sentence of reason each.

Rubric. 2 points: six machines, each with sense, think and act filled in or marked "missing". 1 point: at least one "not a robot" with a clear reason. 1 point: at least one machine that is "in between", with your argument. 1 point: neat enough that a friend can read it.

Summary

  • A robot senses, thinks and acts, again and again.
  • Sensors are its senses, the program is its brain, and actuators (mostly motors) are its muscles.
  • The loop matters: after acting, the robot must sense again, because the world has changed.
  • A machine that only acts on a timer, without sensing, is not a robot in this course's sense.
  • In this course you test robots in tiny text simulators first.
  • Sensing once, outside the loop, makes a robot blind to its own movement.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Sense, think, act — and then again.
  2. (c) muscles. Eyes and skin match sensors; the brain matches the program.
  3. No. It acts, but it does not sense the bread and change what it does. A toaster that measured the bread's colour and stopped when it was brown would be closer to a robot.
  4. Sense: a bump sensor feels the fence. Think: the program decides to turn. Act: the wheel motors turn the mower.
  5. Good answers say: moving changes where the robot is, so the old measurement is out of date; without a new one the robot cannot notice walls, bends or changes.
  6. Line 11, bool tooClose = distance <= 2;. Line 10 senses, lines 13–18 act.
  7. Square 6. At step 7 the robot is on square 6 and sees 10 − 6 = 4, which is 4 or less, so it stops. (If you said 7, you stopped one step late; if you said 4, you used the rule number as the square.)
  8. Because a bug in a simulator costs nothing: no broken robot, no hurt fingers. Real robots come only after the simulator lab passes (see F9-07).

Forensic lab answer key

Root cause. Line 9 of sensed_once.cpp measures the distance before the loop starts. Inside the loop nothing ever updates distance, so the robot always believes the wall is 10 squares away.

Evidence. Every log line says "wall is 10 squares away", while the square goes 1, 2, … 9. Those two cannot both be true. At step 10 the log shows "BUMP!".

Fix. Move line 9 inside the loop, as line 10 of Listing 1. Verify by running again: the distance should go down by one each step, and the robot should stop on square 8 as in R1.

How the fault was made. The Lab Engineer moved the sensing line of Listing 1 above the loop, made the loop run 12 times, and added a "BUMP" message for a move into the wall.

Wrong answers and why. "The rule <= 2 is wrong": no, the same rule works in Listing 1. "The loop runs too many times": more steps only make the bump visible; with correct sensing the robot keeps saying "stop". Prevention: in every log, check that what the robot senses changes when the robot moves.

Story hook

Ravi rides his bicycle along a painted line in the school yard. His teacher has made a game: stay on the white line all the way to the gate.

Ravi keeps his eyes on the line. When the line looks a little to the left, he steers a little left. When the sun goes behind a cloud, everything looks darker. For a moment the grey yard and the line look almost the same. Ravi slows down and looks harder.

His friend Noor rides with her eyes closed for one second, to try it. She wobbles at once. "I can't feel the line!" she laughs.

Without senses, you cannot follow a line. A robot is the same. Today you give your robot its senses, and you find out why a robot's eyes are never perfect.

What you will be able to do

  • Name three kinds of robot sensors and what each one notices.
  • Explain what a sensor reading is, and why two readings of the same thing can differ a little.
  • Choose a threshold that separates "line" from "floor" using measured readings.
  • Run a simulated light sensor and read its log.
  • Diagnose a robot that "sees a line everywhere" from its log.
Jargon box
Reading
Simple words: the number a sensor gives when the robot asks it "what do you notice now?" Analogy: how bright the line looks to Ravi at one moment. Precise: one measurement value produced by a sensor at one moment, in the sensor's own units. D3
Light sensor
Simple words: a sensor that tells how bright something is. Analogy: your eyes telling light from dark. Precise: a sensor whose output changes with the amount of light reaching it; pointed at the floor with a small lamp beside it, it reports how much light the floor reflects. D4
Distance sensor
Simple words: a sensor that tells how far away the nearest thing in front is. Analogy: judging with your eyes how far the wall is. Precise: a range sensor; some send out a signal (sound or light) and measure the echo that comes back from an object. D3
Bump sensor
Simple words: a sensor that only says "I touched something" or "I did not". Analogy: the skin on your hand feeling a wall. Precise: a contact switch that closes (or opens) when pressed; its reading has only two values. D4
Sensor noise
Simple words: small random wobbles in a sensor's readings. Analogy: the line looking slightly different every time a cloud moves. Precise: the part of a measurement that differs from the true value in ways that change from reading to reading; real sensors always have some. D3
Threshold
Simple words: a dividing number: below it means one thing, above it means another. Analogy: "if the yard looks this dark or darker, I am on the line". Precise: a fixed value a program compares a reading with to turn it into a yes/no decision.
Calibrate
Simple words: to measure known things first, so you can set your numbers well. Analogy: looking at the white line and the grey yard before the race starts. Precise: to determine how a sensor's readings relate to known conditions (here: readings on floor and on line) and set the program's constants from those measurements. D3

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the real readings from our simulated light sensor as bars. The robot passed over ten floor squares. Three of them were on a dark line.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

You have many senses. Your eyes see light. Your ears hear sound. Your skin feels touch. A robot has sensors instead. Each sensor notices only one kind of thing.

A light sensor notices how bright something is. Point it down at the floor. A white floor bounces back lots of light. Dark tape bounces back little. So the sensor can tell "floor" from "line".

A distance sensor notices how far away a wall is. A bump sensor is the simplest of all. It is a tiny button on the front. When the robot touches a wall, the button is pressed.

When the program asks a sensor, the sensor answers with a number. That number is called a reading. A bright floor might give a big reading. Dark tape might give a small reading.

Here is the surprise. Ask the same sensor about the same floor twice, and the numbers can be a little different. The light changes. The robot shakes a tiny bit. These little wobbles are called noise. Real sensors always have some.

So how does the robot decide "line or floor"? It uses a dividing number called a threshold. If the reading is below the threshold, it says "line". Otherwise it says "floor".

A good threshold sits in the middle, far from both kinds of reading. Then a small wobble cannot fool the robot. Ravi does the same when the cloud comes: he looks for "clearly darker", not "a tiny bit darker".

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A sensor turns something in the world into a value the computer can read. A light sensor's output changes with the amount of light that reaches it. Pointed down with a small lamp beside it, it measures the light reflected by the floor: light surfaces reflect more than dark ones. D4

Some distance sensors send out a pulse of sound or light and measure the echo that comes back from an object. A bump sensor is a switch: its reading has only two values, pressed or not pressed. D3 D4

Every real measurement differs a little from the true value. Robotics books model this as noise, and they treat a reading as "true value plus a random error". D3 Our simulator does exactly that: line 15 of Listing 1 adds a fixed list of small wobbles to the true brightness. The list is fixed so that every run prints the same numbers, which makes the lab repeatable. R1

To turn a reading into a decision, the program compares it with a threshold. You set a good threshold by calibrating: measure on the floor, measure on the line, and pick a value between the two groups, with room on both sides for noise. D3

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Engineers describe noise with numbers: how big the wobbles are on average, and how they spread. That needs probability, which the university teaches in MA202. Later courses then combine several noisy sensors into one better estimate (the Kalman filter, in RB302). Some errors are not random at all: a sensor might always read a bit too high. That kind of error is called a bias, and calibration is how you find it. D3

How the hardware actually does it

Inside a light sensor is a part whose electrical behaviour changes with light. The robot's small computer measures a voltage that depends on it and turns that voltage into a number. D4 How big the numbers are, and which light colours the part responds to, depends on the exact part, and only its datasheet can tell you. This chapter does not quote numbers for any real sensor (AH-21); our simulator's numbers are made up for the simulator and labelled "simulator units".

Worked example

Lucía calibrates her robot's light sensor. She reads the floor four times and the line three times. Here are her numbers (the same ones our simulator printed, R1):

  • Floor readings: 83, 80, 80, 77, 84, 75, 82.
  • Line readings: 20, 20, 21.

Step 1. Find the darkest floor reading: the smallest floor number is 75.

Step 2. Find the brightest line reading: the biggest line number is 21.

Step 3. Any threshold above 21 and up to 75 sorts all these readings correctly. That is a wide gap.

Step 4. Choose the middle, so noise has the most room on both sides: (21 + 75) ÷ 2 = 96 ÷ 2 = 48. Our listing uses 50, which is also safely in the gap: 50 − 21 = 29 units above the brightest line reading, and 75 − 50 = 25 units below the darkest floor reading.

Step 5. Check a bad choice. A threshold of 76 would call the floor reading 75 a "line". A single wobble would fool the robot. That is why "in the middle" beats "just past the edge".

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — light_sensor.cpp: a simulated light sensor looking down at ten floor squares.

// F9-02 Listing 1: a simulated light sensor looking down at the floor.
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    // How bright each floor square really is (simulator units, 0 = black).
    // Squares 4, 5 and 6 are covered by the dark line.
    const std::vector<int> floor = {80, 82, 79, 81, 20, 18, 22, 80, 78, 81};
    // Small wobbles a real sensor adds to every reading ("noise").
    const std::vector<int> noise = {3, -2, 1, -4, 0, 2, -1, 4, -3, 1};
    const int threshold = 50;   // darker than this means "line"

    for (int square = 0; square < 10; ++square) {
        int reading = floor[square] + noise[square];   // what the sensor reports
        std::cout << "square " << square << ": true " << floor[square]
                  << ", sensor reads " << reading << " -> ";
        if (reading < threshold) {
            std::cout << "LINE\n";
        } else {
            std::cout << "floor\n";
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Your eyes see a whole picture; a simple light sensor sees one spot. Ravi sees the whole line ahead and where it bends. Our light sensor only reports one number for the spot right under it. It cannot tell where the line goes next. R1
  • Your brain hides noise from you; a robot gets it raw. You do not notice your eyes' tiny wobbles. A robot's program receives every wobble in the number and must deal with it, for example with a well-placed threshold. D3
  • Sensor errors are specific and measurable. "Eyes get tired" is vague. A real sensor's errors can be measured and written down, and a careful engineer does that during calibration. D3

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: the robot says "LINE" on every square. Cause: the threshold is above all the readings. How to find it: compare the threshold with the floor readings in the log. Fix: calibrate again and pick a value between the two groups. The forensic lab shows a real run. R2
  • Symptom: the robot never sees the line. Cause: the threshold is below all line readings. How to find it: look at the line squares in the log; their readings are above the threshold. Fix: raise the threshold into the gap.
  • Symptom: the robot sometimes flickers between LINE and floor on the same square. Cause: the threshold is right at the edge of one group, so noise pushes readings across it. How to find it: look for readings close to the threshold. Fix: move the threshold to the middle of the gap.
  • Symptom: the comparison is the wrong way round (dark squares say floor). Cause: > written instead of <. How to find it: the decisions in the log are exactly backwards. Fix: remember: dark means small readings.
Transition box

Where you came from: F9-01 used a perfect "distance to the wall" number, and F0-06 called such things inputs. What carries over: the sense–think–act loop and the idea that a sensor gives the program a number. What changes: real readings are not perfect: they wobble (noise), so a decision needs a well-chosen threshold, found by calibrating. D3 What comes next: F9-03 gives the robot muscles: two wheel motors, and a sensor that counts their turns.

Check yourself

  1. Match each sensor to what it notices: light sensor, distance sensor, bump sensor → touch, brightness, how far.
  2. What is a reading?
  3. Why did square 0 read 83 when its true brightness was 80?
  4. Which threshold is best for the readings in Figure 1? (a) 22 (b) 50 (c) 74 (d) 90
  5. Explain in your own words why a threshold in the middle of the gap is safer than one near the edge.
  6. Apply it to a new case: on a dark floor with a white line, the floor reads about 20 and the line about 80. How must line 18 change?
  7. A bump sensor's reading has how many possible values?

Lab

Goal. Run the simulated light sensor, then calibrate a new floor and set your own threshold.

Hardware and software needed. A computer with a C++ compiler, set up by an adult (this build used g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). No hardware. Paper version: write the ten readings on cards, choose a threshold, and sort the cards into "line" and "floor".

Safety. None beyond normal computer use.

Steps.

  1. Run light_sensor.cpp from university/labs/F9-02. You should see squares 4, 5 and 6 marked LINE.
  2. Now pretend the floor is a grey carpet. Change line 9 so the floor squares are 52, 54, 51, 53, 20, 18, 22, 52, 51, 52. Keep the noise.
  3. Before running: work out the readings (true + noise) by hand. Which squares does threshold 50 get wrong?
  4. Run it. Compare with your prediction.
  5. Calibrate: find the darkest floor reading and the brightest line reading. Pick the middle as your new threshold. Change line 12 and run again.

Expected observations. With the original numbers the output matches the listing's output above. R1 With the grey carpet, the readings become 55, 52, 52, 49, 20, 20, 21, 56, 48, 53, so threshold 50 wrongly calls squares 3 and 8 LINE. Calibrating gives darkest floor 48 and brightest line 21; the middle is (21 + 48) ÷ 2 = 34.5, so 34 or 35 marks exactly squares 4, 5 and 6. (Checked by the Lab Engineer with a scratch run of the edited program in this build.)

Verification. Your final run marks exactly squares 4, 5 and 6 as LINE, and your threshold is at least a few units away from every reading.

Troubleshooting.

  • "expected '}'" or similar error → a comma or brace was lost when editing line 9 → each list needs exactly ten numbers separated by commas.
  • Fewer than ten lines print, or a crash message → the list has fewer than ten numbers → count them.
  • All squares LINE → threshold too high → recalibrate (see Common mistakes).

Extension. Make the noise bigger (for example double every number in line 11). How small can the gap get before no threshold works? Explain what a real robot builder could do then (a better sensor, a darker line, or a lamp next to the sensor).

Forensic lab

Scenario. Mei's line-following robot behaves strangely: it acts as if it is on the line all the time, even on the plain floor. She changed "one number" in the sensor program yesterday but does not remember which.

Evidence pack. The log of a real run of Mei's program (bad_threshold.cpp), produced in this build: R2

square 9: true 81, sensor reads 82 -> LINE

// F9-02 forensic evidence: the same sensor program with one number changed.
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    // How bright each floor square really is (simulator units, 0 = black).
    // Squares 4, 5 and 6 are covered by the dark line.
    const std::vector<int> floor = {80, 82, 79, 81, 20, 18, 22, 80, 78, 81};
    // Small wobbles a real sensor adds to every reading ("noise").
    const std::vector<int> noise = {3, -2, 1, -4, 0, 2, -1, 4, -3, 1};
    const int threshold = 90;   // darker than this means "line"

    for (int square = 0; square < 10; ++square) {
        int reading = floor[square] + noise[square];   // what the sensor reports
        std::cout << "square " << square << ": true " << floor[square]
                  << ", sensor reads " << reading << " -> ";
        if (reading < threshold) {
            std::cout << "LINE\n";
        } else {
            std::cout << "floor\n";

}

Questions.

  1. Observation: what do the readings for squares 0–3 and 4–6 look like? What does the program decide for each?
  2. Hypotheses: give two possible causes (a broken sensor? a program change?). Which evidence tells them apart?
  3. Root cause: which number did Mei change? Prove it from the log.
  4. Fix: what value would you choose, and why?
  5. Prevention: what quick test could Mei run after every change to the sensor program?

Method hints. First ask: are the readings themselves normal? Compare them with Figure 1. If the readings are fine but the decisions are wrong, the problem is in the "think" part, not the "sense" part.

Mini-project

A sensor diary. Pick one of your own senses (sight, hearing or touch). For one day, write down three times when it was "noisy" or fooled, like a cloud making the line hard to see. For each, write what a robot builder could do about it: calibrate, choose a better threshold, or add a second sensor.

Rubric. 2 points: three real examples, described clearly. 2 points: a sensible robot fix for each, using the words reading, noise or threshold. 1 point: one example that explains why a threshold in the middle helps.

Summary

  • Sensors are a robot's senses; each notices one kind of thing.
  • Light sensors tell bright from dark, distance sensors tell how far, bump sensors tell "touched or not".
  • A reading is one number from a sensor at one moment.
  • Readings wobble a little: that is noise, and real sensors always have some.
  • A threshold turns a reading into a yes/no decision.
  • Calibrate first, then put the threshold in the middle of the gap.
  • If readings look normal but decisions are wrong, look at the thinking, not the sensor.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Light sensor → brightness; distance sensor → how far; bump sensor → touch.
  2. The number a sensor gives at one moment, when the program asks it.
  3. Noise: the simulator added +3 to that reading, as real sensors add small wobbles. The sensor is not broken.
  4. (b) 50. 22 is only 1 above the brightest line reading (21), and 74 is only 1 below the darkest floor reading (75), so a small wobble could fool either. 90 is above every reading, so everything becomes "line" (that is the forensic lab).
  5. Good answers say: readings wobble; if the threshold is near one group, a small wobble can push a reading across it; in the middle, a wobble has to be very big to cause a wrong decision.
  6. Now the line is bright, so it must say "line" when the reading is above the threshold: if (reading > threshold), with a threshold in the middle (about 50 here, after calibrating).
  7. Two: pressed or not pressed.

Forensic lab answer key

Root cause. Line 12 sets threshold = 90. Every reading in the log (the largest is 84) is below 90, so every square is called LINE.

Evidence. The readings are the same as in the healthy run (83, 80, 80, 77, 20, 20, 21, 84, 75, 82), so the sensor works. Only the decisions changed. The comparison of the two listings shows one changed number on line 12.

Fix. Recalibrate and choose the middle of the gap, for example 48 or 50. Verify: run again; exactly squares 4, 5 and 6 say LINE.

How the fault was made. The Lab Engineer copied Listing 1 and changed only the threshold on line 12 from 50 to 90 (and the comment on line 1).

Wrong answers and why. "The sensor is broken": its readings match the healthy run. "The noise is too big": the noise is identical to the healthy run. Prevention: after every change, run a test with known squares and check that line and floor are both recognised.

Story hook

Kofi is pushing his little sister Ines around the yard in a cart. The cart has two big wheels at the back. Kofi has an idea: "Ines, you push the left wheel with your hand, and I'll push the right one."

When they push equally hard, the cart rolls straight. When Ines pushes harder than Kofi, the cart swings to the right. When Kofi pushes harder, it swings left. When nobody pushes, it stops.

"We're steering without a steering wheel!" Ines shouts.

Then Kofi counts out loud each time the right wheel goes all the way round. "One, two, three…" After ten turns they have rolled past the tree. "Next time," says Kofi, "I'll know how far ten turns is."

Kofi and Ines have discovered how the robots in this course move and measure. Their hands were the motors. Kofi's counting was the encoder.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a motor does for a robot, using the "muscles" picture.
  • Predict which way a two-wheeled robot goes when its wheels turn at different speeds.
  • Calculate how far a wheel rolled from its turn count.
  • Run a simulation of two wheel motors with turn counters.
  • Diagnose a robot that drives in circles from its encoder log.
Jargon box
Motor
Simple words: a part that turns electricity into turning. Analogy: a muscle that pulls when your brain tells it to. Precise: an electric motor converts electrical energy into rotation of its shaft; a robot's program controls it indirectly, through a motor driver that switches the power. D4
Motor command
Simple words: the instruction the program gives a motor, such as "turn this fast". Analogy: your brain telling a leg how hard to push the pedal. Precise: the value a control program sends to a motor driver; what the motor then really does also depends on the load, the battery and friction. D2
Encoder
Simple words: a sensor that counts how much a wheel has turned. Analogy: counting the turns of a wheel. Precise: a sensor on a motor or wheel shaft that produces counts as the shaft rotates; distance travelled is estimated from the counts and the wheel size. D2
Differential drive
Simple words: steering by turning two side wheels at different speeds. Analogy: Kofi and Ines pushing the two cart wheels. Precise: a wheeled robot with two independently driven wheels on one axle; equal wheel speeds drive straight, different speeds turn it toward the slower wheel's side. D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows a two-wheeled robot from above, in three situations. The arrows on the wheels show how fast each wheel turns: a longer arrow means faster.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Your muscles move your body when your brain tells them to. A robot's muscles are its motors. A motor turns electricity into turning. Fix a wheel to the motor, and the wheel turns too.

Many small robots have two wheels, one on each side, each with its own motor. They have no steering wheel at all. They steer like Kofi and Ines's cart.

Both wheels turn at the same speed? The robot goes straight. The left wheel turns faster? The robot curves to the right. The right wheel turns faster? It curves to the left. Look at Figure 1 and try it with your hands on a toy car.

Here is a puzzle. The program tells both motors "go at speed 4". Does the robot surely go straight? Not always! One motor might be a bit weaker. One wheel might rub on something. The program told the muscles what to do, but it does not know what they really did.

That is why robots often count their wheel turns. A sensor called an encoder counts how far each wheel has turned. It is like Kofi counting "one, two, three" out loud.

Counting turns also tells you how far you went. If one turn of the wheel rolls 10 units along the floor, then 20 turns roll 20 × 10 = 200 units. You will do this sum in the worked example.

So the motor is a muscle, and the encoder is a sense that feels the muscle's work. Sense, think, act again.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

An electric motor converts electrical energy into rotation of its shaft. A small robot's computer cannot power a motor from its own pins, so it sends a motor command to a motor driver, which switches the battery's power to the motor. D4

A robot with two independently driven wheels on one axle is called a differential drive. Equal wheel speeds drive it straight; different speeds turn it toward the side of the slower wheel. D2 Our simulator does not model the turning itself. It compares how far each wheel rolled and names the direction, using exactly this rule (lines 22–30 of Listing 1). R1

A motor command is a wish, not a fact. What the motor really does also depends on load, battery and friction. An encoder measures what really happened: it produces counts as the shaft turns. From the counts and the wheel size, the robot estimates how far each wheel rolled. D2

In our simulator, one "count" is one full turn, and one turn rolls 10 simulator units. Real encoders give many counts per turn, and the real distance per turn comes from measuring the real wheel. D2 R1

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. From the two wheels' distances and the gap between the wheels, an engineer can calculate how much the robot turned and where it is now. This is called odometry, and it needs a little geometry. You will do it in RB201 (F9-09). Engineers also use the encoder counts to control motor speed in a loop: "too slow? push harder". That is the PID loop of RB202. D2 D1

How the hardware actually does it

Inside a simple electric motor, current through coils of wire makes magnetic forces that turn the shaft. More power makes it try to turn harder or faster. A gearbox can sit between motor and wheel, trading speed for pulling force. D4 How fast or strong a real motor is, and how many counts per turn a real encoder gives, come only from that part's datasheet (AH-21). Our simulator's numbers are made up for practice.

Worked example

Arjun's simulated robot runs for 5 steps. Each step, the left wheel turns 4 times and the right wheel 2 times. One wheel turn rolls 10 units.

  1. Left count: 4 turns each step, 5 steps: 4 × 5 = 20 turns.
  2. Right count: 2 × 5 = 10 turns.
  3. Left distance: 20 turns × 10 units = 200 units.
  4. Right distance: 10 × 10 = 100 units.
  5. Direction: the left wheel rolled further, so the robot curved toward the slower, right side: it curves to the right.

The second line of the program's output says exactly this: "counts 20 and 10, wheels rolled 200 and 100 units -> curves to the right". R1

Now backwards: the encoder log says the right wheel counted 35 turns. How far did it roll? 35 × 10 = 350 units.

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — two_wheels.cpp: two wheel motors with turn counters.

// F9-03 Listing 1: two wheel motors and their turn counters (encoders).
#include <iostream>

// Drive for 5 steps. Each step, each wheel turns the number of times asked.
void drive(int leftTurnsPerStep, int rightTurnsPerStep)
{
    const int unitsPerTurn = 10;   // our simulated wheel rolls 10 units per turn
    int leftCount = 0;             // left encoder: counts the left wheel's turns
    int rightCount = 0;            // right encoder: counts the right wheel's turns

    for (int step = 1; step <= 5; ++step) {
        leftCount = leftCount + leftTurnsPerStep;
        rightCount = rightCount + rightTurnsPerStep;
    }
    int leftDistance = leftCount * unitsPerTurn;
    int rightDistance = rightCount * unitsPerTurn;

    std::cout << "left " << leftTurnsPerStep << ", right " << rightTurnsPerStep
              << " per step: counts " << leftCount << " and " << rightCount
              << ", wheels rolled " << leftDistance << " and " << rightDistance
              << " units -> ";
    if (leftDistance == 0 && rightDistance == 0) {
        std::cout << "stands still\n";
    } else if (leftDistance == rightDistance) {
        std::cout << "straight line\n";
    } else if (leftDistance > rightDistance) {
        std::cout << "curves to the right\n";
    } else {
        std::cout << "curves to the left\n";
    }
}

int main()
{
    drive(4, 4);
    drive(4, 2);
    drive(2, 4);
    drive(0, 0);
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Wheels slip. An encoder counts turns of the wheel, not distance on the floor. On a slippery floor the wheel can spin without moving the robot, and the count still goes up. Kofi's counting would be fooled the same way on ice. D2
  • Your muscles have feeling built in; a motor does not. You feel how hard your legs push. A simple motor has no idea what it did. Only an added sensor, like an encoder, tells the program. D2
  • A motor never gets tired, but its battery runs down. Muscles tire and recover. A motor does the same work all day, but as its battery empties the same command may give less turning. That is one reason commands and real turns can differ. D4

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: the robot curves although both motors get the same command. Cause: the motors do not really turn equally (weak motor, rubbing wheel). How to find it: compare the two encoder counts in the log. Fix: fix the mechanical problem, or later (RB202) let a control loop correct each motor's speed. See the forensic lab. R2
  • Symptom: you predict "curves left" but the robot curves right. Cause: mixing up which wheel is faster with which way it turns. How to find it: look at Figure 1 again: the robot turns toward the slower wheel. Fix: draw the robot from above and the two arrows before predicting.
  • Symptom: the distance is 10 times too big or too small. Cause: counts used as distance without multiplying by units per turn (or multiplied twice). How to find it: check the units in your sum. Fix: distance = turns × units per turn.
  • Symptom: the robot goes backwards. Cause: a negative command, or (on a real kit) a motor wired the other way round. How to find it: in the simulator, look at the command values; on a kit, an adult checks the wiring. Fix: change the sign of the command.
Transition box

Where you came from: F9-02 gave the robot senses; F0-06 called motors outputs. What carries over: sensors give readings, and the program decides from them; an encoder is another sensor. What changes: now the robot acts on the world, and a command is not the same as what really happened: you must measure the result (with encoders) to know. D2 Moving parts also bring safety rules (F9-07). What comes next: F9-04 builds the brain: a program loop that keeps sensing, thinking and acting.

Check yourself

  1. What does a motor do, in one sentence?
  2. The left wheel turns slower than the right one. Which way does the robot curve?
  3. One wheel turn rolls 10 units. The encoder counted 12 turns. How far did the wheel roll?
  4. Why might a robot curve even though both motors got the same command?
  5. Explain in your own words the difference between a motor command and an encoder count.
  6. Apply it to a new case: a robot should spin on the spot. What could the two wheel commands be? (Hint: one can be negative.)
  7. An encoder says the wheel turned 30 times, but the robot did not move at all. What happened?

Lab

Goal. Use the two-wheel simulator to predict and test which way a robot goes, and how far.

Hardware and software needed. A computer with a C++ compiler, set up by an adult (this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Paper version: use a toy car or two coins and walk them across a table, one per wheel.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use. (Real motors come only after the simulator, with an adult: F9-07.)

Steps.

  1. Run two_wheels.cpp from university/labs/F9-03. Check that you get the four lines shown above.
  2. Add a line drive(3, 5); before return 0;. Before running, write down the counts, the distances and the direction.
  3. Run it and compare.
  4. Change line 7 to a wheel that rolls 15 units per turn. Predict the new distances for drive(4, 4), then run.
  5. Add drive(5, -5);. What does the program print? Is that a good description of spinning on the spot? (Look carefully at the rules on lines 22–30.)

Expected observations. drive(3, 5) gives counts 15 and 25 and "curves to the left"; with 15 units per turn, drive(4, 4) rolls 300 units per wheel. For drive(5, -5) the program says "curves to the right", although a real robot would spin in place: our simple rule does not know about spinning.

Verification. All your predictions in steps 2 and 4 match the output. For step 5 you can explain why the program's words are not quite right.

Troubleshooting.

  • Error "was not declared in this scope" → drive misspelled → copy the name exactly, with the small d.
  • Your new line has no output → it was placed after return 0; → put it before.
  • Distances look wrong → you changed line 7 but predicted with 10 → redo the sum.

Extension. Improve the rules so drive(5, -5) prints "spins on the spot". (Hint: one distance is above zero and the other below zero.) Run it to check.

Forensic lab

Scenario. Yara's simulated robot was told to drive straight across the room, but it drove in a big circle. She saved the encoder log.

Questions.

  1. Observation: what did the program command each motor? What did each encoder count after 8 steps?
  2. How many turns per step did each wheel really make? Show the sum.
  3. Hypotheses: list two causes that could make one wheel turn less than commanded.
  4. Which way did the robot circle, left or right? Explain with Figure 1.
  5. Fix and prevention: what would you check on the robot, and what could a program do with the encoder counts to keep it straight?

Method hints. Compare the command column with the counts. Divide each final count by the number of steps. Then use the rule "the robot turns toward the slower wheel".

Mini-project

Draw a dance. Plan a short "dance" for a two-wheeled robot: five moves, each written as a pair of wheel commands (for example 4, 4 then 4, 2). Draw the path you expect from above. Then add all five as drive lines to the simulator and check each direction.

Rubric. 2 points: five moves with commands and a drawn path. 2 points: every predicted direction matches the simulator, or a wrong one is explained. 1 point: one move uses a negative command, explained in words.

Summary

  • Motors are a robot's muscles: they turn electricity into turning.
  • A two-wheeled robot steers by turning its wheels at different speeds; it turns toward the slower wheel.
  • A motor command is a wish; what really happened must be measured.
  • An encoder counts wheel turns: distance = turns × distance per turn.
  • Comparing commands with encoder counts finds weak motors and rubbing wheels.
  • Encoders count turns, not floor distance: wheels can slip.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. It turns electricity into turning (rotation), which can turn a wheel.
  2. To the left, toward the slower wheel. (If you said right, redraw Figure 1's arrows.)
  3. 12 × 10 = 120 units.
  4. The motors may not really turn equally: one may be weaker, a wheel may rub, or the battery may give one less power. The command is not what really happened.
  5. Good answers say: the command is what the program asks the motor to do; the encoder count is a measurement of what the wheel really did. They can differ.
  6. For example left 4 and right −4 (or −4 and 4): one wheel forward, the other backward at the same speed, so the robot turns in place.
  7. The wheel slipped (spun on a slippery floor) or the robot was lifted. An encoder counts turns, not distance on the floor.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation. Both motors were commanded 4/4 every step, but after 8 steps the left encoder counted 24 and the right 32.

Real turns per step. Left 24 ÷ 8 = 3; right 32 ÷ 8 = 4. The left wheel turns one less per step than commanded.

Direction. The left wheel is slower, so the robot turns toward the left: it circles to the left.

Root cause. The left motor (or its wheel) delivers less turning than commanded: in this simulation a weaker left motor. On a real robot, hypotheses to check would be: something rubbing the left wheel, a weaker or damaged left motor, a loose connection. A slipping wheel would not explain it, because slipping wheels still turn and are still counted.

How the fault was made. The Lab Engineer's program commands 4 turns for both wheels but adds only 3 per step to the left counter (a simulated weak motor), and prints the log.

Fix and prevention. Fix the mechanical cause. In software, compare the encoder counts every step and give the slower motor a bit more command until the counts match: a feedback loop, taught properly in RB202. Prevention: always log both commands and encoder counts.

Story hook

Sione is riding his bicycle to his grandmother's house. He knows the way: "Ride along the river. When you see the blue gate, stop."

So he rides. Look: is that the blue gate? No. Keep pedalling. Look again: blue gate? No. Pedal. Look. Pedal. Look. He does not think about it much. His brain keeps going round the same small plan.

Then, there it is. Blue gate! He brakes and stops.

But one day the gate has been painted green. Sione rides and rides. He looks for blue and never finds it. After a long time he thinks, "I have gone much too far. Something is wrong." He stops and calls home.

Sione's plan had two ways to end: "I found the gate" and "I have gone much too far". A good robot brain needs both, too.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain a robot's brain as a program that runs a loop: sense, think, act, again.
  • Trace a robot loop by hand, round by round, in a table.
  • Write a loop's stopping rule, including a safety limit.
  • Read a robot's log to see what it did in each round.
  • Diagnose a robot that loops forever, from its log.
Jargon box
Program
Simple words: exact steps that a computer follows, one after another. Analogy: Sione's plan for the ride. Precise: a sequence of instructions that a computer executes exactly as written; a robot's program turns sensor readings into motor commands. D5
Loop
Simple words: a part of a program that repeats. Analogy: look, pedal, look, pedal. Precise: a control structure that executes its body repeatedly; a while loop in C++ repeats as long as its condition is true. D6 R1
Condition
Simple words: a question with the answer yes or no. Analogy: "Is that the blue gate?" Precise: an expression that evaluates to true or false and decides whether an if branch runs or a loop goes round again. D6
Safety limit (step limit)
Simple words: a rule that stops the robot after too many rounds, even if the job is not done. Analogy: "I have gone much too far, I will stop and call home." Precise: a maximum number of loop iterations (or a maximum time) after which the program stops on purpose, so that a wrong rule cannot make the robot run forever. R2
Log (trace)
Simple words: the lines a program prints about what it did, one after another. Analogy: a diary of the ride. Precise: a time-ordered record of a program's actions and values, used to understand and debug its behaviour. R1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 is a flowchart of the robot's brain in Listing 1. Follow the arrows with your finger. Notice the two ways out: "flag found" and "safety limit reached".

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A robot's brain is a computer. The computer follows a program: exact steps, one after another. You met programs as recipes in F0-01.

A robot program has a special shape. Most of it is a loop: steps that repeat. Inside the loop are the three jobs. Sense. Think. Act. Then back to the top.

Why a loop? Because the robot can never be sure it is done. It moved, so the world looks different now. It must look again, like Sione looking for the gate.

Every loop needs a way to end. The robot asks a yes/no question each round, called a condition. "Am I on the flag?" If yes, stop. If no, keep going.

But what if the flag is missing? Or the rule is wrong? Then the answer is "no" forever, and the robot never stops. That can be dangerous with a real robot. So good robot programs add a second way out: a safety limit. "If I have gone round 20 times, stop anyway."

How do you know what the robot's brain did? You make it write a diary. Each round, it prints one line. This is the robot's log. Reading logs is a robot engineer's daily job.

The loop also goes round very quickly in a real robot, many times every second. You cannot watch each round. That is another reason the log matters.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

In C++, a while loop repeats its body as long as its condition is true. Listing 1's condition is !atGoal && step < maxSteps: "not at the goal, and fewer rounds than the limit". The loop ends as soon as either part becomes false. D6 R1

Inside the body the program senses (atGoal = (position == goal)), thinks (if (atGoal)) and acts (moves or stops). This repeating read–decide–command structure is the skeleton of every control program, from this toy to industrial controllers. D1

Notice an important detail in the run: the robot reaches square 6 in loop 6, but only knows it in loop 7. A robot learns about its world only when it senses, and it senses at the start of each round. R1

The safety limit (maxSteps) makes the program end even when the goal condition never becomes true. A program that waits forever for a condition that cannot happen is a common bug; the step limit turns it into a visible, safe stop. R2

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Real robot controllers can run their loop at a fixed rate: for example, "sense, think, act" a set number of times per second, controlled by a clock. Being on time matters: a control loop that runs late can make the robot behave badly. That idea is called real-time, and it is taught in RB304. Later courses also meet the "watchdog": a timer outside the main program that stops the motors if the loop stops reporting in. Our step limit is a tiny cousin of that idea. D1 D7

How the hardware actually does it

The robot's computer runs the loop's instructions one after another, very fast. Each round it reads its input pins (the sensors), calculates, and writes to its output pins (the motor driver). D5 How many rounds per second a real robot can do depends on its computer and program; you would measure it, not guess it (AH-22).

Worked example

Trace Listing 1 by hand. The flag is on square 6; the robot starts on square 0; the limit is 20 rounds.

RoundSquare at start of roundSense: on flag?ActSquare after round
10noforward1
21noforward2
32noforward3
43noforward4
54noforward5
65noforward6
76yesstop6

After round 7, atGoal is true, so the loop condition is false and the loop ends. The program prints "loop finished after 7 rounds". The real run agrees. R1

Question: what if the flag were on square 25? The robot would move one square per round. After round 20 it would stand on square 20, and the condition step < maxSteps would be false. The safety limit stops it at square 20, without the flag.

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — robot_loop.cpp: the robot's brain as a loop.

// F9-04 Listing 1: the robot's brain is a loop: sense, think, act, again.
#include <iostream>

int main()
{
    const int goal = 6;        // a flag on the floor at square 6
    const int maxSteps = 20;   // safety limit: never loop more than this
    int position = 0;
    int step = 0;
    bool atGoal = false;

    while (!atGoal && step < maxSteps) {
        step = step + 1;
        atGoal = (position == goal);          // SENSE: am I standing on the flag?
        if (atGoal) {                         // THINK
            std::cout << "loop " << step << ": flag found at square " << position
                      << " -> stop\n";       // ACT
        } else {
            position = position + 1;          // ACT
            std::cout << "loop " << step << ": no flag -> forward to square "
                      << position << '\n';
        }
    }
    std::cout << "loop finished after " << step << " rounds\n";
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Sione notices surprises; the program does not. Sione realised "I have gone much too far" by common sense. A program only stops for reasons someone wrote into it. Without line 7's limit, the robot would never "feel" that something is wrong. R2
  • A loop runs in separate rounds. Sione watches the road the whole time. The program looks only at the start of each round, so it learns about the flag one round late (round 7, not round 6). R1 D1
  • The program does exactly the same thing every time. Sione might take a shortcut today. Given the same start, our program prints the same log every run. That is good for testing: you can repeat a bug and study it.

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: the robot keeps going until the safety limit, never reaching the goal. Cause: the rule can never make the goal condition true. How to find it: read the log and look for repeating lines (the same squares again and again). Fix: change the rule, not only the limit. The forensic lab is a real example. R2
  • Symptom: the program never ends and prints nothing new. Cause: the round counter is never increased (line 13 deleted), so the safety limit is never reached. How to find it: the loop runs on forever; stop it with Ctrl+C. Fix: make sure the counter goes up every round. (F0-33 has a whole forensic lab on this.)
  • Symptom: the robot stops immediately, in round 1. Cause: the condition is the wrong way round, for example while (atGoal …) without the !. How to find it: the log has no lines from the loop. Fix: read the condition aloud: "while not at the goal".
  • Symptom: you think the loop ran 6 times but the log says 7. Cause: forgetting the extra round needed to sense the goal. How to find it: trace it in a table like the worked example. Fix: remember: arriving and knowing are two different rounds.
Transition box

Where you came from: F0-07 showed decisions and loops without a computer, and F9-01–F9-03 gave the robot senses and muscles. What carries over: exact steps, yes/no decisions, repeating. What changes: a robot's loop must end safely even when its plan fails, so you add a safety limit, and you read logs because the loop runs too fast to watch. D1 What comes next: F9-05 uses the loop for something clever: steering back to a line with a rule that corrects a little each round.

Check yourself

  1. What three jobs are inside a robot's loop?
  2. Why does a robot program use a loop instead of sensing just once?
  3. In Listing 1, what are the two ways the loop can end?
  4. The robot reaches square 6 in round 6. Why does the log say the flag was found in round 7?
  5. Apply it to a new case: the flag is on square 3 and maxSteps is 2. What is the last log line?
  6. Explain in your own words why the safety limit matters more for a real robot than for a simulated one.
  7. Which line would you delete to make the loop never end? (Do not do it on a real robot!)

Lab

Goal. Change the robot's world and limits, predict how many rounds the loop runs, and check with the log.

Hardware and software needed. A computer with a C++ compiler, set up by an adult (this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Paper version: draw squares, use a coin, and fill in a trace table like the worked example.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use.

Steps.

  1. Run robot_loop.cpp from university/labs/F9-04. Check that it says "loop finished after 7 rounds".
  2. Move the flag to square 10 (line 6). Predict the number of rounds. Run and check.
  3. Move the flag to square 30. Predict where the robot stops, and why. Run and check.
  4. Change the robot to move 2 squares per round (line 19). Put the flag on square 5. Predict, then run. What goes wrong?
  5. Fix step 4's problem by changing the sense line to "at or past the flag": atGoal = (position >= goal);. Run again.

Expected observations. Step 2: 11 rounds. Step 3: the safety limit stops the robot on square 20 after 20 rounds. Step 4: the robot jumps from square 4 to 6, never stands exactly on 5, and runs until the safety limit. Step 5: it stops once it is at or past the flag.

Verification. Each prediction matches the last line of the log, or you can point to the round where your trace and the log first differ.

Troubleshooting.

  • Error about >= → a space between > and = → write them together.
  • The log is very long → the safety limit is working; read the last line first.
  • The program seems stuck → you removed line 13 → press Ctrl+C and put it back.

Extension. Add a second sensor: a wall at square 12. Make the loop also stop if the next square is the wall, and print which way out was used.

Forensic lab

Scenario. Tomasz built a robot for an empty room with a flag in the middle. Its only rule is: "if a wall is ahead, turn right; otherwise go forward". He pressed start and the robot "went on and on" until its safety limit stopped it. He saved the log.

Questions.

  1. Observation: list the squares the robot visited. Which steps repeat earlier steps?
  2. Draw the room (5 by 5) and the robot's path. What shape is it?
  3. Hypotheses: is the safety limit too small, or is the rule unable to reach the flag? How does the log decide between them?
  4. Root cause: why can this rule never reach column 2, row 2?
  5. Fix: suggest a different rule that would reach the flag, and how you would test it.

Method hints. Look for the first step whose square and direction exactly equal an earlier step's. From then on, a robot that follows a fixed rule must repeat itself forever. Ask: does the repeating path ever touch the flag?

Mini-project

Be the robot brain. With a friend, play "robot and brain". The brain writes a loop on a card: what to sense, what to decide, how to act, and two ways to stop. The robot follows it exactly across a room (slowly, clear floor, an adult nearby). Write a log of every round on paper.

Rubric. 2 points: the card has sense, think and act inside a loop. 1 point: two clear ways to stop, one of them a safety limit. 1 point: a written log of at least five rounds. 1 point: one bug you found and fixed by reading the log.

Summary

  • A robot's brain is a program; most of it is a loop of sense, think, act.
  • The loop repeats because the world changes after every action.
  • A condition (yes/no question) decides when the loop ends.
  • A safety limit gives a second way out, so a wrong rule cannot run forever.
  • A robot only knows what it sensed at the start of a round.
  • Logs show what happened in each round; repeating lines mean the robot is stuck in a cycle.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Sense, think, act.
  2. Because acting changes the world (the robot moves), so an old reading goes out of date; it must sense again to notice the change.
  3. When the flag is found (atGoal true), or when the safety limit of 20 rounds is reached.
  4. Because it senses at the start of each round. In round 6 it sensed on square 5, then moved to 6. Only at the start of round 7 does it sense square 6.
  5. "loop finished after 2 rounds". Rounds 1 and 2 move it to squares 1 and 2; then step < maxSteps is false. (If you said the flag was found: the robot never got there.)
  6. Good answers say: a real robot that never stops can crash, break things or hurt someone; a simulated one only wastes time. The limit makes a wrong rule end safely.
  7. Line 13 (step = step + 1;) — then the counter never grows. If the goal is also unreachable, the loop never ends. (Deleting line 7 would not compile, because line 12 uses maxSteps.)

Forensic lab answer key

Observation. Steps 21–24 repeat steps 1–4 exactly (column 1 to 4 along row 0, facing east). Step 20 turned the robot back to east at column 0, row 0, which is where it started. The path is a square around the edge of the room.

Root cause. The rule "wall ahead → turn right, else forward" only ever turns at walls, so the robot follows the walls forever. The flag at column 2, row 2 is not next to a wall, so the path never touches it. A bigger safety limit would only make the log longer.

Evidence. The repeat starting at step 21, and the fact that no logged square is column 2, row 2; the last line says "safety limit: stopped after 24 steps, flag not reached".

How the fault was made. The Lab Engineer wrote the wall-following rule for an empty room with the flag in the middle, and a safety limit of 24 steps, then ran it.

Fix. For example: "go forward 2 squares, turn right, go forward 2 squares" for this room; or a rule that senses the flag's direction. Test it in the simulator and check the log ends with "reached the flag".

Wrong answers and why. "The limit of 24 is too small": the path repeats from step 21 on, so no limit will help. "The robot is broken": every line is exactly what the rule says. Prevention: always keep a safety limit, and watch logs for repeats.

Story hook

Lucía has a new challenge: ride her bicycle along a chalk line in the playground. Her cousin Arjun watches.

On her first try, Lucía drifts a little to the right. She panics and yanks the handlebars hard to the left. Now she shoots over the line to the left side! She yanks hard to the right. Over the line again. Left, right, left, right: she zig-zags across the line, and almost falls off.

"Gently!" Arjun calls. "When you are a little off, steer a little. When you are far off, steer more."

On her second try, Lucía drifts right again. This time she steers back just a bit. She comes closer to the line, steers a bit less, closer still, a tiny bit less… and rolls smoothly along the chalk.

Notice what she did: she sensed how far off she was, compared it with where she wanted to be, and corrected by an amount that fit. Then again, and again. That loop is the heart of this chapter. Today you build it.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain a control loop as sense, compare, correct, again and again, using the bicycle picture.
  • Calculate by hand a few steps of a robot steering back to a line with the rule "steer = − gain × error".
  • Write (change) a C++ program that steers a simulated robot back to a line.
  • Read a text plot of a robot's distance from the line and recognise over-correction.
  • Fix a zig-zagging robot by choosing a gentler gain, and show the fix with a real run.
Jargon box
Control loop
Simple words: a loop that keeps checking how far you are from what you want, and corrects a bit each time. Analogy: riding a bicycle and correcting your balance. Precise: a feedback loop that repeatedly measures a system's output, compares it with a target, and computes a command that reduces the difference. D1
Feedback
Simple words: using what you just measured to decide your next action. Analogy: seeing that you drifted, and steering because of it. Precise: the use of a measured output of a system to influence its input; a loop with feedback is called closed loop, one without is open loop (taught in F9-16). D1
Target (setpoint)
Simple words: where you want to be. Analogy: right on the chalk line. Precise: the desired value of the controlled quantity; here, a distance from the line of zero. Engineers call it the setpoint. D1
Error (control)
Simple words: how far you are from where you want to be. Analogy: how far Lucía's wheel is from the chalk. Precise: the difference between the target and the measured value; in this chapter, the measured distance from the line (target zero), positive to the right and negative to the left. Not the same as a program "error" or bug (F0-08). D1
Gain
Simple words: a number that says how strongly to correct. Analogy: how hard Lucía turns the handlebars for each bit she is off. Precise: the constant that multiplies the error to produce the correction; in a proportional rule, correction = − gain × error. D1
Proportional correction
Simple words: a little off, steer a little; far off, steer a lot. Analogy: Arjun's advice, "gently". Precise: a control law in which the command is proportional to the error; it is the P of PID, taught fully in F9-17. D1
Over-correction
Simple words: correcting so hard that you shoot past the target to the other side. Analogy: Lucía yanking the handlebars and zig-zagging. Precise: a response that crosses the target (overshoot) because the correction is too large for the system; with this chapter's rule it happens when the gain is larger than 1. R3
Line follower
Simple words: a robot that drives along a line on the floor. Analogy: Lucía riding along the chalk. Precise: a mobile robot that uses one or more floor sensors to measure its position relative to a line and steers to stay on it. D2

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 is the control loop at kid level. It is a simpler version of the control-loop diagram that later courses use (the PID loop of RB202). Follow the arrows: sense, compare, correct, and back.

Figure 2 shows two real runs of our simulator, drawn as a graph: one with a gentle gain and one with a gain that is too strong.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

Think about riding a bicycle. You never sit perfectly still on it. You wobble a little, notice, and correct. Wobble, notice, correct. You do it so often that it feels like one smooth thing. Engineers call this a control loop.

A line-following robot does the same. Its sensor senses how far it is from the line. Its program compares that with where it wants to be: right on the line. The difference is called the error: "I am 8 units too far to the right." Then the robot corrects: it steers back toward the line.

But how hard should it steer? That is the whole secret of this chapter. The robot multiplies the error by a number called the gain. A small gain means "steer gently". A big gain means "steer hard".

The rule is: steer = − gain × error. The minus sign means "steer the opposite way to the error". If you are off to the right, steer left. If you are off to the left, steer right.

Try it with gain 0.5. You are 8 to the right. Steer = − 0.5 × 8 = − 4. So you move 4 to the left, and now you are 4 to the right. Next time: steer − 2, now you are 2 off. Then 1. Then a half. You glide smoothly onto the line, like Lucía's second try.

Now try gain 1.8. You are 8 to the right. Steer = − 1.8 × 8 = − 14.4. You move 14.4 to the left. But you were only 8 off! Now you are 6.4 to the left of the line. You over-corrected. Next round you steer hard right, and shoot over again. That is the zig-zag of Lucía's first try.

So the lesson is surprising: steering harder does not get you there faster. Too strong, and you zig-zag. Gentle is better here. Finding a good gain is called tuning, and you will do a lot of it.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

A control loop measures the output of a system, compares it with a target (engineers say setpoint), and computes a correction from the difference. Because the measurement is fed back into the decision, this is called feedback, or closed-loop control. D1

Our rule makes the correction proportional to the error: correction = − gain × error. This is proportional control, the P of the PID controller you will study in RB202. D1

Our simulator is deliberately simple. Each step, the robot moves sideways by exactly the steering amount. So the new distance is: new distance = distance − gain × distance = (1 − gain) × distance. You can check this against the printed numbers: with gain 0.5 the distance halves each step (8, 4, 2, 1 …); with gain 1.8 it is multiplied by −0.8 each step (8, −6.4, 5.12 …). R1 R2

That one number, (1 − gain), explains everything in our simulator. Listing 2 tries seven gains and shows it: R3

  • Gain between 0 and 1: (1 − gain) is between 0 and 1, so the distance shrinks without crossing the line (0 crossings for 0.2, 0.5 and 1.0). A smaller gain is slower: gain 0.2 is still 0.55 away after 12 steps.
  • Gain between 1 and 2: (1 − gain) is negative, so the robot crosses the line every step, but the swings shrink (12 crossings for 1.5 and 1.8).
  • Gain 2: the robot jumps from +8 to −8 and back forever (still 8.00 away after 12 steps).
  • Gain above 2: the swings grow. With gain 2.2 the robot is 71.33 away after 12 steps: it has driven off the course. Too much correction is worse than none.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious: why gain 1.0 is not "perfect" in real life. In our simple simulator, gain 1.0 lands exactly on the line in one step. Real robots are not that tidy. Their sensors report a little late, and their motors take time to respond. Listing 3 makes one small change: the robot steers using the reading from one step ago. Now gain 1.0 swings to ±8 forever (7 crossings in 20 steps), gain 0.5 crosses the line 5 times before settling, and only the gentler gain 0.25 approaches without crossing. R4 Control books explain that delays make feedback loops more likely to oscillate, which is one reason engineers tune gains carefully and test in simulation first. D1 Also, a real line-following robot does not slide sideways: it turns, and then drives at an angle, so its distance changes over several steps. RB202 models that properly.

Listing 3 — late_sensor.cpp (for the curious):

// F9-05 Listing 3 (for the curious): what if the sensor reading arrives one step late?
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    const std::vector<double> gains = {0.25, 0.5, 1.0};
    std::cout << "gain  crossings in 20 steps  distance after 20 steps\n";
    for (double gain : gains) {
        double previous = 8.0;   // the distance one step ago (what the sensor reports)
        double distance = 8.0;   // the distance now
        int crossings = 0;
        for (int step = 1; step <= 20; ++step) {
            double next = distance - gain * previous;   // correct using the OLD reading
            if ((distance >= 0 && next < 0) || (distance <= 0 && next > 0)) {
                crossings = crossings + 1;
            }
            previous = distance;
            distance = next;
        }
        std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << std::setw(4) << gain
                  << std::setw(14) << crossings << std::setw(25) << distance << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

gain  crossings in 20 steps  distance after 20 steps
0.25             0                     0.00
0.50             5                    -0.01
1.00             7                    -8.00

Real output, copied from university/labs/F9-05/late_sensor.out; run record late_sensor.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:26:13Z; exit code: 0.

Line 15 is the only real change from Listing 2's rule: it uses previous (the old reading) instead of distance. Lines 19–20 move "now" into "one step ago" before the next round.

How the hardware actually does it

A real line follower cannot measure "8 units right" directly with one light sensor; one sensor only says "line" or "floor" (F9-02). Real designs can use two or more light sensors side by side and work out from which ones see the line how far off the robot is; the program then sets the two wheel speeds differently to turn (F9-03). D2 The control loop is the same idea: measure the error, multiply by a gain, correct. A kit's sensor layout and the numbers it reports come from its own documentation, recorded in the dossier.

Worked example

Noor tests gain 1.8, starting 8 units to the right of the line. She fills in a table, rounding to two decimal places:

StepDistance (error)Steer = −1.8 × errorNew distanceSide of the line
08.00−14.408.00 − 14.40 = −6.40right → left (crossed)
1−6.40+11.52−6.40 + 11.52 = 5.12left → right (crossed)
25.12−9.225.12 − 9.22 = −4.10right → left (crossed)
3−4.10+7.38−4.10 + 7.38 = 3.28left → right (crossed)

Every step crosses the line. Each swing is 0.8 times the one before (6.40 ÷ 8.00 = 0.8; 5.12 ÷ 6.40 = 0.8). The program's own printout agrees: 8.00, −6.40, 5.12, −4.10, 3.28. R2 (The computer keeps more decimal places than Noor's table, so with longer tables the last digit can differ by 0.01.)

Now gain 0.5: steer = −0.5 × 8 = −4, new distance 4; then −2 → 2; then −1 → 1; then −0.5 → 0.5. It never crosses the line. The program prints 8.00, 4.00, 2.00, 1.00, 0.50. R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — steer.cpp: a robot steering back to the line with gain 0.5.

// F9-05 Listing 1: steering back to the line with a gentle correction.
#include <cmath>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>

int main()
{
    const double gain = 0.5;    // how strongly the robot corrects (try other values!)
    double distance = 8.0;      // start 8 units to the right of the line

    std::cout << "step  distance      -10.......0.......+10\n";
    for (int step = 0; step <= 12; ++step) {
        // Draw one row of the text plot: '|' is the line, '*' is the robot.
        std::string row(21, ' ');
        row[10] = '|';
        long column = 10 + std::lround(distance);
        if (column >= 0 && column <= 20) {
            row[static_cast<std::size_t>(column)] = '*';
        }
        std::cout << std::setw(4) << step << std::setw(10) << std::fixed
                  << std::setprecision(2) << distance << "      " << row << '\n';

        double error = distance;            // SENSE: how far from the line am I?
        double steer = -gain * error;       // COMPARE and decide: steer back, sized by gain
        distance = distance + steer;        // CORRECT: the move changes the distance
    }
    return 0;
}

// F9-05 Listing 2: try many gains and count the zig-zags.
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    const std::vector<double> gains = {0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2};
    std::cout << "gain  crossings  distance after 12 steps\n";
    for (double gain : gains) {
        double distance = 8.0;
        int crossings = 0;                       // times the robot jumped over the line
        for (int step = 1; step <= 12; ++step) {
            double next = distance - gain * distance;

                crossings = crossings + 1;
            }
            distance = next;
        }

                  << std::setw(11) << crossings << std::setw(16) << std::setprecision(2)
                  << distance << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Where the analogy breaks

  • Lucía corrects all the time; the program corrects in steps. A computer loop runs at separate moments and sees only what its sensor measured at that moment. Between steps it is blind. D1
  • Lucía's eyes see the line ahead; our sensor sees only "how far off now". A rider looks ahead and turns early for a bend. Our robot reacts only to the error it has already got. R1
  • Lucía learns; the gain stays fixed. After one zig-zag, Lucía steered more gently by herself. The robot will zig-zag forever with gain 1.8 until a person changes line 9. R2
  • Real robots have delays and limits. Our simulator moves the robot sideways instantly by exactly the steering amount. Real motors respond late and have a top speed, and Listing 3 shows that even a one-step delay changes which gains work. R4 D1

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: the robot zig-zags across the line. Cause: gain too strong (between 1 and 2 here). How to find it: in the text plot, the * jumps from one side of | to the other every step; the distances change sign. Fix: lower the gain. R2
  • Symptom: the robot flies off the course, further each step. Cause: gain above 2 in this simulator. How to find it: the distances grow; the * disappears from the plot. Fix: a much smaller gain. R3
  • Symptom: the robot drifts further away smoothly, never coming back. Cause: the minus sign was forgotten: steer = gain * error steers away from the line. How to find it: the distance grows without changing sign. Fix: put the minus sign back: steer opposite to the error.
  • Symptom: the robot takes very long to reach the line. Cause: gain too small (0.2 is still 0.55 away after 12 steps). How to find it: the distance shrinks only a little each step. Fix: raise the gain a little, and watch for crossings. R3
Transition box

Where you came from: F9-04 built a loop that senses and decides yes/no ("on the flag or not"). What carries over: the loop, the log, sensing at the start of each round. What changes: the decision is no longer yes/no: the robot measures how much it is off and corrects by an amount set by the gain, and a gain that is too strong makes things worse, not better. D1 R3 What comes next: F9-06 puts a robot in a bigger simulated world (a course with walls) and you program it from start to goal. Later, RB202 turns today's rule into a full PID controller.

Check yourself

  1. Name the three steps of a control loop in this chapter.
  2. The robot is 6 units to the left of the line (distance −6) and the gain is 0.5. What is the steer, and what is the new distance?
  3. Which gain gives a zig-zag in our simulator? (a) 0.3 (b) 0.8 (c) 1.6 (d) 1.0
  4. What does the minus sign in "steer = − gain × error" do?
  5. Explain in your own words why a stronger correction does not always bring the robot back faster.
  6. Apply it to a new case: a thermostat heats a room. The room is 3 degrees too cold. What is the "error", and what would "over-correction" look like?
  7. In the text plot, how can you see over-correction without reading the numbers?
  8. With a sensor that reports one step late (Listing 3), what happened with gain 1.0?

Lab

Goal. Tune the gain of a simulated line follower: find a gain that brings the robot back quickly without crossing the line.

Hardware and software needed. A computer with a C++ compiler, set up by an adult (this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). No hardware. A real line-following kit robot is optional and comes only after this lab passes, under the rules of F9-07.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use (simulator only).

Steps.

  1. Run steer.cpp from university/labs/F9-05. Check that the distance halves each step (8.00, 4.00, 2.00 …).
  2. Copy the table below into your notebook. For each gain, predict first: smooth, zig-zag shrinking, zig-zag forever, or flying off?
  3. Change line 9 to each gain, run, and write what really happened and the distance at step 12.
  4. Find the gain that is at the line (shows 0.00) soonest without ever crossing it.
  5. Change line 10 to start 5 units to the left (-5.0). Run with your best gain. Does it still work?
