R1 Your table should agree with the rule in Layer 2: gains below 1 approach smoothly, gains between 1 and 2 zig-zag with shrinking swings, gain 2 swings forever. In this ideal simulator, gain 1.0 lands in one step; Layer 3 explains why real robots need more care.

Verification. Run Listing 2 (gain_table.cpp) and compare its crossing counts with your observations for 0.2, 1.0 and 2.0.

Troubleshooting.

  • The plot shows no * on some rows → the robot is more than 10 units from the line, outside the plot → read the distance column.
  • Strange distances like -0.00 → a tiny negative number rounded to two decimals → it means "almost exactly on the line".
  • Build error near line 9 → a comma instead of a decimal point (0,7) → C++ needs 0.7.

Extension. Add a steady "wind" that pushes the robot 1 unit right every step: change line 26 to distance = distance + steer + 1.0;. With gain 0.5, where does the robot settle? Why does it not reach 0? (This "stuck a bit off" behaviour is what the I in PID fixes, in F9-18.)

Questions.

  1. Observation: in the team's plot, on which side of the line is the robot at each step? How many times does it cross the line in 12 steps?
  2. Measure: divide each distance by the one before (for steps 1, 2 and 3). What number do you get each time, and what does its sign mean?
  3. Hypotheses: list two possible causes of zig-zagging (for example a noisy sensor, or too strong a correction). Which evidence rules one of them out?
  4. Root cause: explain, using "steer = − gain × error", why gain 1.8 over-corrects.
  5. Fix and verification: which gain would you choose, and which numbers in the second plot prove that it works?
  6. Prevention: what test should the team run before every race?

Method hints. Look at the sign of the distance in each row: + means right of the line, − means left. A healthy loop's error gets smaller without flipping sign. Then use the rule from Layer 2: the new distance is (1 − gain) times the old one.

Mini-project

Explain it to a friend. This is the start of the course project. Make a one-page explanation, for a friend who has never programmed, of how your simulated line follower steers back to the line. Include: Figure 1 redrawn in your own words, one gentle run and one zig-zag run (copied from your real runs), and a sentence about how you chose your gain.

Rubric. 2 points: sense, compare and correct each explained with the bicycle picture. 1 point: real runs included and labelled with the gain used. 1 point: the friend can say why "steer harder" can be worse (ask them!). 1 point: one honest limit of the simulator mentioned.

Summary

  • A control loop senses, compares with a target, corrects, and repeats.
  • The error is how far off you are; here it is the distance from the line.
  • Proportional correction: steer = − gain × error. The minus sign steers back toward the line.
  • In our simulator, the new distance is (1 − gain) times the old one.
  • Gentle gains (below 1) approach smoothly; gains between 1 and 2 zig-zag; above 2 the robot flies off.
  • Over-correction shows in a plot as the robot crossing the line at every step.
  • Delays in real robots make strong gains even riskier: tune in a simulator first.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Sense (measure how far off), compare (with the target, to get the error), correct (steer by gain × error). Then repeat.
  2. Steer = −0.5 × (−6) = +3, so it moves 3 to the right: new distance −6 + 3 = −3 (3 units left of the line).
  3. (c) 1.6, because it is between 1 and 2. 0.3 and 0.8 approach smoothly; 1.0 lands exactly in our ideal simulator.
  4. It makes the robot steer the opposite way to its error: off to the right → steer left. Without it the robot steers away from the line.
  5. Good answers say: if the correction is bigger than the error, the robot passes the line and ends up off on the other side, then corrects hard again, and zig-zags; with gain above 2 the swings even grow.
  6. The error is "3 degrees too cold". Over-correction: the heater heats so hard that the room becomes too warm, then it switches off and the room becomes too cold again, swinging up and down.
  7. The * jumps from one side of the | to the other on every row.
  8. It swung to ±8 forever: 7 crossings in 20 steps and still −8.00 away at the end (R4).

Forensic lab answer key

Observation. The robot's distance changes sign at every step: 8.00, −6.40, 5.12, −4.10, 3.28, −2.62, 2.10, −1.68, 1.34, −1.07, 0.86, −0.69, 0.55. It crosses the line 12 times in 12 steps and is still 0.55 away at step 12.

Measure. −6.40 ÷ 8.00 = −0.8; 5.12 ÷ −6.40 = −0.8; −4.10 ÷ 5.12 ≈ −0.8. The size 0.8 means each swing is a bit smaller; the minus sign means the robot ends up on the other side each time.

Root cause. The gain 1.8 is too strong. With steer = −1.8 × error, the robot moves 1.8 times as far as it is off, so it overshoots by 0.8 times the error: new distance = (1 − 1.8) × old = −0.8 × old. A noisy sensor is ruled out: the swings are perfectly regular (exactly −0.8 each time), and this simulator has no noise.

Fix and verification. Make the correction gentler: gain 0.5 (or anything below 1 here). The second plot proves it: 8.00, 4.00, 2.00, 1.00, 0.50 … never changes sign and shows 0.00 from step 11.

How the fault was made. The Lab Engineer copied Listing 1 and changed only line 9 (gain 0.5 → 1.8) and the comment on line 1, then ran both with run_lab.sh.

Wrong answers and why. "The robot needs a bigger gain to settle faster": a bigger gain makes it worse, and above 2 it flies off (R3). "The start position is wrong": the gentle run starts at the same 8.00. Prevention: before every race, run the gain on the plot and check that the distance does not change sign; keep the gain table (Listing 2) as a test.

Story hook

Before Mei rides her bicycle to the new library for the first time, she and her aunt sit at the kitchen table with a paper map. Mei traces the route with her finger. "Along this street, turn right at the bakery, then left at the park…"

Her finger hits a dead end. "Oops! There's no road there." She laughs, goes back, and tries another turn. Nobody fell off a bicycle. Nobody got lost. The mistake cost two seconds.

On the real ride the next day, Mei knows the way. At one corner she almost turns the wrong way, but she remembers the dead end from the map, and goes the right way.

Practising on a map is cheap and safe. Robot engineers have a map like that too: a simulator. Today you program a robot through a whole course, in a simulator, and learn to fix its mistakes before any real wheel turns.

What you will be able to do

  • Explain what a robot simulator is and why robots are tested in one first.
  • Program a simulated robot through a course using the commands F, L and R.
  • Predict the robot's position and direction after a list of commands.
  • Read the simulator's printed map and result line to find where a program went wrong.
  • Diagnose a robot that bumps into a wall because of a left/right mix-up.
Jargon box
Grid world
Simple words: a pretend world made of squares, like a board game. Analogy: Mei's paper map with streets. Precise: a simulated environment divided into cells; each cell is free or blocked, and the robot moves from cell to cell. D3 R1
Command
Simple words: one instruction for the robot, like "go forward one square". Analogy: "turn right at the bakery". Precise: in this chapter's simulator, one character: F moves forward one cell, L turns 90 degrees left, R turns 90 degrees right, on the spot. R1
Heading
Simple words: the direction the robot is facing. Analogy: which way your bicycle's front wheel points. Precise: the robot's orientation; in the grid world one of east, south, west or north. "Left" and "right" are measured from the robot's own heading, not from the map. D2
Test run
Simple words: trying the program to see if it does what you wanted. Analogy: tracing the route on the map with your finger. Precise: an execution of a program with known inputs whose output is compared with the expected result. R1
Simulator
Defined in F9-01: a program that pretends to be the robot and its world. R1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the course. The robot starts on S, facing east (to the right of the map). The goal is G. Shaded squares marked # are walls. The thick line shows one route that works.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A simulator is a program that pretends to be a robot and its world. Our simulator's world is a grid world: a board of squares. Some squares are floor. Some are walls. One is the start, S. One is the goal, G.

You program the robot with three commands. F means "forward one square". L means "turn left on the spot". R means "turn right on the spot". You write them in a row, like FFRFF, and the simulator follows them one by one.

The tricky part is left and right. They are the robot's left and right, not yours. Imagine sitting on the robot. If the robot faces down the map (south), its right hand points to the left of the map (west)! Mei had the same problem with her paper map when she turned it upside down.

The robot also senses. Before each step forward, it looks at the square in front. If it is a wall, the robot stops and reports a BUMP. In a real robot that would be a crash, so the simulator stops there and tells you exactly where it happened.

After the run, the simulator prints the map with your robot's path marked by stars (*). It also prints where the robot ended, which way it faced, and what happened: reached the goal, bumped, or ran out of commands.

Why bother with a simulator? Because mistakes are free in it. A real robot that bumps can break, or bump into a person. In the simulator you change a letter and try again. That is why every robot lab in this university starts in a simulator, and moves to a real robot only after the simulator lab passes (F9-07).

Layer 2 — the student explanation

Our simulator keeps the robot's state in three numbers: its row, its column and its heading (0 = east, 1 = south, 2 = west, 3 = north). A right turn adds 1 to the heading, and a left turn adds 3; the remainder after dividing by 4 keeps the heading between 0 and 3. R1

Turning right four times brings you back to where you started facing, and so does turning left four times. A left turn is the same as three right turns, which is why line 34 adds 3. R1

A forward command first senses the cell ahead, using two small tables of moves (one for rows, one for columns) indexed by the heading. If the cell is a wall, the run ends with a BUMP report; if it is the goal, the run ends with GOAL. R1

Notice what kind of program you write here: a fixed list of commands that never looks at the sensors to change its plan. Engineers call such a plan open loop: it works only if the world is exactly as you expected. D1 The robot of F9-04 and the line follower of F9-05 instead decided every round from what they sensed. Real robots combine both: a plan, and a control loop that corrects as they go. D2

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Professional robot simulators model much more than squares: masses, friction, motors, sensors with noise, cameras, even light and shadows. They let engineers test the same program that will later run on the real robot. But every simulator is a model, and models leave things out. A program that works in simulation can still fail on hardware, which is why engineers test in simulation first and then carefully on the real machine. Later courses (RB303, RB401) use a full robot simulator, named and recorded in their dossiers. D2 S1

How the hardware actually does it

A real robot has no "squares". To move "forward one square" it would run both wheel motors until the encoders have counted the right number of turns (F9-03); to turn on the spot it would run one wheel forward and one backward. Because wheels slip and motors differ, a real robot drifts from its plan, and it needs sensors and control loops to correct (F9-05). D2

Worked example

Trace the start of the working route by hand. The robot is on S (row 1, column 1), facing east.

CommandHeading afterSquare after (row, column)Why
Feast1, 2East adds 1 to the column.
Feast1, 3Column 4 is a wall, so stop going east.
Rsouth1, 3Right of east is south. Turning does not move.
F Fsouth3, 3South adds 1 to the row, twice.
Rwest3, 3Right of south is west.
F Fwest3, 1West takes 1 from the column, twice.
Lsouth3, 1Left of west is south. (Sit on the robot facing west: your left hand points down the map.)
F Fsouth5, 1Down to the bottom row.

Continue: L (east), FFFF to (5, 5), L (north), FFFF to (1, 5), R (east), FF to (1, 7), R (south), FFFF to (5, 7), which is G. The whole program is FFRFFRFFLFFLFFFFLFFFFRFFRFFFF: 29 commands. The simulator agrees: "GOAL reached at step 29". R1

Listing 2 — grid_world.hpp: the simulator itself. You do not need to understand every detail yet; the table groups lines by job.

// F9-06 Listing 2: the university's tiny grid-world robot simulator.
#pragma once
#include <array>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

// Runs one robot program on the course and prints what happens.
// Commands: F = forward one square, L = turn left, R = turn right.
inline void runCourse(const std::string& commands)
{
    std::vector<std::string> map = {
        "#########",
        "#S..#...#",
        "###.#.#.#",
        "#...#.#.#",
        "#.###.#.#",
        "#.....#G#",
        "#########",
    };
    const std::array<int, 4> moveColumn = {1, 0, -1, 0};   // east, south, west, north
    const std::array<int, 4> moveRow = {0, 1, 0, -1};
    const std::array<std::string, 4> name = {"east", "south", "west", "north"};

    int row = 1;
    int column = 1;
    int facing = 0;                       // the robot starts facing east
    int step = 0;
    std::string result = "program ended before the goal";

    for (char command : commands) {
        step = step + 1;
        if (command == 'L') {
            facing = (facing + 3) % 4;    // turning left = three right turns
        } else if (command == 'R') {
            facing = (facing + 1) % 4;
        } else if (command == 'F') {
            int nextRow = row + moveRow[facing];
            int nextColumn = column + moveColumn[facing];
            char ahead = map[nextRow][nextColumn];   // SENSE: what is in front?
            if (ahead == '#') {
                result = "BUMP at step " + std::to_string(step) + ": wall ahead at row " +
                         std::to_string(nextRow) + ", column " + std::to_string(nextColumn) +
                         " while facing " + name[facing];
                break;
            }
            row = nextRow;
            column = nextColumn;
            if (ahead == 'G') {
                result = "GOAL reached at step " + std::to_string(step);
                break;
            }
            map[row][column] = '*';       // mark the path
        } else {
            result = "unknown command '" + std::string(1, command) + "' at step " +
                     std::to_string(step);
            break;
        }
    }
    std::cout << "program: " << commands << '\n';
    for (const std::string& line : map) {
        std::cout << "  " << line << '\n';
    }
    std::cout << "robot at row " << row << ", column " << column << ", facing "
              << name[facing] << '\n';
    std::cout << result << "\n\n";
}
LinesCodeWhat it doesWhy it matters
1–7comment, #pragma once, includes#pragma once makes sure the file is pasted in only once.Standard header setup.
8–11inline void runCourse(const std::string& commands)Starts the simulator recipe; it receives one robot program.inline allows the recipe to live in a header used by several programs.
12–20std::vector<std::string> map = {…};The course: seven rows of text. # wall, . floor, S start, G goal.Change these rows to make a new course.
21–23moveColumn, moveRow, nameFor each heading (east, south, west, north): how the column and row change, and its name.One table instead of four ifs.
24–29int row = 1; … std::string result = …;The robot's state: on S, facing east, no steps yet, result not decided.The simulator's "memory".
31–32for (char command : commands) { step = step + 1;Goes through the commands one by one and counts them.Step numbers in the result line.
33–36if (command == 'L') … 'R'Turns: left adds 3, right adds 1, then % 4 keeps 0–3.Turning on the spot.
37–40else if (command == 'F') … char ahead = map[nextRow][nextColumn];Works out the square in front and looks at it.Sense before moving.
41–46if (ahead == '#') { … break; }A wall ahead: write the BUMP report and stop the run.A crash in real life; a message here.
47–52row = nextRow; … if (ahead == 'G') { … break; }Move; if this is the goal, report GOAL and stop.Act, then check success.
53map[row][column] = '*';Marks the path on the map.So you can see the route afterwards.
54–58else { result = "unknown command …"; break; }Any other letter stops the run with a message.A typo (like f or a space) is reported, not ignored.
60–67std::cout << …Prints the program, the map with the path, the final position and heading, and the result.The evidence you read.

Where the analogy breaks

  • The simulator's world is perfect; the real world is not. On a paper map, a street is exactly where it is drawn. In our grid, "forward" always moves exactly one square. A real robot's wheels slip and its motors differ, so it ends up slightly off, and the errors add up. D2
  • Mei could adapt on the ride; our command list cannot. Mei changed her mind at a corner. A fixed list of commands does not look at the sensors to change its plan; if one wall moves, the program bumps. D1 R2
  • A simulator only contains what someone put in it. Our simulator has no people, no pets, no slopes and no battery. Passing in it shows that your logic is right, not that a real robot will be safe. That is why real-robot labs still need the safety rules of F9-07. S1

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: "BUMP" right after a turn. Cause: left and right mixed up, thinking of the map's left instead of the robot's left. How to find it: read the heading in the result line ("while facing north") and compare with the heading you wanted. Fix: sit on the robot in your mind (or turn the paper) at each turn. See the forensic lab. R2
  • Symptom: "BUMP" after a straight run. Cause: one F too many. How to find it: count the free squares in Figure 1 before the wall. Fix: remove one F. The first program in grid_sim.in is an example. R1
  • Symptom: "program ended before the goal". Cause: the program is too short. How to find it: look at where the stars end on the map. Fix: add the missing commands from there.
  • Symptom: "unknown command". Cause: a small letter (f), a space or another character in the line. How to find it: the message names the character and the step. Fix: use only capital F, L and R, with no spaces.
Transition box

Where you came from: F9-04 ran a robot loop in a corridor and a room; F9-05 steered back to a line in a one-dimensional simulator. What carries over: exact commands, sensing before acting, reading logs, safety stops. What changes: the world now has two dimensions and walls, the robot has a heading, and left and right depend on which way it faces; you test whole programs, not single rules. R1 What comes next: F9-07 covers what must be true before any program leaves the simulator and drives a real robot: robot safety.

Check yourself

  1. What do the commands F, L and R do?
  2. The robot faces south. You send R. Which way does it face now?
  3. The robot faces north. You send L L (two left turns). Which way does it face?
  4. Why is it safer to test a robot program in a simulator first?
  5. Explain in your own words why "turn right" on the map and "turn right" for the robot can be different.
  6. Apply it to a new case: on the course of Figure 1, which command list takes the robot from S to the square at row 3, column 1?
  7. What is the difference between a fixed list of commands and the line follower of F9-05?

Lab

Goal. Program the simulated robot from S to G on the course, and on a course you design yourself. (This is also the practical exam task of RB101: program the simulated robot through a course.)

Hardware and software needed. A computer with a C++ compiler, set up by an adult (this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0). Files: grid_sim.cpp, grid_world.hpp, grid_sim.in in university/labs/F9-06.

Safety. None beyond normal computer use (simulator only).

Steps.

  1. Run the simulator with the given input (run_lab.sh university/labs/F9-06, or run ./grid_sim < grid_sim.in after building). You should see a BUMP for FFFF and GOAL for the long program.
  2. Cover the worked example. Using only Figure 1, write the whole program from S to G yourself. Is there any other route through this maze? Look carefully, and explain your answer.
  3. Write your program as a new line at the end of grid_sim.in. Before running, trace it on paper with a coin and a pencil arrow for the heading.
  4. Run and compare the printed map with your paper trace.
  5. Design your own course: change the rows in grid_world.hpp (keep every row the same length and keep a wall all around). Write a program that solves it, and give it to a friend to solve too.

Expected observations. Step 1 matches the output in the code walk-through. R1 In step 4 the stars on the printed map follow your paper trace exactly; if not, the first difference shows your mistake.

Verification. The result line of your program says "GOAL reached at step N", and N equals the number of letters in your program.

Troubleshooting.

  • A result with "program: " and nothing after it → an empty line in grid_sim.in → remove empty lines.
  • Strange results or a sanitizer error message after editing the map → a row is shorter than the others or the outer wall has a gap, so the robot looked outside the map → make all rows the same length with # all around.
  • "unknown command" → a space or small letter → see Common mistakes.

Extension. Write a program for a sensing robot: change runCourse so that F on a wall turns right instead of bumping. Can that rule solve the course without any R or L? Compare with the forensic lab of F9-04.

Forensic lab

Scenario. Sami copied the working route from a friend, but typed one letter from memory. "The robot crashed into a wall in the middle of the maze!" Sami says. You get the simulator's printout and nothing else.

Evidence pack. The printout of a real run of Sami's program (mixup.cpp, which runs Sami's command list on the same course) in this build: R2

program: FFRFFRFFRFFLFFFFLFFFFRFFRFFFF
  #########
  #S**#...#
  ###*#.#.#
  #***#.#.#
  #.###.#.#
  #.....#G#
  #########
robot at row 3, column 1, facing north
BUMP at step 10: wall ahead at row 2, column 1 while facing north

Real output, copied from university/labs/F9-06/mixup.out; run record mixup.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:26:16Z; exit code: 0.

Questions.

  1. Observation: at which step did the robot bump? Where was it, and which way was it facing?
  2. Compare Sami's program with the working one (in the worked example) letter by letter. Where is the first difference?
  3. Hypotheses: was it one F too many, or a wrong turn? Which line of the printout decides?
  4. Root cause: which way should the robot have faced at that moment, and which turn gives that?
  5. Fix and prevention: correct Sami's program, and suggest a habit that prevents left/right mix-ups.

Method hints. The printout tells you the step number of the bump. Count that many letters into Sami's program. Then sit on the robot: which way is it facing just before the last turn?

Mini-project

Maze for a friend. Design a course of at least 7 by 9 squares with at least four turns needed. Solve it in the simulator. Then give the map (not the solution) to a friend, and watch them solve it. Write down every bump they get and why.

Rubric. 2 points: a valid map that the simulator runs, with your own working program. 1 point: at least four turns needed. 1 point: a written list of your friend's bumps and their causes. 1 point: one improvement to your map or instructions after watching.

Summary

  • A simulator is a program that pretends to be the robot and its world; mistakes in it cost nothing.
  • Our grid world uses three commands: F (forward), L and R (turn on the spot).
  • Left and right are the robot's, measured from its heading, not from the map.
  • The simulator senses the square ahead before moving and reports a BUMP instead of crashing.
  • The printed map, final position, heading and result line are your evidence.
  • A fixed command list is open loop: it works only if the world is exactly as expected.
  • Every robot lab starts in a simulator; real robots come after it passes.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. F moves forward one square in the direction the robot faces; L turns it left on the spot; R turns it right on the spot.
  2. West. (Sit on the robot facing down the map: your right hand points to the map's left.)
  3. South: two left turns make a half turn.
  4. Mistakes cost nothing: no broken robot, nobody hurt, and you can repeat the run exactly to find the bug.
  5. Good answers say: "right" depends on which way you face. The map is always seen from above with north at the top, but the robot turns with its own heading; when it faces south, its right is the map's west.
  6. FFRFFRFF: east to (1, 3), turn to south, down to (3, 3), turn to west, along to (3, 1).
  7. The command list never changes its plan from what it senses (open loop); the line follower measured its error every step and corrected (feedback).

Forensic lab answer key

Observation. The run ended with "BUMP at step 10: wall ahead at row 2, column 1 while facing north". The robot stood at row 3, column 1.

First difference. Sami: FFRFFRFFRFF…; working route: FFRFFRFFLFF…. The 9th letter differs.

Root cause. At (3, 1) the robot faces west. The route continues down the map (south). Left of west is south, so the turn must be L. Sami's R turned it to north, toward the wall at (2, 1), and the next F (step 10) bumped. The printout's "while facing north" proves a wrong turn rather than an extra F: an extra F would have bumped while still facing west.

How the fault was made. The Lab Engineer changed the 9th command of the working program from L to R and ran it through the same simulator (mixup.cpp).

Fix. FFRFFRFFLFFLFFFFLFFFFRFFRFFFF; verify that the run says "GOAL reached at step 29". Prevention: at every turn, write the heading before and after next to the program, or turn the paper map so the robot's heading points up.

Story hook

Ravi is finally allowed to ride his bicycle to the park on his own. Before he goes, his grandmother asks him the same questions as always.

"Brakes?" Ravi squeezes them: they work. "Helmet?" On his head. "Where will you ride?" On the path, not the road. "How fast?" Slowly near the playground, where small children run around.

Ravi rolls his eyes a little. He knows all this! But on the way, a ball bounces onto the path, and a little boy runs after it. Ravi squeezes the brakes, stops in time, and smiles at the boy.

That evening he tells his grandmother. She nods. "Checking the brakes is boring," she says, "until the day you need them."

Robots are the same. Before a real robot moves, someone checks the stop, the space, the speed and the battery. Every time. This chapter is about those boring, important checks.

What you will be able to do

  • Follow this university's robot safety rules: simulator first, adult supervision, clear zone, emergency stop within reach, speed limit, battery rules.
  • Explain why each rule exists, using the bicycle picture.
  • Program a speed limit and a latched emergency stop into a simulated robot's loop.
  • Diagnose a robot that kept moving after the stop was pressed, from its log.
  • Prepare a safety checklist for an optional, supervised kit-robot session.
Safety

The robot safety rules of this university (F9). (1) Simulator first, always. A real robot runs a program only after that program's simulator lab has passed. (2) Adult supervision for every real-robot activity of learners below level L3, which includes everyone in this course. (3) A clear zone around the robot: no people, pets or loose objects inside while it can move. (4) An emergency stop within reach of the supervising adult, tested before every session; it must be a physical switch that does not depend on the robot's program. (5) Speed limits configured in the program before the first run, starting at the lowest useful speed. (6) Battery rules: only battery-powered kits designed for children of the learner's age; no LiPo batteries and no mains electricity in this course; follow the kit maker's instructions for charging, storing and disposing of batteries. Moving parts can pinch fingers, and motors can start unexpectedly: keep fingers away from wheels whenever the robot is switched on. S1

Jargon box
Emergency stop
Simple words: a big, easy button or switch that makes the robot stop at once. Analogy: the brakes on your bicycle. Precise: a stop control that removes the power to the robot's motors (or otherwise forces them to stop) immediately and stays active until a person deliberately resets it; in this university it must be a physical switch that does not rely on the robot's program. S1
Latched
Simple words: once switched on, it stays on until someone switches it off on purpose. Analogy: a door that locks when it shuts, and needs a key to open. Precise: a state that, once set by an event, remains set after the event ends, until an explicit reset. R1
Speed limit
Simple words: the fastest the robot is allowed to go, whatever its program asks for. Analogy: riding slowly near the playground. Precise: an upper bound applied to every motor command before it is sent, so that no part of the program can command a faster speed. R1 S1
Clear zone
Simple words: an empty space around the robot that people stay out of while it can move. Analogy: the path being clear before you ride fast. Precise: a marked area around a robot that is kept free of people, animals and objects whenever the robot is powered and able to move. S1
Supervision
Simple words: a grown-up who watches, helps and can stop everything. Analogy: Amara's uncle walking next to her bicycle. Precise: the continuous presence of a responsible adult who has read the kit's instructions and controls the emergency stop during a real-robot activity. S1

The idea in pictures

Figure 1 shows the path from a program to a moving real robot. Every gate must be passed in order. On the right is the clear zone seen from above.

Layer 1 — the kid explanation

A real robot is a machine with motors. Motors can pinch fingers. A robot can drive off a table, or into a person's foot. Robots do not know they are hurting anyone. So people must keep things safe.

The first rule is simulator first. You already did this in F9-05 and F9-06. If a program bumps or zig-zags in the simulator, it will surely misbehave on a real robot too. Fix it where mistakes are free.

The second rule: a grown-up is always there when a real robot moves. Like Amara's uncle walking next to her bicycle. The grown-up has read the kit's instructions and can stop everything.

The third rule: a clear zone. Before the robot moves, clear a space on the floor. Mark it with tape if you can. Nobody stands inside it while the robot is switched on. No toys, no pets, no feet.

The fourth rule: an emergency stop within reach. It is like your bicycle's brakes. It must stop the robot at once, and stay stopped until someone resets it on purpose. You test it before every session, as Ravi squeezed his brakes.

The fifth rule: a speed limit. Your program might ask for "speed 9" by mistake. The speed limit says: never more than 5, whatever happens. Start slow. You can always go faster later.

The sixth rule is about batteries. Use only kits made for children your age, with the batteries the kit maker says. No big rechargeable batteries of the kind used in drones (LiPo), and never anything plugged into the wall socket. Charge and store batteries exactly as the kit's instructions say.

These rules can feel boring. But remember Ravi's grandmother: checking the brakes is boring until the day you need them.

Layer 2 — the student explanation

This university's rules for every robot lab are: simulator first; real-robot labs only after the simulator lab passes; an emergency stop within reach; a clear zone; speed limits configured; adult supervision for learners below L3; and the battery rules of the safety section (for this course: kits designed for children, no LiPo, no mains). S1

Two of these rules can also be built into the program, and Listing 1 shows how. The speed limit clamps every command: std::min(wanted, speedLimit) picks the smaller of the two, so a mistaken "9" becomes "5". The stop is latched: once set, nothing in the loop clears it, and it overrides every other decision. R1

The order inside the loop matters. Listing 1 checks the stop at the start of every round, before computing the speed, so the robot stops in the same round the stop is pressed. A program that checks the stop only now and then keeps driving in between, as the forensic lab shows. R2

A software stop is not enough on its own. If the program itself has a bug, or the computer freezes, a software check may never run. That is why this university requires a physical kill switch for real robots: a switch that cuts motor power without asking the program. S1 The software stop in Listing 1 is an extra layer, not a replacement.

Layer 3 — the engineer's depth

Note

For the curious. Engineers who build robots for factories and homes follow written safety standards and do a careful study of what could go wrong (called a hazard analysis) before a robot is used. They design several independent layers of protection, so that one failure is not enough to hurt someone. The F11 faculty of this university teaches safety-critical engineering in depth; the exact standards are named in its dossiers, not here. S1

How the hardware actually does it

On a real kit, the safest stop is the simplest: a switch between the battery and the motors. When it is off, the motors get no power, whatever the program does. On a kit, a speed limit can be set in the program as a maximum motor command, like Listing 1. D4 S1 Which switch your kit has, and how its batteries must be charged and stored, comes only from the kit maker's instructions and datasheets, recorded in the dossier.

Worked example

Ines tests Listing 1's speed limit and stop by hand. The plan wants speeds 2, 4, 9, 9, 9, 9 … The limit is 5. The stop is pressed at step 6.

  1. Steps 1–2: wanted 2 and 4, both below 5, so allowed 2 and 4. Position: 2, then 2 + 4 = 6.
  2. Steps 3–5: wanted 9, but the limit allows only 5. Position: 6 + 5 = 11, 16, 21.
  3. Step 6: the stop is pressed. Speed 0. Position stays 21.
  4. Steps 7–10: the stop is latched, so speed stays 0. Position stays 21.

Without the speed limit, steps 3–5 would have moved 9 + 9 + 9 = 27 instead of 5 + 5 + 5 = 15: 12 units further, at nearly double speed. The program's log matches Ines's table exactly. R1

Code walk-through

Listing 1 — safe_drive.cpp: a speed limit and a latched emergency stop inside the loop.

// F9-07 Listing 1: a speed limit and an emergency stop in the robot's loop.
#include <algorithm>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main()
{
    const int speedLimit = 5;   // the fastest this robot is allowed to go (simulator units)
    // What the robot's plan asks for at each step:
    const std::vector<int> wanted = {2, 4, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9};
    const int stopPressedAt = 6;   // in this test, someone presses the stop at step 6
    bool stopped = false;
    int position = 0;

    std::cout << "step  wanted  allowed  stop?  position\n";
    for (int step = 1; step <= 10; ++step) {
        if (step == stopPressedAt) {
            stopped = true;                        // the stop is latched: it stays on
        }
        int speed = std::min(wanted[step - 1], speedLimit);   // obey the speed limit
        if (stopped) {
            speed = 0;                             // the stop beats everything else
        }
        position = position + speed;
        std::cout << std::setw(4) << step << std::setw(8) << wanted[step - 1]
                  << std::setw(9) << speed << std::setw(7) << (stopped ? "yes" : "no")
                  << std::setw(10) << position << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}

Build command (the one actually used): g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -g -fsanitize=address,undefined safe_drive.cpp -o safe_drive, toolchain g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0.

Where the analogy breaks

  • Ravi sees the ball; a robot may not. Ravi braked because he saw the boy. A simple robot has no sensor for people at all. That is why a human, not the robot, holds the emergency stop. S1
  • Bicycle brakes need a hand; a robot's software stop needs working software. If the program has a bug or freezes, a stop that lives in the program may never run. A real robot needs a physical switch that cuts motor power, which does not depend on the program. S1 R2
  • A bicycle slows when you stop pedalling; a robot does not get tired. A robot keeps doing exactly what its program says, at full power, until something stops it. S1

Common mistakes and debugging

  • Symptom: the robot keeps moving for a while after the stop is pressed. Cause: the program checks the stop only now and then. How to find it: in the log, find rounds where the button is down but the robot still moves. Fix: check the stop at the start of every round, and keep a physical switch as well. See the forensic lab. R2
  • Symptom: the robot starts moving again by itself after a stop. Cause: the stop is not latched: it was set back to "not stopped" when the button was released. How to find it: the log shows stop? yes followed later by no without a reset. Fix: only a deliberate reset may clear the stop.
  • Symptom: the robot drives faster than the limit. Cause: one part of the program sends commands without going through the limit. How to find it: compare the "allowed" column with the limit. Fix: apply the limit in one place, right before every command goes to the motors.
  • Symptom: during a real session, the emergency stop does nothing. Cause: it was not tested before the session. How to find it: rule 4: test it first. Fix: stop the session, switch off with the main switch, and let the adult check the kit against its instructions before anyone continues.
Transition box

Where you came from: F9-06 ran robots only in simulators, where a bump costs nothing. What carries over: loops, logs, testing before trusting, and the safety limit idea of F9-04. What changes: on a real robot, mistakes can hurt people and break things, so safety comes before everything: a physical stop, a clear zone, a speed limit, an adult, and safe batteries, checked every time. S1 What comes next: this is the last chapter of RB101. Next comes the course project. Then RB202 turns your steering rule into a full PID controller, ending with supervised motor control on a real kit in F9-22, under these same rules.

Check yourself

  1. Name the six robot safety rules of this course.
  2. Why must the emergency stop be a physical switch, and not only a check in the program?
  3. What does "latched" mean for an emergency stop?
  4. The plan wants speed 8 and the limit is 3. What speed does Listing 1 allow?
  5. Explain in your own words why we run the simulator lab before the real robot.
  6. Apply it to a new case: your friend wants to show a robot on the kitchen table at a family party. Which rules are broken, and what should you do instead?
  7. Which batteries are allowed in this course? (a) LiPo packs from a drone (b) whatever fits (c) the batteries the kit maker says, in a kit designed for children (d) a power adapter plugged into the wall

Lab

Goal. Test a speed limit and a latched stop in the simulator; then, optionally and only under supervision, prepare and run a first real-robot session.

Part A — simulator (required).

Hardware and software needed. A computer with a C++ compiler, set up by an adult (this build: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0).

Safety. None beyond normal computer use.

Steps.

  1. Run safe_drive.cpp from university/labs/F9-07. Check: the "allowed" column never goes above 5, and from step 6 the speed is 0.
  2. Change the stop to step 3 (line 12). Predict the final position, run and check.
  3. Change the limit to 3 (line 9). Predict the position at step 5, run and check.
  4. Make a deliberate mistake: delete the if (stopped) block (lines 22–24). Run. What does the log show? Then put it back and run again.

Expected observations. The original run matches the output above (final position 21). R1 Stop at step 3: the robot moves only in steps 1 and 2, final position 6. Limit 3 (stop still at step 6): positions 2, 5, 8, 11, 14 at step 5. Without lines 22–24, the "stop?" column says yes but the robot keeps moving: a stop that is noticed but not obeyed.

Verification. All predictions match, and the restored program gives exactly the original output.

Troubleshooting.

  • Error about std::min → #include <algorithm> was removed → put line 2 back.
  • Build error after step 4 → a brace was removed with the block, or left behind → delete exactly lines 22–24, all three.
  • Strange speeds after changing line 11 → the list must still have ten numbers.

Part B — optional supervised kit robot.

Not verified — check before relying on this

Untested on hardware (AH-26). This part was not run on any real robot during this build: no kit was available, and this chapter names no kit. What is untested: every step below on real hardware. What would be needed: the kit chosen by the owner, its manufacturer's instructions and datasheets (motor, battery, charger, switch) recorded in the RB101 dossier, and a supervised trial run by an adult following this checklist, with the result written into the QA record.

Decision for the owner. (1) Which kit, if any, RB101 uses: a battery-powered robot kit designed for children of the learners' age, with two driven wheels, at least one floor (light) sensor and a physical power switch that cuts motor power. (2) Whether Part B is offered at all, or RB101 stays simulator-only. (3) How the kit is programmed (it must accept a program equivalent to Listing 1 of F9-05). Until these are decided and recorded, Part B stays optional and untested.

Safety

Only with a supervising adult who has read the kit's instructions. Only after Part A and the simulator lab of F9-05 have passed. Floor only (never on a table). Clear zone marked and empty. Physical power switch within the adult's reach and tested first. Lowest useful speed. The kit's own batteries, charged and stored as its maker says; no LiPo, no mains. Fingers away from the wheels while the robot is switched on.

  1. The adult reads the kit maker's safety instructions aloud and keeps them at hand.
  2. Mark a clear zone on the floor with tape. Remove everything inside it. Everyone except the robot stays outside.
  3. With the robot switched off, check the battery as the kit maker describes.
  4. Hold the robot with its wheels off the floor, switch it on, and test the physical power switch: the wheels must stop at once. Switch off.
  5. Load your gentle line-following program with the speed limit set to the lowest useful value.
  6. Place the robot on a line inside the clear zone. The adult holds the switch. Switch on and watch.
  7. At the first surprise (zig-zag, wrong direction, leaving the zone), the adult switches off. Fix the program in the simulator first, then try again.
  8. Finish: switch off, and handle the battery as the kit maker says.

Extension. In the simulator, add a "reset" step after which the robot may move again, but only if the reset happens while the wanted speed is 0. Why might that extra condition be a good idea?

Forensic lab

Scenario. During a simulator test, Yara pressed the emergency stop at step 6. The robot kept going and only stopped at step 8. "I pressed it!" she says. "Is the button broken?" You get the robot's log.

Evidence pack. The log from a real run of the program (late_stop.cpp) in this build. The "button" column shows the real button; the "stopped?" column shows what the program believed. R2

step  button  wanted  allowed  stopped?  position
   1      up       2        2        no         2
   2      up       4        4        no         6
   3      up       9        5        no        11
   4      up       9        5        no        16
   5      up       9        5        no        21
   6    down       9        5        no        26
   7    down       9        5        no        31
   8    down       9        0       yes        31
   9    down       9        0       yes        31
  10    down       9        0       yes        31

Real output, copied from university/labs/F9-07/late_stop.out; run record late_stop.log: g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; 2026-10-09T18:26:17Z; exit code: 0.

Questions.

  1. Observation: at which step did the button go down? At which step did the program believe it was stopped?
  2. How many extra units did the robot travel after the button was pressed? Show the sum.
  3. Hypotheses: is the button broken, or does the program look at it too rarely? Which column of the log decides?
  4. Root cause: how often does the program seem to check the button? Use the step numbers.
  5. Fix and prevention: what must change in the program, and what must a real robot have as well?

Method hints. Compare the "button" and "stopped?" columns row by row. A healthy stop changes both in the same row. Then look for a pattern in the step number where "stopped?" finally changes.

Mini-project

The course project: a line-following robot in simulation, explained to a friend. Bring together everything from RB101. Use your tuned program from F9-05 and add a speed limit and a latched stop (from this chapter). Then explain it to a friend, using your one-page explanation from F9-05, and add a safety page: the six rules and how your program follows two of them.

Rubric. 2 points: a working simulated line follower with a gentle gain, shown by a real run. 1 point: speed limit and latched stop in the program, shown in the log. 1 point: the friend can explain sense–compare–correct and why steering harder can be worse. 1 point: the safety page lists all six rules correctly and says which ones software cannot replace.

Summary

  • Real robots can pinch, bump and hurt; people keep them safe.
  • Simulator first, always: real robots only after the simulator lab passes.
  • An adult supervises every real-robot activity in this course.
  • A clear zone, an emergency stop within reach (physical, tested first) and a low speed limit come before any motion.
  • Batteries: kits designed for children, as the kit maker says; no LiPo, no mains.
  • In software, apply the speed limit to every command and check a latched stop at the start of every round.
  • A software stop is an extra layer, never a replacement for a physical switch.

Sources

  1. University Authoring Guide (this project), sections "Honesty first" (safety: simulator first, physical kill switch, clear zone, young learners supervised, low voltages, kits for their age, no mains), 5.5 (F0 faculty safety: battery-powered kits designed for children, no LiPo) and 5.14 (F9 faculty safety: emergency stop within reach, clear zone, speed limits, adult supervision below L3, battery rules). Opened and read during this build. These are this university's rules; the exact safety instructions of any kit come from its maker (dossier).
  2. Charles Platt, "Make: Electronics" (tier 3). Used for: a switch between battery and motor cuts the motor's power. Title only — not opened during this build; the Source Researcher must confirm the edition and section (dossier gate G1 open).
  3. R1 — lab run of Listing 1 (university/labs/F9-07/safe_drive.cpp) in this build; toolchain g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0; exit code 0 (from safe_drive.log).
  4. R2 — lab run of the forensic program (university/labs/F9-07/late_stop.cpp) in this build; same toolchain; exit code 0 (from late_stop.log).

Next chapter

This is the last chapter of the course. Back to the course: RB101 Robots for kids: sense, think, act (project and exams). Previous: F9-06 A robot in the simulator. Where this leads: RB202 Control I: PID, starting with F9-16 Open loop and closed loop. Safety rules: safety.

Answers to Check yourself

  1. Simulator first; adult supervision; clear zone; emergency stop within reach (physical, tested); speed limit set; battery rules (kits designed for children, as the maker says, no LiPo, no mains).
  2. Because the program itself might have a bug or freeze, and then a stop that lives in the program would not work. A physical switch cuts the motor power without asking the program.
  3. Once pressed, it stays active until someone deliberately resets it; releasing the button does not restart the robot.
  4. 3: std::min(8, 3) is 3.
  5. Good answers say: mistakes in a simulator cost nothing; a program that misbehaves there would misbehave on the real robot too, where it could break things or hurt someone.
  6. A table is not a clear zone on the floor (the robot can fall off), a party means people (and maybe pets) close by, and there may be no tested stop or supervising adult with the instructions. Instead: test in the simulator, then show it on the floor in a marked, empty zone, with an adult holding the tested switch and a low speed limit.
  7. (c). (a) LiPo is not allowed in this course; (b) "whatever fits" ignores the maker's instructions; (d) no mains electricity in this course.

Forensic lab answer key

Observation. The button is "down" from step 6, but "stopped?" only becomes "yes" at step 8. In steps 6 and 7 the robot still moved at speed 5.

Extra travel. Position 21 at step 5; it ends at 31. Extra: 31 − 21 = 10 units (2 steps × 5). A correct stop would have kept it at 21, as R1 shows.

Root cause. The button works (the "button" column changes at step 6). The program only looks at it on steps 4 and 8 (every 4th step: step % 4 == 0). The first check after step 6 is step 8.

How the fault was made. The Lab Engineer copied Listing 1 and made the stop check run only when the step number is a multiple of 4, keeping the real button in a separate variable so the log can show both.

Fix and prevention. Check the stop at the start of every round, before computing the speed (Listing 1, lines 18–20). On a real robot, also have a physical power switch that does not depend on the program at all. Prevention: every stop test logs both the button and the program's belief, and fails if they ever differ for even one step.

Wrong answers and why. "The button is broken": the log shows it went down at step 6. "The speed limit failed": the speed never exceeded 5.

Bridge chapters

Learners get lost not inside a technology but between technologies: the day C++ becomes CUDA, the day one GPU becomes eight, the day the simulator becomes a real robot. The university handles every such step twice: a dedicated bridge chapter (BR-01 to BR-10) placed exactly where the step happens, and a mandatory Transition box in every chapter that introduces something new relative to an earlier technology.

6.1 The Transition box (required in chapters)

Every chapter has a Transition box (template position 13, 7.3). It answers four questions in this order, each in one to three sentences, with source tags for every technical claim:

  1. Where you came from: the earlier technology or chapter (by id).
  2. What carries over: knowledge and habits that still apply unchanged.
  3. What changes: the differences that will bite, most dangerous first.
  4. What comes next: the next chapter and how today's idea will be used there.
Transition box (example from F6-04)

Where you came from: SP102 taught you functions and std::vector on the CPU. What carries over: the same C++ syntax, types and functions; host code is ordinary C++. What changes: the kernel runs on the GPU and cannot read your std::vector directly; data must be in GPU memory first; a launch returns before the GPU finishes; errors arrive as return codes you must check. What comes next: F6-05 shows how to check every call and find bugs with Compute Sanitizer.

(Source tags omitted in this guide's example; in a chapter each claim is tagged.)

6.2 The ten bridges

Each bridge chapter follows the full chapter template, is at most one level above the chapters before it, has its own lab, and is listed as a prerequisite of the first chapter after the step.

BR-01 From C++ to CUDA C++: the same language, a second place to run L2
Placement
Between SP203 and CU201 (prerequisite of F6-01).
Carries over
C++ syntax, types, functions, templates (within the limits CUDA documents for device code), headers, build discipline, testing habits, RAII for host-side resources.
Changes
Two processors and two memories (host and device); function execution-space qualifiers; the execution configuration of a launch; explicit allocation and copies (or managed memory with its own costs); asynchronous execution; error handling through return codes and a "last error"; many standard-library facilities and exceptions are not available in device code (the dossier cites the Programming Guide's C++ language support section for the exact list); a new compiler driver (nvcc) that splits host and device code.
Traps
Reading results before the GPU finished; forgetting the bounds check; passing a host pointer to a kernel; not checking errors so failures look like zeros.
Lab
Rewrite a CPU vector-add program step by step into CUDA C++, checking each step; deliberately break it three ways and read the errors.
BR-02 From CUDA to HIP: a second kitchen building with the same recipes L3
Placement
Before F7-01.
Carries over
The programming model (grids, blocks, threads, shared memory, streams, events); most runtime calls have HIP counterparts with similar names (each mapping cited from the HIP documentation's porting guide and API reference); kernel code is largely the same C++.
Changes
API prefixes and headers; the hipcc driver and the ROCm toolchain; the warp size is not a constant 32 (64 on CDNA; 32 or 64 on RDNA); lane masks become 64-bit; LDS instead of "shared memory" in AMD's documents; different profilers; hardware support listed in the ROCm compatibility matrix; HIP can also target NVIDIA through the CUDA back end.
Traps
Hard-coded 32; 32-bit ballot masks; tuning parameters copied from NVIDIA; assuming a CUDA library has a drop-in HIP equivalent without checking.
Lab
hipify a CU201 lab, run it on both back ends, fix the warp-size assumption planted in the starter code.
BR-03 From CPU threads to GPU warps and wavefronts L2–L3
Placement
Between F6-03 and F6-04 for readers coming from SP203; referenced again in F7-08.
Carries over
Data races, the need for synchronization, atomics, the idea of a memory model, Amdahl-style reasoning about serial parts.
Changes
CPU threads are few, heavy and scheduled by the OS; GPU threads are many and light, created by the launch and scheduled by hardware in groups (warps of 32 on NVIDIA, wavefronts of 64 on AMD CDNA); divergence inside a group costs time; there are no OS context switches per GPU thread; synchronization is cheap inside a block and expensive or unavailable across the whole grid; memory access patterns of the whole group matter (coalescing).
Traps
Using a mutex-like spin lock across threads of the same warp; expecting one GPU thread to be fast; ignoring divergence.
Lab
The same histogram written with std::thread and with CUDA; measure and explain the difference with the kitchen analogy and the profiler.
BR-04 From one GPU to many GPUs to many machines L4
Placement
Before F8-01.
Carries over
Kernels, streams and events; measurement protocol; roofline thinking applied to links instead of memory.
Changes
Data must move between devices over links of very different speeds (PCIe, NVLink, xGMI, network); topology decides performance; collectives replace point-to-point thinking; failures of one process stop everyone; time is dominated by communication unless overlapped.
Traps
Assuming all GPU pairs are equally connected; benchmarking with one message size; deadlocks from mismatched collective calls.
Lab
F1 peer bandwidth matrix, then predict a ring all-reduce time with the alpha-beta model before running it.
BR-05 From bare metal to an RTOS to Linux L3
Placement
Inside OS305 (between F3-38 and F3-39), referenced by RB304 and DN302.
Carries over
Interrupts, timers, drivers, memory maps, the debugger, the discipline of measuring timing.
Changes
Bare metal: one loop, you own everything. RTOS: tasks with priorities, a scheduler, kernel objects, deterministic timing, small memory, usually no MMU-based process isolation. Linux: processes with virtual memory, rich drivers and networking, much larger footprint, real-time behaviour only with configuration (PREEMPT_RT) and care.
Traps
Blocking calls inside interrupt handlers; priority inversion; assuming Linux is real-time by default; dynamic allocation in time-critical paths.
Lab
The same sensor-to-actuator loop implemented bare metal, on Zephyr or FreeRTOS, and on Linux with and without PREEMPT_RT; compare measured jitter.
BR-06 From x86 to ARM to RISC-V L4
Placement
Before F4-23.
Carries over
The arch-neutral kernel core; the platform checklist (curriculum 9.1); C++ code with correct atomics.
Changes
Privilege models (rings, exception levels, M/S/U modes); boot contracts (UEFI and ACPI, devicetree, SBI); interrupt controllers (APIC, GIC, PLIC/AIA); memory ordering (x86's strong ordering versus weakly ordered Arm and RISC-V); cache maintenance for DMA on non-coherent devices.
Traps
Missing barriers; hard-coded page sizes; assuming an APIC; endianness of device and on-disk data (curriculum 10.2).
Lab
Fill the checklist for the three QEMU machines and run the arch-neutral test suite on each.
BR-07 From a PC to an SoC board L4
Placement
Before F4-31; referenced by RB403 and DN302.
Carries over
Drivers written against specifications; the universal method; the devicetree knowledge from DR402.
Changes
No enumeration; boot ROMs and vendor boot chains; explicit clocks, resets, pins and regulators; non-coherent DMA; documentation quality varies by vendor (curriculum 11.1, 11.4).
Traps
A device that "reads zeros" because its clock is off; wrong bus-address translation; writing to on-board storage without a recovery path.
Lab
Boot a known-good image on the board, dump its devicetree, and write the bring-up plan before writing any code.
BR-08 From simulator to real robot or drone (sim-to-real) L3–L4
Placement
Before the first real-hardware lab of RB304 and DN401; revisited in F9-71.
Carries over
The software stack, interfaces, tests and logs; the controller structure.
Changes
Noise, delays, friction, vibration, battery sag, calibration errors, unmodelled dynamics, timing jitter, and physical danger. Parameters that worked in simulation often need re-tuning.
Traps
Trusting simulation gains on hardware; skipping the bench test; testing without an e-stop or without propellers removed; changing two things at once.
Lab
Run the same controller in simulation and on the supervised kit, log both, and explain every difference from the logs.
Safety

Bench first, propellers off, e-stop in hand, supervision for learners below L3, local drone rules read and recorded.

BR-09 From hobby code to production L3–L4
Placement
Before SE301.
Carries over
Working code, tests, the habit of reading sources.
Changes
Other people depend on it: reviews, CI, versioning, compatibility, documentation, monitoring, security updates, on-call, licences, and the cost of being wrong.
Traps
"Works on my machine"; no tests for failure paths; undocumented assumptions; ignoring licences of copied code.
Lab
Take a learner's earlier project and make it production-grade: CI, review, release notes, a known-issues list.
BR-10 From a laptop to a server cluster L3–L4
Placement
Before DS303 and DG402.
Carries over
Programs, tests, measurement discipline.
Changes
Many machines fail independently; remote management (BMC, Redfish); schedulers decide where code runs; shared storage and networks become bottlenecks; NUMA inside each server; observability is required because you cannot "just look".
Traps
Benchmarking on a noisy shared node; assuming clocks agree; no timeouts.
Lab
Run the same job on a laptop and on a three-node virtual cluster under Slurm; compare and explain.

Mega projects

Mega projects are long (one to two semesters each), done alone or in small learner teams, with design-review gates. Each reuses curriculum milestones as building blocks and adds integration, scale and real-world constraints. Every mega project has: milestones, deliverables, a grading rubric and review gates (R0 proposal, R1 design review, R2 mid-project review, R3 readiness review, R4 final defence). A gate is passed only with written reviewer approval (peer learners and, where available, a human mentor; agent reviewers may assist but the owner decides who signs).

MP1 Own OS on a real board and on a server, with SMP and networking
Prereqs
OS304, DR302, DR402, DR403; DS304 recommended.
Milestones
  1. Kernel from OS302–OS304 passes the full B-track regression in QEMU (x86-64 and AArch64).
  2. Boots on a real SoC board through the standard boot chain (D10) with console, timer, SMP and storage.
  3. Boots on a server (or a server-class virtual machine) via UEFI network boot, with SMP on all cores, NVMe storage and a NIC with the TCP/IP stack (C9).
  4. A shell and user programs over the network (remote shell or file service).
  5. Measured boot timeline compared with Linux on the same hardware.
Deliverables
Source repository with CI; design notes per subsystem; device records for every device on both machines (M1); test reports; a 20-minute demo.
Rubric
Works on both platforms with one kernel image or a documented minimal difference (30 %); test coverage and regression discipline (20 %); real-hardware evidence and device records (20 %); design quality (15 %); defence (15 %).
Gates
R1 after milestone 1; R2 after milestone 2; R3 before server boot; R4 final.
MP2 A small distributed OS service layer with consensus
Prereqs
DS302, DS402, DS403.
Milestones
  1. Raft library passing deterministic fault-injection tests and a linearizability check.
  2. A replicated key-value service with membership changes.
  3. Cluster membership and a job scheduler on top (submit, place, restart on failure).
  4. Runs on three or more nodes of the learner's own OS (from MP1) or on Linux virtual machines as a fallback (documented).
  5. Observability: metrics, logs, traces; an SLO and a game-day incident.
Deliverables
Code, test harness, a written protocol specification, an incident post-mortem, demo.
Rubric
Safety under faults (35 %); test rigour (20 %); performance evidence (15 %); operability (15 %); defence (15 %).
Gates
R1 protocol design; R2 after milestone 2; R3 game-day readiness; R4.
MP3 A CUDA kernel library (GEMM and attention) benchmarked against cuBLAS
Prereqs
CU401. Hardware: an NVIDIA GPU (or cloud GPU).
Milestones
  1. Harness and correctness suite (shapes, precisions, tolerances justified per MA302).
  2. SGEMM reaching the pre-agreed percentage of cuBLAS at three sizes.
  3. Mixed-precision GEMM on tensor cores.
  4. Fused attention forward pass compared with the library implementation available on the platform.
  5. Profiler-backed gap analysis and a roofline chart.
Deliverables
Library, benchmarks with raw data, a report with all measurements labelled by GPU, driver and toolkit versions.
Rubric
Correctness (30 %); performance against pre-set targets (25 %); measurement methodology (20 %); explanation of gaps (15 %); code quality (10 %).
Gates
R1 targets agreed before coding (never lowered afterwards without owner approval, curriculum 13.4); R2; R4.
MP4 The HIP port benchmarked against rocBLAS
Prereqs
HP401, MP3 (or its GEMM part). Hardware: an AMD GPU in the ROCm compatibility list.
Milestones
  1. One source tree building for both vendors.
  2. All MP3 correctness tests pass on AMD.
  3. AMD-specific tuning (wave64, LDS, MFMA) to pre-set targets versus rocBLAS/hipBLASLt.
  4. A portability report: each kernel's percentage of the vendor library on both GPUs, with reasons.
Deliverables
Code, benchmark data, portability report.
Rubric
As MP3, plus portability analysis (15 % taken from code quality and methodology).
Gates
R1, R2, R4.
MP5 A multi-node all-reduce
Prereqs
DG402. Hardware: two nodes with GPUs and a network (RDMA for the performance part).
Milestones
  1. Single-node ring all-reduce (F2) correct for all sizes.
  2. Hierarchical two-node version over MPI or verbs.
  3. Comparison with NCCL/RCCL bus bandwidth; GPUDirect RDMA on/off where possible.
  4. Overlap with a training step (F6) and fault handling (F8).
Deliverables
Code, bandwidth curves, a model-versus-measurement report (alpha-beta).
Rubric
Correctness (30 %); performance versus pre-set targets (25 %); model accuracy and explanation (25 %); robustness (20 %).
Gates
R1, R2, R4.
MP6 A robot software stack: ROS 2, real-time control and micro-ROS firmware, in simulation then on a kit robot
Prereqs
RB403, RB401, SS402.
Milestones
  1. Simulated robot: drivers (simulated), EKF localisation, navigation, one manipulation or delivery task.
  2. Real-time control loop on Linux with PREEMPT_RT meeting a measured jitter requirement; ros2_control hardware interface.
  3. micro-ROS firmware on the motor or sensor microcontroller with an RTOS.
  4. Custom OS image for the robot computer (RB403), booting into the stack.
  5. Sim-to-real on the kit robot (supervised): the same task, logs compared with simulation.
  6. Safety case with e-stop, watchdog and safe-state tests.
Deliverables
Repository, OS image build scripts, simulation worlds, logs, safety case, demo video recorded by the learner (optional), live demo.
Rubric
Task success in simulation and on hardware (25 %); real-time evidence (20 %); safety case and tests (20 %); software quality (15 %); sim-to-real analysis (10 %); defence (10 %).
Gates
R1; R2 after simulation; R3 safety and readiness review before any real-robot run; R4.
Safety

R3 must check: e-stop tested, speed limits set, clear zone, supervision arranged, battery handling per maker instructions.

MP7 A drone flight stack on PX4 or ArduPilot: SITL → HITL → supervised outdoor test
Prereqs
DN401, DN302 or DN303, SS402.
Milestones
  1. Own module(s) in PX4 (or ArduPilot) adding a feature (for example a custom estimator check, a mission behaviour, or a companion-computer interface) with tests in SITL.
  2. Failsafe test matrix in SITL (RC loss, low battery, geofence, estimator failure).
  3. HITL on the bench flight controller.
  4. Bench tests with propellers removed; tethered or netted hover if available.
  5. Supervised outdoor test where legal, following the field-test checklist, with logs analysed afterwards.
Deliverables
Code, SITL and HITL test reports, safety case, field-test checklist signed by the supervisor, flight logs and their analysis.
Rubric
Feature correctness in SITL/HITL (25 %); failsafe evidence (25 %); safety process (25 %); log analysis (15 %); defence (10 %). A learner may pass without the outdoor flight if regulations or supervision do not allow it; the gate records why.
Gates
R1; R2 after SITL; R3 go/no-go before any flight; R4.
Safety

R3 checks the national aviation authority's current rules (recorded), location permission, weather, supervision, failsafe configuration, battery condition, and propeller-off bench tests completed.

MP8 The final integrated project
Prereqs
SE404, at least two of MP1–MP7.
Milestones
  1. Proposal combining at least two goal areas (examples: a robot whose perception kernel is the learner's own CUDA or HIP code and whose computer runs the learner's OS image; a drone ground station backed by the learner's consensus-replicated service; a GPU cluster job service running on the learner's OS).
  2. Design document and threat model, reviewed.
  3. Integration milestones defined by the learner and approved at R1.
  4. Incident game-day and post-mortem.
  5. Public defence.
Deliverables
Everything above plus a retrospective on what the learner would do differently.
Rubric
Technical depth (25 %); integration quality (20 %); evidence and testing (20 %); leadership and communication (20 %); reflection (15 %).
Gates
R0–R4.

QA records

One record per written chapter (guide 3.7). Gates follow guide 12.3.

How this file was built

This page is generated by university/build/build.py from the three source files in the repository (UNIVERSITY_AUTHORING_GUIDE.html, SYSTEMS_CURRICULUM.html; DRIVERS.html is the learning page the forensic-lab idea comes from) and from the chapter fragments in university/chapters/. Course cards, the analogy registry, the safety rules, the ladder, the goal paths and the bridge and mega-project cards are copied from the guide unchanged. Listings and outputs are copied byte for byte from university/labs/. See university/README.md for the folder layout and how to rebuild.

Companion documents: University Authoring Guide · Systems Curriculum · Windows drivers learning page.

Bare Metal to GPU University · one-file edition · 2026-10-09 · no scripts; all diagrams are inline SVG using the colour tokens of the style block, in light and dark mode.
